Entre las medidas principales contenidas en el Proyecto de Presupuestos Generales del Estado me interesa hacer mencin especial a la aplicacin del nuevo sistema de financiacin autonmica de las Comunidades Autnomas de rgimen comn, que si bien debe valorarse positivamente en sus elementos de incremento de la corresponsabilidad fiscal, tambin plantea la necesidad de establecer los mecanismos que garanticen la transparencia informativa en relacin con las actividades de las Administraciones Territoriales. Este es un elemento esencial para el desarrollo adecuado de cualquier proceso de descentralizacin fiscal, pero se ve reforzado en el caso espaol por la magnitud de las responsabilidades de gasto e impositivas asumidas por las Comunidades Autnomas en relacin con el conjunto de las actividades del sector pblico. Por otro lado, el principio de transparencia es consustancial a las disposiciones del Pacto de Estabilidad y de Crecimiento y del Proyecto de Ley de Estabilidad Presupuestaria, que establecen unas normas de disciplina fiscal estricta. Los Presupuestos Generales del Estado para el ao 2002 prolongan la estrategia de poltica fiscal desarrollada en los ltimos aos, que ha consistido en un descenso gradual de la presin impositiva y en el control del gasto pblico corriente. Esta estrategia ha permitido situar las finanzas pblicas en una posicin prxima al equilibrio presupuestario en el medio plazo, tal como se entiende en el Pacto de Estabilidad y Crecimiento, y recuperar el margen de maniobra necesario para poder acometer polticas estabilizadoras ante un eventual empeoramiento de la situacin econmica, sin sobrepasar el umbral del 3% establecido por el Tratado. El logro del equilibrio presupuestario en 2002 en el contexto econmico sealado supone imprimir un tono neutral a la poltica fiscal y permite que acten los estabilizadores automticos, en coherencia con la filosofa del Pacto de Estabilidad y Crecimiento. Dicho tono neutral, frente al carcter ligeramente restrictivo de la poltica fiscal durante los ltimos aos, parece adecuado en las circunstancias actuales de desaceleracin econmica. Como se desprende de mis consideraciones anteriores, el riesgo principal al que se enfrentan los Presupuestos para el ao 2002 surge de una desaceleracin del producto y del empleo superior a la que contempla el escenario macroeconmico del Gobierno. Si se materializara este riesgo, como parece difcilmente evitable, no habra que descartar un ligero dficit de carcter cclico de las cuentas pblicas en el ao 2002, como consecuencia del juego de los estabilizadores automticos. Lo importante es que, aceptando el papel positivo de los estabilizadores en la actual coyuntura, se preserve el tono neutral del componente estructural de la poltica fiscal que subyace a las cifras presupuestarias de 2002 y no adoptar medidas discrecionales adicionales que aumenten permanentemente el dficit. Existen varias razones que justifican mi argumentacin anterior. En primer lugar, las perspectivas de crecimiento de la economa espaola en este momento no demandan actuaciones discrecionales de signo expansivo de la poltica fiscal ms all de los estabilizadores automticos, ya que el estmulo de dichas actuaciones vendra a sumarse al impulso monetario, tambin expansivo, que se deriva de los ltimos descensos de los tipos de intervencin por parte del Banco Central Europeo. Por otra parte, el mantenimiento de una posicin fiscal saneada es necesario para que los estabilizadores automticos puedan actuar libremente en el caso en que la desaceleracin econmica alcance mayor intensidad de la prevista o tenga una duracin superior a la esperada, sin que se desborden las posiciones fiscales. Este argumento adquiere especial relevancia en el caso de la economa espaola, dada la elevada inercia que han mostrado en el pasado determinadas partidas de gasto pblico en situaciones de desaceleracin econmica y el elevado coste que supone recuperar una posicin fiscal saneada, esencial para preservar un entorno de estabilidad macroeconmica. Por ltimo, el proceso de consolidacin fiscal desarrollado en los ltimos aos no debe darse por concluido, ya que, por un lado, es necesario seguir avanzando en el desarrollo de estrategias de gasto e ingresos pblicos que mejoren los fundamentos del crecimiento econmico de la economa espaola y, por otro, es preciso asegurar la sostenibilidad de las finanzas pblicas en el medio plazo, cuando se produzca el envejecimiento de la poblacin. En este sentido, hay que valorar positivamente la dotacin realizada al fondo de reserva de las pensiones y la mejora en el tratamiento fiscal de las aportaciones a los fondos de pensiones que contemplan los Presupuestos y su Ley de Acompaamiento, respectivamente. La sostenibilidad de las finanzas pblicas en el medio plazo requiere, sin embargo, una estrategia ms global y decidida que, entre otros aspectos, explote plenamente las posibilidades que proporciona la excelente situacin que viene mostrando la Seguridad Social en los ltimos aos mediante dotaciones ms cuantiosas al fondo de reserva o la adopcin de un ritmo ms rpido de consolidacin fiscal. En resumen, la incertidumbre que rodea las perspectivas de crecimiento de la economa mundial en los prximos meses y su impacto sobre la economa espaola exige una gestin cauta de la poltica fiscal en el ao 2002, que preserve los logros alcanzados en este mbito, para que, al mismo tiempo, pueda utilizar el margen de maniobra que proporciona una situacin de partida de equilibrio presupuestario. En este sentido, debern mantenerse los esfuerzos realizados en los ltimos aos en el apoyo a la capacidad productiva del pas a travs de las polticas de investigacin, desarrollo e innovacin y, en general, a travs de la inversin pblica. Por otra parte, el diseo de las polticas econmicas deber reforzarse a travs de la profundizacin de las reformas del mercado de trabajo que fomenten la generacin de empleo en la economa, y de la introduccin de nuevas reformas estructurales que mejoren la flexibilidad de los mercados y su capacidad de respuesta ante cambios bruscos en el entorno exterior, como el que acaba de tener lugar. De esta forma se garantizar que la economa conserve la estabilidad macroeconmica necesaria para aprovechar plenamente la recuperacin econmica externa, cuando esta tenga lugar, a la vez que siga mejorando su potencial de crecimiento.

Title: Some reflections on the International Role of the Euro in the official sphere. Intervention at the International Seminar on the International Role of the Euro, organized by the EU Presidency, within the framework of the Council of Ministers of Economy and Finance of the EU. Oviedo.
text: Oviedo,14 de abril de 2002 Some reflections on the International Role of the Euro in the official sphere Seminario Internacional sobre el Papel Internacional del Euro Presidencia de la UE. Consejo de Ministros de Economia y Hacienda de la UE Jose Vinals Director General de Asuntos Internacionales del Banco de Espana 1. An analysis of the international role of the euro should start with the acknowledgment that, in spite of its youth, the euro is nowadays the second most widely used currency internationally, still behind the dollar but nevertheless well ahead of the yen. This is the case in both the private and official spheres. There are three key reasons behind this: the inheritance from the former national currencies the euro has now replaced, the significant economic and financial weight of the euro area, and the high standards of macroeconomic stability already achieved in the euro area since its creation in 1999. 2. Having said that, the main ideas I want to stress in this short presentation are the following: The international role of a currency -and, in particular, of a recent currency such as the euro- is subject to long transitions and to inertia so that, in general, we should not expect major changes in the international role of a currency except over the longer term. Admittedly, the overwhelmingly important role of private markets in a globalised economic and financial system means that the private use of the euro is likely to be of far greater quantitative significance than the official use. But the factors that enhance the private use of the euro are, to a large extent, also very important in enhancing its official use. Eventually, then, both the private and official roles are likely to move in the same direction, although not necessarily with the same intensity or pace. In particular, in the light of the predominance of financial transactions over commercial transactions on global foreign exchange markets, financial considerations and, in particular, the size, depth and liquidity of the financial markets in the respective currencies of denomination are likely to exert a most considerable influence on both the private and official role of the euro as official reserves. Indeed, liquidity is -together with security- of paramount importance in the decisions to allocate foreign reserves among various currencies. The larger the international use of the euro, the stronger the influence of financial conditions in the euro area on other countries and areas. 3. Concerning more specifically the use of the euro as a reserve currency, it should be noted that it ranks second in the world, with a share of around 13% of official reserves, compared to nearly 70% for the dollar and 5% for the yen. This ranking mirrors that in respect of the private use. Over the last few years, these shares have remained very stable and very close to what would have been the case with the euro-legacy currencies, showing no significant reallocations within official portfolios Perhaps the key reasons behind the still-sizeable differences between the respective shares of the dollar and euro in official reserves are: the starting advantage enjoyed by the dollar as the most widely used intervention currency; and, closely linked to this, the as yet significant differences in terms of size, depth and liquidity between euro and dollar denominated financial markets. 4. While inertial factors always play a role in the demand for reserves, there is a potential enhanced international role for the euro as a reserve currency. This is so given the already very high standards of stability of the internal value of the currency achieved in the euro area, and insofar as European financial market integration may deepen further with the removal of the legal, regulatory and technical barriers currently hampering it. 5. This favorable framework could also interact positively with the potentially higher demand for official reserves in euros that could result from the growing use of the euro as an anchor and reference currency in a number of countries, as explained by President Duisenberg. Here again, the size, depth and liquidity of financial markets are crucial to ensure that the choice of reserve currency reflects that of intervention currency.

Title: EMU and Latin America. Intervention in the panel of the Conference on Monetary Union, organized by the National Bank of Austria. Vienna, Austria. Only in English.
text: Viena,16/04/02 EMU and Latin America Conference on Monetary Union. osterreichische Nationalbank Jose Vinals Banco de Espana and CEPR Participating in a panel at the end of a conference poses the risk of either repeating something that has already been widely discussed and accepted or sounding too controversial. In any case, I will try to deal with the following two issues: what are the pros and cons of EMU; and what are the prospects for monetary union in Latin America. Concerning the desirability of EMU, I want to emphasize that traditional economic analyses of the pros and cons of monetary unions are likely to be at least incomplete and, in any case, very complex. On the one hand, since we economists lack a sound microeconomic theory of money we are at best capable of providing a very rough and somewhat inaccurate approximation to the costs and benefits of monetary unions. On the other, since economic systems are not static but rather evolve over time, an appropriate analysis should adopt a dynamic view where not just past or current but also prospective costs and benefits are assessed. The above notwithstanding, I will still say that the creation of EMU was very appropriate. Indeed, after having established a single market in the European Union, going forward towards a monetary union was a natural development. EMU certainly helps fully reap all the potential benefits deriving from the free circulation of goods, services and capital within the euro area. Furthermore, we should not forget that many European countries were for sometime already importing their monetary policy from the Bundesbank in a sort of 'de facto asymmetric monetary union'. The creation of EMU allowed in this way for a 'de iure' symmetric monetary union where monetary policy decisions are made taking into account the interests of the euro area as a whole and not just of the "anchor country", as it was previously the case. I should also add that in its first three and a half years of life, EMU has functioned very well in the presence of a number of complications. These stem from the differences in cyclical conditions among member countries as well as from the occurrence of several external shocks, like the US recession, the crises in Brazil in 1999 and Argentina at present or the bursting of the IT bubble. Finally, I would like to mention that the main problems observed in the economic performance of the euro area are not those that many observers envisaged. In particular, before the creation of EMU it was feared that the participation of the so-called "peripheral" countries -like Spain or Italy- would be a source of tensions given their different economic structures relative to the "core" countries. Nevertheless, what has been observed is that countries like Spain or Italy have significantly increased their economic flexibility so as to cope with the requirements posed by their participation in the euro area. In contrast, the two largest countries have not shown the degree of economic flexibility and dynamism that is required to support a higher rate of potential output growth in the euro area as a whole. Consequently, it is of great importance that structural reforms are vigorously pursued in the single currency area and, in particular, in the largest economies. Turning now towards the issue of monetary union in Latin America, it is important to ask if there are any lessons that can be drawn from the European experience. A key lesson is that the road towards European monetary integration has been long, uneven and sometimes with dangerous turns. EMU represents the culmination of an integration process that started nearly fifty years ago and which evolved gradually. In Europe, the process started fostering trade integration, then went on to pursue deeper financial integration in an environment of closer monetary cooperation, and then achieved a significant degree of economic convergence prior to the creation of monetary union. Of course, there have been naturally reinforcing interactions among the various steps of the European integration process. In this regard, it is also worth recalling that for many years achieving monetary union was not even on the agenda of European policymakers, which shows that the goals of integration became increasingly ambitious as time went on and previously set objectives were realized. We shouldn't forget however that there was a failed attempt to establish a monetary union in Europe in 1970 -the so-called Werner Plan-. With hindsight, the reason why this earlier attempt failed is that the economic and political conditions for it to succeed were not there. Or, in other words, the time was not ripe. Another useful lesson from the European experience is that monetary union cannot be regarded as a purely technical process but as part of a regional integration project which has wide economic, institutional and ultimately political dimensions. While, as I have mentioned, EMU represents the culmination of the European integration process set in motion in the fifties, it should not be forgotten that such process started with an important political motivation after the painful experiences of two world wars. So, what are, in my view, the main differences between Europe and Latin America in the path towards monetary unification? A first difference has to do with the lack of a unique, well defined regional economic integration project in Latin America in contrast with the single, open-to-all with clean entry conditions European project. In Latin America, the juxtaposition of several sub-regional integration projects often with different levels of ambition -Nafta, Mercosur, Andes region, Central America, etc.- has not, in spite of the attempts made, been very effective in promoting economic integration in the region as a whole. In fact, according to a number of estimates, the degree of effective regional economic integration existing nowadays in Latin America is like that of Europe about thirty years ago. Thus if, as I have tried to emphasize earlier on, regional monetary integration needs to be preceded by a significant degree of regional economic integration, the time doesn't seem to be at all ripe for the establishment of a monetary union in Latin America. A second difference with Europe, closely related to the first, is the lack of a supra-national institutional framework in Latin America. In the European case, the existence of a clean, well defined supra-national institutional framework, like that embedded in the Union Treaty after Maastricht was critical for the success of the monetary unification process. Such a framework interacted in a virtuous way with national policies, reinforcing macroeconomic stability and convergence. Specifically, the determination of national policymakers in carrying out the appropriate policies was strengthened by the existence of the supra-national framework and, in particular, by the incentives for EMU participation. For instance, it would be difficult to explain why countries like Spain, Italy or Portugal undertook decisive policies aimed at structural reforms, fiscal consolidation and low inflation in the nineties without taking into account the drive to become members of EMU. Taking all of the above into account, what prospects are there for a Latin American monetary union? I think it is clear that it remains a very distant goal. Indeed, there seems to be no social or political demand for it except in some very small countries and there is not even demand for other less ambitious forms of monetary cooperation. The main reason for this lack of demand is that Latin American countries are confronted with such intense domestic economic problems that regional integration processes -and in particular monetary integration- are not at the top of the policy agendas. As a result, significant advances will need to be made in the domestic economic front before monetary cooperation makes some progress in the region. To conclude, before asking about the prospects for monetary union in Latin America it is critical that countries in the region significantly improve their domestic economic institutions, increase macroeconomic stability and significantly advance along the road of regional economic integration. If so, maybe sometime in the future we may once again gather in this wonderful place to discuss with more realism than today what are the prospects for monetary integration in Latin America.

Title: Intervention in the LXXXV ordinary general assembly of the Spanish Confederation of Savings Banks
text: GONZALO GIL BANK OF SPAIN Deputy Governor INTERVENTION IN THE LXXXV ORDINARY GENERAL ASSEMBLY SPANISH CONFEDERATION OF SAVINGS BANKS 24 April 2002 I would like to begin my speech by thanking the Spanish Confederation of Savings Banks for the opportunity it offers me on the occasion of its annual meeting to address all of you. I shall devote the minutes available to me to commenting on certain aspects of our situation which I consider particularly significant in order to meet with due guarantees of success the new demands that arise in the economic field and in the supervisory field. In the ecological field, a first set of changes is associated with the change in the phase of the cycle. Although there is no lack of uncertainties, for example those associated with the price of energy, most of the available indicators seem to show that the phase of slowdown that, since the past a, has been going through the world economy, and with it the Spanish economy, would be bottoming out. Thus, despite the fact that the Japanese deflaci and its financial crisis And the Argentine crisis continues to worsen d1although contained within national bordersd1, the good data of the US economy, the strong economic fundamentals of the euro zone and the absence of serious imbalances in it are factors that allow us to affirm that, if unforeseen events do not arise, throughout the present a, the external demand of our economy will recover and, With it, exports and business investment, the two variables that are most severely affected by the unfavorable external environment of the months scams. While it is true that, in the global environment, the performance of our economy has generally been satisfactory, it is no less true that, for the expected recovery to be sustainable, it is essential to continue promoting the policies of modernisation, budgetary austerity, cost containment and flexibility of our markets for factors, products and, Of course, financial. The intensification of these policies is all the more necessary, bearing in mind that this change in the phase of the cycle must be placed in a second, broader and much more far-reaching transitional scenario: that defined by the perspectives opened after the full introduction of the euro in twelve European economies, including ours. The success of this operation, attributable to all, must be an incentive for all of us to assume our responsibilities to ensure that we are all responsible for the purpose of to achieve the levels of progress and economic and social well-being that the opinion associates an increasingly cohesive Europe. A key factor in achieving the benefits of this increased cohesion is to be increasingly competitive in increasingly integrated and efficient European markets. Achieving this objective poses, both for the economic authorities and for the agents, a series of demands which, given the hearing, I will focus on the field of savings banks. Among the demands made of the authorities, in addition to continuing to promote economic policies that I mentioned earlier, I would like to stress the need to continue to alleviate the institutional difficulties that still remain, both nationally and internationally, for the creation of the European financial market. At international level, I am convinced that, under the Spanish presidency of the European Union, this easing of obstacles will experience a strong advance. At the national level, a good example of an initiative along the same lines is the recent Bill on Financial System Reform Measures. I am not going to comment on the ambitious content of this initiative, which cannot be undertaken in the time available to me. I will only mention two aspects of the Bill directly related to savings banks, to which the Banco de Espa attaches particular importance. The first is the reinforcement of the essential characteristic of Savings banks are their status as private credit institutions. Assuming the responsibilities of all kinds implied by this condition, a subject to which I will return later, savings banks can satisfactorily face the implications of their differentiating characteristics (private foundational nature, social character and territorial linkage); characteristics that must be maintained, as they are at the basis of many of the transcendental contributions of savings banks to the stability, solvency and efficiency of our financial system. The second aspect is the consideration and treatment of the participatory quotas of savings banks. For some time, the Bank of Spain has been in favour of regulating flexibly and rigorously this instrument for raising own resources specific to savings banks, respectful of their foundational nature and, to the extent that it is well designed, called upon to grant them greater possibilities of expansion and operation, which require a parallel increase in market discipline. The Financial Bill is an ideal means of realizing this old aspiration, shared with the sector itself, establishing a regulation that incorporates the least possible intervention, and is based on principles as basic as full respect for the state sphere of competence, freedom of emission, the clear determination of the rights that will confer the possession of the participatory quotas, and their listing on official secondary markets, to provide them with liquidity. The advantages of all kinds that participatory quotas can bring to savings banks, and therefore to the Spanish financial system, should not make us forget that their introduction must be gradual, based on particularly rigorous studies until we have sufficient experience, and adopting the necessary precautions to avoid diluting the high social value of savings banks. Despite their importance, the replies I have just mentioned are not the key factor in seizing the opportunities and overcoming the challenges that will arise with the change in the cycle phase and the increasing integration of European financial markets. As befits a market economy, the key factor will be the attitudes and behaviour of private economic actors. In this sense and for the savings bank sector, it is worth dwelling briefly on some features of the evolution in the past a. In 2001, credit grew at a strong rate, 15.5%, well above the 9.1% of Spanish banks, despite the slowdown in economic growth, which makes the quality of investment and its profitability particularly relevant. It must be recognized, however, that NPL ratios remain at minimum levels, 0.8%, and the coverage of non-performing loans continues to grow, standing at 225% at the end of 2001, thanks largely to the FCEI. However, it should not be forgotten that the non-performing loans implicit in the strong growth in credit recorded in recent years will manifest itself even if the best prospects for a change in trend are fulfilled. Therefore, although the provisions represent an undoubted safety buffer against possible impairments of assets and reinforce the good image of solvency of the sector, we must not stop monitoring excessive concentrations of risks and applying rigorous policies. The own resources of the savings banks declared as a whole are, at the end of 2001, 45% higher than the legally required minimums, which all together says a lot about this image of solvency. Although provisions for statistical provisions had a clear negative impact on the 2001 income statement, net accounting profit grew by 6.1%, despite the fact that extraordinary profits have fallen sharply. In terms of expenditure, the expansion of savings banks has not ceased, as evidenced by the fact that in 2001 563 new net offices were opened and the number of staff increased by 3,835 people. This has generated a growth in structural costs of 8.5%, although the increase in turnover has made it possible for the efficiency ratio to improve by 2.1 percentage points, which remains at levels 62.1% substantially worse than those of Spanish banks, 53.5%. Therefore, although the increases in intermediation margins and ordinary, make the operating increase in absolute values by almost 20%, the effort to achieve greater containment of operating expenses must continue. It is necessary to emphasize the importance of the rationalization of these expenses as a defense against the pressure that competition exerts on the margins of the business. I would now like to comment on some of the changes that are taking place in the supervisory field. The first is the New Capital Agreement, which, as you all know, has been delayed in publishing its final text because of the difficulties in calibrating the proposals of January last year and the desire to refine them, incorporating the best of the many suggestions made during the consultation phase. Nor can this delay lead to a stage of relaxation. Far from it, it must constitute a stage of active preparation so that all, supervisors and supervised, are able to assume the proper and reciprocal responsibilities that the New Agreement will pose to us, some of whose basic features I will comment on. In its quest for a regulation of minimum own resources more in line with current financial systems and more sensitive to risk than the current one, the Basel Committee explicitly starts from the basic principle that the fundamental responsibility for the evolution and behaviour of any entity lies with its administrators and senior managers. His is the merit of the successes, but also the responsibility for the errors, of the deficient and problematic behaviors in which the entity may incur. Supervisors should not try to replace the task of direction and supervision that our legal system entrusts to administrators; the task of control that, within the framework of correct corporate governance, corresponds to shareholders; nor the work of discipline that, based on transparent corporate information, corresponds to the market. Respecting these private areas of action, it is up to us supervisors to establish and enforce a consistent, transparent and proactive regulatory framework that, by providing institutions with the right incentives, contributes efficiently to avoiding systemic risk, to the proper functioning of institutions and markets, and to enhancing the protection of the depositor and the investor. With regard to the supervisory approach, I would like to highlight how the New Agreement deepens the tendency, already present in previous recommendations of the Basel Committee, to complement the necessary mandatory rules with an incentive system, aimed at improving qualitative aspects of the management and risk control of institutions. These supervisory incentives permeate the entire text of the New Deal. The greater supervisory emphasis on qualitative aspects responds, basically, to well-known motivations: the growing Complexity of the current financial systems, with increasingly larger and more diversified entities and groups and the growing dynamism of the markets, whose situation and perspectives can change with a speed unknown until recently, as they are increasingly competitive and deregulated, more integrated and geographically interdependent, and by having the best information and operational agility that new technologies are providing. If changes of this magnitude are affecting supervision, enhancing its qualitative aspect, there must necessarily be a symmetrical reflection in the entities, which, therefore, must affect with special intensity the qualitative aspects of their activity. Earlier, I mentioned the need to improve some of these aspects, such as management and internal control, both generally and, especially, of risks. Within this qualitative area, and to conclude my intervention, I would like to comment on a topic that has been dealt with in depth by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and which has brought to the forefront recent national and international events, which, although of very unequal importance, are on everyone's mind. It is about the need to improve the governance of our societies. So far, the greatest impetus for improvement raised on this issue has been the so-called Olivencia Report, prepared at the request of the Council of Ministers to achieve, and I quote literally "greater Levels of efficiency, accountability and transparency in the governance of societies that appeal to financial markets." Since the publication of this Report in March 1998, many listed companies have formally adopted it. Despite the progress, I believe that, in the current circumstances, this is insufficient and the gap between the reality of our corporate governance and the demands posed by a society and an economy, increasingly attentive to how companies are governed, and by markets that, increasingly, They incorporate deficiencies in this area into their risk premiums. It is a problem that transcends national borders and, while it has not had systemic effects, it does deserve, and is receiving, careful attention in all countries. If the issue of corporate governance is important for all types of companies, I believe that it is specifically important for credit institutions, in which, in addition, it must be complemented by rigorous conduct and strict Chinese walls, as a result, among other issues, of the special complexity of the agency relationships that develop within them; the powerful conflicts of interest that may arise in the allocation of credit resources; inside information on debtor companies to which institutions have access; and the very high information asymmetry that affects depositors. In its document "Empowerment of corporate governance in the banking organizations", of September 1999, the Basel Committee draws from these characteristics the basic principles that corporate governance in credit institutions must meet: transparency, responsibility, professionalism, qualification and independence are some of the characteristics that the document considers necessary in managers to ensure the good governance of all entities. Addressing an audience composed of top savings bank managers, I can complement these recommendations by emphasizing their importance given the special complexity and significance that corporate governance has for savings banks, due to their peculiar ownership system. It is clear that these qualitative improvements that I have just mentioned d0 in the management and control of entities, in their corporate governance and in their due diligence with customers d0 are of special importance for an economic sector as dependent on the confidence of the plico as the financial sector. However, it is no less evident that these improvements respond to a widespread social demand and that, therefore, they must be placed within a much more general framework of reforms, which includes non-financial companies, external auditors, consultants, investment analysts, etc. These issues, which, as you know, are being discussed both in international forums and institutions and at national level, have been discussed in depth at the recent ECOFIN meeting in Oviedo, where the EU High Level Group on Commercial Law was mandated to analyse internal control systems. to Corporate Governance practices and Audit practices. To sum up my speech, the change in the cyclical situation of our economy and the economies around us, together with the prospects opened up after the full introduction of the euro, present opportunities, not without risks, the use of which requires us all to tackle, immediately, reforms of high scope and profound significance. I am sure that our economy, our financial system, and not the savings banks, will once again rise to the occasion. Thanks a lot.
