As, a pesar de que la deflaci japonesa y su crisis financiera contin, y la crisis argentina sigue agravndose aunque contenida dentro de las fronteras nacionales, los buenos datos de la economa estadounidense, los sidos fundamentos econmicos de la zona euro y la ausencia en ella de graves desequilibrios son factores que permiten afirmar que, si no surgen acontecimientos imprevistos, a lo largo del presente a, la demanda externa de nuestra economa se ir recuperando y, con ella, las exportaciones y la inversi empresarial, las dos variables que ms severamente se estn viendo afectadas por el desfavorable entorno exterior de los timos meses. Si bien es cierto que, en el entorno global, el comportamiento de nuestra economa ha sido, en general, satisfactorio, no lo es menos que, para que la esperada reactivaci sea sostenible es imprescindible continuar potenciando las polticas de modernizaci, de austeridad presupuestaria, de contenci de costes y de flexibilizaci de nuestros mercados de factores, de productos y, por supuesto, financieros. La intensificaci de estas polticas es an ms necesaria, teniendo en cuenta que este cambio en la fase del ciclo hay que situarlo en un segundo escenario de transicin, ms amplio y de mucho mayor calado: el definido por las perspectivas abiertas tras la plena introducci del euro en doce economas europeas, entre ellas la nuestra. El xito de esta operaci, atribuble a todos, debe constituir un acicate para que todos asumamos nuestras responsabilidades con el fin de alcanzar las cotas de progreso y de bienestar econmico y social que la opinin plica asocia a una Europa cada vez ms cohesionada. Un factor clave para alcanzar los beneficios de esta mayor cohesi es ser cada vez ms competitivos en unos mercados europeos cada vez ms integrados y eficientes. Lograr este objetivo plantea, tanto para las autoridades econmicas como para los agentes, una serie de exigencias que, dada la audiencia, centrar en el mbito de las cajas de ahorros. De entre las exigencias planteadas a las autoridades, adems de continuar impulsando polticas econmicas que antes he mencionado, quiero destacar la necesidad de continuar allanando las dificultades institucionales que todava subsisten, tanto a nivel nacional como internacional, para la creaci del mercado financiero ico europeo. A nivel internacional, estoy convencido que, bajo la presidencia espaola de la Uni Europea, este allanamiento de trabas experimentar un fuerte avance. A nivel nacional, un buen ejemplo de iniciativa en la misma lnea lo constituye el reciente Proyecto de Ley de Medidas de Reforma del Sistema Financiero. No voy a comentar el ambicioso contenido de esta iniciativa, tarea inabordable en el tiempo de que dispongo. nicamente voy a mencionar dos aspectos del Proyecto de Ley directamente relacionados con las cajas de ahorros, a los que el Banco de Espa concede especial importancia. El primero es el reforzamiento de que la caracterstica esencial de las cajas de ahorros es su condici de entidades privadas de crdito. So asumiendo las responsabilidades de todo tipo que implica esta condici, tema sobre el que volver ms adelante, pueden las cajas de ahorros afrontar satisfactoriamente las implicaciones de sus caractersticas diferenciadoras (naturaleza fundacional privada, carcter social y vinculaci territorial); caractersticas que hay que mantener, por estar en la base de muchas de las trascendentales aportaciones de las cajas de ahorros a la estabilidad, solvencia y eficiencia de nuestro sistema financiero. El segundo aspecto es la consideraci y el tratamiento de las cuotas participativas de las cajas de ahorros. Desde hace tiempo, el Banco de Espaa se ha manifestado a favor de regular flexible y rigurosamente este instrumento de captaci de recursos propios especfico de las cajas de ahorros, respetuoso con su naturaleza fundacional y, en la medida en que est bien disedo, llamado a otorgarles unas mayores posibilidades de expansi y operativas, que exigen un incremento paralelo de la disciplina de mercado. El Proyecto de Ley Financiera es un medio ideo de concretar esta vieja aspiracin, compartida con el propio sector, estableciendo una regulaci que incorpore la menor intervenci plica que sea posible, y est sidamente asentada en principios tan bsicos como el pleno respeto del mbito estatal de competencias, la libertad de emisi, la clara determinacin de los derechos que vaya a conferir la tenencia de cuotas participativas, y su cotizacin en mercados secundarios oficiales, para aportarles liquidez. Las ventajas de todo tipo que las cuotas participativas pueden aportar a las cajas de ahorros, y por tanto al sistema financiero espal, no deben hacernos olvidar que su introducci ha de ser gradual, basada en estudios especialmente rigurosos hasta disponer de suficiente experiencia, y adoptando las cautelas necesarias para evitar la diluci del elevado valor social de las cajas de ahorros. Pese a su importancia, las actuaciones plicas que acabo de comentar no son el factor clave para aprovechar las oportunidades y superar los desafos que van a plantearse con el cambio en la fase del ciclo y la creciente integraci de los mercados financieros europeos. Como corresponde a una economa de mercado, el factor clave van a ser las actitudes y comportamientos de los agentes econmicos privados. En este sentido y para el sector de cajas de ahorros, merece la pena detenerse brevemente en algunos rasgos de la evoluci en el pasado a. En 2001, el crdito ha crecido a un fuerte ritmo, 15,5%, muy superior al 9,1% de la banca espala, y ello a pesar de la ralentizaci del crecimiento econico, lo que hace que sea especialmente relevante la calidad de la inversi y la rentabilidad de la misma. Debe reconocerse, no obstante, que los ratios de morosidad se mantienen en niveles mnimos, 0'8%, y la cobertura de la morosidad, sigue creciendo, situndose a finales de 2001 en el 225%, gracias en buena medida al FCEI. No obstante, conviene no olvidar que la morosidad implcita en los fuertes crecimientos del crdito registrados en los ltimos as, se va a ir manifestando incluso si las mejores perspectivas de cambio de tendencia se cumplen. Por ello, aunque las provisiones suponen un indudable colch de seguridad ante posibles deterioros de los activos y refuerzan la buena imagen de solvencia del sector, no hay que dejar de vigilar las excesivas concentraciones de riesgos y de aplicar polticas rigurosas. Los recursos propios de las cajas de ahorros declarados en su conjunto son a, finales de 2001, un 45% superiores a los mnimos legalmente exigibles, lo que todo unido dice mucho de esa imagen de solvencia. Aunque las dotaciones a las provisiones estadsticas han tenido una clara incidencia negativa en la cuenta de resultados de 2001, el resultado neto contable a ha crecido un 6,1%, a pesar de que los beneficios extraordinarios se han reducido drsticamente. En cuanto a gastos, no ha cesado la expansi de las cajas de ahorros, como lo demuestra el hecho de que en 2001 se hayan abierto 563 nuevas oficinas netas y las plantillas se hayan incrementado en 3.835 personas. Ello ha generado un crecimiento de los costes de estructura del 8,5%, si bien, el aumento del volumen de negocio ha hecho posible que el ratio de eficiencia haya mejorado en 2,1 puntos porcentuales, que a se mantiene en niveles 62,1% sustancialmente peores que los de la banca espaola, 53,5%. Por ello, aunque los aumentos de los mrgenes de intermediaci y ordinario, hagan que el de explotaci aumente en valores absolutos casi un 20%, debe continuarse con el esfuerzo por conseguir una mayor contenci de los gastos de explotaci. Hay que remarcar la importancia de la racionalizaci de estos gastos como defensa ante la presi que la competencia ejerce en los mrgenes del negocio. Me gustara ahora comentar alguno de los cambios que se estn produciendo en el terreno supervisor. El primero es el Nuevo Acuerdo de Capital, que, como todos ustedes saben, ha visto retrasada la publicacin de su texto definitivo por las dificultades que plantea la calibraci de las propuestas de enero del pasado a y por el deseo de perfeccionarlas, incorporando lo mejor de las numerosas sugerencias formuladas durante la fase de consulta. Tampoco este retraso puede dar lugar a una etapa de relajacin. Lejos de ello, debe constituir una etapa de activa preparaci para que todos, supervisores y supervisados, seamos capaces de asumir las responsabilidades propias y recprocas que va a plantearnos el Nuevo Acuerdo, algunos de cuyos rasgos bsicos paso a comentar. En su bsqueda de una regulaci de los recursos propios mnimos ms acorde con los sistemas financieros actuales y ms sensible al riesgo que la actual, el Comit de Basilea parte explcitamente del principio bsico de que la responsabilidad fundamental de la evoluci y comportamiento de cualquier entidad corresponde a sus administradores y altos gestores. Suyo es el mrito de los aciertos, pero tambin la responsabilidad de los errores, de los comportamientos deficientes y problemticos en los que la entidad pueda incurrir. Los supervisores no debemos intentar sustituir la labor de direcci y vigilancia que nuestro ordenamiento jurdico encomienda a los administradores; la labor de control que, en el marco de un correcto gobierno corporativo, corresponde a los accionistas; ni la labor de disciplina que, a partir de una informaci societaria transparente, corresponde al mercado. Respetando estos mbitos de actuaci privados, a los supervisores plicos nos corresponde establecer y hacer cumplir un marco normativo consistente, transparente y proactivo que, proporcionando a las entidades los incentivos correctos, contribuya eficientemente a evitar el riesgo sistmico, al buen funcionamiento de entidades y mercados, y a potenciar la proteccin del depositante y del inversor. Respecto al enfoque supervisor, quiero destacar co el Nuevo Acuerdo profundiza la tendencia, ya presente en anteriores recomendaciones del Comit de Basilea, a complementar las necesarias normas de obligado cumplimiento con un sistema de incentivos, orientado a mejorar aspectos cualitativos de la gesti y del control de riesgos de las entidades. Estos incentivos supervisores impregnan todo el texto del Nuevo Acuerdo. El mayor nfasis supervisor en los aspectos cualitativos responde, bsicamente, a motivaciones bien conocidas: la creciente complejidad de los actuales sistemas financieros, con entidades y grupos cada vez mayores y ms diversificados y el creciente dinamismo de los mercados, cuya situacin y perspectivas pueden cambiar con una rapidez desconocida hasta tiempos recientes, al ser cada vez ms competitivos y desregulados, ms integrados y geogrficamente interdependientes, y al contar con la mejor informaci y la agilidad operativa que estn aportando las nuevas tecnologas. Si cambios de esta magnitud estn incidiendo en la supervisi, potenciando su vertiente cualitativa, necesariamente tiene que haber un reflejo simtrico en las entidades, que, por tanto, debe afectar con especial intensidad a los aspectos cualitativos de su actividad. Anteriormente, ya he mencionado la necesidad de mejorar algunos de estos aspectos, tales como la gesti y el control interno, tanto con carcter general como, muy especialmente, de los riesgos. Dentro de este mbito cualitativo, y para cerrar mi intervenci, voy a comentar un tema del que se ha ocupado en profundidad el Comit de Supervisi Bancaria de Basilea y que han puesto de actualidad recientes acontecimientos nacionales e internacionales, que, aunque de importancia muy desigual, estn en la mente de todos. Se trata de la necesidad de mejorar el gobierno de nuestras sociedades. Hasta ahora, el mayor impulso de mejora planteado en este tema ha sido el denominado Informe Olivencia, preparado a instancias del Consejo de Ministros para alcanzar, y cito literalmente "mayores cotas de eficacia, responsabilidad y transparencia en el gobierno de las sociedades que apelan a los mercados financieros". Desde la aparici de este Informe, en marzo de 1998, han sido numerosas las sociedades cotizadas que lo han adoptado formalmente. Pese a los avances, creo que, en las actuales circunstancias, sto es insuficiente y cada vez est siendo mayor el desfase entre la realidad de nuestro gobierno corporativo y las exigencias planteadas por una sociedad y una economa, cada vez ms atentas a cmo se rigen las empresas, y por unos mercados que, cada vez ms, incorporan a sus primas de riesgo las deficiencias en esta materia. Se trata de un problema que rebasa las fronteras nacionales que, si bien no ha tenido efectos sistmicos, s que merece, y est recibiendo, una cuidadosa atenci en todos los pases. Si el tema del gobierno corporativo es importante para todo tipo de sociedades, creo que lo es especficamente para las entidades de crdito, en las que, adems, debe complementarse con rigurosos cigos de conducta y estrictas murallas chinas, como consecuencia, entre otros temas, de la especial complejidad de las relaciones de agencia que se desarrollan en su seno; de los potentes conflictos de intereses que pueden surgir en la asignaci de los recursos crediticios; de la informaci privilegiada sobre las empresas deudoras a la que tienen acceso las entidades; y de la elevadsima asimetra informativa que afecta a los depositantes. En su documento "Potenciaci del gobierno corporativo en las organizaciones bancarias", de septiembre de 1999, el Comit de Basilea extrae de estas caractersticas los principios bsicos que debe reunir el gobierno corporativo en las entidades de crdito: transparencia, responsabilidad, profesionalidad, cualificaci e independencia son algunas de las caractersticas que el documento considera como necesarias en los gestores para asegurar el buen gobierno de todas las entidades. Dirigindome a una audiencia compuesta por responsables mximos de cajas de ahorros, so me queda complementar estas recomendaciones enfatizando su importancia dada la especial complejidad y significaci que el gobierno corporativo tiene para las cajas de ahorros, por su peculiar sistema de propiedad. Es evidente que estas mejoras cualitativas que acabo de mencionar en la gesti y control de las entidades, en su gobierno corporativo y en su debida diligencia con los clientes son de especial trascendencia para un sector econico tan dependiente de la confianza del plico como es el financiero. Ahora bien, no es menos evidente que dichas mejoras responden a una demanda social ampliamente generalizada y que, por tanto, hay que situarlas en un marco de reformas mucho ms general, que incluye a las empresas no financieras, a los auditores externos, a los consultores, a los analistas de inversiones, etc. Estas cuestiones que, como ustedes saben, estn siendo discutidas tanto en foros e instituciones internacionales como en mbitos nacionales, han sido debatidas en profundidad en la reciente reuni del ECOFIN, celebrada en Oviedo, en el que se ha dado un mandado al Grupo de Alto Nivel de Derecho Mercantil de la UE para que analice los sistemas de control interno, a las prcticas de Gobierno Corporativo y las prcticas de Auditora. Resumiendo mi intervenci, el cambio en la situaci cclica de nuestra economa y de las economas de nuestro entorno, junto con las perspectivas abiertas tras la plena introducci del euro, plantean unas oportunidades, no exentas de riesgos, cuyo aprovechamiento nos exige a todos abordar, con carcter inmediato, reformas de alto alcance y profundo calado. Estoy seguro de que nuestra economa, nuestro sistema financiero, y co no, las cajas de ahorros, sabrn estar, una vez ms, a la altura de las circunstancias. Muchas gracias.

Title: Appearance before the Committee on Economy and Finance of the Congress of Deputies
text: Jaime Caruna Governor of the Bank of Spain May 8, 2002 APPEARANCE OF THE GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF SPAIN, JAIME CARUANA, BEFORE THE ECONOMY AND FINANCE COMMITTEE OF THE CONGRESS OF DEPUTIES Mr. President, Honourable Members, It is an honour and a source of satisfaction for me that this Committee on Economic Affairs and Finance has established a calendar of hearings that allows me to report to you on the activities of the Banco de Espa96a within the framework of the functions entrusted to it by statute. The completion of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has changed some of these functions, since it is up to the Eurosystem as a whole, consisting of the European Central Bank (ECB), and the national central banks of the area, to define the strategy and objectives of the common monetary policy and to adopt at all times the decisions required for its correct implementation. However, the common monetary policy of the euro area is our own monetary policy and its evolution is fraught with implications for the Spanish economy. As Governor of the Banco de Espa96a, I am part - together with the governors of the central banks of the other countries integrated in the Monetary Union and with the members of the Executive Board - of the Governing Council of the ECB, which is the body responsible for directing this policy. And the Bank of Spain is responsible for implementing it in our monetary and financial markets and monitoring its transmission through credit institutions and its implications for the Spanish economy and for other aspects of economic policy that remain under national sovereignty. All this - together with other tasks of the Banco de Espa96a - must be the subject of a fruitful dialogue with this Parliamentary Committee, within the limits of the confidentiality commitments that derive both from membership of the Governing Council of the ECB, on the one hand, and from supervisory legislation, on the other. Euro area and monetary policy The first part of my speech will focus on analysing the monetary policy that the Eurosystem has been implementing and the future challenges facing the euro area, as well as the evolution and prospects of the Spanish economy. The second part will be devoted to aspects of financial stability and supervisory activities, and within this section I want to summarize the actions of the Bank of Spain in relation to BBVA. In any case, allow me to begin by referring to the most outstanding event that has taken place in our recent past, which is only the culmination of EMU through the introduction of euro banknotes and coins. The exchange process has involved enormous complexity, and although it had been carefully scheduled, it has required considerable effort on the part of numerous actors in both the public and private sectors. The result would not have been so brilliant without the close cooperation of the financial system, the distribution sector and, especially, the European citizens, who have been the real protagonists in unequivocally supporting the currency exchange. Judging by the results, this collective - albeit demanding - effort has been worthwhile, since the exchange has generally proceeded without serious incidents and with great speed. Thus, three years after the beginning of EMU, the euro is already a currency in the full extent of the term, and can be used in any type of economic transaction by three hundred million Europeans. It is hoped that this far-reaching and irreversible step will strengthen economic integration in Europe and contribute to the full exploitation of the benefits that this process brings to the economies of the participating countries. Although the potential benefits of EMU will be reaped as the integration process progresses, many favourable effects of the single currency have already been felt. Among them, it is noteworthy that, from the outset, the euro area has shown a high degree of macroeconomic stability, consistent with the primary objective of the Eurosystem's monetary policy, which is the maintenance of price stability. This has meant that EMU countries have been able to overcome, in a relatively satisfactory way, the shocks that have occurred in their external environment since 1999 and which, in the past, would probably have entailed higher costs in the past. in terms of growth and employment, especially in those countries that lacked their own sufficiently deep-rooted experience of macroeconomic discipline. Despite this, EMU was, of course, affected during the past year by successive shocks and by the significant deterioration in economic activity in the main industrialized countries. This cyclical evolution showed high synchrony at the global level, although the slowdown, which was intense, lasted only for a relatively short period, thanks in large part to the appropriate policy response. In this way, the sharp slowdown in activity has not prevented output from continuing to register positive growth rates in some countries, including Spain. The rapid onset of the economic slowdown in 2001, the uncertainty about its impact on the European economy and the initially unfavourable trend in inflation observed complicated the Eurosystem's assessment of the outlook for price behaviour. However, as the deterioration of the economic outlook and the transitory nature of the price tensions became apparent, monetary policy adapted to the new context, implementing gradual reductions in interest rates, which became more intense as a result of the worsening of the international economic scenario after the attacks of 11 September. From the decision taken in May 2001 to cut interest rates, for the first time in this new cyclical phase, until November, when the ECB decided to cut the last hair, interest rates on the main refinancing operations fell by 150 basis points. These declines were consistent with the maintenance of relatively reassuring outlook on price behaviour over the medium term. With these cuts, real rates reached levels close to the lowest levels of recent decades in all the economies that make up EMU. It must therefore be recognized that monetary conditions have been conducive to the revival of economic activity and have helped to moderate the extent of the cyclical slowdown. Monetary policy also obviously took into account the authorities' actions in other areas of economic policy. Thus, on the budgetary side, the policies implemented in EMU contributed, in general, to macroeconomic stability, since they took into account both the cyclical position - allowing automatic stabilisers to act - and the commitment contained in the Stability and Growth Pact to maintain a path of budgetary balance in the medium term. The increase in the structural deficit observed in the euro area as a whole was modest and was mainly due to the impact of tax cuts that were adopted at the beginning of the year in some countries, earlier that the weakening of activity would become apparent. In any case, I would like to stress here that, as the conclusions of the Barcelona Council point out, the action of the budgetary stabilisers must be symmetrical, so that, in the boom phases, their operation must lead to an improvement in the situation of the public accounts. Thus, it would be facilitated that, even in times of economic weakness, its stimulating action can reach a sufficient intensity, without violating the established limits. The recent evolution of prices in the euro area - with the harmonised index increasing by 2.7% in January, falling to 2.2% in the first Eurostat estimates for April - has been less satisfactory than expected a few months ago. Given the temporary nature of the factors contributing to price developments, both in the past months and in the years 2000 and 2001, their effects should be cushioned and should not affect the medium-term inflation outlook. Despite the upswing in consumer prices at the beginning of this year - mainly linked to climatic factors, the increase in indirect taxes and higher oil prices - it is still possible that the inflation rate in the euro zone will be below the 2% benchmark contained in the definition of price stability adopted by the ECB in the coming months. This will depend, to a large extent, on the behaviour of oil prices. In the light of the information available, at its last meeting on 2 May, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank concluded that the inflationary outlook in the euro area is now less favourable than it was at the end of last year. At the same time, uncertainties in the economic outlook and the influence of temporary factors on past price behavior were recognized. In the medium term, the reduction in inflation could be compromised if wage demands lead to exaggerated cost increases and if oil prices maintain an upward path. As for the foreseeable evolution of economic activity, the latest indicators show a recovery of positive GDP growth rates in the first quarter of this year, which should normally mark the end of the phase of economic slowdown. The dynamism of foreign markets, driven by the recovery of the US economy, should favour the acceleration of output and employment throughout the year. The indicators that have appeared are compatible with growth in the area at the end of the year, in line with its potential growth. However, there are still uncertainties, As for the strength of the recovery, related to the evolution of oil prices and the existence of imbalances outside the euro area. The prospects for sustained growth in the euro area depend mainly on the dynamism of gross capital formation, following the stagnation experienced in 2001. In principle, the ease of monetary and financial conditions, the exhaustion of the inventory adjustment process and the foreseeable expansion of exports should contribute to the increase in investment in the area, as the available indicators for the first months of this year seem to suggest. Moreover, the European economy faces this phase of recovery with relatively solid fundamentals. Thus, despite their decline in recent years, European households have a higher savings rate and a debt, in terms of their disposable income, lower than those of the US economy; The current account balance is balanced, and private sector exposure to a possible correction in equity prices is moderate. However, the limited duration and scope of the previous expansionary phase and the relative intensity of the subsequent slowdown suggest that the euro area is struggling to maintain a high pace of output growth over an extended period. These problems are related to the rigidities that European markets still present, which damage the adjustment mechanisms of the economy and discourage the expansion and modernization of the productive apparatus. These shortcomings are reflected in low labour productivity growth in Europe, both historically and in comparison with the United States, which has direct effects on the well-being of citizens, hindering the growth of their per capita income, damaging the competitiveness of the economy and thus hindering sustained job creation. Thus, it seems logical that one of the priorities of the European authorities is the adoption of reforms aimed at creating a framework conducive to investment, which promotes productivity growth. In this regard, the initiatives recently agreed by the European authorities are particularly timely. If the ambitious objectives set are to be achieved, so that the potential growth of the European economy rises substantially - and with it job creation - it seems necessary to deepen and accelerate reforms aimed at increasing the flexibility of labour markets, liberalising and integrating network industries, promoting technological innovation and boosting the integration of the European Union. financial markets. These reforms are also essential if we are to exploit intensively the potential benefits of the European single market, to which I referred at the beginning of my speech. Spanish economy I now turn to the Spanish economy. The slowdown and uncertain environment in which world economic activity developed during 2001 also affected our economy, which, as you all know, gradually reduced its rate of growth, ending the year with an average growth in real GDP of 2.8 per cent, significantly lower than the previous year. The variables most directly affected by external conditions - exports and investment - were those that set the pace of slowdown. Exports suffered from the collapse of foreign markets, especially European markets, while the climate of pessimism and uncertainty that took over the international economic scene did not create a favorable framework for the expected take-off of business investment, despite the favorable situation of companies. On the other hand, those variables that respond to a greater extent to factors of an internal nature, such as household expenses, maintained greater dynamism, to which the strength in employment growth contributed. The reactivation that is leading the North American economy and the increasingly favorable expectations about its progressive consolidation throughout the year are already extending, as we have seen, to Europe and, of course, to Spain. As the Bank of Spain has recently advanced in its latest quarterly report, the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP of the Spanish economy in the first quarter of 2002 is estimated at 2.1% and the quarter-on-quarter rate calculated from the seasonally adjusted series, which provides more immediate information, in line with European practices. Although more volatile, it has already recovered significantly with respect to the values reached in the previous quarter, marking a turning point in economic activity that extends to a significant part of the industrial sector, which had suffered a phase of contraction in recent months. As the recovery period consolidates and exports and business investment are incorporated into this process, the Spanish economy will gradually approach its potential growth rate and employment will return to a path of sustained growth, although more moderate than in the past. The Spanish economy is therefore completing a cyclical phase that is moving away from the usual patterns in our recent economic history. The boom period was particularly long and fruitful in terms of job creation and falling unemployment, and marked an important step forward in real convergence with euro area countries. The slowdown phase has been particularly benign, not only because of its short duration, but also because considerable growth rates in output and employment have been maintained during it, without real convergence having stopped. Therefore, as in previous cycles, we have not entered a period of sluggish demand and job destruction in which economic agents were cleaning up the imbalances accumulated in the expansionary phase. It is worthwhile for me to refer, albeit briefly, to the specific factors that have contributed to this change in behaviour, since relevant lessons can be drawn from them about the patterns we should follow in the future, in order to make the most of this climate of resuscitation that is beginning to be perceived. The Spanish economy is increasingly conditioned by the evolution of the external environment, not only that marked by the European economic area, but also by the one formed by other economic areas with which our relations are increasingly intense. The importance of cross-border flows of direct investment in recent years, inwards and, above all, and this is the highlight, outwards, speak of their growing integration into the international environment. But, as everyone well knows, Spain's growing involvement in the world economic sphere has reached its maximum expression with the full integration of our economy into EMU. The benefits of participating in an area of monetary and financial stability have materialised not only through exchange rate stability in the euro area, but also, in our case, through substantial reductions in interest rates - a consequence of the success achieved in convergence - which induced a significant revaluation of wealth and stimulated the dynamism of spending. The fall in interest rates initially boosted the increase in investment, until the change in the international environment and the consequent worsening of expectations conditioned companies' investment plans in capital goods. The latest available data indicate that we may already be reaching a floor in the slowdown in business investment, which will become more vigorous as the recovery of the world economy is transmitted to our foreign markets. The construction sector also received a strong boost through the decline in mortgage rates. The increase in house prices and the decline in the profitability of other alternative investments also stimulated the demand for housing for investment, accentuating the pressure on prices in a spiral that is already beginning to subside. During these years, therefore, the Spanish economy has received a temporary monetary boost as a result of the entry into EMU, without its nominal stability being compromised, since other economic policies - macroeconomic and microeconomic - have contributed to counteract its effects. Fiscal policy has been aimed at achieving full fiscal consolidation, in line with the requirements of the Stability and Growth Pact. As you all know, last year the budget balance was achieved for all public administrations, and the available data on the execution of the State budget in the current year anticipate that we will not move away from that result. The maintenance of a significant primary structural surplus - above 2.5% in 2001 - is the best guarantee of the solvency achieved by the public accounts. The contribution of fiscal policy to macroeconomic stability has received very important support through, precisely, the Budget Stability Act, recently enacted in this House. Another norm of this legislature, the Law of Financing of the Autonomous Communities, is especially suitable to advance in the discipline and fiscal co-responsibility of the territorial entities. In this brief review of the factors that have contributed to the Spanish economy maintaining particularly favourable patterns of behaviour throughout the cycle that is now ending, I must refer, finally, to the structural reforms undertaken in recent years, which have continued to make progress in making the labour market more flexible and improving the functioning of numerous markets for goods and services. These changes have allowed, among other things, as I have already said, that the current cycle has been particularly fruitful in terms of employment growth, which, in turn, by boosting family incomes and clearing uncertainty about their future, have allowed high growth rates in household spending. Although employment has tended to slow down recently - and with it household disposable income - it has done so moderately and private consumption continues to grow considerably. This is compatible with the fact that, after several years of considerable expansion, Some components of household spending, such as car purchases, show signs of some exhaustion. It must be other variables, to which I have already mentioned - investment and exports - that have to take a greater role and become the engines of growth in the coming years. Challenges of the Spanish economy But the Spanish economy has important challenges that it must face decisively, deepening the reforms already initiated. Belonging to an area that gives special priority to the values of efficiency and stability provides, as we have had occasion to verify, notable benefits to the economies that integrate it, but it is equally demanding and severe with those that deviate from these postulates. This being so, in order for the Spanish economy to continue advancing firmly in its process of real convergence, a series of problems that have become evident over the years must be faced. Some are typical of an economy that has experienced a long expansionary period and will tend to correct themselves. But others have a deeper nature and demand concrete actions to solve them. I will now refer to them. In recent years there has been a notable increase in the debt ratios of the private sector - households and companies - which, in part, is due to a structural change, as agents adapt to a situation in which relatively low interest rates can be sustained in the medium and long term. In fact, these ratios are even lower than those in other neighbouring economies, which have been moving for several years in a context of low interest rates. In any case, the speed with which indebtedness has increased and the strong concentration of it, in the case of households, in the purchase of real estate assets, whose prices may vary in the future, advises to be cautious and closely monitor the evolution of these variables, which do not seem to be a hindrance to spending decisions as the reactivation of the economy takes hold. In this respect, credit to the private sector has been slowing significantly over the past year, consistent with the slower tone of activity, although it still maintains high growth rates and even seems to have picked up slightly in the first quarter of 2002. Another of the less favourable features of our recent economic developments that should be analysed is low productivity growth, while recognising the Difficulties in its measurement and interpretation. As I have said on other occasions, the Spanish economy must maintain a pattern of growth that allows it to continue to substantially increase the level of employment and incorporate into the labour market important sectors of the population that remain outside it. This employment-intensive pattern, which implies a certain moderation in the observed increase in productivity, has made it possible to bring our levels of well-being closer to those prevailing in neighbouring countries. But low productivity also reflects inadequacies in the incorporation of new technologies into production processes. The challenge is therefore to ensure that employment growth is compatible with long-term improvements in the genuine productivity of factors of production. Productivity gains are necessary to be competitive, especially in today's world, in which the profound technological changes that are taking place drive less efficient firms out of the market, or force them to compete in the technologically less advanced segments with newly industrializing economies that, lacking the social welfare systems of advanced economies, They start from a more favourable cost ratio. In order to make progress along these lines, it is necessary to increase investment in the economy, in its broadest sense, which includes investment in physical capital, technological capital and human capital. Finally, it is necessary to have flexible markets that allow technological advances to spread effectively through all sectors of the economy. This is one point, the reform of the markets, where there is still an important task to be completed. The progress made in reforming the labour market must continue, until its efficient functioning reduces disincentives to participation and allows the incorporation of important segments of the population: the unemployed, women and young people, who remain on the margins of productive activities. And they must do so in such a way that wage remuneration is adapted to the circumstances of the different sectors and companies of the economy and to the characteristics of the workers themselves, which is the best way to guarantee the stability of jobs. The reforms should be extended to other markets - for goods, and especially for services - which continue to carry out a significant part of their activity in uncompetitive situations. The persistence of a dual inflation problem in the Spanish economy is the clearest example of this situation. The high growth rates that continue to register the prices of services in the Spanish economy and the differential that we maintain with the countries of the euro zone, contrast with the results we observe in other sectors that, being open to competition - abroad and in the domestic market - , adapt their prices to those in force in international markets. I am referring to many industrial sectors and our exporting companies, which must absorb cost pressures, whatever their origin, through reductions in their operating margins, because they cannot systematically pass them on to their prices. The persistence that our prices and costs grow above those of our European partners, ends up undermining the foundations on which the competitiveness of the economy must be based, and its solution passes, as has been repeated so many times, by a decisive advance in the reforms that act on the supply side of the economy. Finally, I would like to refer to fiscal consolidation, which, as I said before, is one of the most important assets that the Spanish economy has achieved in recent years, we must try to preserve and consolidate. For this, it is necessary to undertake the pertinent reforms to face in a fair and efficient way the future challenges that will arise as a result of the changes that are taking place in the structure of the population of our country and that will affect very important aspects of our welfare state. I believe, ladies and gentlemen, that the Spanish economy is in a favourable situation to deal with the new expansionary stage that is making its way, still with certain hesitations, in the international environment. Our current growth is higher than that of most countries in our environment and is expected to remain so throughout the year. The levels of macroeconomic stability, with which we have completed the recent expansionary phase, are satisfactory, and private economic agents have sound financial positions. But the challenges we face are significant. The Spanish economy must consolidate its integration into the European Union and approach the levels of well-being typical of the area. And for that to be so, we must grow more than the other countries and do it in a sustained manner, which requires us to be more efficient and competitive. I now come to the second part of my speech, which will focus on issues relating to financial stability. Firstly, I will comment on the situation of the Spanish banking system in this regard; I will then summarize some aspects of the supervisory activity of the Banco de Espa96a. The health of the financial system in the US, Europe and Spain has been one of the key elements of this greater resistance to which I referred in the first part of my speech and which has allowed the recent crisis to be successfully overcome. The channels of interaction between the financial system and the real economy are increasingly powerful, rapid and complex, and experience shows how fragile financial systems can extend cycles, deepening their declining phases, making the necessary adjustments extremely costly. Financial stability is necessary for the sustained growth of the economy, and achieving and consolidating it requires constant attention and work. Therefore, the strengthening of financial systems is one of the basic priorities of many international organizations and, of course, of national authorities. I will return later to the international aspects of banking supervision, but first I will summarize the situation of our banking system, commenting on the evolution of its activity, its risks, its profitability and its solvency. Evolution .- At a consolidated level, the total assets of Spanish depository institutions grew by 7.3% in 2001 compared with the previous year, confirming in the second half of the year the slowdown already observed in the first half of 2001. The economic slowdown has been translated into a moderation in the pace of credit growth and a stabilisation of the NPL ratio slightly below 1%, after years of continued declines. However, it should not be forgotten that the non-performing loans implicit in the strong growth in credit recorded in recent years will tend to manifest itself even if the improvement in the economic outlook consolidates. This development has occurred in an international environment characterized by the intensity of shocks affecting the financial system, including the bursting of the bubble in technology and telecommunications stocks; an intense financial crisis in Turkey; the collapse of Enron, among other large companies; the direct and indirect effects of the terrorist attacks of 11 September and, finally, the deterioration of the situation in Argentina, which continues to be plunged into a crisis, differentiated and its own, of great proportions. Risks.- The Spanish financial system has been relatively little affected by these shocks, with the exception of the Argentine problem. International expansion strategies provide great opportunities, but they necessarily involve the assumption of corresponding risks. The important thing is that institutions know how to identify and manage them, that they have the capacity to generate recurring income and have adequate provisions and own resources to face possible expected and unexpected losses. This is the case of Spanish banks, which are showing their capacity to face the Argentine crisis and have adequately provisioned their risks in this country. The serious difficulties that Argentina is going through have not spread to those countries that concentrate most of the presence of Spanish banks in the area, in particular, Mexico, Brazil and Chile. With regard to liquidity risk, over the past year it has been possible to verify the capacity of national and international financial systems to overcome very satisfactorily shocks such as that of 11 September, thanks to the rapid and appropriate coordinated action of the monetary authorities. Once the immediate negative impact that the events of September 11 had on market risk has been overcome, there has been an advance in stock indices, although the profit prospects of companies seem generously valued in the stock markets, worldwide. Profitability.- The slowdown in economic growth in Spain, the unfavourable evolution of national and international financial markets and the Argentine crisis have resulted in a general moderation in the growth of the net result of Spanish depository institutions. The net result after tax attributed to the group grew by 6.9% in 2001. This growth represents a substantial moderation compared to the two years immediately preceding (21.6 per cent in 2000 and 13.4 per cent in 1999). However, the fall in the profitability of equity has been more moderate (from 15% in 2000 to 13.3% in 2001), compared very advantageously with that obtained by its international competitors, even after the impact of the new statistical provision, an element that reinforces the medium-term solvency of Spanish banks and allows us to face the future with confidence. Solvency.- The solvency ratio of Spanish deposit institutions, both under the terms established by the Basel Committee and by the much more demanding Spanish regulations, has increased in 2001, truncating a four-year downward trend. The The slowdown in credit growth, which has resulted in a substantial moderation in the increase in requirements, has been greater than that of own resources, which have continued to grow, thanks to the increase in second-category funds. In the preference shares, which count as first-class equity, on which the Bank of Spain had been recommending prudence, there has been a change in trend, reducing their importance in those entities with a greater weight of preferred equity in their own resources. Despite the economic slowdown, the increase in non-performing assets and the slowdown in earnings growth, Spanish banks show good efficiency, profitability and solvency ratios, which, together with the anticipatory effect of the statistical provision, places the Spanish banking system in a favourable comparative situation. International Principles of Banking Supervision I will now comment on the supervisory activity of the Banco de Espa96a. However, I would firstly like to highlight some of the internationally accepted principles on which banking supervision is based. (1) Responsibility of administrators and managers. The starting point is to remember that those most responsible for the evolution and behavior of a credit institution are its administrators and managers. They must be credited with the successes, but also the responsibility for mistakes and deficient or irregular behaviour. This does not mean that these decisions are only internal affairs of each financial institution, which do not concern the others. On the contrary, one of the main causes of the banking sector being specially regulated is its powerful externalities; in particular, the significant impact on third parties that may have failures in an entity. This requires, on the one hand, a special dose of responsibility on the part of the directors and managers of the entities; on the other, the existence of efficient supervision. Both requirements are complementary, without it being up to the supervisors to replace the managerial work of the administrators, or even the control work that corresponds to the shareholders or the discipline that the market must exercise. (2) National jurisdiction and international coordination. Even in progressively integrated economic areas, such as Europe, banking supervision follows the principle of subsidiarity and is therefore a national competence. This makes sense given that the structure of European banking systems continues to have an essentially national dimension, while significant regulatory differences persist. To this must be added the convenience of maintaining supervision close to the supervised. However, the need for greater international supervisory coordination is becoming increasingly apparent. In this area, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, linked to the G10, is the most important body in this area. In February of last year, given the relevance of our banking system and recognizing the quality of the Spanish supervisory model, the Bank of Spain joined it as a full member and, since then, actively participates in all its work. Although this committee is best known for the international impact of its "Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision" and its "Capital Agreement", now under review, the significance of its work on the code of good governance of banking entities cannot be overlooked; its recommendations on the relations of these entities and their supervisors with internal and external auditors; or their considerations about the obligation that banks have to know their customers, to avoid using the financial system for illicit purposes. I do not want to dwell on this point. To conclude with this, I would just like to mention that, at European Union level, there are also three cooperation committees in the field of banking supervision, in which we also actively participate: the Banking Advisory Committee, the Committee on Banking Supervision and the so-called Contact Group. This is the international reference framework in which the Spanish legal system must be placed, which designates the Bank of Spain as the competent body to ensure the stability and solvency of the credit system. Law 13/1994, of 1 June (Article 7, paragraph 6), on the Autonomy of the Bank of Spain, states: "The Banco de Espa96a must supervise, in accordance with the provisions in force, the solvency, performance and compliance with the specific regulations of credit institutions and any other financial institutions and markets whose supervision has been attributed to it,...." (3) Independence of the supervisor. Listed by the Basel Committee as one of its "Basic Principles for Effective Banking Supervision", supervisory independence is contemplated in Spanish legislation in art. 1 of Law 13/1994, of June 1, on the Autonomy of the Bank of Spain, when it states: "In the development of its activity and for the fulfillment of its purposes, it will act with autonomy with respect to the General Administration of the State, performing its functions in accordance with the provisions of this Law and in the rest of the legal system." (4) Obligation of professional secrecy. The obligation for the supervisor to maintain professional secrecy over its actions is also another of the "Basic principles for effective banking supervision" of the Basel Committee, included in the regulations of all supervisors in developed countries and which, as a transposition of two Community directives (73/183 and 77/780), also appear in Spanish legislation. Specifically, Royal Legislative Decree 1298/1986, of 28 June, establishes that: "The data, documents and information held by the Banco de Espa96a by virtue of all the functions entrusted to it by law will be reserved and may not be disclosed to any person or authority." This obligation of secrecy has, logically, certain exceptions, assessed and protected by due precautions (Cortes Generales, criminal proceedings, money laundering, etc.). Strict compliance is a condition required by both EU directives and international practices for the exchange of information between supervisors in different countries. Obviously, this does not exclude the information contemplated by Spanish legislation at the end of a sanctioning process. Supervisory activities of the Banco de Espa96a The principles I have just mentioned are some of the principles in which banking supervision activities in our country must be framed. Its head is the Bank of Spain, which is entrusted with the supervision of 510 entities, of which 367 are credit institutions The Banco de Espa96a exercises over these entities, in the first place, a process of continuous supervision, consisting of the analysis and monitoring of economic and financial information, which is complemented by frequent contact with the representatives of the entities. This ongoing process is reinforced, secondly, by an extensive programme of on-site inspections. During 2001, around 150 on-site inspections were carried out. Finally, I would like to mention two issues. The first is that we are working on an annual monitoring report, which we are going to publish for the first time this year, covering the financial year 2001. The second theme is that we have launched a new publication on financial stability, which, based on the conviction that banking supervision must be increasingly transparent, aims to create a platform for communication and dialogue with industry and academia on financial stability issues, with a particular focus on prudential regulatory and supervisory issues. Supervisory actions of the Banco de Espa96a in relation to BBVA I now summarize the most relevant actions of the Bank of Spain that have led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings against Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria (BBVA) and 16 of its administrators and senior managers. I want to emphasize that the BBVA group today and after 150 years of effort and good work, is a solvent and profitable group, which constitutes an international reference. It currently has high equity, a solvency ratio of 12.6%, measured by the criteria of the Basel Committee (well above, therefore, the minimum of 8%) (December 2001 figures). Quantitatively, the facts that gave rise to the file have no material impact on the solvency of the group or its profitability and are exceptional, isolated and completely unrelated to the behavior of our banking system. But bank managers are obliged not only to manage well, but to do so from the highest ethical standards, of maximum integrity and professional probity. The Banco de Espa96a must ensure that these standards are respected. For this reason, and because it has to act with the objectivity and autonomy that I mentioned before, the Bank of Spain decided to investigate and open a sanctioning file, to determine and assess the facts and sanction them, where appropriate. The Bank of Spain initiated the investigation necessary to establish the facts in January 2001, as soon as the first information was obtained. Investigation contained in the report of the Inspection Services of 11 March 2002. On the occasion of the facts related in that report, and taking into account the analysis carried out by our Legal Service, the Executive Committee of the Banco de Espa96a, at its meeting of March 15 of this year, decided to initiate disciplinary proceedings against BBVA, to the 12 persons who had been members of the Permanent Executive Committee of the Board of Directors of BBV between March 15, 1997 and the date of the merger with Argentaria and 4 other senior officials of the bank related to the facts. Simultaneously, and in order to assess the possible criminal significance of some of the facts reflected in the aforementioned Inspection Report, mainly in the context of corporate crimes, the Executive Committee of the Bank of Spain requested BBVA to carry out as soon as possible, and within a maximum period of one month, an assessment of the danger or harm of such conduct, and proceed to communicate to the Bank of Spain its results with an indication of the actions of any kind that it deems appropriate to initiate and its term of execution, to which the entity replied on April 12, 2002, stating that the consideration of the possible criminal relevance of the facts has already been made by a judicial authority, therefore, it considers that the valuation request made by the Bank of Spain has become devoid of purpose. Subsequent to the opening by the Banco de Espa96a of the disciplinary proceedings, the Magistrate-Judge of the Central Court of Instruction No 5 of the National High Court requested the Banco de Espa96a to provide him with information on this matter, having proceeded to send the requested information and, as usual, to provide maximum cooperation. As a result of the analysis of the Report of the Inspection Services, on 9 April 2002 the Magistrate-Judge issued an order extending preliminary proceedings 161/00 in progress in that Court to the facts and possible offences that were being inspected, requiring that the sanctioning procedure initiated by the Banco de Espa96a be suspended. For your better understanding, I would like to highlight some of the characteristics of the facts investigated contained in the Inspection Report. They all relate to funds generated and held outside the bank's accounts through two structures: one in Liechtenstein and one in Jersey. The funds have their origin in obtaining profits in operations with securities carried out by third parties, without financing from the entity, and without, therefore, remaining in the bank's accounts any trace that would make it possible for the Inspection of the Bank of Spain to detect the existence of such facts. Given the parallel nature of this activity, the decisions on it and its management have apparently been made by a very small number of people, without any record of it having been found in any act or corporate document that could have been known by the Inspection of the Bank of Spain in its actions. Finally, I would like to emphasize that the very age of the facts, their opaque nature and their implementation in tax havens have made it very difficult to obtain information that allows the facts investigated to be reconstructed and accredited. Without pretending to make a complete and detailed description of the actions of the Bank of Spain, I think it would be clarifying to make a summary of them. The existence of extraordinary results amounting to ESP 37,343 million in BBVA's accounts for 2000 was communicated to me on 19 January 2001 at a meeting held with the two presidents of the bank. Faced with such an anomalous fact, we consider it necessary to open an investigation by the Inspectorate of the Bank of Spain, which immediately began its proceedings, holding a first meeting with BBVA, on February 1, 2001, the summary of which is annexed to the Inspection Report mentioned above. At the aforementioned meeting, the BBVA representation offered various explanations, without providing any documentation, and expressed the existing limitations to know the origin and evolution of the funds investigated, indicating that, in Spain, there was no documentation to support the operation carried out. As a result, the Banco de Espa96a requested the compilation of all existing information on this issue and its delivery to the Inspectorate, as soon as it was available. A month and a half later, BBVA's interlocutor handed over all the information he said he had been able to obtain. A period of analysis of that documentation then began, after which the Inspectorate concluded that the information received was insufficient to explain both the origin of the funds and the evolution of the operations that were intended to be known. For all the above, the Bank of Spain decided to commission the entity a report on the origin, evolution and cancellation of the funds belonging to it and that had been outside its accounting. To this end, after informing the presidents, the Chairman of the Control Committee of the Board of Directors of BBVA was summoned to a meeting, which took place at the Bank of Spain on June 7. At the meeting, which was attended by the Deputy Governor and the Director General of Supervision, the Chairman of the BBVA Control Committee was informed that the purpose of this meeting was to specify the terms of the required report and clarify any doubts that may exist about them. On the same day, a letter was sent to it indicating that the report should be finalized by 15 September 2001 at the latest and that, in addition to specifying the origin, evolution and cancellation of those funds, it should contain details of all payments made, clarify the extent to which those funds were used to finance own shares or those of group companies and specify which members of the Board of Directors and General Directors of the bank had been involved in this operation, or knew of its existence. It was also requested to expressly state whether, after the incorporation of funds mentioned, there was any balance belonging to BBVA outside its accounts. As an annex to the requested report, all the documentation that supports and justifies it should be included, documentation that would be made, together with the report, available to the Bank of Spain. By letter of 18 September, the Chairman of BBVA's Control Committee stated that, in accordance with the order received, a report had been drawn up which, together with the accompanying documentation, was available to the Banco de Espa96a. On September 20, the Chairman of BBVA's Control Committee held a meeting with the Deputy Governor and the Director General of Supervision of the Bank of Spain, in order to present the content of the aforementioned report. Following instructions from the Director General of Supervision, the inspectors went to BBVA's headquarters in Madrid on 24 September, where they collected the requested report, together with the attached documentation. This report, dated September 17 and without signature, consists of 24 pages and is complemented by three filing cabinets with documentation of different nature, all of them referenced in the report. On September 25, the Chairman of BBVA, Mr. Ybarra, and his 1st Vice President and CEO, Mr. Uriarte, held a meeting at the Bank of Spain with the Deputy Governor and me, in which we were informed that the 19.3 million that came out of Sharington's account in Jersey in March 2000, had been used to set up pension funds in the name of certain persons in American Life Insurance Company (ALICO), in case it was necessary to take a position in Bancomer. As this position was not finally necessary, the corresponding balances returned. After analyzing the report presented by BBVA and reviewing all the documentation provided, the Inspection concluded that the request made on June 7 by the Bank of Spain could not be considered completed, nor in relation to the justification of the origin and evolution of the funds that had originated the 37,343 million pesetas of extraordinary results, nor in determining which directors-general and members of the Board of Directors of the bank had been involved in this operation, or knew of its existence. As regards the other two questions raised in the letter from the Bank of Spain, with regard to the financing of own shares or group companies, it was stated literally in the report received that, after May 1992, no type of treasury stock operation had been carried out in respect of BBVA shares, or BBVA, other than those reflected at any time in the financial statements of said entities"; With regard to the possible existence of other balances outside the bank's accounts, the conclusions of the report literally state that "once the operation has been terminated on the date described by decision of the entity, from the same there is no type of equity, nor business that does not appear in BBVA's financial statements." As a result of all the above, the Executive Committee of the Bank of Spain was informed of the ongoing investigation, and it was decided to submit a proposal for a request to the entity. Thus, on October 19, 2001, the Executive Committee of the Banco de Espa96a requested BBVA to send the Bank of Spain clarifications and documentary support within 20 days on 13 specific points that were insufficiently documented in the report of September 17, 2001. In addition to requiring it to clarify these 13 points, BBVA was also asked to collect and provide the Bank of Spain with the necessary documentation to verify the operations carried out by one of the structures (Amelan Foundation) that existed outside the entity's accounts. Finally, in the aforementioned letter it was indicated that, in the event that any of the points indicated could not be adequately documented, the cause of that lack or impossibility should be explained. BBVA replied to the Bank of Spain by means of two letters dated November 14. The first, addressed to the Director General of Supervision, was sent by the Presidency of BBVA, signed by Mr Ybarra and Mr Gonz87lez, and was accompanied by seven annexes with supporting documentation. The second, addressed to me, was signed only by Mr. Ybarra and was accompanied by two annexes. In that second letter, Mr Ybarra stated that, in relation to the persons involved in the transaction with ALICO, an envelope containing the information requested was in his possession and at the disposal of the Banco de Espa96a. By letter of 5 December, it was asked to forward it to the Banco de Espa96a, which it did on the same day. On 27 December, the Director General of Supervision of the Banco de Espa96a sent a letter to Mr Gonz87lez, Chairman of BBVA, asking him to ask ALICO for confirmation of the list of persons who entered into a pension fund contract, indicating the amount corresponding to each of them. On 13 February 2002, the Banco de Espa96a received a reply to this request. After analyzing the available information, it was concluded that it was not sufficient to verify Amelan's operations, so on January 24, 2002, a letter was sent to the Chairman of BBVA, requesting that the entity obtain and validate the documentation that would allow it to know and prove the operations carried out by Amelan and order the aforementioned documentation. indicating the time you needed to complete the application, and justifying any limitations or problems that may exist. On February 19, 2002, BBVA received a response, stating that the time needed to sort and classify the archived documentation was estimated at about two months. On 10 April 2002, the Banco de Espa96a, in accordance with the letter received the previous day from the Central Court of Instruction No 5 of the National High Court, informed BBVA that that documentation should be sent directly to that court before 19 April. Collecting all the actions I have just mentioned, on March 11 the Report of the Inspection Services was signed that describes and evaluates these facts. Subsequently, once the sanctioning file has been opened, and in addition to the actions described at the beginning of this exhibition, we have sent the Report of the Inspection Services to the Tax Agency and the National Securities Market Commission. Once the suspension of the sanctioning administrative file has been agreed, the proceedings will not be resumed until there is a final sentence in criminal proceedings. Future of prudential supervision Having concluded this summary of the actions of the Bank of Spain regarding BBVA, I will end my speech with some reflections on the foreseeable evolution of banking supervision in the immediate future. What has happened at our borders and beyond requires rigorous analysis to draw conclusions that will help strengthen financial systems. As a starting point, I would like to say that banking supervision, as it was conceived a few years ago, is now insufficient in the face of the new characteristics that They present the financial systems: increasing integration and complexity, greater competition and a more varied and powerful interaction with the rest of the economy. It is therefore necessary to constantly update our prudential apparatus, if we do not want it to be outdated with the new realities. An important feature of this renewal process is that it cannot, and should not, be considered in isolation, but within the framework of the international coordination movement to which I referred earlier. Some problems, such as failures in the governance of entities or internal and external controls, go beyond the national level and require internationally valid solutions. This explains our growing presence in international supervisory forums, with the aim of actively participating in the definition and implementation of the best banking and supervisory criteria and practices. To face the changes I have just mentioned, which will undoubtedly accelerate in the future, we need prudential supervision with a more preventive and incentivizing approach, aimed at promoting the good management of institutions, at least in two ways: "A priori", promoting the quality and consistency of risk management systems, structures, techniques, procedures and culture; "a posteriori", devoting more resources to complement traditional monitoring with the evaluation of the above-mentioned qualitative aspects. Codes of good governance should be improved and strengthened through internal structures and procedures that facilitate controls by managers and supervisors; the creation and effective functioning of specialized committees, such as internal control and remuneration; the internal rules of operation of the board, which promote adequate information, and collegiate decisions; The importance of written minutes and references are examples of how internal structures and procedures can increase the effectiveness of good governance codes. I would like to remind you that this incentive approach is one of the essential features of the New Capital Deal that we are finalising in the Basel Committee and that it is based on three elements: sufficient own resources, supervisory action and market discipline. This is the orientation in which the Bank of Spain has been working in recent years and which is reflected in a methodology called Supervision of Banking Activity under the Risk Approach. In short, I believe that we must continue working to achieve an adequate combination of regulation, internal control of entities, supervision, international coordination and market discipline, leading to solvent banking systems that fulfill their function with a high degree of quality and service.
