Espaa comienza a participar en este proceso en el a 1999 como pas invitado al grupo de trabajo de riesgo de crdito, el grupo clave del Acuerdo, y se incorporplenamente al mismo a partir del momento en que fue seleccionado como miembro del Comit de Basilea (febrero de 2001). Desde julio de este a el Gobernador preside el Comit. La fecha establecida para el cierre del Acuerdo es diciembre de este a y a partir de ese punto se iniciar el proceso de implantaci de tres as de duraci que, dada la complejidad del Acuerdo, exigir un intenso trabajo a entidades y supervisores. En principio, la fecha de entrada en vigor del nuevo acuerdo es finales de 2006. ESTRUCTURA DEL ACUERDO: LOS TRES PILARES. Basilea II se estructura en torno a tres pilares. El Pilar 1 contempla los requisitos de capital mnimo para cubrir tres categoras de riesgos: riesgo de crdito, para el que se permiten tres enfoques, riesgo de mercado (que no sufre cambios respecto a la situaci actual) y se ade la cobertura del riesgo operacional. El Pilar 2 contiene la revisi de la adecuaci de capital por parte del supervisor y, finalmente, el Pilar 3 fomenta la disciplina de mercado a travs de la exigencia de una mayor transparencia informativa a las entidades.  Pilar 1: requerimientos de capital mnimo El numerador del ratio de capital; es decir, la definici del capital regulatorio, queda inalterado en relaci con Basilea I. El 8% mnimo tampoco cambia. Lo que cambia es la definici de los activos ponderados; es decir, el clculo de los riesgos en que incurren los bancos. Las novedades del Pilar 1 son los cambios sustanciales en el tratamiento del riesgo de crdito y el tratamiento explcito de riesgo operativo. En ambos casos hay tres posibles opciones, cada una de las cuales incrementa la sensibilidad al riesgo y la sofisticaci de los mtodos de medici para que cada banco escoja el ms adecuado. Para el riesgo de crdito, el ms importante desde el punto de vista prudencial, Basilea II plantea tres enfoques: enfoque estndar y enfoque de los modelos internos de rating (IRB) con dos variantes, enfoque bsico y enfoque avanzado. El enfoque estndar establece una mayor sensibilidad al riesgo mediante el uso de ratings externos (proporcionados por las agencias de calificaci autorizadas a tal efecto por los supervisores). Asimismo, establece, como en el Acuerdo anterior, carteras (soberanos, bancos, empresas no financieras y negocio minorista) con ponderaciones que dependen de los ratings externos y, tambin de la existencia o no de garantas hipotecarias. Adicionalmente, se mejora el tratamiento de las tcnicas de compensaci de riesgos (garantas, derivados de crdito, etc.). En el enfoque IRB, la diferencia fundamental es que el clculo de los requerimientos de capital se basa en la medici de los factores de riesgo (probabilidad de impago, prdida en caso de impago, exposicin en el momento del impago y vencimiento) proporcionados por la propia entidad y resultado de sus modelos internos utilizados para la medici y gesti de sus riesgos. No obstante, los bancos no determinan todos los elementos necesarios para el clculo de los recursos propios ya que las fmulas que relacionan los factores de riesgo con el nivel de capital las ofrecen los supervisores. Dichas fmulas trasladan los datos cuantitativos a requerimientos de capital. La diferencia entre los enfoques bsico y avanzado radica en el nero, mayor en el caso avanzado y menor en el bsico, de factores procedentes de la propia entidad que se utilizan para el clculo de sus recursos propios. Hay tambin un reconocimiento de las tcnicas de mitigaci de riesgos empleadas por las entidades y un tratamiento especfico para la titulizaci de activos. El riesgo operacional se define como la probabilidad de incurrir en prdidas por inadecuaci o fallos en los procesos internos, personal o sistemas o como resultado de acontecimientos externos. Se incluye el riesgo legal pero no el estratgico ni el de reputaci. Existen tambin tres alternativas para medir este riesgo: enfoque bsico, estndar y Avanzado. De nuevo la diferencia se basa en una mayor sofisticaci de los clculos y una creciente finura en la medici del riesgo. En el bsico y en el estndar, que se aplicar a los bancos con menores riesgos en esta rea, se les requiere mantener un nivel de capital directamente proporcional a una variable representativa de su volumen de negocio, dado que a mayor volumen mayor es la posibilidad de incurrir en dicho riesgo.  Pilar 2: Revisin supervisora La adecuaci de capital es algo que va ms all del cumplimiento de los requerimientos mnimos fijados en el Pilar 1. La complejidad y el rpido cambio de los mercados y los productos as como los cambios en la gesti del riesgo por parte de las entidades podran hacer que el Acuerdo, en el Pilar 1, se quedara atrasado respecto a lo que seran las mejores prcticas de control de riesgos. Por ello, es necesario reforzar el papel del supervisor (Pilar 2) con el fin de introducir las correcciones que se consideren necesarias. El Pilar 2 se basa en cuatro principios clave y otros elementos adicionales ms especficos. El Principio 1 establece que los bancos deben tener procedimientos para valorar su nivel de capital en relaci con su perfil de riesgos y una estrategia para mantener sus niveles de capital. El Principio 2 exige que los supervisores valoren la adecuaci del capital de las entidades y su capacidad para satisfacer los ratios mnimos de capital. El Principio 3 autoriza a los supervisores a imponer niveles de capital superiores al mnimo. Finalmente el Principio 4 indica que los supervisores deben intervenir rpidamente para impedir que el capital descienda por debajo del nivel apropiado al perfil de riesgo de cada entidad. En cuanto a los elementos especficos, el Pilar 2 puede destinarse a cubrir riesgos no cubiertos en el Pilar 1 y en particular, cuestiones relacionadas con las titulizaciones (transmisi efectiva o no del riesgo) y con el ciclo econmico (realizaci y comprobaci de los ejercicios de stress tests desarrollados por las entidades). Los reguladores/supervisores debern ofrecer opiniones explcitas de lo adecuado de los niveles de capital por encima del mnimo regulatorio del Pilar 1. Para ello tendrn que valorar de una manera proactiva las polticas de los bancos, la evoluci del capital econmico y el control de los riesgos por parte de la empresa. Todo ello implicar por parte de los supervisores un intenso esfuerzo para desarrollar capacidades tecnolicas, incrementar el personal, etc. Existe el riesgo que el supervisor ms sofisticado tienda a dar ms flexibilidad a sus entidades mientras que el menos preparado tender a ser ms conservador poniendo en desventaja competitiva a sus bancos. La soluci a esta cuesti se consigue a travs de la convergencia de las prcticas supervisoras, algo en lo que el Comit est ya trabajando, siguiendo la lnea de los desarrollos de otros comits en los timos aos.  Pilar 3: Disciplina de mercado Se trata de un complemento imprescindible de los dos pilares anteriores. Establece una serie de requerimientos que permiten a los participantes en los mercados valorar adecuadamente el perfil de riesgos de la entidad y su capitalizacin. La transparencia en este sentido es un componente equilibrador del mayor nfasis que pone el Acuerdo en metodologas internas que dan a los bancos un mayor grado de discrecionalidad en el clculo de sus necesidades de capital. La poltica de transparencia debe ser formalmente aprobada por el Consejo de Administraci. Se aplicar a nivel consolidado, pero los supervisores tendrn la capacidad para exigirla a un nivel de subconsolidaci. Deber suministrarse informaci detallada de los recursos propios y sus componentes, de la relaci entre capital y riesgos, de los riesgos. La publicaci de las cuentas financieras no es sustituto de ninguna de las exigencias anteriores. La frecuencia ser distinta segn la naturaleza de la informaci. 5. Caractersticas y naturaleza de las normas del Comit de Basilea Constituyen un marco de referencia para una supervisin bancaria efectiva que ayude a proteger la estabilidad de los sistemas financieros. Aunque las normas elaboradas abarcan muy distintos aspectos relacionados con el objetivo general mencionado, merece la pena citar aqu so las de carcter ms general: en primer lugar los 25 principios bsicos (core principles) que constituyen los requisitos para alcanzar una supervisi bancaria efectiva, en segundo lugar, el Acuerdo de Basilea de 1988, todava vigente y, finalmente, el Acuerdo de Basilea II que sustituye al anterior y que se ha explicado en el epgrafe anterior. El Comit de Supervisi Bancaria de Basilea es un organismo creado en 1974 para coordinar la supervisi de los bancos activos a nivel internacional. Est formado por representantes de los bancos centrales y de los supervisores (grupo de los 10, adems de Luxemburgo y Espaa desde enero del 2001). No es un organismo internacional ni tiene entidad jurdica propia. Sus recomendaciones no son normas internacionales aunque tienen extraordinaria influencia. Lo anterior quiere decir que el proceso de elaboraci del Acuerdo en el que el Comit est involucrado es de una naturaleza completamente distinta de la de los procesos nacionales de elaboraci de normas supervisoras. El Comit se ocupa de elaborar estndares internacionales e identificar las mejores prcticas para el desarrollo de una supervisi y regulaci efectiva, desde un punto de vista tcnico. Al margen de este proceso est la labor de los representantes parlamentarios que son los que libremente decidirn sobre las normas a aprobar. Quiere esto decir que el conjunto de normas que constituyen el Acuerdo no tienen fuerza legal hasta que las instancias parlamentarias hayan decidido sobre ellas en cada pas. Lo mismo ocurri por supuesto, con el Acuerdo hoy vigente de Basilea I, que se ha transformado en norma legal, en todo o en parte, en prcticamente todos los pases en base al prestigio de los miembros del Comit.  Proceso en la Unin Europea El inicio de la discusi del nuevo Acuerdo coincidicon la fecha en la que empezaron a darse los primeros pasos en la creacin del Mercado nico Europeo. Por ello, el tratamiento del tema se integren el Plan de Acci de los Servicios Financieros. A travs de los grupos de la Comisi en los que participan miembros y no miembros de Basilea, se est desarrollando el marco normativo europeo, que plantea la adaptaci del Acuerdo a las especificidades de la Uni (mayor presencia de PYMES en el tejido productivo europeo, bancos de tama muy distinto, etc.). De igual forma que en Basilea, ha existido un dilogo muy fluido con la industria. Como ocurre con las otras directivas, tambin sta debe aplicarse a todas las instituciones financieras (bancos y sociedades de inversi). La normativa no tiene por qu suponer un incremento de los requerimientos de capital. Existen incentivos para que las entidades locales no especializadas adopten el enfoque estndar, las peques especializadas adopten el IRB bsico y los grandes bancos internacionales operen con el avanzado. La cartera minorista marca la diferencia entre unas y otras entidades. La Directiva (que debera estar lista en el primer trimestre de 2004 y traspasarse a la normativa nacional antes de 2006) fija tambin un marco normativo adecuado para entidades pequeas y centradas en operativa con valores. La directiva incorporar algunos matices respecto a Basilea II: ms atenci a los crditos hipotecarios, tratamiento de cdulas hipotecarias y territoriales, tratamiento ms amplio de los elementos de mitigaci, mayor flexibilidad en el tratamiento del riesgo operativo en las ESIS. Su elaboraci est siguiendo ya el esquema Lamfalussy: nivel 1 y nivel 2, de carcter legal, aprobado por codecisi (Consejo y Parlamento), nivel 3, que no forma parte del derecho positivo (convergencia de prcticas supervisoras). El nivel 1 es el cuerpo de la directiva y contiene los principios bsicos de la regulaci y los elementos considerados esenciales desde el punto de vista de la seguridad jurdica. El nivel 2 se articula mediante anexos e incorpora las cuestiones tcnicas y otros aspectos que pueden necesitar cambios con flexibilidad. El nivel 3 busca la homogeneizaci en su aplicaci a los distintos temas a travs de la convergencia supervisora. Fuera de la Uni Europea existe tambin debate y se estn adoptando los pasos necesarios para la adaptaci a Basilea II. Concretamente, en estos momentos en Estados Unidos se est desarrollando un debate parlamentario de extraordinaria intensidad sobre Basilea II. El caso europeo es distinto y las normas que contiene el Acuerdo so estarn vigentes en los pases de la Uni cuando se cierre el proceso legislativo europeo que desembocar en una directiva de aplicaci en todos los pases, que podr seguir finalmente el Acuerdo o con toda probabilidad marcando diferencias. 6. Implantacin del nuevo Acuerdo El proceso de aplicaci del Acuerdo no ser en ningn caso un proceso automtico en el que las entidades libremente escojan el enfoque que ms les conviene. Al contrario, los requisitos para la utilizaci de los modelos internos (enfoque IRB) son muy exigentes. Se trata de requisitos tanto cuantitativos (datos para largos periodos de tiempo, exigencias determinadas a los sistemas de rating, etc.) como cualitativos. Entre estos timos destaca el que los modelos que se utilicen estn prcticamente integrados en la propia gestin de la entidad. La valoraci de riesgos no ser algo aislado de la gestin sino producto directo de la misma. No se autorizarn modelos desarrollados exclusivamente para el clculo de los recursos propios regulatorios. La aplicaci podr ser desigual entre pases y, dentro de un pas, entre bancos. En Estados Unidos, los supervisores han anunciado ya que solo exigirn Basilea II a unas 10 entidades, las ms sofisticadas y las que concentran la mayor parte de activos internacionales. En Europa, se aplicar a todos los bancos y a las sociedades de inversi, sin distinci de tama. Los supervisores debern decidir entre las opciones posibles. Basilea II est enfocado, en sus variantes avanzadas, a los bancos ms sofisticados y con presencia internacional. Tampoco es necesario pasar automticamente a Basilea II en 2006. Los pases emergentes que tengan muy reciente la implantaci de Basilea I pueden posponer el cambio actuando mientras tanto mediante la incorporaci a sus sistemas de elementos de los pilares 2 y 3. Esta flexibilidad y adaptabilidad del Acuerdo (que tiene como consecuencia una mayor complejidad) requiere prestar atenci especial a los problemas de consistencia transfronteriza, en particular, en el caso de bancos multinacionales sometidos a diferentes jurisdicciones. Existe un grupo de trabajo Grupo para la implantaci del Acuerdo (AIG) que, partiendo del hecho anterior, va a seguir con atenci la implantaci del Acuerdo, proporcionando un espacio en el que se analicen los problemas y se coordinen las respuestas a los inevitables problemas que plantear su implantaci. El grado de consistencia debe ser mantenido en base a la tarea de los supervisores. Los supervisores seguirn enmarcando su actividad y desarrollando sus responsabilidades en el marco selado por los core principles. La nueva situaci aconseja, no obstante, un refuerzo de los mismos, haciendo nfasis en el intercambio de informaci y coordinaci, as como en la elaboraci de planes prcticos. As, el AIG ha elaborado seis principios bsicos adicionales, que refuerzan los aspectos comentados: 1) El Acuerdo no cambia las responsabilidades. 2) El supervisor del pas de origen del banco (home supervisor en la jerga de Basilea) es responsable de la aplicaci del Acuerdo en base consolidada. 3) El supervisor del pas de acogida de la entidad (host supervisor), en el caso de filiales, tiene responsabilidades que deben considerarse 4) Incrementar el esfuerzo de cooperaci, liderado por el home. 5) Evitar las redundancias en la validaci y la aprobaci de los modelos. 6) Comunicaci lo ms clara posible, a las entidades, de los respectivos papeles. 7. Retos de Basilea  Retos para los bancos La literatura en torno al Acuerdo se centra con frecuencia en sus efectos sobre la medici de riesgos y la estabilidad financiera, pero Basilea tambin supondr uno de los ms grandes shocks estructurales de la industria bancaria en las timas dcadas ya que el nuevo Acuerdo influir sobre sus estrategias de negocio (consolidaciones, fusiones, nfasis en determinadas lneas de negocio, etc.). Adems, los bancos debern mejorar la medici, gesti y control de los riesgos. En cuanto a sus modelos internos debern estar a la altura de las exigencias tcnicas, de datos y cumplir con los requerimientos cuantitativos y cualitativos para su utilizaci. Al mismo tiempo, debern simultanear el nuevo acuerdo con el importante cambio en las normas contables desde 2005. Conviene insistir en que es un error tener una visi puramente mecanicista del nuevo Acuerdo. No basta con tener un sistema de rating interno bien diseado, es necesario tenerlo bien integrado en el proceso diario de gesti de riesgos. Adems, no basta con tener un volumen suficiente de recursos propios, tiene que haber una estrategia (permanencia de los mismos, capacidad de acceso al mercado, equilibrio entre remuneraci al accionista y capitalizacin, etc.) y una valoraci del nivel y composici del capital a medio y largo plazo.  Retos para los supervisores El primer reto es implantar Basilea II en 3 as, tarea nada fcil debido a la inevitable mayor complejidad que supondr Basilea II. En segundo lugar, hay que prepararse para cumplir con las exigencias del Pilar 2: valorar la adecuaci del capital al perfil de riesgo de cada entidad, lo que requerir un conocimiento detallado de los riesgos, incluida su evoluci a lo largo del ciclo econmico, la interacci entre los diferentes riesgos as como valorar la capacidad de los directivos de la entidad para gestionar y controlar dichos riesgos. El supervisor necesitar juzgar la cantidad y la calidad de los recursos propios de la entidad y entender, valorar y validar los modelos internos de riesgo de crdito y riesgo operacional. Dado que si el capital regulatorio obtenido a partir del Pilar 1 no le parece al supervisor adecuado al nivel de riesgo, ste puede exigir, a travs del Pilar 2, ms capital, aumenta la discrecionalidad del supervisor. Esta mayor discrecionalidad del supervisor obliga a una mayor transparencia hacia los supervisados y a un incremento en la convergencia de las prcticas supervisoras para evitar discriminaciones entre pases. El supervisor deber prestar mayor atenci a los elementos cualitativos. Sin dejar de inspeccionar la calidad de los activos y la rentabilidad de las entidades, deber evaluar la informaci suministrada por las entidades al plico, estudiar los principios de gesti del riesgo que aplica cada entidad, analizar sus mecanismos de gobierno corporativo y sus sistemas de informaci y control interno. A los anteriores retos, el supervisor debe adir tambin la interaccin de Basilea II con las nuevas normas contables. Para ello se ha abierto un dilogo permanente entre contables y supervisores bancarios. La entrada en vigor de las normas IAS en la Uni Europea en 2005 obligar a destinar una atenci preferente a la valoraci de activos y a las provisiones para riesgos ya que afectan a la definici del capital de las entidades. De hecho, el Comit de Basilea ha estado trabajando con el International Accountancy Standard Board (IASB) para asegurar la consistencia entre las obligaciones de informaci y cumplimiento de Basilea II con las normas contables (IAS). En este sentido las normas IAS ms importantes son la 32 y la 39, que tratan de la valoraci de los activos y pasivos financieros. Al igual que ocurre con el acuerdo de capital, las IAS tambin van mucho ms all de una alteraci de normas o circulares. Son autnticas innovaciones que afectarn no so a la transparencia, sino a las estrategias mismas de negocio. Aunque el Banco de Espaa como supervisor, con intereses legtimos sobre la contabilidad, continuar ejerciendo un papel activo en la configuraci de la normativa, es importante que las entidades asuman los cambios cualitativos que va a suponer. Impone a las entidades y a sus gestores una mayor responsabilidad al dar mayor flexibilidad. Ahora las normas contables limitaban la discrecionalidad. El mayor impacto provendr, sin duda, del cambio de enfoque. Cabra destacar, en primer lugar, la mayor amplitud interpretativa, principios abiertos con opciones de tratamiento contable. En segundo lugar, la informacin financiera plica ser mayor que la actual y con una clara orientaci hacia los inversores. La realizacin de provisiones requerir dosis ms fuertes de estimaciones frente al modelo actual que es muy mecnico. La utilizaci mayor del valor razonable (fair value) introducir una mayor sensibilidad en las cuentas y en el patrimonio como resultado de la evoluci de los mercados financieros. Conviene destacar, finalmente, que las normas contables interaccionan directamente con los 3 pilares de Basilea reforzando los efectos del Acuerdo: incrementarn la estandarizaci de la contabilidad y el desarrollo de las metodologas de valoracin que debern tener en cuenta el efecto de la volatilidad, tendrn que transmitir a las agencias el autntico sentido de la mayor volatilidad predecible aunque podran aumentar la ciclicidad, ayudarn a allanar los problemas legales con los derivados de crdito y harn ms fcil para los reguladores valorar si el riesgo est realmente transferido cuando se produzca la revisi supervisora de las titulizaciones. 8. Enfoque supervisor del Banco de Espaa Finalmente, me gustara concluir valorando, siquiera someramente, la situaci en la que se encuentra el Banco de Espaa de cara a Basilea II. La supervisi se ha desarrollado histicamente en 3 fases. En la primera, hasta la crisis bancaria de finales de los as 70 del siglo pasado, la supervisi se centraba en la revisi metica de un conjunto de normas que limitaban enormemente la actividad bancaria. La segunda fase, despus de la crisis mencionada, se basen una completa liberalizacin del sistema financiero y se empeza poner nfasis en aspectos cuantitativos. En la tercera etapa, la metodologa de supervisin del Banco de Espa se ha reorientado hacia los riesgos, su gesti y control. En esta tercera etapa, para hacer frente a los nuevos desafos de la supervisi, el banco ha desarrollado lo que denomina enfoque SABER (Supervisi de la Actividad Bancaria bajo el Enfoque Riesgo). Merece la pena recordar brevemente co funciona. En primer lugar, se cuantifica el nivel de riesgo inherente asumido por una entidad en las diferentes reas (se consideran, entre otros, el riesgo de crdito, de mercado, de tipo de inters). En segundo lugar, se pone en relacin dicho nivel con la calidad de los sistemas de control establecidos. De esta forma se obtiene el riesgo residual de la entidad. La comparaci entre dicho riesgo residual y la solvencia de la entidad (nivel y calidad de los recursos propios) es lo que determina el riesgo para el supervisor. Este esquema de supervisi enfocado al riesgo nos coloca plenamente en la lnea Basilea II. Adems del enfoque SABER, la existencia de la provisin estadstica establecida en el a 2000 y fundada en la utilizacin, con los debidos controles, de modelos internos para calcular las prdidas esperadas en el conjunto de operaciones de las entidades, nos ha permitido ganar en experiencia sobre los modelos internos de riesgo de crdito los timos as, incluso antes de que se cierre Basilea II. El hecho de haber estado trabajando durante los timos as en esos principios y conceptos facilitar sin duda nuestra adaptaci al nuevo esquema. En el mismo sentido act la existencia de la CIR y su explotaci para la construcci de modelos de referencia para la medici del riesgo con empresas. Basilea II ser, sin duda alguna, ms sensible al riesgo que Basilea I. Sin embargo, ser tambin ms complejo. Esta mayor complejidad obligar a una reorganizaci interna del supervisor que requerir la adecuaci de medios y personal a las nuevas tareas. Si somos capaces de completar est tarea con xito, habremos dado un gran paso a favor de la estabilidad del sistema financiero espal que redundar en beneficio de toda la sociedad.

Title: Conference "Perspective of the new regulatory framework and its impact on the financial system"
text: BANK OF SPAIN Seminar for Financial Markets Expansin -IBM MADRID, 17 SEPTEMBER 2003 PERSPECTIVE OF THE NEW REGULATORY FRAMEWORK AND ITS IMPACT ON THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM GONZALO GIL Deputy governor 1. INTRODUCTION The purpose of my intervention is to share with you some reflections that serve as a conceptual framework for the Seminar that will be developed on "Reference practices and latest trends in financial processes". There are currently two processes, in their last stages of preparation, which will mean, from their application, a change of great importance for all financial and non-financial companies. I am referring to Basel II and the adoption of the new international accounting standards. The latter will need another seminar session given their importance and the fact that they have been somewhat obscured by the parallel process of drafting the Capital Agreement. As you well know, the Basel Committee has been working intensively for quite some time, more than 4 years, to develop a new Capital Agreement, known as Basel II, which will replace the current Agreement dating from 1988 and which, according to reputable international publications, "It will be one of the most significant structural shocks to the banking industry in recent decades." This new agreement substantially modifies the solvency rules of credit institutions with regard to the most important risk they must assume in their normal activity: credit risk. In addition, it incorporates into the scheme an explicit treatment of operational risk, which is a risk that has given significant displeasure to a relatively high number of entities. Although the direct subject of this regulation are the banking entities, it interests and affects very directly all the economic sectors that need bank financing to carry out their activity. Large companies and SMEs looking for credits and loans to finance their projects, or individuals who need mortgage loans to access their home, and their credit card or personal loans, for their daily work. This banking activity therefore facilitates economic growth and the well-being of citizens, which is of interest both to economic policy managers and to companies, and of course to the banks themselves. Undoubtedly, when banks are adequately capitalized and well managed, they are better able to promote economic growth in countries through the financing of economic agents, and can help more effectively to promote sustained growth and, above all, more resilient to the materialization of the risks inherent in the economic cycle. Encouraging this better internal management of banking risks and greater bank capitalization has been the recurring objective of the Committee since the beginning of its work. 2. THE 1988 AGREEMENT It is worth asking why a Capital Agreement that establishes minimum regulatory capital requirements is necessary. The answer lies in a proper assessment of the importance of capital for the solvency of a credit institution. Capital is the last line of defense of the entity. When risk management is not sufficient, when the accounting provisions that would cover the expected losses have been consumed, then capital is the last hope of the entity. And when capital is extinguished, when it is not enough, the entity must close its doors. To put it more simply, capital is what allows you to deal with unexpected losses. The objective of Basel I was, on the one hand, to strengthen solvency after a period of rapid deregulation and liberalization of financial systems, which had led to a dangerous decline in capital, and, on the other, to level the competitive playing field of internationally active banks. Among the merits of the 1988 Agreement is its simple structure, which has contributed significantly to the harmonization of banking regulation between countries (more than 100 countries have acceded to the Agreement). At the same time, it has made a very important contribution to international financial stability through an increase in the capital ratios maintained by banks. However, despite its contributions, the Agreement was becoming outdated, owing to the new possibilities offered to banks by innovation in products and financial markets as well as the considerable improvement in risk management carried out by institutions since 1988 (more precise measurement of risk, better coverage, consideration of new risks, etc.). In addition, the linkage between capital requirements and the risk assumed by institutions was somewhat crude (for example, all exposures to non-financial corporations were required to have the same capital, without differentiating according to their credit quality) and perverse incentives were beginning to be produced leading to regulatory arbitrages in which capital reductions occurred without an effective reduction in the risks assumed. In short, the loss of meaning and the diminishing comparability of capital ratios raises the need to revise the old 1988 Agreement. This fact of non-differentiated treatment, in terms of capital requirements, according to quality, has ended up generating imbalances in the way in which companies have obtained financing. There is evidence that, in the current Agreement, capital requirements for transactions with the most solvent companies overestimate the risk of those companies. Therefore, this Agreement discourages bank financing of companies with higher credit quality. In fact, since these operations require the same capital as other entities, and the remuneration of capital is a component that is normally taken into account when determining the price, the interest rate that these companies can obtain in their bank financing is worse than the one they can obtain in the capital markets. where in fact its good credit quality is taken into account. In capital markets, external ratings are a crucial element in determining price. The opposite is true, logically, with companies of lower credit quality that may be better treated by banks than in capital markets, where their poor credit quality is taken into account. This has ended up causing companies with better credit quality to end up financing themselves off bank balance sheets, through direct access to the capital market. This situation is expected to change with the new solvency regulations, which are more sensitive to the risk assumed. The new Agreement takes into account the external credit rating of companies, in the standard method, or the internal rating generated by the banks themselves, in the IRB method. In this way, capital requirements are more sensitive to the quality of the borrower and, therefore, the previous distortion on the destination of bank financing flows is significantly reduced. It will be other reasons than the different perception of risk, which will end up determining the financing decision that companies finally take. 3. BASE II The objectives of the new Agreement continue to be to promote the solvency of banking systems and the promotion of competitive equality, as well as better hedging of risks and extending it to others not explicitly considered in the existing Agreement (in particular operational risk). Basel II seeks to link capital requirements much more closely to the risk incurred and become a stimulus for institutions to improve their risk management. All this framed in the so-called principle of neutrality of capital. This last principle simply wants to make it clear that the Committee is not seeking with the new Agreement to increase regulatory capital requirements, since it is satisfied with the capital that entities currently have, but to technically improve the Agreement so that entities have the capital they need to cover the risk they really assume. Ultimately, the agreement aims to reduce the potential costs of potential financial fragility for society. At the heart of the Agreement is the idea that it is necessary to extend the framework of the current Agreement, which has been clearly supported by industry. This idea has been reflected in the introduction of the so-called 3 pillars (capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline) and a set of methods offered to entities for the measurement of each of their risks, which gives the Agreement great flexibility compared to the current situation, as well as inevitable greater complexity. The 3 pillars have been introduced with an idea of complementarity since it is not prudent to rely only on the requirement of a minimum capital (pillar 1), given the increasing complexity of the institutions and their risks, but also the other two pillars of the Agreement. A second pillar that gives a fundamental role to supervisors, who must assess the capital held by each bank and its adequacy to the level of risks that the entity is assuming. The supervisor shall proactively assess risk policies and may impose above-minimum levels. And a third pillar to strengthen market discipline by increasing the information available to economic agents of key elements to understand the level of risk and capitalization of entities. This third pillar is a necessary complement to the previous two and is based on increasing transparency as a balancer of the greater emphasis that advanced risk assessment methods place on the use of internal valuations of the entities themselves. The elaboration of the new Agreement has been a complex process but open to the entities that have participated in the different calibration exercises carried out by the Basel Committee as well as through countless suggestions to improve the Agreement, many of which have been incorporated. The road has been long. The first concept paper is from June 1999. From then until now: 3 impact studies, 3 additional consultative documents, numerous working groups set up by the Committee, hundreds of meetings with representatives of banks, etc. After each consultative document, an extensive discussion process has been developed with more than 300 banks from around the world, including five Spanish banks, which have collaborated on the quantitative impact studies necessary to properly calibrate the required capital curves and, at the same time, ensure that the reform was consistent, with the aim of maintaining the level of own resources. Spain began to participate in this process in 1999 as a guest country to the credit risk working group, the key group of the Arrangement, and joined it fully from the moment it was selected as a member of the Basel Committee (February 2001). Since July of this year, the Governor has chaired the Committee. The date established for the closing of the Agreement is December of this year and from this point the process of implementation of 3 years of duration will begin, which, given the complexity of the Agreement, will require intense work from entities and supervisors. In principle, the date of entry into force of the Agreement is the end of 2006. It has therefore been a long but transparent process. It should come as no surprise that despite the fact that the objectives pursued are clear and shared with all, and the consensus on the necessary change of Basel I is practically unanimous, the process is so long. Several factors help explain the long time period. First, financial products are becoming increasingly complex and require complicated processes to measure their risk. They must be fully understood by bankers and supervisors. Secondly, the Committee intends (and the industry also demands) that the new Agreement can be applied to as many entities and countries as possible. There is no desire to renounce the fact that the Agreement remains a benchmark in the international market. For this reason, institutions can choose from a set of methods to assess their risks, which they can use depending on their level of sophistication. In fact, at the moment, the Agreement in its Pillar 1 provides for 3 methods, with different levels of complexity (increasingly incorporating internal valuations of the entities themselves) so that institutions can measure their credit risk and another 3 methods to do the same with operational risk. That is, greater coverage has been sought, different options have been contemplated, which inevitably leads to more complexity. Thirdly, the new Agreement, by wanting to be more sensitive to the risk actually assumed by the entities than the current Agreement, generates "winners" and "losers"; That is, there are entities that will need less regulatory capital than in the current situation, but there will also be entities to which the opposite happens, for example, because their portfolio has a higher level of risk. Obviously, these latter entities try to ensure that the new proposals harm them as little as possible, even if this implies a waiver, at least partially, of one of the basic objectives pursued by the Committee, that is, that the capital requirements are sensitive to the risk assumed. Finally, consultative processes and impact analyses that channel industry views are time-consuming. Analyzing the hundreds of comments received, trying to find a reasonable solution for all of them, as well as to carry out studies of the quantitative impact of the Committee's proposals, are processes carried out with extreme seriousness that have allowed the incorporation of very valid observations from the industry. 4. CHARACTERISTICS AND NATURE OF THE BASEL COMMITTEE RULES These constitute a framework for effective banking supervision that helps protect the stability of financial systems. Although the standards developed by the Committee cover many different aspects related to the general objective mentioned, it is worth mentioning here only those of a more general nature: first, the 25 core principles that constitute the requirements for achieving effective banking supervision; secondly, the Basel Accord of 1988, still in force and, finally, the Basel II Accord which replaces the previous one and which has been explained in the previous section. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is a body created in 1974 to coordinate the supervision of internationally active banks. It is made up of representatives of central banks and supervisors (group of 10, plus Luxembourg and Spain since January 2001). It is not an international organization nor does it have its own legal entity. Its recommendations are not international standards although they have extraordinary influence. This means that the process of drafting the Agreement in which the Committee is involved is of a completely different nature from that of national supervisory rule-making processes. The Committee is responsible for developing international standards and identifying best practices for the development of effective supervision and regulation, from a technical point of view. Apart from this process is the work of parliamentary representatives who are the ones who will freely decide on the rules to be approved. This means that the set of rules that constitute the Agreement do not have legal force until the parliamentary bodies have decided on them in each country. The same happened, of course, with the Basel I Agreement in force today, which has become a legal norm, in whole or in part, in practically all countries based on the prestige of the members of the Committee. 5. THE QIS3 IMPACT STUDY AND THE THIRD CONSULTATIVE DOCUMENT (COP3) This third impact study, which contains the data provided by the entities at the end of last year, has been the most complete and sophisticated of all and has allowed the Committee to refine the proposals included in the third consultative document. The results obtained in QIS3 are satisfactory and consistent with the objectives announced by the Committee. In other words, in general terms, the Committee's proposals generate regulatory capital requirements that, on average, remain at current levels and, in addition, there are certain incentives, in terms of lower capital requirements, for institutions to adopt more sophisticated methods to measure their risks. The third consultative document takes up many of the industry's requests in its responses to the second consultative process. Particularly relevant is the improvement in the treatment of SMEs and the inclusion of a complete treatment of operational risk and securitization. Undoubtedly, the treatment of loans to small and medium-sized enterprises has been one of the most relevant issues in Europe given that it is a basic sector for our economies. That is why I will dwell briefly on the treatment of these in the current draft. The proposals made by the Committee in its second consultative process generated significantly higher capital demands than the current ones and sparked a wide debate between regulators and industry. The Committee echoed the criticisms and carried out further studies which showed the need to take account of the greater diversification of this portfolio and therefore its lower relative risk. The new proposals basically consisted of the possibility of including SMEs in the retail portfolio, where there are lower regulatory capital requirements, and reducing the slope of the capital curve that must be applied to all companies, introducing a size adjustment for those companies with a size of less than 50 million euros. In addition, the basic IRB approach introduces greater recognition of collateral typically used by this sector such as bill and bill discounting and physical collateral. It seems that these changes have been welcomed by the industry. It is also worth saying a few words about the portfolio of shareholdings, which is important for many Spanish entities, and to which the new rules impose higher capital requirements than the current ones, which has been one of the criticisms of the new project included in CP3. However, it must be noted that this treatment is necessary because the current standards, in their simplicity, do not adequately assess this risk. In addition, a smooth transition is foreseen, so that all equity investments existing at the date of approval of the new Agreement will have a transitional period of 10 years during which they can continue to apply the rules currently existing. 6. CURRENT SITUATION Approaching the end of my speech, I would like to comment briefly on where we stand today. As you know, the third consultative period ended on 31 July. A very large number of comments have been received and are available on the BIS website, demonstrating once again the great desire for transparency with which the Committee has conducted this whole process. Most of the comments not only highlight that the overall objectives of the new Agreement are shared, but also accept that there has been a substantial improvement in the proposals since the previous consultative process, further recognising that the new Agreement represents a major step forward in solvency regulation. However, it should not be ignored that there have been a large number of observations on particular elements of the proposals, which have to be analyzed and to which an adequate response must be given. Some of these criticisms are of a general nature and, as I have already anticipated, are difficult to solve. They refer to the complexity and conservatism of the proposals, as well as the need to promote competitive equality. Undoubtedly, the new Agreement is more complex than the current one, but this greater complexity is the result both of the Committee's desire to offer an adaptable scheme to entities with different degrees of sophistication (Basel I offered homogenization and Basel II offers differentiation) and of the requests of the industry itself that has always wanted to take into account the specific complexities of its businesses and that capital requirements are more sensitive to risk. 7. IMPLEMENTATION OF THE NEW AGREEMENT The process of implementing the Agreement shall in no case be an automatic process in which entities freely choose the approach that suits them best. On the contrary, the requirements for the use of internal models (IRB approach) are very demanding. These are both quantitative (data for long periods of time, requirements determined to rating systems, etc.) and qualitative. Among these last highlights the fact that the models used are practically integrated into the management of the entity itself. The assessment of risks will not be something isolated from the management but a direct product of it. Models developed exclusively for the calculation of regulatory own resources shall not be authorised. The Agreement is based on national discretion that requires cross-border consistency. Application may be uneven between countries and, within a country, between banks. In the United States, supervisors have already announced that they will only require Basel II from about 10 entities, the most sophisticated and those that concentrate the largest part of international assets. In Europe, it will apply to all banks and investment companies, regardless of size. Supervisors will have to decide between possible options. Basel II is focused, in its advanced variants, on the most sophisticated banks with an international presence. There is also no need to automatically move to Basel II in 2006. Emerging countries that are very recent to implement Basel I can postpone change by acting in the meantime by incorporating pillar 2 and 3 elements into their systems. This flexibility and adaptability of the Agreement (which results in greater complexity) requires particular attention to cross-border consistency issues, in particular for multinational banks in different jurisdictions. There is a working group, the Group for the Implementation of the Agreement (AIG), which, based on the above fact, will follow closely the implementation of the Agreement, providing a space in which the problems are analyzed and the responses to them are coordinated. The degree of consistency should be maintained based on the task of supervisors. Supervisors will continue to carry out their activity and responsibilities within the framework established by the core principles. The new situation suggests, however, a reinforcement of them, emphasizing the exchange of information and coordination, as well as the elaboration of practical plans. Thus, the AIG has developed and published six additional basic principles, which reinforce the aspects discussed: 1) The Agreement does not change responsibilities. 2) The home country supervisor of the bank (home supervisor in Basel jargon) is responsible for the implementation of the Agreement on a consolidated basis. 3) The supervisor of the host country of the institution (host supervisor), in the case of subsidiaries, has responsibilities that must be considered. 4) Increase the cooperative effort, led by the home. 5) Avoid redundancies in the validation and approval of models. 6) Communication as clearly as possible, to the entities, of the respective roles. On the other hand, but in clear connection with the above, the Committee is working on greater cooperation with the supervisors of non-Committee countries, since although the entities on which the new Agreement focuses and which, in principle, would be affected by the reform are still internationally active banks, the Committee hopes that the new Agreement will remain an international benchmark for solvency. 8. MORE SPECIFIC MATTERS Apart from these criticisms affecting the general nature of the Agreement, I would like to highlight some more specific technical issues that have emerged in the consultation process and that are currently being analysed by the various working groups involved in the reform of the Agreement. Regarding the criticism of the calibration of the Agreement, some banks continue to believe that the current proposals do not provide them with the appropriate incentives to move to the most sophisticated calculation methods, and others have again expressed their disagreement with the IRB commitment solution to cover both expected and unexpected losses with capital and argue that only unexpected losses should be covered by capital. The issue of double default in risk mitigation techniques has also been raised. In the risk mitigation rules contained in CP3, a loan with a guarantee is weighted by the guarantor (substitution treatment). The industry has considered this treatment very conservative, since it does not take into account the fact that for this loan to be unpaid, the default of both the obligor and the guarantor must occur simultaneously. However, while the reduction in the probability of default is theoretically clear, its practical application is hampered by the non-availability of data on correlations between guarantors and obligors. There are also concrete proposals to modify the treatment of operational risk, of which very few argue that the correct treatment of this risk must be given in pillar 1, that is, with explicit capital requirements. Finally, I will highlight the many comments from the industry on the treatment of securitization. They criticize the great conservatism of the current proposals and their great complexity and difficulty of interpretation, which has led to the proposal of a simplification in the treatment that would affect several of the basic aspects of the treatment of securitization in the new Agreement, such as the weightings of the method based on external ratings (RBA) or the supervisory formula. All these comments made by the industry will be analyzed and some of them are very likely to generate changes in the proposals, given the considerable interest in achieving the best possible capital agreement in a period of time, which should already be reasonably short. Although there is concern that the estimated deadlines for the finalization of the Agreement (end of this year) are too narrow, which could jeopardize the quality of the Agreement, it is important to finalize this phase of discussions and proposals and open the way to the effective implementation of the Agreement. However, in my opinion, the credibility of the new Agreement and its success certainly does not depend so much on strict compliance with certain commitments in terms of dates, but will have to be measured by taking into account the improvements that it may have made in the internal management that institutions make of their risks and by the achievement of a greater strength of the global financial system that makes it more resistant to economic crisis situations. In conclusion, we have before us a new Capital Agreement which has been the product of several years of hard work and which, in my opinion, will be very positive in improving the strength and soundness of credit institutions and the economic system in general. However, it should be remembered that this Agreement is just one more step in the attempt to bring regulatory capital as close as possible to the risks actually assumed by the entities. It is important to be aware that there are certain additional issues that have not been considered appropriate to include in the current proposals but that will be studied in the next steps that the Committee intends to progressively improve the solvency regulations of credit institutions. These additional issues include, for example, the possibility of fully recognising the effects of diversification and concentration of portfolios or the need to seek to harmonise solvency rules with the accounting treatment of provisions. Additional steps will continue to be taken but do not doubt that the chosen line is the correct one.

Basilea II busca vincular mucho ms estrechamente los requerimientos de capital al riesgo incurrido y convertirse en un estmulo para que las entidades mejoren la gestin de sus riesgos. Todo ello enmarcado en el llamado principio de neutralidad del capital.
