Title: The European economy at the crossroads. Speech at the III Annual Conference on Economic Policy, Business, and Society of the Crculo de Empresarios. Madrid.
text: Madrid, 25 November 2003 The European economy at a crossroads* II Annual Conference on Economic Policy, Enterprise and Society C92rculo de Empresarios Jose Vials Director General of International Affairs of the Bank of Spain * The judgments and opinions expressed in the text are exclusively of a personal nature Ladies and Gentlemen: It is an honour for me to have been invited to address such a distinguished audience on the occasion of the Third Annual Conference on "Economic Policy, Business and Society" of the C92rculo de Empresarios. Therefore, my gratitude to all of you, to the Board of Directors of the C92rculo and, in particular, to its President, Manuel Azpilicueta, and its Secretary General, Vicente Boceta. Undoubtedly, the full integration of Spain into the European Union and, moreover, our affiliation to the euro area enter into strong and deep economic, financial and monetary links between our country and the rest of the member states that make the European economy an indispensable reference for the progress of the Spanish economy. It is therefore not surprising that the conferences given in the same way as this one in the last two years have dealt with the construction of the European monetary union, in one case, and with the margins for manoeuvre of Spanish macroeconomic policy in the euro zone, in the other. The title I have chosen d0 'The European economy at the crossroads' d0 seeks to emphasise that Europe is currently at a difficult but decisive economic moment resulting from the confluence of two factors. On the one hand, the manifest inability of all EU economies to grow at a satisfactory pace, not only during these last years of marked international economic slowdown but, what is much more worrying, over the last decades. On the other hand, the formidable challenge of successfully completing the imminent enlargement of the European Union to absorb ten new members in May next year and two more in 2007, in an environment in which globalisation, technological change and unfavourable demographic dynamics will exert an additional pressure on the so-called "European economic and social model"; This model emphasizes preserving not only macroeconomic stability but also d0 and this is its main distinguishing feature compared to the North American model d0 an adequate degree of economic and social cohesion, through the existing social protection networks at both national and community level. Growth, stability and cohesion would therefore be the three aspects that, with greater or lesser fortune as I will explain later, the European model tries to conjugate. In the course of my speech, Europe's economic future depends decisively on whether it emerges from the current crossroads and, in particular, how it faces the challenges mentioned in the coming years. I shall therefore devote the first part of my presentation to examining European economic developments from a medium-term perspective, with a view to identifying, beyond the ups and downs of the current economic situation, the underlying problems facing the European economy, and then analysing what their causes are and exploring what consequences could arise from the persistence of these problems within an enlarged Europe. Finally, I would like to make some reflections on the steps that, in my opinion, could be taken to restore the strength of the European economy on a lasting basis so that its greater capacity for growth translates into sustained improvements in the living standards and well-being of citizens and into a greater weight of Europe in the international context. Institutional developments and economic developments When one examines the evolution of the EU over the last two decades, there is no doubt that it has achieved institutional successes of enormous importance in welcoming new members into its midst in successive enlargements while witnessing the creation of the Single Market in 1993 and, most recently, from the Monetary Union in 1999. And today, as the euro area countries mark the fifth anniversary by sharing the same monetary policy, the institutional vitality of the integration process is manifested in the imminent enlargement of the European Union to welcome new members from Central and Eastern Europe and in the preparation of the European Constitution. However, this succession of first-rate institutional developments contrasts with the widespread perception that things are not working so well as far as the European economy is concerned. Thus, in recent years, the countries of the area have gone through a phase of notable economic slowdown in an extremely adverse international environment fostered, mainly, by the crisis in the computer and communications sector that was associated with the bursting of the technological bubble, by the successive shocks of confidence triggered by the terrorist attacks of September 11 and increased, later, because of the scandals in some large companies and, recently, because of the geopolitical uncertainties derived from the situation in Iraq and, in general, in the Middle East. The difficult situation that the economies of the European Union have gone through in recent years has been reflected, in most cases, in a notable decline in their rates of activity that has led to recession in several countries, including Germany, the main economy in the area. All this, in turn, has made it particularly difficult in some cases to comply with the rules on budgetary discipline laid down in the Stability and Growth Pact, which has given rise to a lively debate on the appropriateness of maintaining or amending some of the central elements of that pact. However, it would be wrong to conclude that the current difficulties in the European economy are only cyclical or, moreover, mainly due to a particularly adverse international environment. On the contrary, the difficulties that have become apparent in recent years are palpably due to the persistence of certain fundamental problems which the European Union has been suffering internally for some time and whose most negative consequences tend to emerge in less favourable circumstances. Hence, instead of being content to wait for the international economic recovery currently under way to restore normality to the European economic situation, it is particularly urgent to confront these problems decisively and courageously with determination. Growth, stability and cohesion The idea that the difficulties of the European economy have a deep root that goes far beyond the temporal limits of the current conjuncture is corroborated by looking at the trajectory of European economic growth during the last decades. A benchmark of average growth over the last four decades shows that the EU has seen a gradual but inexorable decline in its capacity to grow. Thus, while the average annual growth was 4.8% in the sixties, this figure fell to 3% in the seventies, to 2.4% in the eighties and to 2.1% in the nineties and, currently, is less than 1%. This fact, which clearly reveals the increasing difficulties that the EU has been encountering in growing at a sustained high pace, is particularly worrying for several reasons. On the one hand, because the progressive weakness of growth over this long period has coincided with the realization of intense progress in the European integration process, which was expected to result in substantial efficiency gains in the processes of allocation of resources and, ultimately, in a greater growth potential of the European area. On the other hand, because the EU's economic trajectory has not only been frustrating in relation to the golden sixties and the expectations raised around the integration process, but also in comparison with the United States, the other major world economic area. Thus, although the US economy has also experienced a reduction in its growth rate in the last three decades in relation to the sixties, however, in these thirty years it has grown annually by 3.4%, on average, which is almost one point above the 2.5% registered in the EU. But, although this is disturbing from the European perspective, it is even more so that the growth differential between the EU and the United States has become increasingly unfavourable for Europe over time, since, compared to the gradual decline observed in the European case, the American economy has not maintained growth rates of 3.3% and 3.2% respectively in the seventies and eighties. but, thanks to the intense technological changes that occurred in the second half of the nineties, it has managed to raise its rate of progress to 3.6% in the last decade. Acknowledging the obvious difficulties that the EU has been facing in growing in the medium term is essential to understand the magnitude of the problems that arise when, as has been happening in recent years, the economic cycle enters the contractionary phase. It is precisely the fact of moving from average growth rates, already modest, to smaller ones that magnifies the adverse consequences of the cyclical worsening. However, the above analysis, based on growth, would be insufficient and, to some extent, also unfair to the EU if it were not completed by an examination of the other two vertices of the triangle that, together with growth, make up the European model; namely, macroeconomic stability and economic and social cohesion. If we understand stability in its most commonly accepted sense, such as maintaining low inflation rates and sound public finances, the EU has made significant progress on both fronts over the past few decades. Thus, from an average annual inflation rate in the seventies to more than 10% in the EU as a whole, it has gone to rates slightly below 7% in the eighties, 3% in the nineties and around 2% today. At the same time, the last decade has reversed the trend towards deterioration of public accounts evidenced in previous periods, which d0 despite the most recent difficulties encountered in some countries d0 has contributed very favourably to the process of deficit reduction and to improving the sustainability of public debt. Undoubtedly, the sharp reduction in inflation and public deficits that took place mainly in the nineties was due to the macroeconomic stability policies implemented by the Member States in order to meet the convergence criteria established in the Maastricht Treaty for accession to the Monetary Union; stability policies which have sought to consolidate through the technical monetary policy and the Stability and Growth Pact. In the area of cohesion too, considerable progress has been made in the past. The importance attached within the EU to economic and social cohesion reflects the preferences of European citizens and is expressed at both national and Community level. In the first case, through social protection networks and policies aimed at improving the distribution of income and wealth; and, in the second, through Community funds designed to reduce differences in per capita income between Member States and between regions. Regardless of the variables chosen to approximate how cohesion has evolved within the EU, the fact is that, in the last three decades, the distances separating the least prosperous countries from the rest in terms of per capita income have been narrowing while various synthetic indicators of the degree of inequality between countries have improved. overall, despite successive enlargements of the EU over the years. Therefore, from the analysis carried out so far, it can be concluded that over the last thirty years, during which the EU has made considerable institutional progress in the integration process, its economic trajectory has been characterized by lights and shadows. Lights, which correspond to improvements in the areas of macroeconomic stability and cohesion; and shadows, emanating from the prolonged decline in European growth. Nature and causes of the European growth problem Since the problem of growth is the most worrying feature of European economic developments, I shall now examine the reasons which may have contributed most decisively to this. In particular, I will focus on the role of macroeconomic stability policies, cohesion and other factors. A debate has now raged in Europe about whether stability policies could be responsible, to a greater or lesser extent, for the EU's persistent difficulties in maintaining sustained growth at higher rates. Undoubtedly, this debate is sparked by the unfavourable European economic situation in recent years, which has led to criticism from some quarters of the institutional and strategic framework governing European macroeconomic policy and, in particular, monetary policy and fiscal policies. This has also been helped by the suspicion on the part of some whether the progress made by the EU in the area of stability following the Maastricht convergence process would not have diminished its capacity for growth. However, I believe that, without going into depth to discuss whether any specific aspect of the mechanisms that govern these policies in practice should be reconsidered, it can be said that the above position is wrong. On the one hand, according to economic principles and experience confirms, macroeconomic stability is essential to achieve and maintain a satisfactory growth rate in a sustained manner, while recognizing that, in certain cases, the adjustment policies needed to achieve such stability in advance may have a negative impact on activity in the short term. On the other hand, blaming stability policies for the critical weakness of European growth is inconsistent with the fact that stability weakness is a medium-term phenomenon that has been observed decade after decade, long before macroeconomic stability policies were put in place in the nineties. And, finally, if we compare what happened in Europe with the United States, it turns out that in the latter country similar progress has also been made to the European countries in achieving a high degree of stability but, as I have explained earlier, with a very satisfactory performance of growth. As far as cohesion is concerned, the key question is whether the concrete way in which cohesion is articulated within the European model may have had a negative impact on growth. In this regard, it must be recognized that ensuring a reasonable degree of economic and social cohesion has been essential in the past to advance the integration process and will continue to be so in the future. However, there is ample evidence to suggest that the design of cohesion policies, both at Community and national levels, has not sufficiently taken into account that some of their elements could have a particularly adverse impact on efficiency and growth. At Community level, there is empirical evidence that agricultural and regional funds would have limited, in many cases, the natural processes of reallocation of resources resulting from the establishment of the Single Market, which would have prevented the potential efficiency gains that it entails by preventing factors of production from shifting to more productive sectors or activities. At the national level, on the other hand, the adverse effects on efficiency and growth would have been the unintended result of social and tax measures that would have had a negative impact, for example, on the degree of flexibility of wage structures, on labour mobility and on the incentives of agents to save, invest or produce. Cohesin is d0 and must remain d0 a basic element of the European model and this is established both in the current treaties and in the draft of the future European Constitution. However, we cannot close our eyes to the prospect that, if Europe fails to return to higher economic growth rates on a sustained basis, it will be increasingly difficult to finance cohesion, jeopardising the survival of the European model. Furthermore, it seems unavoidable to review some of the basic elements of national and Community cohesion policies in order to make them as complementary as possible with an efficient allocation of resources and, ultimately, with the growth process. But it is not the design of cohesion policies that is solely responsible for the weakness of European growth in the medium and long term. According to numerous analyses, other serious supply problems would also have contributed to slowing down the increase in total factor productivity, the rate of accumulation of human, physical and technological capital and job creation. These problems, in turn, would be rooted in an extremely complex and far from effective and insufficiently oriented economic governance model for the EU towards economic growth. It is clear that, if one distinguishes the trajectory followed by European countries over time, very notable differences in their growth rates are highlighted, as It happens, for example, if we compare Ireland or Spain d0 to name several of the most dynamic d0 with Germany or France, which are the largest economies in the area, but are among the least dynamic. This disaggregation also serves to confirm that it is precisely the countries that have most decisively and promptly introduced the necessary reforms in their product and factor markets that have achieved the best results in terms of growth. The comparison between the European case and that of the United States may, once again, be useful for a better understanding of the nature of our problems. Thus, if GDP growth is broken down into productivity gains (per hour worked) and job creation (hours worked) it can be clearly seen that during the last three decades, the differential factor that explains the higher growth of the United States in relation to Europe is job creation, while the rates of increase in productivity are very similar and, on the whole, slightly favourable to the EU. It should come as no surprise, however, that our productivity has grown more rapidly, given that it was significantly lower than in the United States. What is frustrating is that their current level is almost ten percent below that of the US economy and that, in recent years, the gap between the two has widened again. At the same time, given the high unemployment rate in the European economy, it is disheartening that hardly any jobs have been created. However, the experience is that, in the European case, when job creation intensifies d0 even modestly d0 the counterpart is a slowdown in the rate of productivity growth and vice versa. Thus, for example, as the EU has increased its average annual rate of job creation from -0.5% in the seventies, to 0% in the eighties and to a very meagre 0.3% in the nineties, the rate of average annual increase in productivity has fallen significantly, respectively in each of these periods. 3.5%, 2.4% and 1.8% and at lower rates at present. This experience contrasts markedly with that of the United States, which has seen its annual rate of job creation remain very close to 2% in each of the same periods while its annual productivity increased from 1.4% to 1.7%, being currently clearly higher than these figures. As a result, the US economy has been able to improve its productivity while maintaining considerably higher rates of job creation, which has doubly favoured the growth process. The European experience, on the other hand, highlights the serious difficulties encountered so far in improving in one direction without worsening in the other, which is a formidable brake on the capacity for growth. But what are the roots of Europe's growth problem? According to the most recent research on this question, although it is not easy to unravel the Last causes that govern the processes of growth, it can be concluded that having an appropriate economic environment, fully respectful of the incentives of the agents and that facilitates productive dynamism in a framework of efficient allocation of resources, is essential. In particular, according to modern theories of endemic growth, the processes of technological innovation and the continuous adaptation of organizational structures to the demands of a changing environment are a very important force whose contribution to growth is decisive. However, reality shows that the transition from a traditional economic system, based on large-scale production within the framework of stable and protected markets and inflexible industrial relations, to what is currently regarded as a modern economic system has not been completed throughout the EU. This system is characterized by the importance of technological innovation processes to survive in a world characterized by globalization and external competition, which makes it necessary to adopt new organizational forms, promote research and development, improve the quality of education, establish regulatory frameworks that encourage the free entry of companies and competition in the markets for goods and services, improve the degree of flexibility of wage structures and functional, geographical and sectoral mobility in labour markets, have better tax structures and, finally, sufficiently flexible and diversified sources of financing in integrated financial markets at European level. All these supply-side dynamising elements, which are present in the United States, suffer from a very insufficient degree of development in the EU as a result of the fact that economic growth has not been, so far, the main priority of European economic policies, both at national level d0 in most cases d0 and at Community level. This concern is what inspires the so-called "Lisbon strategy", through which EU governments agreed to relaunch Europe's growth capacity on the basis of three basic elements: completing the Single Market; promoting the information, research and development society; and modernising the European social model. However, given the appropriate aims and given the short time spent with this framework, the poor results achieved since the adoption of the "Lisbon strategy" in 2000 make it seriously doubtful whether the ultimate objectives can finally be achieved with the shortcomings of the current European economic system and the absence of sufficiently powerful mechanisms to improve it. In this respect, my opinion is that, as long as the EU equips itself with a very Effective in encouraging Member States to adopt macroeconomic stability policies, the Lisbon process does not seem to have, for the time being, sufficiently effective reward and penalisation mechanisms to favour the implementation of the micro-economic policies required to boost Europe's capacity for growth. Consequently, it can be argued that the weakness of microeconomic policies, closely linked to the low presence of structural reforms, is what is at the root of the serious supply shortfalls suffered by the EU economic system and which have such serious consequences on its growth potential. It should not be forgotten, however, that this situation is also influenced by the complexity of the Community's economic governance system and by the different assignment of responsibilities between national and European decision-making areas. This has led to a state of affairs that can clearly be improved, since the current coordination mechanisms between the aforementioned decision-making areas do not seem to guarantee coherence and effectiveness in terms of their joint impact on growth capacity. Hence, the need, not only to promote micro-economic policies but also to improve the quality of EU economic governance. Future challenges The EU's poor balance sheet in terms of growth poses a serious threat to the future living standards of European citizens, while, as I mentioned earlier, it puts the European model in check. On the one hand, the low rates of growth, if it continues in the future, necessarily imply a slow progression of per capita income in the area; and, on the other hand, since maintaining cohesion requires sufficient growth rates to finance social safety nets, the absence of economic dynamism could put too much pressure on public accounts in the future, thus making cohesion increasingly difficult to finance and calling into question macroeconomic stability, This would seriously threaten the survival of the European model. This problem is all the more important in view of the increasing demands that this model will have to bear in the coming years as a result of the new needs for health expenditure and pensions associated with the ageing of Europe's population. But it is also necessary to consider that globalisation and, in particular, strong international competition make it necessary for the countries of the Union to improve their competitiveness and move up a few steps in the technological ladder, so as not to be subjected to the problems that higher unemployment and its adverse repercussions on public accounts would entail. However, in the immediate term, the most important challenge facing the EU is to ensure the success of the accession of ten new members in May next year and another two in 2007. Enlargement to include the countries of Central and Eastern Europe is a political event of extraordinary importance, since it means bringing together again in a framework of democracy and respect for freedoms the majority of the members of the great European family, separated and confronted for half a century as a result of the Second World War. At the economic level, enlargement is an opportunity but also a formidable challenge since, although it is true that the new Member States together account for just over 5% of the GDP of the current EU, their population is equivalent to almost a third and, what is more worrying, their average per capita income is not even half that of the current EU. although there are considerable differences between the situation of the two countries of Central and Eastern Europe. Since enlargement means increasing the Single Market and given the greater economic dynamism of the new members, which are engaged in processes of structural reform and real convergence, it is to be hoped that their entry will contribute favourably, to some extent, to the overall dynamism of the EU. However, Europe faces the challenge of fully integrating d0 and not just de jure d0 the economies of these countries and facilitating the approximation of their low levels of per capita income to those prevailing in the EU as a whole through European cohesion policies, always counting on the new member states to continue to improve the efficiency of their economies and to make progress towards macroeconomic stability. You will agree with me that an enlarged Europe, which starts from such substantial differences in per capita income between the current and the new Member States and where the Community funds necessary to facilitate the integration of more than one hundred million people into a new reality must be raised more than ever, it is necessary to carry out the reforms that will make it possible to boost European growth. On the other hand, the economic governance of an EU of 25 27 countries, instead of the current 15, acquires a very remarkable degree of institutional complexity that is all the more so if one takes into account the considerable economic and social heterogeneity among its members. Hence, the response to the challenge of enlargement must also have mechanisms that guarantee the efficiency of the decision-making processes of such a large, complex and diverse structure. The preparatory tasks for the European Constitution must be devoted to solving the institutional problems I have just mentioned, in their most general form. How to face the challenges? Having reached this point, I would like to make some reflections below on what ways could be explored to meet the dual challenge currently facing the countries of the European Union: on the one hand, to ensure the sustainability of the European model and, on the other, to ensure the success of enlargement, in order to meet the legitimate aspirations of European citizens to enjoy higher standards of living and well-being in the future. From my analysis of the three vertices of the European model d0 growth, stability and cohesiveness d0 several conclusions emerge. First, that maintaining macroeconomic stability is an extremely valuable asset in itself and essential as a frame of reference for growth; secondly, that preserving cohesion necessarily requires a modernisation of cohesion, so that this is consistent with the incentives for operators to work, invest and produce in a more demanding economic environment; and finally, that boosting growth capacity requires very important structural reforms both at national level and in Community policies, while improving the quality of European economic governance. In other words, what is needed is for the EU's economic system to be genuinely d0 and not just nominally d0 oriented towards the objective of boosting growth within a framework of high macroeconomic stability and a reasonable degree of cohesion, since growth is the cornerstone on which the European economic and social model is based. But this implies very considerable changes, both in economic policies and in European governance methods, so that the action of the national and Community authorities is generally consistent with these objectives. As regards policies to promote growth, the role of national authorities is crucial. The continuity of reform processes in the various countries is key to improving the functioning of goods and services markets and labour markets; to ensure the future solvency of public pension systems; to promote and encourage innovation, research and development processes; and to raise the quality of education. In this respect, the future course of events in Germany and France is of the utmost importance because, if reforms in these countries finally make decisive progress, their economic and political impact will be very healthy, not only for their own economies, but for the EU as a whole, given their considerable specific weight and the favourable impact this would have on further deepening reforms in other countries. In line with policies at European level, it is essential to complete the single market and make it more dynamic and competitive. This is very important for services and, in particular, financial services, given the benefit of having more developed and integrated financial markets in an already commercially and monetarily integrated area; and it is also very relevant as far as labour markets are concerned, given the Very low degree of labour mobility between Member States. Along with the above, Initiatives to improve the quality of Community competition regulations, to increase coordination between national regulators in certain sectors, and to facilitate the geographical connection of markets through the necessary infrastructures can also help to complete the single market and make it more dynamic. Finally, it should also be possible to revise the criteria behind the preparation of the Community budget so that it is more clearly in line with the primary objective of stimulating the most innovative and productive processes throughout the European Union. Conclusin As I have tried to explain during my speech, the European economy is currently at a crossroads from which it must succeed in order to ensure the future living standards of its citizens, the continuity of the integration process and the sustainability of the European model. But this will require far-reaching reforms in the area of economic policies d0 national and Community d0 over the next few years and improving the quality of European economic governance in order to ensure the effectiveness of decision-making processes in a wider and more heterogeneous Europe. The EU is not a state, it is not a nation, but an entity that articulates a set of member states. It is therefore essential to achieve unity of action in economic policy decisions in the economic field in pursuit of a unitary objective: to enhance the capacity for economic growth under conditions of stability and ensuring a reasonable degree of cohesion. It is therefore the EU's economic system d0 consisting of the combination of national and Community actions d0 that must be reformed in order to make it more efficient. If this is done, by articulating a body of micro-economic policies consistent with the promotion of growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability policies and modernising cohesion policies to adapt them to the current environment of globalisation and strong external competition, Europe will be carving out a brighter future and gaining weight in the international arena. And for a country like Spain, which participates so decisively in European integration, this will be a source of dynamism that we can take advantage of if we too d0 from the authorities to the economic and social actors d0 join forces to continue improving the efficiency and competitiveness of the Spanish economy in an environment of stability. Thanks a lot.

Por lo que se refiere a la cohesin, la pregunta clave es si la forma concreta a travs de la que sta se articula dentro del modelo europeo puede haber incidido negativamente sobre el crecimiento. En este sentido, debe reconocerse que asegurar un grado razonable de cohesin econmica y social ha sido bsico en el pasado para avanzar en el proceso de integracin y lo seguir siendo en el futuro. Ahora bien, existe abundante evidencia que indica que el diseo de las polticas de cohesin, tanto a nivel comunitario como nacional, no ha tenido suficientemente en cuenta que algunos de sus elementos podran incidir de manera particularmente lesiva sobre la eficiencia y el crecimiento. A nivel comunitario, existe evidencia emprica de que los fondos agrcolas y regionales habran limitado, en no pocos casos, los naturales procesos de reasignacin de los recursos derivados del establecimiento del Mercado nico, lo que habra impedido materializar las ganancias potenciales de eficiencia que ste lleva consigo al impedir que los factores de produccin se desplacen hacia sectores o actividades ms productivas. A nivel nacional, por su parte, los efectos desfavorables sobre la eficiencia y el crecimiento habran sido el resultado no deseado de medidas sociales y tributarias que habran incidido negativamente, por ejemplo, sobre el grado de flexibilidad de las estructuras salariales, sobre la movilidad laboral y sobre los incentivos de los agentes para ahorrar, invertir o producir. La cohesin es y debe seguir siendo un elemento bsico del modelo europeo y as lo establecen tanto los actuales tratados como el borrador de la futura Constitucin Europea. Sin embargo, no se pueden cerrar los ojos ante la perspectiva de que, si Europa no consigue retornar a tasas de crecimiento econmico ms elevadas de forma sostenida, ser cada vez ms difcil financiar la cohesin, poniendo en riesgo la pervivencia del modelo europeo. Asimismo, segn se desprende de lo que he argumentado, parece tambin ineludible revisar algunos de los elementos bsicos de las polticas nacionales y comunitarias de cohesin con objeto de que stas sean lo ms complementarias posible con una eficiente asignacin de los recursos y, en ltimo trmino, con el proceso de crecimiento. Pero no es el diseo de las polticas de cohesin el nico responsable de la endeblez del crecimiento europeo en el medio y largo plazo. Segn han puesto de relieve numerosos anlisis, otros serios problemas tambin de oferta habran contribuido a ralentizar el incremento de la productividad total de los factores, el ritmo de acumulacin del capital humano, fsico y tecnolgico y la creacin de empleo. Estos problemas, a su vez, tendran su raz en un modelo de gobierno econmico para la UE sumamente complejo y que dista de ser lo bastante eficaz y en una insuficiente orientacin, tanto de las polticas nacionales como europeas hacia el crecimiento econmico. Es evidente que, si se distingue la trayectoria seguida por los pases europeos a lo largo del tiempo, se ponen de relieve diferencias muy notables en sus ritmos de crecimiento, tal y como sucede, por ejemplo, si comparamos Irlanda o Espaa por citar varios de los ms dinmicos, con Alemania o Francia, que son las economas ms grandes del rea, pero que estn entre las menos dinmicas. Esta desagregacin sirve tambin para constatar que han sido precisamente los pases que con mayor decisin y prontitud han introducido las reformas necesarias en sus mercados de productos y factores los que mejores resultados han cosechado en trminos de crecimiento. La comparacin entre el caso europeo y el de Estados Unidos puede, de nuevo, resultar til para comprender mejor la naturaleza de nuestros problemas. As, si se descompone el crecimiento del PIB en avances de la productividad (por hora trabajada) y creacin de empleo (horas trabajadas) se aprecia claramente cmo, durante las ltimas tres dcadas, el factor diferencial que explica el mayor crecimiento de los Estados Unidos en relacin a Europa es la creacin de empleo, mientras que las tasas de incremento de la productividad son muy similares y, en conjunto, ligeramente favorables a la UE. No obstante, no debe sorprender que nuestra productividad haya crecido ms rpidamente habida cuenta de que su nivel era bastante inferior al de los Estados Unidos. Lo que resulta frustrante es que su nivel actual an est casi un diez por ciento por debajo de de la economa norteamericana y que, en estos ltimos aos, se haya vuelto a ensanchar la brecha entre los dos. A su vez, dada la elevada tasa de paro existente en la economa europea, es descorazonador que apenas se haya creado empleo. Sin embargo, la experiencia seala que, en el caso europeo, cuando se intensifica siquiera modestamente la creacin de empleo, la contrapartida es una ralentizacin del ritmo de incremento de la productividad y viceversa. As, por ejemplo, a medida que la UE ha ido incrementando su tasa media anual de creacin de empleo desde el -0,5% en los aos setenta, al 0% en los ochenta y al muy exiguo +0,3% en los noventa, el ritmo de aumento medio anual de la productividad ha descendido de manera significativa, respectivamente en cada uno de esos perodos, del 3,5%, al 2,4% y al 1,8% y a tasas an ms reducidas en el presente. Esta experiencia contrasta notablemente con la de los Estados Unidos, que ha visto cmo su ritmo de creacin anual de empleo se ha mantenido muy cercano al 2% en cada uno de esos mismos perodos mientras que su productividad anual aumentaba del 1,4% al 1,7%, siendo en la actualidad claramente superior a estas cifras. La economa norteamericana ha podido, en consecuencia, mejorar su productividad sin dejar de mantener por ello unas tasas de creacin de empleo considerablemente ms elevadas lo que ha favorecido doblemente el proceso de crecimiento. La experiencia europea, por el contrario, pone de manifiesto las serias dificultades encontradas hasta el presente para mejorar en un sentido sin empeorar en el otro, lo que supone un formidable freno a la capacidad de crecimiento. Ahora bien, cules son las races del problema de crecimiento europeo? Segn concluyen las investigaciones ms recientes sobre esta cuestin, aunque no resulta sencillo desentraar las causas ltimas que gobiernan los procesos de crecimiento, s puede concluirse que contar con un entorno econmico apropiado, plenamente respetuoso con los incentivos de los agentes y que facilite el dinamismo productivo en un marco de asignacin eficiente de los recursos, es imprescindible. En particular, segn las modernas teoras del crecimiento endgeno, los procesos de innovacin tecnolgica y de continuada adaptacin de las estructuras organizativas a las exigencias de un entorno cambiante son una fuerza muy importante cuya contribucin al crecimiento resulta decisiva. Sin embargo, la realidad muestra que en el conjunto de la UE no se ha completado an el trnsito desde un sistema econmico tradicional, basado en la produccin a gran escala en el marco de unos mercados estables y protegidos y de unas relaciones laborales escasamente flexibles, a lo que actualmente se considera un sistema econmico moderno. Dicho sistema se caracteriza por la importancia que revisten los procesos de innovacin tecnolgica para sobrevivir en un mundo caracterizado por la globalizacin y la competencia exterior, lo que hace necesario adoptar nuevas formas organizativas, promocionar la investigacin y el desarrollo, mejorar la calidad de la educacin, establecer marcos regulatorios que fomenten la libre entrada de empresas y la competencia en los mercados de bienes y servicios, mejorar el grado de flexibilidad de las estructuras salariales y la movilidad funcional, geogrfica y sectorial en los mercados de trabajo, disponer de mejores estructuras impositivas y, finalmente, contar con unas fuentes de financiacin suficientemente flexibles y diversificadas en unos mercados financieros integrados a nivel europeo. Todos estos elementos dinamizadores por el lado de la oferta, que se encuentran presentes en los Estados Unidos, adolecen de un grado de desarrollo muy insuficiente en la UE como consecuencia de que el crecimiento econmico no ha sido, hasta el momento, la prioridad principal de las polticas econmicas europeas, tanto en el mbito nacional en la mayor parte de los casos como comunitario. Esta preocupacin es la que inspira la denominada "estrategia de Lisboa", mediante la cual los gobiernos de la UE acordaron relanzar la capacidad de crecimiento europeo a partir de tres elementos bsicos: completar el Mercado nico; promocionar la sociedad de la informacin, la investigacin y el desarrollo; y modernizar el modelo social europeo. No obstante, con ser adecuados los fines y an teniendo en cuenta el escaso tiempo transcurrido con este marco, los pobres resultados cosechados desde la adopcin de la "estrategia de Lisboa" en el 2000 hacen dudar seriamente acerca de que puedan alcanzarse finalmente los objetivos ltimos con las carencias del actual sistema econmico europeo y la ausencia de mecanismos suficientemente potentes para mejorarlo. En este sentido, mi opinin es que, mientras que la UE se doten Maastricht de un sistema muy eficaz para incentivar la adopcin de unas polticas de estabilidad macroeconmica por parte de los estados miembros, el proceso de Lisboa no parece contar, por el momento, con unos mecanismos de recompensa y penalizacin lo bastante eficaces como para favorecer la instrumentacin de las polticas microeconmicas que se requieren para impulsar la capacidad de crecimiento en Europa. En consecuencia, puede afirmarse que la debilidad de las polticas microeconmicas, ligada ntimamente a la escasa presencia de las reformas estructurales, es la que est en la base de las serias insuficiencias de oferta que padece el sistema econmico de la UE y que tan graves consecuencias han tenido y tienen sobre su potencial de crecimiento. No debe olvidarse, sin embargo, que esta situacin tambin viene influida por la complejidad del sistema de gobierno econmico comunitario y por la diferente adscripcin de responsabilidades entre los mbitos de decisin nacionales y europeos. Ello ha llevado a un estado de cosas manifiestamente mejorable ya que no parece que los actuales mecanismos de coordinacin entre los mencionados mbitos de decisin garanticen la coherencia y la eficacia por lo que se refiere a su impacto conjunto sobre la capacidad de crecimiento. De ah, la necesidad, no solo de impulsar las polticas de carcter microeconmico sino de mejorar la calidad del gobierno econmico de la UE. Retos futuros El pobre balance de la UE en trminos de crecimiento supone una seria amenaza para los futuros niveles de vida de los ciudadanos europeos, al tiempo que, segn he mencionado anteriormente, coloca en jaque al modelo europeo. De una parte, los reducidos ritmos de crecimiento, de continuar en el futuro, necesariamente implican una lenta progresin de la renta per cpita en el rea; y, de otra, puesto que el mantenimiento de la cohesin requiere unas tasas de crecimiento suficientes que permitan financiar las redes de proteccin social, la ausencia de dinamismo econmico podra presionar en exceso sobre las cuentas pblicas en el futuro haciendo, de esta forma, cada vez ms difcilmente financiable la cohesin y cuestionando la estabilidad macroeconmica, lo que amenazara gravemente la pervivencia del modelo europeo. Esta problemtica reviste an mayor importancia si se tiene en cuenta las crecientes exigencias que dicho modelo deber soportar en aos venideros como consecuencia de las nuevas necesidades de gastos sanitarios y de pensiones asociadas con el envejecimiento de la poblacin europea. Pero tambin es necesario considerar que la globalizacin y, en particular, la fuerte competencia internacional hacen preciso que los pases de la Unin mejoren su competitividad y suban algunos peldaos en la escala tecnolgica, para no verse sometidos a los problemas que supondra un desempleo ms elevado y sus repercusiones adversas sobre las cuentas pblicas. Sin embargo, con carcter inmediato, el reto ms importante al que tiene que enfrentarse la UE es asegurar el xito de la incorporacin de diez nuevos miembros en mayo del ao que viene y de otros dos en 2007. La ampliacin a los pases de Europa central y del este es un hecho poltico de extraordinaria importancia ya que supone volver a congregar en un marco de democracia y respeto a las libertades a la mayor parte de los miembros de la gran familia europea, separados y enfrentados durante medio siglo a raz de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. En el plano econmico, la ampliacin constituye una oportunidad pero tambin un reto formidable ya que, si bien es cierto que el conjunto de los nuevos estados miembros no supone sino algo ms del 5% del PIB de la actual UE, su poblacin equivale a casi una tercera parte y, lo que es ms preocupante, su renta per cpita media ni siquiera llega a la mitad de la correspondiente a la actual UE, aunque existen notables diferencias entre la situacin de unos y otros pases de Europa central y del este. Puesto que la ampliacin supone aumentar el Mercado nico y dado el mayor dinamismo econmico de los nuevos miembros, que estn inmersos en procesos de reforma estructural y convergencia real, es de esperar que su entrada contribuya favorablemente, en cierta medida, al dinamismo global de la UE. No obstante, Europa se enfrenta al desafo que supone lograr integrar plenamente y no solo "de iure" las economas de estos pases y facilitar la aproximacin de sus reducidos niveles de renta per cpita hacia los prevalecientes en el conjunto de la UE mediante las polticas europeas de cohesin, contando siempre con que los nuevos estados miembros sigan mejorando la eficiencia de sus economas y avanzando en el logro de la estabilidad macroeconmica. Convendrn conmigo en que, una Europa ampliada, que parte de unas diferencias tan sustanciales de renta per cpita entre los actuales y los nuevos estados miembros y en donde hay que allegar los fondos comunitarios necesarios para facilitar la integracin de ms de cien millones de personas en una nueva realidad, precisa, ms que nunca, realizar las reformas que permitan potenciar el crecimiento europeo. Por otra parte, el gobierno econmico de una UE de 25 27 pases, en lugar de los 15 actuales, adquiere un grado de complejidad institucional muy notable que an lo es ms si se tiene en cuenta la considerable heterogeneidad econmica y social entre sus miembros. De ah que, la respuesta al reto de la ampliacin deba contar tambin con mecanismos que garanticen la eficiencia de los procesos de toma de decisiones de una estructura tan amplia, compleja y diversa. A resolver los problemas de carcter institucional que acabo de aludir, en su forma ms general, deben dedicarse las tareas preparatorias de la Constitucin Europea. Cmo hacer frente a los retos? Habiendo llegado a este punto, quisiera hacer algunas reflexiones a continuacin sobre qu caminos podran explorarse para hacer frente al doble reto al que actualmente se enfrentan los pases de la Unin Europea: por un lado, garantizar la sostenibilidad del modelo europeo y, por otro, asegurar el xito de la ampliacin, con objeto de satisfacer las legtimas aspiraciones de los ciudadanos europeos a gozar de unos niveles de vida y bienestar ms elevados en el futuro. Del anlisis que he realizado de los tres vrtices del modelo europeo crecimiento, estabilidad y cohesin se desprenden varias conclusiones. En primer lugar, que el mantenimiento de la estabilidad macroeconmica es un activo sumamente valioso por s mismo e imprescindible como marco de referencia para el crecimiento; en segundo lugar, que preservar la cohesin pasa necesariamente por una modernizacin de la misma, de forma que ello resulte coherente con los incentivos de los agentes a trabajar, invertir y producir en un entorno econmico ms exigente; y finalmente, que la potenciacin de la capacidad de crecimiento requiere de reformas estructurales muy importantes tanto en el mbito nacional como en el de las polticas comunitarias, al tiempo que se mejora la calidad del gobierno econmico europeo. Dicho de otro modo, lo que se precisa es que el sistema econmico de la UE se oriente realmente y no solo nominalmente al objetivo de potenciar el crecimiento en un marco de elevada estabilidad macroeconmica y un grado razonable de cohesin, por ser el crecimiento la piedra angular sobre la que se asienta el modelo econmico y social europeo. Pero ello implica modificaciones muy considerables, tanto de las polticas econmicas como de los mtodos de gobierno europeo, de modo que la actuacin de las autoridades nacionales y comunitarias resulte globalmente coherente con estos objetivos. Por lo que respecta a las polticas de fomento del crecimiento, el papel de las autoridades nacionales es decisivo. La continuidad de los procesos de reforma en los diversos pases se revela como fundamental para mejorar el funcionamiento de los mercados de bienes y servicios y de los mercados de trabajo; para garantizar la solvencia futura de los sistemas pblicos de pensiones; para promover e incentivar los procesos de innovacin, investigacin y desarrollo; y para elevar la calidad de la educacin. En este sentido, el curso futuro de los acontecimientos en Alemania y Francia reviste suma importancia porque, si finalmente avanzan decisivamente las reformas en estos pases, su impacto econmico y poltico ser muy saludable, no solo para sus propias economas, sino para el conjunto de la UE, dado su considerable peso especfico y la repercusin favorable que ello tendra para seguir profundizando con las reformas en otros pases. En relacin con las polticas de mbito europeo, resulta imprescindible completar el mercado nico y hacerlo ms dinmico y competitivo. Esto es muy importante por lo que respecta a los servicios y, en particular, a los servicios financieros, dado lo beneficioso que resulta contar con unos mercados financieros ms desarrollados e integrados en un rea comercial y monetariamente ya integrada; y tambin es muy relevante por lo que concierne a los mercados de trabajo, dado el muy reducido grado de movilidad laboral existente entre los pases miembros. Junto a lo anterior, las iniciativas tendentes a mejorar la calidad de las regulaciones comunitarias en el mbito de la competencia, a incrementar la coordinacin entre los reguladores nacionales en ciertos sectores, y a facilitar la conexin geogrfica de los mercados mediante las necesarias infraestructuras, pueden tambin contribuir a completar el mercado nico y hacerlo ms dinmico. Por ltimo, debera resultar tambin posible revisar los criterios que inspiran la confeccin del presupuesto comunitario para que ste se site ms claramente en lnea con el objetivo primordial de estimular los procesos ms innovadores y productivos en el conjunto de la Unin Europea. Conclusin Segn he tratado de exponer durante mi intervencin, la economa europea se encuentra actualmente en una encrucijada de la que debe salir airosa para asegurar los niveles de vida futuros de sus ciudadanos, la continuidad del proceso de integracin y la sostenibilidad del modelo europeo. Pero ello requerir llevar a cabo, durante los prximos aos, reformas de un profundo calado en el mbito de las polticas econmicas nacionales y comunitarias y mejorar la calidad del gobierno econmico europeo con objeto de garantizar la eficacia de los procesos de toma de decisiones en una Europa ms amplia y heterognea. La UE no es un estado, no es una nacin, sino un ente que articula un conjunto de estados miembros. Por ello, resulta primordial conseguir en el mbito econmico una unidad de accin en las decisiones de poltica econmica en pos de un objetivo tambin unitario: potenciar la capacidad de crecimiento econmico en condiciones de estabilidad y asegurando un grado razonable de cohesin. Es, por tanto, el sistema econmico de la UE consistente en la combinacin de actuaciones nacionales y comunitarias el que debe reformarse para dotarse de mayor eficiencia. Si as se hace, articulando un cuerpo de polticas microeconmicas coherentes con la promocin del crecimiento al tiempo que se mantienen las polticas macroeconmicas de estabilidad y se modernizan las polticas de cohesin para adaptarlas al entorno actual ms exigente, de globalizacin y fuerte competencia exterior, Europa estar labrndose un futuro ms prspero y ganando peso en el concierto internacional. Y para un pas como Espaa, que tan decididamente participa en la integracin europea, ello supondr una fuente de dinamismo que podremos aprovechar si nosotros tambin desde las autoridades hasta los agentes econmicos y sociales aunamos esfuerzos para seguir mejorando la eficacia y la competitividad de la economa espaola en un entorno de estabilidad. Muchas gracias.

Title: Governor's Appearance: Senate Budget Committee, in relation to the General State Budget Bill for 2004
text: APPEARANCE OF THE GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF SPAIN BEFORE THE SENATE BUDGET COMMITTEE November 2003 Ladies and Gentlemen Senators In October, when I appeared before the Congressional Committee on Budgets on the occasion of the discussion of the Draft General Budget for 2004, I reflected on the factors that have allowed the Spanish economy to be among those economies that lead growth in Europe, in an external context dominated by considerable uncertainty. I also referred to the challenges facing our economy, in order to project into the future a dynamism that will allow it to achieve further improvements in welfare levels and convergence with the core of the most advanced European countries. In my speech to the Congressional Committee, I presented the growth prospects for the Spanish economy in 2003 and 2004, which point to a moderate acceleration in activity, and I also pointed out the desirability of this growth being based to a greater extent on the impulse from foreign demand d0 now that the signs of recovery of the international economy are consolidating. surpassing the pattern followed so far, in which domestic demand has played a preponderant role. This change in composition would favour the intensification of productive investment and avoid the imbalances that can result from a pattern in which the sources of growth are poorly diversified. Accordingly, the framework within which next year's Draft Budget should be assessed is that of an economy that must continue to grow, preserving its levels of competitiveness and increasing its profitability, for which it is necessary that macroeconomic policies be firmly oriented towards stability. I would like to take this opportunity to reaffirm the balance sheet I outlined then and to update it with the latest developments and information on the economic situation. As usual, I will begin by referring to the international economic context, and the European economic context in particular, to then comment on the outlook for the Spanish economy in this autumn of 2003 and the outlook for 2004, ending with some considerations on the Draft Budget. In general, the latest information on international economic developments, activity, agents' confidence indicators and the trajectory of financial markets confirms a gradual establishment of the recovery. Among the positive data that have appeared in recent weeks, mention should be made of the second estimate of the growth of the US economy in the third quarter of 2003, which, in addition to being remarkably high and higher than the first estimate, has revealed as the most encouraging element a significant rebound in productive investment, while there are symptoms of a certain improvement in the labor market. In Japan, after the summer break, there have been signs of recovery, largely linked to trade with the rest of the Asian countries, which have led to an increase in the level of orders from Japanese industry. The thrust of the economies of this geographical area, especially China, is being remarkable, as well as, with less intensity, that observed in the European countries not belonging to the EMU. However, in other areas, such as Latin America, although there is a clear improvement, we still cannot speak of recovery. It can therefore be said that following the impetus provided by the monetary and fiscal policies adopted to counter the slowdown that began in 2001, there are already some signs of expansion in the main economies that make up the euro area's external environment. In fact, timid expectations have begun to appear that this change in climate could affect the future tone of monetary policies, although, for the moment, only the Bank of England has recently decided to increase its official interest rates. Signs of a gradual consolidation of the international recovery do not, however, imply that uncertainties about the medium-term trajectory of the world economy have disappeared. The recovery depends significantly on the impulse provided by the US, where the maintenance of important macrofinancial imbalances, such as those represented by high fiscal and current account deficits, suggests a certain vulnerability of its dynamism, despite high productivity growth. For their part, the structural problems that continue to afflict the Japanese economy also support doubts about the intensity and duration of its incipient revival. These risk factors are finally joined by the rigidity of exchange rate regimes in some Southeast Asian economies, which is hampering some of the possible adjustments that may lead to an orderly correction of global imbalances. The euro area, however, is lagging behind the recovery of the international economy, as evidenced by growth figures in the first half of the year. In this period, activity and demand stagged, with falls in investment and exports, in a context of appreciation of the euro and financial consolidation in the European business sector, which have led to a poor performance of employment. The information available for the second half of the year, however, indicates that there would be a moderate recovery, favoured by expansionary monetary and financial conditions and the rebound in the stock markets, in response to better earnings expectations. Although the indicators closest to expenditure and activity d0 which are only observed with some delay d0 have not yet shown a clear improvement, the preliminary estimate for the third quarter has placed quarter-on-quarter GDP growth in the area at 0.4%, due to the contribution of foreign demand. In addition, the various qualitative and opinion indicators have generally reflected greater optimism on the part of European businesses and consumers, and the recovery is expected to become more intense and broad at the beginning of 2004. Although the area faces this coming expansion without significant macroeconomic imbalances and with favourable financial conditions, a number of factors may contribute to delaying the recovery in EMU and moderating the intensity of the recovery. These include a process of rapid appreciation of the euro, the possibility that European companies have not yet completed the adjustment of their balance sheets and the effects that uncertainty on employment behaviour and the state of national public finances may have on consumer spending. In this regard, it is clear that an important source of concern comes from the behavior of fiscal policies in some countries of the area, which did not make sufficient progress in the consolidation process, in the phase of most intense growth, and which have not been able to contain public deficits within the legally established limits. These developments have tested the effectiveness of the corrective mechanisms provided for in the EU Treaty and the Stability and Growth Pact. In this respect, the conclusions of the EU Council of Ministers of 25 November on the excessive deficit procedures open to Germany and France are regrettable, as have the European Commission and the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. These conclusions, as they do not comply with the existing disciplinary rules, pose a risk to the maintenance of the credibility of the institutional framework and confidence in the soundness of the public finances of euro area Member States. It is therefore imperative that the national authorities take effective action to limit the adverse effects that these events may have generated. For its part, the single monetary policy has taken advantage of the fact that the outlook for the inflation rate in the area has evolved around levels compatible with price stability to maintain an appropriate tone to overcome the situation of stagnation in the economy. It should be noted, however, that, despite the low dynamism, the inflation rate in the euro area has shown some persistence, which has been supported by the behaviour of food prices, and may be encouraged by the increases in indirect taxes introduced in some countries to contain government deficits in 2004. In this situation, the European authorities face the challenge in the coming quarters of making the recovery of the area's economy compatible with the return to the reference values established by the Stability and Growth Pact, preserving the fiscal consolidation framework, and promoting, decisively, structural reform measures that will increase the growth capacity of the European economy. In Spain, as I said at the beginning, the behavior of the economy has been considerably more dynamic. In the third quarter of 2003, the year-on-year rate of GDP growth stood at 2.4%, with quarter-on-quarter growth of 0.7%, slightly higher than those of the previous quarter, confirming the continuation of a path of gradual revival, once a cyclical minimum was exceeded in the central months of the previous year. These data also indicate that the growth differential with the euro area, which widened in the first half of the year, has continued to widen in the second part, even though the European economy has already begun to emerge from its weaker growth phase. At the same time, employment has continued to grow in Spain at comparatively high rates, also marking a notable difference with the euro area. GDP growth continues to be supported by domestic demand and, within it, by consumption and construction. The generation of household incomes d0 supported mainly by job creation d0 the improvement in stock markets, increases in the value of household real estate assets and low interest rates have continued to contribute, to varying degrees, to maintaining, and even intensifying, growth in private consumption. In addition, the purchase of housing, also influenced by the increase in income, by favorable financing conditions, by demographic factors and demand from abroad, has maintained a very lively pace, in a context of increased construction, so that household indebtedness and house prices have maintained the patterns of previous quarters. The thrust of civil works has also converged in the impulse of investment in construction, which has continued to register high increases in recent months, although the most immediate indicators point to a gentle slowdown, which has its origin in the section of non-residential private construction. On the other hand, purchases of capital goods, which had already emerged from the slump they suffered in 2001, have, however, slowed their rate of expansion in that period. Several factors may have contributed to this, such as the weak recovery in the European countries closest to Spain. However, the situation of Spanish companies continues to be healthy and their profitability levels high, so it is expected that this will be a temporary episode, so that productive investment regains greater momentum when the international recovery is consolidated. Exports, meanwhile, which had strengthened markedly since the summer of 2002 and maintained high growth rates in the first half of this year, also slowed down in summer. Available information suggests that this loss of dynamism became more intense in sales to the euro area and was much softer in sales to other geographical areas. In the latter case, it should be borne in mind that, due to the appreciation of the euro, Spanish exporters to these markets have had to assume price declines to protect their shares. The lower dynamism of exports in recent months seems to mainly reflect the sluggishness of the European market, although the compression of margins in the sector has also begun to play a role. In any case, this behaviour, together with a less pronounced slowdown in imports d0 whose growth has been supported by the strength of domestic demand and the appreciation of the euro itself d0 has resulted in a negative contribution of external demand to GDP growth. This scenario suggests that the growth prospects for the Spanish economy in the nearest horizon are based on solid foundations, since its main support d0 consumption and construction d0 maintain stable and high rates of growth, and the other components will be encouraged as the international recovery d0 and that of the euro area, in particular. is strengthened. It is therefore to be expected that, in line with the diagnosis I outlined in Congress, the Spanish economy will close 2003 with an average GDP growth of around 2.3% d0 or even somewhat higher d0 a result that provides the appropriate starting point for growth rates of around 3% in 2004 to be achieved in a context of external expansion. consistent with the figures included in the macroeconomic table on which the budget programming is based. This is not obvious, however, to the existence of some features in the performance of the Spanish economy that must be improved in order to take better advantage of the external impulse and provide greater sustainability to growth in the medium term. The hesitations shown, in the most recent period, by investment in equipment and exports illustrate the need for the recovery to be based on the competitiveness of those sectors most open to the outside, on which the weight of the expansionary phase should rest, in order to avoid accumulating pressures on the sectors that have contributed most to growth so far. It is particularly important that price and cost developments in Spain are aligned with those of our main trading partners. Labour cost growth in the Spanish economy continues to be higher than in the euro area, reflecting both reduced gains in labour productivity and higher wage growth, despite the moderation patterns that have been accepted. In this regard, productive investment must play a leading role, since only progress in it can make the maintenance of employment generation compatible with higher productivity gains. As for wages, it is important to avoid that temporary deviations in inflation feed upward pressures on them. To this end, it is necessary to limit the indexation mechanisms that survive in collective bargaining and that hinder the processes of reducing the inflation rate. In any case, it is not only labour cost differentials per unit of output that explain the inflation differential that Spain maintains with the euro area, but also the widening of margins in some sectors, linked both to demand pressure and to the inefficient functioning of some markets, are contributing to maintaining price increases. That is why it is essential to continue deepening the flexibility of product markets and the economy in general. In the period since 2003, the Spanish inflation rate, as measured by the CPI, has fallen sharply, from 4% at the end of 2002 to 2.6% in October. This significant cut reflects, in part, the discounting of a number of factors, which affected prices during the past year d0 such as certain increases in indirect taxation, or the introduction of euro banknotes and coins d0 whose effects on the inflation rate have been reabsorbed in the first part of 2003. Despite this, the inflation differential with EMU continues to stand at seven tenths of a percentage point, indicating the persistence of some factors that tend to limit the necessary reduction in it. Mention should be made, in this regard, of wage review clauses, the effects of which on the price-forming process will take time to absorb, and the persistence of relatively high price increases in services and commercial distribution, which, as I have just mentioned, are in some cases linked to the strength of demand and, in others, they reflect the existence of insufficiently competitive market structures. At this time, when the Spanish economy is resuming a path of gradual acceleration, in a European situation that allows us to predict monetary conditions that will remain comfortable for domestic needs, it is of great importance that fiscal policy preserve its stabilising stance and help to temper demand pressures, also contributing to the rebalancing in the composition of expenditure. In this context, it is necessary to assess positively the Government's forecast, announced in Congress during the debate on the General State Budget for 2004, of a slight surplus in the closing of the public accounts for the year 2003. This result, better than that anticipated in the draft budget under discussion, is in line with the stabilising function of fiscal policy and highlights the possibility of making this function compatible with compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact. In fact, in the years in which the Spanish economy experienced a certain cyclical slowdown, Spanish public administrations continued to make progress in budgetary consolidation, while contributing positively to sustaining activity, through their influence on household disposable income d0 and, in this way, on private consumption d0 and through a significant contribution to the development of infrastructure investment. It should not be forgotten, however, that this stabilizing stance of fiscal policy would not have been possible without the consolidation effort made during the previous cyclical phase, in which there were significant increases in revenue, even in the years of tax reform, while significant adjustments were made in primary current expenditure. This strategy contrasts, as I pointed out earlier, with that followed by other European countries, with much less positive results for fiscal policy room for manoeuvre. For 2004, the General State Budget establishes the objective of placing public accounts in a position of balance. This objective would be compatible with a certain expansionary orientation in certain items of expenditure d0 social benefits, public employment, compensation of employees and public investment d0 and, on the income side, with some expansionary effect derived from the reform of personal income tax, implemented in 2003. However, starting from a surplus situation such as that projected in FY2003, it may be useful to deepen the stabilizing role that fiscal policy has been playing, especially when a cyclical upswing is expected. At this juncture, it would be advisable - especially if the profile of acceleration of domestic spending is accentuated - for a surplus of similar magnitude to that already achieved during the next year. In this way, the cyclically-adjusted balance and interest rates (known as the primary structural balance) would continue to improve. This type of action would also make it possible to face the challenges that, in the short term, involves advancing in the process of separating the sources of financing of the State and Social Security, as stipulated in the recent agreement on pensions within the framework of the Toledo Pact and, more in the medium term, improve the quality of public finances and deepen budgetary consolidation, which are necessary to successfully overcome the challenges associated with population ageing. In this way, budgetary policy would continue to play the role that is required of it, since monetary policy, being dictated by the needs of the euro area as a whole, cannot meet the specific stabilisation needs of the Spanish economy.
text_original: COMPARECENCIA DEL GOBERNADOR DEL BANCO DE ESPAA ANTE LA COMISIN DE PRESUPUESTOS DEL SENADO Noviembre 2003 Sras. y Sres. Senadores En el mes de octubre, cuando comparec ante la Comisin de Presupuestos del Congreso, con ocasin de la discusin del Proyecto de Presupuestos Generales para el ejercicio 2004, realic una reflexin sobre los factores que han permitido a la economa espaola situarse entre aquellas economas que lideran el crecimiento en Europa, en un contexto exterior dominado por una notable incertidumbre. Hice referencia tambin a los retos a los que se enfrenta nuestra economa, para proyectar hacia el futuro un dinamismo que le permita conseguir nuevas mejoras en los niveles de bienestar y en la convergencia con el ncleo de pases europeos ms avanzados. En mi intervencin ante la Comisin del Congreso, expuse las perspectivas de crecimiento para la economa espaola en 2003 y 2004, que apuntan a una moderada aceleracin de la actividad, y seal tambin la conveniencia de que este crecimiento se base en mayor medida en el impulso proveniente de la demanda exterior ahora que los signos de recuperacin de la economa internacional se afianzan, superando el patrn seguido hasta este momento, en el que la demanda interna ha tenido un papel preponderante. Este cambio de composicin favorecera la intensificacin de la inversin productiva y evitara los desequilibrios que puede acarrear un patrn en el que las fuentes del crecimiento estn poco diversificadas. De acuerdo con ello, el marco en el que se debe valorar el Proyecto de Presupuestos del prximo ao es el de una economa que debe seguir creciendo, preservando sus niveles de competitividad y aumentando su rentabilidad, para lo que es necesario que las polticas macroeconmicas estn firmemente orientadas hacia la estabilidad. Quisiera aprovechar esta oportunidad para reafirmar el balance que entonces esboc y actualizarlo con los acontecimientos y las informaciones ms recientes sobre la situacin econmica. Como es habitual, comenzar haciendo referencia al contexto econmico internacional, y al europeo en particular, para comentar posteriormente el panorama de la economa espaola en este otoo de 2003 y las perspectivas para 2004, terminando con algunas consideraciones sobre el Proyecto de Presupuestos. En general, la informacin ms reciente sobre la evolucin econmica internacional, la actividad, los indicadores de confianza de los agentes y la trayectoria de los mercados financieros viene a confirmar un progresivo asentamiento de la recuperacin. Entre los datos positivos aparecidos en las ltimas semanas hay que mencionar la segunda estimacin del crecimiento de la economa de EEUU en el tercer trimestre de 2003, que adems de ser notablemente elevado y superior a la primera estimacin, ha revelado como elemento ms alentador un significativo repunte de la inversin productiva, al tiempo que se observan sntomas de una cierta mejora del mercado laboral. En Japn, tras la pausa del verano, se han percibido signos de recuperacin, ligados en gran medida al comercio con el resto de los pases asiticos, que han llevado a un aumento en el nivel de pedidos de la industria japonesa. El empuje de las economas de esta rea geogrfica, especialmente de China, est siendo notable, as como, con menor intensidad, el observado en los pases europeos no pertenecientes a la UEM. Sin embargo, en otras zonas, como Latinoamrica, aunque se observa una clara mejora, todava no se puede hablar de recuperacin. Puede decirse, por tanto, que tras el impulso impartido por las polticas monetarias y fiscales adoptadas para contrarrestar la desaceleracin iniciada en 2001, se observan ya algunos sntomas de expansin en las principales economas que conforman el entorno exterior de la zona del euro. De hecho, han comenzado a aparecer tmidas expectativas de que este cambio de clima pueda llegar a afectar al tono futuro de las polticas monetarias, aunque, por el momento, slo el Banco de Inglaterra ha decidido incrementar recientemente sus tipos de inters oficiales. Los signos de una consolidacin gradual de la recuperacin internacional no implican, sin embargo, que hayan desparecido las incertidumbres sobre la trayectoria a medio plazo de la economa mundial. La recuperacin depende significativamente del impulso impartido por EEUU, donde el mantenimiento de desequilibrios macrofinancieros importantes, como los que representan los elevados dficit fiscal y por cuenta corriente, sugiere una cierta vulnerabilidad de su dinamismo, a pesar del elevado crecimiento de la productividad. Por su parte, los problemas estructurales que siguen aquejando a la economa japonesa tambin sostienen las dudas sobre la intensidad y duracin de su incipiente reanimacin. A estos factores de riesgo se une, finalmente, la rigidez de los regmenes cambiarios en algunas economas del sudeste asitico, que est dificultando algunos de los posibles ajustes que pueden propiciar una correccin ordenada de los desequilibrios globales. La zona del euro, sin embargo, est evolucionando con retraso en relacin con la recuperacin de la economa internacional, como se puso de manifiesto en las cifras de crecimiento en la primera mitad del ao. En ese perodo, la actividad y la demanda registraron un estancamiento, con cadas en la inversin y las exportaciones, en un contexto de apreciacin del euro y de saneamiento financiero en el sector empresarial europeo, que han conducido a un mal comportamiento del empleo. La informacin disponible respecto al segundo semestre del ao, indica sin embargo, que se estara registrando una moderada reactivacin , favorecida por unas condiciones monetarias y financieras expansivas y por el repunte de las bolsas, en respuesta a unas mejores expectativas de beneficios. Aunque los indicadores ms prximos al gasto y a la actividad que slo se observan con cierto retraso- no han mostrado todava una mejora clara, la estimacin preliminar para el tercer trimestre ha situado el avance intertrimestral del PIB de la zona en el 0,4%, debido a la aportacin de la demanda exterior. Adems, los distintos indicadores cualitativos y de opinin han reflejado, de forma general, un mayor optimismo de las empresas y de los consumidores europeos, por lo que cabe esperar que la recuperacin gane una mayor intensidad y amplitud al comienzo de 2004. A pesar de que la zona afronta esa prxima expansin sin desequilibrios macroeconmicos significativos y con condiciones financieras favorables, hay diversos factores que pueden contribuir a retrasar la recuperacin en la UEM y a moderar la intensidad de la misma.
