Basel II represents a new, more comprehensive and inclusive supervisory approach, in which, through its three pillars - the first relating to the minimum regulatory capital more sensitive to risk, the second relating to the more coordinated and risk-focused supervisory process and the third pillar dedicated to improving the transparency of institutions - it seeks not only to maintain regulatory capital closer to the economic capital calculated by institutions, but also create incentives that support the improvement of the risk management of institutions. The end result we hope to achieve is a more solid, resilient and efficient financial system that is capable of fulfilling its functions in all kinds of cyclical conditions and thus contributes to the growth of the economy as a whole. The Basel II preparation process, which resulted in the publication two weeks ago of the text of the new framework for determining and measuring regulatory capital, has been long, nearly six years, and very open and participatory. Thanks to the hundreds of comments and proposals received from industry, supervisors and academics around the world, the New Regulatory Capital Framework has changed and improved substantially over the years. One of the examples where there have been notable improvements is the treatment of SMEs: being aware of the importance of SMEs in our economies, the Committee devoted considerable efforts to the analysis of the financing of small and medium-sized enterprises with the dual objective of not adversely affecting their access to credit and, At the same time, that the sensitivity to risk that Basel II has set itself as one of its objectives should be maintained. The analysis showed that banks' loan portfolios to SMEs show a high degree of diversification. This diversification, by making a joint analysis of the portfolio and not an individualized study of each of the loans, facilitates the reduction of losses of the portfolio as a whole and, consequently, allows to reduce the regulatory capital required. With this basic idea of taking into account the effect of diversification on the portfolio as a whole, changes were introduced that have led to a more favourable treatment of SMEs. Both the studies of the Basel Committee and those carried out by the Bank of Spain show that, on average and depending on the case, reductions can range from 3% to 30% reduction on the regulatory capital required in the current agreement. In particular, three relevant modifications were introduced: a5 Firstly, for those companies with annual sales of less than 50 million euros (definition of SMEs in Basel II), a diversification factor is introduced that reduces capital, depending on the size, which may be 20% lower than that required for large companies. a5 Secondly, for loans to small and medium-sized enterprises individually below db1 million, they are allowed to be treated as retail risks and portfolios of this type of risk receive a lower capital requirement in both the standard and advanced approaches. a5 The third modification, also important in loans to SMEs, is a greater recognition of guarantees and guarantors, which allows to reduce losses and, therefore, reduce the capital required. As I indicated earlier, the final result is satisfactory to the extent that it does not hinder access to credit for small and medium-sized enterprises and, at the same time, incorporates incentives for non-financial companies to improve their fundamental parameters, so as to increase their credit rating, and their practices in terms of transparency in their information. I trust that this small foray into financial and microeconomic issues has not diverted too much attention from the center of this meeting, which is the recovery of the economy and its differentiated characteristics in various geographical areas. Thank you very much for your attention.

Jaime Caruana Gobernador Seoras y seores: Quiero agradecer a los organizadores la oportunidad que me brindan para dirigirme a ustedes en esta jornada de apertura del Cuarto Encuentro Financiero Internacional de Caja Madrid. Para ello, van a contar con la presencia de personalidades muy desatacadas y especialistas que los harn partcipes de su experiencia y sus conocimientos. No es aventurado pronosticar un gran xito a estos encuentros. En los ltimos das, he tenido la oportunidad de expresar mi opinin sobre la situacin en la que se encuentra nuestra economa y de cul es el entorno internacional en el que se desenvuelve. Lo he hecho con ocasin de la presentacin del Informe Anual del ao 2003 ante el Consejo de Gobierno del Banco de Espaa y, ms recientemente, con motivo de mi comparecencia ante la Comisin de Economa del Congreso. No quiero, por eso, resultar reiterativo y repetir un diagnstico que estoy seguro que muchos de ustedes conocen y, posiblemente, comparten. S quisiera aprovechar la ocasin para centrar la atencin en algunas ideas, concretamente en cuatro temas, que pueden resultar ilustrativas de los problemas que hemos de afrontar y que conviene que tengamos presentes en cualquier debate sobre el futuro de la economa mundial y sus implicaciones para la economa espaola. El programa de estas jornadas se pregunta sobre si la recuperacin es ya una realidad. Creo que la economa mundial est entrando en una fase de clara expansin, liderada por los Estados Unidos y que cuenta con la colaboracin de otros destacados protagonistas; entre ellos, muy especialmente, algunas economas asiticas. Los datos ms recientes nos indican, tambin, que este proceso de recuperacin est extendindose a las principales economas europeas y que el conjunto de pases de la zona euro parece que abandona, al fin, el estancamiento de los ltimos aos. La economa espaola se encuentra en una posicin ventajosa para aprovechar este entorno estimulante. Ha dado muestras de una gran capacidad de resistencia durante la ltima fase de desaceleracin cclica y mantiene, desde hace ya varios trimestres, un ritmo de crecimiento sostenido. Pudiera ser que nos encontrsemos, por tanto, al comienzo de una etapa de crecimiento relativamente generalizado. No podemos decir, sin embargo, que este panorama se encuentre exento de incertidumbres y que la fase de recuperacin econmica est garantizada. La economa norteamericana se ha adentrado en una nueva fase de crecimiento que confirma su extraordinaria vitalidad, pero arrastra unos importantes desequilibrios que, si no se enderezan, podran comprometer su empuje. Europa sigue dando muestras de rigideces que limitan su capacidad de expansin, y que deben corregirse para que pueda desarrollar todo su potencial y contribuir, en la medida en la que le corresponde, a un crecimiento mundial ms equilibrado. Espaa, en fin, se enfrenta al reto de mantener e intensificar su proceso de convergencia real con las economas ms destacadas de nuestro entorno, para lo que precisa fortalecer su posicin competitiva. As pues, en esta ocasin, he preferido elegir los tres temas econmicos que he esbozado ms un tema financiero, en lugar de tratar de hacer un anlisis extensivo de la situacin econmica. Los cuatro asuntos son: En economa internacional, los desequilibrios econmicos globales que persisten a pesar de la recuperacin, sus posibles vas de ajuste y sus implicaciones para la recuperacin. De la situacin de la economa europea me parece interesante reflexionar sobre la relacin entre los retos estructurales que tiene la zona, un tema de medio largo plazo, y las dificultades que est mostrando la confianza en retomar un dinamismo similar a otras situaciones cclicas parecidas. En la economa espaola, creo que un tema central para el futuro prximo, ms all de 2005, es la competitividad. Finalmente, en el rea financiera, me gustara explicar el favorable trato de las pequeas y medianas empresas en Basilea II. 1) Desequilibrios econmicos globales. La fase actual de crecimiento de la economa mundial se caracteriza por la presencia de notables desajustes en los flujos de ahorro e inversin internacionales, de los que el dficit por cuenta corriente de Estados Unidos es el principal exponente. Hasta la fecha, la financiacin del dficit norteamericano no ha planteado ningn problema, por la predisposicin de los inversores extranjeros a continuar absorbiendo activos emitidos por los agentes econmicos de ese pas. Este fenmeno se ha visto alentado por diversos factores, entre ellos, los avances de productividad de la economa americana desde la segunda mitad de los 90 que han aumentado el rendimiento esperado de sus activos, el desarrollo y la eficiencia con la que actan los mercados financieros mundiales, reforzada, en el caso de Estados Unidos, por el papel preponderante del dlar dentro del sistema monetario internacional. Adems, las polticas cambiarias llevadas a cabo por numerosos pases asiticos encaminadas a evitar la apreciacin de los tipos de cambio de sus monedas y seguir apoyando la recuperacin de sus economas les han llevado a ejercer una fuerte demanda de activos denominados en dlares. Aunque la confluencia de estos factores haya resultado, hasta el da de hoy, fructfera, no debemos pensar que esta situacin pueda prolongarse indefinidamente e introduce un elemento de riesgo en el proceso de recuperacin mundial. Como ustedes saben, las vas clsicas de absorcin de los desequilibrios por cuenta corriente son, bsicamente, dos. La primera discurre a travs de los movimientos de los tipos de cambio y su impacto en los precios relativos de los bienes comerciables. La segunda est relacionada con las polticas de estmulo de la demanda aplicadas en las distintas reas. Los pases que han acumulado excedentes comerciales deben impulsar el crecimiento de sus economas para equilibrar los flujos de bienes y servicios con las reas deficitarias, y permitir la apreciacin de sus monedas. Ambos mecanismos de ajuste son, hasta cierto punto, complementarios, por lo que ambos pueden desempear un papel relevante en la correccin de los desequilibrios. En todo caso, la contribucin que cabe esperar de los movimientos de los tipos de cambio a la correccin de los desequilibrios exteriores globales es limitada, por lo que son necesarios ajustes en las polticas econmicas de los principales pases. La experiencia de los dos ltimos aos resulta, en este sentido, suficientemente ilustrativa: la prdida de valor de la moneda norteamericana coexisti con una ampliacin del dficit de Estados Unidos y de los supervit de Japn y del resto de Asia, debido, fundamentalmente, a que la depreciacin del dlar no se concentr en las monedas de esas regiones, que son las que originan, en mayor medida, el desequilibrio comercial norteamericano, sino, sobre todo, frente al euro, moneda de una regin que presenta un saldo exterior relativamente equilibrado. No se puede excluir, por tanto, que un ajuste de este tipo, lejos de solucionar el desequilibrio exterior norteamericano, acabe afectando a la recuperacin de las economas europeas, que son las que se encuentran en una fase cclica ms retrasada. Lograr un reparto del crecimiento mundial ms acorde con unas posiciones exteriores ms equilibradas sin poner en riesgo la recuperacin es, por lo tanto, uno de los principales desafos que afronta la economa mundial. Un primer riesgo es que la persistencia de los desequilibrios por cuenta corriente pueda exacerbar la volatilidad en los mercados cambiarios y financieros internacionales. Por estas razones, parece aconsejable que sean las polticas econmicas de las distintas reas mundiales las que adopten una orientacin que permita mitigar los riesgos asociados a los desequilibrios globales, sin comprometer su estabilidad. As, en Estados Unidos, la retirada gradual del estmulo fiscal introducido en los ltimos aos podra hacer una contribucin fundamental a la moderacin del crecimiento de la demanda interna y, por tanto, a la contencin de las elevadas necesidades de apelacin al ahorro mundial que se viene registrando. No en vano, se ha acuado la terminologa de "dficit gemelos" para referirse al doble desequilibrio de esta economa, ya que, aunque los agentes privados tambin han contribuido al desequilibrio exterior, ste ha sido, sobre todo, la contrapartida del elevado dficit pblico. Por su parte, la contribucin de las polticas econmicas de la zona del euro a la correccin de los desequilibrios mundiales pasa por la aplicacin decidida de las reformas de los mercados de productos y factores que permitan elevar su crecimiento potencial y su demanda de bienes producidos en el exterior. La evolucin de la zona euro a lo largo de los ltimos aos ha sido un tanto decepcionante. Su ritmo de crecimiento ha permanecido, prcticamente, estancado y no han podido materializarse todava muchas de las ganancias de bienestar que cabe esperar de la adopcin de una moneda nica y de la profundizacin en un nico mercado. Destacada la importancia de las polticas econmicas de las diversas reas en el ajuste ordenado de los desequilibrios globales, la importante contribucin que un mayor crecimiento en la zona euro tendra en este proceso, me permite centrarme en el segundo de los temas que quera tratar. 2) Reformas y confianza en Europa En estos aos ha ido forjndose un amplio consenso sobre las causas de esta situacin de dificultad para impulsar su crecimiento, as como sobre los posibles remedios. Me gustara destacar, a este respecto, dos puntos que, a mi juicio, son muy relevantes. En primer lugar, el modesto crecimiento de la productividad, que podra estar relacionado, a su vez, con el escaso ritmo de generacin de innovaciones tecnolgicas y las dificultades para la difusin de las ya existentes, muy por debajo, ambos, de los que han tenido lugar en otras reas geogrficas. Es posible que a ello haya contribuido la relativa rigidez regulatoria y administrativa a la que se enfrentan las empresas europeas. Adems, la eficiencia en el funcionamiento de los mercados de trabajo europeos contina ofreciendo un amplio margen de mejora. Un uso ms intenso y eficiente del factor trabajo requiere una profundizacin en las reformas emprendidas y, en particular, en la puesta en prctica de medidas que reduzcan los costes de contratacin, en la aplicacin de reformas de los sistemas impositivos y, de manera especial, en la revisin de aquellos elementos de los mecanismos de prestaciones sociales que, habiendo sido concebidos en una etapa de mayor crecimiento econmico, revelan ahora sus elevados costes en trminos de una distorsin de los estmulos para una asignacin eficiente de los recursos. Sin embargo, el consenso que, como he indicado, se ha ido construyendo en torno a este diagnstico y que qued consagrado en los ambiciosos objetivos de la agenda de Lisboa, no se ha correspondido con una accin decidida por parte de las autoridades nacionales, que han adoptado, en general, una actitud vacilante en la aplicacin del catlogo de medidas trazado. A mi juicio, una de las razones que explican la debilidad del impulso reformador radica en el hecho de que las autoridades no han sido siempre capaces de transmitir a los ciudadanos que las reformas se presentan como una oportunidad para obtener un mayor crecimiento futuro y no como una prdida de bienestar. Se ha exagerado la idea de que los costes de las reformas se perciben enseguida mientras que sus frutos tardan aos en llegar o, incluso, en el caso de las reformas de los sistemas de pensiones, dcadas o generaciones. Creo que esta idea hay que matizarla mucho porque el avance en la agenda reformadora y en su comprensin por parte del ciudadano, ayudara a incrementar el crecimiento potencial y tambin a espolear la dbil confianza de los agentes europeos que ha inhibido su propensin al gasto en los ltimos aos. Una voluntad reformadora ms decidida es un ingrediente necesario para apuntalar la fase actual de mayor dinamismo de la actividad. En este sentido, la esperanzadora recuperacin del producto de la UEM iniciada a mediados del pasado ao proporciona una ocasin para la aceleracin de las reformas que no debe desperdiciarse, ya que la mejora de las perspectivas de empleo y renta contribuye a mitigar los posibles costes en el ms corto plazo. 3) La competitividad de la economa espaola En relacin a la economa espaola, he preferido elegir como el elemento ms relevante para el futuro de nuestra economa la competitividad. La economa espaola ha logrado mantenerse al margen del tono poco estimulante que han vivido las principales economas europeas en los ltimos aos y ha sabido beneficiarse del entorno de estabilidad en el que viene desenvolvindose desde nuestra entrada en la UEM. Ello le ha permitido seguir recortando sus diferencias de renta y bienestar con los pases ms avanzados de la UE. Este dinamismo se asienta en unas bases relativamente slidas. Por un lado, las favorables condiciones monetarias y financieras y el dinamismo del empleo continan sustentando la expansin del gasto de las familias en bienes de consumo y vivienda. Por otro, cabe esperar que, en los prximos meses, la saneada situacin financiera de las empresas espaolas y la expansin de la economa mundial que, como ya he dicho, es cada vez ms intensa y generalizada, tiendan a ampliar las bases de nuestro patrn de crecimiento, de forma que vaya sustentndose, cada vez en mayor medida, en aquellos componentes del gasto que contribuyen a elevar el potencial productivo, como la inversin y la exportacin. En este sentido, ya se aprecian signos de recuperacin en la inversin productiva de las empresas, una vez superada la fase de saneamiento financiero que han tenido que afrontar algunos grandes grupos empresariales, al tiempo que las exportaciones se pueden ver favorecidas por el mejor tono de los mercados internacionales. Este comportamiento favorable no debe restar importancia, sin embargo, a la exigencia de preservar las cotas de estabilidad macroeconmica alcanzadas y de profundizar y ampliar las reformas estructurales que necesita la economa. Quiero referirme hoy, como ya lo hice con ocasin de la presentacin del Informe Anual, a la necesidad de afrontar algunos elementos de riesgo que se han ido gestando a lo largo de los ltimos aos y que, de materializarse, podran dificultar la total incorporacin de la economa espaola a la fase de expansin econmica global y la continuidad del proceso de convergencia real. Estoy aludiendo, en concreto, a la persistencia de diferenciales de inflacin con el conjunto de pases de la zona euro y al bajo crecimiento de la productividad, dos factores que pueden terminar daando la competitividad en la que se ha de asentar el crecimiento futuro de nuestra economa. La persistencia de un diferencial de inflacin positivo frente a los pases de la zona euro responde, en parte, a la posicin cclica ms avanzada que mantiene la economa espaola, pero tambin refleja la presencia de imperfecciones y rigideces que se ponen de manifiesto en incrementos ms notorios en aquellos sectores, como los servicios, que se encuentran al amparo de la competencia exterior. Adems, como algunas de estas actividades son proveedoras de inputs intermedios, sus aumentos de precios se transmiten al resto del entramado productivo, lo que acenta la presin de los costes, con el consiguiente deterioro de las condiciones de concurrencia de aquellas empresas que compiten en los mercados internacionales. Esta situacin ha obligado a numerosos sectores industriales, sobre todo aquellos con una mayor vocacin exportadora, a ajustar, tras varios aos de compresin de sus mrgenes de explotacin, el crecimiento del empleo, con el fin de reducir sus costes por unidad de producto y defender sus cuotas de mercado. La estabilidad de costes y precios constituye un elemento esencial de la estrategia de poltica econmica dentro de la UEM, y preservarla es un reto fundamental para nuestra economa. Pero no debemos olvidar que, en un contexto de internacionalizacin creciente, las ventajas competitivas que tradicionalmente ha disfrutado la economa espaola, basadas en unos niveles de precios y costes inferiores a los de nuestros principales competidores, se pueden ver afectadas por las de aquellos pases de industrializacin ms reciente que se estn incorporando con rapidez a la actividad exportadora. De esta manera, la defensa de la posicin competitiva de la economa espaola est cada vez ms vinculada a las mejoras en la eficiencia y en la productividad, un reto que compartimos con otros pases europeos, en la lnea que he esbozado en la primera parte de mi intervencin. Como ya he expuesto en numerosas ocasiones, el escaso crecimiento de la productividad de la economa espaola en los aos recientes se encuentra relacionado, sin duda, con la solidez e intensidad del proceso de creacin de empleo, que se ha visto impulsado por las medidas de flexibilizacin adoptadas en el mercado de trabajo. La fortaleza del empleo no solo ha permitido reducir de forma apreciable nuestra elevada tasa de paro, sino que, adems, ha sustentado el crecimiento de la renta disponible de las familias. Se pueden identificar, no obstante, algunos otros factores, de carcter ms estructural, que tambin contribuyen a explicar el menor dinamismo de la productividad, incluso en relacin con los otros pases de la zona del euro, y que deben afrontarse adecuadamente, si no queremos ver limitada nuestra capacidad de crecimiento a medio plazo. Entre ellos hay que destacar, por su importancia, el escaso protagonismo de la innovacin tecnolgica y al papel de la difusin del conocimiento en la modernizacin del aparato productivo. Para que la economa espaola logre aumentos genuinos de productividad debe aumentar, de forma decidida, la capitalizacin de sus procesos productivos, reforzando, en particular, aquellas infraestructuras de transporte y telecomunicaciones, que tanta influencia tienen sobre el crecimiento a largo plazo. Al mismo tiempo, se debe intensificar el esfuerzo innovador, el nivel de educacin y la cualificacin de la mano de obra, con el fin de mejorar la capacidad de las empresas espaolas para adecuar su estructura productiva y comercial a las pautas de la demanda internacional, impulsando una especializacin creciente en aquellos productos de mayor valor aadido y mercados ms dinmicos. La experiencia de otros pases muestra la importancia de combinar, de una parte, el importante esfuerzo inversor necesario para producir e incorporar nuevas tecnologas en los distintos procesos productivos y, de otra, la configuracin de un entorno econmico competitivo y flexible, favorecedor de la difusin hacia el conjunto de la sociedad de los cambios organizativos y del uso de las aplicaciones derivadas de las nuevas tecnologas. De esta forma podremos hacer frente a la presin competitiva cada vez ms intensa que ejercen los pases que se han incorporado recientemente a la UE, con unas estructuras productivas y comerciales similares a las nuestras y que estn acometiendo intensos procesos de capitalizacin, financiados, en gran parte, desde el exterior. La economa espaola se enfrenta, por tanto, -como el resto de las economas europeas- a la necesidad de avanzar en las reformas necesarias para mejorar sus estructuras productivas y flexibilizar el funcionamiento de los mercados de bienes y servicios. A su vez, las polticas macroeconmicas deben seguir garantizando el actual entorno de estabilidad. En este sentido, conviene reiterar una vez ms la importancia que para Espaa tiene el mantenimiento de una poltica presupuestaria disciplinada que permita continuar mejorando el saldo de las cuentas pblicas, de manera que frente a las condiciones monetarias holgadas que van a prevalecer, en coherencia con los requerimientos del conjunto del rea del euro, se puedan moderar los impulsos expansivos y preservar la estabilidad presupuestaria a medio y largo plazo. Slo con esta orientacin se podrn soslayar los riesgos de medio plazo a los que me he referido, y aprovechar las oportunidades que brinda la nueva etapa de crecimiento generalizado que puede disfrutar la economa mundial y sobre cuyas perspectivas van ustedes a reflexionar a los largo de estas jornadas, por lo que no quiero restarles ms tiempo de lo que prometen ser unas provechosas sesiones de trabajo. 4) Basilea II y las pymes. Aprovechando la oportunidad que me brinda este encuentro y siguiendo con la idea de centrarme en temas concretos, me gustara saltar de lo macro a lo micro y de la economa real a la financiera, para dedicar mis ltimas palabras al acuerdo de Basilea II, aprobado la ltima semana de junio y especficamente a su favorable tratamiento de las pequeas y medianas empresas, algo que todos reconocemos como muy necesario para el desarrollo econmico. Basilea II representa un nuevo enfoque supervisor, ms global e integrador, en el que, a travs de sus tres pilares - el primero relativo al capital regulatorio mnimo ms sensible al riesgo, el segundo relativo al proceso supervisor ms coordinado y enfocado al riesgo y el tercer pilar dedicado a mejorar la transparencia de las entidades - se busca no slo mantener una capital regulatorio mas prximo al capital econmico calculado por las entidades, sino tambin crear incentivos que apoyen la mejora de la gestin de riesgos de las entidades. El resultado final que esperamos obtener es un sistema financiero ms slido, resistente y eficiente, que sea capaz de cumplir sus funciones en todo tipo de condiciones cclicas y de esa manera contribuya al crecimiento del conjunto de la economa. El proceso de preparacin de Basilea II, que dio como resultado la publicacin hace dos semanas del texto del nuevo marco para la determinacin y medida del capital regulatorio, ha sido largo, cerca de seis aos, y muy abierto y participativo. Gracias a los cientos de comentarios y propuestas recibidos de la industria, supervisores y acadmicos de todo el mundo, el Nuevo Marco de Capital Regulatorio ha cambiado y mejorado sustancialmente a lo largo de estos aos. Uno de los ejemplos en los que se han producido notables mejoras es el tratamiento de las pymes: siendo conscientes de la importancia de las pymes en nuestras economas, el Comit dedic notables esfuerzos al anlisis de la financiacin de las pequeas y medianas empresas con el doble objetivo de que no se viese perjudicado su acceso al crdito y, simultneamente, que se mantuviese la sensibilidad al riesgo que Basilea II se ha marcado como uno de sus objetivos. El anlisis mostr que las carteras de prstamos de la banca a las pymes presentan un elevado grado de diversificacin. Esta diversificacin, al hacer un anlisis conjunto de la cartera y no un estudio individualizado de cada uno de los prstamos, facilita la disminucin de las prdidas del conjunto de la cartera y, en consecuencia, permite reducir el capital regulatorio requerido. Con esta idea de fondo de tener en cuenta el efecto de diversificacin en el conjunto de la cartera, se introdujeron cambios que han llevado a un tratamiento ms favorable de las Pymes. Tanto los estudios del Comit de Basilea como los realizados por el Banco de Espaa muestran que, en promedio y segn los casos, las reducciones pueden oscilar entre un 3% a un 30% de reduccin sobre el capital regulatorio requerido en el vigente acuerdo. En particular, se introdujeron tres modificaciones relevantes:  En primer lugar, para aquellas empresas con unas ventas anuales inferiores a 50 millones de euros (definicin de pyme en Basilea II), se introduce un factor de diversificacin que reduce el capital, en funcin del tamao, pudiendo llegar a ser ste un 20% inferior al requerido para grandes empresas.  En segundo lugar, para prstamos a pequeas y medianas empresas individualmente inferiores a 1 milln de euros, se permite que sean tratadas como riesgos detallistas y las carteras de este tipo de riesgos reciben un menor requisito de capital tanto en el enfoque estndar como en los avanzados.  La tercera modificacin, tambin importante en los prstamos a pymes, es un mayor reconocimiento de garantas y garantes, lo que permite reducir prdidas y, por tanto, reducir el capital requerido. Como indiqu anteriormente, el resultado final es satisfactorio en la medida que no se dificulta el acceso al crdito a la pequea y mediana empresa y, simultneamente, incorpora incentivos a las empresas no financieras para que mejoren sus parmetros fundamentales, de forma que aumenten su calificacin crediticia, y sus prcticas en cuanto a transparencia en su informacin. Confo en que esta pequea incursin en temas financieros y microeconmicos no haya desviado demasiado su atencin del centro de este encuentro, que es la recuperacin de la economa y sus diferenciadas caractersticas en diversas reas geogrficas. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Opening remarks at the "Basel Sessions 2004"
text: Madrid, 6 July 2004 Opening Remarks Basel Sessions 2004. Sponsored by the Institute of International Finance Jaime Cauana Governor of Banco de Espana Chairman of the Basel Committe on Banking Supervision Thank you for that kind introduction. I would like to thank as well Daniel Bouton, Charles Dallara, and the Institute of International Finance for inviting me to participate in this very timely seminar on Basel II. As you know, less than two weeks ago the Basel Committee published the text of Basel II, a document that we have officially named the International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: a Revised Framework. This marked the culmination of an intensive, nearly six-year process of discussion, debate, and consultation to specify the structure and rules for Basel II. I. Preview First of all, Basel II represents the recognition of the good work done by banks in recent times to develop and improve their risk management and measurement systems. It is also an encouragement to continue this work. Therefore, Basel II offers an unparalleled opportunity for banks to improve their capital strategies and risk management systems. Likewise, it offers supervisors with an opportunity to align supervision more closely to sound industry practices and to enhance the dialogue with the industry and among banking supervisors. In our discussions today, we will consider the challenges and opportunities ahead under Basel II from the perspective of banking organisations, supervisory authorities, and the financial industry more broadly. I would like to address these topics from my perspective as Chairman of the Basel Committee. First, I would like to share my views on the significance of Basel IIs recent publication. As I will explain, the conclusion of the work to develop the framework does not mark the end of our work on Basel II. Indeed, in the second part of my remarks this morning, I will identify four transitional matters that we must address during the period leading up to implementation of the new framework. Finally, I will conclude my remarks by sharing with you the Committees plans for future work on regulatory capital. II. The conclusion of the work to specify Basel II Allow me to begin my remarks by sharing some thoughts on the recent conclusion of the work to specify the Basel II framework. The release of the Basel II text marks the end of a challenging but very worthwhile process. Bankers and supervisors alike devoted considerable efforts to this project because we agreed that a new framework was necessary to maintain the relevance of capital supervision to the needs of banking in the twenty-first century. We also recognise that the capital framework serves as a cornerstone to the safe and sound operation of the banking system. Given the importance of the issues at stake, the Committee sought to conduct its discussions in a highly transparent process. We discussed the new framework with many interested parties on the domestic and international levels. I would like to express my appreciation to two groups of external organisations and individuals in particular who supported our efforts. First, I should mention the numerous representatives of banking organisations, industry associations, and other private sector bodies who devoted considerable time and energy to sharing their views. Organisations such as the IIF and its member banks engaged us in a very active dialogue, something that was enormously helpful to improving the quality of the framework. Above all, banks and other private sector bodies helped us to ensure that supervision would be more closely aligned to sound industry practices. A second group I would like to acknowledge consists of those supervisory authorities, central banks, multilateral financial institutions, and other public authorities around the world who shared with us the perspectives and needs of banking systems that are based in many different markets, economies, and legal systems. Thanks to discussions with these colleagues in regional consultations and meetings, the Committee was better able to ensure that the new framework would be relevant to many different kinds of banks and economies that are in various stages of growth and development. Basel II represents a success story in promoting international cooperation and in enhancing the quality of dialogue between banks and their supervisors. And it is a success story for all of us. We have concluded an important phase in our efforts to ensure that the supervision of capital will remain robust and relevant in the future. But we cannot stop to rest yet. As the poet and former banker T.S. Eliot once wrote, What we call a beginning is often the end, and to make an end is to make a beginning. The end is where we start from. Similarly, banks and supervisors know that our work on Basel II has not ended. Indeed, our most important work is in many ways only just beginning, as we must now prepare for the implementation of the new framework. III. The transition to the new framework This leads to my second topic today, namely the work that we will do to move toward the implementation of Basel II. During the upcoming period of transition, banks and supervisors will prepare to embrace a new approach to banking supervision. Basel II represents a new philosophy for supervision, as supervisors have in recent years been turning their focus away from point-in-time assessments of a banks financial condition. Under Basel II, we will look more deeply into the processes and control structures that banks put in place to safeguard their financial health into the future. At the same time, Basel II introduces a new set of incentives for internal controls. The increased use of internal measures of risk as inputs to capital requirements will encourage banking organisations to review, update, and renew their approaches to risk measurement and management constantly. In the short to medium run, these new approaches will require national authorities and banks to invest time, talent, and treasure to adapt their practices and processes to Basel II. In the long run, however, I am confident that these investments will yield stronger controls over risks, a more stable flow of rewards, and a strengthening in our resilience. To implement the new framework successfully, and to realise these longer term benefits, I believe that there are four important transitional matters that we must address in the years leading up to implementation. They are,  first, to transform the framework into enforceable rules;  second, to ensure that the schedule for implementation reflects the overall readiness for new approaches to risk management;  third, to commit our best resources to the parallel calculations or field tests that we will conduct; and,  fourth, to confirm that the new framework will meet its quantitative objectives to maintain broadly the level of overall capital in the system. I would like to take a few moments to address each of these four transitional matters.  Transforming the Basel II framework into national rules Certainly one of the most important legal matters ahead for our transitional period is to transform Basel II into national rules. The text that describes Basel II serves in some ways like a lighthouse, acting as a beacon to guide banks and supervisors in their journey toward the new framework. If Basel II is a lighthouse, then the national rules that actually implement Basel II serve a bit like nautical charts. Just as ships rely on charts for precise information on safe passages and dangers to avoid as they approach the shoreline, national rules provide specific guidance on how the international standards will be applied and enforced with respect to domestic circumstances. Consequently, from the perspective of supervisors, the text that was published in June will now serve as the basis for national rule-making and approval processes to continue. That work is of critical importance to the successful application of the new framework. Each jurisdiction has its own process to follow to articulate those rules. The Committee recognises the need to respect these national processes. Similarly, in publishing the text, the Committee sought to clear the fog that might otherwise have obscured the expectations that supervisors have for banks preparations. Banking organisations now have a stable framework on which to assess their own readiness. They will need to discuss their plans with national supervisors and, equally important, work to understand the national rules that will apply Basel II domestically.  Implementation timing In addition to transforming the framework into national rules, a second matter that we must address during the transition period is to permit banks to apply the new approaches to risk only when they are fully ready to do so. All of us have a keen interest in making sure that the seas we cross from the existing rules to Basel II are not rougher than what we can manage. One way to do so is to launch the journey only when banks systems can master the potential storms they may encounter. The Committee has confirmed that the simpler approaches to credit and operational risks will be available for implementation as of year-end 2006. This is important because many banks have already made considerable investments to prepare for Basel II, and we expect that many will be ready by that point. For banks choosing the advanced IRB approach to credit risk or the advanced measurement approach to operational risk, there is more work to complete. We think that an extra year of preparation and analysis will permit a more successful implementation. It has been said that haste makes waste: in the case of Basel IIs advanced approaches, none of us will benefit from an overly hasty implementation if our systems are not sufficiently ready for actual use as risk management tools. Likewise, national authorities must be sufficiently comfortable with the expected results that the new approaches will offer. Consequently, in order to allow banks and supervisors to benefit from an additional year of impact analysis or parallel capital calculations under the existing and new rules, the most advanced approaches to risk measurement will be available for implementation as of year-end 2007. The IIF has expressed important views about the need to manage a staggered implementation schedule carefully, something that the Committee is working hard to address. In this sense, it is important to notice that the availability of the standard and foundation IRB approaches as of year-end 2006 means that Basel II in fact allows banks to stay on Basel I for an additional year. Therefore, I would encourage all banks to be proactive and to consult carefully with their national supervisors. This would include discussing your plans for the transition period and any arrangements that may help to reduce the potential for a burdensome transition. Bankers and supervisors have a mutual interest in a smooth crossing to the new framework for all banks, whether they are adopting advanced approaches or simpler ones. The Committee will take steps to reduce potential disruptions to competition during the very short period that implementation will be staggered. In this sense, the Committee has agreed to adopt a 95% capital floor for banks using the foundation IRB approach during 2007. Likewise, we are working to encourage cooperation and coordination among home and host supervisors during the period of transition. Supervisors must carry out their legal responsibilities to promote the safety and soundness of their banking systems, while seeking to manage and minimise the degree of burden that may arise as we move toward Basel II. I will allude a bit later to some of the relevant work that is already well underway within the Committees Accord Implementation Group. Nick LePan, the Canadian Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the Vice Chairman of the Committee, will provide a more detailed overview of the AIGs work toward the conclusion of this conference.  Parallel capital calculations and national field tests This second matter regarding the timing of implementation is related closely to a third transitional matter that we must all address, namely running parallel capital calculations or conducting national field tests in 2006 and 2007. These are some of the most important preparations that banks and supervisors will conduct prior to implementation. Parallel calculations and field tests will serve as our best source of information on the effects of Basel II on banks capital requirements. Having access to accurate results will help to ensure the successful implementation of the advanced approaches under Basel II. Parallel calculations will also be important for banks as they prepare for Basel II. Performing the calculations will allow them to ensure that their systems are performing as expected, that they are aware of the impact of the move to Basel II and that they make adjustments as necessary. Parallel calculations and field tests deserve much more attention and commitment from industry leaders than the question of when particular approaches will be available does. Indeed, if advanced approaches have not been calibrated effectively, it does not matter at all when they are implemented. An improperly calibrated framework will never deliver the improved sensitivity to risk and the increased efficiency that we expect. Such a result is clearly not in the interest of the industry or of regulators.  Confirm that the new framework meets the objective of maintaining the overall level of capital This leads to a fourth transitional matter that we must address, namely to confirm that the new framework will meet its quantitative objective to maintain the overall level of capital in the system. The Committee has long stated that its intent is to maintain broadly the aggregate level of capital that is required for the banking system, while still providing incentives for banks to adopt more risk-sensitive approaches to risk measurement and management. Parallel capital calculations and national field tests will help the Committee to review its objectives for the calibration of the new framework prior to its implementation. Should we determine that our objective will not be achieved, we are prepared to address the situation. In particular, if the new framework is found to fall short of maintaining broadly the aggregate level of required capital in the banking system, the Committee may decide that adjustments should be made to the framework. This could include applying a single scaling factor to the capital charges that arise from the internal ratings-based approach to credit risk. The Committee believes that it would be preferable to apply such a factor if the resulting capital requirements conflict with our objectives rather than to make last-minute changes to the IRB approach. Late changes to the fundamental construction of the capital requirement could be disruptive to banks efforts to prepare for its implementation. The IIF has shared its views with the Committee about the potential application of a scaling factor to IRB capital requirements. I want to emphasise that the use of a scaling factor is fully consistent with our long-held objective to avoid increasing or decreasing the overall level of capital required for the banking system. Moreover, it in no way undermines the potential for individual banks to achieve reductions in their capital requirements if they adopt advanced methods and can demonstrate that their exposures to risk are indeed lower. In fact, we recognise that Basel II will allow for capital requirements to be redistributed among individual banks I should moreover emphasise that the scaling factor, if applied, might be less than or greater than one. While the introduction to the Basel II text cites a factor that might be slightly higher than 1.0, I want to emphasise that we provided this figure purely to give the industry insight into our best and most current sense of where the factor may lie. During the transition period, we may learn from banks calculations that this figure was too conservative  or perhaps not conservative enough. This re-emphasises the importance of the parallel calculations and field tests and the reasons why we must all devote our best efforts to them. IV. The Committees future agenda for regulatory capital Together, these four matters  namely, transforming Basel II into national rules, implementing the approaches at appropriate times, conducting parallel calculations and field tests, and verifying that Basel IIs objectives will be met  constitute the issues that banks and supervisors must address immediately in the months ahead as we make the transition from the existing rules to the new framework. I would like to conclude my remarks today by giving you some insight into the Basel Committees agenda for future work on regulatory capital relevant to Basel II. The new framework is intended to be a more forward-looking approach to capital supervision, and certainly the Committee intends to keep Basel II up to date with changes underway in risk management in the industry. We must continue to monitor industry developments to make sure that Basel II reflects sound practices. We intend to do so in part by continuing to cultivate a dialogue with industry participants and with other supervisors in the coming months and years. We expect that dialogue will be particularly important in the area of double default  that is, the likelihood that both a borrower and a guarantor default on the same obligation may be lower than the likelihood of the guarantor defaulting alone. The Committee believes that we must recognise double default in the new framework, though it is also essential that we consider all of the implications, especially those related to measurement, before we agree to a particular solution. We intend to continue to work on this issue with the goal of finding a prudentially sound solution as promptly as possible prior to the implementation of the new framework. Alongside this work, we have begun joint work with the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) on various issues related to trading activities, such as the potential future exposure of derivative positions. Similarly, as I suggested earlier, the Committees Accord Implementation Group has developed a detailed agenda for its work through 2005. As you all know, implementation issues have become very important as we enter into this new phase of the work of the Committee. They are important both for supervisors and banks, as you have mentioned in many of your comments recently. These are difficult issues where it is essential that we give the right answers, and develop adequate and clear implementation solutions. As Nick LePan will discuss later today, the AIG is studying issues may arise in the cross-border application of the new Framework and how home and host supervisors may work through such issues. It is also studying Pillar 2 issues and considering principles and options for implementing Pillar 2 and will take up important technical work on how banks should best develop estimates of losses given default in economic downturns, among other issues. Over the longer term, the Committee intends to undertake work on the definition of capital. This is motivated in part by changes to the Basel II framework related to the treatment of expected versus unexpected losses, which, together with changes to the treatment of provisions, tend to reduce Tier 1 capital requirements relative to total capital requirements. Likewise, we have to consider the impact of International Accounting Standards that will begin to be applied in many countries from next year onwards. A final area related to capital that the Committee intends to discuss with the industry over the longer term includes risk management practices that aim to quantify measures of risk and economic capital. Leading institutions have invested substantial resources in modelling credit risk, something that Basel II stops short of recognising for regulatory capital requirements. Nonetheless, we know that the IIF and many banks are deeply interested in moving toward greater recognition of these practices in the future. We recognise the need to continue to discuss such practices with banks. We intend to use Basel II as a means of developing experience in the performance of such models. The Committee will continue this discussion with a view toward potentially allowing the greater use of credit risk modelling for regulatory capital purposes in the future and working towards the recognition of diversification effects. These discussions will focus on addressing concerns such as those regarding the reliability, comparability, validation, and competitive equity that might arise when greater recognition of full credit risk modelling is permitted. V. Conclusion The recent publication of the text of Basel II marks the end of an important phase in our work. But, let me repeat T.S. Eliots words that to make an end is to make a beginning. It is now time for all of us to redouble our efforts to build the necessary infrastructure that will support the successful implementation of the new framework. For supervisors and other authorities, this means converting Basel II into national rules and providing guidance to banks to help smooth the transition to the new framework. For banks, this means working to enhance internal systems and controls to improve the quality of their risk management. Ultimately, our goal for Basel II is to encourage prudent risk-taking and the adequate capitalisation of banking organisations. We expect that, when banks have the right incentives to manage their risks appropriately and to hold sufficient levels of capital, the financial system as a whole will become more resilient, more stable, and better able to serve as a source for credit and growth. Those characteristics matter greatly to the health of the overall economy, to the livelihood of consumers, and to the outlook for commerce and business. To harvest the benefits of Basel II, we must avoid the tendency to view this as merely an exercise in compliance. Banks should, of course, work to comply with the letter of Basel IIs requirements, but I would encourage you to seek to achieve its spirit as well. We should view Basel II as an opportunity to do those things that make good economic sense to strengthen the quality of risk management and to enhance the stability of the financial system. Thank you for your attention this morning.

Title: Opening Conference: Banking and regional integration: Lessons from the European Union for Central America (III Central American Regional Conference, organized by the Central American Monetary Council, the International Monetary Fund, and the Central Bank of Honduras)
text: San Pedro Sula Honduras, 8 July 2004 Banking supervision in the twenty-first century Third Central American Regional Conference "Economic growth and bank resolution issues". Central American Monetary Council and International Monetary Fund Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. Ladies and gentlemen: My first words should be of gratitude both to the Central American Monetary Council and to the International Monetary Fund, organizers of this Conference, as well as to the institution that hosts it, the Central Bank of Honduras. The gratitude that I express to you, for giving me the opportunity to participate in it, joins the recognition and congratulations that I send you for enabling this forum for debate, in which, without a doubt, there is an invaluable exchange of ideas about such central aspects as the identification of the factors and policies that would enhance the economic development of the region. as well as those aimed at the establishment of solid financial systems capable of favoring such economic development. I sincerely believe that sound financial systems require robust regulatory and supervisory frameworks and prudential supervision has made significant progress over the past 20 years, contributing to greater financial stability, which is essential for sustaining the growth of our economies. Today I would like to share with you some thoughts on the elements that, in my opinion, should be part of a supervisory model that has the necessary capacity to face the new challenges posed by the many and rapid changes in financial systems. Such a supervisory model, due to the variety of existing financial systems and the very dynamism of the sector, will need to be able to adapt to the situation of each banking system and should be able to evolve. In fact, banking supervision is, to a large extent, the result of the experience of banking crises, for different reasons and with varying intensity, in a number of countries. The need to combine theoretical advances with lessons learned, both from past experiences and from the analysis of the evolution of best banking practices, requires flexibility, adaptability, willingness to learn and a certain critical spirit. For this reason, I will begin by criticizing the title that I myself have chosen for this conference: "Banking supervision in the twenty-first century". In a world as dynamic as the one in which we live, where financial structures and instruments, as well as risks and their distribution, are increasingly complex and global, there is little about which we can be sure in order to face this century that has just begun, is the need to be in a position to face the innovations and surprises that, They will undoubtedly test our level of preparation, adaptability and learning, as well as the supervisory framework itself. The reflections that I will share with you today are the product of an attempt to combine two types of experiences. On the one hand, that of the Bank of Spain, from its perspective as a supervisory entity of the banking system and a central bank that ensures financial stability, to the extent that we too have suffered banking crises, coming to understand the high associated costs. On the other hand, the experience gained from the work of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, especially those aimed at preparing Basel II, which, as you know, was adopted in the last week of last June. The amendment of the 1988 Agreement has led the Committee to an intensive and very open consultation and discussion process, addressing central issues of banking supervision, such as capital, the supervisory process, market discipline and cooperation between supervisors. This process has been long and has involved different institutions and organizations, the industry itself and, of course, supervisors, central banks and academics from all over the world. I believe that the New Regulatory Framework for Capital has required a reflection that has great value in itself, while it has allowed to establish very consistent principles and bases on which to build a solid, effective and forward-looking supervision. Trying to integrate the different experiences of the different countries and an analysis as deep as that carried out over these years, implies combining very specific aspects, such as, for example, in the Spanish case, the important role that elements such as provisions, emphasis on the consolidated group, have in our supervisory model, or as the intense surveillance of the quality of bank assets through on-site inspections, with more theoretical analyses that relate the risks with capital, economic and regulatory, that they require. Basel II represents a new supervisory approach in which concepts such as risk sensitivity, establishment of incentives, consistency in the application of rules, process supervision, transparency, etc., become more relevant and integrated into a single regulatory framework. I believe that this combination of elements adequately reflects the nature of prudential supervision, which should make the best theoretical foundations compatible with practical and organisational elements learned from experience. Throughout my speech, I will try to organize my reflections around a set of basic aspects that, of course, are not intended to cover all areas of banking supervision but simply to emphasize some of the issues that seem to me to be particularly relevant. 1. Search for financial stability. Cooperation between industry and supervision in response to the dynamism of the financial sector. As I have pointed out earlier, the financial sector in general, and the banking sector in particular, is characterized by its high dynamism. Although general trends have not manifested themselves with equal intensity in all countries, there are four factors that, I believe, are fundamental to understanding the dynamics of the sector in recent decades and that can help to understand the necessary evolution of supervisory models. First, growth in banking and financial activity has been proportionally higher than in the real sector, driven both by significant technological advances and institutional developments that have made it possible to have more mature financial markets and reliable and efficient payment systems. It is precisely the process of technological advancement that helps explain the second of the elements I would like to mention: the growing sophistication of the banking business. This process of sophistication is evident when observing the wide and varied range of products, increasingly complex, that, based on previously unthinkable data processing, are now at our disposal. At the same time, the sophistication of the banking business has allowed entities to offer a set of solutions that, on the one hand, enable a greater approach to the customer by improving the services they have traditionally been providing to society and their quality and, on the other, has made it possible for them to operate with a higher level of efficiency. The third element is the increasing degree of competition that institutions have had to face, and which has required them, and I believe that it will undoubtedly continue to demand of them, a continuous effort to contain their costs in order to guarantee their own survival through more efficient behaviour. The increase in competition has not only occurred within national borders, a consequence, among other factors, of the process of financial disintermediation, but in recent decades, the banking and financial sectors in general have experienced a strong process of internationalization. Precisely, the increasing sophistication and internationalization of financial institutions, together with the greater sophistication of the business, have contributed to the emergence of new risks and to the intensification and transmission of existing ones, which poses challenges to which banking supervision will have to respond that, however, does not imply a brake on financial innovation. Let me recall, and this is the fourth element I will mention, that it has been the bank managers themselves who, as a counterweight to this growing complexity and diversification of their business, have devoted preferential attention to improving their risk management systems, allocating more technical and human resources to the implementation of the necessary means to identify them. measure and control them. A few years ago, being in charge of supervision at the Bank of Spain, I attended an international conference on risk management. One of the speakers, the chief risk officer of a large international bank, showed on one slide the private banking sector represented by an impressive sports car, while, on the next slide, he represented supervisors using a turtle. The speaker wondered how to make a turtle go at high speed to be able to follow the pace of a sports car. The answer was reflected in the next slide, in which the turtle was seen climbing in the sports car. Comparison aside, there is some merit in thinking that supervisors and industry should travel together to build more stable financial systems. The experience and discussion process of Basel II show the possibility and desirability of establishing a richer dialogue to improve banking practices, without abandoning our focus and mission as supervisors. 2. Importance of the macroprudential approach. Beyond this need for ongoing dialogue between supervisors and industry, the importance of integrating a macroprudential approach into prudential supervision requires several considerations. Traditionally, there has been broad consensus on the importance of the institutional framework and macroeconomic stability as necessary preconditions for sustained economic growth. Moreover, many financial crises have not been caused by shocks originating in the financial system, but by macroeconomic causes. In this regard, it is therefore necessary to be clear that prudential supervision is only one part of the set of policies necessary to achieve stability in the banking system. Economic policies aimed at macroeconomic stability are therefore essential, especially price stability and fiscal discipline. It should also not be forgotten that the crises experienced in different countries highlight the importance of strengthening other macroeconomic policy mechanisms, including: 1) ensure flexibility and consistency between the exchange rate scheme chosen and the internal policies themselves; 2) limit the vulnerabilities associated with exchange rate instability processes in the balance sheets of the different sectors of the economy; and 3) consider that certain economies have a high sensitivity to the volatility of capital flows, sometimes altered by factors external to the country in question. In this regard, allow me to make a final double thought. First, supervision should be based on a comprehensive analysis of internal and external vulnerabilities to the banking sector, including the necessary macroeconomic, institutional and stability elements of the money and capital markets in which institutions operate and implement their investment, hedging and financing strategies. Financial stability reports are being produced and even published in many countries. The Bank of Spain, for example, has been doing this for two years and I must say that, although its preparation is complex and resource-intensive, the results are very positive. On the other hand, prudential regulation and supervision should extend its objectives beyond the attempt to avoid the occurrence of crises, also seeking to achieve greater financial stability, a concept that is undoubtedly broader, including resistance to external shocks and the ability to contribute to the proper functioning of the economy in different circumstances. I believe that prudential supervisors, central banks or not, must also analyse to what extent the conditions exist for the banking system to fulfil its function and also its micro and macro vulnerabilities. In pursuit of these broader objectives, collaboration between prudential supervisors and central banks, when they do not coincide, may be particularly relevant. 3. Don't forget the basics. An effective monitoring system requires a set of preconditions that serve as foundations on which to solidly build the system architecture. In addition to the need to adopt a set of sound and prudent macroeconomic policies, it will be necessary to have an adequate structure of commercial and civil laws, including the treatment of bankruptcy situations, accounting obligations that guarantee a homogeneous representation of economic facts, external audit requirements, guarantee funds that provide adequate protection, supervisors with operational capacity and independence, etc. The legal structure and its application by the judicial system must provide respect for property rights, equality before the law... In short, legal certainty. Tomorrow a session is devoted to discussing one of these important elements, the design of an appropriate crisis resolution framework, and the search for best practices, which, as the programme rightly says, is important both for preventing crises and for managing them in ways that make them less costly. The need for this set of minimum preconditions is reinforced by the "Core Principles for an Effective Banking Supervision", without which, today, it is not possible to describe the structure of supervisory systems. The Core Principles, published by the Committee in September 1997, are based on the best practices identified in the world, and not only allow each country to develop self-assessment processes, but also play a central role in the Financial Sector Assessment Programs (FSAP) of international organizations. The brevity, for reasons of time, in enumerating the above elements does not do justice to the importance that each and every one of them has in achieving a stable and efficient financial system. I think we all have first-hand experiences of how the lack of effective compliance with these principles has brought serious negative consequences for our banking systems. Without going any further, Spain had a major banking crisis between 1978 and 1983 in which more than 50 banks of the 108 initially existing failed and at least 10 of the 25 principles were breached: - Banking licensing principles were not complied with. Many of those granted, since the creation of new banks had been authorized in 1962, were under the protection of influences that did not take into account the professional and moral quality of managers and shareholders with significant holdings, nor the prevention of possible conflicts of interest between the objectives of these shareholders. - The principles relating to the need to assess asset quality, monitor concentration, avoid risks with related entities or the need for an adequate provisioning and capital system were also not complied with. - Finally, the legal regulations were not adequate for the supervisor to have the ability to take supervisory measures with sufficient speed, efficiency and legal certainty. The list could go on, the important thing is that, as a result of the crisis, there was a legislative change and a substantial extension of resources which is the basis of our present supervisory system. In short, the Core Principles, in their role of defining and outlining the minimum criteria for an effective monitoring system, remain fully in force. This recognition, together with the accumulated experience - and, in this sense, the FSAP and the work of the IMF, have been very enlightening - points to the desirability of continuing to deepen the effective implementation of the principles and also to the desirability of a certain small revision, rather adjustments, so that they remain current and adequate to the new realities. 4. Regulation based on incentives: improvement of risk management. Always bearing in mind the basic elements necessary for effective supervision, I believe that the future of financial regulation and supervision lies in strengthening the necessary incentives to promote the proper functioning of institutions and, in particular, the continuous improvement of their risk measurement and management systems. Despite great strides made by the banking sector in the use of models and new technologies, the banking business still depends, in large part, on the knowledgeable and expert judgment of risk managers. However, these judgments can and should be reinforced by processing the available information using the best techniques and tools available at any given time. Risk assessment and control methods, to the extent that they acquire a greater degree of formalization and rigor, will reduce the probability of making failures in decision-making and will help to promptly detect deviations from the initial objectives or, simply, errors, allowing institutions to implement corrective measures early. In recent years, financial institutions have made significant achievements in the field of risk measurement and management, and I believe that advances in quantification methods, which we are already seeing, will experience enormous momentum in the coming decades. Public policies must also collaborate in the development of incentive systems, trying not to impose unnecessary burdens on entities, avoiding an excessive degree of interventionism and encouraging healthy and prudent action by managers. In particular, the necessary measures should be developed so that they identify and understand the risks they face, consider those that may arise in the future and respond promptly and actively to both. As I have had occasion to repeat on numerous occasions, Basel II is much more than a new system for setting the regulatory minimum capital and, possibly, the main change compared to the 1988 agreement is precisely the incorporation of incentives to encourage improvement in risk management. Good risk management, supported by good corporate governance structures and practices, will also help to strengthen a bank's first line of defence, i.e. strengthen and sound its income statement. It will also help to measure and determine the provisions and capital necessary to meet expected and unexpected losses, so that sufficient certainty is given to the continuity of the banking enterprise and sufficient room for manoeuvre to carry out its functions without restriction, even in difficult circumstances. 5. Gain room for manoeuvre. Relevance of the time horizon and countercyclical factors. Indeed, the need to create provisions to cover expected losses and to have sufficient capital to restore unexpected losses, allowing institutions to have a certain margin for manoeuvre, is among the basic principles set out in any risk management manual. Therefore, capital and provisions are an essential part of any supervisory framework and I would venture to point out that Basel II reinforces the need to implement good policies in both areas. In this sense, it is important to analyze provisions and capital considering an adequate time horizon that allows to take into account the experience throughout at least one complete cycle, assessing, in addition, different potential future scenarios, taking into account past experience and the present situation. An action in this direction does not imply that there is a tendency towards uniformity in the time horizons of the investment decisions of market participants, but rather on the contrary, greater heterogeneity in the time horizons would be desirable in order to avoid imitation behaviour between agents. What does seem important is that risk managers are fully aware of how the elements that determine risk are modified and evolve over economic cycles, so that they incorporate that knowledge into their models and thus be able to design appropriate risk management policies, provisions, equity and liquidity. I also personally believe that, as far as possible, it would be appropriate to induce a certain countercyclical behaviour, thus trying to compensate for the natural tendency of banking systems to behave procyclically. It seems sensible that institutions have, during the good times of the economic cycle, sufficient room for manoeuvre to strengthen their financial situation, thus being able to face less favorable circumstances with greater guarantees of success and without the need to suddenly change their investment decisions. This idea of gaining room for manoeuvre and strengthening during the good times of the cycle, through both capital and provisions, is the reflection of prudent policy, but it is also consistent from a theoretical point of view of risk management. In general, it is common to think that the risks increase in bad times. However, this is only partly true. From my point of view, the exposures committed by financial institutions, and therefore the risks, increase in the bullish phases of the cycle and it is in times of difficulty when these risks materialize. Not surprisingly, banks' credit policy errors, despite the fact that credit risk is the most important they face and perhaps therefore the best known, tend to be concentrated in the expansionary phases of the cycle. When establishing a correct capital policy, it must be borne in mind that, due to the existence of transaction costs and given the presence of information asymmetries in financial markets, it can be difficult to increase capital in times of difficulty when it will be most needed. In short, with the intention of strengthening in good times, managers must design capital and provisions strategies, adopting an appropriate time horizon and remembering that the imbalances that make financial instability possible tend to accumulate in expansionary phases. 6. The risk approach as a complement to traditional supervision. As banking systems have evolved, supervisory procedures have had to be improved and modernised in many respects, and the concept of 'risk' is beginning to play a predominant role. The banking supervision that we could call traditional has sought to ensure the solvency of entities by emphasizing the accounting review of their financial and patrimonial situation. This approach is increasingly limited, and, today, it is necessary to incorporate and systematize elements of analysis that provide a greater capacity for anticipation. Moreover, in a globalized, changing and competitive environment, in which institutions assume risk positions or incorporate new complex products that can drastically and quickly modify their financial situation, it is essential to complement the accounting approach with a greater emphasis on the analysis of the risks that affect the entities and the management and control systems they implement to limit them. I would like to insist on the word complement, since it is not a question of replacing traditional supervision, but of enhancing it with a more systematic analysis of the risks of the entity and its management capacity. In my opinion, the work of reviewing asset quality and ensuring a correct provisioning or diversification policy, among others, will continue to be of vital importance to contribute to the health of banking systems. The implications of the change in the orientation of supervision are important, both in terms of its internal organisation and the relationship to be established with the institutions, with which it has to work closely and fostering a richer dialogue. The Bank of Spain has been working since 1999 to incorporate a more formalized risk approach into its supervisory model and, although there is still a long way to go, I believe that the experience is positive and is preparing us for the future implementation of Basel II, which will undoubtedly represent a fundamental boost to this approach. 7. Transparency. In this process of change, the exercise of market discipline is already a factor that must be present in any supervisory model as an essential element for the success of prudential policies. In particular, in order to ensure responsible and prudent behaviour of bank managers, not only supervisory action is necessary, but minority shareholders, depositors and debt holders should have the ability to assess institutions, rewarding well-managed banks and penalising others who behave recklessly. In order for market discipline to be exercised, a necessary prerequisite is that of information transparency, and banks must publish quantitative and qualitative information that enables market participants to assess the equity situation, the results obtained by the bank, its risk profile and the practices used in its management and control. Again, I would like to highlight that Basel II, through pillar 3, facilitates greater transparency in these last elements, the risk profile and its management, complementing, in a valuable way, the more traditional accounting data. 8. Cooperation between supervisors. The increasing internationalisation and complexity of banking groups and financial markets in recent years, together with the evolution of supervision, including the introduction of Basel II, makes it necessary to intensify the degree of international cooperation between supervisors. This issue is not new, but it is becoming increasingly important. Effectively integrating the necessary supervision at local level in the host country (host) with effective supervision at consolidated level in the home country (home) requires greater cooperation, greater exchange of information and better knowledge of financial instruments and linkages within financial groups. All this is especially relevant, as is logical, in those situations in which banks with a systemic impact in a country are part of international groups or, in those others, in which the operations carried out in a country by an international group are systemically important for the entire group. Basel II adds additional reasons for coordination, for example, due to the need to validate internal rating models used at the level of an international banking group. Therefore, in the future it will be necessary to promote greater cooperation, coordination and consistency in the way of evaluating the capital that entities have to maintain according to the risks they assume, thus favoring consistency in the implementation of standards, competitive equality and the reduction of unnecessary regulatory burdens for entities, while reducing the incentives they may have to practice regulatory arbitrage between different jurisdictions. In conclusion, I would like to share with you some thoughts on the contribution of Basel II in promoting financial stability, as well as on the appropriateness of all countries adopting, as they become ready, this new approach. 9. Basel II: a big step in the right direction. As you all know, the 1988 Capital Accord has been adopted by a huge number of countries and is one of the most influential jobs in the financial world. In recent years, and after recognizing that the successful 1988 Agreement was no longer fully satisfactory to meet the increasingly complex reality in which major international entities operate, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has worked hard to introduce the necessary reforms to achieve a New Capital Regulatory Framework capable of overcoming the limitations of its predecessor. The New Capital Regulatory Framework will represent a substantial advance in the development of a framework that promotes a more stable behavior of the financial system and, perhaps, its greatest guarantee of success is that its design has taken into account, among others, the set of principles to which I have been referring. In particular, Basel II is aware of the importance of the time horizon in risk management and has numerous clauses on the importance of considering low cycle periods and stressful situations. The New Capital Regulatory Framework is based on the idea that to the extent that entities are better capitalized and managed, they will be more stable and able to cope with periods of stress, not acting as mechanisms that amplify problems.
