On the other hand, the approach proposed by the New Capital Regulatory Framework has a comprehensive character, which is evidenced not only by the joint action of the three famous pillars (minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline), but also in that it covers a wide set of risks, takes into account the existence of increasingly complex transactions that must be properly considered and incorporates numerous Risk mitigation, with the aim, without a doubt, of achieving a more effective approximation of regulatory capital to economic capital. The need to introduce appropriate incentive systems is also present in the design of Basel II. In fact, in my opinion, it is one of the great innovations compared to Basel I. In particular, the New Capital Regulatory Framework establishes the necessary means to ensure that those with a higher risk profile are obliged to allocate a higher level of capital. Moreover, Basel II has been sensitive to concerns about the need to consider an appropriate time horizon for the calculation of model variables, the need to use broad time horizons in the design of internal rating systems, and also the need to incorporate stress test analysis. With regard to the principles on which Basel II is based, which I believe will guarantee their future validity, allow me to indicate two additional ones: The first is its evolutionary character. That is, the Committee itself recognizes that the banking sector is dynamic and complex enough to seek to achieve a Capital Regulatory Framework that remains unchanged over a given period of years. The second concerns the recognition that international cooperation between supervisors in different countries is important. Basel II establishes the necessary mechanisms to promote greater cooperation, coordination and consistency in the way of applying the Capital Regulatory Framework. Moreover, Committee members, as well as other supervisors, are working to find ways to foster communication and cooperation between supervisors in an institution's home country and those in the host country. All in all, Basel II is a major step in the right direction and will undoubtedly contribute to a more resilient, stable banking system capable of promoting sustainable economic growth. However, I have sometimes detected a certain degree of concern about whether Basel II would be appropriate for the banking systems of emerging countries. I have also noted some concern on the part of non-Committee members about the proposed implementation timetable. Let me conclude my speech by giving you, albeit briefly, my point of view on these two issues. Firstly, the supervisory approach on which the New Framework is based and the set of alternatives offered in it, I believe make it valid for all markets and for all institutions. This is not to say that more advanced approaches are not reserved for internationally active banks. In the case of Spain, for example, we expect that both due to the type of operations developed by Spanish entities, and the requirement of the minimum requirements necessary to access the different methodologies, the number of these that opt for the most advanced models will be reduced and the result of a gradual process over time. We in the Committee have defended and defend the idea that, although we believe that Basel II is the direction in which we must evolve, no country should adopt Basel II if it feels that it is not yet ready and, if it chooses to do so, the timetable must be the one that best suits its circumstances. We believe that Basel II is the best reference to guide future changes and therefore, we expect that, over time, the number of countries accessing the New Regulatory Framework for Capital will increase. It is up to the national authorities who, in accordance with their responsibilities, must analyse the appropriateness, procedure and timetable for the adoption of Basel II. The discussions I have had with various supervisors have been very positive; we all want to have the best supervisory system and Basel II is the right direction to go. Recently, an ISF/BIS survey on Basel II implementation showed that of 107 responses received from non-Committee countries, 88 intend to adopt Basel II and many by 2009. If we add the member countries of the Committee, more than 100 countries are likely to adopt the New Framework. In this transition process, a three-stage approach may be most appropriate: First, focus on the fundamentals of the banking system and supervision. That is, an appropriate legal and accounting framework, which provides legal certainty, compliance with the 'core principles', a good system of verification of the quality of assets, classification of credits, concentrations, etc. Second, to strengthen the three pillars, without having to comply with the detailed Basel rules. That is, improve the capitalization of the banking system, strengthen supervision by improving its ability to introduce the risk approach and improving transparency. And third, implement the transition from the 1988 Agreement to Basel II, selecting the alternatives that best suit the situation of the particular banking system. This three-stage approach recognizes that Basel II is not simply a set of rules, but that there is a real concern to improve quality in risk management. 10. Conclusions. Let me, by way of conclusion, emphasize that supervisors have a responsibility to promote the solvency and stability of our financial systems, and to this end we must devote our resources and efforts to ensuring that banking supervision in the twenty-first century is: More dynamic, able to adapt to the evolution and innovations of the sector and to offer an agile response to the phenomena of innovation and concentration. More preventive, always completing the necessary diagnostic tasks with extensive vulnerability analysis and a risk approach, which allows a greater capacity for anticipation and crisis prevention. More flexible, recognizing that the complexity of banking groups and the different class and performance of entities requires, in many cases, tailored supervisory criteria. More inclusive, combining rules, some supervisory discretion based on dialogue with the industry and market discipline. And finally, in line with the last comment, more transparent, favoring an adequate understanding of the supervisory function by citizens, thus responding to their growing demand for more information. In short, I am sure that despite everything said, reality will be surprising and rich in nuances, so we will have to continue adapting and learning. I believe that the ultimate goal of financial stability increasingly requires that industry, markets and supervisors, each taking their respective place, have the incentives aligned and join forces. Thank you very much for your attention.

Este enfoque en tres etapas reconoce que Basilea II no es simplemente un conjunto de reglas, sino que existe una preocupacin verdadera por mejorar la calidad en la gestin del riesgo. 10. Conclusiones. Permtanme que, a modo de conclusin, enfatice que los supervisores tenemos la responsabilidad de propiciar la solvencia y la estabilidad de nuestros sistemas financieros, y para ello hemos de dedicar nuestros recursos y esfuerzos a que la supervisin bancaria del siglo XXI sea: Ms dinmica, capaz adaptarse a la evolucin e innovaciones del sector y de ofrecer una respuesta gil a los fenmenos de innovacin y concentracin. Ms preventiva, completando siempre las necesarias tareas de diagnstico con amplios anlisis de vulnerabilidades y un enfoque riesgo, que permita una mayor capacidad de anticipacin y de prevencin de crisis. Ms flexible, reconociendo que la complejidad de los grupos bancarios y la diferente clase y actuacin de las entidades exige, en muchas ocasiones, criterios supervisores a la medida. Ms integradora, combinando reglas, cierta discrecin supervisora basada en el dilogo con la industria y la disciplina de mercado. Y finalmente, en lnea con el ltimo comentario, ms transparente, favoreciendo una adecuada comprensin de la funcin supervisora por parte de los ciudadanos, respondiendo as a su creciente demanda de mayor informacin. En definitiva, estoy seguro de que a pesar de todo lo dicho, la realidad ser sorprendente y rica en matices, por lo que deberemos seguir adaptndonos y aprendiendo. Creo que el objetivo final de la estabilidad financiera requiere cada vez ms que la industria, los mercados y supervisores, cada uno ocupando su respectivo lugar, tengamos los incentivos alineados y aunemos esfuerzos. Title: Conference: Towards an effective implementation of the New Basel Capital Accord (International seminar "The New Basel Capital Accord: Challenges and Opportunities for the Americas", organized by the Association of Banking Supervisors of the Americas, the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies, and the Latin American Federation of Banks)
text: Mexico City July 12, 2004 Towards an effective implementation of the Basel New Capital Framework Basel II: challenges and opportunities for the Americas Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA) Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA) Latin American Federation of Banks (FELABAN) Jaime Caruana Jaime Caruana, Governor of the Bank of Spain Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Ladies and gentlemen: I would like to begin by expressing my sincere thanks to Jonathan Davis, President of the National Banking and Securities Commission of Mexico for his words of welcome, to ASBA (Richard Spillenkothen), CEMLA (Kenneth Coates) and FELABAN (Ignacio Salvatierra) for the kindness of having invited me to pronounce these words, and for the wisdom of convening this seminar at a fundamental moment in the development of the new proposals of the Basel Committee. I would also like to congratulate you on the careful selection of topics, speakers and participants. I have very good memories of the ASBA and CEMLA meetings: The last time I participated in an ASBA assembly was in Puerto Rico 4 years ago and about a year ago I had the opportunity to participate in the CEMLA meeting held in Seville. It is a great satisfaction for me to be in Mexico City today to take part in this joint initiative of ASBA, CEMLA and FELABAN to talk about an issue to which I have paid some attention in recent years. As you know, just over two weeks ago the Basel Committee published the document entitled "International convergence of capital measurement and capital standards: a revised framework", which we have commonly referred to as Basel II. The publication of Basel II begins a new stage for supervisory bodies and financial institutions: the adoption and transposition of regulations in each of the jurisdictions, as well as the effective implementation of Basel II. This new phase will be characterized by the need for efforts of a different nature from those that have been carried out so far, but it will still be necessary to have the same degree of collaboration and constructive dialogue on the part of banks, supervisory bodies, central banks and other stakeholders around the world. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision concludes almost six years of work to design a new regulatory framework for regulatory capital, which we believe provides an adequate response to the profound changes experienced in financial markets and in much of international banking activity. I believe that Basel II is a success for international cooperation on prudential regulation, and communication between regulators and the banking sector around the world. The very process of consultations, seminars, meetings etc. that has been followed has great value in itself: it has helped us to define concepts better, to know each other better and to better understand the nature of risks and banking practices. Basel II represents, in my opinion, a great opportunity for both banks and their supervisors. With Basel II, banks are recognized for their efforts to improve risk management and have incentives to continue working in that direction. For supervisors, Basel II represents a great opportunity to enrich the dialogue with industry and improve collaboration between us. Today I would like to make two general comments on the new Capital Regulatory Framework, including the additional work that we are going to undertake, and three comments on the most important part, namely the development of the implementation or implementation work. 1) New supervisory approach in response to the dynamism of changes in the financial sector. Improvement in the stability of the banking system. As is well known, the Basel Accord of 1988, commonly known today as Basel I, established the first internationally accepted capital requirement. Its simplicity was one of the elements of its success and this is reflected in the fact that today it is applied in more than one hundred countries and has become a market standard. However, this same simplicity means that more than fifteen years after its approval it has become obsolete for many supervisors and banks, due to the tremendous development of the methodologies of management and risk measurement of the entities in these years. Advances in technology and developments in financial markets have led banks to apply increasingly sophisticated systems for measuring and managing risks, which allow them to make increasingly accurate measurements of risks. In addition, these new techniques have been applied not only to what is traditionally their most important risk, that is, credit risk, but also to other risks, such as operational risk. Market developments have also provided certain tools, such as risk transfer, including securitisation, that offer additional opportunities for management. These advances meant that the simplicity of the rules contained in Basel I increasingly clashed with the practices and business needs of the most sophisticated entities, and caused some dissatisfaction among supervisors who lacked a tool adapted to the new realities. It was becoming increasingly clear that the simplicity of the supervisor's risk measurement rules was not in line with reality. In other words, it was necessary to bring the calculation of regulatory capital closer to the calculation of the economic capital of entities. Thus begins the work aimed at modifying the existing framework, replacing it with another more sophisticated and in line with the new realities. And one of the important features of this work was the ongoing dialogue between the Committee, banks, non-committee supervisors, and other stakeholders. To replace the 1988 Framework, a scheme based on three pillars was decided: a5 The first pillar is a thorough review of the minimum capital requirements set out in Basel I, aligning risk measurement with the techniques used by institutions that have demonstrated best practices. a5 The other two pillars are new, not because they were not already exercised by supervisors, but because it is the first time they have been integrated into the capital regulatory framework. a5 The second pillar is the so-called supervisory review, which requires banks to internally assess the capital they need based on their particular risk profile, and instructs supervisors to review this internal assessment, facilitating a richer dialogue with the institution. a5 Finally, the third pillar, that of market discipline, reinforces the external incentives that banks have to prudently manage their business through information transparency. These three pillars constitute a much more sophisticated and comprehensive approach than the single-pillar approach of 1988. But, in addition to this, they constitute a profound change in the prudential supervision of institutions. The incentives introduced by Pillar 1, together with the necessary interaction with the other two pillars, make Basel II much more than quantitative capital requirements. It is also, and in particular, a stimulus to the continuous development and extension of best practices in risk management and measurement. In addition, I would like to recall that Basel II offers a real menu of options, from the simplest to the most sophisticated, so that its basic principles can be applied to very different types of banks in different countries. The simplified standard approach, the simplest possible version of the new framework, is included as Annex 9 and has 11 pages. In this regard, I believe that Basel II represents an excellent opportunity for all types of banks in all types of economies. I would like to make a brief comment on this. In particular, there have been views that raised uncertainties about the influence of the new Capital Framework on capital flows and financing in emerging countries. The basic argument is that because Basel II is more sensitive to risk, exposures to countries with a higher level of risk will lead to increased capital requirements and this may decrease financing flows. I think there are several comments that appreciably qualify the effects of this argument: a5 First, what the New Capital Framework does is approach the best practices that banks are effectively using today. It tries to approximate regulatory capital to economic capital, that is, to the calculation of capital that banks themselves are using to make their decisions. To the extent that this economic capital, more or less sophisticated and formalized, is the main element in decision-making and is not altered by the change to the new Capital Framework, it does not seem that Basel II necessarily has to produce major changes in the behavior of banks. a5 Analysis carried out on the behavior of banks suggests that in making decisions about investments or on prices of e.g. syndicated loans, the degree of risk of the investment is taken and the expected income is adjusted. All this regardless of the regulatory capital required, which is undoubtedly important and may pose a global constraint, but which, in practice, has less influence on individual decisions. a5 In fact, at present, in many countries, the requirements that supervisors demand are significantly higher than the minimum regulatory requirements and banks, by their own decision, maintain ratios even above these levels. For all these reasons, I believe that, in general, excessive importance is given to regulatory capital in the behavior of banks and perhaps not enough attention is paid to the other channel of influence that Basel II has, which is to encourage improvement in risk management and which can undoubtedly bring significant improvements to financial stability. I believe, for example, that adequately capitalized banking systems, well managed with risk analyses that incorporate sufficiently long time horizons, are more stable, tend to behave less abruptly and can help mitigate the excessive volatility of funding flows in emerging countries. a5 In addition to the above, it is worth remembering that, in many cases, as a result of dialogue with supervisors around the world, elements have been introduced in Basel II that mitigate the tendency to raise regulatory capital. For example, in retail loans, in home mortgages, in small businesses and also in well-provisioned damaged loans. Clauses are also included to avoid dependence on external rating agencies when the supervisor deems it appropriate, being able to base external credit ratings on those provided by official export credit agencies. a5 Finally, there are two related issues to which I will refer later: On the one hand, the insufficient consideration of the benefits of diversification and, on the other, the different implementation of Basel II that can generate problems of inconsistency and competition. Let me now turn to the next item: the programme of work on the subject of diversification. 2) Future work programme: Evolutionary, calibration and additional work: However, the publication of Basel II does not mean that everything is finished. We have completed a first stage, but we are facing a second phase of great importance, not only because of the important challenges of implementation, to which I will refer later, but also because the Committee has provided itself with a rich programme of work related to the new Framework. This programme of work was a tangible demonstration of the Committee's new approach. As we have repeated on numerous occasions, the Committee considers Basel II to be an evolutionary framework. With this, we believe that although its fundamental structure is valid in the long term, it must also have the necessary flexibility to allow it to adapt as quickly as possible to new developments in institutions' systems and to developments in financial markets in general. On the other hand, the Committee also understands that it is desirable to have stable regulation. One of our objectives now is precisely to strike the right balance between the necessary evolution and the desired stability. Calibration Within this work programme, one of the tasks we have to carry out before the entry into force of the new Framework is to ensure that the dual objective of maintaining the overall level of capital, as well as adequate incentives, is met. This is what has come to be called the calibration of the agreement which, until now, has been based on the quantitative impact studies carried out (QIS). In relation to these impact studies, I would like to mention the valuable collaboration of many supervisors in the last QIS3 exercise. With regard to Latin America, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Mexico collaborated in this work and I would like to take this opportunity to thank these countries for their contribution to the results obtained through QIS 3. The Committee considers it a priority to have a clear view of the quantitative impact of the new proposals. For this reason, the Committee Secretariat has created the appropriate structure to coordinate the efforts of the different supervisors who want to carry out new studies, or who begin the preparation of the double calculation of requirements prior to the entry into force of the New Capital Framework. In the event that these studies result in some adjustment, which could be positive or negative but in any case minimal, a simple scale factor has been introduced that would be applied to the capital calculations obtained for the internal approaches. 3) Additional work Continuing with the aforementioned work program, those most immediate related to the content of the new framework are now focused on the treatment of the so-called double default (or double default) and on concluding those that have already begun, in collaboration with the International Organization of Securities Commissions d0 IOSCO, on the treatment of risks derived from the trading book. We hope that these works can be completed before the implementation of the agreement. In software terminology, we expect to have 'version II.1' before the implementation date. In the longer term, the Committee will address diversification and the treatment of comprehensive credit risk models and review the definition of capital, among other issues. Treatment of diversification. Although in this presentation I do not want to focus so much on the work on the framework itself, but rather on developing issues relating to implementation, let me nevertheless say a few words on the subject of models for two reasons. First, because it illustrates well the working method that has been followed for the development of Basel II. And, secondly, because I know that the recognition of diversification, intimately linked to models, is one of the topics that is of particular interest to some members of the audience gathered here today. The Committee is fully aware that the path taken to achieve more risk-sensitive capital requirements is not exhausted. The evolution of banking practices has been closely monitored, and to the extent that confidence was gained that these practices, in addition to being conceptually sound, could be validated by the bank and reviewed by the supervisor, they have been incorporated into the proposals. The treatment of credit risk illustrates this. Building on the 1988 Agreement, the Committee proposes through Basel II the standard method as a greater awareness of credit risk through the use of external ratings and also allowing greater recognition of risk reduction techniques. As a next step, the Committee accepts the use of internal ratings for those banks that meet minimum requirements. Finally, and within the use of internal ratings, the Committee recognizes different methods that allow each entity, depending on its development in risk management, to weight assets by estimating one or more risk factors by the bank. This evolving treatment of credit risk arises from the dialogue with banks, and following this dialogue, the Committee hopes to be able to take what it considers to be the next natural step in the reasonably near future: the start of work aimed at the recognition for prudential purposes of internal credit risk models. But first we need to have clear evidence that enough banks have robust models and use their results in their day-to-day risk management. To the extent that there is a good practice in the industry, it will be easier for us to incorporate it into the regulatory framework. This would allow banks to estimate internally, among other elements, the values of asset correlations and thus the recognition of the effects of diversification. In addition, thanks to the momentum of the Basel II process, in particular internal rating methods (IRBs) and internal capital assessments in Pillar 2, work is progressing at a rapid pace and banks are increasingly in a position to deliver results that can have value for prudential purposes. But the work is not yet finished. Today, IRB methods present significant challenges that supervisors and banks still need to work on to gain greater confidence. 4) Implementation of the Agreement, cooperation between supervisors. Turning now to the second important theme of my speech today, which is the implementation of the new Framework, I would like to mention the challenges posed by its cross-border implementation. For many supervisors and banks, this is a prominent issue. It is likely that, if we could only talk about one issue today, many of you here would choose the problems arising from the cross-border implementation of Basel II. Proper implementation of Basel II is going to require us to delve into three key ideas or concepts: collaboration, communication, and trust. As the Committee has repeated on numerous occasions, the effective implementation of the New Capital Framework will require a greater degree of collaboration, at a practical level, between different supervisors. However, the need for collaborative arrangements and exchange of information is not new within the work of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. It should be remembered that the Committee itself was born in response to a need for information and collaboration between supervisors. What Basel II has contributed in this regard is, on the one hand, to have introduced it within the perimeter of the Agreement thanks to Pillar 2, thus giving it the relevance and attention it deserves and, secondly, to have added reasons and mechanisms to improve this necessary cooperation. In addition, this need for collaboration is reinforced by the increasing globalization of banking groups, especially in cases where a country's banking system has a strong presence of foreign capital and also vice versa, in cases where operations in a country are systemically important for a banking group. Basel II adds reasons for collaboration because the validation of models and the assessment of the correct application of the technical requirements posed by the three pillars - with the existence of different options, methodologies, supervisory practices, banking management practices, legal frameworks, etc. - certainly requires enhanced collaboration if we are to use supervisory resources efficiently, Reduce the regulatory cost of banking entities and ensure a sufficient level of consistency in implementation. Basel II adds mechanisms because we are devoting significant resources to ensuring this consistency and collaboration. This work is being carried out mainly in the Accord Implementation Group (AIG), chaired by Nick Le Pan, Vice-Chair of the Committee, with significant collaboration from CPLG. Along these lines, in August 2003, the Committee published a document entitled: "High-level principles for the cross-border implementation of the New Capital Framework". The basic ideas contained in the principles are: a5 Basel II does not change the responsibilities of national supervisors for the regulation of their respective institutions, nor the arrangements for consolidated supervision already established by the Committee. a5 What is changing, however, is the need to strengthen and encourage practical and pragmatic collaboration between supervisors. a5 The principles also point to the need to avoid, as far as possible, duplication of work. This is necessary to save resources for both supervisors and banking groups and will require not only enhanced collaboration but also a certain amount of trust between supervisors, especially in some respects. a5 The other idea contained in the principles is that, in coordination functions, the parent supervisor of the group has to have a certain leadership role. With the publication of the principles, the basis has been prepared for starting work on how to reach these agreements in a practical way. Thus, the AIG working group has begun to see how to reach these collaboration agreements through case studies based on real banking groups and that bring together supervisors from both member countries of the Committee and other countries, with selection criteria in terms of significant subsidiaries, both by the weight of the subsidiary in the banking group, and by the systemic importance of the subsidiary in the host country. This work on the case study is proving to be the most effective way to address the problems of cross-border enforcement. A first conclusion of the work of the AIG indicates that there is no common pattern of management and organization among the different banking groups with a significant international presence. There is also no pattern of collaboration agreement between supervisors. Each case requires individualized attention. However, we hope that we will be able to draw some practical lessons from this exercise which we want to share, and which I also hope will facilitate the adoption of real collaboration agreements between supervisors. Work is also being done to better understand the choices that each country makes in matters where there is national discretion and it is intended to provide information, even if it has a certain provisional character, since we believe it will be useful for everyone. The work of the AIG group led in May to publish some further elaboration of the principles published last year, in three areas that I would like to summarize below. . Firstly, the coordination of requests for information. In this regard, the members of the Committee decided that when one of us acting as host supervisor wants detailed information about the Basel II implementation plan of a subsidiary of a foreign group, he will first ask the home country supervisor for the information. Logically, this agreement should be interpreted with flexibility and common sense and in no case limits the direct access of the supervisor to the bank, but tries to rationalize the flow of information. We hope to discuss this agreement among the members of the Committee with other supervisors and that it can be accepted. a5 Secondly, to avoid duplication of work in the area of model validation, an additional step was taken and we consider it desirable for the origin supervisor to have a leading role in the approval and validation of certain types of advanced techniques. Specifically, it is expected that the validation of advanced approaches in the case of large companies will be led by the supervisor of origin with the inputs provided by the host supervisor and, therefore, with a greater degree of confidence of the host supervisor in the work of the home supervisor. a5 Finally, also in the area of the assessment of advanced models for operational risk, it is considered that the supervisor of origin has to have a leading role. Another conclusion drawn from the actual cases is, on the one hand, the importance of creating the necessary environment of mutual trust d0 trust on the basis that each party efficiently fulfils its role d0 and, on the other, the importance of the exchange of information and that there is an adequate degree of transparency between the supervisor of origin and the host supervisor. To this end, both reception and home supervisors should pragmatically weigh what information we need to feel comfortable with cooperation schemes such as those mentioned. To conclude this point, I would like to stress that, with or without Basel II, supervisors in different countries need a greater degree of cooperation to exercise effective consolidated supervision in an environment characterized by the strong globalization of banking activities, and the greater weight of foreign banking in different countries. In this context, I believe that in some areas, Basel II can play a catalytic role in this dialogue between the various parties involved in the consolidated supervision of a group. Finally, I would like to stress that the phase we are now entering, where implementation becomes the main focus, we will have to intensify the work and communication between supervisors in order to effectively implement the collaboration I have mentioned. But I must add that this applies not only to supervisors; Communication within banking groups must also be intensified if we are to be prepared for effective implementation. 5) Transition to Basel II The second issue I want to highlight today in relation to the implementation of Basel II is its broad international application of Basel II. I believe that the New Capital Framework has been designed so that it can become an internationally applicable standard, similar to what the 1988 Agreement has been. To this end, we have already seen that efforts have been made to ensure that the proposals are also an appropriate response for economies and banks of various sizes and characteristics, so I believe that Basel II is the direction in which we must look. The transposition of Basel II into the regulations of each country, including the decision on its date of entry into force and the graduation of the elements that are incorporated, is the sole and exclusive responsibility of the national authorities. The member countries of the Committee have reached consensus on its entry into force and scope. The rest of the regulators will have to carefully decide on its implementation. In doing so, they will have to consider various factors in each case, such as the characteristics of their financial system, their experience with the 1988 Agreement or the resources available for effective supervision under Basel II. In some cases, it may be advisable to defer the date of entry into force of the New Capital Framework; In others, the current agreement may be a valid solution for less sophisticated banks. The discussions I have had with various supervisors have been very positive; we all want to have the best supervisory system and Basel II is the right direction to go. Recently, a Financial Stability Institute (FSI)/BIS survey on the implementation of Basel II showed that of 107 responses received from non-Committee countries, 88 intend to adopt Basel II, and many of them, by 2009. If we add the member countries of the Committee, more than 100 countries are likely to adopt the New Framework. Having said that, let me nevertheless point out that, in those countries where the adoption of Basel II is not a priority, national supervisors could consider certain work that would facilitate the preparation of the ground for the future adoption of proposals. I have mentioned on occasion that it is a good option to do it in several phases: the first would be to concentrate on strengthening the fundamental foundations of the system and supervision. An effective system of supervision requires a set of preconditions that operate as foundations on which to solidly build the system architecture that is known to all of us. In addition to the need for prudential supervision to be supported by a set of sound and prudent macroeconomic policies, it will be necessary to have an adequate structure of commercial and civil laws, including the treatment of bankruptcy situations, accounting obligations that ensure a homogeneous representation of economic facts, external audit requirements, guarantee funds that provide adequate protection, supervisors with operational capacity and independence, etc. The legal structure and its application by the judicial system must provide respect for property rights, equality before the law and, in short, legal certainty. The need for this set of minimum preconditions is reinforced by the "Core Principles for an Effective Banking Supervision", without which, today, it is not possible to describe the structure of supervisory systems. The second phase would be to strengthen the three pillars, without focusing on the details of Basel II; i.e. achieving a well-capitalised banking system, strengthening Pillar 2 by complementing national supervision with a risk approach; Supervisors could consider the extent to which greater attention can be paid to the quality of bank management and the ability of bankers and supervisors to assess risks. Similarly, supervisors could improve processes for assessing banks' capital needs, as suggested by Pillar 2, and foster transparency towards the market, as suggested by Pillar 3. Finally, the third phase would be the full implementation of the new Framework, choosing the options that best suit the country's needs. Thus, while Basel II may not be a priority in the short term, I do believe that the discussion of its different basic elements and principles, and how they affect the national regulatory and supervisory framework, should be part of the work programmes of all supervisors. On this point, I would like to elaborate a little more on what I consider to be the main merit of the proposals and which, in my opinion, benefits everyone. As I mentioned, viewing Basel II as a set of mechanistic rules to improve the measurement of credit and operational risks would be too simplistic a reduction and therefore unfortunate for what is intended. Since the best measurement of risk is a very important element of the proposals, the main merit of Basel II is to be found in its role as a catalyst for progress in the management of banking risks and the better knowledge of them, both by banks and by supervisors themselves. Today, after six years of work in the Committee and open discussion with all stakeholders, internal systems for scoring and estimating risk factors are widely pervasive. Moreover, an increasing number of banks, from member and non-member countries of the Committee, are developing them sufficiently robust so that, in addition to serving their internal purposes, supervisors can use them for prudential purposes. The same can be said about operational risk. Prior to the Committee's commencement, operational losses occurred without banks having a clear understanding of their true impact and potential risk. Advances in banking management and technological improvements led to an increase in the volume of activity and the appearance of new products of increasing complexity, causing operational losses to have an increasing incidence or, at least, a greater risk of incidence. Concern began to grow among bankers and supervisors about the need to obtain a reasonable estimate of its potential impact. Today, work continues to progress, but confidence is already beginning to be gained about the modelling of operational risk and the effect that expected and unexpected losses due to operational risk can have. Pillar 2 also plays an important role as a catalyst for advancement. Under Pillar 2, banks take responsibility for presenting to their supervisors the internal processes on which they base their capital policies: processes that must include not only credit, market and operational risks, but all banking risks to which the entity is exposed. This does not necessarily require the use of internal economic capital models, but for more sophisticated banks this is likely to be the solution they adopt. This dialogue will give rise to a new impetus to improve and strengthen banking management techniques and supervisory activity, from which I trust we can all benefit. 6) Dialogue of the Committee with non-member countries. In view of some of the main tasks that the Committee intends to carry out, and the challenges posed by the implementation of Basel II, I would like to conclude my speech by referring to what will undoubtedly be a priority during this stage of implementation: that is, the Committee's dialogue with the other supervisors. Basel II is a proposal for reasonable regulation, not only for the member countries of the Committee, but for all those supervisors who wish to make further progress in the correct assessment of banking risks. To this end, the Committee has maintained and wishes to continue to maintain a dialogue with the other supervisors. The detailed list of all communication channels that have been opened so far would be extensive. It could be listed, among others, the numerous comments received to the various consultative documents, all of which are available on the website of the Bank for International Settlements and which have been a fundamental input in the development of Basel II. Similarly, meetings, seminars, working groups and meetings of regional groups have always had the active participation of the Committee. I would like to stress that the publication of Basel II at the end of June makes dialogue even more necessary. Therefore, I would like to point out the channels that I understand will play an important role in strengthening and ensuring this mutual dialogue: First, it is worth highlighting the work of the Core Principles Liaison Group, which the Committee established following the work on the preparation of the Basic Principles and which brings together representatives of member countries of the Committee with other national supervisory bodies, in such a way as to ensure a regional balance and diversity of the economies represented, together with representatives of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. This working group regularly provides the Committee with a first contrast of its work against the other points of view of the international financial community. The Committee also maintains, through the AIG working group, regular contacts with non-Committee supervisors through various channels. This fulfils the objective of sharing experiences on the implementation of the New Capital Framework and thus promoting consistent implementation. Let me simply say that I am personally committed to finding formulas that will strengthen the role of the SLCP, and that will make it possible to make better use of regional structures, which certainly also requires greater effort on their part and, in general, improving dialogue with all supervisors. Second, the most far-reaching communication channel may be the International Conferences of Supervisors of Banks (ICBS) held every two years. These conferences facilitate the exchange of views and experiences for representatives of different countries. The level of discussions is high and their conclusions are present in the Committee's programme of work. In this line, the next international conference, to be held in Madrid and will be organized by the Bank of Spain, will have as one of its main topics the application and implementation of Basel II, with a selection of presentations that will cover the problems of countries with different degrees of financial development. I look forward to seeing many of my supervisory colleagues at this new meeting. (7) Conclusion I would like to conclude these words by emphasising once again that the new proposals are, above all, correct mechanisms for driving improvements in banks' risk management and banking supervision, while at the same time promoting collaboration and exchange of information between supervisors. Basel II, in my opinion, represents a great opportunity for industry, supervisors and countries that adopt it. With the publication of Basel II on June 26, the Committee enters a new stage to implement the new proposals effectively and consistently. In this regard, the Committee remains seriously committed to ensuring and deepening its dialogue with other supervisors and industry. Personally, it is my intention that this dialogue will be a priority of the Committee's efforts going forward. I would like to join everyone in their efforts and offer the support of both the Committee and the Banco de Espa96a in the various initiatives in the region and in the implementation of Basel II as a means of strengthening banking systems. Thanks a lot

En alguna ocasin he mencionado que una buena opcin es hacerlo en varias fases: la primera sera concentrarse en reforzar las bases fundamentales del sistema y la supervisin. Un sistema efectivo de supervisin requiere un conjunto de condiciones previas que operan como cimientos sobre los que poder asentar slidamente la arquitectura del sistema que son conocidas por todos nosotros. Adems de la necesidad de que la supervisin prudencial est apoyada por un conjunto de polticas macroeconmicas sanas y prudentes, ser preciso disponer de una estructura adecuada de leyes mercantiles y civiles, incluyendo el tratamiento de las situaciones concursales, obligaciones de contabilidad que garanticen una representacin homognea de los hechos econmicos, exigencias de auditora externa, fondos de garanta que proporcionen una adecuada proteccin, supervisores con capacidad operativa e independencia, etc. La estructura legal y su aplicacin por el sistema judicial han de proporcionar respeto a los derechos de propiedad, igualdad ante la ley y, en suma, seguridad jurdica. La necesidad de que exista este conjunto de condiciones previas mnimas se refuerza con los Core Principles for an Effective Banking Supervision, sin los cuales, hoy en da, no es posible describir la estructura de los sistemas de supervisin. La segunda fase sera la de reforzar los tres pilares, sin centrarse en los detalles de Basilea II; es decir, conseguir un sistema bancario bien capitalizado, reforzar el pilar 2 complementando la supervisin nacional con un enfoque riesgo ; los supervisores podran considerar en qu medida es posible prestar mayor atencin a la calidad de la gestin bancaria y la habilidad de banqueros y supervisores de evaluar los riesgos. Del mismo modo, los supervisores podran mejorar los procesos para la evaluacin de las necesidades de capital de los bancos, como sugiere el Pilar 2, y fomentar la transparencia hacia el mercado, como sugiere el Pilar 3. Finalmente, la tercera fase sera la implantacin completa del nuevo Marco, eligiendo las opciones que mejor se adaptan a las necesidades del pas. De este modo, an cuando Basilea II puede no ser una prioridad a corto plazo, sin embargo, s considero que la discusin de sus diferentes elementos y principios bsicos, y el modo en que stos inciden en el marco de regulacin y supervisin nacional, deberan formar parte de los programas de trabajo de todos los supervisores. Siguiendo este punto, me gustara extenderme un poco ms sobre lo que considero es el principal mrito de las propuestas y que, en mi opinin, a todos beneficia. Como he mencionado, ver Basilea II como un conjunto de reglas mecanicistas para mejorar la medicin de los riesgos de crdito y operacional sera una reduccin demasiado simplista y, por tanto, desafortunada para lo que se pretende. Siendo la mejor medicin del riesgo un elemento muy importante de las propuestas, el principal mrito de Basilea II lo tenemos que encontrar en su funcin como catalizador de avances en la gestin de los riesgos bancarios y el mejor conocimiento de stos, tanto por parte de los bancos como de los supervisores mismos. Hoy, despus de seis aos de trabajos en el Comit y discusin abierta con todas las partes interesadas, los sistemas internos de calificacin y estimacin de los factores de riesgo son conceptos ampliamente generalizados. Es ms, un nmero cada vez mayor de bancos, de pases miembros y no miembros del Comit, los estn desarrollado con la solidez suficiente para que, adems de servir a sus fines internos, los supervisores los puedan utilizar con fines prudenciales. Lo mismo se puede decir sobre el riesgo operacional. Antes de iniciarse los trabajos del Comit, las prdidas operacionales ocurran sin que los bancos tuvieran una nocin clara de su verdadera incidencia y riesgo potencial. Los avances en la gestin bancaria y mejoras tecnolgicas propiciaron un aumento en el volumen de actividad y la aparicin de nuevos productos de creciente complejidad, haciendo que las prdidas operacionales tuvieran cada vez mayor incidencia o, al menos, un mayor riesgo de incidencia. Comenz a crecer la preocupacin entre banqueros y supervisores sobre la necesidad de obtener una estimacin razonable de su impacto potencial. Hoy los trabajos siguen avanzando, pero ya se empieza a ganar confianza sobre la modelizacin del riesgo operacional y el efecto que pueden tener las prdidas esperadas e inesperadas por riesgo operacional. El Pilar 2 tambin juega un papel importante como catalizador de avances. Con el Pilar 2, los bancos asumen la responsabilidad de presentar a sus supervisores los procesos internos sobre los que fundamentan sus polticas de capital: procesos que han de incluir no slo los riesgos de crdito, mercado y operacional, sino todos los riesgos bancarios a los que la entidad se vea expuesta. Esto no requiere necesariamente el uso de modelos internos de capital econmico, pero para la banca ms sofisticada es probable que sta sea la solucin que adopten. De este dilogo surgir un nuevo impulso para mejorar y reforzar las tcnicas de gestin bancarias y la actividad supervisora, del que confo todos nos podamos beneficiar. 6) Dilogo del Comit con pases no miembros. Vistas algunas de las principales tareas que el Comit piensa llevar a cabo, y los desafos que supone la implantacin de Basilea II, me gustara terminar mi intervencin haciendo referencia a lo que sin duda constituir una prioridad durante esta etapa de implantacin: esto es, el dilogo del Comit con el resto de supervisores. Basilea II constituye una propuesta de regulacin razonable, no slo para los pases miembros del Comit, sino para todos aquellos supervisores que deseen seguir avanzando en la evaluacin correcta de los riesgos bancarios. Para ello, el Comit ha mantenido y desea seguir manteniendo un dilogo con el resto de supervisores. La lista detallada de todos los canales de comunicacin que se han abierto hasta ahora sera extensa. Se podran enumerar, entre otros, los numerosos comentarios recibidos a los distintos documentos consultivos, todos ellos disponibles en la pgina web del Banco de Pagos Internacionales y que han supuesto un input fundamental en el desarrollo de Basilea II. Asimismo, las reuniones, seminarios, grupos de trabajo y reuniones de grupos regionales han contado siempre con una participacin activa del Comit. Por eso, quisiera sealar los canales que entiendo que jugarn un papel importante en fortalecer y asegurar este dilogo mutuo: En primer lugar, cabe resaltar la labor del Core Principles Liaison Group, que el Comit estableci a raz de los trabajos de preparacin de los Principios Bsicos y que rene a representantes de pases miembros del Comit con otros organismos supervisores nacionales, de tal forma que se asegure un equilibrio regional y diversidad de las economas representadas, junto con representantes del Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. Este grupo de trabajo ofrece al Comit, de forma regular, un primer contraste de sus trabajos frente al resto de puntos de vista de la comunidad financiera internacional. El Comit tambin mantiene, a travs del grupo de trabajo AIG, contactos regulares con los supervisores no miembros del Comit a travs de diversos canales. Se cumple as con el objetivo de compartir experiencias sobre la aplicacin del Nuevo Marco de Capital y, de este modo, promover una aplicacin consistente. Permtanme simplemente decir que, personalmente estoy comprometido con la bsqueda de frmulas que refuercen el papel del CPLG, y que permitan utilizar mejor las estructuras regionales, lo que sin duda requiere tambin un mayor esfuerzo por parte de stas y, en general, mejorar el dilogo con todos los supervisores. En segundo lugar, el canal de comunicacin con mayor alcance puede que sean las Conferencias Internacionales de Supervisores Bancarios (ICBS) que se celebran cada dos aos. Estas conferencias facilitan a los representantes de los distintos pases el intercambio de puntos de vista y experiencias. En esta lnea, la prxima conferencia internacional, que se celebrar en Madrid y estar organizada por el Banco de Espaa, tendr como uno de sus temas principales la aplicacin y puesta en marcha de Basilea II, con una seleccin de presentaciones que cubrirn la problemtica de pases con distinto grado de desarrollo financiero. Confo ver a muchos de los colegas supervisores en este nuevo encuentro. 7) Conclusin Quisiera concluir estas palabras enfatizando de nuevo que las nuevas propuestas constituyen, ante todo, unos mecanismos correctos para impulsar mejoras en la gestin de riesgos de las entidades y en la supervisin bancaria, y que, al mismo tiempo, favorecern la colaboracin e intercambio de informacin entre supervisores. Basilea II, en mi opinin, representa una gran oportunidad para la industria, los supervisores y los pases que lo adopten. Con la publicacin de Basilea II el pasado 26 de junio, el Comit entra en una nueva etapa para poner en prctica las nuevas propuestas de forma efectiva y consistente. En este sentido, el Comit contina seriamente comprometido a asegurar y profundizar su dilogo con el resto de supervisores y con la industria. En lo personal, es mi intencin que este dilogo sea una prioridad de los esfuerzos del Comit de aqu en adelante. Quisiera sumarme al esfuerzo de todos y ofrecer el apoyo tanto del Comit como del Banco de Espaa en las distintas iniciativas de la regin y en la puesta en marcha de Basilea II como medio de fortalecer los sistemas bancarios. Title: Governor's Appearance: Budget Committee of the Congress of Deputies, Madrid
text: Madrid, 13 October 2004 APPEARANCE OF THE GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF SPAIN BEFORE THE BUDGET COMMITTEE OF THE CONGRESS CONGRESS OF DEPUTIES Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain Mr. Chairman, Ms. and Honourable Members: It is very pleasant for me to appear before this Congressional Budget Committee, on the occasion of the presentation of the General State Budget of 2005. These are the first budgets of the new legislature, which respond to the economic policy guidelines established by the new Government. They also come at a crucial moment for the future evolution of the Spanish economy, when the tone adopted by economic policy d0 and fiscal policy in particular d0 will be highly influential on its prospects for growth and convergence with Europe. My contribution will pivot, as usual, on the assessment of the state of the economy in the current international environment and the monetary policy of the Eurosystem that we share with the other members of the euro area. I shall therefore begin by commenting on the external context and, within it, the outlook for the euro area. In recent months, the recovery phase has continued to consolidate in the international economy and spread to the different regions, despite the tensions experienced by the price of oil. The most recent forecasts discussed in various international forums remain cautiously optimistic about the prospects for continued expansion in 2005, highlighting in particular the expected growth in the United States and Asian countries as well as the progressive broadening of the geographical base on which global growth is based. The more intense acceleration of growth in the world economy since mid-2003 allowed the euro area to begin a gradual recovery, which over the past four quarters has shown rates of expansion close to the region's potential growth rate. According to the latest available data, the area's output expanded at a year-on-year rate of 2% in the second quarter of 2004 and growth is expected to reach a similar figure for the present year, after three years of low activity dynamism. In any case, the production gap accumulated in recent years has not yet been absorbed. The recovery was initially supported by external demand, given the strong IRR in world trade, but domestic spending has also experienced a greater boost more recently, although the improvement in domestic demand has been relatively slow, with confidence indicators not showing significant progress in recent months. In any case, the evolution of the euro area as a whole is the result of quite different behaviour, as there are countries (such as Spain or France) with premium expansion rates of 3% and with a significant contribution from domestic demand, while in others (such as the Netherlands or Germany) growth has been weaker and has rested significantly on external demand. In this relatively positive but not unbalanced international scenario, the main source of uncertainty in the short term is the behaviour of the price of petreo, after the significant increase in prices experienced in recent months, although it is difficult to detect, for the moment, an appreciable impact of this disturbance on growth in EMU. Activity in the euro area is expected to strengthen in the first quarters, thanks to the support that the expansion of world trade will continue to provide, if, as seems likely, the main industrialised countries maintain relatively high growth rates. Domestic demand in the lagging economies in EMU is also expected to start to show greater dynamism, as the boost in foreign trade feeds investment and employment, and these variables, in turn, support household income expectations and spending. In the area of inflation, on the other hand, the effects of the increase in oil prices have been faster and more noticeable. Inflation in EMU has risen above 2% over the past few months and is unlikely to fall below that figure until the first half of 2005, provided that so-called second-round effects do not occur as a result of agents' attempts to protect their incomes by increasing their wage demands or margins. It is obvious that the ECB will monitor whether these defence mechanisms are put in place, as in that case there would be substantial risks to the maintenance of price stability. In this context, the Eurosystem has maintained short-term interest rates at 2% since June 2003, a level which represents a historic low and which, in real terms, means, for most countries, zero or negative premium rates. Long-term interest rates, meanwhile, are also at very low levels. Thus, monetary and financial conditions have remained very favourable for the consolidation of the recovery. These comments on the European situation cannot ignore the debate that has been taking place over the past few months on the monitoring of economic policies and, in particular, budgetary policy within the European Union, following the failures to implement the excessive deficit procedure provided for in the Stability and Growth Pact in the cases of Germany and France. Firstly, it is important to note that, despite the difficulties that have arisen, the European framework for fiscal discipline, although it has not acted with the expected rigour, has served as a brake on the deterioration of budgetary positions in the cyclical slowdown, which in the absence of such a pact would have been even more serious. However, it is obvious that serious problems have become apparent in the application of these disciplinary mechanisms which need to be corrected in order to safeguard their effectiveness and credibility. Recently, the European Commission has launched a series of proposals around which the debate is taking place in the European institutions. Without going into a detailed assessment of these proposals, I would like to emphasise that, in my opinion, in view of recent experience, it is crucial to carry out strict surveillance of budgetary policy in the boom phases, because if the appropriate adjustment then takes place, the finances will be prepared to face the stages of slowdown without generating excessive fiscal deficits. I also think it appropriate to pay more attention to the debt criterion when assessing budgetary policies, because this criterion sometimes provides very valuable information on the real state of finances. Obviously, this task of monitoring and coordination can only be carried out if reliable and timely information on budgetary developments is available, which takes into account the accounting criteria and established timetables. The discussion on these issues will continue over the first few months and I remain in the hope that ways will be found to improve the implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact, so as to restore the effectiveness and credibility of the essential mechanisms of fiscal discipline and to provide a framework for sufficient coordination of the economic policies of the euro area countries. In any case, these revisions do not require regulatory changes which, in any case, are restricted by the provisions of the current Treaty d0 also included in the new Constitutional Treaty d0 according to which the limits of 3% of GDP for the flat deficit and 60% of GDP for the public debt ratio cannot be modified. I would also like to point out that the review of progress on the objectives set out in the Lisbon agenda points to a clearly insufficient result, so it is a priority to restore the reform momentum. The ability to achieve high and sustained medium-term growth in the euro area will depend on the success of this strategy. In this context of the expansion of the world economy and the progressive consolidation of economic prospects in Europe, the Spanish economy has tended to stabilise its growth rate around the comparatively high levels it had reached at the end of last year. Specifically, according to the most recent estimates of the Quarterly Accounts, in the second quarter of 2004 the year-on-year increase in GDP was 2.6%, after having registered slightly higher increases in the previous two quarters d0 of 2.8% and 2.7%, respectively. These estimates indicate that the growth differential with the euro area remains positive and that, therefore, the Spanish economy continues to converge, in real terms, with the income levels of the most advanced countries in the euro area, although the pace of convergence is now lower, because the recent slight weakening of our pace of expansion has coincided with the recovery that these economies are experiencing. Growth continues to be accompanied by comparatively high employment generation. In fact, the indicators of the labor market point to a stabilization of the rate of job creation, which increased 2% in the second quarter. However, these estimates also confirm that the rate of growth in apparent labour productivity remains low. The most positive aspect of the recent situation has undoubtedly been the progress of investment as a team in the second quarter of 2004, a period in which it has begun to overcome the stagnation that had been recorded since 2003. Short-term information seems to confirm the continuation of this improvement. However, other aspects of the drivers of growth are less novel. Private consumption has maintained higher rates of increase of more than 3 per cent, higher than those observed in 2003; the advance of the plico consumption has exceeded 4%; and construction, with increases of around 4.2%, has continued to provide basic support to the expansion of spending, driven by the plica work and residential investment. This scam continues to progress, despite the high levels it had already reached in the previous years. Foreign demand, meanwhile, has increased its contractionary nature significantly in the first quarters of 2004, slowing down the growth of activity. On the one hand, the Quarterly Accounts data would indicate that exports of goods have begun to benefit from the momentum of world trade, growing at rates similar to this, and it seems that the most up-to-date foreign trade data reflect this momentum. However, in contrast, tourism recorded a rather weak performance in the second quarter of 2004 which, according to all indications, has been somewhat attenuated to the summer season. More importantly, imports have rebounded strongly since the start of the year, helping to curb output. In short, the results of the Spanish economy continue to settle on a pattern of growth very similar to that of the scams. The increase in demand is largely based on the support that the comfortable financial conditions lend to household spending on residential consumption and investment and on the increase in expenditure on civil works and on retail consumption. Although productive investment and exports have tended to recover, they have done so with an even lower intensity than desirable. The dynamism of household spending has generated tensions on prices, especially in those sectors with less flexibility in supply. Data received since spring have shown a significant uptick in the inflation rate, amid pressures from commodity markets d0 particularly oil markets d0 and some foods. Specifically, the inflation rate stood at 3.1% in September, according to the preliminary advance, bringing the spread with the euro area back to the euro area by one percentage point. It is likely that the rise in the price of oil has had a relatively stronger impact on our economy than on other European economies. However, the most permanent increase in the inflation differential comes from the most stable components of the CPI: Spanish core inflation has approached 3% in recent months, around six or seven tenths above its level in the euro area, and in the case of services, the spread remains around one percentage point. The persistence of this behavior is having negative effects on competitiveness that are beginning to be noticeable in the trade deficit and in the weakening of tourism. As regards the financial implications of household behaviour, it should be noted that there is still no change in the growing trend in indebtedness. Indeed, financing to households accelerated in the early part of 2004, driven by strong growth in mortgage lending. Likewise, the various indicators on the effort represented by the acquisition of housing show that this continues to increase, without, on the other hand, reducing the pressure on the price of these assets, which has only given lukewarm moderaci. Although the patrimonial position of families is still AIDS, the weight of the financial burden in relation to income has increased. For its part, financing to companies, which had maintained a more moderate tone, has accelerated in the months months, possibly reflecting the rebound in investment, which is supported by a financial situation and high levels of profitability for its continuity. The information available suggests that the economy will continue to grow in the second half of the year at rates similar to those of the first part of the year. In this way, the year could end with GDP growth slightly below 2.8%, depending, above all, on the contractionary effect of net foreign demand. And from here, the scenario for 2005 will be conditioned by the intensity of the impulses coming from the external context and by the evolution of the internal conditions of the economy. If the euro area continues to gain strength, in an expansionary international environment, the Spanish economy would also have the opportunity to strengthen its dynamism and achieve growth rates that could approach 3%. However, in the current circumstances, this rate is, rather, in the high zone of the possible range of forecast. In this direction, he points out the risk that the rise in oil prices will be prolonged or even reach a higher intensity than initially expected or that the recovery of the European economies will show greater hesitation. The implications of adverse behaviour in the price of oil in our economy, both in reducing the rate of economic growth and job creation and in its upward pressure on prices, depends, to a large extent, on the behaviour of economic agents. To the extent that these companies and workers try to avoid the loss of real income, which is caused by the increase in the price of petreo, through increases in margins and wage increases they will tend to produce more lasting deterioration of the inflationary situation, growth and employment. It should not be forgotten, however, that several factors, such as less dependence on oil and lower price increases in real terms, qualify the direct impact in relation to past experiences; It is therefore important to avoid the aforementioned second-round effects and possible trade-offs that could diminish the incentives needed to improve energy efficiency. Internally, there are also factors that can act to slow growth, such as the possible materialization of some risks underlying the pattern of growth that the Spanish economy has followed or with the exhaustion of some of the impulses received after its entry into the euro. It is these risks that call for an active response from economic policy to mitigate them and establish the best conditions for harnessing external impulses. The instruments available at the national level should be aimed at preserving the macroeconomic stability framework, moderating household demand, while simultaneously promoting productive investment and competitiveness, so as to rebalance the components of expenditure that sustain demand growth and support productivity gains and competitiveness. Monetary policy has so far determined relatively loose monetary and financial conditions for the needs of the Spanish economy. As the overall situation of the euro area economy improves, the tone of monetary conditions is expected to gradually return to more neutral patterns, so that the financial slack that has prevailed can be absorbed, at least in part. However, even if the monetary policy stance moves in a direction more in line with domestic needs, this shift is more than likely to be sufficient to achieve the overall policy tone that the economy needs at the moment, and the role of domestic policies is therefore of great importance. The situation I have described on budgetary policy is the task of trying to channel demand and expenditure in a manner consistent with the containment of the risks that have begun to emerge, and to this end it is essential to deepen the path of budgetary consolidation of the scams. As I said last year in this very Committee, the General Budgets for the current year, which were then under discussion, had an objective of balancing the account of all the administrations, which in those cyclical circumstances had a moderately expansionary character, which made it advisable to use any available margin for a tighter instrument and to move more decisively towards the surplus. in line with the requirements of the macroeconomic situation. The figures on budget execution in 2004 are affected by the recognition of some adjustments in the expenditure of the Administrations in terms of National Accounts that were not contemplated by the Budgets and the assumption of debt of some companies, such as RTVE and RENFE. As a result, the estimated balance has been in deficit by an amount which essentially reflects these one-off operations, which are intended to reflect more comprehensively the financial situation. The commitment to improving transparency in the accounts of the accounts, manifested in the presentation of budgets as a necessary objective to improve the efficiency of the tax sector, must be positively valued since this is an essential element to guarantee fiscal discipline. In this sense, any effort at transparency should serve to strengthen discipline mechanisms and avoid the continuation of spending trends in healthy units. This shows that it should be accompanied by the necessary reforms to prevent the future reappearance of the imbalances that have arisen in the past in companies, such as those mentioned above, which have led to the adjustments in 2004, so that these adjustments do not serve to provide greater slack to the budget that could favour a permanent increase in budgetary expenditure. Transparency as a mechanism of discipline is particularly important when the structure of expenditure is strongly decentralised, as is the case in Spain. It is essential that the situation of the finances of all the Administrations is known with a frequency and a punctuality similar to that of the State, for which greater transparency of the Autonomous Communities is required. It is also important that, beyond the rigor of the accounting criteria, the different public administrations explain those commitments or activities that they do not consolidate within the sector but that may represent risks of higher payments or debts in the future. In any event, once the accounting adjustments made are taken into account, the assessment of the tone of budget execution in 2004 indicates, according to the available year-end forecasts, that it has been indeed expansionary, even if the slight weakening of the recovery is taken into account. Thus, the effort to consolidate the budget would have fallen short of what would have been desirable in order to achieve AIDS protection against the risk factors that were becoming present. The general budget for 2005 presents a surplus target for all administrations of one tenth of GDP, which is compatible with the criteria of budgetary stability and which would allow Spain to be among the small number of euro area countries with a surplus balance in their accounts for all administrations. From the point of view of its macroeconomic effects, with all the cautions that derive from an analysis that in this case is surrounded by greater uncertainty than usual as a result of the accounting adjustments made, this figure could mean that the aforementioned moderately expansionary stance of fiscal policy is not sufficiently corrected. resulting in a contribution to stability that could be less than desirable in the current situation of the Spanish economy. Given the lack of sufficient room for manoeuvre in the 2005 budget, it is particularly important that the implementation of the budget by the various administrations be particularly rigorous, that every opportunity be taken to deepen the path of budgetary consolidation and that overflows of the programmed figures are avoided, even if economic growth or revenues are slightly lower than those envisaged in the Budget planning. The tone of fiscal policy required by the Spanish economy is not limited to an overall balance that is appropriate for the current situation, but also refers to the composition and quality of revenues and expenditures. Policies that favor the increase of the potential growth of the economy also allow social spending to be financed in a sustained manner, so it is necessary to properly prioritize the promotion of investment and productivity growth and a containment of other spending areas, especially if some components of social spending are to be promoted in parallel. Overall, a less loose combination of policies, monetary, and fiscal, is the right macroeconomic response to address risks on the ground. competitiveness, rising house prices and household indebtedness. This poses a special demand and responsibility in the fiscal field, a stricter tone will favor the containment of price and cost increases in the sectors less exposed to competition, the gradual containment of house prices towards a path compatible with the evolution of their fundamentals and the slowdown in the pace of household indebtedness towards more sustainable patterns. But just as important as the aggregate tone of macroeconomic policy is the push for structural reforms that address the problems of rigidities or inadequate regulation in some markets. These reforms are also essential to boost productivity growth, to which the Draft Budget attaches so much importance and to this end they must contribute, in the short term, to boosting entrepreneurship and the capacity for innovation of the economy as a whole. Action must be aimed, above all, at creating the conditions for actors to take their decisions in a sufficiently competitive environment, avoiding interventionism that hinders the dynamism and adaptability of our economy. It is very important to maintain a liberalizing impulse that dispels the doubts that may have arisen about the nature of some regulations, as in the case of the opening hours of commercial establishments, which affect a sector that plays a prominent role in the diffusion of productivity gains and in the formation of final prices. The reform drive must cover a very wide range of sectors and measures in response to the specific problems of the Spanish economy and in line with the objectives of the Lisbon agenda. In relation to proposals relating to specific sectors, in the field of housing, for example, measures aimed at promoting access must be accompanied by reforms which effectively increase the flexibility of supply, which depends fundamentally on the regulation of the land market, otherwise the pressures will always end up manifesting themselves through price increases. Great importance should be attached to measures to consolidate the foundations for growth that will lead to productivity improvements and, in parallel, continued employment generation in the economy. The reforms introduced in the nineties made it possible to reduce the unemployment rate significantly and, by increasing the potential for job creation, have helped to sustain economic dynamism. However, the inertia and rigidity that wage determination mechanisms continue to present and the elements of inflexibility that persist in other aspects of the labour market make it necessary to deepen reforms in this market, which are key to the functioning of the economy. The strategy to improve competitiveness should adopt a general approach, ranging from the promotion of investment in physical and human capital, the basis of productivity gains, to the revision of some sectoral strategies and to the pattern of productive specialization itself. But these are far-reaching issues that go beyond the scope of this hearing. Let me conclude by stressing the importance of the role of budgetary policy in taking advantage of the improved external environment and in ensuring that emerging risks do not jeopardise the continued recovery and convergence. Likewise, the deepening of budgetary consolidation is necessary to face with greater guarantees the long-term challenges that the accounts will have to face, especially those associated with the effect of the aging of the population.
