Title: Reflections on the different social models and economic trajectories of Europe and the United States. Presentation at the Seminar "Europe and the United States: Comparison and Relations" organized by the Carolina Foundation, the Rafael del Pino Foundation, and the Free College of Emeritus of Madrid. Madrid.
text: Madrid, 25 February 2005 Reflections on the different social models and economic trajectories of Europe and the United States* Cycle of Seminars "Europe/United States: comparison and relations". Carolina Foundation-Rafael del Pino Foundation-Free School of Emeritus Jose Vi96als Director General of International Affairs of the Banco de Espa96a * The opinions and judgments contained in this article are solely of a personal nature. Introduction The United States and the European Union are the most important economic areas in the international economic context, with shares of 19% and 21% respectively in world GDP. However, there are important differences between the two areas in terms of their political institutions, the economic and social models they have adopted and their economic trajectories. At the political level, the United States is a single nation with a government and legislative institutions structured around the achievement of well-defined national objectives in a way that guarantees the necessary unity of action. On the other hand, still far from being the United States of Europe, the European Union is a grouping of nations, each with its own government and parliament, which seek to achieve both its own objectives and those established for the Union as a whole through European economic governance mechanisms that do not always succeed in coordinating adequately actions at national and Community level in pursuit of those objectives or ensuring due proportionality between the ends pursued and the means available for it. However, it should be remembered that, as a result of the significant institutional advances made in the European Union over the last twenty years, since 1993 it has had a single market based in each and every one of the twenty-five countries of the Union and, since 1999, with the euro, which is currently the common currency of twelve of these countries and which is also trusted to be the rest of the European Union. Member States in the future. Finally, it is important for the European Union to be currently in the process of ratifying its Constitution in the process of ratifying its Constitution in order to widen and deepen its institutional framework. As for the economic and social models adopted, there are also very notable differences between Europe and the United States, given that in the European case special attention is paid to the values of solidarity, cohesion, equity, equality or social justice while in the case of the United States a less social and more individualistic tone is adopted. Another common way of differentiating the two models is that, while in the European model equity prevails over efficiency, in the North American model it is efficiency that enjoys preference over equity. Finally, it is also possible to explain the difference between the two models on the basis that, while in the European case it is about ensuring equality of results (ex post), in the North American model it is, rather, about achieving equality of opportunities (ex ante). There are also important differences in the economic evolution of both areas to the extent that the growth rates achieved by the United States have not only traditionally been higher than in Europe, but this gap has tended to widen since the mid-nineties, coinciding with the technological revolution that took place in the American economy. In recent years, European countries have gone through a phase of strong economic slowdown in an international environment that was initially adverse, as a result of the unfavourable impact of the bursting of the technology bubble and the crisis in the information technology and telecommunications sector, and the successive shock of confidence triggered by the terrorist attacks of 11 September and increased, later, because of corporate scandals and geopolitical uncertainties in Iraq and, in general, in the Middle East. And at the present time, in which the United States and China are leading the international economic recovery, Europe is finding it very difficult to recover more reasonable growth rates. As a result, many European countries have violated the rules on budgetary discipline laid down in the Stability and Growth Pact, which has given rise to a lively debate about the appropriateness of maintaining or modifying certain elements of this payment. There is, on the basis of all the above, serious concern on the part of European authorities and citizens about the economic trajectory of Europe and the adverse consequences that result from it for the living standards of European citizens, both in absolute terms and in comparison with other more dynamic areas such as the United States and, in general, for Europe's role in the international economic and political concert. The result of this concern has been the very recent reports investigating what are the causes of European economic problems and what could be the possible solutions to them, carried out at the request of the President of the Commission, such as the Sapir Report1, or the European Council, such as the Kok2 Report. These reports have led the new Commission President, Durao Barroso, to adopt from the outset the position of prioritising the promotion of European economic growth. The obvious concern about the low level of European economic vitality becomes all the more intense when we consider that Europe will have to face far-reaching challenges in the coming years, such as ensuring the success of the recent enlargement and future enlargements to include members such as Romania, Bulgaria or, most especially, Turkey; confronting the formidable external competition associated with the globalization process; and to alleviate the adverse consequences for productivity and financial burdens that demographic developments leading to population ageing entail in the medium and long term. Since European economic developments are clearly unsatisfactory, not only in absolute terms but also in comparison with the United States, the world's other major economic area, and given the differences between the degrees of political-institutional structuring and the economic and social models adopted by Europe and the United States, it makes sense to ask to what extent Europe's economic problems may be related to their weaknesses. institutional, which are projected to the scope of economic government, with the type of economic and social model chosen or with the way in which it has been managed. To address these issues, the rest of the intervention is structured as follows. First, it defines the peculiarities of the European model and explains the preference of European citizens for "their" model, in contrast to the model prevailing in the United States. Secondly, it assesses European economic developments over the last decades and in relation to that of the United States, and examines the extent to which the basic objectives of the European model have been achieved. Thirdly, the main factors responsible for Europe's economic problems are identified. Finally, some reflections are made on the steps that should be taken to restore the strength of the European economy in order to guarantee the survival of the European model, improve the living standards of the citizens of an enlarged Europe and strengthen its weight in the international arena. 3 1 An Agenda for a Growing Europe. The Sapir Report, por A. Sapir y otros, Oxford University Press, 2004 2 Facing the Challenges: The Lisbon strategy for growth and employment, por W. Kok y otros, Comisi97n Europea, 2004 The European economic and social model and its differences from the North American model The European model is often characterised as a system which, unlike the North American model, seeks to preserve an adequate degree of equality and economic and social cohesion through existing social safety nets at both national and Community level and which ultimately shape Europe's commitment to the welfare state. At the national level, this is reflected in progressive taxation systems, in the weight of transfers and other items of a social nature in the budget d0 such as unemployment insurance d0 as well as in laws and regulations such as those that, for example, regulate the labour market. At Community level, the most important mechanisms are the transfers that the EU makes through cohesion funds, regional funds or the common agricultural policy. But what reasons explain Europeans' demonstrated preference for a more social model, as opposed to the more individualistic model prevalent in the United States? Although there are numerous reasons that are often put forward to explain or justify Europeans' preference for a more social model, the most systematic and rigorous analysis is that recently carried out by professors Alesina and Glaeser of Harvard University4 . In their work, which considers economic, sociological and political explanations, they conclude that the reasons that explain the preference of Europeans for the social are several. On the one hand, political institutions, since the European political system is proportional, compared to the majority system in the United States. It is well known that a proportional system makes it relatively easier for there to be more significant penetration into the institutions of new parties, as was the case with centre-left and left-wing parties in Europe, particularly after the state of devastation and poverty in which many European countries were plunged after the First World War. These circumstances led to the introduction of proportional systems and the advance of left and center-left formations, which were the ones that proposed and implemented the social protection networks that currently make up the welfare state. On the contrary, in the United States, the individualistic principles of the eighteenth century enshrined in its constitution have been preserved over time by a political system of a majority nature that precisely has the mission of avoiding important changes in the legal system derived from the emergence of new political and ideological forces. Undoubtedly, the peculiar geography of the United States, with a large size, a low population density and the possibility of conquering the new frontier of the west, served to dilute social tensions and also made it more difficult to form parties of the left or center-left, similar to those that were emerging in Europe in the first half of the twentieth century. In turn, the absence on American soil of the devastating effects of the First World War also avoided the social and political effervescence that did exist in Europe and, as a result of which, constitutional changes were carried out tending to evolve towards systems of proportional representation. 3 Some parts of the article are based on the author's publications: La econom92a europea en la encrucijada, Conferencias del C92rculo, 4, C92rculo de Empresarios, 2003, and "El modelo econ97mico y social europeo: c0una trinidad inconsistente?", Informaci97n Comercial Espa96ola, January 2005. 4 Fighting Poverty in the US and Europe. A world of difference, por A. Alesina y E. Glaeser, Oxford University Press, 2004 But not only would the different political systems be responsible for preferences for one or the other model on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the strong differences in the degree of ethnic and racial homogeneity would have an important weight. Thus, the ethnic and racial fragmentation of American society, the result of its history, would have made it much more difficult for the egalitarian ideas that had been assumed in a very homogeneous Europe ethnically and racially to penetrate, since it is easier to accept than to help those who are of the same ethnic or racial group because they understand that they are not so different from oneself. Another factor that, finally, could also have contributed to the adoption of different models is the diversity of attitudes of the population of both areas regarding the risk and value of individual effort. In particular, since the United States is a nation formed from its origin by emigrants, it seems reasonable to think that those who were willing to leave their countries of origin and embark on the American adventure were precisely those capable of taking greater risks, of valuing their own initiative more and of believing more in the fruit of personal effort. Much more suspicious of the need or desirability of social safety nets designed to protect certain social sectors and that, ultimately, could blur the correspondence between personal effort and the degree of well-being achieved. On the contrary, those who decided to stay in Europe would have been more in favour of supporting solutions based on the establishment of more extensive social coverage networks, aimed at limiting inequalities. The three dimensions of the European economic and social model Although the analysis carried out serves to explain why the social dimension is much more important in the European model than in the North American one, there are two other elements that make up the European model and that must be taken into account when analysing the European economic trajectory and assessing to what extent the various objectives that are present in this model have been achieved. The three dimensions of the European social economic model, which have always been present in the Community Treaties, are summarised in Article I-3 of the text of the European Constitution as follows: "The Union shall work for the sustainable development of Europe based on balanced economic growth and price stability, in a highly competitive social market economy, aiming at full employment and social progress..." That is, the EU's economic and social objectives can be described as a "trinity", consisting in achieving a satisfactory rate of growth in a sustained manner, under conditions of macroeconomic stability while ensuring an appropriate degree of economic and social cohesion, both within the Union as a whole and in individual Member States. Figure 1 provides a schematic representation of the European economic and social model around its three dimensions: growth, economic and social cohesion and macroeconomic stability. The graph also provides a useful starting point for analysing the EU's past economic trajectory on the basis of each of the three dimensions mentioned above and thus assessing the extent to which the growth, stability and cohesion objectives that shape the European model have or have not been achieved. The European model under review: growth, stability and cohesion The idea that the difficulties of the European economy have a deep root that goes far beyond the temporal limits of the current conjuncture, is corroborated by observing the trajectory of European economic growth during the last decades. Taking the average growth over the last four decades as a benchmark shows that the EU has seen a gradual but inexorable decline in its capacity to grow. Thus, as can be seen in Graph 2, while the average annual growth was 4.8% in the sixties, this figure fell to 3% in the seventies, 2.4% in the eighties, 2.1% in the nineties and is below 2% in the present decade. This fact, which clearly reveals the increasing difficulties that the EU has been encountering in growing at a sustained high pace, is particularly worrying for several reasons. On the one hand, because the progressive weakness of growth over this long period has coincided with the realization of intense progress in the European integration process, which was expected to result in substantial efficiency gains in the processes of allocation of resources and, ultimately, in a greater growth potential of the European area. And, on the other hand, because the economic trajectory of the EU has not only been frustrating in relation to the golden sixties and the expectations raised around the integration process, but also in comparison with the United States, the other great world economic area. Thus, although d0 as can be seen in Graph 3 d0 the US economy also experienced a reduction in its growth rate in the last three decades in relation to the sixties, nevertheless, in these thirty years it has grown annually by 3.4%, on average, which is almost one point above the 2.5% registered in the EU. But, although this is disturbing from the European perspective, it is even more worrying that the growth differential between the EU and the United States has become increasingly unfavorable for Europe over time, since, compared to the gradual decline observed in the European case, the North American economy has not only maintained growth rates of 3.3% and 3.2% respectively in the seventies and eighties, but, thanks to the intense technological changes that occurred in the second half of the nineties, it has managed to raise its rate of progress to 3.6% in the last decade. Acknowledging the obvious difficulties that the EU has been facing in growing in the medium term is essential to understand the magnitude of the problems that arise when, as has been happening in recent years, the economic cycle enters the contractionary phase. It is precisely the fact of moving from average growth rates, already modest, to even lower ones that magnifies the adverse consequences of the cyclical worsening. Turning to Europe's macroeconomic stability trajectory, if we understand this in its most commonly accepted sense, as maintaining low inflation rates and sound public finances, the EU has made very significant progress on both fronts in recent decades. Thus, from an average annual inflation rate in the seventies above 10% in the EU as a whole, it has gone to rates slightly below 7% in the eighties, 3% in the nineties and around 2% today. At the same time, the last decade has reversed the trend towards deterioration in public accounts evidenced in previous periods, which d0 despite the most recent difficulties encountered in some countries d0 has contributed very favourably to the process of reducing the deficit and improving the sustainability of public debt. Undoubtedly, the sharp reduction in inflation and public deficits that has taken place mainly in the nineties has been due to the macroeconomic stability policies implemented by the member states in order to meet the convergence criteria established in the Maastricht Treaty to accede to monetary union; stability policies that have sought to consolidate through the single monetary policy and the Stability and Growth Pact. Again, the comparison with the United States is illustrative, because in that country, as can be seen in the Table, inflation has also fallen significantly from the peaks of 8% of GDP reached in the seventies, being today very similar to that of the EU. However, the same cannot be said of public finances which, although they had managed in the nineties to eliminate the public deficits of previous periods, have seen deficits widen to 5% of GDP in recent years. In the area of cohesion, there have also been notable advances in Europe in the past. As has been explained, regardless of the variables chosen to approximate how cohesion has evolved within the EU, the fact is that, in the last three decades, the distances that separate the least prosperous countries from the rest in terms of per capita income have been narrowing while various synthetic indicators of the degree of inequality between countries have improved, on the whole, despite successive enlargements of the EU over the years. Finally, from the analysis carried out so far, it can be concluded that over the last thirty years, during which the EU has made considerable institutional progress in the integration process, its economic trajectory has been characterized by lights and shadows. Lights, which correspond to improvements in the areas of macroeconomic stability and cohesion; and shadows, emanating from the prolonged decline of European growth over time and relative to the United States. Factors explaining the weakness of European economic growth Since the manifest weakness of growth is the most worrying feature of European economic developments, it is necessary to examine what reasons may have contributed most decisively to this, from a medium- and long-term perspective. The comparison between the European case and that of the United States may, once again, be useful for a better understanding of the nature of our problems. Thus, if GDP growth is broken down into productivity gains (per hour worked) and job creation (hours worked), it is clear how, over the last three decades, the differential factor that, together, explains the higher growth of the United States in relation to Europe is job creation, while the rates of increase in productivity are higher in the EU. It should come as no surprise, however, that our productivity has grown more rapidly given that its starting level was well below that of the United States. What is frustrating is that its current level is still almost ten percent below that of the US economy and that, in recent years, the gap between the two has widened again. At the same time, given the high unemployment rate in the European economy, it is disheartening that hardly any jobs have been created. However, experience shows that, in the case of Europe, when job creation intensifies d0 even modestly d0 the counterpart is a slowdown in the rate of productivity growth and vice versa. Thus, for example, as the EU has increased its average annual rate of job creation from -0.5% in the seventies, to 0% in the eighties and to the very meager 0.3% in the nineties, the rate of average annual increase in productivity has fallen significantly, respectively in each of these periods, 3.5 per cent, 2.4 per cent and 1.8 per cent and at even lower rates at present. This experience contrasts markedly with that of the United States, which has seen its annual rate of job creation remain very close to 2% in each of the same periods while its annual productivity increased from 1.4% to 1.7%, being currently clearly higher than these figures. As a result, the US economy has been able to improve its productivity while maintaining considerably higher rates of job creation, which has doubly favoured the growth process. The European experience, on the other hand, highlights the serious difficulties encountered so far in improving in one direction without worsening in the other, which is a formidable brake on the capacity for growth. How have stability and cohesion policies affected European growth? After examining the evidence, the question that arises is what reason(s) explain the inability of the European economy to create jobs more rapidly and to maintain higher rates of productivity growth, given its relatively lower levels than in the United States? In this sense, it is worth asking whether and in what direction the European model d0 macroeconomic stability and cohesion d0 have influenced the growth process in Europe. A debate has now raged in Europe about whether stability policies could be responsible, to a greater or lesser extent, for the EU's persistent difficulties in maintaining sustained growth at higher rates. Undoubtedly, this debate is triggered by the unfavourable European economic situation in recent years, which has led to criticism from some quarters of the institutional and strategic framework governing European macroeconomic policy and, in particular, the single monetary policy and fiscal policies. This has also been helped by the suspicion on the part of some whether the progress made by the EU in the area of stability following the Maastricht convergence process would not have diminished its capacity for growth. However, even without going into depth to discuss whether any specific aspect of the mechanisms that govern such policies in practice should be reconsidered, it can be said that the previous position is wrong. On the one hand, according to economic principles and experience confirms, macroeconomic stability is essential to achieve and maintain a satisfactory growth rate in a sustained manner, while recognizing that, in certain cases, the adjustment policies required to achieve such stability in advance may have a negative impact on activity in the short term. On the other hand, blaming stability policies for the chronic weakness of European growth is inconsistent with the fact that stability weakness is a medium-term phenomenon that has been observed decade after decade, long before macroeconomic stability policies were put in place in the nineties. The other particularly important question is whether the concrete way in which the search for cohesion is articulated within the European model through the welfare state may have had a negative impact on growth. In this sense, the evidence indicates that the design of cohesion policies, both at Community and national level, has not sufficiently taken into account that some of their elements could have a particularly harmful impact on efficiency and growth. At Community level, there is empirical evidence that agricultural and regional funds would have limited, in many cases, the natural processes of reallocation of resources resulting from the establishment of the Single Market, which would have prevented the potential efficiency gains that it entails by preventing factors of production from shifting to more productive sectors or activities. At the national level, on the other hand, the adverse effects on efficiency and growth would have been the unintended result of social and tax measures that would have had a negative impact, for example, on the degree of flexibility of wage structures, on labour mobility and on the incentives of agents to save, invest or produce. Cohesion is d0 and must remain d0 a basic element of the European model and this is established both in the current treaties and in the text of the European Constitution. However, we cannot close our eyes to the prospect that, if Europe does not manage to return to higher economic growth rates in a sustained manner, it will be increasingly difficult to finance cohesion, putting at risk the survival of the European model. Furthermore, as can be seen, it also seems unavoidable to revise some of the basic elements of national and Community cohesion policies so that they are as complementary as possible with an efficient allocation of resources and, ultimately, with the growth process. Supply factors When the empirical evidence on the roots of Europe's economic problems is analysed, it is concluded that the decline in European growth over recent years is basically due to supply-side reasons which, as mentioned, some elements of cohesion policies would also have had an adverse impact. Thus, a number of problems, affecting aggregate supply, would have contributed to the decline in growth by slowing down the increase in total factor productivity, the rate of accumulation of human, physical and technological capital and job creation. These problems, in turn, would be rooted in a highly complex and not fully efficient model of economic governance for the EU and in an insufficient orientation of national and European policies towards economic growth. According to the most recent research, although it is not easy to unravel the root causes that govern growth processes, it can be concluded that having an appropriate economic environment, fully respectful of the incentives of agents and that facilitates productive dynamism within a framework of efficient allocation of resources, is essential. In particular, according to modern theories of endogenous growth, the processes of technological innovation and the continuous adaptation of organizational structures to the demands of a changing environment are a very important force whose contribution to growth is decisive. However, reality shows that the transition from a traditional economic system, based on large-scale production within the framework of stable and secure markets and inflexible industrial relations, to what is currently considered a modern economic system has not yet been completed throughout the EU. This system is characterized by the importance of technological innovation processes to survive in a world characterized by globalization and external competition, which makes it necessary to adopt new organizational forms, promote research and development, improve the quality of education, establish regulatory frameworks that encourage the free entry of companies and competition in the markets for goods and services, improve the degree of flexibility of wage structures and functional, geographical and sectoral mobility in labour markets, have better tax structures and, finally, sufficiently flexible and diversified sources of financing in integrated financial markets at European level. All these supply-side driving elements, which are present in the United States, suffer from a very insufficient degree of development in the EU as a result of the fact that economic growth has not been, until now, the main priority of European economic policies, both at national level d0 in most cases d0 and at Community level. This concern is what inspired the so-called "Lisbon Strategy", through which EU governments agreed to relaunch Europe's growth capacity based on three basic elements: completing the Single Market; promoting the information, research and development society; and modernising the European social model. However, even if the aims are appropriate and even taking into account the short time that has elapsed with this framework, the poor results achieved since the adoption of the "Lisbon strategy" in 2000 make it impossible to think that the ultimate objectives can finally be achieved with the shortcomings of the current European economic system and the absence of sufficiently powerful mechanisms to improve it. In this sense, while the EU provided itself in Maastricht with a very effective system to encourage the adoption of macroeconomic stability policies by the member states, the Lisbon process does not seem to have, for the moment, mechanisms of reward and penalization sufficiently effective to favor the implementation of the microeconomic policies that are required to boost the capacity for growth in Europe. Consequently, it can be said that the weakness of microeconomic policies, closely linked to the low presence of structural reforms, is what is at the root of the serious supply shortfalls suffered by the EU economic system and which have such serious consequences on its growth potential. It should not be forgotten, however, that this situation is also influenced by the complexity of the Community's economic governance system and by the different assignment of responsibilities between national and European decision-making areas. This has led to a state of affairs that can clearly be improved, since the current coordination mechanisms between the aforementioned decision-making areas do not seem to guarantee coherence and effectiveness as regards their joint impact on growth capacity. Hence, the need, not only to promote microeconomic policies but also to improve the quality of the EU's economic governance. Check the European model The EU's poor balance sheet in terms of growth poses a serious threat to the future living standards of European citizens, while jeopardizing the European model and casting serious doubt on its sustainability. On the one hand, the low rates of growth, if continued in the future, necessarily imply a slow progression of per capita income in the area; and, on the other hand, since maintaining cohesion requires sufficient growth rates to raise the resources needed to finance social safety nets, the absence of economic dynamism could put too much pressure on public accounts in the future, thus making cohesion increasingly difficult to finance and/or calling macroeconomic stability into question. This, in turn, would adversely affect growth and seriously threaten the survival of the European model. Consequently, only if the EU succeeds in growing at a satisfactory pace in a sustained manner will it be possible to maintain macroeconomic stability and, ultimately, the elements of cohesion that characterise the European model. But, in order to boost growth, it is essential, at the same time, to strengthen macroeconomic stability policies and review the design of the welfare state so that the promotion of cohesion is compatible, and does not hinder, economic growth. The sustainability d0 without reforms d0 of the European model is even more problematic if one takes into account the increasing demands that this model will have to bear in the coming years as a result of the new needs for health and pension expenses associated with the ageing of the European population. But it is also necessary to consider that globalisation and, in particular, strong international competition make it necessary for the countries of the Union to improve their competitiveness and climb some rungs on the technological ladder, so as not to be subjected to the problems that higher unemployment and its adverse repercussions on public accounts would entail. Finally, it is clear that an enlarged Europe, which starts from such substantial differences in per capita income between the current and the new Member States and where the necessary Community funds must be raised to facilitate the integration of more than one hundred million people into a new reality, needs, more than ever, to carry out the reforms that allow European growth to be enhanced. In turn, the economic governance of an EU of 25 countries acquires a very remarkable degree of institutional complexity that is even more so if one takes into account the considerable economic and social heterogeneity among its members. Hence, the response to the challenge of enlargement must also have mechanisms to ensure the efficiency of the decision-making processes of such a large, complex and diverse structure. The European Constitution is aimed at resolving these institutional problems in their more general form. Economic policy and methods of European governance Having reviewed the challenges that the EU will have to face in the future, it is necessary to ask what avenues could be explored to meet the challenge currently faced by the countries of the European Union to ensure the sustainability of the European model in order to meet the legitimate aspirations of European citizens to enjoy higher standards of living and well-being in the future in the future. an enlarged EU. From my analysis of the three vertices of the European model d0 growth, stability and cohesion d0 several conclusions emerge. First, that maintaining macroeconomic stability is an extremely valuable asset in itself and essential as a frame of reference for growth; secondly, that preserving cohesion necessarily requires a modernisation of cohesion, so that this is consistent with the incentives of actors to work, invest and produce in a more demanding economic environment; and finally, that boosting growth capacity requires very important structural reforms both at national level and in Community policies, while improving the quality of European economic governance. In other words, as the Sapir and Kok reports have concluded, what is needed is for the EU's economic system to be genuinely d0 and not just nominally d0 oriented towards the objective of boosting growth within a framework of high macroeconomic stability and a reasonable degree of cohesion, as growth is the cornerstone on which the European economic and social model is based. But this implies very considerable changes, both in economic policies and in European governance methods, so that the action of the national and Community authorities is generally consistent with these objectives. As regards policies to promote growth, the role of national authorities is crucial. The continuity of reform processes in the various countries is key to improving the functioning of goods and services markets and labour markets; to ensure the future solvency of public pension systems; to promote and encourage innovation, research and development processes; and to raise the quality of education. In this respect, the future course of events in Germany and France is of the utmost importance because, if reforms in these countries finally make decisive progress, their economic and political impact will be very healthy, not only for their own economies, but for the EU as a whole, given their considerable specific weight and the favourable impact this would have on further deepening reforms in other countries. With regard to policies at European level, it is essential to complete the single market and make it more dynamic and competitive. This is very important for services and, in particular, financial services, given the benefit of having more developed and integrated financial markets in an already commercially and monetarily integrated area; And it is also very relevant as far as labour markets are concerned, given the very low degree of labour mobility between Member States. In addition to this, initiatives aimed at improving the quality of Community competition regulations, increasing coordination between national regulators in certain sectors, and facilitating the geographical connection of markets through the necessary infrastructures can also contribute to completing the single market and making it more dynamic. Finally, it should also be possible to revise the criteria behind the preparation of the Community budget so that it is more clearly in line with the primary objective of stimulating the most innovative and productive processes throughout the European Union. Conclusions Only a few days have passed since Spain supported the text of the European Constitution in a popular referendum. The ratification process to which the constitutional text is currently subject in each and every one of the countries of the European Union is the latest example of the institutional vitality of the process of European construction. However, it is disturbing that the institutional dynamism shown by the EU contrasts so sharply with the widespread perception that things are not going well in the economic field and that, without courageous, determined and urgent action by national governments, Europe's economic future could be seriously jeopardised. consequently, to make it impossible to achieve the objectives of economic growth, macroeconomic stability and social progress contained in the constitutional text. For all these reasons, it is absolutely essential to reorient all the priorities, actions and methods of decision-making throughout the Union, on the part of the national authorities and the Community governing bodies, in order to avert the serious danger that the objectives of growth, stability and social cohesion that underpin the European model will not be achieved, making such a model unfeasible, eroding the living standards of European citizens and reducing the role played by Europe in the international arena. Europe faces enormous challenges but also extraordinary opportunities that must be exploited. And now is the time to act, all together, giving priority to relaunching European economic growth, the true cornerstone of our model. Only if we citizens understand how much is at stake in the coming years will we be able to boost the political will of the national and Community authorities and commit them to carrying out the reforms needed to secure Europe's economic future. Segn se ha expuesto, independientemente de cules sean las variables escogidas para aproximar cmo ha evolucionado la cohesin en el seno de la UE, el hecho es que, en las ltimas tres dcadas, se han ido estrechando las distancias que separan a los pases menos prsperos del resto en trminos de renta per cpita al tiempo que diversos indicadores sintticos del grado de desigualdad entre pases han mejorado, en conjunto, a pesar de las sucesivas ampliaciones de la UE llevadas a cabo durante todos estos aos. En fin, del anlisis llevado a cabo hasta ahora puede concluirse que a lo largo de los ltimos treinta aos, durante los que la UE ha llevado a cabo considerables avances institucionales en el proceso de integracin, su trayectoria econmica ha venido caracterizada por luces y sombras. Luces, que corresponden a las mejoras logradas en los mbitos de la estabilidad macroeconmica y la cohesin; y sombras, que emanan del prolongado declive del crecimiento europeo en el tiempo y en relacin con los Estados Unidos. Factores explicativos de la debilidad del crecimiento econmico europeo Puesto que la manifiesta debilidad del crecimiento constituye el rasgo ms preocupante de la evolucin econmica europea, resulta necesario examinar qu razones pueden haber contribuido ms decisivamente a ello, desde una perspectiva de medio y largo plazo. La comparacin entre el caso europeo y el de Estados Unidos puede, de nuevo, resultar til para comprender mejor la naturaleza de nuestros problemas. As, si se descompone el crecimiento del PIB en avances de la productividad (por hora trabajada) y creacin de empleo (horas trabajadas), se aprecia claramente cmo, durante las ltimas tres dcadas, el factor diferencial que, en conjunto, explica el mayor crecimiento de los Estados Unidos en relacin a Europa es la creacin de empleo, mientras que las tasas de incremento de la productividad son mayores en la UE. No obstante, no debe sorprender que nuestra productividad haya crecido ms rpidamente habida cuenta de que su nivel de partida era bastante inferior al de los Estados Unidos. Lo que resulta frustrante es que su nivel actual an est casi un diez por ciento por debajo de de la economa norteamericana y que, en estos ltimos aos, se haya vuelto a ensanchar la brecha entre los dos. A su vez, dada la elevada tasa de paro existente en la economa europea, es descorazonador que apenas se haya creado empleo. Sin embargo, la experiencia seala que, en el caso europeo, cuando se intensifica  siquiera modestamente  la creacin de empleo, la contrapartida es una ralentizacin del ritmo de incremento de la productividad y viceversa. As, por ejemplo, a medida que la UE ha ido incrementando su tasa media anual de creacin de empleo desde el -0,5% en los aos setenta, al 0% en los ochenta y al muy exiguo +0,3% en los noventa, el ritmo de aumento medio anual de la productividad ha descendido de manera significativa, respectivamente en cada uno de esos perodos, del 3,5%, al 2,4% y al 1,8% y a tasas an ms reducidas en el presente. Esta experiencia contrasta notablemente con la de los Estados Unidos, que ha visto cmo su ritmo de creacin anual de empleo se ha mantenido muy cercano al 2% en cada uno de esos mismos perodos mientras que su productividad anual aumentaba del 1,4% al 1,7%, siendo en la actualidad claramente superior a estas cifras. La economa norteamericana ha podido, en consecuencia, mejorar su productividad sin dejar de mantener por ello unas tasas de creacin de empleo considerablemente ms elevadas, lo que ha favorecido doblemente el proceso de crecimiento. La experiencia europea, por el contrario, pone de manifiesto las serias dificultades encontradas hasta el presente para mejorar en un sentido sin empeorar en el otro, lo que supone un formidable freno a la capacidad de crecimiento. Cmo han afectado las polticas de estabilidad y de cohesin al crecimiento europeo? Tras examinar la evidencia, la pregunta que surge es qu razn o razones explican la incapacidad de la economa europea para crear empleo ms rpidamente as como para mantener ritmos de crecimiento de la productividad ms elevados, habida cuenta de sus niveles relativamente ms reducidos que en los Estados Unidos? En este sentido, conviene preguntarse si las otras dos dimensiones del modelo europeo  estabilidad macroeconmica y cohesin  han influido y en qu direccin sobre el proceso de crecimiento en Europa. Actualmente se ha desencadenado un debate en Europa acerca de si las polticas de estabilidad podran ser responsables, en mayor o menor medida, de las persistentes dificultades de la UE para mantener un crecimiento sostenido a ritmos ms elevados. Indudablemente, este debate viene suscitado por la desfavorable coyuntura econmica europea de estos ltimos aos, que ha llevado a criticar desde algunos crculos el marco institucional y estratgico que rige la poltica macroeconmica europea y, en particular, la poltica monetaria nica y las polticas fiscales. A ello tambin ha contribuido la sospecha, por parte de algunos, acerca de si los progresos realizados por la UE en el mbito de la estabilidad a raz del proceso de convergencia de Maastricht no habran mermado su capacidad de crecimiento. Sin embargo, an sin entrar a fondo a discutir si debera replantearse algn aspecto concreto de los mecanismos que en la prctica rigen dichas polticas, puede afirmarse que la posicin anterior est equivocada. Por una parte, segn postulan los principios econmicos y confirma la experiencia, la estabilidad macroeconmica resulta indispensable para alcanzar y mantener un ritmo de crecimiento satisfactorio de manera sostenida aun reconociendo que, en ciertos casos, las polticas de ajuste que se precisan para alcanzar dicha estabilidad previamente pueden tener un impacto negativo sobre la actividad en el corto plazo. Por otra parte, achacar a las polticas de estabilidad la debilidad crnica del crecimiento europeo resulta inconsistente con el hecho de que dicha debilidad es un fenmeno de medio plazo que viene observndose dcada tras dcada, mucho antes de que se pusieran en marcha las polticas macroeconmicas de estabilidad en los aos noventa. La otra cuestin particularmente importante es si la forma concreta en que la bsqueda de la cohesin se articula dentro del modelo europeo a travs del estado del bienestar puede haber incidido negativamente sobre el crecimiento. En este sentido, la evidencia indica que el diseo de las polticas de cohesin, tanto a nivel comunitario como nacional, no ha tenido suficientemente en cuenta que algunos de sus elementos podran incidir de manera particularmente lesiva sobre la eficiencia y el crecimiento. A nivel comunitario, existe evidencia emprica de que los fondos agrcolas y regionales habran limitado, en no pocos casos, los naturales procesos de reasignacin de los recursos derivados del establecimiento del Mercado nico, lo que habra impedido materializar las ganancias potenciales de eficiencia que ste lleva consigo al impedir que los factores de produccin se desplacen hacia sectores o actividades ms productivas. A nivel nacional, por su parte, los efectos desfavorables sobre la eficiencia y el crecimiento habran sido el resultado no deseado de medidas sociales y tributarias que habran incidido negativamente, por ejemplo, sobre el grado de flexibilidad de las estructuras salariales, sobre la movilidad laboral y sobre los incentivos de los agentes para ahorrar, invertir o producir. La cohesin es  y debe seguir siendo  un elemento bsico del modelo europeo y as lo establecen tanto los actuales tratados como el texto de la Constitucin Europea. Sin embargo, no se pueden cerrar los ojos ante la perspectiva de que, si Europa no consigue retornar a tasas de crecimiento econmico ms elevadas de forma sostenida, ser cada vez ms difcil financiar la cohesin, poniendo en riesgo la pervivencia del modelo europeo. Asimismo, segn se desprende de lo argumentado, parece tambin ineludible revisar algunos de los elementos bsicos de las polticas nacionales y comunitarias de cohesin de forma que resulten lo ms complementarias posible con una eficiente asignacin de los recursos y, en ltimo trmino, con el proceso de crecimiento. Los factores de oferta Cuando se analiza la evidencia emprica acerca de las races de los problemas econmicos europeos, viene a concluirse que el declive del crecimiento europeo a lo largo de los ltimos aos obedece bsicamente a razones de oferta sobre las que, como se ha mencionado, habran incidido desfavorablemente tambin algunos elementos de las polticas de cohesin. As, una serie de problemas, que afectan a la oferta agregada, habran contribuido al declive del crecimiento al ralentizar el incremento de la productividad total de los factores, el ritmo de acumulacin del capital humano, fsico y tecnolgico y la creacin de empleo. Estos problemas, a su vez, tendran su raz en un modelo de gobierno econmico para la UE sumamente complejo y no plenamente eficiente y en una insuficiente orientacin de las polticas nacionales y europeas hacia el crecimiento econmico. Segn concluyen las investigaciones ms recientes, aunque no resulta sencillo desentraar las causas ltimas que gobiernan los procesos de crecimiento, s puede concluirse que contar con un entorno econmico apropiado, plenamente respetuoso con los incentivos de los agentes y que facilite el dinamismo productivo en un marco de asignacin eficiente de los recursos, es imprescindible. En particular, segn las modernas teoras del crecimiento endgeno, los procesos de innovacin tecnolgica y de continuada adaptacin de las estructuras organizativas a las exigencias de un entorno cambiante son una fuerza muy importante cuya contribucin al crecimiento resulta decisiva. Sin embargo, la realidad muestra que en el conjunto de la UE no se ha completado an el trnsito desde un sistema econmico tradicional, basado en la produccin a gran escala en el marco de unos mercados estables y protegidos y de unas relaciones laborales escasamente flexibles, a lo que actualmente se considera un sistema econmico moderno. Dicho sistema se caracteriza por la importancia que revisten los procesos de innovacin tecnolgica para sobrevivir en un mundo caracterizado por la globalizacin y la competencia exterior, lo que hace necesario adoptar nuevas formas organizativas, promocionar la investigacin y el desarrollo, mejorar la calidad de la educacin, establecer marcos regulatorios que fomenten la libre entrada de empresas y la competencia en los mercados de bienes y servicios, mejorar el grado de flexibilidad de las estructuras salariales y la movilidad funcional, geogrfica y sectorial en los mercados de trabajo, disponer de mejores estructuras impositivas y, finalmente, contar con unas fuentes de financiacin suficientemente flexibles y diversificadas en unos mercados financieros integrados a nivel europeo. Todos estos elementos dinamizadores por el lado de la oferta, que se encuentran presentes en los Estados Unidos, adolecen de un grado de desarrollo muy insuficiente en la UE como consecuencia de que el crecimiento econmico no ha sido, hasta el momento, la prioridad principal de las polticas econmicas europeas, tanto en el mbito nacional en la mayor parte de los casos como comunitario. Esta preocupacin es la que inspir la denominada "Estrategia de Lisboa", mediante la cual los gobiernos de la UE acordaron relanzar la capacidad de crecimiento europeo a partir de tres elementos bsicos: completar el Mercado nico; promocionar la sociedad de la informacin, la investigacin y el desarrollo; y modernizar el modelo social europeo. No obstante, con ser adecuados los fines y an teniendo en cuenta el escaso tiempo transcurrido con este marco, los pobres resultados cosechados desde la adopcin de la "estrategia de Lisboa" en el 2000 hacen imposible pensar que puedan alcanzarse finalmente los objetivos ltimos con las carencias del actual sistema econmico europeo y la ausencia de mecanismos suficientemente potentes para mejorarlo. En este sentido, mientras que la UE se dot en Maastricht de un sistema muy eficaz para incentivar la adopcin de unas polticas de estabilidad macroeconmica por parte de los estados miembros, el proceso de Lisboa no parece contar, por el momento, con unos mecanismos de recompensa y penalizacin lo bastante eficaces como para favorecer la instrumentacin de las polticas microeconmicas que se requieren para impulsar la capacidad de crecimiento en Europa. En consecuencia, puede afirmarse que la debilidad de las polticas microeconmicas, ligada ntimamente a la escasa presencia de las reformas estructurales, es la que est en la base de las serias insuficiencias de oferta que padece el sistema econmico de la UE y que tan graves consecuencias han tenido y tienen sobre su potencial de crecimiento. No debe olvidarse, sin embargo, que esta situacin tambin viene influida por la complejidad del sistema de gobierno econmico comunitario y por la diferente adscripcin de responsabilidades entre los mbitos de decisin nacionales y europeos. Ello ha llevado a un estado de cosas manifiestamente mejorable, ya que no parece que los actuales mecanismos de coordinacin entre los mencionados mbitos de decisin garanticen la coherencia y la eficacia por lo que se refiere a su impacto conjunto sobre la capacidad de crecimiento. De ah, la necesidad, no solo de impulsar las polticas de carcter microeconmico sino de mejorar la calidad del gobierno econmico de la UE. Jaque al modelo europeo El pobre balance de la UE en trminos de crecimiento supone una seria amenaza para los futuros niveles de vida de los ciudadanos europeos, al tiempo que coloca en jaque al modelo europeo y siembra serias dudas sobre su sostenibilidad. De una parte, los reducidos ritmos de crecimiento, de continuar en el futuro, necesariamente implican una lenta progresin de la renta per cpita en el rea; y, de otra, puesto que el mantenimiento de la cohesin requiere unas tasas de crecimiento suficientes que permitan allegar los recursos necesarios para financiar las redes de proteccin social, la ausencia de dinamismo econmico podra presionar en exceso sobre las cuentas pblicas en el futuro, haciendo, de esta forma, cada vez ms difcilmente financiable la cohesin y/o cuestionando la estabilidad macroeconmica. Esto, a su vez, redundara desfavorablemente sobre el crecimiento y amenazara gravemente la pervivencia del modelo europeo. En consecuencia, slo si la UE consigue crecer a un ritmo satisfactorio de forma sostenida resultar posible mantener la estabilidad macroeconmica y, en ltima instancia, los elementos de cohesin que caracterizan al modelo europeo. Pero, para potenciar el crecimiento resulta imprescindible, a su vez, reforzar las polticas macroeconmicas de estabilidad y revisar el diseo del estado de bienestar con el fin de que el fomento de la cohesin resulte compatible, y no dificulte, el crecimiento econmico. La sostenibilidad  sin reformas  del modelo europeo resulta an ms problemtica si se tiene en cuenta las crecientes exigencias que dicho modelo deber soportar en aos venideros como consecuencia de las nuevas necesidades de gastos sanitarios y de pensiones asociadas con el envejecimiento de la poblacin europea. Pero tambin es necesario considerar que la globalizacin y, en particular, la fuerte competencia internacional hacen preciso que los pases de la Unin mejoren su competitividad y suban algunos peldaos en la escala tecnolgica, para no verse sometidos a los problemas que supondra un desempleo ms elevado y sus repercusiones adversas sobre las cuentas pblicas. Finalmente, resulta evidente que una Europa ampliada, que parte de unas diferencias tan sustanciales de renta per cpita entre los actuales y los nuevos estados miembros y en donde hay que allegar los fondos comunitarios necesarios para facilitar la integracin de ms de cien millones de personas en una nueva realidad, precisa, ms que nunca, realizar las reformas que permitan potenciar el crecimiento europeo. A su vez, el gobierno econmico de una UE de 25 pases adquiere un grado de complejidad institucional muy notable que an lo es ms si se tiene en cuenta la considerable heterogeneidad econmica y social entre sus miembros. De ah que, la respuesta al reto de la ampliacin deba contar tambin con mecanismos que garanticen la eficiencia de los procesos de toma de decisiones de una estructura tan amplia, compleja y diversa. A resolver estos problemas de carcter institucional, en su forma ms general, se encamina la Constitucin Europea. Poltica econmica y mtodos de gobierno europeo Una vez repasados los desafos a los que la UE va a tener que hacer frente en el futuro, resulta necesario preguntarse qu caminos podran explorarse para hacer frente al reto al que actualmente se enfrentan los pases de la Unin Europea de garantizar la sostenibilidad del modelo europeo con objeto de satisfacer las legtimas aspiraciones de los ciudadanos europeos a gozar de unos niveles de vida y bienestar ms elevados en el futuro en una UE ampliada. Del anlisis que he realizado de los tres vrtices del modelo europeo  crecimiento, estabilidad y cohesin  se desprenden varias conclusiones. En primer lugar, que el mantenimiento de la estabilidad macroeconmica es un activo sumamente valioso por s mismo e imprescindible como marco de referencia para el crecimiento; en segundo lugar, que preservar la cohesin pasa necesariamente por una modernizacin de la misma, de forma que ello resulte coherente con los incentivos de los agentes a trabajar, invertir y producir en un entorno econmico ms exigente; y finalmente, que la potenciacin de la capacidad de crecimiento requiere de reformas estructurales muy importantes tanto en el mbito nacional como en el de las polticas comunitarias, al tiempo que se mejora la calidad del gobierno econmico europeo. Dicho de otro modo, segn han concluido los informes Sapir y Kok, lo que se precisa es que el sistema econmico de la UE se oriente realmente y no solo nominalmente al objetivo de potenciar el crecimiento en un marco de elevada estabilidad macroeconmica y un grado razonable de cohesin, por ser el crecimiento la piedra angular sobre la que se asienta el modelo econmico y social europeo. Pero ello implica modificaciones muy considerables, tanto de las polticas econmicas como de los mtodos de gobierno europeo, de modo que la actuacin de las autoridades nacionales y comunitarias resulte globalmente coherente con estos objetivos. Por lo que respecta a las polticas de fomento del crecimiento, el papel de las autoridades nacionales es decisivo. La continuidad de los procesos de reforma en los diversos pases se revela como fundamental para mejorar el funcionamiento de los mercados de bienes y servicios y de los mercados de trabajo; para garantizar la solvencia futura de los sistemas pblicos de pensiones; para promover e incentivar los procesos de innovacin, investigacin y desarrollo; y para elevar la calidad de la educacin. En este sentido, el curso futuro de los acontecimientos en Alemania y Francia reviste suma importancia porque, si finalmente avanzan decisivamente las reformas en estos pases, su impacto econmico y poltico ser muy saludable, no solo para sus propias economas, sino para el conjunto de la UE, dado su considerable peso especfico y la repercusin favorable que ello tendra para seguir profundizando con las reformas en otros pases. En relacin con las polticas de mbito europeo, resulta imprescindible completar el mercado nico y hacerlo ms dinmico y competitivo. Esto es muy importante por lo que respecta a los servicios y, en particular, a los servicios financieros, dado lo beneficioso que resulta contar con unos mercados financieros ms desarrollados e integrados en un rea comercial y monetariamente ya integrada; y tambin es muy relevante por lo que concierne a los mercados de trabajo, dado el muy reducido grado de movilidad laboral existente entre los pases miembros. Junto a lo anterior, las iniciativas tendentes a mejorar la calidad de las regulaciones comunitarias en el mbito de la competencia, a incrementar la coordinacin entre los reguladores nacionales en ciertos sectores, y a facilitar la conexin geogrfica de los mercados mediante las necesarias infraestructuras, pueden tambin contribuir a completar el mercado nico y hacerlo ms dinmico. Por ltimo, debera resultar tambin posible revisar los criterios que inspiran la confeccin del presupuesto comunitario para que ste se site ms claramente en lnea con el objetivo primordial de estimular los procesos ms innovadores y productivos en el conjunto de la Unin Europea. Conclusiones Tan solo han transcurrido unos das desde que Espaa apoyara en referndum popular el texto de la Constitucin Europea. El proceso de ratificacin al que actualmente se halla sometido el texto constitucional en todos y cada uno de los pases de la Unin Europea constituye el ltimo exponente de la vitalidad institucional del proceso de construccin europea. Sin embargo, resulta inquietante que el dinamismo institucional mostrado por la UE contraste de forma tan patente con la percepcin generalizada de que las cosas no van bien en el mbito econmico y que, de no mediar actuaciones valientes, decididas y urgentes por parte de los gobiernos nacionales, el futuro econmico de Europa podra quedar seriamente comprometido y, en consecuencia, hacer imposible alcanzar los objetivos de crecimiento econmico, estabilidad macroeconmica y progreso social que figuran en el texto constitucional. Por todo ello, resulta de todo punto imprescindible reorientar el conjunto de las prioridades, de las actuaciones y de los mtodos de toma de decisiones en el conjunto de la Unin, por parte de las autoridades nacionales y de los rganos de gobierno comunitarios, para conjurar el serio peligro de que los objetivos de crecimiento, estabilidad y cohesin social que vertebran el modelo europeo no se alcancen, haciendo inviable dicho modelo, erosionando los niveles de vida de los ciudadanos europeos y reduciendo el papel desempeado por Europa en el concierto internacional. Europa tiene ante s enormes retos pero tambin extraordinarias posibilidades que deben ser aprovechadas. Y ste es el momento para actuar, todos juntos, concediendo prioridad a relanzar el crecimiento econmico europeo, verdadera piedra angular de nuestro modelo. Solo si los ciudadanos entendemos lo mucho que nos jugamos en estos prximos aos, seremos capaces de impulsar la voluntad poltica de las autoridades nacionales y comunitarias y comprometerlos en la realizacin de las reformas que se precisan para asegurar el futuro econmico de Europa.
