Title: Notes: Opening Speech at XII Meeting of the Financial Sector (Theme: "Strategies to consolidate the leadership of Spanish financial institutions")
text: Madrid, 11 May 2005 Strategies to consolidate the leadership of Spanish financial institutions. Opening remarks notes XII Meeting of the Financial Sector. Organized by Deloitte SAP, Genworth Financial and ABC Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain Introduction It is a pleasure for me to be here with all of you today. I would like my first words to be of thanks for the invitation to participate in this meeting, which has already become a traditional occasion to discuss the economy and the financial sector. It is difficult to begin a presentation on financial systems without referring to the profound changes that they have undergone in recent years, and that will undoubtedly continue in the future. In the case of Spain, the evolution has been, if possible, more profound, since it has been accompanied by our participation in the creation of Monetary Union, and therefore, by a very substantial change in the framework in which our economic agents carry out their activity. In this sense, the title of this meeting seems to me especially appropriate since, in general, I think it can be said that Spanish entities have been able to adapt to changes in the financial markets, in the international economy and in the institutional environment. They have also done so, gaining in positioning and leadership, something that says a lot about the improvements in management and the adaptability of our entities. However, the changes will continue to take place, the challenges are high, and therefore, the debate on the strategies that allow consolidating the positions reached seems to me very timely. This debate will undoubtedly be enriched thanks to the topics chosen for the presentations that will take place throughout these two days, since they will allow analyzing issues as relevant as, for example, the international strategy of the entities, the regulatory impacts, the priorities required by our market or the integral management of risks. For my part, throughout my presentation I will try to contribute some reflection to the subsequent debate. To that end, let me begin with a brief reminder of the state of our economy and then raise a few questions about the banking system. Economic situation. Since the middle of the last decade, the Spanish economy has been experiencing a long phase of expansion that has significantly shortened the differences in welfare with the most advanced countries in our environment (about 10 points of GDP in the last 10 years). Although this favourable trend is based primarily on the strong demand stimuli resulting from the process of joining the Economic and Monetary Union, it has also benefited from supply-side developments, such as reforms in goods and factor markets and the sharp increase in the immigrant population. Other key defining features of our evolution have been: the remarkable process of fiscal consolidation, a fundamental element of our macroeconomic stability, which has led us to balance the budget of all general government; and the extraordinary performance of the labour market, where the structural reforms introduced, wage moderation in relation to previous situations, and the important demographic changes that have taken place in recent years have boosted the process of job creation. These comparatively positive results for the Spanish economy do not, however, prevent less favourable aspects in its behaviour that need to be redirected to guarantee the continuity of the expansionary phase. However, the Spanish economy is in a good relative situation for this dynamism and convergence process to continue in the future and therefore I believe that we have room for manoeuvre to face the present challenges. In this context, and in a positive international environment, with the exception of the euro area, but with certain risks arising from oil prices and still unresolved global imbalances, the available data indicate that last year GDP increased by 2.7% d0 two tenths more than in 2003 d0 a slightly lower rate than that which seems to have been recorded in the first quarter of this year. These figures, which are already indicative of the remarkable dynamism of the Spanish economy d0 especially when compared with that shown by the euro area as a whole d0 will also be revised upwards once the INE applies the methodological changes of the new National Accounts based on 2000 and, above all, reflects in the macroeconomic aggregates the new information available on population, participation and employment derived from the municipal register and the EAPS, where the phenomenon of immigration is more accurately collected. Recent figures continue to show considerable strength in household spending on consumption and residential investment, which has been a constant during this prolonged expansionary period of the Spanish economy. This strength is supported by the advances in disposable income in the sector d0which, in turn, are linked to the good performance of employmentd0; in the slack of financing conditions; and in the revaluation of the wealth of families that, as you all know, materializes fundamentally in real estate assets. A logical consequence of maintaining growth rates in domestic demand that are persistently higher than those of our main trading partners has been the accumulation of deficit balances in our trade balance. However, recent data on export shares and import penetration suggest that the economy may also be starting to experience the effect of losses in competitiveness caused by higher prices and labour costs than those observed in the euro area as a whole. Indeed, inflation, which the most recent provisional information puts at 3.5% per annum, has long maintained a relatively stable spread of around one percentage point with respect to the EMU average. Wages, on the other hand, although they have maintained a higher degree of moderation than that observed in previous expansionary phases, continue to advance at rates of around 3%, well above the average for the area. Unfortunately, it is not possible to explain the evolution of prices and wage costs in terms of productivity gains in the Spanish economy that could allow an increase in relative nominal incomes without generating competitiveness problems. On the other hand, productivity over the current cycle has shown a low dynamic behaviour, largely as a result of the high rate of job creation. Undoubtedly, the generation of new jobs is one of the most positive features of recent economic developments in our country, given the low rates of use of this factor. However, adverse productivity trends also reflect insufficient capacity to incorporate technical progress into the improvement of production processes. In this way, improving competitiveness, particularly if it is based on a strategy to promote productivity, is one of the main challenges that must be faced to ensure the maintenance in the medium and long term of growth rates that allow further progress in the process of real convergence. Undoubtedly, a necessary condition for the fulfillment of these objectives is the dynamism of productive investment. Precisely for this reason, the incipient recovery of this variable is particularly encouraging, which, after several years of practical stagnation, closed 2004 with a growth rate close to 6%. The improvement in corporate performance and the gradual completion of the balance sheet clean-up process undertaken by large national groups could, in a context of very low financial costs, be providing the necessary stimulus for the sustained expansion of corporate capital expenditure. Likewise, other challenges facing our economy are those derived from the adaptation of the balance sheets of Spanish families to a new context of macroeconomic stability, intense employment growth and low interest rates. Thus, households have increased their indebtedness very sharply and, accordingly, their available savings have been reduced, once the service of the debts contracted has been discounted. Consequently, although the segment of the population that registers a clearly vulnerable patrimonial situation is small, the sector as a whole has increased its exposure to possible shocks that could adversely affect their incomes, the installments they pay for their loans or the value of the main component of their wealth: housing. With regard to the latter, you are already well aware of our diagnosis of the real estate market, although it is perhaps appropriate to recall it here briefly: for some time now, we have been pointing out that the observed growth in prices is not easily explained in terms of the fundamental long-term determinants of demand for residential assets, including household income or the level of interest rates. Consequently, although econometric and statistical techniques do not allow us to estimate with the precision that we would like the magnitude of the imbalance, it is evident in our opinion that there is a significant degree of overvaluation of housing that has been growing progressively. However, although prices still do not show clear signs of moderation, a gradual correction of the existing imbalance remains predictable and desirable, as has in fact happened in previous episodes of real estate boom both in our country and in others. In any case, as a central bank we are obliged to take into account not only the most likely events but also others that are less likely to the extent that they may have particularly negative effects. Let me highlight some elements that justify the low probability of these more adverse scenarios. In this sense, in addition to noting the low probability that can be assigned to a scenario of disorderly adjustment of house prices, it is necessary to check the springs that the Spanish economy maintains to face this eventuality. Thus, it is pertinent to emphasize that Spanish households, contrary to what happened in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom or the Netherlands, have not notoriously exploited the revaluation of their homes to contract debts destined to the financing of current consumption. Therefore, the behavior of this important component of national demand is less dependent on the vicissitudes of the real estate market than in other countries. But, above all, the soundness of the Spanish banking system makes it highly unlikely that a situation such as the one described could significantly weaken its ability to continue efficiently financing economic activity, thus mitigating the macroeconomic impact of this type of shock. Like central banks, which in our risk analysis we have to consider adverse scenarios even if they are not the most likely, it is important that banks incorporate more unfavourable macroeconomic contexts into their risk management. This is one of the reflections I wanted to make when talking about the financial system, to which I will devote the rest of my speech. Financial system Spanish depository institutions have been able to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the favourable situation of our economy. In particular, the strength they have shown in terms of results, as well as the processes of cost rationalisation undertaken, are reflected in the favourable evolution of return on equity, which continues to register levels relatively higher than those observed for the average of euro area banks. Likewise, the soundness of the Spanish banking system as a whole is reinforced by its level of solvency. In aggregate terms, capital ratios remain above the minimum required, standing around the European average. This solvency has been strengthened by the prudential nature of the insolvency endowment model, which since mid-2000 incorporated the statistical endowment, and which has contributed to a greater solidity of Spanish financial institutions. However, the high consumption of own resources as a result of the rapid growth of credit has reduced the high solvency ratios that have traditionally characterized our banking system. Similarly, this rate of progress, which has been observed in financing the resident private sector, has not been accompanied by a similar growth in deposits from this sector. This has forced entities to seek financing through the issuance of securities and by going to the foreign interbank market, which puts pressure on the average cost of their liabilities. However, Spain's integration into an area of stability such as the euro area has made an important contribution to financing credit expansion without any particular tensions. These favourable economic and financial results to which I have been referring have also occurred at a time characterised by the notable changes experienced by the international financial system and, in particular, by the Spanish financial system. Without wishing to be exhaustive, let me remind you that, in recent decades, in a context of continuous technological advance, there has not only been a strong growth in activity, but also in the sophistication and complexity of the banking business. In addition, financial disintermediation and the emergence of new competitors introduce greater competitive pressures into markets. Partly in response to these pressures, and partly by strengthening them, there is also a growing internationalization of entities. In short, new opportunities have arisen, but also numerous challenges. Many of them, in force today, are motivated, in large part, by the development of the banking business in a more varied and interdependent world. The managers of the entities have had to face them and, their response, which in the Spanish case has benefited from the good relative position of our economy in recent years, has made possible the strength of the deposit institutions to which I have referred. This response is based on diverse business strategies, which depend on a multitude of factors, but which, in general, have recognized as a common element the importance of assigning a central role in decision-making processes to the risks assumed, developing procedures that allow them to be identified, measured and controlled. The growing geographical expansion that has been taking place implies challenges for institutions, but also for supervisors. Thus, the increasing complexity of banking groups, both in terms of their organizational structure and the geographical scope of their operations, makes it necessary to deepen the field of international cooperation between banking supervisors. In fact, this is not something new, although, as I say, its importance is growing. Greater cooperation, materialised through a more intensive exchange of information, should lead to a better understanding of financial instruments, entities and the relationships between them. It is also necessary, and even essential for effective international cooperation to be carried out, that entities with a presence in several countries have policies and management criteria consistent with the various geographical areas in which they operate, although, of course, implementing the appropriate adaptations to the characteristics of the different local environments. In the euro area, the single currency has served as a catalyst for progress towards a single financial market, and indeed, in certain segments, such as interbank, this progress has been very profound, while in others, such as retail banking, there is still a need to continue deepening the integration process. In this respect, the European Commission's initiatives are moving in the right direction and I believe that they should be supported. Given these developments, it has been shown in the EU that a cooperative solution between supervisors is not only appropriate, but rather essential. In fact, this is the line that prevails today, through, for example, the ECB's Committee on Banking Supervision, or the recently created European Committee of Banking Supervisors, a level three committee in the application to the banking sector of the so-called Lamfalussy approach. The European Committee of Banking Supervisors maintains among its powers to promote the convergence of supervisory practices in the Member States of the European Union, as well as to increase and improve cooperation between supervisors. Finally, in the field of changes we are experiencing, an important source of changes is coming from the intense regulatory process to which the banking sector has recently been subjected. The adaptation to the new accounting standards issued by the IASB, in the Spanish case specified in the new accounting circular, and the preparation for the implementation of the new capital agreement are two major challenges that, without a doubt, are requiring great efforts on the part of European entities. Efforts that are absorbing substantial resources and that deserve our full support. In this sense, I believe in the convenience that after an intense process of regulatory changes, we concentrate our efforts on achieving a good implementation and allow a moderation in the regulatory intensity in these areas. In this way, it is a question of making it possible to digest the profound changes recently introduced. I would now like to dwell on two elements: the need to introduce macro aspects into risk analysis and management, that is, the need to be prepared for variations in the macroeconomic scenario, even if these changes are not the most likely; and second, I will point out some aspects of the aforementioned regulations, and in particular, of the International Accounting Standards. Macro approach to banking risks: credit growth As I mentioned earlier, over the last few decades there has been a remarkable advance in banking activity in the broad sense. Thus, for example, entities have sought to expand their operations towards the provision of financial services with greater added value. This dynamism is also reflected in the notable expansion that has occurred in the so-called off-balance sheet operations, which generally include operations that in the future could have equity repercussions for institutions, but which, by their very nature, incorporate risks that are sometimes more difficult to assess, requiring special attention from managers. Having said all of the above, I believe that none of those present is unaware that, however, in Spain, in recent years, the dynamism of banking activity has been led by the sharp increase in credit. Moreover, the growth of financing granted to the resident private sector presents a marked dichotomy, since it has been particularly intense in the financing of those activities related to the real estate sector in the broad sense. As you know, we have been noticing for some time a continuous increase in household debt in proportion to their gross annual disposable income, which has gone from levels of around 45% in the mid-nineties to 100% in the third quarter of 2004. Thus, the degree of indebtedness of this sector, which started from values well below those of the average of the EMU countries, has come to be, in a short space of time, above these, although they still remain at lower levels than those of the United States and the United Kingdom. This process has caused significant changes in the spending and financing decisions of families that have produced noticeable modifications in their balance sheets. These changes have direct implications, both from a macroeconomic point of view and from the point of view of financial stability. For example, an increase in household debt usually entails greater credit risk for lenders. At the same time, it implies for households an increase in their future financial obligations in the form of interest and amortization of outstanding capital, and therefore, a lower disposable income for consumption, which could, eventually, translate into a downward adjustment of this aggregate. All this makes it more necessary that, as I have already pointed out, institutions take into account the possible evolution of risks in more adverse macroeconomic environments, even if these are not the most likely. It seems clear that in the case of our economy, entities must consider scenarios that include higher interest rates and adjustment processes in the real estate market that lead to lower mortgage credit growth figures. Given the wide time lag between credit growth phenomena such as that experienced in our economy and the emergence of non-performing loans, this indicator, which is currently at historic lows, should not lead to excessive confidence and to relax credit policy. And this despite recognizing that this low delinquency is explained not only by cyclical phenomena, but also by the improvement in the management of the Spanish banking system. On the contrary, it should be remembered that mistakes tend to be made during the expansionary phase of the credit cycle. It is also necessary to analyse the risks in depth, avoiding risk concentrations and appropriately differentiating those corresponding to the financing of final housing and development activities. The dynamism of mortgage credit that we have been observing in recent years should lead us to some reflections: Firstly, and given the changes that our economy has undergone over the last 20 years, it is possible that the historical experience available in terms of potential losses in adverse situations does not correspond to the size and characteristics of the current market, something that from the point of view of risk management and preparation towards Basel II, It shall be taken into account in the models of institutions. From this perspective, it is possible that the expectations of reduction in consumption of regulatory capital in the mortgage loan portfolio, as a result of the application of advanced Basel II models, are exaggerated. The second reflection has to do with the role played by appraisal companies, since the maximum percentage to be financed by the entity depends, to a large extent, on them, which is important to respect effectively. In particular, valuations carried out by appraisers need not be fixed solely at the time of grant. Taking into account the cyclical behavior of the real estate sector, it seems not only more prudent, but also more realistic, to consider a longer period of time, where the appraisal reflects the sustainable value in the medium term of the property in question. From a different point of view, allow me one final reflection through which I intend to reiterate the importance of providing adequate information to the user of financial services. Institutions must help customers understand the products offered to them, evaluate them properly and, to do so, identify the risks associated with each product and put them in relation to their degree of tolerance and their ability to assume them. In this sense, the Bank of Spain has always recognized that the proper functioning of the financial system requires well-informed consumers capable of making their decisions responsibly. For this reason, in February of this year, an Internet portal dedicated to banking customers has been created that is receiving about 2,000 daily accesses. It is not intended to give advice or make recommendations, but to guide consumers in their relationship with credit institutions, helping them to have more information. A well-informed consumer, together with a transparent attitude on the part of institutions, contributes to increasing market discipline with the consequent favourable effect on competition and the efficiency of the Spanish banking system. IAS and the new accounting circular of the Bank of Spain I mentioned that different initiatives have been developed at EU level aimed at promoting genuine integration of the Union's financial markets. One of those initiatives, and to which I would like to devote the last minutes of my speech, has been the approval by the European Union of the International Accounting Standards emanating from the IASB. The European Union decided that the consolidated accounts of groups with securities listed on any regulated market in the European Union should be drawn up, since January 2005, in accordance with those rules. The objective, as I mentioned, is to promote the consolidation of a single financial market, for which it is important to ensure that participants in it have access to financial information that enjoys the highest degree of homogenisation possible. Likewise, a second objective would be to strengthen the integration of the international financial system, which involves favoring the convergence of IAS with North American accounting standards. The Banco de Espa96a, for its part, recognizes and shares the benefits derived from the efforts aimed at achieving a greater degree of accounting harmonization, while as supervisor maintaining a legitimate interest in the quality of accounting standards and their effective implementation. For this reason, and in accordance with its competences in terms of accounting regulation of Spanish credit institutions, it decided to modify its regulations. The new accounting circular (CBE 4/2004) was issued in December 2004. Likewise, and in view of the fact that the process of approval and adoption of the new international standards was characterized by its complexity and there were certain calendar difficulties, through the new accounting circular the Bank of Spain has also sought to grant, as far as possible, a greater degree of certainty to the process. The complexity incorporated in the new accounting standards comes not only from the process to which I have just referred, but basically from the modifications contained in them, since they involve notable changes in many aspects very relevant to the management of the entities. Although it is too early to make a detailed assessment of the implementation of the new accounting standards, which have only been in force for a few months, the initial assessment of this process made by the Bank of Spain is positive, also recognizing the important effort and work that financial institutions have done. One of the messages that, from the outset, the Bank of Spain wanted to convey was that we were aware of the difficulties associated with implementation and that therefore, from our role as banking supervisors, we considered a certain flexibility appropriate. Thus, for example, when considering the treatment of the equity of stable holdings in industrial projects, i.e. in the treatment of associated companies, the new accounting rules introduce the figure of 20% and refer to the concept of significant influence. I remember that in the old accounting circular, shares in listed companies greater than 3% were assumed under the method of equivalence, something that was far from the international practice that mostly considered the figure of 20%. The transition was therefore significant and the Bank of Spain expressed its willingness to contribute to making it as easy as possible and without relevant consequences. Today it can be said that the sector itself, in fact a large part of the entities that maintain this type of participation, has decided, from its own conviction, to count these shares as "available for sale", that is, not as "associated companies accounted for by equivalence". I think this rapid transition made by the sector is very positive, which allows us to affirm without nuances that the 20% rule does not require special considerations in our country. In short, this type of investment of a permanent nature and with a vocation to exert a certain influence on the management of non-financial corporations, implies long-term commitments and incorporates additional risks that require greater responsibilities on the part of managers. These greater responsibilities translate into more demands from the point of view of the corporate governance of the entities. Conclusion Let me conclude my statement by conveying to you a message of confidence. Confidence that Spanish entities will demonstrate, as they have been doing in the past, that they have sufficient capacity to face the whole set of challenges to which I have referred today, as well as those others that, no less important, I have not addressed in this intervention. This confidence leads me to think that the managers of the entities will behave in a professional and prudent way, designing business strategies with a medium and long-term vision. In this way, they will not only contribute to the stable functioning of the entities for which they are responsible, but also to the financial system as a whole. I am sure that the reflections you will share throughout these two days will contribute to these achievements. Thank you very much for your attention.

Sistema financiero Las entidades de depsito espaolas han sabido aprovechar las oportunidades ofrecidas por la favorable situacin de nuestra economa. Estos favorables resultados econmico-financieros a los que he venido haciendo referencia se han producido, adems, en un momento caracterizado por los notables cambios experimentados por el sistema financiero internacional y, en particular, por el espaol. Sin nimo de ser exhaustivo, permtanme recordarles que, en las ltimas dcadas, en un marco de continuo avance tecnolgico, no slo se ha producido un fuerte crecimiento de la actividad, sino tambin de la sofisticacin y de la complejidad del negocio bancario. Asimismo, la desintermediacin financiera y la aparicin de nuevos competidores introducen mayores presiones competitivas en los mercados. En parte como respuesta a dichas presiones, y en parte reforzndolas, se observa tambin una creciente internacionalizacin de las entidades. En definitiva, han surgido nuevas oportunidades, pero tambin numerosos retos. Muchos de ellos, vigentes hoy en da, vienen motivados, en buena parte, por el desarrollo del negocio bancario en un mundo ms variado e interdependiente. Los gestores de las entidades han debido enfrentarse a ellos y, su respuesta, que en el caso espaol se ha beneficiado de la buena posicin relativa de nuestra economa durante los ltimos aos, ha posibilitado la fortaleza de las entidades de depsito a la que he hecho alusin. Esta respuesta se basa en estrategias de negocio diversas, que dependen de multitud de factores, pero que, en general, han reconocido como elemento comn la importancia de asignar un papel central en los procesos de toma de decisiones, a los riesgos que se asumen, desarrollando procedimientos que permiten identificarlos, medirlos y controlarlos. La creciente expansin geogrfica que se ha venido produciendo, implica desafos para las entidades, pero tambin para los supervisores. As, la cada vez mayor complejidad de los grupos bancarios, tanto en trminos de su estructura organizativa como del mbito geogrfico de su operativa, hace necesario profundizar en el terreno de la cooperacin internacional entre supervisores bancarios. De hecho, esto no es algo novedoso, aunque, como digo, su importancia es creciente. La mayor cooperacin, materializada a travs de un intercambio de informacin ms intenso, ha de posibilitar un mejor conocimiento tanto de los instrumentos financieros, como de las entidades y de las relaciones existentes entre ellas. Tambin es necesario, e incluso imprescindible para que pueda realizarse una efectiva cooperacin internacional, que las entidades con presencia en varios pases tengan polticas y criterios de gestin consistentes en las diversas reas geogrficas en las que operan, si bien, como es lgico, implementando las debidas adaptaciones a las caractersticas propias de los distintos entornos locales. En la zona del euro la moneda nica ha servido de catalizador para avanzar en el camino hacia un mercado financiero nico, y de hecho, en determinados segmentos como, por ejemplo, en el interbancario dicho avance ha sido muy profundo, mientras que en otros, como el de la banca minorista, todava es necesario continuar profundizando en el proceso de integracin. En este sentido, las iniciativas de la Comisin Europea van en la direccin correcta y creo que deben ser apoyadas. Ante estos desarrollos, en la UE se ha demostrado que una solucin cooperativa entre los supervisores no solo es apropiada, sino ms bien imprescindible. De hecho, esta es la lnea que prevalece en la actualidad, a travs, por ejemplo, del Comit de Supervisin Bancaria del BCE, o del recientemente creado Comit Europeo de Supervisores Bancarios, un comit de nivel tres en la aplicacin al sector bancario del conocido como enfoque Lamfalussy. El Comit Europeo de Supervisores Bancarios mantiene entre sus atribuciones la de favorecer la convergencia de las prcticas supervisoras de los Estados Miembros de la Unin Europea, as como la de aumentar y mejorar la cooperacin entre supervisores. Finalmente, en el terreno de los cambios que estamos viviendo, una importante fuente de modificaciones est proviniendo del intenso proceso regulador al que ltimamente est sometido el sector bancario. La adaptacin a las nuevas normas contables emitidas por el IASB, en el caso espaol concretadas en la nueva circular contable, y la preparacin para la implantacin del nuevo acuerdo de capital son dos grandes retos que, sin duda, estn requiriendo grandes esfuerzos por parte de las entidades europeas. Esfuerzos que estn absorbiendo cuantiosos recursos y que merecen todo nuestro apoyo. En este sentido, creo en la conveniencia de que despus de un intenso proceso de cambios regulatorios, concentremos nuestros esfuerzos en lograr una buena implementacin y permitamos una moderacin en la intensidad regulatoria en estas reas. Se trata, de este modo, de posibilitar una cierta digestin de las profundas modificaciones introducidas recientemente. Me gustara ahora detenerme en dos elementos: la necesidad de introducir en el anlisis y en la gestin de los riesgos los aspectos macro, es decir, la necesidad de estar preparados ante variaciones del escenario macroeconmico, incluso aunque estos cambios no sean los ms probables; y segundo, sealar algunos aspectos de las regulaciones antes mencionadas, y en particular, de las Normas Internacionales de Contabilidad. Planteamiento macro de los riesgos bancarios: crecimiento del crdito Como he mencionado anteriormente, a lo largo de las ltimas dcadas se ha producido un notable avance de la actividad bancaria en sentido amplio. As, por ejemplo, las entidades han procurado expandir su operativa hacia la prestacin de servicios financieros con un mayor valor aadido. Este dinamismo tambin se refleja en la notable expansin que se ha producido en las denominadas operaciones fuera de balance, que con carcter general, recogen operaciones que en el futuro podran tener repercusiones patrimoniales para las entidades, pero que por su propia naturaleza, incorporan riesgos que son a veces ms difciles de evaluar, lo requiere una especial atencin por parte de los gestores. Dicho todo lo anterior, creo que a ninguno de los presentes se le escapa, sin embargo, que en Espaa, en los ltimos aos, el dinamismo de la actividad bancaria ha venido protagonizado por el fuerte incremento del crdito. Es ms, el crecimiento de la financiacin concedida al sector privado residente presenta una marcada dicotoma, ya que ha sido especialmente intenso en la financiacin de aquellas actividades relacionadas con el sector inmobiliario en sentido amplio. Como saben, venimos advirtiendo desde hace algn tiempo un incremento continuado de la deuda de las familias en proporcin a su renta bruta anual disponible, que ha pasado de niveles en torno al 45% a mediados de los aos noventa a alcanzar el 100% en el tercer trimestre de 2004. De este modo, el grado de endeudamiento de este sector, que parta de valores muy inferiores a los de la media de los pases de la UEM, se ha llegado a situar, en un breve espacio de tiempo, por encima de estos, aunque se mantienen todava en registros inferiores a los de Estados Unidos y del Reino Unido. Este proceso ha ocasionado cambios significativos en las decisiones de gasto y financiacin de las familias que han producido modificaciones notorias en sus balances patrimoniales. Estos cambios tienen implicaciones directas, tanto desde el punto de vista macroeconmico, como desde el de la estabilidad financiera. Por ejemplo, un aumento de la deuda contrada por los hogares normalmente supone un mayor riesgo de crdito para las entidades prestamistas. Al mismo tiempo, implica para los hogares un incremento de sus obligaciones financieras futuras en forma de intereses y amortizacin del capital pendiente, y por lo tanto, una menor renta disponible para el consumo, que podra, eventualmente, traducirse en un ajuste a la baja de dicho agregado. Todo ello hace ms necesario que, como ya he sealado, las entidades tengan muy en cuenta la posible evolucin de los riesgos en entornos macroeconmicos ms adversos, aunque estos no sean los ms probables. Parece evidente que en el caso de nuestra economa, las entidades deben considerar escenarios que incluyan tipos de inters ms elevados y procesos de ajuste en el mercado inmobiliario que lleven a cifras de crecimiento del crdito hipotecario ms reducidas. Dado el desfase temporal amplio entre los fenmenos de crecimiento del crdito como el experimentado en nuestra economa y la aparicin de morosidad, este indicador, que en estos momentos se sita en mnimos histricos, no debe inducir a una excesiva confianza y a relajar la poltica crediticia. Y ello a pesar de reconocer que esa baja morosidad se explica no solo, por fenmenos cclicos, sino tambin por la mejora en la gestin del sistema bancario espaol. Por el contrario, conviene recordar que los errores tienden a cometerse durante la fase expansiva del ciclo crediticio. Asimismo es necesario que se analicen los riesgos en profundidad, evitando concentraciones de riesgo y diferenciando apropiadamente los correspondientes a la financiacin de vivienda final y a las actividades promotoras. El dinamismo del crdito hipotecario que venimos observando en los ltimos aos nos debe llevar a algunas reflexiones: En primer lugar, y dados los cambios que ha experimentado nuestra economa en los ltimos 20 aos, es posible que la experiencia histrica disponible en materia de prdidas potenciales en situaciones adversas, no responda al tamao y a las caractersticas del mercado actual, algo que desde el punto de vista de la gestin de riesgos y de la preparacin hacia Basilea II, deber ser tenido en cuenta en los modelos de las entidades. Desde esa perspectiva, es posible que las expectativas de reduccin de consumo de capital regulatorio en la cartera de crditos hipotecarios, como consecuencia de la aplicacin de modelos avanzados de Basilea II, sean exageradas. La segunda reflexin tiene que ver con el papel jugado por las sociedades de tasacin, ya que de ellas depende, en buena medida, el porcentaje mximo a financiar por parte de la entidad, que es importante respetar de manera efectiva. En particular, las valoraciones realizadas por las tasadoras no han de fijarse nicamente en el momento de la concesin. Teniendo en cuenta el comportamiento cclico de sector inmobiliario parece no solo ms prudente, sino tambin ms realista, que se considere un perodo temporal ms amplio, donde la tasacin recoja el valor sostenible a medio plazo del inmueble en cuestin. Desde un punto de vista diferente, permtanme una ltima reflexin a travs de la que pretendo reiterar la importancia de proporcionar una informacin adecuada al usuario de servicios financieros. Las entidades han de contribuir a que los clientes entiendan los productos que le son ofrecidos, a que los evalen adecuadamente y a que, para ello, identifiquen los riesgos asociados a cada producto y los pongan en relacin con su grado de tolerancia y con su capacidad para asumirlos. En este sentido, el Banco de Espaa siempre ha reconocido que el buen funcionamiento del sistema financiero precisa de consumidores bien informados y capaces de tomar sus decisiones de forma responsable. Por este motivo, en febrero de este ao, se ha creado un portal de Internet dedicado a los clientes bancarios que est recibiendo cerca de 2.000 accesos diarios. A travs de l no se pretende dar consejos ni hacer recomendaciones, sino orientar a los consumidores en su relacin con las entidades de crdito, contribuyendo a que stos dispongan de una mayor informacin. Un consumidor bien informado, junto con una actitud transparente por parte de las entidades, contribuye a aumentar la disciplina de mercado con el consiguiente efecto favorable sobre la competencia y la eficiencia del sistema bancario espaol. Las NIC y la nueva circular contable del Banco de Espaa He mencionado que en el mbito de la UE se han desarrollado diferentes iniciativas que persiguen fomentar una verdadera integracin de los mercados financieros de la Unin. Una de esas iniciativas, y a la cual querra dedicar los ltimos minutos de mi intervencin, ha sido la aprobacin por parte de la Unin Europea, de las Normas Internacionales de Contabilidad emanadas del IASB. En efecto, la Unin Europea tom la decisin de que las cuentas consolidadas de los grupos con valores cotizados en cualquier mercado regulado de la Unin, se elaboren, desde enero de 2005, de acuerdo con dichas normas. El objetivo, como he mencionado, es fomentar la consolidacin de un mercado financiero nico, para lo cual es importante garantizar que los participantes en l tengan acceso a una informacin financiera que goce del mayor grado de homogeneizacin posible. Asimismo, un segundo objetivo sera reforzar la integracin del sistema financiero internacional, lo cual pasa por favorecer la convergencia de las NIC con los estndares contables norteamericanos. El Banco de Espaa, por su parte, reconoce y comparte los beneficios derivados de los esfuerzos encaminados a lograr un mayor grado de armonizacin contable, al tiempo que como supervisor mantiene un legtimo inters en la calidad de los estndares contables y en su efectiva implementacin. Por ello, y de acuerdo con sus competencias en materia de regulacin contable de las entidades de crdito espaolas, decidi modificar su normativa. En diciembre de 2004 vio la luz la nueva circular contable (CBE 4/2004). Asimismo, y a la vista de que el proceso de aprobacin y adopcin de los nuevos estndares internacionales se caracterizaba por su complejidad y existan ciertas dificultades de calendario, a travs de la nueva circular contable el Banco de Espaa ha pretendido tambin otorgar, en la medida de lo posible, un mayor grado de certidumbre al proceso. La complejidad que incorporan los nuevos estndares contables no viene slo del proceso al que acabo de hacer referencia, sino bsicamente de las propias modificaciones contenidas en ellos, ya que suponen cambios notables en numerosos aspectos muy relevantes para la gestin de las entidades. Si bien es pronto para hacer una evaluacin detallada de la implantacin de las nuevas normas contables, que tan solo llevan en vigor unos pocos meses, la valoracin inicial de este proceso que hace el Banco de Espaa es positiva, reconociendo, asimismo, el importante esfuerzo y el trabajo que han realizado las entidades financieras. Uno de los mensajes que, desde un primer momento, se quiso transmitir desde el Banco de Espaa, fue que ramos conscientes de las dificultadas asociadas a la implantacin y que por tanto, desde nuestra funcin de supervisores bancarios, estimbamos conveniente una cierta flexibilidad. As, por ejemplo, al considerar el tratamiento de la puesta en equivalencia de las participaciones estables en proyectos industriales, es decir, en el tratamiento de las empresas asociadas, las nuevas normas contables introducen la cifra del 20% y se refieren al concepto de influencia significativa. Recuerdo que en la antigua circular contable, las participaciones en sociedades cotizadas superiores al 3% se suponan bajo el mtodo de la puesta en equivalencia, algo que estaba lejos de la prctica internacional que mayoritariamente consideraba la cifra del 20%. La transicin era, pues, significativa y el Banco de Espaa manifest su voluntad de contribuir a que fuese lo mas fcil posible y sin consecuencias relevantes. Hoy se puede afirmar que el propio sector, de hecho una gran parte de las entidades que mantienen este tipo de participaciones, ha decidido, desde su propio convencimiento, contabilizar estas participaciones como disponible para la venta, es decir, no como empresas asociadas contabilizadas por puesta en equivalencia. Creo muy positiva esta rpida transicin realizada por el sector que nos permite afirmar sin matices que la regla del 20% no requiere consideraciones especiales en nuestro pas. En definitiva, este tipo de inversiones de carcter permanente y con vocacin de ejercer una cierta influencia en la gestin de las sociedades no financieras, implican compromisos de largo plazo e incorporan riesgos adicionales que exigen mayores responsabilidades por parte de los gestores. Estas mayores responsabilidades se traducen en ms exigencias desde el punto de vista del gobierno corporativo de las entidades. Conclusin Permtanme que concluya mi intervencin transmitindoles un mensaje de confianza. Confianza en que las entidades espaolas demuestren, como lo han venido haciendo en el pasado, que disponen de la capacidad suficiente para afrontar todo el conjunto de retos a los que me he referido hoy, as como aquellos otros que, no por menos importantes, no he abordado en esta intervencin. Esta confianza me lleva a pensar que los gestores de las entidades se comportarn de un modo profesional y prudente, diseando estrategias de negocio con una visin de medio y largo plazo. De este modo no solo contribuirn al funcionamiento estable de las entidades de las que son responsables, sino tambin al del conjunto del sistema financiero. Estoy seguro de que las reflexiones que compartirn a lo largo de estos dos das contribuirn a estos logros. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Notes: Presentation at the Strategic Forum of Savings Banks (Theme: "Savings banks, precursors in corporate social responsibility")
text: Madrid, 9 June 2005 Notes for the Governor's Presentation Strategic Forum of Savings Banks. Corporate Social Responsibility Spanish Confederation of Savings Banks (CECA) Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain Mr President of the Government, Mr President of the ECSC, ladies and gentlemen, 1. Introduction First of all, I would like to thank the ECSC for inviting you to these important days. Savings banks are a key element of our financial system, to which, for more than a hundred years, they have brought stability and competition. I would also like to welcome the creation of this Savings Banks Forum and celebrate the fact that in this first meeting the theme of corporate social responsibility has been chosen. A concept very close, I would almost dare to say redundant, to the nature of the savings banks, which as credit institutions of a private foundational nature, of a social nature, have always been linked to the promotion and mobilization of popular savings and, in general, to the attention of the needs of society. Within this broad theme, you will allow me to take advantage of this opportunity to share with you some reflections on the good governance of deposit institutions, and to do so, within the framework of the growing interest that initiatives in corporate governance are receiving at the international level. You already know the emphasis that the Bank of Spain places on remembering that if savings banks want to fulfill their social function, if they want to continue creating value for society and for the region in a sustained manner, savings banks must be, above all, solvent financial institutions and managed with professional criteria and proportionate to the great confidence that savers place in them. This implies, on the one hand, the recognition of the defining features and specific operational characteristics of the savings banks, which are the basis of their legal consideration and also fidelity to their model which, together with their social character and regional vocation, requires as a central axis the recognition of their nature as deposit institutions above other considerations. This double characteristic of financial institutions, but with a special legal nature, makes the corporate governance of savings banks especially relevant and complex. The history of the Savings Banks in this country is, without a doubt, a success story in which they have shown their ability to adapt and grow based on their strengths, have provided the financial system with stability, solvency and competition, and have also done so maintaining their social orientation and their special link with their regional environment. But this positive analysis that undoubtedly deserves the Savings Banks, should not make us forget that the financial system is increasingly complex, more competitive and poses more difficult challenges and the Savings Banks have been increasing their field of action, now covering a wide range in terms of risks and complexity. All this leads to insist on the convenience of continuing to deepen its good governance adapted to its peculiarities. The bulk of my intervention will focus on the ongoing efforts of the Basel Committee of Banking Supervisors to strengthen the governance of banking enterprises, thereby helping to maintain and stimulate the stability of the international financial system. But first I will briefly refer to recent responses by regulators to various episodes of lack of good corporate governance that led to scandals such as those of Enron and Parmalat. It should be noted that the above problems have not appeared in any type of deposit institution. 2. Some episodes of bad corporate governance On everyone's mind are the cases of Enron, Worldcom, Parmalat, etc. In most cases, these were well-known, large, listed and even highly reputable companies with a high reputation and credit rating in which severe corporate governance problems were seen and ended in bankruptcy or in a very difficult situation. Although each case contains specific and particular elements, and some of the details are not yet fully understood, it seems that the cases of corporate governance collapse in recent years share some common elements. First, the members of the board of directors did not understand the risks that the company was incurring and did not exercise adequate supervision over the top-level executives, did not ask properly, did not question their actions. Secondly, there were conflicts of interest between the directors and executives of the companies that highlighted the lack of independence and the negative consequences that this can have for the rest of the shareholders and stakeholders in the company. Thirdly, internal controls were very weak or even conspicuous by their absence, or although they were correct, even very good, on paper they were never implemented in reality. Internal and external auditors were unable to detect serious problems. In the case of the latter, they could even help to hide the problems, largely because of the conflict of interests that hampered their independence. Fourth, certain complex transactions and structures were designed to reduce transparency and thus mask problems from investors and supervisors. Finally, and probably the most important aspect, company culture encouraged unethical behavior, discouraging the formulation of questions about the strategy developed by the company, promoting those who contributed to hide or increase them and punishing those who openly exposed them. Therefore, a company culture was promoted just at the antipodes of corporate social responsibility. In addition to the direct damage to shareholders, debt holders, suppliers and workers, the poor governance of these companies by their directors and directors caused a very important negative externality, on the set of companies listed on the main stock markets, in particular, in the United States, consisting of the loss of confidence in business managers. For some analysts, the situation was very close to translating into a problem of financial instability, which would have had serious consequences on investment, production and employment. Again, I would like to stress the importance of trust for the functioning of the market and the key contribution of good governance to it. The direct and indirect costs that can occur in situations of sudden loss of confidence are always difficult to estimate but possibly considerable. The reaction was immediate. In the first place, on the part of the market itself, with a discipline effect as clear as it is rapid on poorly governed entities: collapse of stock prices, abrupt and very marked increase in the risk premium implicit in its debt, drastic reductions in its credit rating, loss of liquidity and, in some cases, bankruptcy of the company. In addition, market discipline not only reached these companies but went further and also rigorously affected their auditors, that is, those companies responsible for certifying that the financial statements faithfully reflect the company's financial situation, that the risks incurred are adequately reflected and that, ultimately, the company provides truthful information to the market, to investors and other interested parties in its operation, so that, at all times, they can make their decisions in the best possible way. The suspicions also extended to stock analysts and investment banks, responsible for placing the securities issues of these companies among the public, in exchange for the corresponding commissions, both under the same roof on many occasions. Regulators reacted promptly while assessing the scale of the potential problem that poor corporate governance had caused to the international financial system. In the European Union, different directives echoed the concerns unleashed by the aforementioned financial scandals, although the Financial Services Action Plan launched in 1999 by the European Commission to promote the integration of European financial markets, already contemplated measures to improve corporate governance, particularly in its aspect of external control and transparency. The European Union adopted an action plan on corporate governance in May 2003. Among the elements to be considered are, first, the strengthening of non-executive directors; improve shareholder access to information about the company, facilitating the exercise of their rights, and improve information transparency in matters of corporate governance. In Spain, although no significant company was involved in problems of bad governance that ended in bankruptcy or serious difficulties, the Ministry of Economy promoted several laws to improve the governance of companies in general, and banking companies in particular. Thus, it is worth mentioning Law 44/2002 on the reform of the financial system and Law 26/2003 on transparency. This last law introduced the obligation for companies with securities traded on official financial markets to issue an annual report on their corporate governance, as well as the obligation to attend to the right to information of shareholders and investors through a website. Recently, the CNMV, in charge of its functions, has issued a circular regulating the minimum content of said corporate governance report in the case of savings banks. In short, the above shows a decisive action of the regulator in the face of a serious problem of confidence in the functioning of financial markets, as a result of poor corporate governance. I must confess that the regulation by official gazette of corporate governance, has always seemed to me an optimal second and that, in general and also in the case of the Savings Banks, it would have been desirable for the sector to have adopted, by itself, effectively a good code. Since this did not happen and the pressure derived from the aforementioned business cases, regulation became the next optimum. 3. Good governance of depository institutions Importantly, during this turbulent period in the corporate governance of some companies, no bank was forced into bankruptcy. I think this speaks to the government of depository institutions who are well aware of the value of good reputation and the cost of losing it. I would also like to think that the presence of banking regulators and supervisors could have contributed significantly to this outcome. The reputation of the banking company is, in many cases, its main asset because it is directly and closely correlated with the trust of the public and, therefore, with the ability to continue developing its business. Illegal or unethical behavior deteriorates the reputation of the entity, sometimes irreparably. However, it is true that some banks were involved laterally in the problems to which I referred earlier. Thus, I have already mentioned the possible conflict of interest between some investment banks, which counted poorly governed companies among their clients, and the recommendations that they themselves made through their company analysts, some of them very listened to by investors. Another element to consider is the role that some banks could play by facilitating complex operations with vehicles domiciled, often in opaque centers and therefore with less supervision. Despite not having directly experienced any bankruptcy due to corporate governance problems and excluding the indirect relationships I have just mentioned, the central role played by depository institutions in the payment system, as liquidity providers, and their high vulnerability to the lack of confidence of depositors, make the good governance of depository institutions, banks, savings banks and cooperatives, is a fundamental piece to preserve the stability of the financial system. Markets and financial intermediaries channel savers' money to investors, thus contributing to the efficient allocation of resources and the distribution of risk among different economic agents. The previous mechanism, in principle simple, is based on the trust that savers have deposited in the companies receiving their money. If savers are wary of the good end investors will put to their money, they will not acquire assets, or they will quickly and abruptly sell those assets or rush to withdraw their deposits. In more academic terms, good corporate governance can help alleviate the problem of information asymmetry that exists between company managers and their owners, shareholders. And this does not exclude, especially in the case of financial institutions, the interests of the rest of the parties involved in the operation of the company (debtors of the company, through bonds, obligations or other securities; suppliers, depositors, in the case of deposit institutions, and also employees). This broad vision of good corporate governance, which has been progressively making its way among academics, is what connects with the central theme of this first edition of the Savings Banks Forum, which is none other than corporate social responsibility. In the broad conception of corporate governance, where all the interested parties in the company must be taken into account, in the case of depository institutions, consideration towards depositors stands out. Therefore, of course, banking supervisors have an interest in promoting the good governance of deposit institutions, good governance that necessarily involves adequate management and control of the different risks, credit, market, operational, legal, reputational, strategic, business, etc., incurred by banks, savings banks and credit unions. 4. Contribution of the Basel Committee of Banking Supervisors Through Basel II As you know, the Basel committee, which brings together the banking supervisors of the most developed countries, has been working intensively for the past six years on a new equity arrangement, a process known colloquially as Basel 2. Although Basel II is best known for its requirements for calculating regulatory minimum capital, much of the new capital framework is dedicated to improving important elements of depository governance. I am convinced that Basel II will contribute significantly to better depository institution governance, for three reasons. First, the supervisor's acceptance of institutions' internal models should take into account how institutions control risk management. Effective risk controls are essential for a successful implementation of the new capital framework. Supervisors expect each bank's board of directors to ensure that the entity has a sufficiently rigorous risk control system. We also expect the members of the executive committee and the CEOs to assume their responsibility for the implementation of the risk control system chosen by the directors. In the case of savings banks, the control committee is also intended to play a very important role in monitoring the risk control system. In addition, Basel II places clear responsibilities on internal auditors to carry out an independent review of internal models and thus of the minimum level of capital needed by institutions to address their risk profile. I believe that the emphasis being placed on the role that directors and top executives have in controlling risk will make an important contribution to depository institutions being properly managed. Secondly, the greater responsibility placed on directors and executives will translate into a greater culture of risk in banks and, also, why not say it, in banking supervisors. The key is, therefore, that the vigilant attitude towards risk begins at the top of the organization and that, therefore, it will be adequately transmitted to all organizational and decision-making levels in the entity, impregnated to the whole company of the aforementioned risk culture. Third, Basel II will contribute to better governance of depository institutions through greater transparency in risk measurement and management. The third pillar, market discipline, enhanced by increased investor transparency requirements will help discipline institutions and incentivise prudent risk management. Precisely, greater transparency focuses on information about risks and their management, so that investors can adequately penalize the riskiest entities and reward, with a lower cost of capital, those that carry out a more prudent risk management. Logically, if institutions know that they are better monitored by investors, thanks to the greater information provided, they will tend to pay greater attention to the proper management and control of risks. Greater responsibility of the directors and top executives of depository institutions, actively involved in the control and management of risk, the dissemination throughout the organization of a culture of risk, anticipation and surveillance of them in reality, and greater transparency and market discipline, will contribute to improving the good governance of depository institutions and, In short, to strengthen the confidence of investors and depositors in entities that play a central role in any economic system. Beyond Basel II On a broader note, we are reviewing past guidance on corporate governance of depository institutions, which reflect best practices developed by banks and supervisors in Basel Committee countries. It is not, therefore, guidelines aimed at savings banks but in general at deposit institutions. The Committee in 1999 issued general principles on this issue, which we are revising in the light of recent experiences and updates and work on the OECD Code. In addition to the revision of the 1999 document, we are incorporating the convenience of depository institutions knowing their structure, including the most complex products and, above all, the operations they can carry out from off-shore centers, subject to less regulatory and supervisory pressure. While we hope to soon submit our new thinking on depository governance to the banking industry, I would like to share with you some of these reflections, based on supervisors' experience on corporate governance issues, and suggest practices that could help avoid such problems. Objectives and values The board of directors must set what the strategic objectives of the entity are and what are the acceptable ethical standards to achieve them. These objectives and standards are those that must direct the activities of the entity and must respond to the interest of all parties involved (shareholders, debt holders, depositors, etc.). It is important for counselors to establish and transmit a culture that rewards ethical behaviors. Strategic objectives must be accompanied by ethical standards. The general tone on values, ethical principles and risk culture should start at the top of the company and extend to the whole company. At this point it is convenient to stop and make some reflection on the specificities of the Savings Banks model. When analyzing corporate governance, two important elements are considered, among others: the defense of shareholders, so that the interests of the various parties involved are aligned and that the operation of the entity is consistent with them and also highlights the role of the market as an element of discipline that enhances good governance. Some analyses, see market discipline, including the possibility of poorly managed companies being acquired by others and their managers replaced, as an important external pillar of corporate governance. Given the specificities of the Savings Banks in both aspects mentioned, the lack of identification of ownership and the absence of some market discipline mechanisms, the governance structures of the Savings Banks have deserved greater attention. It has been repeated on numerous occasions: the need to strengthen the professionalism, stability and control of the management of the Savings Banks and the need to avoid interference that leads to confusing social purposes with public policy objectives. Without going into the many nuances that should be introduced in this debate, it seems convenient that the weaknesses in the corporate governance of the Savings Banks require a greater demand in the other pillars (internal governance and transparency) so that management is perfected, creating structures that establish counterweights, hinder personalisms and external interferences and facilitate the definition of clear strategies according to their nature and encourage professional management and transparent. A starting principle is to make it clear that only a solvent and efficient entity can guarantee, in a sustained manner, the protection of the depositor and the fulfillment of its social function. Consequently, the members of the administrative bodies must put the good management of the entity above any other objective. It is also the responsibility of board members to ensure that executives implement the necessary policies to identify and prevent potential conflicts of interest. This responsibility is put into practice by ensuring independence between different business areas (between analysts and investment banks, for example) and ensuring that the information provided to clients is clear and does not lead them to confusion. Directors should ensure that the entity's executives implement and implement an internal code of conduct that promotes integrity and professionalism. In addition, transactions that by their very nature may weaken the quality of corporate governance (related-party transactions, for example) should be strictly limited. One way to do this is through the requirement of market conditions in such transactions. They should pay increasing attention to transactions carried out in offshore centers or through vehicles that decrease transparency and that can contribute to a loss of reputation of the entity. Finally, the above ethical policies and behaviors must be reviewed periodically and verified that they are actually applied. Qualification of directors, responsibility and independence of judgment The members of the board of directors are ultimately and ultimately responsible for the financial situation of an entity. We must never lose sight of this element. By the way, no one is obliged to be a director of an entity. To carry out their work properly, they must receive in due time, that is, sufficiently in advance to be able to react, relevant information to judge the actions of the executives who run the bank. Directors have a duty of loyalty to the bank and its shareholders. Therefore, they must select, monitor and, if necessary, replace the top executives of the entity, as well as supervise their renewal over time. The directors must exercise a task of control and balance against the executives who carry out the day-to-day management of the bank. They should not interfere in the day-to-day management of the entity but they should provide their common sense and a dispassionate, even distant, analysis of decisions. Among their obligations, but also forming part of their rights, is their ability to ask questions to managers, however simple they may seem and as many times as they consider it necessary. In addition to the above supervisory tasks, it is desirable that a sufficient number of directors be able to exercise judgment independent of that of managers and large shareholders. For this, it is essential that these independent directors have a high qualification. In the cases of malfunctioning corporate governance that I mentioned before, almost always complex, non-transparent and difficult to follow products or transactions appeared. It should be the responsibility of the management board to approve it in advance. Executive control and supervision Senior executives play a central role in good corporate governance. Senior management should play a supervisory role of middle managers similar to that exercised by directors over them. To do this, with the help of the directors, they must establish an adequate system of internal control. For example, key management decisions should not be made by just one person but at a minimum involve two (four-eyes principle). Role of internal and external auditors Another key piece of the good governance of depository institutions or, in general, of any company, is the work carried out by independent, competent and qualified auditors. Directors should use the work of internal and external auditors as an independent control over the information provided by managers. They must therefore ensure that internal audit can be carried out independently and that it is sufficiently equipped with the material and human resources to do so. In the case of external auditors, it is necessary to ensure that their independence of judgment is not conditioned by the existence of conflicts of interest that lead the auditors, for example, not to contradict the executives in order to maintain other business with the entity. Transparency Transparency in corporate governance matters reinforces the practice of good governance. By knowing that they are observed by the different stakeholders in the entity, its agents, directors and executives have a greater incentive to improve the corporate governance of the entity. This transparency also reinforces investor confidence and can affect the cost of financing, reducing it. The elements on which the Basel Committee recommends transparency are, among others, structure of the board of directors (size, selection process, qualification, independence, etc.), structure of senior management (responsibilities, qualifications, experience), ownership structure and presence of ownership on the board, information on the incentive structure, including remuneration policy, the Bank's Code of Conduct, nature and scope of transactions between the entity and its subsidiaries and related parties to directors or officers. Role of supervisors So far I have only talked about, fundamentally, the responsibility that others have in relation to the good governance of entities. I would not like to end this speech without mentioning the role that supervisors can and must play. First of all, we should be aware of the importance of good corporate governance and its positive impact on institutions. I do not think that anyone present here, at this point in my presentation, doubts the importance that the Bank of Spain attributes to good governance. Secondly, although our most direct responsibility is on the solvency of the entities, we must be vigilant to any sign that we perceive of deterioration in the managers of the entities because, sooner or later, it will end up manifesting itself in the risk, profitability or solvency of the entity. Thirdly, and this is a very important element, supervisors must assess the quality of the internal controls applied by institutions. It is very important that these controls are not only theoretical or formal, but that they are actually applied and function. In addition, we must ensure that internal and external audits carry out an effective and independent review of the aforementioned internal controls. Last but not least, we must ensure that institutions carry out proper risk management, with a sufficient amount of prudence to protect the interests of the normally weaker party of the providers of funds, the depositors. In short, by carrying out adequate supervision of institutions and being attentive to the good governance of banks and savings banks, we can contribute to strengthening confidence in our entities and strengthening financial stability. In addition to the work we are developing within the Basel Committee, both that directly related to the new capital agreement and the rest of the issues, it should be remembered that the adoption in Spain, and throughout the European Union, of the new international accounting standards attributes greater responsibility to the directors in the definition of the accounting policies of the entity. 5. Final Thoughts I would like to conclude my speech with a final reflection on the desirability of all parties interested in the proper functioning of depository institutions to contribute to their good governance to the best of our ability. Although I will not tire of repeating that the maximum responsibility for the good governance of companies, banks and savings banks, lies with the directors and top executives, shareholders, through the effective exercise of their rights, auditors, through fluid communication and with the board and professional work, employees, revealing illegal or unethical behaviour observed, governments, by promoting laws and regulations and monitoring their effective compliance, and, finally, banking supervisors, by issuing guidance based on best banking practices and monitoring the risks and, more generally, management practices of institutions, They are also responsible for creating an appropriate framework conducive to the development of good governance of banking enterprises. With this, confidence in our financial system will be strengthened and society as a whole will be able to benefit from an efficient allocation of resources from savers to investors as well as the consequent reallocation of risk between economic agents. Thank you very much for your attention

Algunos episodios de mal gobierno corporativo En la mente de todos estn los casos de Enron, Worldcom, Parmalat, etc. En la mayor parte de casos se trataba de empresas muy conocidas, de elevado tamao, cotizadas en bolsa e, incluso, con una elevada reputacin y calificacin crediticia en las que se apreciaron severos problemas de gobierno corporativo y que terminaron en quiebra o en una situacin muy difcil. Adems del perjuicio directo para los accionistas, tenedores de deuda, proveedores y trabajadores, el mal gobierno de estas empresas por parte de sus directivos y consejeros provoc una externalidad negativa muy importante, sobre el conjunto de empresas cotizadas en los principales mercados burstiles, en particular, en el estadounidense, consistente en la prdida de confianza en los gestores empresariales. Para algunos analistas la situacin estuvo muy cerca de traducirse en un problema de inestabilidad financiera, que hubiera tenido consecuencias graves sobre la inversin, la produccin y el empleo. De nuevo, quiero insistir en la importancia de la confianza para el funcionamiento del mercado y la contribucin clave del buen gobierno a ella. En primer lugar, por parte del propio mercado, con un efecto de disciplina tan claro como rpido sobre las entidades mal gobernadas: desplome de cotizaciones burstiles, aumento abrupto y muy marcado de la prima de riesgo implcita en su deuda, reducciones drsticas de su calificacin crediticia, prdida de liquidez y, en algunos casos, quiebra de la empresa. Adems, la disciplina de mercado no solo alcanz a estas empresas sino que fue ms all y afect tambin con rigor a sus auditores, es decir, a aquellas empresas encargadas de certificar que los estados financieros reflejan fielmente la situacin patrimonial de la empresa, que los riesgos incurridos estn adecuadamente reflejados y que, en definitiva, la empresa suministra informacin veraz al mercado, a los inversores y dems partes interesadas en su funcionamiento, para que, en todo momento puedan tomar sus decisiones de la mejor forma posible. Las sospechas se extendieron tambin hacia los analistas burstiles y los bancos de inversin, encargados de la colocacin de las emisiones de valores de dichas empresas entre el pblico, a cambio de las correspondientes comisiones, ambos bajo el mismo techo en no pocas ocasiones. Los reguladores reaccionaron con prontitud valorando al tiempo la dimensin del problema potencial que el mal gobierno corporativo haba ocasionado al sistema financiero internacional. En Espaa, aunque ninguna empresa significativa se vio envuelta en problemas de mal gobierno que acabaran en una quiebra o en dificultades serias, el Ministerio de Economa impuls varias leyes para mejorar el gobierno de las empresas en general, y de las bancarias en particular. Esta ltima ley introdujo la obligatoriedad de que las empresas con valores negociados en mercados financieros oficiales, emitieran un informe anual sobre su gobierno corporativo, as como la obligatoriedad de atender el derecho de informacin de los accionistas e inversores a travs de una pgina web.
