Las prioridades de las polticas de gasto que incorporan los Presupuestos parecen adecuadamente orientadas hacia reas especialmente importantes para la mejora de la productividad, como el fomento de la innovacin, el incremento de la inversin en infraestructuras, el aumento de recursos para la educacin y el impulso de los servicios pblicos de calidad, pero comportan incrementos significativos de las correspondientes dotaciones presupuestarias, a los que se aaden los compromisos de gasto que se han asumido en el mbito de la vivienda, pensiones mnimas o de la financiacin sanitaria. Sobre este ltimo punto, resulta preocupante que el acuerdo alcanzado se base fundamentalmente en un mayor recurso a la financiacin del Estado, frente a la utilizacin de las vas de financiacin complementarias que ofrece el sistema de financiacin autonmico vigente y que no aborde la introduccin de medidas de mejora de eficiencia en el gasto sanitario. En la fase que atraviesa la economa espaola es muy importante que la poltica presupuestaria desempee un papel de contencin efectiva de los riesgos que laten tras el fuerte dinamismo del gasto, por lo que sera altamente deseable, como ya he dicho, avanzar hacia un mayor supervit de las cuentas pblicas. La contribucin fiscal debe provenir no solo de la mejora del saldo presupuestario sino tambin del aumento de la eficiencia en la actuacin del sector pblico, a travs de la revisin de las polticas de gasto y de las figuras tributarias que pueden ayudar al perfeccionamiento de los incentivos. Las reformas impositivas anunciadas han de tener en cuenta estos objetivos y han de estar bien calibradas para no suponer un coste recaudatorio excesivo. En este sentido, no hay que olvidar que el dinamismo actual de los ingresos pblicos puede incorporar algn componente transitorio que podra desaparecer en coyunturas menos favorables. Estas consideraciones se refuerzan cuando se tienen en cuenta las perspectivas demogrficas espaolas. Estas apuntan a un intenso proceso de envejecimiento de la poblacin, a pesar de los intensos flujos de inmigracin que se vienen registrando en los ltimos aos. Es preciso que la poltica presupuestaria anticipe con suficiente antelacin las presiones sobre el gasto pblico que generar una sociedad ms envejecida, tanto en su componente de pensiones como en el de cobertura de las situaciones de dependencia, adoptando objetivos fiscales ms ambiciosos y abordando las reformas necesarias en los sistemas de proteccin social. El marco institucional en el que se desenvuelve la poltica fiscal tiene gran importancia para asegurar una evolucin disciplinada de las finanzas pblicas. En la actualidad se est discutiendo la reforma de las Leyes de Estabilidad presupuestaria, que suministran la base para limitar conductas indisciplinadas y distribuir por agentes el objetivo de poltica fiscal establecido. El aspecto ms novedoso en el proyecto de reforma es la introduccin de una mayor flexibilidad en la definicin de las reglas de estabilidad presupuestaria, permitiendo que el Estado y las CCAA adapten su objetivo de dficit o supervit a la situacin cclica de la economa. Esta modificacin de la Ley est orientada a permitir el funcionamiento de los estabilizadores automticos existentes, aunque no introduce los incentivos suficientes para la generacin de los supervit adecuados en situaciones cclicas favorables. Por otra parte, el Proyecto de reforma refuerza la disciplina fiscal, al introducir requisitos especficos para los diferentes agentes del sector pblico. Estos requisitos estn claramente definidos en el caso de la Administracin Central, cuyo saldo, a efectos del cumplimiento del objetivo de estabilidad presupuestaria, pasar a computarse de forma independiente al de la Seguridad Social, pero en el caso de las Comunidades autnomas no se establece una distribucin transparente del esfuerzo fiscal que corresponde a cada una de ellas, lo que puede comportar algn riesgo de que se produzcan desviaciones. Por ltimo, quiero hacer especial hincapi en las provisiones que incorpora la norma para mejorar la transparencia y la disponibilidad de informacin sobre las cuentas pblicas, objetivo que ha resultado fallido en ocasiones anteriores, pero que considero de vital importancia como elemento de disciplina en estructuras fiscales en las que el gasto est fuertemente descentralizado, como ocurre en Espaa. En el plano de las reformas estructurales, el Gobierno ha tomado a lo largo de este ltimo ao una serie de iniciativas, dirigidas a impulsar la productividad y la innovacin con el objetivo de establecer las bases para un crecimiento slido en el largo plazo. Me refiero, al Plan de Dinamizacin de la economa, el Programa Ingenio 2010 y, prximamente, el Plan nacional de reforma econmica. Estas iniciativas establecen una orientacin adecuada para que la poltica econmica aborde los retos que tiene planteados la economa espaola, en concreto, la necesidad de impulsar la productividad y de establecer las bases para un crecimiento slido en el largo plazo que permita alcanzar mejoras sostenidas en el bienestar econmico de la sociedad espaola. Es necesario, sin embargo, una mayor concrecin y profundizacin de los compromisos adquiridos y acometer simultneamente otras reformas de mayor calado, que son de vital importancia en el caso del mercado de trabajo. Estas reformas resultan imprescindibles para mantener el dinamismo en el empleo y promover la innovacin en el tejido empresarial, particularmente en las empresas de las ramas de servicios y en las de dimensin reducida, que representan una parte muy importante del panorama empresarial de este pas y que son las que acumulan el mayor desfase innovador y tecnolgico. Para ello, el mercado de trabajo debe proporcionar la flexibilidad suficiente para que las empresas puedan organizar el uso de los factores de produccin de forma eficiente y han de continuar los procesos de liberalizacin de los mercados de bienes y servicios emprendidos en los ltimos aos. Tiene tambin gran importancia que la descentralizacin de competencias que caracteriza a la estructura autonmica del Estado no genere discrepancias reguladoras que puedan suponer una erosin de la unidad del mercado nacional, como ya ha ocurrido en algunas parcelas como la del comercio al por menor. Un desarrollo de esas caractersticas sera contradictorio con los procesos de integracin europea y de globalizacin y daara la posicin competitiva de la economa espaola. En relacin con este tema, a nadie se le escapa la enorme trascendencia que tiene el debate de posibles reformas del marco institucional de las Comunidades Autnomas y, muy particularmente, de la propuesta del Estatuto de Autonoma de Catalua. Dicha propuesta conlleva modificaciones de orden poltico, cultural y social, sobre cuya constitucionalidad y conveniencia se pronunciarn los rganos parlamentarios y jurisdiccionales competentes. Desde el punto de vista de la poltica econmica, adems, la redaccin actual comporta alteraciones en la distribucin de competencias entre el Estado y las Comunidades Autnomas y en los sistemas de financiacin de estas ltimas que pueden afectar, no solo a la cohesin interna, sino tambin a la capacidad de las polticas pblicas para mantener la integracin del mercado y la eficiencia en el funcionamiento de la economa. Se trata de decisiones de gran alcance que pueden llegar a incidir sobre la posicin a medio y largo plazo de la economa espaola en un escenario mundial caracterizado por una acendrada competencia y una apertura e integracin cada vez mayores. Cambios institucionales de esta naturaleza pueden tener consecuencias econmicas importantes y duraderas, debilitar la eficiencia y capacidad de crecer de la economa y afectar al bienestar del conjunto de los espaoles. Por ello, debe cuidarse con especial atencin que el diseo institucional permita gestionar de manera eficaz las polticas econmicas, promueva un entorno que favorezca la iniciativa privada y la competencia, evite excesivos intervencionismos, as como incertidumbres y riesgos regulatorios y finalmente sea coherente con la plena integracin econmica. El Banco de Espaa contempla con especial preocupacin las propuestas de modificacin del sistema de regulacin y supervisin de las entidades de crdito que suponen una fragmentacin de competencias, que podra interpretarse como contraria a la copiosa jurisprudencia del Tribunal Constitucional, particularmente en lo que se refiere a la estabilidad y solvencia del sistema financiero. Esta disgregacin podra fragmentar el sistema financiero espaol, generar conflictos de inters en el gobierno y supervisin de las Cajas de Ahorro, (al ganar competencias supervisoras los poderes pblicos regionales que ya estn presentes en los rganos de gobierno de estas instituciones), podra llegar a comprometer la eficacia de la supervisin financiera y dificultara avanzar en la direccin de convergencia y coordinacin en este mbito, que demandan las autoridades europeas y los foros internacionales de estabilidad financiera. En definitiva, en el panorama que he tratado de esbozar, corresponde a la poltica econmica una especial responsabilidad, en mltiples parcelas, para promover el establecimiento de unas bases adecuadas para que el dinamismo que est viviendo la economa espaola pueda proyectarse de manera sostenible hacia el futuro.

Title: ABC Forum: The Spanish economy and its financing within the framework of the EU
text: Madrid, 18 October 2005 The Spanish economy and its financing within the framework of the EU ABC Forum. ABC and Deloitte Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain Allow me to begin my speech by thanking the organisers of this ABC Forum for the opportunity they give me to share here with you today some reflections on the Spanish economy and the challenges posed by financing our growth within the framework of Economic and Monetary Union. I will try to reflect on questions such as: What is the meaning and importance of the financing needs of our economy? How is it funded? What role does our banking system play? How can we make it easier for it to continue in the future by providing the efficient financing that the growth of our economy needs? Talking about financing growth illustrates in itself that we are referring to a particularly prosperous period for the Spanish economy. As you all know, this economy has been experiencing a prolonged period of expansion for more than a decade now, which has been the result of combining an implementation of economic policies conducive to growth and macroeconomic stability with the emergence of different impulses on the demand and supply side. The firm commitment to fiscal consolidation, in the second half of the nineties, and the maintenance of balanced public accounts, have contributed decisively to the process of entry and subsequent participation in the Monetary Union has resulted in a permanent improvement in the financial conditions of the economy. The boost to household and business spending in this context has been matched by a positive response from the supply side of the economy, stimulated by some reform measures and, above all, by the significant increase in the labour force resulting from the increasing participation in the labour market, mainly of women and, more importantly in recent years, high immigration flows. The results, in terms of growth in production and employment, have been and are being very positive. Spain has emerged as one of the economies with the highest growth rate in the euro area, maintaining its dynamism even in those periods in which the external context has been less propitious and resisting the slowdown impulses experienced by other economies in our environment at the beginning of the current decade. In this way, progress has been made on what was one of the main objectives of our participation in EMU, namely the progressive reduction of the gap that, in terms of well-being, separated us d0 and still separates us d0 from our European partners. At present, the growth rate in Spain has risen to levels of 3.4%, after having closed 2004 with GDP growth of 3.1%, favoured by the maintenance of monetary and financial conditions that have become more comfortable, in response to the prolonged sluggishness that the euro area is experiencing. Although growth is still based on the boost in household consumption spending and on the construction of housing and public works, the high profitability that characterises the Spanish business sector as a whole and the improvement in demand prospects have allowed investment in equipment to join the most dynamic components of spending. This fact seems to point towards a desirable change in the composition of growth, although not yet sufficiently established. However, the healthy performance of our economy over the years does not eliminate the need to rigorously analyze the elements of risk that have been appearing and that may condition the sustainability of the expansionary stage in the medium and long term. I would therefore like to take this opportunity to reflect on some of them and on their link with the financial situation of the economy. These risk elements undoubtedly include the imbalance shown by the growth pattern, which is excessively dependent on components linked to household spending, while net foreign demand detracts, according to the most recent information, by just over two points from output growth. This trade imbalance is, in large part, a direct consequence of the growth differential between Spain and the euro zone, to which our main trading partners belong. It also partially responds to short-term developments such as the recent boom in the import of capital goods in our country, associated with the incipient recovery of productive investment, and the atypically weak behavior of exports in the first months of this year. But, in addition, behind this bulky external deficit is detected the influence of the progressive accumulation of losses of competitiveness of the Spanish economy. In this regard, the increasing degree of import penetration and the gradual loss of export share are particularly informative. Thus, the persistence of price and labour cost differentials d0 in a context of poor productivity growth d0 which our economy has been experiencing for years, is no longer just a risk element for economic dynamism in the medium term, but a factor that has begun to exert a visible contractionary effect. It is very likely, in fact, that improving the competitive position of the Spanish economy will currently be the main challenge to consolidate the current dynamism based on a greater balance between the internal and external components of demand. However, the sustainability of growth rates such as the current ones will also require a more balanced composition of domestic demand growth, with a greater relative role for investment in equipment. As I have pointed out previously, one of the most positive characteristics of the current expansionary phase of the Spanish economy is its marked intensity in job creation, a bias that is adapted to the relative abundance of the labour factor in the Spanish economy and the need to reduce unemployment in a context of high growth of the active population, due, as is well known, to the increase in female participation and, above all, to the large immigration flows. Growth of around 3% per year in the number of equivalent jobs, according to data from the National Accounts, has translated, even in the presence of a certain wage moderation, into substantial increases in household income, which have come to add to the strong incentives to spending provided by unusually low interest rates in historical terms. and that they are especially expansive when the current cyclical position of the economy is taken into account. Under these conditions, it is not surprising that the dynamism of domestic demand has been based mainly on the growth of private consumption and residential investment. Nor is it true that the confidence generated by the expansion of employment and the low financing costs have led to households' consumption and investment expenditure increasing to a greater extent than their incomes, and that, consequently, there has been a marked expansion in the demand for credit. In fact, it is striking that, according to the latest data available from the Financial Accounts of the Spanish Economy, households have decreased their savings rate and have become net claimants of funds. From the Bank of Spain we have repeatedly pointed out the macroeconomic and financial implications that derive from the evolution of the indebtedness of Spanish families in recent years. Let me remind you that in just ten years households have more than doubled their debt ratio in terms of household income, which is already above the European average, although it is still some distance from the values corresponding to the main Anglo-Saxon economies. This variation reflects, to a large extent, a natural process of adjustment to changes in some of the fundamental determinants of savings such as interest rates and income expectations. In fact, the sector's equity position, taken as a whole, remains very healthy, as shown by the fact that its net assets are more than six times the GDP of the entire economy. However, it is clear that the current rates of growth in household debts are not sustainable. Nor can it be ignored that the predominance of variable-rate loans and the allocation of a substantial part of new liabilities to the purchase of housing have significantly increased the exposure of this sector to changes in interest rates and in the prices of real estate assets. Given the historically low level of interest rates and the increase in inflationary risks, in the short term, mainly as a result of oil price developments, it seems appropriate to insist on the necessary prudence on the part of both financial institutions and borrowers. Non-financial corporations have also been maintaining high funding needs. This trend contrasts with the performance of investment in capital goods, which has shown a lower expansion over recent years than might have been expected, in line with both cyclical circumstances and similar financing conditions. In fact, until practically last year there have been no signs of reactivation of this component of domestic demand, whose evolution, on the other hand, usually conditions the growth of the economy's productivity and, in this way, may also end up affecting its competitiveness. The expansion of corporate credit in the last decade was due, at first, to the demand of large business groups immersed in internationalization processes. More recently, it has been mainly companies linked to the construction and real estate development sector that have required more financial resources, more than making up for the low dynamism of credit for industrial activities. Thus, the financial counterpart to the imbalance between domestic and external demand in the pattern of growth, as well as the dynamism of household spending, has been the maintenance of high financing needs of the private sector. Fortunately, progress in the field of fiscal consolidation has meant that these funding needs have not been exacerbated by the behaviour of general government, which has had a financial balance that has been only slightly in deficit or even slightly in surplus in the last two years. It is pertinent, however, to point out, also from this perspective, that the expansionary behavior of private spending would have required, and still requires d0 as I said recently in the Congressional Budget Committee d0 a greater degree of fiscal restriction that contributes to a greater extent to mitigate the macroeconomic and financial imbalances observed. In short, the imbalances that accompany the current pattern of growth of our economy are generating net annual financing needs for the nation as a whole that can be around 6% of GDP. Either because of its relative proximity to the level currently exhibited by the US economy, to which all analysts tend to attribute a problem of acute external imbalance; Whether because they are higher than the levels reached by our own economy in previous historical moments that led to episodes of exchange rate crisis, this figure is viewed with special attention by analysts. In this regard, it is important to bear in mind first of all that Spain's membership of the euro area has substantially changed the way in which the risks arising from the current account deficit of our economy should be considered. In an open economy with monetary sovereignty and inflexible prices, the usual mechanism for correcting an excessive level of external deficit runs through a depreciation of the exchange rate, which allows the economy's price-competitiveness to be restored. Seen from a purely financial perspective, the imbalance tends to generate a loss of attractiveness of assets issued in the domestic currency for non-resident savers, which reduces their relative value compared to similar instruments issued in other currencies. The depreciation of the exchange rate thus reduces the demand for funds in foreign currency that requires the financing of the domestic deficit and facilitates the gradual correction of the trade imbalance. It should also be noted that, under these conditions, uncertainty about exchange rate developments tends to make the cost of external financing more expensive and, thus, limits the economy's ability to maintain, persistently, negative balances in its current account balance that cause a sustained increase in its debts to non-residents. Membership of a common monetary area such as EMU obviously short-circuits the above mechanism since the link is established, in this case, between the euro exchange rate and the external deficit not of the Spanish economy individually considered but of the euro area as a whole. Thus, the increase in the financing needs of an economy does not have the brake represented by exchange rate uncertainty and the increase in financing costs. Consequently, the connection between a current account deficit and the possible difficulties in financing it now runs through a much more indirect channel that passes, first, through the implications of the imbalance on the economy's growth capacity and, secondly, through the impact of the latter on the equity position of each borrower. It is important to stress that this does not mean at all that the problems arising from a high level of current account deficit disappear. It is rather a change in its nature. If I may use a medical simile here, it could be said that the external deficit ceases to be a disease in itself and becomes principally the symptom of a different disease. A disease that consists of the gradual loss of competitiveness. The symptoms, in any case, are relevant and must be observed carefully, as they provide valuable information about the evolution of the underlying problem. But in addition, they must be analyzed in detail because they require treatment, both in the underlying problem, and to help prevent the appearance of complementary difficulties that complicate the diagnosis. From this perspective, I would like to dedicate the next few minutes of my presentation to briefly analysing how the current account deficit of the Spanish economy is being financed and analysing its implications for the conduct of public policies. At the beginning of this decade, when the financing needs of the Spanish economy were around 3% of GDP, our Balance of Payments showed an approximately equitable distribution between the three main components of net financing inflows: direct investment; portfolio investment; and the rest of investments, which mainly include loans, deposits and temporary operations of financial institutions. Since 2003, however, we have witnessed a gradual contraction in direct investment which, according to the latest information available, accounted for barely 6% of resource inflows during the first six months of this year. Initially, the gap left by lower foreign direct investment was mainly filled by the advance of "other investments", that is, by greater recourse by credit institutions to international interbank markets. Subsequently, we have witnessed a very significant growth in portfolio investment, which now accounts for approximately three quarters of the total funds raised from the rest of the world. A closer analysis of this item reveals, however, that the recent boom is mainly due to the expansionary trend in the acquisition by foreign investors of fixed-income securities issued by both credit institutions and securitisation funds. In this way, the external financial resources necessary to finance the current deficit of the Spanish economy are being channelled towards their ultimate recipients through, mainly, the intermediation of Spanish credit institutions. They are appealing to international markets to fill the growing gap between the demand for credit and the evolution of traditional bank liabilities. In this way, the expansion of domestic demand and the external imbalance it has generated have led to a notable increase in both the loan portfolio and the liabilities vis-88-vis abroad of the resident banking sector, which has increased the complexity of risk management and control in a way that cannot go unnoticed by those of us who have the task of ensuring the good health and efficiency of this fundamental piece of the Spanish financial system. In this regard, I must point out that the entities are responding diligently to the evolution of the scenario in which they operate. Given the strong growth in the demand for credit and the consequent increase in the requirements derived from the different solvency ratios, the entities have made some use of the cushion provided by the traditional maintenance of levels of own resources substantially higher than those legally required. Thus, despite the slight downward trend shown by the ratios in recent years, their current levels continue to be comfortably above the minimum required. At the same time, both the dynamism of credit itself and the continued expansion of the economy and its consequent contractionary effects on non-performing loans have been accompanied by significant increases in the provisions maintained by institutions and, therefore, in the coverage available against potential insolvencies. This process, in which statistical provision has played an important role, is serving to strengthen the solidity of banks in a context in which the strong growth of loans makes it advisable to take extreme precautions against the risks of future defaults. At the same time, there have been progressive advances in its results, which currently place Spanish institutions among the most profitable in the European concert, in a context that is not easy for banks such as low interest rates. This trend has undoubtedly been fostered by the very dynamism of intermediation activity. But it is also important to note that it has also benefited from a significant effort to contain costs, the most obvious reflection of which is the continued improvement in the average efficiency ratio of the sector. An important conclusion of all this is the importance of having had and being able to count in the future on an integrated, efficient and solvent financial system to finance the growth of our economy. Growth that has brought our levels of well-being closer to that of our European partners. It has been the integration of the European financial market, within the framework of the single currency, that has made it possible to finance our economy without the restrictions to which it was accustomed in the past. In addition, the Spanish financial system has been able to adapt to new circumstances and, as in the past, has not only been able to channel domestic savings towards the most profitable allocations, thus contributing to development, but also to lead a process of international expansion with remarkable success. An integrated, efficient and competitive financial system provides the best conditions for depositors and investors and contributes to greater soundness from a prudential perspective. Under these conditions, it is the responsibility of the Bank of Spain to ensure that the current regulatory framework favours the preservation of the solidity, profitability and efficiency of the sector, in a context characterised by a growing complexity of financial instruments and a progressive internationalisation of capital flows. Such a framework should also promote the integration of markets, be shaped in compliance with basic market principles in such a way as to reduce interference in their normal functioning to the minimum necessary and take as a basic reference when defining strategies and priorities, the challenges posed by globalisation and the advantages provided by the European single market. The Banco de Espa96a is making significant efforts in this area, which are part of broader processes developed at European and international level. There are major challenges at European level. On the one hand, the creation of the euro and European regulatory initiatives (among which the European Commission's Financial Services Action Plan stands out) has achieved the integration in a very short space of time of wholesale markets, such as monetary and interbank. However, this integration is progressing much more slowly in the area of retail banking, and there is still a lack of resistance in cross-border banking operations. I believe that the European Commission's approach of considering the new phase of its action plan in the area of financial services as an integral and fundamental part of its economic and social agenda is very appropriate. Indeed, challenges such as globalisation, the need to increase its potential growth, to create an environment conducive to entrepreneurship and innovation, the sustainability of the tensions that population ageing poses on the financing of pension and health systems, require the EU to undertake reforms and one of the main ones is to perfect a single financial market, Integrated and dynamic that channels savings, diversifies risks and provides companies with the means to invest and grow. Responsibility in these areas lies not only with the Community bodies and authorities, but also, and in many cases, most especially, with the authorities of the Member States. I believe that all authorities must push in the same direction: market integration, better regulation that reduces costs for companies, incentives for better risk management, risk-based supervision, supervisory coordination and convergence, improvement of corporate governance structures, transparency, market discipline, etc. The list is long and varied, therefore, I would like to dedicate the end of my speech to commenting schematically on some of these aspects, whose choice responds to their particular relevance in a situation such as the current one in which, as I have been pointing out throughout my presentation, the complexity of the business has increased significantly as a result of the transformations of our economy and the national and international financial system. In the regulatory framework known as Lamfalusy, the so-called CEBS (European Committee of Banking Supervisors), chaired by the Bank of Spain in its first two years of existence, has been working, I believe in a recognized efficient way, in several of the lines of action: Coordination and convergence of supervisory practices. This is particularly relevant for achieving consistency in the implementation of Basel II, whose directive, as you know, was recently adopted by the European Parliament. Basel II and more especially the European Capital Directive reinforces the role of the supervisor of origin, both as a dynamizer of the coordination of destination supervisors, and in the processes of validation of models. In the single European financial market, where 25 national supervisory authorities coexist alongside pan-European banks, common regulation is not enough, but a broad consensus among supervisors is needed on how this directive will be implemented in practice. This process, called convergence of supervisory practices, is essential in order not to impede integration processes between institutions and to provide the banking industry with a cost-efficient European supervisory system. CEBS has also launched two initiatives in the field of information and transparency by seeking common formats in the European Union for accounting and capital reporting requirements, known as FINREP and COREP. It is the first time that European financial supervisors have succeeded in establishing common EU-wide reporting requirements, with obvious cost advantages for industry. In addition, this harmonisation of information will also favour that of supervisory practices. Finally, these initiatives include computer developments using the latest techniques in financial information transmission, such as XBRL. With the Basel II Directive recently adopted by the Council and the European Parliament, I think it is appropriate to spend a little time reflecting on its role in strengthening the financial system in various ways. On the one hand, Basel II will provide incentives for better risk management and will encourage the directors of the entities to assume greater responsibility for their effective control. On the other hand, transparency requirements will be substantially increased which, among other things, will make the risk management decisions taken much more visible, thus amplifying the ability of markets to reward, in the form of lower financing costs, those institutions that pursue with greater commitment and success the objective of creating value with a medium and long-term perspective. Improvement in risk management must be anchored in good corporate governance. While Basel II will provide an overall framework conducive to better governance of institutions, each regulator will need to outline the specific elements that can be adapted to the specific characteristics of institutions or groups of entities. The need to normatively articulate a series of principles of good corporate governance arises when market mechanisms, including the possibility of self-regulation by the sector, are not sufficient to guarantee a correct alignment of the interests of the managers of the companies with those of their ultimate owners. It is also reasonable to think that the existence of sound principles of good governance will contribute positively to increasing the confidence of those who, without necessarily becoming owners of companies, contribute in one way or another to financing their activity. The importance of good corporate governance is, in my opinion, even greater in the case of the banking business since the essence of it consists precisely in taking funds from agents and channeling them to third parties. Terms such as trust and reputation therefore take on an additional dimension. In this regard, I would like to recall that the Committee of Banking Supervisors in Basel has published a consultative document in which it has sought to adapt the OECD code of good governance to the specificities of credit institutions. These initiatives that I have summarized in a schematic way: supervisory convergence and cooperation, the implementation of Basel II and initiatives to strengthen the good governance of financial institutions are just some examples that go in the aforementioned directions of deepening the integration and competition of financial markets and the efficiency and solvency of credit institutions. I will conclude by recalling that the long period of growth of the Spanish economy has required access to foreign savings that has been possible, without introducing restrictions on growth, thanks mainly to the European financial market in the context of the euro, highlighting the important role played by Spanish credit institutions. This financing facility must not obscure the need to correct the underlying imbalances if the period of convergence with our European partners is to be prolonged. In this process, budgetary and structural reform policies are key. Likewise, we must not ignore that the concrete way in which the entry of this greater volume of foreign savings is being implemented implies an additional pressure on the ability of Spanish credit institutions to effectively intermediate the flows of financial resources between savers and lenders and a change in their risk profile. An exercise of minimum prudence therefore requires special attention to monitor the evolution of this process in the future and to continue advancing in the aforementioned lines of action. Thank you very much for your attention.
