Title: Notes for the speech given on the occasion of the inauguration of the III Congress of Economy of the Valencian Community
text: 13th XBRL International Conference Jaime Caruana Governor of the Banco de Espa Introduction Good afternoon. I would like to begin by thanking the organisers of this 13th XBRL International Conference for their kind invitation to participate. I am delighted to have this opportunity to close todays session by sharing with you some reflections on financial information from the standpoint of a banking supervisor. And it is, of course, a special pleasure for me to be able to address this audience in my home country. I guess that, looking from the outside, it might seem somewhat strange that banking supervisors and other regulators are taking such an active interest in a computer language. But I think that all of us here are very well aware of the role that tools such as XBRL can play in promoting the effective and efficient flow of financial information, and it is on this wider objective that I want to focus my intervention today. I will begin with a brief introduction to recall the important role that information plays in financial markets from a macroeconomic perspective. But I would like to devote the main part of my presentation to five initiatives that I believe regulators - as one of the sources of information demands on the industry - can take to contribute to ensuring that financial information can be generated, transmitted and used in the most efficient and effective way, to the benefit of stakeholders and interested parties, in todays complex financial markets. In doing so, I will draw on my experience as the Governor of an EU central bank with prudential supervisory responsibilities, and also as the current Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. The importance of financial information So, why is information so important? Quite simply, because information is the fabric from which financial markets are made. Let me elaborate on this statement. In economic terms, an efficient market is defined as one in which prices reflect all available information. Extrapolating this, we can say that the efficient functioning of financial markets requires that the prices within those markets reflect all the information on the financial asset being traded. For markets to be efficient, therefore, it is necessary that sufficient information flows with sufficient speed. However, information is neither created nor transmitted spontaneously. First, it must be generated. Then, it must be transmitted to users, through the appropriate channels and in the appropriate format and presentation. These users, in turn, must incorporate the information into their own decision-making processes. This is a process which clearly implies costs, both in terms of time and resources. Regulators are one of the stakeholders in this process. In order to fulfil our objectives and functions, we need information from the entities and markets that we supervise. But financial institutions are faced with requirements from other sources too. They have to produce information for a whole range of other purposes, for example to fulfil mercantile, fiscal and statistical requirements, as well as to run their own business, of course. On top of this, changes in the financial markets themselves are having a major impact on information flows. Increases in the complexity and volume of financial transactions are contributing to an increase in the complexity and volume of information that entities need to produce and manage, even if only for their own internal purposes. And if we add in the ever more prevalent international dimension, the situation becomes even more complicated. In the face of these developments, it seems important to me that we find new ways to manage the information process. So what can we do, as regulators, to promote the most effective and efficient processes for the generation, transmission and use of financial information, and therefore the most efficient markets? I believe there are five key elements in this process, and it is on these elements that I will focus in the remainder of my intervention. 1 Convergence of regulatory requirements The first of these involves starting at the beginning of the value chain of information requirements. In my view, a greater degree of convergence in the underlying regulation which applies to financial institutions and markets will provide us with an excellent basis for making progress on other aspects. Let me refer to some initiatives that have been taken in this respect. Of course, the first initiative that I must mention is that of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Given the importance of accounting data as the basis of information flows, the development and application of these standards is providing a valuable opportunity to enhance the efficiency and comparability of information, especially on an international basis. Indeed, with effect from 1 January 2005, all EU listed companies have been required by law to use IFRS for their consolidated financial statements. The significance of this development should not be underestimated. It means that market participants and other interested parties should be able to compare and contrast information relating to companies in different jurisdictions on a like-for-like basis, and thereby make more informed decisions. Common accounting standards increase transparency and comparability for investors, thus promoting greater cross border investment. And let me give you a less direct, but nonetheless important example of a regulatory convergence initiative, from my perspective as Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. As you may well be aware, at the end of the nineties, we embarked on a review of the so-called Basel Accord, an agreement reached back in 1988 to determine minimum regulatory capital requirements for international banks. The result of this review, the new Basel II framework, will, like its predecessor, be applied not only in the thirteen countries which are members of the Committee, but in many other countries of the world, including the 25 countries of the European Union  in fact, in probably more than 100 countries in total. And Basel II is much more than a capital requirements regime. It is a major shift in regulatory philosophy. First, although it still sets minimum capital requirements, these are based on a menu of approaches with built-in economic incentives to encourage banks to develop and use more sophisticated risk measurement and management systems which can be recognised for supervisory purposes. Second, banks are encouraged to conduct their own assessments of their overall risk profile in order to determine whether they need additional capital buffers and/or other risk mitigants. Supervisors will evaluate these assessments and both parties will engage in dialogue on the basis of their findings. Thirdly, the new regime sets out requirements for increased transparency and disclosure by institutions to the markets. This is intended to leverage the ability of markets to provide discipline to banks to ensure that they are not holding unrealistically low levels of capital. In sum, Basel II will have wide-ranging effects, both on banks and on supervisors, across many countries. Many aspects of the supervisory process which are currently subject to different requirements in different countries will be captured within a common international framework for the first time. This will not only help banks that operate on an international basis to establish more convergent information bases across the countries in which they are present. It will also facilitate the exchange of information among supervisors, because we will be speaking a more common language. And, more directly, the transparency requirements will, in themselves, lead to the availability of more, and more comparable, data for market participants and users. Both these initiatives are international in nature. However, as I noted earlier in my intervention, information demands also come from a range of sources including at the domestic level, and it is certainly worth looking to see what can be done at this level too. One such initiative could be to look at the possibility of using IFRS data for market, corporate law, prudential and tax purposes. 2 Convergence of reporting requirements So, having common regulatory standards and approaches on an international basis can provide a natural basis for more efficient information flows. However, without convergence of the reporting requirements that stem from these standards and approaches, entities will still have to produce and transmit different information, in different formats, to the regulators in the countries in which they are present. In other words, common regulation does not automatically translate into common reporting requirements - the second element that I want to mention today. This has been highlighted as a particular issue in the European Union context, given the political objective to promote a fully integrated financial market. Differences in reporting requirements can be seen as a barrier to achieving the full potential of this single market, to the extent that they impose an additional cost on those entities operating, or planning to operate, across borders. Not surprisingly, therefore, there have been a number of calls for regulators to work together to streamline the reporting requirements that apply to institutions which are active on a pan-European basis. The Committee of European Banking Supervisors, or CEBS, established two years ago and charged with promoting convergence of supervisory practices and cooperation and information sharing between supervisors, has risen to this challenge and has taken a major initiative in this respect, culminating in the publication of two sets of common reporting templates, one set for institutions to report their solvency ratio results under Basel II, and the other set for institutions to report financial information based on IFRS. These two projects take advantage of the two initiatives for convergence in international regulatory requirements I have already mentioned. Indeed, it would have been very difficult, if not impossible, to have made progress without them. Both the introduction of International Financial Reporting Standards and the implementation of Basel II are obliging supervisors to modify their existing reporting requirements and systems. This presents a window of opportunity to make progress on more convergent approaches. The benefits of a common reporting framework are clear, both for the institutions generating the information and for banking supervisors. From the standpoint of financial institutions, administrative costs will decrease, particularly for cross-border banks. At the same time, supervisors will benefit from easier exchange of information. And the framework offers the flexibility to incorporate future modifications with lower costs. Overall, these positive effects should lead to higher quality in the information flows generated. I should say at this point that neither of these projects has been easy. If you consider that the European Union is currently made up of 25 countries, you can well imagine that the starting situation was complex, with each country requiring its banks to submit different information. In fact, the differences were not limited to the definitions used by each Member State, but also related to the reporting systems, and the technologies and formats used. But I would argue that it has been a very worthwhile initiative, and one that will reap benefits for years to come. 3 Increased reliance on business information Let me turn now to the third element that I believe is important for success. I believe that regulators should put increased reliance on information generated and used by institutions within their own business. Let me set the context for this remark. I dont think it is an exaggeration to say that, over recent years, the Basel II initiative has driven a paradigm shift in regulatory attitudes. Regulation used to be something that was rather imposed on institutions to be complied with, and seen by them as completely separate from their own internal business processes, and therefore an additional cost. But it has been evolving to something which increasingly goes in the direction of recognising and harnessing the best risk management practices of the industry itself, and encouraging institutions to further improve their own risk management practices. As I have already mentioned, Basel II includes explicit economic incentives for institutions to adopt more sophisticated risk measurement and management systems. And to the extent that it is based on institutions own capital evaluation processes, it brings regulatory capital closer to economic capital. Such an approach means that regulation becomes less of a separate cost for institutions, which can use the same systems for both business and regulatory purposes. Whats more, such regulation can have business benefits, because improved risk management also makes good business sense. I think the same philosophy is applicable to regulatory reporting. In my view, regulatory reporting requirements should, to the extent possible, be based on internal data used by managers to run their business, and should encourage the effective collection, generation and use of this information for internal risk management purposes. There is clearly a cost in asking for information that is not used within the business. But more than this, it may well be that internal information is of better quality, more reliable and more accurate than information generated for external purposes. To the extent that Basel II recognises internal risk management systems, the resulting reporting requirements should naturally be based more on the internal information produced by those systems. But I think that over the coming years, we should continue to explore ways to encourage institutions to improve the way they collect and use internal information to run their business and manage their risks, as well as the possibilities for harnessing and using this information as regulators. 4 Increased feed-back to reporting institutions So far, I have mainly talked about initiatives which regulators can take that should have the impact of reducing the costs of producing financial information. But I think it is possible to go further than this. In fact, I think that we can take initiatives that actually give something back to the reporting entities - in other words, initiatives that provide them with clear benefits. This is the fourth element that I wanted to mention, and perhaps is best explained with a couple of examples. Let me take my first example from the Spanish context. In Spain, as in some other countries, we maintain a central credit register. This contains information about all the direct and indirect credit exposures  i.e. loans and guarantees  with a value of 6000 or more, which have been granted by banking institutions and other lenders to their clients. As a central bank and banking supervisory authority, we use this database to assist us in evaluating macro-prudential trends and the credit risk in the economy as a whole. Of course, the data doesnt get into the register of its own accord but rather must be reported by the lending institutions. Reporting this data is complex and costly for the institutions. But they receive useful feedback in return. As contributors to the register, they are entitled to have access to aggregate information on the credit extended by other lenders to potential and actual borrowers. This can be helpful to them in making their own credit decisions and evaluating their credit risk situation. Let me also mention another international initiative that I think will give something useful back to reporting institutions. This is the initiative to promote increased supervisory transparency, or supervisory disclosure as part of the EU implementation of the Basel II framework. CEBS has developed a framework for supervisory disclosure, with information to be published on CEBS website, via a set of common templates. While much of the information to be published under the framework relates to supervisory rules and processes, it will also include aggregate national information on the banking sector, on credit risk, operational risk, market risk, and on supervisory actions and measures. Given that this information will be published in a single location for all EU countries, and in a format that facilitates country-by-country comparisons, institutions will be able to use it see where they stand in certain key respects against other banks, both on a national and international basis. This will be valuable to them in making evaluations and decisions about their position. In sum, I think that the general move towards greater transparency by regulators is positive and should be encouraged. But, more than this, we should explore the possibilities to give greater feed-back to reporting institutions, from which they can derive benefits. 5 Taking advantage of new technologies The final element that I want to mention today is certainly not the least important. I believe that we should make full use of the possibilities offered by new technologies and tools to collect, transmit, manage and analyse the increasing amounts of data we are faced with. A standard like XBRL can and should play a central role in enhancing information flows. Its great advantage is that it allows for a more precise, reliable and rapid interface between the generators and users of information. But XBRL is not only a tool for transmission of data. Through the development of taxonomies or dictionaries of terms, it allows information to be generated and interpreted on a consistent basis. XBRL therefore means that financial information from entities can be understood and assimilated in other parts of the world in an accurate and timely manner. In the banking sector, XBRL could be a means of finding a common language for financial information needs. It could thereby facilitate supervisory co-operation and promote a level playing field. It is for these reasons that CEBS has decided to promote the use of XBRL in the two common reporting initiatives that I mentioned earlier in my intervention. While national supervisory authorities are free to decide on the technical transmission specifications to implement the new reporting frameworks, CEBS considers that XBRL can be a helpful tool in constructing a harmonised European reporting mechanism, and is therefore developing an XBRL platform which will be available free of charge to national authorities and supervised institutions. XBRL taxonomies are being developed for both frameworks. Of course, we all recognise that it is not cheap to develop these technologies. But I do believe that the benefits will greatly outweigh the costs in the medium to longer term, and I would encourage every effort to be made to harness those benefits. Conclusions Let me finalise my intervention by briefly recapitulating the five elements that I believe are important for progress: First, convergence of the underlying regulation that affects financial institutions and markets. Second, convergence of reporting requirements on the basis of this more harmonised regulation. Third, increased use of internal information, generated for business purposes, for external reporting purposes. Fourth, increased feedback and information to the reporting institutions. And finally, the use of new technologies. I think the examples I have given from the banking perspective show that we are already making some good progress, although there is of course more that could, and should, be done. In closing, I would like to thank you for your attention and wish you a productive and enjoyable time here in Madrid.

Title: Conference: Business Meeting of the Financial Club of Vigo (Governor's Participation)
text: Madrid, 24 November 2005 Appearance before the Senate Budget Committee Senate Jaime Caruana Lacorte Governor of the Bank of Spain Ladies and gentlemen, I come before this Senate Budget Committee today in order to report on the analysis carried out by the Bank of Spain of the General State Budget Project for the year 2006. In these analyses, the Banco de Espa96a adopts a comprehensive approach, placing budgetary policy in the Spanish macroeconomic context and taking into account its interaction with other economic policies, especially with the monetary policy of the Eurosystem. At the beginning of October I appeared before the homonymous Commission of the Congress of Deputies for the same purpose. My statement before you today naturally takes up many of the arguments that I then outlined, and which I will try to set out below, duly updated and nuanced with those relevant events that have taken place in recent weeks. As usual, I will begin by briefly reviewing the international and European economic environment, and then focus on the Spanish situation. The notable rise in oil prices on international markets has been the feature that has most conditioned the evolution of the international economy throughout this year. Thus, since the summer, the price of a barrel of crude oil has been around 60 dollars per barrel, levels that are 50% higher than the average of 2004. A set of specific factors have contributed to the rise in oil prices that would not necessarily have to be repeated in the future, such as geopolitical uncertainties and the series of hurricanes that have hit various areas of the Gulf of Mexico. However, this phenomenon responds, above all, to the confluence of reasons of a more structural nature. In particular, in a context where rapid progress towards the incorporation of large regions of the world into all developed countries exerts high pressure on the demand for this raw material, the crude oil extraction and refining industries are operating in conditions close to their maximum capacity level. In the short and medium term, it is not foreseeable that these supply restrictions can be overcome, because although the persistence of high oil prices encourages investment in new capacity, it will take several years until it is operational. For these reasons, rising oil prices may not be a passing phenomenon. The good news is that, to date, the pace of expansion of global activity has suffered only moderately as a result of higher oil prices. This may have been due to reasons such as the decrease in the degree of energy dependence of the main economies compared to previous historical episodes or the fact that the increase in oil prices is largely due to demand pressure (reflecting the general economic boom). In any case, global GDP is likely to close the year growing above 4%, driven by the still accommodative tone of the economic policy set, the persistence of favourable financial conditions and the consolidation of corporate balance sheets. However, this dynamism of activity in aggregate terms hides differentiated regional behaviour. Thus, the economies of the United States and those of Southeast Asia have continued to exhibit remarkable strength, while Japan seems to be finally leaving behind its long phase of reduced growth. However, this context of generalized prosperity contrasts with the low dynamism exhibited by the euro area economy. In any case, while the outlook for developments in the global economy remains relatively satisfactory, risks have been increasing over the course of the year. On the one hand, as I have indicated, the phase of high oil prices may last for an extended period of time. On the other hand, persistent global imbalances d0 which are most expressed in the US external deficit d0 have continued to intensify, carrying the risk of sharp adjustments in exchange rates between major currencies. As I pointed out a moment ago, in the period since 2005, the euro area has not been able to take full advantage of the period of relative prosperity that the world economy is going through. Thus, in the first half of the year, the rates of expansion of the area's output have been relatively modest. The advance in the third quarter confirms the first signs of a revival, although the outlook for the year as a whole remains for moderate growth. The causes of this development lie in the impact of the rise in oil prices and, to a lesser extent, in the delayed effects of the cumulative appreciation of the euro exchange rate. The most recent indicators point to a recovery in the tone of activity in the final part of the year, so that, according to the various forecasts available, the area's output could register an average growth of around 1.3% in 2005. In the coming year, according to the forecasts just released by the European Commission, activity is expected to expand at rates close to 2%, favoured by the persistence of favourable monetary and financial conditions and the continuation of the dynamism of world trade. This greater support in activity should be helped by an expansionary tone in exports and a recovery in investment, while private consumption would take a little longer to accelerate, in line with the expected improvement in job creation and the consequent strengthening of household confidence. However, the materialisation of these prospects is subject, as for the world economy as a whole, to uncertainties arising from oil price developments and global imbalances. As regards the evolution of the inflationary situation, the annual growth rate of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices in the euro area has been clearly above 2% since the spring, reflecting the increase in the energy goods component. In the coming months, it is foreseeable that inflation in the area will continue to be above 2%. In a more distant horizon, the existing evidence that rising oil prices are being passed on to other groups of goods and services is, for the moment, limited. Thus, the rate of change of the price index that excludes unprocessed food and energy goods has recently remained at around 1.5%. In addition, wage demands have for the moment been consistent with the maintenance of price stability in the medium term, which has possibly been favoured by the modest strength of economic activity and employment. However, the continued high levels of energy prices and their potential second-round effects on wages are emerging as a significant upside risk to inflation in the euro area. The Governing Council of the ECB has kept key interest rates unchanged at 2%. However, in the communiqu8es issued following its meetings on 6 October and 3 November, the Governing Council clearly expressed its concern at the persistence of inflationary pressures arising from oil price developments. In recent years, the maintenance of conditions conducive to stronger economic growth contrasts with the relatively mediocre results that have been achieved. This apparent paradox highlights the existence of structural constraints limiting potential growth. These obstacles are not an insurmountable obstacle. However, overcoming them requires a more determined application than has been carried out to date of policies aimed at promoting aspects such as greater use of the labour factor or the intensification of the introduction and use of new technologies. This need was recognised last March by the European Council when it decided to relaunch the structural reform agenda designed in Lisbon five years ago. In order to increase the commitment of the various authorities to the reform processes, the review of the Lisbon strategy has more clearly identified the areas of responsibility at Community and national level. On the one hand, Member States retain responsibility for most of the policies necessary to achieve the final objectives, for which they must make explicit, through the National Reform Programmes, how they will translate the generic commitments they have made into concrete actions. These Programmes are being discussed and agreed upon with the national social partners, since success in achieving the objectives is all the more likely the greater the involvement of the different groups involved. On the other hand, contribution at Community level to the reform process is equally necessary. In July, the Commission presented all the actions within its scope. In particular, the benefits of completing the single market in terms of economic growth and employment are still far from being fully exploited, which is particularly true for services markets. In the area of public finances, high structural deficits are again present in a large number of countries this year. Moreover, according to the budgetary plans for next year, there will be no significant correction of existing imbalances in 2006 either. The inadequacy of adjustment efforts is, in my view, unsatisfactory, since, as I have said, it is necessary for individual countries to face the budgetary consequences of population ageing from as healthy a starting point as possible. Moreover, as has been seen in recent years of modest economic growth in Europe, the maintenance of high structural deficits deprives fiscal policy of the necessary room for manoeuvre for automatic stabilisers to operate in the downturn of the cycle. Finally, the absence of ambitious fiscal consolidation strategies, part of a broader reform framework, contributes to undermining the confidence of economic operators, who adopt a more cautious attitude when undertaking their spending decisions. For all these reasons, it is of the utmost importance that the revised rules of the Stability and Growth Pact are rigorously applied and that Member States show a high degree of compliance with these rules. The Spanish economy continues to show high dynamism, closer to that of the US economy than to the tone of weakness that characterises the euro area. However, the close link between our economy and that of the other EMU countries means that our external environment is somewhat less expansionary than the world economy, although monetary and financial conditions, set at the level of the euro area, are very comfortable for a situation, such as Spain's, of strong growth in domestic spending. These circumstances condition the appropriate design of domestic economic policies and, in particular, that of fiscal policy, to which I will refer in detail when commenting on the Draft General State Budget for 2006. First, allow me to briefly review the economic situation and the outlook for the coming year. The important revision of the National Accounts of Spain that took place last spring has confirmed the solidity of the expansionary phase that the Spanish economy is going through, characterized by a high dynamism of activity and employment, in a context of strong increase in the active population derived from immigration. Since the end of 2003, there has also been a continuous trend towards higher GDP growth, which has continued in the period since 2005, reaching a year-on-year rate of 3.5% in the third quarter, one tenth more than in the previous quarter. Likewise, employment growth, which was above 3% in the first half of the year, has remained remarkably strong in the summer months. Therefore, the rate of growth in labour productivity remains low, which reflects, in part, the type of productive activities that grow the most, such as services and, above all, construction. On the expenditure side, output growth reflects the extraordinary buoyancy of domestic demand, growing at rates of around 5 per cent since the second half of 2004. Part of this demand has filtered outwards, contributing to the detraction of growth that net foreign demand is exerting, close to two percentage points. Estimates for the third quarter of 2005 point to a certain correction in the composition of expenditure, towards a lower negative contribution from foreign demand. The component that is contributing most to sustaining domestic demand is household consumption which, after growing by 4.8% in the first half of the year, has slightly moderated its rate of change in recent months. The disposable income of households, whose growth is linked to job creation, continues to constitute the basic support of expenditure, despite the fact that the recent upswing in inflation has reduced, to some extent, their purchasing power. Even so, consumption is advancing at rates higher than those of income, mainly as a result of the wealth effects that continue to be generated by the high increases in house prices and the revaluation of financial assets. In turn, favourable mortgage financing conditions, together with the boost derived from the revaluation of wealth, explain the intense boom in home purchases, a component of gross capital formation that maintains a growth rate of around 6%. To finance this increase in spending, especially on residential investment, households have had to incur a growing debt, which already exceeds 100% of their disposable income. The decline in savings and the increase in investment have determined that families have become net demanders of financing. On the other hand, productive investment is the component of expenditure that has experienced the strongest recovery since 2004, as can be seen from the rapid acceleration shown by investment in equipment. The latter reached rates of change close to 10 per cent in the first half of 2005, which, according to the available indicators, seem to have tended to soften, to some extent, in the second part of the year. The favourable financing conditions, the rise in corporate profits and the completion of the financial restructuring processes undertaken by some large companies have stimulated business investment, despite the fact that demand prospects in the most dynamic markets may be conditioned by the losses of competitiveness that accumulate in the sectors most open to the outside. I have already pointed out that net foreign demand is exerting a sharp detraction on the rate of output growth, which has been accompanied by very sharp increases in the trade deficit and the economy's need for financing. The contraction reached very negative levels at the end of 2004 and at the beginning of 2005, when a very weak performance of exports was combined with a notable rebound in imports, associated with the recovery in domestic demand. Since the second quarter, exports of goods and tourism receipts have recovered, somewhat mitigating the contractionary effect of the external contribution. Several factors are contributing to the drain on external demand, including the higher rate of growth recorded by the Spanish economy, in relation to the surrounding countries, as it has a more advanced cyclical position and a higher growth potential. The composition of demand, in which the weight of investment in equipment has increased, has also contributed to raising import intensity. However, these elements are not sufficient to explain the sharp deterioration in the external balance that has been observed since 2004. It also affects the losses of competitiveness accumulated by the Spanish economy in recent years. The increasing penetration of imports into the domestic market and the fall in export share, which was already evident in 2004, indicate that losses in competitiveness are already translating into worse trade performance. Price and cost developments indicate continued losses in competitiveness. The inflation rate measured by consumer prices stood at 3.5% in October, which represents an improvement over the 3.8% recorded in the harmonised index the previous month. In any case, Spanish inflation is still one percentage point higher than that of EMU as a whole. Wages also maintain systematically higher growth rates than those registered in the countries with which Spain competes internationally, which, together with the low growth in productivity, leads to comparatively high increases in unit labour costs. These differences tend to worsen in situations such as the current one, of higher prices of imported energy, due to the existence of safeguard clauses that facilitate the transfer to wages of increases in consumer energy prices, which tends to make it difficult for the economy to adjust to oil price increases. These suppose a drain of real disposable income that agents have to assume to make possible the continuity of a non-inflationary growth. From this perspective, measures aimed at softening, directly or indirectly, the impact that higher energy prices have on the costs and performance of certain sectors, such as transport or fisheries, through effective reductions in taxes on hydrocarbon purchases or increases in subsidies, may also have counterproductive effects. Although this type of measure can help to wipe out the possible losses that are generated in the short term, they do so at the cost of delaying and hindering the introduction of changes in production processes that favor greater energy efficiency or the use of alternative energies, which constitute, in the end, the appropriate response in the long term. The rise in oil prices is an external shock to which the Spanish economy must adapt by accepting the loss of purchasing power that it implies for the incomes of national factors (whether wages or corporate profits) and allowing the relative increase in the price of this raw material to drive the necessary adjustments in terms of a more efficient use of energy in production and lower domestic consumption. As I pointed out in my appearance before the Congressional Budget Committee, the current trends of the Spanish economy and its behaviour in the first three quarters of 2005 indicate that GDP growth this year could be some tenth above the forecast incorporated in the Government's macroeconomic scenario, which is 3.3%. Logically, the growth forecast for next year, which the macroeconomic picture accompanying the Budgets also places at 3.3%, is surrounded by greater uncertainties. These come both from the external environment d0 partly due to the possibility of outdated impacts of oil price increases d0 and from the internal risks that have been generated in the current expansionary stage. The Spanish economy continues to grow and create jobs at high rates, but the role of private consumption and residential construction in growth remains excessive, without the recent recovery in productive investment having yet induced a sufficient rebalancing, and labour productivity continues to advance at very low rates. The prolongation of a period of growth with these characteristics has favoured the generation of losses in competitiveness and the rapid indebtedness of households, factors that pose risks to the very sustainability of the expansion. In the short term, it is foreseeable that the Spanish economy will maintain its current dynamism, supported by the expansionary influence of extraordinarily low levels of interest rates and the increase in the active population. However, in order to consolidate this growth scenario over a longer horizon, it is necessary to tackle the elements of risk that I have just mentioned. This is the biggest challenge facing domestic economic policies right now. Demand policies, and fiscal policy in particular, should be geared towards redirecting domestic demand growth towards rates more in line with the economy's potential, favouring a change in its composition towards a more moderate increase in household spending and a strengthening of productive investment. It should be borne in mind that budgetary policy is the most effective instrument available to the economic authorities for this task. On the other hand, the action of demand policies must be supported by structural reform policies that improve the functioning of goods and factor markets, and make it possible to reconcile job creation with greater productivity gains. As I have just pointed out, in the current phase of the Spanish economy it is important that budgetary policy adopts a relatively stabilising tone, which favours the containment of demand pressures. In principle, the fiscal forecasts for 2005 assume that the accounts of the Public Administrations will be closed, as planned at the beginning of the year, with a surplus of 0.1% of GDP and that the ratio of public debt to GDP could be below 45%. These results, which would make it possible to comfortably meet the European commitments made under the Stability and Growth Pact, would, however, mean a certain slowdown in the fiscal effort made. In fact, the usual fiscal stimulus measures indicate that if the public accounts were closed as expected in the liquidation advance, budgetary policy would have acquired a slightly expansionary tone in 2005. However, the strong dynamism shown by tax collection throughout this year, well above the estimates incorporated in the closing forecasts now available, would allow a surplus higher than budgeted and more in line with the requirements of the economy. The State's budget execution figures for recent months support the strength of revenues, although recently some additional spending commitments have also been assumed d0 such as those derived from agreements with the transport, fishing and mining sectors d0 towards which a part of this surplus of collection could be derived. In any case, it has recently been announced that the State could end the year with a positive balance, instead of with the expected deficit of 0.4 of GDP. In this case, the surplus of the general government as a whole would be more than half a point of GDP and the fiscal tone would have been closer to what the Spanish economy currently requires. The Budgets for 2006, which are now the subject of parliamentary discussion, set as an objective for the joint balance of the Public Administrations the obtaining of a surplus of 0.2% of GDP, which would not imply a significant change in the tone of fiscal policy. It is therefore very important that if the dynamism of revenue again exceeds the budgeted figures, as is expected to happen in 2005, the excess revenue translates into a higher surplus, in line with the results expected for this year. In my speech before the Congressional Committee on Budgets, I already pointed out that the priority orientation of spending policies towards those areas that can most favor the advancement of productivity - such as education - is adequate and consistent with the general framework established by the Government for its economic policy. However, in addition to the significant increase in the corresponding budgetary allocations, we must add other spending commitments made in the area of housing, minimum pensions, health financing and, more recently, those linked to agreements reached with sectors particularly affected by increases in energy prices or in the process of conversion. All this translates into a growth in public expenditure of the State higher than that of nominal GDP and entails the risk of overflows in budget execution, given that it is not expected to undertake compensatory cuts in other items or implement policies of greater efficiency of public spending in the horizon of the 2006 budgets. Increasing efficiency in public sector action is also essential to generate an environment more prone to increases in productivity and long-term growth, and this must be contributed not only by the reorientation of spending policies but also by a tax structure that generates the right incentives. The tax reforms announced must take this objective into account, while they must be well calibrated so that they do not entail a collection cost that may be excessive in less dynamic public revenue situations. The need to design more rigorous fiscal policies to achieve surplus positions more quickly is reinforced when medium-term considerations are introduced and Spanish demographic prospects are taken into account. These point to an intense process of population ageing, which will entail significant upward pressure on public spending, both in its pension component and in the coverage of situations of dependency. Faced with this prospect, which is unlikely to be broken as a result of intense emigration flows, more ambitious fiscal targets must be adopted and the necessary reforms in social protection systems addressed. The National Reform Program of Spain, presented by the Government in mid-October, is committed to promoting the adoption of some of the recommendations that emerged from the revision of the Toledo Pact two years ago, such as establishing greater correspondence between contributions and pensions or introducing elements of rationality in early retirement processes. After the loss of momentum in the adoption of measures of this nature in recent years, with the exception of the significant contributions to the Social Security Reserve Fund, this initiative is a good starting point, although complementary measures should begin to be discussed, in line with those that other European countries are beginning to apply. The institutional framework within which fiscal policy operates is of great importance in ensuring disciplined developments in public finances. The reform of the Budget Stability Laws is currently being discussed and a new revision of the regional financing system has been proposed. Among the most innovative aspects in the draft reform of the Budget Stability Laws is the introduction of greater flexibility in the definition of budgetary stability rules, allowing the State, the Autonomous Communities and the large municipalities to adapt their deficit or surplus target to the cyclical situation of the economy and the obligation to obtain a surplus when economic growth exceeds a certain threshold, although it is not established that this is greater the higher the growth. On the other hand, the Reform Project reinforces fiscal discipline, by establishing that the balance of the Central Administration will be computed, for the purposes of compliance with the objectives of budgetary stability, independently of that of Social Security. However, in the case of the Autonomous Communities, a transparent distribution of the fiscal effort corresponding to each of them is not defined, which may entail the risk of deviations. Finally, as I mentioned in my October appearance, I would like to highlight the importance of fully applying the provisions incorporated in the standard to improve transparency and the availability of information on public accounts, as I believe that it is a fundamental element to ensure discipline in fiscal structures in which spending is strongly decentralized. as in Spain. The beginning of a process of revision of the regional financing system makes this effort of transparency and fiscal discipline more necessary. In terms of structural reforms, the Government has taken a series of initiatives over the past year, which have been subsumed in Spain's recently approved National Reform Programme aimed at boosting productivity, innovation and, ultimately, real convergence. These initiatives establish an appropriate orientation for economic policy to address the challenges facing the Spanish economy, in particular the need to boost productivity and lay the foundations for solid growth in the long term. It is necessary, however, to complement this set of measures with the application of other reforms that entail longer negotiating timetables, but which are of vital importance to maintain dynamism in employment and promote the competitiveness of the Spanish business fabric. In this sense, the labour market must provide sufficient flexibility for firms to organise the use of factors of production efficiently, and the processes of liberalisation of markets for goods and services undertaken in recent years must continue. In my recent appearance before the Committee on Budgets of the Congress, I referred, within the chapter of the structural requirements arising from the situation of the Spanish economy, to the need to maintain the unity of the national market within the decentralization of competences that characterizes the autonomous structure of the State. I also expressed, in this area, a concern about the current wording of the proposal for the Statute of Autonomy of Catalonia. From the point of view of the functions attributed to the Banco de Espa96a, it is particularly important that the distribution of competences between the State and the Autonomous Communities and the latter's financing systems make it possible to manage economic policies effectively and are consistent with full economic integration and the proper functioning of market mechanisms. Therefore, special care must be taken that institutional design promotes an environment that favors private initiative and competition and avoids excessive interventionism and uncertainties and regulatory risks. As I said then, for the Bank of Spain, the integrity of the current system of regulation and supervision of credit institutions is of particular importance, particularly with regard to the stability and solvency of the financial system, in line with the copious jurisprudence of the Constitutional Court and with the demands for greater coordination and harmonization that are being raised by the European authorities and international financial stability forums. Ladies and gentlemen, the Spanish economy has made significant progress in recent years, achieving results that could hardly have been foreseen beforehand. Its high growth has allowed it to deepen the process of real convergence towards the countries with higher levels of income in our environment, leading to an unprecedented increase in employment. The great challenge for the coming years is to continue taking advantage of the circumstances, which at least in the short term, will continue to be propitious, to consolidate the foundations of this growth. This is the objective towards which economic policies must be oriented, and in particular fiscal policy, which has in the Budget one of its most important instruments.
text_original: Madrid, 24 de noviembre de 2005 Comparecencia ante la Comisin de Presupuestos del Senado Senado Jaime Caruana Lacorte Gobernador del Banco de Espaa Seoras: Acudo hoy ante esta Comisin de Presupuestos del Senado con el fin de informar acerca del anlisis que realiza el Banco de Espaa del Proyecto de Presupuestos Generales del Estado para el ejercicio 2006. En cualquier caso, aunque las perspectivas de evolucin de la economa mundial continan siendo relativamente satisfactorias, los riesgos se han ido acrecentando en el curso del ao. Esta aparente paradoja pone de manifiesto la existencia de rmoras estructurales que limitan el crecimiento potencial. Estas trabas no constituyen un obstculo insalvable. Por un lado, los Estados miembros retienen la responsabilidad sobre la mayor parte de las polticas necesarias para la consecucin de los objetivos finales, para lo que deben explicitar, a travs de los Programas Nacionales de Reforma, cmo traducirn en acciones concretas los compromisos genricos que han adquirido. Estos Programas estn siendo discutidos y consensuados con los agentes sociales nacionales, pues el xito en el logro de los objetivos es tanto ms probable cuanto mayor sea la implicacin de los distintos colectivos involucrados. Por otro lado, la contribucin a nivel comunitario al proceso de reformas es igualmente necesaria. En particular, los beneficios que se derivan de la culminacin del mercado nico en trminos de crecimiento econmico y de empleo distan an de ser explotados plenamente, lo cual es especialmente cierto en el caso de los mercados de servicios. En el mbito de las finanzas pblicas, en el presente ejercicio se vuelven a presentar elevados dficit estructurales en un nmero alto de pases. Adems, de acuerdo con los planes presupuestarios para el prximo ao, tampoco en 2006 tendr lugar una correccin significativa de los desequilibrios existentes. La insuficiencia de los esfuerzos de ajuste resulta, a mi juicio, insatisfactoria, puesto que, como he comentado, es necesario que los distintos pases afronten desde una posicin de partida lo ms saneada posible las consecuencias presupuestarias del envejecimiento de la poblacin. Adems, como se ha podido comprobar en los aos recientes de modesto crecimiento econmico en Europa, el mantenimiento de elevados dficit estructurales priva a la poltica fiscal del necesario margen de maniobra para que operen los estabilizadores automticos en la fase baja del ciclo. Por ltimo, la ausencia de estrategias ambiciosas de consolidacin presupuestaria, insertas en un marco ms amplio de reformas, contribuye a minar la confianza de los agentes econmicos, que adoptan una actitud ms cautelosa a la hora de emprender sus decisiones de gasto. La economa espaola sigue registrando un dinamismo elevado, ms prximo al de la economa de Estados Unidos que al tono de debilidad que caracteriza a la zona del euro. No obstante, la estrecha vinculacin de nuestra economa con la de los restantes pases de la UEM hace que nuestro entorno exterior sea algo menos expansivo que la economa mundial, aunque las condiciones monetarias y financieras, establecidas al nivel de la zona del euro, resultan muy holgadas para una situacin, como la espaola, de fuerte crecimiento del gasto interior. Estas circunstancias condicionan el diseo apropiado de las polticas econmicas internas y, en particular, el de la poltica fiscal, a la que me referir de forma detallada al comentar el Proyecto de Presupuestos Generales del Estado para 2006. Antes, permtanme que haga un breve repaso de la situacin coyuntural y de las perspectivas para el prximo ejercicio. Por tanto, el ritmo de avance de la productividad del trabajo sigue siendo reducido, lo que refleja, en parte, el tipo de actividades productivas que ms crecen, como son los servicios y, sobre todo, la construccin. Desde el punto de vista del gasto, el crecimiento del producto responde al extraordinario dinamismo que ha alcanzado la demanda interna, al avanzar a tasas en torno al 5% desde la segunda mitad de 2004. Parte de esta demanda se ha filtrado hacia el exterior contribuyendo a la detraccin del crecimiento que est ejerciendo la demanda exterior neta, prxima a los dos puntos porcentuales. An as, el consumo avanza a tasas superiores a las de la renta, como consecuencia, principalmente, de los efectos riqueza que siguen generando los elevados incrementos del precio de la vivienda y la revalorizacin de los activos financieros. Ya he sealado que la demanda exterior neta est ejerciendo una abultada detraccin sobre la tasa de crecimiento del producto, que ha venido acompaada de aumentos muy pronunciados del dficit comercial y de la necesidad de financiacin de la economa. La detraccin alcanz cotas muy negativas a finales de 2004 y a comienzos de 2005, al unirse un comportamiento muy dbil de las exportaciones con un notable repunte de la importacin, asociado a la recuperacin de la demanda interna. A partir del segundo trimestre, las exportaciones de bienes y los ingresos por turismo se han recuperado, mitigando algo el efecto contractivo de la aportacin exterior. Al drenaje de la demanda externa estn contribuyendo varios factores, entre ellos, el mayor ritmo de crecimiento que registra la economa espaola, en relacin con los pases de su entorno, al tener una posicin cclica ms avanzada y un potencial de crecimiento ms alto. La composicin de la demanda, en la que ha aumentado el peso de la inversin en equipo, ha contribuido, asimismo, a elevar la intensidad importadora. Sin embargo, estos elementos no son suficientes para explicar el fuerte deterioro del saldo exterior que se ha observado desde 2004. En l inciden tambin, las prdidas de competitividad acumuladas por la economa espaola en los aos ms recientes. La creciente penetracin de las importaciones en el mercado interior y la cada de la cuota de exportacin, que ya fue evidente en 2004, indican que las prdidas de competitividad se estn traduciendo ya en unos peores resultados comerciales. La evolucin de los precios y los costes indica la continuidad de las prdidas de competitividad. La tasa de inflacin medida por los precios de consumo se situ en octubre en el 3,5%, lo que representa una mejora en relacin con el 3,8% contabilizado el ndice armonizado el mes anterior. En cualquier caso, la inflacin espaola sigue siendo un punto porcentual ms elevada que la del conjunto de la UEM. Tambin los salarios mantienen ritmos de crecimiento sistemticamente mayores que los registrados en los pases con los que Espaa compite internacionalmente, lo que, unido al escaso avance de la productividad, da lugar a incrementos de los costes laborales unitarios comparativamente elevados. Estas diferencias tienden a agravarse en situaciones como la actual, de encarecimiento de la energa importada, debido a la existencia de clusulas de salvaguarda que facilitan la traslacin a los salarios de las subidas de los precios de consumo de la energa, lo que tiende a dificultar el ajuste de la economa ante las alzas del precio del petrleo. Estas suponen un drenaje de renta real disponible que los agentes han de asumir para hacer posible la continuidad de un crecimiento no inflacionista. Desde esta perspectiva, tambin pueden tener efectos contraproducentes las medidas orientadas a suavizar, directa o indirectamente, el impacto que el encarecimiento energtico tiene sobre los costes y los resultados de algunos sectores, como el de transporte o el pesquero, mediante reducciones efectivas de los impuestos que gravan las compras de hidrocarburos o aumentos de las subvenciones. Aunque este tipo de medidas puedan ayudar a enjugar las posibles prdidas que se generen a corto plazo, lo hacen a costa de retrasar y dificultar la introduccin de cambios en los procesos productivos que favorezcan una mayor eficiencia energtica o el uso de energas alternativas, que constituyen, a la postre, la respuesta adecuada a largo plazo. La subida del petrleo es una perturbacin externa a la que la economa espaola debe adaptarse aceptando la prdida de poder adquisitivo que supone para las rentas de los factores nacionales (ya sean salarios o beneficios empresariales) y permitiendo que el encarecimiento relativo de esta materia prima impulse los ajustes necesarios en trminos de un uso ms eficiente de la energa en la produccin y un menor consumo domstico. Como ya apunt en mi comparecencia ante la Comisin de Presupuestos del Congreso, las tendencias actuales de la economa espaola y su comportamiento en los tres primeros trimestres de 2005 indican que el crecimiento del PIB en este ao podra situarse alguna dcima por encima de la previsin incorporada en el escenario macroeconmico del Gobierno, que es del 3,3%. Lgicamente, el crecimiento previsto para el prximo ejercicio, que el cuadro macroeconmico que acompaa a los Presupuestos sita tambin en el 3,3%, est rodeado de mayores incertidumbres. Estas provienen tanto del entorno exterior en parte por la posibilidad de que aparezcan impactos desfasados de los aumentos del precio del petrleo como de los riesgos internos que se han ido generando en la actual etapa expansiva. La economa espaola sigue creciendo y creando empleo a ritmos elevados, pero el protagonismo del consumo privado y de la construccin residencial al crecimiento sigue siendo excesivo, sin que la reciente recuperacin de la inversin productiva haya inducido todava un reequilibrio suficiente, y la productividad del trabajo contina avanzando a tasas muy bajas. La prolongacin de una etapa de crecimiento con estas caractersticas ha favorecido la generacin de prdidas de competitividad y el rpido endeudamiento de los hogares, factores que suponen riesgos para la propia sostenibilidad de la expansin. En el corto plazo, es previsible que la economa espaola mantenga su dinamismo actual, apoyada en la influencia expansiva de los niveles extraordinariamente bajos de los tipos de inters y en el aumento de la poblacin activa. Sin embargo, para consolidar ese escenario de crecimiento en un horizonte ms dilatado es preciso atajar los elementos de riesgo que acabo de sealar. Este es el mayor reto al que se enfrenta las polticas econmicas internas en este momento. Las polticas de demanda y, en particular, la poltica fiscal, deben orientarse a reconducir el crecimiento de la demanda interna hacia ritmos ms acordes con el potencial de la economa, favoreciendo un cambio en su composicin hacia un avance ms moderado del gasto de las familias y un fortalecimiento de la inversin productiva. Debe tenerse en cuenta que la poltica presupuestaria es el instrumento ms eficaz del que disponen las autoridades econmicas para este cometido. Por otro lado, la accin de las polticas de demanda debe venir apoyada por polticas de reforma estructural, que mejoren el funcionamiento de los mercados de bienes y factores, y permitan compatibilizar la generacin de empleo con la obtencin de mayores ganancias de productividad. Como acabo de sealar, en la fase que atraviesa actualmente la economa espaola es importante que la poltica presupuestaria adopte un tono relativamente estabilizador, que favorezca la contencin de las presiones de demanda. En principio, las previsiones fiscales para 2005 suponen que las cuentas de las AAPP se cerrarn, de acuerdo con lo previsto al inicio del ejercicio, con un supervit del 0,1% del PIB y que la ratio de deuda pblica sobre el PIB podra situarse por debajo del 45%. Estos resultados, que permitiran cumplir con holgura los compromisos europeos, adquiridos en el mbito del Pacto de Estabilidad y de Crecimiento, supondran, sin embargo, una cierta ralentizacin del esfuerzo fiscal realizado. De hecho, las medidas habituales de impulso fiscal indican que si las cuentas pblicas se cerrasen como se prev en el avance de liquidacin, la poltica presupuestaria habra adquirido un tono ligeradamente expansivo en 2005. No obstante, el fuerte dinamismo que ha mostrado la recaudacin tributaria a lo largo del presente ejercicio, muy por encima de las estimaciones incorporadas en las previsiones de cierre ahora disponibles, permitira alcanzar un supervit superior al presupuestado y ms acorde con los requerimientos de la economa. Las cifras de ejecucin presupuestaria del Estado de los ltimos meses avalan la fortaleza de los ingresos, aunque recientemente se han asumido tambin algunos compromisos adicionales de gasto -como los derivados de los acuerdos con los sectores del transporte, la pesca y la minera- hacia los que podra derivarse una parte de este excedente de recaudacin. En todo caso, recientemente se ha anunciado que el Estado podra terminar el ejercicio con un saldo positivo, en vez de con el dficit previsto del 0,4 del PIB. En tal caso, el excedente del conjunto de las Administraciones Pblicas sera superior al medio punto del PIB y el tono fiscal se habra acercado ms a lo que requiere la economa espaola en estos momentos. Los Presupuestos para el ao 2006, que son ahora objeto de discusin parlamentaria, fijan como objetivo para el saldo conjunto de las AAPP la obtencin de un supervit del 0,2% del PIB, que no supondra un cambio significativo en el tono de la poltica fiscal. Por ello, es muy importante que si el dinamismo de los ingresos vuelve a superar las cifras presupuestadas, como previsiblemente suceder en 2005, el exceso de recaudacin se traduzca en un supervit ms elevado, en lnea con los resultados que se esperan para este ejercicio. En mi intervencin ante la Comisin de Presupuestos del Congreso, ya seal que la orientacin prioritaria de las polticas de gasto hacia aquellas reas que ms pueden favorecer el avance de la productividad -como la educacin- es adecuada y coherente con el marco general establecido por el Gobierno para su poltica econmica. Sin embargo, al significativo aumento en las correspondientes dotaciones presupuestarias que ello supone, hay que aadir otros compromisos de gasto adquiridos en el mbito de la vivienda, las pensiones mnimas, la financiacin sanitaria y, ms recientemente, los vinculados a los acuerdos alcanzados con sectores particularmente afectados por las subidas en los precios de la energa o en proceso de reconversin. Todo ello se traduce en un crecimiento del gasto pblico del Estado superior al del PIB nominal y comporta el riesgo de que se produzcan desbordamientos en la ejecucin presupuestaria, dado que no se prev acometer recortes compensatorios en otras partidas o poner en prctica polticas de mayor eficiencia del gasto pblico en el horizonte de los presupuestos del 2006. El aumento de la eficiencia en la actuacin del sector pblico es por otra parte imprescindible para generar un entorno ms proclive a los incrementos de la productividad y del crecimiento a largo plazo, y a ello deben contribuir no solo la reorientacin de las polticas de gasto sino tambin una estructura tributaria que genere los incentivos adecuados. Las reformas impositivas anunciadas han de tener en cuenta este objetivo, al tiempo que deben estar bien calibradas para que no supongan un coste recaudatorio que pueda resultar excesivo en coyunturas de menor dinamismo de los ingresos pblicos. La necesidad de disear polticas fiscales ms rigurosas que permitan alcanzar ms rpidamente posiciones de supervit, se refuerza cuando se introducen consideraciones de medio plazo y se tienen en cuenta las perspectivas demogrficas espaolas. Estas apuntan a un intenso proceso de envejecimiento de la poblacin, que comportar importantes presiones al alza sobre el gasto pblico, tanto en su componente de pensiones como en el de cobertura de las situaciones de dependencia. Ante esta perspectiva, que difcilmente se va a quebrar como consecuencia de los intensos flujos de emigracin, se han de adoptar objetivos fiscales ms ambiciosos y abordar las reformas necesarias en los sistemas de proteccin social. El Programa Nacional de Reformas de Espaa, que present el Gobierno a mediados del pasado mes de octubre se compromete a impulsar la adopcin de algunas de las recomendaciones que surgieron de la revisin del Pacto de Toledo hace dos aos, como son la de establecer una mayor correspondencia entre aportaciones y pensiones o la de introducir elementos de racionalidad en los procesos de jubilacin anticipada. Tras la prdida de impulso en la adopcin de medidas de esta naturaleza en los ltimos aos, con la excepcin de las importantes aportaciones al Fondo de Reserva de la Seguridad Social, esta iniciativa constituye un buen punto de partida, aunque deberan empezar a discutirse medidas complementarias, en lnea con las que comienzan a aplicar otros pases europeos. El marco institucional en el que se desenvuelve la poltica fiscal tiene gran importancia para asegurar una evolucin disciplinada de las finanzas pblicas. En la actualidad se est discutiendo la reforma de las Leyes de Estabilidad Presupuestaria y se ha planteado una nueva revisin del sistema de financiacin autonmica. Entre los aspectos ms novedosos en el proyecto de reforma de las Leyes de Estabilidad Presupuestaria est la introduccin de una mayor flexibilidad en la definicin de las reglas de estabilidad presupuestaria, permitiendo que el Estado, las Comunidades Autnomas y los grandes Ayuntamientos adapten su objetivo de dficit o supervit a la situacin cclica de la economa y la obligacin de obtener supervit cuando el crecimiento econmico supere un determinado umbral, si bien no se establece que este sea mayor cuanto mayor sea el crecimiento. Por otra parte, el Proyecto de reforma refuerza la disciplina fiscal, al establecer que el saldo de la Administracin Central pase a computarse, a efectos del cumplimiento de los objetivos de estabilidad presupuestaria, de forma independiente al de la Seguridad Social. No obstante, en el caso de las CCAA no se define una distribucin transparente del esfuerzo fiscal que corresponde a cada una de ellas, lo que puede comportar el riesgo de que se produzcan desviaciones. Por ltimo, como mencion en mi comparecencia del mes de octubre quiero resaltar la importancia de aplicar en toda su extensin las provisiones que incorpora la norma para mejorar la transparencia y la disponibilidad de informacin sobre las cuentas pblicas, pues considero que es un elemento fundamental para asegurar la disciplina en estructuras fiscales en las que el gasto est fuertemente descentralizado, como ocurre en Espaa. El inicio de un proceso de revisin del sistema de financiacin autonmica hace ms necesario este esfuerzo de transparencia y de disciplina fiscal. En el plano de las reformas estructurales, el Gobierno ha tomado a lo largo de este ltimo ao una serie de iniciativas, que han quedado subsumidas en el Programa Nacional de Reformas de Espaa, recientemente aprobado, y que se dirigen a impulsar la productividad, la innovacin y, en ltimo trmino, la convergencia real. Estas iniciativas establecen una orientacin adecuada para que la poltica econmica aborde los retos que tiene planteados la economa espaola, en concreto la necesidad de impulsar la productividad y de establecer las bases para un crecimiento slido en el largo plazo. Es necesario, sin embargo, complementar este conjunto de medidas con la aplicacin de otras reformas que conllevan calendarios ms dilatados de negociacin, pero que resultan de vital importancia para mantener el dinamismo en el empleo y promover la competitividad del tejido empresarial espaol. En este sentido, el mercado de trabajo debe proporcionar la flexibilidad suficiente para que las empresas puedan organizar el uso de los factores de produccin de forma eficiente, y han de continuar los procesos de liberalizacin de los mercados de bienes y servicios emprendidos en los ltimos aos. En mi reciente comparecencia en la Comisin de Presupuestos del Congreso me refer, dentro del captulo de las exigencias de carcter estructural que se derivan de la situacin de la economa espaola, a la necesidad de mantener la unidad del mercado nacional dentro de la descentralizacin de competencias que caracteriza a la estructura autonmica del Estado. Tambin expres, en este mbito, una inquietud sobre la redaccin actual de la propuesta del Estatuto de Autonoma de Catalua. Desde el punto de vista de las funciones que tiene atribuidas el Banco de Espaa tiene especial importancia que la distribucin de competencias entre el Estado y las Comunidades Autnomas y los sistemas de financiacin de estas ltimas permitan gestionar de manera eficaz las polticas econmicas y sean coherentes con la plena integracin econmica y un buen funcionamiento de los mecanismos de mercado. Por ello, debe cuidarse con especial atencin que el diseo institucional promueva un entorno que favorezca la iniciativa privada y la competencia y evite intervencionismos excesivos e incertidumbres y riesgos regulatorios. Como dije entonces, para el Banco de Espaa tiene especial importancia la integridad del sistema actual de regulacin y supervisin de las entidades de crdito, particularmente en lo que se refiere a la estabilidad y solvencia del sistema financiero, en lnea con la copiosa jurisprudencia del Tribunal Constitucional y con las demandas de mayor coordinacin y armonizacin que estn planteando las autoridades europeas y los foros internacionales de estabilidad financiera. Seoras, la economa espaola ha realizado importantes avances en los ltimos aos, alcanzando resultados que difcilmente podan haberse previsto con anterioridad. Su elevado crecimiento le ha permitido profundizar en el proceso de convergencia real hacia los pases con mayores niveles de renta de nuestro entorno, propiciando un aumento sin precedentes del empleo. El gran reto para los prximos aos es seguir aprovechando las circunstancias, que al menos a corto plazo, seguirn siendo propicias, para consolidar las bases de este crecimiento. Es este el objetivo al que deben orientarse las polticas econmicas y, en particular, la poltica fiscal, que tiene en los Presupuestos uno de sus instrumentos ms importantes.

Title: Credit Unions: Current Situation and Future Prospects
text: Valencia, 16 February 2006 Credit unions: current situation and future prospects XV Conference of the Rural Savings Banks of the Valencian Community Gonzalo Gil Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain Introduction It is a pleasure for me to be here with all of you today, and I would like my first words to be of thanks for the kind invitation I have received to participate in this forum. Cooperative banking has been characterized by its proximity to its customers, to whom it has traditionally offered a close and quality service. These are also entities that have provided financial services to a range of economic operators, SMEs and rural dwellers, for example, who may have greater difficulties in accessing these services through other channels. In fact, historically cooperative banking arises, among other reasons, to try to alleviate the absence of adequate banking services in certain areas, and that is why they have been contributing to favor the economic development of their operational scope. These defining characteristics of credit unions must be compatible, however, with their operation under market rules, which, in turn, is characterized by a high degree of competition. Cooperatives must focus their management on achieving a solid financial structure capable of ensuring their business model over time. Throughout my speech I will try to highlight some circumstances that credit unions have to face in order to achieve the above objective. To a large extent, they are similar to those faced by all Spanish depository institutions and are located in the areas of generating recurring resources, risk management, transparency and solvency with which the entities must operate. On the other hand, together with the previous areas that, we could say, are the traditional ones, regulatory changes have appeared in recent years that will require, are in fact, demanding important efforts so that the adaptation to them is fruitful. Before addressing the above issues, however, let me take a few minutes to put the credit union sector within the Spanish banking system into context. Current situation of credit unions The Spanish banking system registers high levels of profitability d0 the ROE has been 10% higher than the yield on long-term Spanish public debt d0 and also solvency levels that are clearly above the minimum levels required by regulation. This solid situation of Spanish banks is reinforced by the important prudential role played by provisions in our accounting framework, as well as by the low NPL ratio that has been observed in recent years. The comparison with the financial institutions of the European Union reinforces the above, since the levels of profitability and efficiency of the Spanish ones are clearly above the average, while those of solvency are in line with it. This favourable framework has not only been boosted by short-term issues related to the good moment of the Spanish economy, which allows a strong pace of activity and a low level of non-performing loans, but also that banks have been making significant efforts in areas such as cost containment, the search for recurring income or the improvement of risk management and measurement systems. In this context, the credit union business has grown significantly in recent years, with an average annual growth of its balance sheet from 1995 to September 2005 of 13%, compared to 10% observed for deposit institutions. This has allowed the sector to gain market share in terms of its total assets, rising from 3.1% in 1995 to 3.8% in September 2005. The gain in market share is more significant in terms of credit to the resident private sector, rising from 4% in 1995 to 5.6% in September 2005. This data shows that cooperatives continue to show an activity closely linked to their more traditional business. In fact, the relative weight of credit to the resident private sector on its total balance sheet stood at 81% in September 2005, compared with 67% in savings banks and 44% in banks. Cooperatives have historically been small entities linked to a local operational scope, that is, with little presence outside their province. While this is still true for the vast majority of them, in recent years there has been some expansion that has contributed to progressively reducing the degree of atomization of the sector. Thus, total assets held by the 10 largest cooperatives have risen from 56% in 1995 to 68% in September 2005. This process of growth in the activity of cooperatives, common to that observed for the aggregate of Spanish deposit institutions, although somewhat more accentuated in terms of credit to the private sector, occurs in a context of reduction in the financial margins with which all entities have been operating, although the intermediation margin was traditionally higher in cooperatives. In the context of recent times of low interest rates and strong competitive pressure on the financial markets, margins have been shrinking, converging to the levels of other deposit institutions. For example, the intermediation margin on average total assets has risen from 4.5% in 1995, almost two percentage points higher than for depository institutions, to 2.3% in September 2005, only 0.7 percentage points higher than for all depository institutions. As I have already pointed out, the efficiency ratio of all Spanish depository institutions is favourable compared to the European Union average. Somewhat lower is the level of efficiency of cooperatives within Spanish deposit institutions. Moreover, and contrary to what happened in other groups of entities, there is no clear trend that points in the direction of a gradual improvement in this variable. Part of the explanation could lie in the typical activity of cooperatives that, based on proximity to the customer, requires them to have, in relative terms, an extensive network of offices and a large staff, which hinders the processes of cost reduction. Despite the above-mentioned increase in activity, the narrowing of margins and the evolution of operational efficiency help to explain why the ROE of this group of institutions, traditionally above that observed for all depository institutions (4 percentage points in 1995), has maintained a downward trend to be below that recorded by all depository institutions since 1999. Thus, in September 2005 there was an ROE of 10%, almost 2 percentage points lower. In terms of their solvency, cooperatives also show a downward trend, although always remaining above the regulatory minimum .4 percentage points in June 2005., and of all deposit institutions .almost 2 percentage points on the same date.. The strength of the sector is reinforced by the trend in the NPL ratio which, although slightly higher than that of all depository institutions in September 2005, stood at 1%, four percentage points less than 10 years ago. However, the greater delinquency of cooperatives, probably boosted by the development of a large part of their activity with small companies, justifies their need for greater provisions, which further pressures the ROE downwards. In any case, the financial situation of cooperatives is, in line with that of all Spanish depository institutions, solid. However, and also in line with what has been observed for all Spanish deposit institutions, their favourable situation does not imply the absence of future risks that the managers of the entities must adequately consider in the design of their business strategies. In the particular case of cooperatives, the above data also reflect that in a market characterized by strong competition and low levels of interest rates, both financial margins, profitability and solvency, have tended to converge with the levels recorded by banks and savings banks, traditionally lower.
