Allow me to devote the remainder of my speech to setting out a set of reflections on some of the circumstances that, in my view, the credit union sector is facing and which, as you will see, do not affect them exclusively, but could, to a large extent, be extended to all depository institutions. Future needs Ability to generate resources on a recurring basis As I have already shown, in the last 10 years there has been a process of narrowing of financial margins in business in Spain for all deposit institutions and, in particular, for cooperatives. This is part of a process of convergence of our economy with that of the euro area, as well as in a context of strong competition in the financial markets. In fact, it is not foreseeable that these competitive pressures will be reduced in the future. In general, Spanish banks have responded adequately to this important management problem. Among other issues, they have made a notable effort to offer their customers products with greater added value, while increasing the volume of activity and assuming cost containment processes that have translated, in many cases, into improvements in efficiency ratios. In the case of cooperatives, however, and despite a certain trend towards cost reductions in recent years, no significant reductions have been observed in the efficiency ratio, which continues to show a higher level in this group of institutions than that corresponding to other depository institutions. Improving in this area, probably from the reduction of operating costs, is a future purpose to be taken into consideration. However, to achieve greater efficiency there is no single answer, but each entity must look for the best strategy that allows it to achieve this objective. In this sense, the evidence does not show a clear relationship between size and profitability. Therefore, territorial expansion strategies must properly assess the additional costs involved and that could, apart from other considerations, negatively affect operational efficiency. From the point of view of the generation of recurring resources, the greater proximity to the client characteristic of cooperative banks can mean advantages for these entities in terms of favoring the better knowledge of customers, and therefore, increasing the possibilities of offering value-added services appropriate to their particular characteristics. Risk management In the banking sector, trust is a crucial element. Maintaining it undoubtedly involves developing appropriate risk measurement and management systems. This need to measure and manage risks correctly becomes, if possible, more necessary at a time of strong credit expansion such as, as I have already mentioned, is being experienced in Spain. During expansionary phases, in which banks' loan portfolios increase, risks tend to accumulate and subsequently become apparent when the cycle changes. In other words, in good times, bank managers sometimes make credit policy mistakes. Excessive optimism, lack of foresight or imitation behaviors are just some of the factors that help explain these errors, whose probability of occurrence is also increased in situations of strong competitive pressure. Historical experience confirms this and, in fact, in Spain, during the last recessionary phase of our economy, which occurred in 1993, bank delinquencies increased substantially as a reflection of the errors made in the previous expansionary moment. Managers of institutions must therefore act by maintaining adequate time horizons, i.e. avoiding giving excessive importance to the short term. Likewise, and this is something in which progress has been made in recent years, we must persevere in the development and improvement of the mechanisms for admission, concession, monitoring and coverage of credit risk. In this sense, cooperatives could continue to exploit the advantages offered by proximity to their customers and their operations at the local level, which allows them to obtain more information to evaluate the credit quality of their customers. An important part of the credit granting process has to do with risk quantification mechanisms. In fact, more formal risk assessment processes based on rigorous quantitative techniques are essential complements to the necessary expert judgment of risk managers, and help to detect problems early. In recent years, many banks have improved their risk measurement and management systems, especially credit. Moving in this direction, according to the complexity of the operations developed, is an open challenge for all entities, including cooperatives. Basel II, the New Capital Arrangement well known to most of you, introduces the necessary incentives to favour and enhance this sound risk management. The joint application of its three pillars allows, through the first, a greater sensitivity to risk in the calculation of minimum capital requirements; through the second, a better consideration of the global capital strategy and through the third, greater information to the market. Greater information to the market, and in general greater transparency in management, in combination with good corporate governance, are today essential tools to deepen a relationship of trust with banking customers. Moving in this direction seems a challenge for the future that is difficult to renounce. I have mentioned that the application of one or another risk measurement and management system depends on the complexity of the operations carried out by the entities. This principle applies, in fact, to Basel II. The Bank of Spain expects, therefore, that the number of entities that access the most advanced methods will be small, and in any case, the result of a gradual process over time. What is certain is that Basel II introduces the necessary incentives to make progress in improving risk management. Solvency Depository institutions must have a sufficient level of own resources in relation to the risks assumed, since these become a fundamental line of defense against the event of difficulties. In fact, in recent years it has been observed how maintaining adequate solvency levels has been an explanatory factor that has contributed to strengthening the resilience of institutions. These own resources must not only be sufficient, but also complete and of sufficient quality. For this to be the case, own resources must be characterised by a sufficient degree of permanence so that they are stable, while at the same time having sufficient loss-absorbing capacity. In a context of strong credit growth, in which, therefore, capital requirements are increasing, institutions must make efforts not only to increase their own resources adequately, but to do so through those that are of sufficient quality to act as a line of defense against the possible occurrence of difficulties. Likewise, it is no less true that in times of financial difficulties, even the most solid levels of capital have proved insufficient in those entities that did not have their loan portfolio correctly valued. Therefore, the capital policy of institutions must be complemented by appropriate provisioning policies. The provisions incorporated in the Spanish accounting framework have traditionally been part of our prudential regulatory framework. This was reinforced by the introduction of statistical provision in mid-2000, which undoubtedly contributes to the stability of our financial system. Since January 1 of last year, the New Accounting Circular of the Bank of Spain has been in force, which, as you know, adapts the International Accounting Standards approved and adopted by the European Union since that same date. In terms of provisions, the new Accounting Circular, respecting international standards, incorporates a macro-prudential component through the generic envelope. This new provision covers losses incurred, but does not apply to those already identified in specific transactions, but also to losses incurred but not identified in particular transactions. In any case, the new Accounting Circular has come to recognize the important role that the Spanish accounting model, and in particular the provisions, play within our prudential policy. Regulatory changes I have just referred to the new Accounting Circular introduced by the Bank of Spain, which has led to profound changes in the Spanish accounting framework as a result of the adoption, by the European Union, of the International Accounting Standards. I have also referred to Basel II, which will be a real step forward in the culture of risk measurement and management, in order to enhance financial stability. The new Accounting Circular, as you know, has involved significant learning and adaptation efforts over the past year, not only for the entities, but also for the Bank of Spain itself. Basel II, although it has not yet entered into force, has already been demanding adaptation efforts on the part of entities, which require investments in technical and human capital to adapt successfully to changes. These changes in the regulatory framework, due to their size, but also because of their development in a relatively short space of time, require an important adaptation process for institutions, which must allocate sufficient resources and assume an adequate level of commitment. As has already been stated on occasion from the Bank of Spain, I believe that now opens a period that makes it possible to adequately assume the changes and, therefore, of relaxation with respect to new proposals. Conclusions Allow me to conclude my speech simply by emphasizing the main message that I have tried to convey to you today: the greatest guarantee of success for the cooperative banking model to last over time while maintaining its main defining features is to continue in the line of achieving solid, solvent and, ultimately, well-managed entities. In a market as demanding and competitive as the Spanish one, this path is not without risks, but also full of possibilities. However, my personal conviction is that, as in the vast majority of cases so far, credit union managers will continue to show a high degree of professionalism to successfully address the changing circumstances to come. Thank you very much for your attention.
text_original: Valencia, 16 de febrero de 2006 Cooperativas de crdito: situacin actual y perspectivas de futuro XV Jornadas de las Cajas Rurales de la Comunidad Valenciana Gonzalo Gil Subgobernador del Banco de Espaa Introduccin Es para m un placer estar hoy aqu con todos ustedes, y querra que mis primeras palabras fueran de agradecimiento por la amable invitacin que he recibido para participar en este foro. La banca cooperativa se ha venido caracterizando por la cercana a sus clientes, a los que tradicionalmente ha ofrecido un servicio prximo y de calidad. Asimismo, se trata de entidades que han prestado servicios financieros a un conjunto de agentes econmicos, PYMES y habitantes de zonas rurales, por ejemplo, que podran tener mayores dificultades para acceder a dichos servicios a travs de otros canales. De hecho, histricamente la banca cooperativa surge, entre otras razones, para tratar de paliar la ausencia de adecuados servicios bancarios en determinadas reas, y es por ello que han venido contribuyendo a favorecer el desarrollo econmico de su mbito operativo. Estas caractersticas definitorias de las cooperativas de crdito han de ser compatibles, no obstante, con su operativa bajo las reglas de mercado que, a su vez, se caracteriza por su elevado grado de competencia. Las cooperativas han de enfocar su gestin al logro de una estructura financiera slida capaz de asegurar su modelo de negocio en el tiempo. A lo largo de mi intervencin tratar de poner de manifiesto algunas circunstancias que han de afrontar las cooperativas de crdito para lograr el objetivo anterior. Las mismas, en buena medida, son similares a las que afrontan el conjunto de entidades de depsito espaolas y se sitan en los mbitos de la generacin de recursos recurrentes, en la gestin de los riesgos, en la transparencia y en la solvencia con la que han de operar las entidades. Por otro lado, junto a los mbitos anteriores que, podramos decir, son los tradicionales, han aparecido en los ltimos aos cambios regulatorios que van a exigir, estn exigiendo de hecho, importantes esfuerzos para que la adaptacin a los mismos sea fructfera. No obstante, antes de abordar los temas anteriores, permtanme que dedique unos minutos a poner en contexto el sector de las cooperativas de crdito dentro del sistema bancario espaol. Situacin actual de las cooperativas de crdito El sistema bancario espaol registra elevados niveles de rentabilidad el ROE viene superando en un 10% a la rentabilidad de la deuda pblica espaola a largo plazo y tambin de solvencia que se sitan claramente por encima de los niveles mnimos exigidos por la regulacin. Esta slida situacin de las entidades espaolas queda reforzada por el importante papel prudencial que juegan las provisiones en nuestro marco contable, as como por la reducida ratio de morosidad que se viene observando en los ltimos aos. La comparacin con las entidades financieras de la Unin Europea refuerza lo anterior, ya que los niveles de rentabilidad y eficiencia de las espaolas se sitan claramente por encima de la media, mientras que los de solvencia estn en lnea con ella. Este favorable marco no solo se ha visto potenciado por cuestiones coyunturales relacionadas con el buen momento de la economa espaola, que posibilita un fuerte ritmo de actividad y un reducido nivel de morosidad, sino que, adems, las entidades han venido realizando importantes esfuerzos en reas como la contencin de costes, la bsqueda de ingresos recurrentes o la mejora de los sistemas de gestin y medicin de riesgos. En este contexto, el negocio de las cooperativas de crdito ha crecido de forma muy notable en los ltimos aos, registrndose un crecimiento medio anual de su balance desde 1995 hasta septiembre de 2005 del 13%, frente al 10% observado para las entidades de depsito. Esto ha permitido que el sector ganara cuota de mercado en trminos de su activo total, pasando del 3,1% en 1995 al 3,8% en septiembre de 2005. La ganancia de cuota de mercado es ms significativa en trminos del crdito al sector privado residente, que pasa del 4% en 1995 al 5,6% en septiembre de 2005. Este dato pone de manifiesto que las cooperativas continan mostrando una actividad muy vinculada a su negocio ms tradicional. De hecho, el peso relativo sobre su balance total del crdito al sector privado residente se situaba en septiembre de 2005 en el 81%, frente al 67% en las cajas y al 44% en los bancos. Las cooperativas han sido, histricamente, entidades de reducido tamao vinculadas a un mbito operativo local, es decir, con escasa presencia fuera de su provincia. Si bien esto sigue siendo cierto para la gran mayora de ellas, en los ltimos aos se ha observado una cierta expansin que ha contribuido a reducir progresivamente el grado de atomizacin del sector. As, los activos totales en manos de las 10 mayores cooperativas han pasado del 56% en 1995 al 68% en septiembre de 2005. Este proceso de crecimiento de la actividad de las cooperativas, comn al observado para el agregado de entidades de depsito espaolas, aunque algo ms acentuado en trminos del crdito al sector privado, se produce en un contexto de reduccin de los mrgenes financieros con los que vienen operando todas las entidades, si bien el margen de intermediacin era tradicionalmente ms alto en las cooperativas. En el contexto de los ltimos tiempos de reducidos tipos de inters y de fuerte presin competitiva en los mercados financieros, los mrgenes se han ido reduciendo, convergiendo a los niveles del resto de entidades de depsito. As, por ejemplo, el margen de intermediacin sobre los activos totales medios ha pasado del 4,5% en 1995, casi dos puntos porcentuales ms que para las entidades de depsito, al 2,3% en septiembre de 2005, slo 0,7 puntos porcentuales ms que para el total de entidades de depsito. Como ya he sealado anteriormente, la ratio de eficiencia del conjunto de entidades de depsito espaolas resulta favorable en comparacin con las de la media de la Unin Europea. Algo menor es el nivel de eficiencia de las cooperativas dentro de las entidades de depsito espaolas. Ms an, y en contra de lo ocurrido en otros grupos de entidades, no se observa una tendencia clara que apunte en la direccin de una paulatina mejora de esta variable. Parte de la explicacin podra residir en la actividad tpica de las cooperativas que, basada en la cercana al cliente, les exige disponer, en trminos relativos, de una extensa red de oficinas y de una amplia plantilla, lo que dificulta los procesos de reduccin de costes. A pesar del mencionado incremento de la actividad, el estrechamiento de los mrgenes y la evolucin de la eficiencia operativa contribuyen a explicar que el ROE de este conjunto de entidades, tradicionalmente por encima del observado para el conjunto de entidades de depsito (4 puntos porcentuales en 1995), haya mantenido una tendencia decreciente hasta situarse por debajo del registrado por el total de entidades de depsito desde 1999. As, en septiembre de 2005 se registr un ROE del 10%, casi 2 puntos porcentuales inferior. En trminos de su solvencia, las cooperativas tambin presentan una tendencia decreciente, si bien mantenindose siempre por encima del mnimo regulatorio 4 puntos porcentuales en junio de 2005, y del conjunto de entidades de depsito casi 2 puntos porcentuales en esa misma fecha. La fortaleza del sector queda reforzada por la evolucin de la ratio de morosidad que, si bien ligeramente superior a la del conjunto de entidades de depsito, se situaba en septiembre de 2005 en el 1%, cuatro puntos porcentuales menos que hace 10 aos. No obstante, la mayor morosidad de las cooperativas, probablemente potenciada por el desarrollo de gran parte de su actividad con empresas de reducido tamao, justifica su necesidad de mayores provisiones, lo que presiona adicionalmente el ROE a la baja. En cualquier caso, la situacin financiera de las cooperativas es, en lnea con la del conjunto de entidades de depsito espaolas, slida. No obstante, y tambin en lnea con lo observado para el conjunto de entidades de depsito espaolas, su favorable situacin no implica la ausencia de riesgos de futuro que los gestores de las entidades han de considerar adecuadamente en el diseo de sus estrategias de negocio. En el caso particular de las cooperativas, los datos anteriores reflejan, adems, que en un mercado caracterizado por la fuerte competencia y los reducidos niveles de tipos de inters, tanto los mrgenes financieros, como la rentabilidad y la solvencia, han tendido a converger con los niveles registrados por bancos y cajas, tradicionalmente inferiores. Permtanme que dedique lo que resta de mi intervencin a plantear un conjunto de reflexiones sobre algunas de las circunstancias a las que, desde mi punto de vista, se enfrenta el sector de las cooperativas de crdito y que, como vern, no les afectan a ellas de forma exclusiva, sino que, en buena medida, podran ser extensibles al conjunto de entidades de depsito. Necesidades de futuro Capacidad de generacin de recursos de forma recurrente Como ya he puesto de manifiesto, en los ltimos 10 aos se ha venido produciendo un proceso de estrechamiento de los mrgenes financieros en los negocios en Espaa para el conjunto de entidades de depsito y, en especial, para las cooperativas. Esto se enmarca en un proceso de convergencia de nuestra economa con la de la zona euro, as como en un contexto de fuerte competencia en los mercados financieros. De hecho, no es previsible que en el futuro estas presiones competitivas se reduzcan. En general, las entidades espaolas han respondido adecuadamente a este importante problema de gestin. Entre otras cuestiones, han realizado un notable esfuerzo por ofrecer a sus clientes productos con un mayor valor aadido, al tiempo que han incrementado el volumen de actividad y han asumido procesos de contencin de costes que se han traducido, en muchos casos, en mejoras de las ratios de eficiencia. En el caso de las cooperativas, sin embargo, y a pesar de una cierta tendencia a la reduccin de costes en los ltimos aos, no se han observado reducciones significativas de la ratio de eficiencia, que contina mostrando en este grupo de entidades un nivel ms elevado que el correspondiente a las otras entidades de depsito. Mejorar en este mbito, probablemente desde la reduccin de los costes operativos, es un propsito de futuro a tener en consideracin. Ahora bien, para lograr una mayor eficiencia no existe una respuesta nica, sino que cada entidad ha de buscar la mejor estrategia que le permita conseguir dicho objetivo. En este sentido, la evidencia no muestra una relacin clara entre tamao y rentabilidad. Por ello, las estrategias de expansin territorial han de valorar adecuadamente los costes adicionales que implican y que podran, al margen de otras consideraciones, afectar negativamente a la eficiencia operativa. Desde el punto de vista de la generacin de recursos recurrentes, la mayor proximidad al cliente caracterstica de los bancos cooperativos, puede suponer ventajas para estas entidades en trminos de favorecer el mejor conocimiento de los clientes, y por tanto, de incrementar las posibilidades de ofrecer servicios de valor aadido adecuados a sus caractersticas particulares. Gestin de los riesgos En el sector bancario la confianza es un elemento crucial. Mantenerla pasa, sin duda, por desarrollar sistemas de medicin y gestin de los riesgos adecuados. Esta necesidad de medir y gestionar correctamente los riesgos se hace, si cabe, ms necesaria en un momento coyuntural de fuerte expansin crediticia como el que, como ya he mencionado, se est viviendo en Espaa. Durante las fases expansivas, en las que las carteras crediticias de las entidades se incrementan, los riesgos tienden a acumularse para, con posterioridad, ponerse de manifiesto cuando se produce el cambio de ciclo. En otras palabras, en los momentos buenos los gestores bancarios, en ocasiones, cometen errores de poltica crediticia. El exceso de optimismo, la falta de previsin o los comportamientos de imitacin son solo algunos de los factores que ayudan a explicar estos errores, cuya probabilidad de ocurrencia se incrementa, adems, en situaciones de fuerte presin competitiva. La experiencia histrica confirma lo anterior y, de hecho, en Espaa, durante la ltima fase recesiva de nuestra economa, ocurrida en 1993, la morosidad bancaria se increment de forma sustancial como reflejo de los errores cometidos en el momento expansivo precedente. Los gestores de las entidades han de actuar, por lo tanto, manteniendo adecuados horizontes temporales, es decir, evitando conceder una importancia excesiva al corto plazo. Asimismo, y esto es algo en lo que se ha avanzado en los ltimos aos, se ha de perseverar en el desarrollo y mejora de los mecanismos de admisin, concesin, seguimiento y cobertura del riesgo de crdito. En este sentido, las cooperativas podran continuar explotando las ventajas que les ofrece la cercana a sus clientes y su operativa a nivel local, que permite obtener ms informacin para evaluar la calidad crediticia de sus clientes. Una parte importante del proceso de concesin del crdito tiene que ver con los mecanismos de cuantificacin de los riesgos. De hecho, procesos de valoracin de los riesgos ms formales y basados en tcnicas cuantitativas rigurosas son complementos esenciales del necesario juicio experto de los gestores de riesgos, y contribuyen a detectar anticipadamente los problemas. En los ltimos aos muchas entidades han mejorado sus sistemas de medicin y gestin de los riesgos, especialmente del de crdito. Avanzar en esta direccin, de acuerdo con la complejidad de la operativa desarrollada, es un reto abierto para el conjunto de entidades, incluidas las cooperativas. Basilea II, el Nuevo Acuerdo de Capitales bien conocido por la mayora de ustedes, introduce los incentivos necesarios para favorecer y potenciar esta correcta gestin de los riesgos. La aplicacin conjunta de sus tres pilares permite, a travs del primero, una mayor sensibilidad al riesgo en el clculo de los requerimientos mnimos de capital; a travs del segundo, una mejor consideracin de la estrategia de capital global y a travs del tercero, una mayor informacin al mercado. La mayor informacin al mercado, y en general la mayor transparencia en la gestin, en combinacin con el buen gobierno empresarial, son hoy en da herramientas imprescindibles para profundizar en una relacin de confianza con la clientela bancaria. Avanzar en esta direccin parece un reto de futuro difcilmente renunciable. He mencionado que la aplicacin de uno u otro sistema de medicin y gestin de los riesgos depende de la propia complejidad de la operativa desarrollada por las entidades. Este principio se aplica, de hecho, a Basilea II. El Banco de Espaa espera, por lo tanto, que el nmero de entidades que accedan a los mtodos ms avanzados sea reducido, y en cualquier caso, fruto de un proceso gradual en el tiempo. De lo que no cabe ninguna duda es que Basilea II introduce los incentivos necesarios para avanzar en la mejora de la gestin de los riesgos. Solvencia Las entidades de depsito han de disponer de un nivel suficiente de recursos propios en relacin a los riesgos asumidos, ya que estos se convierten en una lnea de defensa fundamental ante la eventual ocurrencia de dificultades. De hecho, en aos recientes se ha observado cmo el mantenimiento de adecuados niveles de solvencia ha sido un factor explicativo que ha contribuido a fortalecer la capacidad de resistencia de las entidades. Estos recursos propios no slo han de ser suficientes, sino tambin ntegros y de calidad suficiente. Para que esto sea as, los recursos propios han de caracterizarse por un grado de permanencia suficiente, de tal modo que sean estables, al tiempo que deben disponer de la suficiente capacidad de absorcin de prdidas. En un contexto de fuerte crecimiento del crdito, en el que, por tanto, los requerimientos de capital se incrementan, las entidades han de realizar esfuerzos no solo para incrementar sus recursos propios adecuadamente, sino para hacerlo mediante aquellos que resultan de calidad suficiente como para actuar como lnea de defensa ante la eventual ocurrencia de dificultades. Asimismo, no es menos cierto que en los momentos de dificultades financieras, incluso los niveles de capital ms slidos se han mostrado insuficientes en aquellas entidades que no tenan correctamente valorada su cartera crediticia. Por ello, la poltica de capital de las entidades se ha de ver complementada por adecuadas polticas de provisiones. Las provisiones incorporadas en el marco contable espaol han formado parte, tradicionalmente, de nuestro marco de regulacin prudencial. Esto se vio reforzado con la introduccin de la provisin estadstica a mediados del ao 2000, que sin duda contribuye a la estabilidad de nuestro sistema financiero. Desde el 1 de enero del pasado ao est vigente la Nueva Circular Contable del Banco de Espaa que, como saben, adapta las Normas Internacionales de Contabilidad aprobadas y adoptadas por la Unin Europea desde esa misma fecha. En materia de provisiones, la nueva Circular contable, respetando las normas internacionales, incorpora un componente macro-prudencial a travs de la dotacin genrica. Esta nueva provisin cubre las prdidas incurridas, pero no se cie a las ya identificadas en operaciones concretas, sino tambin a las incurridas pero no identificadas en operaciones particulares. En cualquier caso, la nueva Circular contable ha venido a reconocer el importante papel que el modelo contable espaol, y en particular las provisiones, juegan dentro de nuestra poltica prudencial. Cambios regulatorios Acabo de referirme a la nueva Circular contable introducida por el Banco de Espaa, que ha supuesto cambios profundos en el marco contable espaol como consecuencia de la adopcin, por parte de la Unin Europea, de las Normas Internacionales de Contabilidad. Tambin me he referido a Basilea II que supondr un verdadero avance en la cultura de medicin y gestin de los riesgos, para as potenciar la estabilidad financiera. La nueva Circular contable, como saben, ha supuesto importantes esfuerzos de aprendizaje y adaptacin a lo largo del pasado ejercicio, no solo para las entidades, sino tambin para el propio Banco de Espaa. Basilea II, si bien an no ha entrado en vigor, ya viene exigiendo esfuerzos de adaptacin por parte de las entidades, que precisan de inversiones en capital tcnico y humano para adaptarse exitosamente a los cambios. Estos cambios en el marco regulatorio, por su envergadura, pero tambin por su desarrollo en un espacio de tiempo relativamente reducido, exigen un proceso de adaptacin importante para las entidades, que han de destinar recursos suficientes y asumir un nivel de compromiso adecuado. Como ya se ha manifestado en alguna ocasin desde el Banco de Espaa, creo que ahora se abre un periodo que posibilite asumir adecuadamente los cambios y, por lo tanto, de relajacin respecto de nuevas propuestas. Conclusiones Permtanme que concluya mi intervencin simplemente enfatizando el mensaje principal que hoy he pretendido transmitirles: la mayor garanta de xito para que el modelo de banca cooperativa perdure en el tiempo manteniendo sus principales rasgos definitorios es continuar en la lnea de lograr entidades slidas, solventes y, en definitiva, bien gestionadas. En un mercado tan exigente y competitivo como el espaol, este camino no est exento de riesgos, pero tambin lleno de posibilidades. No obstante, mi conviccin personal es que, como en la gran mayora de los casos hasta ahora, los gestores de las cooperativas de crdito continuarn mostrando un elevado grado de profesionalidad para abordar con xito las cambiantes circunstancias por venir. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Welcome remarks at the International Conference on "The Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey", organized by the Banco de Espaa. Madrid. Only in English.
text: Madrid, March 1, 2006 Welcoming remarks International Conference on the Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey Banco de Espana Jose Vinals Director General of International Affairs Good morning. Let me welcome you on behalf of the Banco de Espana, whose pleasure it is, in collaboration with the International Monetary Fund, to have organised this international conference on the Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey. So, let me take the opportunity to thank the Fund for their excellent partnership in this, as well as in other previous occasions. The most important structural change that has taken place in the world economy over the last two decades has been the very significant degree to which trade and financial relationships have increased across countries. This phenomenon popularly known as globalisation is having a deep impact on the way modern economies work and on how the effects of shocks and policies are transmitted internationally. Thus, it should be no surprise that discussions on the economic and financial effects of globalisation are currently high on the agendas of both policymakers and private-sector players. Because globalisation is simply the reflection of the growing interdependency of national economies, and since Balance of Payments Statistics are precisely designed to record such interdependency in the most faithful possible way, it follows that the more globalisation progresses, the more interest there is in such statistics both from the economic and the policymaking viewpoints. However, the forces unleashed by globalisation also have the potential to weaken, sometimes fundamentally, the connection between the underlying economic phenomena and their statistical representation. By its very nature, globalisation resulting from the liberalisation of trade and capital flows makes it harder to collect the information that allows such flows to be recorded properly. Consequently, while globalisation has made the statistical recording of economic and financial interlinkages all the more relevant, it has also made it harder to record this properly or to continue to draw correct and accurate monetary and economic policy implications from Balance of Payments Statistics. In general, given high financial integration it becomes very difficult if not impossible to know with precision the nationality of portfolio investors. This leads to a loss of information concerning this category of capital flows relative to, say, FDI investors. From a policymaking standpoint, identifying the ultimate holders of the resident issues is important in order to make an accurate assessment of the nature of the capital flows in terms of foreseeable volatility and of the stability and solvency of the financial sector. The Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey, to which we will be devoting the next day and a half, arose in response to these reporting needs which, to some extent, were ahead of their time. Ultimately, the Survey dates back to two reports by the International Monetary Fund in the late 80s and early 90s. The Esteva report and the Godeaux report highlighted the presence of substantial asymmetries between the data on global credits and debits in the global current account and financial account, respectively. This was unquestionably one of the first occasions on which statistics were explicitly and publicly up against one of the biggest nightmares in the field of foreign sector data: cross-country asymmetries. The Godeaux report noted that portfolio investment was, probably, the major source of problems in the financial account, and it recommended conducting an international survey on such investment. Today, almost 25 years after the Godeaux report, we view the Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey as a pioneering response to the challenges posed by globalisation to foreign statistics. The usefulness of the Survey has, no doubt, far exceeded the initial intentions of its original proponents. The Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey sought to analyse, on a one-off basis, the problems caused by the major asymmetries detected, so as to take decisions that would improve data quality. What was involved, therefore, was an instrument of statistical analysis whose usefulness was confined to that area, and it was in this capacity that the Survey was performed in 1997. A main conclusion drawn from this first Survey was, to some extent, discouraging: asymmetries are a difficult problem to resolve, something statisticians already knew. Why, then, was this Survey considered successful? Apart from providing useful information on the sources of asymmetries and acting as a positive force for the dissemination and promotion of suitable methods for increasing the quality of statistics, the Surveys success lay in the fact that it showed that a global approach for resolving, or at least mitigating, a global problem was possible. Indeed, the Survey was seen to be the sole procedure for obtaining information on the country of residence of investors who hold in their portfolios securities issued by the residents of a specific country. Moreover, the roll-out of the Survey disseminated statistical procedures such as security-by-security reporting systems or centralised securities databases, which were scarce in the mid-90s and are today widely used. Thanks to the clear perception of the value it added, the Survey became an annual exercise from 2001 onwards. Thereafter the Survey may be said to have outgrown its initial objective and to have become a statistical source in itself, providing annual information with an itemised geographical breakdown of global portfolio investment. The value of this information source, in terms both of its inclusion in national and regional statistics, and of its analytical worth per se, has undoubtedly exceeded what those who proposed conducting such a survey in the early 90s had in mind. Furthermore, the growth and growing volatility witnessed in international transactions with negotiable securities in recent years, coupled with the need for detailed information on these transactions for monetary, economic and financial stability-related analyses, greatly enhance the value of the Survey, as it is the sole means for gaining reliable, useful information on essential aspects of these transactions. Spain is a clear example of the growing importance of portfolio investment: the Spanish economys stock of portfolio investment assets and liabilities as a percentage of GDP increased by 97% from 1992 to 2004, outpacing the stocks of direct investment and other investment (which grew by 45% and 40%, respectively). The Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey has now been up and running for several years. In addition to the data from the pilot 1997 experience, it has furnished results for the years 2001 to 2004. It may thus be said to have reached maturity. In this connection, the conference has two aims: first, to contribute to the dissemination of the Survey among users and, thereby, to promote the use of the data it provides; and second, to identify potential improvements enabling increasingly useful information to be made available. To achieve both aims we have invited experts who will present various aspects of the Survey and an audience drawn from statisticians, analysts and specialists from academia, the private sector and government, coming from a large number of countries and international organisations. We trust the conference will be a good forum for these groups to exchange information and opinions, and we urge them to participate actively and discuss their ideas. The Banco de Espana feels privileged to have jointly organised this conference with the International Monetary Fund and to have gathered together such an eminent group of speakers and participants. We hope you will all find the conference most useful. Thank you very much.

Title: What have we learned from the international experience of bank restructuring?. Speech at the Spanish-Chinese Conference on experiences in bank restructuring, organized by the CBRB and the Bank of Spain in Shanghai. Only in English.
text: Shanghai, April 10th 2006 What have we learned from the international experience of bank restructuring? Chinese-Spanish Conference on bank restructuring experiences CRBC and Banco de Espana Jose Vinals Director General Introduction It is a pleasure to comment on these two extremely interesting bank restructuring cases from Hungary and Chile. I believe that the experiences of these two countries are of particular relevance today for at least two reasons. The first is that they provide a useful insight into bank restructuring from two apparently very different cases: a former Transition Economy in Central and Eastern Europe, and an Emerging Market economy in Latin America. And the second is that it is possible, drawing on these two cases, to identify some conclusions that might be of interest in the context of the situation of the banking sector in China today. At first sight, it would seem that the experience of Hungary might be of more direct relevance to China, given its background as a former planned economy. The roots of its banking crises, associated with a large build-up of bad debts due to soft-budget constraints from State ownership would seem to be quite close to the experience of China today. In contrast, as we have learned this afternoon, the banking crisis in Chile stands out as a case of twin crises, in which the collapse of the exchange rate resulted in widespread bank and corporate insolvency, due to heavy overborrowing in foreign currency. Such developments prompted a different kind of banking crisis, characterised by high macroeconomic volatility, and also a bank run. While one might think that the collapse of the exchange rate is totally implausible in China today, it is also true that Chile underwent a fast process of financial liberalisation without adequate bank regulation and supervision. This particular dimension of the crisis may be potentially useful to China, given the steady but firm process of financial liberalisation currently under way. In my presentation I will try to organise my comments around four main topics. I will first talk about differences and similarities between Chile and Hungary at the time of bank restructuring. From this comparison, I will attempt to highlight some of the key strengths in China, but also some major challenges. Then I will say something about those aspects of the bank restructuring experiences of Chile and Hungary which may be potentially more relevant for China. After that I would like to add a few remarks on a slightly different matter, but a very relevant one in the context of bank restructuring: the role of the central bank and the importance of coordination between policies. In this regard, I will try to make the case that the coordination of different economic policies is key to successful bank restructuring and also for the sustained development of the financial system thereafter. Finally, I will conclude my presentation with a few more general thoughts. Common factors and key differences between the Chilean and Hungarian experiences Each crisis is unquestionably unique. Its sources as well as the combination of events that led to the problem are probably impossible to repeat in any approximate way, so any generalisation runs the risk of being too simplistic. But bearing in mind these caveats, let me share with you at least three issues in the experiences of Chile and Hungary which to me seem to have much in common. Obviously, there are also several important differences that should be taken into account. The common factors in the two cases include most notably the macroeconomic conditions. Both Chile and Hungary faced huge economic shocks in the run-up to their crises, with a devastating effect on the corporate and banking sectors. In spite of latent vulnerabilities in both financial systems, had it not been for the strong terms-of-trade shock in Chile or for the collapse of large export markets in Hungary, their financial systems might arguably have continued to run for years. The second common factor is the presence of shortcomings in the regulatory and supervisory frameworks. With the benefit of hindsight, it has been acknowledged that regulation and supervision were outdated both in Chile and in Hungary. Risks such as overborrowing, related-party lending or concentration were tackled late, and key prudential regulations such as provisioning or financial disclosure were poor or simply not there. All these faults probably compounded the problem, increasing the costs of the banking crises. Finally, the third common factor is the lack of adequate corporate governance and risk management at the bank level, which have also been acknowledged as key weaknesses that led at least to bad lending decisions, and in some cases even to outright fraud. Let me now turn to those factors which I believe are quite different. In addition to the already mentioned different sources of banking problems in the two countries, the approach to bank restructuring was also different. In the case of Chile, bank restructuring was based on corporate and household debt restructuring and on the recapitalisation of banks, followed by a major revamp of the regulatory and supervisory frameworks. In Hungary, however, key features were the portfolio clean-up, recapitalisation and finally privatisation, which was primarily aimed at reinforcing corporate governance and risk management and which resulted in the very significant presence of foreign banks. How does China compare? I would like now to move on to those experiences of Chile and Hungary in bank restructuring which may be more useful to the specific case of China. But let me first briefly review how I think that the general situation in China today compares to that of Chile and Hungary at the time of bank restructuring. One of the first apparent differences between the cases of Chile and Hungary, on one hand, and that of China, on the other, is the nature of their banking crises. Both in Chile and Hungary, the banking crises were full-blown, in that these were periods of pervasive bank unsoundness coupled with significant bank runs or other substantial portfolio shifts, collapses of financial firms, or massive government interventions. With a varying degree of timeliness, resolution strategies were put in place only after the crisis had severely hit those financial systems. In China, however, we cannot speak of a banking crisis although there are indications of potential bank unsoundness when looking at the volume of NPLs. Therefore, recent bank restructuring initiatives taken by the Chinese authorities since 1998 are, for the most part, in anticipation of what could come later, and this foresight may be taken as one of its principal strengths. A second key difference is economic growth, which continues to be robust in China after years of expansion, and which remains underpinned by the strength of domestic demand, as compared to Chile and Hungary. Sustained high economic growth in China is unquestionably a plus when it comes to the timing of bank restructuring. A third important strength of the Chinese economy is the large stock of international foreign reserves, together with a sound fiscal position and relatively low government debt ratios. Even if the fiscal positions in Hungary or Chile at the time of bank restructuring were considered as relatively healthy, and instrumental in limiting the fiscal costs of restructuring especially compared to many other countries, it should be recalled that the strength of public sector finances has been acknowledged as one of the key lessons from recent financial crises around the world. Weak public sector finances together with high levels of public debt and fiscal deficits have, in too many of the most salient banking crises of late, intensified the magnitude of the crisis by limiting the choices available to manage it, and also jeopardised the conduct of monetary policy. Finally, two interrelated additional sources of strength for China at the present time are the low levels of foreign currency borrowing, which in the particular case of Chile were a significant (and costly) vulnerability when the crisis broke, and the prevalence of capital controls, which for the time being heavily restrain the possibility of capital flight from China. In Chile, most of those controls had already been lifted when the crisis hit the country, and needed to be reintroduced afterwards, while in Hungary financial liberalisation had started much later. All in all, then, it would appear that the Chinese economy has been in recent years and also is at present in a very good position to address bank restructuring and recapitalisation. This, coupled with the fact that challenges are increasing (financial liberalisation and the restructuring of State-owned enterprises), would seem to call for resolute steps forward with the reform process. But within this very positive context, there are also a few issues pending which will need to be faced. The first is the bulk of NPLs in the financial system, which remain high even following substantial recapitalisation in the last few years. Hungary probably faced a similar situation in the run-up to its banking crisis, while in Chile the build-up of NPLs had a different origin. Another key potential weakness is the challenge posed by the ongoing financial liberalisation process, which has moved a long way on the domestic side, but less so externally. In the particular case of China, the liberalisation of the capital account and the heightened competition it would entail could pose a challenge for the banking system, primarily due to the high volume of NPLs, low profitability and limited knowledge of risk management. These challenges also had to be tackled by Chile and Hungary at the time, each one in its own specific way. Aspects of the bank restructuring experiences of Chile and Hungary of most relevance for China There are at least three findings from the experiences of Hungary and Chile that could be relevant for China at this point. One is, obviously, that there are major challenges in the transition from a State-owned banking system to a market-based system. Such challenges encompass issues as important and diverse as radically changing the way in which banking business is conducted, encouraging competition, and learning to manage risk and be profitable in a context of market-determined interest and exchange rates. And last but certainly not least, adapting banking regulation and supervision accordingly. A second finding concerns policy choices in bank restructuring, including privatisation and the entry of foreign banks. In Hungary, recapitalisation was followed by privatisation. Following the positive experience of Hungary but also the negative ones of other transition countries, it became clear that the key aspect of privatisation was to obtain an ownership structure that ensured effective corporate governance. In Hungary this was attained largely by selling banks to strategic investors. In practice, this meant that Hungarian banks were sold mostly to foreign banks, which provided capital, corporate governance, risk management and technology, even if in some cases the privatisation through the local stock exchange to domestic investors also worked well. This obviously meant a major change from the previous ownership structure to one in which competition and the availability of financial products and services has increased as a result of foreign bank participation, even if there is still room for improvement. Today, the Hungarian banking system is widely viewed as one of the strongest in the region. Thirdly, I would also like to highlight some relevant findings from the experience of Chile, which stem from the risks of financial liberalisation with insufficient checks and balances. The first is the importance of anticipating, and of preventing, through a prudent economic policy mix, the problems caused by excessive risk-taking and the accumulation of large financial imbalances. The second is that a sound institutional framework must be in place when a country decides to liberalise, and that the proper timing of financial liberalisation is key to its success. Bank restructuring and the role of the central bank Let me now add a few comments, as mentioned before, on the interaction between bank restructuring and monetary policy. With these comments I want to convey to you the importance of coordinating different policies in pursuing a successful bank restructuring process. Past experience in bank restructuring shows that the role of the central bank has been crucial in all phases of a banking crisis resolution. During the initial containment phase, the central bank is typically in charge of providing sufficient liquidity. At the same time, it will have to manage a potential short-term conflict between its responsibility in safeguarding financial stability and that of preserving monetary stability. If the central bank is credible, and sufficiently flexible monetary policy instruments are available, it will be able to safeguard the smooth functioning of the payments system in order to prevent a further deterioration of economic conditions while at the same time ensuring that inflation expectations remain in check. Later, during the bank restructuring and reintermediation phases, the central bank will also play an important role by adapting monetary conditions to the new environment, with a view to ensuring that the financial system is back on a sound footing and that it can resume its natural role as a provider of credit to the economy. This will facilitate enormously the conduct of bank restructuring, containing some of its costs. General conclusions arising from the international experience of bank restructuring Finally, let me end my presentation by discussing some of the most important general conclusions that can be derived from the very rich international experience of bank restructuring. First, each bank restructuring experience is unique in many ways. Different country-specific circumstances, initial conditions, sources of banking problems, institutional frameworks or even the degree of financial development are bound to determine different approaches to bank restructuring. But it is also important to note that, as we have learnt today, there are also a few common factors in past restructuring experiences which may be of great use to policymakers when they need to address a new process. A second conclusion is that most banking problems can be structured in three phases: one of containment, a second of bank restructuring and a third of financial reintermediation. Since the focus of this conference today is on the latter two, I would like to emphasise that the choice of bank restructuring strategy should be aimed at minimising the net present value of the costs of the crisis. But similarly important is the fact that the financial reintermediation strategy be designed in such a way as to lay the foundations for a financial system which is viable, efficient, sound and resilient. In this regard, it is also appropriate to recall that early detection of problems and firm political resolve to address them are instrumental in reducing the magnitude of the crisis. Delays in tackling banking problems are only likely to end up increasing the costs. Likewise, having in place a clear and consistent restructuring strategy that is transparent and well-communicated to the public so as to make it credible is fundamental to success. Thirdly, restoring and maintaining macroeconomic stability is also a major determinant of the final success of bank restructuring processes. Similarly, it is difficult to make progress in bank restructuring without dealing with corporate restructuring too. A fourth conclusion that can be drawn is the importance of good risk management both at the macro-prudential and individual bank level. From past experience, the coordination of different economic policies is clearly crucial for avoiding some of the key risks related to financial liberalisation and for ensuring successful bank restructuring. Capital-account liberalisation should be sequenced appropriately, i.e. paying particular attention to lifting short-term capital inflow restrictions, and especially those on capital outflows, only after the domestic financial system has built in sufficient buffers and is perceived as sufficiently robust. Incidentally, this is to a large extent the approach that China has rightly been following. Likewise, financial regulation, supervision and enforcement need to be upgraded as liberalisation proceeds, in accordance with the basic principles of risk assessment and risk management. Finally, it is also essential that a strong credit culture and improved corporate governance should be well-established within banks, so that lending decisions are taken on the grounds of risk management to avoid the fresh build-up of NPLs. And finally, I would like to stress the importance of having an adequate institutional framework for a successful bank restructuring process. In this regard, a credible central bank, high-quality financial regulation and supervision, and sound fiscal policies are among the cornerstones of a good policy framework for bank restructuring. But equally important in the process are appropriate disclosure and accounting standards, the respect for property rights, well-designed bankruptcy laws and the effective functioning of the judiciary. To conclude, bank restructuring is certainly a complex process, involving a number of public and private economic agents, that must be designed with care and carried out effectively in order to be successful. I hope that some of the ideas put forward in this discussion can help us better design and pursue such processes in the future.

Title: Notes: The economic situation in 2005 and the beginning of 2006 (Governor's Intervention at the Five-Day Forum)
text: 12 December 2005 III Congress of Economy of the Valencian Community Jaime Caruana Lacorte Governor of the Bank of Spain I am very pleased to participate in these Valencian Regional Economy Days and I thank its organizers for having commissioned me to pronounce a few words at the beginning of them. For an institution like the Bank of Spain, with important responsibilities in the design and management of economic policy, all activities related to improving knowledge of the Spanish economy are of great interest, to which I am sure the debates that you will have these days will contribute. As manager of economic policy, within the monetary and financial areas entrusted to the Bank of Spain, my best contribution is to provide the vision of the current situation of the Spanish economy within the European Economic and Monetary Union. I will focus the first part of my speech on the European situation, on the current international framework, devoting some attention to some of the structural gaps that are becoming apparent, to concentrate later on the Spanish economy. . Despite the sharp rise in oil prices, the world economy continued to show high dynamism in 2005 in a context of moderate inflation, with GDP reaching a growth rate of over 4 per cent (although below the 5.1 per cent observed in 2004). As the year has progressed, the strength experienced by the United States and emerging Asia (including China and India) has expanded into other economic areas such as Japan and Europe, which I will discuss in more detail later. The reasons why, to date, the pace of expansion of global activity has suffered only moderately from the rise in oil prices are diverse. These include the decrease in the degree of energy dependence of the main economies compared to previous historical episodes or the fact that the increase in oil prices is largely due to demand pressure, especially from the most dynamic Asian economies. For its part, the absence of "second-round effects" on wages has made it possible to contain underlying inflationary tensions, and thus allow monetary policies to continue to be encouraging growth. The leading indicators point to the prolongation of this period of economic boom in the coming months - with world GDP growth similar to its potential - favoured by low interest rates, price stability and the boost in demand from the revenues obtained by oil-producing countries. However, the risks surrounding this scenario are predominantly to the downside and are related to the possibility that energy prices will grow further and be transmitted to a greater extent to inflation and to the high US current account imbalance that could trigger episodes of exchange rate volatility and, eventually, lead to a sharp increase in long-term interest rates, which are currently at unusually low levels. In this context, the euro area is likely to achieve growth for 2005 of less than 1.5%, well below that recorded in other relevant economic areas as it has not been able to fully benefit from the favourable situation of the world economy until mid-year. Thus, in the first half of the year, the delayed effects of the accumulated appreciation of the euro exchange rate and the loss of purchasing power of households as a result of the high price of oil weighed down the expansion of the area's output. In the second half, however, the euro area has begun to show signs of greater strength as exports have become more dynamic and external momentum has begun to be transmitted to domestic demand. These developments allow us to expect a sustained recovery in activity in the coming quarters, which will mean maintaining year-on-year GDP growth rates of around 2%. This forecast is based, in addition to the favourable external environment, on the acceleration of productive investment encouraged by the comfortable financial conditions and the good outlook for corporate profits. However, consumption is likely to experience only moderate growth in the near future, in line with developments in disposable income. In any case, the materialisation of these prospects is subject, as for the world economy as a whole, to uncertainties arising from the evolution of oil prices and global imbalances, as well as low levels of consumer confidence. As regards the evolution of inflation, the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices of the euro area has recently been guided by the evolution of energy prices, which explains why its year-on-year growth has been clearly above 2% since spring. To date, however, no signs of persistent inflationary pressures have emerged, as weak labour market strength and strong international competition are allowing for contained growth in wages and domestic prices. In any case, markets expect oil prices to remain high, which will prevent HICP energy growth from easing significantly downwards in the coming months. This increases the risk that higher production costs will end up leading to price increases in all sectors and interrupt wage moderation. On the other hand, there is the possibility of increases in administered prices and indirect taxes in several countries in the area, which would imply greater inflationary pressure. Given these constraints, the Governing Council of the ECB decided to raise interest rates on 1st December by 25 basis points to 2.25%, after having kept them unchanged for two and a half years. The objective is to ensure that the observed increase in inflation rates and the risks surrounding their evolution do not end up affecting expectations, so that they remain anchored at levels consistent with price stability. In any case, monetary policy maintains an accommodative tone that will support the progressive strengthening of domestic demand and job creation. Current monetary conditions are thus appropriate for the euro area to maintain low inflation rates while economic activity gains momentum. This benefits all the states that are part of the monetary union, regardless of whether their cyclical conditions are more or less expansionary than those of the euro area as a whole. This is, of course, the case of the Spanish economy whose dynamism is due, to a large extent, to its belonging to a supranational area with a high degree of macroeconomic stability, favoured by the proper conduct of the single monetary policy by the ECB. At the same time, the rise in interest rates makes it possible to moderate somewhat the particularly relaxed nature of monetary and financial conditions in our country, although it does not exempt us from the need to use the economic policy instruments that remain under national control to contain and channel the imbalances that the continued expansion of spending can generate. I will come to this issue a little more later. Turning to the euro area, I would like to spend the next few minutes highlighting some of the more structural challenges facing its economy. In particular, increasing globalisation, rapid technological progress and the foreseeable ageing of the population make it necessary for the European economy to improve its adaptability and increase its efficiency, if it is to intensify growth in the medium term and ensure the sustainability of its socio-economic model. The low economic dynamism of the euro area is clearly manifested when the recent trajectory of the average income of each euro area inhabitant is contrasted with that of the United States. After the rapid approximation of European living standards towards North Americans during the post-war period, we have witnessed, since the 70s, an interruption of this process, and, since the mid- nineties, a widening of the welfare gap. In order to analyse the causes of this development, it is useful to decompose the rate of expansion of per capita output into the growth in labour use and productivity, which are the ultimate sources of growth in living standards. With regard to the use of the labour factor, the most recent estimates suggest that average hours worked per capita in EMU are 77% of the level for the United States. An accounting decomposition of this variable allows us to inquire about the contributions to this gap in the number of hours worked per employee, the level of unemployment and the activity rate. Thus, an important part of the differential is explained by the fact that each employee in the euro area works, on average, approximately 15% fewer hours at the end of the year than an American. This is mainly due to the fact that the number of working days in the euro area is smaller. In addition, since the mid-90s, the distance between the hours worked in both areas has increased due to the increase in part-time employment and the decrease in working hours. A second factor explaining the lower use of the labour factor in EMU is its higher unemployment rate. Thus, although in the last decade reforms in labor markets and social benefit systems have allowed a substantial reduction in unemployment, the decline has been more intense in the United States, so that currently the differential in unemployment rates is about 3 percentage points. Finally, although these same reforms have also promoted an increase in the activity rate in EMU, progress has not been sufficient to reach the levels of the United States, where the level of this variable continues to be higher by about 10 percentage points. The causes of this lower use of the labour factor in Europe are the subject of recurrent discussion in different forums. Sometimes, the lower number of hours worked in Europe has been explained by a greater preference of its citizens for leisure. It is more likely, in my view, that this phenomenon is due, above all, to the disincentives generated by tax, social security and pension systems, which calls for additional reform measures to further narrow the gap between the United States and the euro area in the intensity of use of available human resources. The analysis of productivity differentials d0 the second factor into which per capita income can be broken down d0 does not reveal a more positive assessment. In fact, the gap between output growth per employee in the United States and Europe has widened markedly since the nineties of the last century and, above all, in the most recent years. Thus, in the last five years, EMU productivity has only grown by around 1% per year, almost two percentage points below the US rate. As is known, the evolution of productivity can be analyzed from its two fundamental components: the intensity in the use of capital - that is, the quotient between the stock of capital and the number of hours worked - and technological progress - known as total factor productivity. Well, there seems to be robust evidence that the low dynamism of productivity in EMU, and in general in all its member countries, has been the result of the worse relative performance of both components. In particular, the growing weight of low-skilled workers and the intense job creation since the mid-nineties have been two elements that have contributed to the slowdown in productivity. Moreover, the euro area has failed to take advantage of the opportunities offered by new information and communication technologies, as a result of insufficient incentives for innovation and the existence of barriers to their diffusion and use, especially in the service sector. In short, I believe that the widening gap between the European economy and the United States in terms of the level of per capita income requires that, with some urgency, the economic policy debate should focus on promoting measures aimed at increasing growth in both the use of labour and productivity. In particular, the latter requires the improvement of education systems (through greater commensurate with the needs of labour markets, for example), reforms in product markets that allow them to operate with a greater degree of efficiency or the achievement of an environment more conducive to innovation and the adoption of new technologies. Moreover, only the implementation of ambitious reforms in the labour market and social protection systems will make it possible to ensure increased participation and job creation. In 2000, the European Council meeting in Lisbon already echoed this need, defining as a strategic goal for Europe by the end of this decade "to become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth with more and better jobs and greater cohesion". To this end, several fields of action were proposed. The first area of reforms focuses on the development of a knowledge society, through the promotion of investment in RD and education and the promotion of information and communication technologies. Secondly, the Heads of State and Government recognised the need to complete the integration of markets, especially in services. The third avenue through which action was advocated was to reform the regulatory environment underlying business. In addition, in the area of the labour market, specific objectives were defined to increase employment rates, with particular attention to women, young people and older citizens. Today, halfway through the deadline set by the Lisbon Agenda, the results are far from satisfactory. Thus, as has been described, while advances in the use of the labour factor have generally been remarkable, the evolution of productivity has not been adjusted to the ambition of the objectives set. Indeed, Europe is not being able to innovate or introduce new technologies to the extent necessary, while the integration of European markets is insufficient and business dynamism is still far from that of the United States. There is a general consensus that the multiplicity of objectives and the lack of definition of priorities between them, as well as the lack of commitment and political will, are the reasons for the limited progress of the Lisbon Agenda. That is why, last March, the European Council decided to relaunch the Agenda by agreeing to concentrate efforts on those areas that had the greatest impact on jobs and growth. In order to increase the commitment of the various authorities to the reform processes, the review of the Lisbon strategy has more clearly identified the areas of responsibility at Community and national level. On the one hand, the Member States retain responsibility for most of the policies necessary to achieve the final objectives, for which, through the National Reform Programmes d0 discussed and agreed with the social groups involved d0 they have made explicit how they will translate the generic commitments they have acquired into concrete actions. Overall, most countries have put forward measures to improve labour market conditions, ensure the sustainability of public finances, encourage investment in research and innovation, and promote educational improvements. While overall, the proposals put forward make a promising start to the relaunch of the revised Lisbon Agenda, it remains to be seen to what extent there is a genuine political commitment to carry out all the reforms set out in the National Reform Programmes. The contribution of initiatives at Community level to the reform process is also necessary. In July, the Commission presented all the actions within its scope. This communication showed that the potential benefits of completing the single market in terms of economic growth and employment are still far from being fully exploited, as a result of insufficient progress in the integration of certain markets, particularly in the services sector. In short, Europe must be aware that its economic prosperity depends primarily on the implementation of a comprehensive and ambitious set of structural reforms, as well as sound macroeconomic policies. The review of the Lisbon Agenda is only the first step, which must be complemented by concrete measures that will require strengthened political will. The period of greater economic dynamism in which the euro area seems to be entering may provide a breeding ground for intensifying the reform process. I now turn to the situation of the Spanish economy. In the year that is about to end, the Spanish economy has continued to show remarkable dynamism, much higher than that of the euro area as a whole, prolonging a long phase of economic expansion, which has lasted a decade. Between 1995 and 2004, the average annual growth of activity in Spain was 3.6%, with annual rates always exceeding 2.5% and a cumulative increase in production of 38%. This prolonged and intense expansion has made it possible to create almost 4 and a half million jobs. The more intensive use of this productive factor, relatively more abundant in the Spanish economy, has allowed to considerably reduce the unemployment rate that existed in the middle of the last decade d0 to be located at 8.4%, in the third quarter of 2005, a level that was not observed in Spain since the seventies d0 but has led, At the same time, to a very limited advance in the apparent productivity of labour, a question on which I shall dwell later. The dynamism of our economy, which the recent revision of Spain's National Accounts has confirmed and reinforced, has been based on a combination of expansionary factors in both supply and demand. On the one hand, there has been a strong increase in the labour force, which in turn has resulted from high immigration flows, which has made it possible to make significant job creation compatible with a containment of pressures on labour costs. On the other hand, the maintenance of interest rates at very low levels has created very favourable financial conditions, which have contributed to the expansion of spending and indebtedness. All these factors d0 population growth, strong job creation and low interest rates d0 have led to an improvement in income prospects and have also driven a process of persistent increases in house prices, which has fed back the strength of demand through the wealth effects they have generated. For this reason, the expansion of activity has been substantially based on the strength of private consumption and investment in construction, while the foreign sector has been showing a negative contribution to output. In 2005, this pattern of growth has been broadly maintained, although since mid-2004 investment in capital goods has also been incorporated into the expansion process. In addition, during the first three quarters of the year there has been a gradual acceleration of activity, which has reached a year-on-year rate of 3.5% in the third quarter, 4 tenths more than that registered a year earlier. Thus, growth for 2005 as a whole is likely to be around 3.4%. In 2005, private consumption continued to show fairly high rates of change, clearly above 4% year-on-year, although they have tended to moderate in recent months. The continuation of strong job creation - with increases very close to those of output expansion - and favourable financial conditions, including the revaluation of housing, which I have already mentioned, and that of equity securities, are the main factors that have driven the dynamism of consumption. These wealth effects have also maintained the growth of spending above that of household disposable income, leading to a decrease in the savings rate in this sector. Within the investment, we must highlight the strength that construction continues to manifest, which has even accelerated gently throughout this year. The environment of low interest rates and the revaluation of real assets have continued to stimulate residential investment. However, some recent indicators suggest that house prices must have slowed somewhat in 2005, which could be a symptom of lower demand pressure, dampening to some extent the magnitude of the wealth effects. In any case, the very inertia of the residential construction cycle d0 as illustrated by the fact that 2005 is likely to close with a new record number of housing starts d0 together with the ambitious infrastructure plans approved, will provide support for construction activity over the coming years. Investment in equipment has also shown significant dynamism, which is one of the most positive aspects of the current economic landscape, insofar as it reflects the effort of companies to equip themselves with new productive capital with which to face future challenges. The growth of corporate margins, low financing costs, the solvent financial situation of companies d0 after the reorganization of the heavy indebtedness accumulated by some companies in the second half of the nineties d0 and the strength of demand are driving the investment effort. However, a significant part of the increase in domestic demand has continued to filter outward. Thus, the negative contribution of net exports to output growth, which continued to expand throughout 2004, has remained close to two percentage points, albeit in slight decline, throughout 2005. This trend is explained by both the behaviour of exports and imports. As was the case in 2004, sales abroad have grown below export markets, while imports have shown a dynamism higher than that of final demand, increasing their degree of penetration in the domestic market. In the case of tourism, although the rate of growth of payments is still much higher than that of income, it is worth noting the notable improvement experienced by the main indicators of the Spanish tourism sector in recent months. The deterioration in the contribution of the external sector and the growing balance of payments imbalance are due to various causes, partly of a cyclical nature, such as the fact that Spain's cyclical position is more advanced than that of the nearest economies, mainly belonging to the euro area. Higher energy prices and higher investment flows also contribute to increasing the external deficit. However, the fall in the market share of Spanish exports since 2004 indicates that our companies have difficulties competing in international markets, in a context of strong international dynamism in some emerging countries - China is perhaps the most paradigmatic case - and of comparatively upward trend in domestic costs. In this respect, the cumulative growth differential in consumer prices vis-88-vis the rest of the euro area has widened steadily since the introduction of the single currency. Certainly, measured in terms of export prices, the loss of price-competitiveness seems less intense. However, it is possible that the export prices set by Spanish companies are, above all, the result of the strong pressure of international competition and, in this way, can only be maintained by assuming a cut in business margins d0 that is, accepting price increases lower than the increase in internal costs d0 which could call into question the very sustainability of export activity. Therefore, the maintenance of a relatively high inflation differential, in terms of consumer prices, vis-88-vis the euro area is possibly one of the most worrying features of the current situation of the Spanish economy. This differential, as I have pointed out, has persistently been around one percentage point since the beginning of the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union in 1999. In addition, it is widespread among the different components of the harmonised index of consumer prices, although it is particularly large for unprocessed foods and services.
