A partir de ah, incidir en las ventajas de la adopcin de este estndar a nivel europeo en un momento, adems, especialmente. Asimismo, argumentar que estas ventajas que aporta XBRL no quedan constreidas al mbito europeo, sino que otros pases podran tambin beneficiarse de ellas. Finalmente, concluir mi intervencin compartiendo con ustedes nuestra experiencia en Espaa, y en particular me centrar en algunas iniciativas recientes desarrolladas por el Banco de Espaa. El Comit de Supervisores Bancarios Europeos (CEBS): iniciativas en el mbito de la generacin y transmisin de la informacin Antes de analizar cules son las principales iniciativas del CEBS en el mbito de la generacin y transmisin de la informacin, permtanme que dedique solo unas palabras para situar a este organismo en el marco europeo. En el ao 2003, la Comisin Europea decidi adoptar el enfoque Lamfalussy, inicialmente desarrollado en el mbito de los valores, a la regulacin de los sectores bancario y de seguros. Dicho enfoque, que debe su nombre al presidente del grupo de expertos que lo desarroll en el ao 2000, ofrece una respuesta a la necesidad de crear en Europa un marco regulatorio que contribuyera a la promocin de un mercado de capitales integrado. En este marco, el CEBS, que formalmente inici sus funciones en enero de 2004, acta como un Comit que rene a los representantes de alto nivel de las autoridades de supervisin bancaria y de los bancos centrales de la Unin Europea, entre los que se incluye el Banco Central Europeo. Las funciones principales del CEBS se aglutinan en torno a tres grandes reas. En primer lugar, este organismo realiza una labor de asesoramiento, aconsejando a la Comisin Europea en cuestiones de poltica bancaria, y en particular, acerca de la preparacin de medidas de carcter preliminar en cuanto a la implementacin de la legislacin de la Unin Europea. En segundo lugar, contribuye a la ejecucin consistente de las Directivas comunitarias estableciendo, para ello, pautas, recomendaciones y principios. Finalmente, pero no menos importante, las tareas de CEBS consisten tambin en promover la cooperacin entre los distintos supervisores bancarios de la Unin Europea, manteniendo y fomentando el intercambio de informacin entre ellos. Permtanme que a continuacin me refiera a este ltimo mbito, y les traslade algunas iniciativas que ha desarrollado el CEBS en el mbito de la generacin e intercambio de la informacin. Si tienen en consideracin que la Unin Europea est formada en este momento por 25 pases, pueden imaginar sin demasiado esfuerzo que la situacin de partida supona un cierto grado de complejidad. Es decir, cada uno de esos pases solicitaba informacin diferente a las entidades. Las diferencias, de hecho, no se limitaban a las distintas definiciones empleadas por cada Estado Miembro, sino que tambin afectaban a los sistemas de informacin, a las tecnologas empleadas o a los formatos que eran utilizados, por ejemplo. Si bien en muchas ocasiones la diversidad es un valor en s mismo, en este terreno creo que las dificultades y los costes adicionales que implicaba, tanto para las entidades, como para los supervisores son obvios. En este marco, el CEBS est llevando a cabo dos iniciativas principales para promover la armonizacin de los requerimientos de informacin que se exigen a las entidades. Por una parte, a travs de un proyecto denominado COREP, se ha trabajado en el desarrollo de informes comunes en el mbito de la ratio de solvencia, que se han publicado en enero de 2006. Por otra, el proyecto denominado FINREP adopta la misma lnea de trabajo en el terreno de la informacin financiera, y los informes comunes se publicaron en diciembre del pasado ao. Estos informes comunes se han desarrollado en un momento especialmente conveniente, puesto que tanto la introduccin de las Normas Internacionales de Informacin Financiera, como la implantacin de Basilea II estn obligando a los supervisores a modificar, en alguna medida, los requerimientos y los sistemas de informacin que hasta la fecha estaban vigentes. En el desarrollo de estos proyectos, FINREP y COREP, el estndar XBRL aporta la tecnologa adecuada. Es ms, lo hace en el momento en el que ms se necesita. Por estos motivos, CEBS ha recomendado, en ambas iniciativas, promover el uso del estndar XBRL, creando para ello dos taxonomas. Ventajas asociadas a la implementacin de XBRL en Europa Las ventajas que aporta la adopcin de XBRL tienen que ver con los beneficios que cabe esperar de un sistema de informacin comn. Disponer de un marco de informacin comn en toda la Unin Europea contribuir no slo a favorecer el terreno de juego en el que operan las entidades o, si se quiere, a potenciar un mayor equilibrio competitivo, sino que es un ingrediente muy relevante a la hora de eliminar potenciales obstculos para la integracin del mercado financiero. Los beneficios que aporta un marco de informacin comn son palpables tanto para las entidades que generan la informacin como para los supervisores bancarios. Desde el punto de vista de las entidades, no cabe duda de que, principalmente los bancos transfronterizos, vern reducidos los costes administrativos a los que se enfrentan. Para los supervisores, las ventajas tienen que ver con las mayores posibilidades y facilidades en el mbito del intercambio de la informacin. En este sentido, un elemento importante que contribuir al incremento de la efectividad, en trminos de su coste, de las actividades supervisoras, es la mayor flexibilidad que, a su vez, posibilita un marco de este tipo. As, en este contexto, solicitar informacin adicional o modificar ligeramente aquella que se est solicitando conlleva unos menores costes. De nuevo, las entidades se beneficiarn de ello. Este conjunto de efectos positivos repercutir, en definitiva, en una mayor calidad de los flujos de informacin generados. Cul es, en este marco, la aportacin de XBRL? La respuesta se puede resumir diciendo que se trata de un estndar que por su rapidez, flexibilidad y precisin, caractersticas a las que ya me he referido, contribuye a la materializacin de los mencionados efectos positivos. Primero, XBRL permitir a los bancos cumplir con las necesidades de informacin de las autoridades supervisoras de la Unin Europea, y ello aplicando un nico estndar de sistemas de informacin. Por lo tanto, los costes asociados a la implementacin de los informes comunes que se derivan de los proyectos iniciados por CEBS en el mbito de la informacin relativa a la solvencia de las entidades, as como a sus estados financieros, se reducir para los grupos bancarios transfronterizos. As, XBRL contribuir a reducir los costes administrativos y de implementacin asociados al proceso. En segundo trmino, las entidades de menor tamao podrn beneficiarse de XBRL por dos motivos. Por una parte, porque se trata de un estndar en el que no se han de pagar royalties, es decir, es de un estndar libre. Por otra, en la medida en la que CEBS desarrolla las taxonomas XBRL, dichas entidades podrn aprovechar las economas de escala asociadas a tal proceso. Lgicamente, ello repercutir en unos menores costes a la hora de implementar tanto Basilea II como las Normas Internacionales de Informacin Financiera. En tercer lugar, los supervisores tambin obtendremos beneficios derivados del empleo de XBRL, y en particular, de las economas de escala derivadas. Sin duda, el uso de este estndar contribuir a mejorar la efectividad de coste de las actividades supervisoras. En cuarto lugar, XBRL va a facilitar el uso y la transmisin de definiciones homogneas que queden expresadas en los informes comunes de la Unin Europea. Sin duda ello incidir favorablemente en la consecucin de uno de los beneficios a los que me he referido anteriormente: la integracin financiera. En resumen, los supervisores se beneficiarn de un sistema de recopilacin de la informacin descentralizado, al tiempo que obtendrn las ventajas que aportan las bases de datos centralizadas. En efecto, la comparabilidad de formatos, contenidos y sistemas de informacin apoyados por XBRL permitir a los supervisores que el modo en el que se recoge la informacin sea descentralizado, pero al tiempo que puedan conservar todas las funcionalidades como si existiera una base de datos centralizada. La mejora que ello aporta en trminos de flexibilidad adicional parece, por lo tanto, clara. Antes me he referido a lo oportuno del momento de la implementacin de XBRL. Actualmente estamos en un proceso de cambio de los requerimientos de informacin, tanto por la introduccin de las Normas Internacionales de Informacin Financiera, como de Basilea II. Permtanme solo dos palabras sobre esto ltimo. En la actualidad, y una vez que el Comit de Basilea public el texto del Acuerdo, el paso siguiente, a nivel europeo, era su traslado a la Directiva comunitaria, de la que, sin entrar en mayores detalles, s quiero sealar que en compatible con Basilea II en su prctica totalidad. A partir de ah, el siguiente paso es su transposicin a la legislacin nacional de cada uno de los Estados Miembros y su desarrollo en lo que se podra denominar regulacin secundaria. Por ejemplo, en el Banco de Espaa se desarrolla una nueva circular en este mbito. Esto supone, sin duda, un reto para el lenguaje XBRL. No obstante, como suele ocurrir en la mayora de los casos en los es preciso afrontar retos importantes, se abre tambin una oportunidad. En este caso, la oportunidad es, desde mi punto de vista, inmejorable. De hecho, algunos aos antes el proceso no estaba suficientemente maduro, y quiz era un poco pronto no ya para el XBRL, sino incluso para CEBS. Ahora bien, el ao que viene, en trminos de la implementacin de Basilea II y de las Normas Internacionales de Informacin Financiera, ser ya demasiado tarde. En el contexto europeo la oportunidad est ah, y me atrevera a decir que es una cuestin de ahora o nunca. XBRL y su papel en la economa global Hasta ahora me he referido al contexto europeo, y he tratado de poner de manifiesto las ventajas asociadas al estndar XBRL. Permtanme que, antes de entrar a valorar nuestra experiencia en Espaa, dedique alguna reflexin al papel de XBRL en la economa global. Por concretar algo ms, es relevante lo que les he contado hasta ahora para Argentina y para otros pases de Latinoamrica? Desde mi punto de vista la respuesta es s, y, al menor, hay tres razones de peso. En primer lugar, y aunque pueda parecer una obviedad, el imparable proceso de globalizacin financiera al que estamos asistiendo en las ltimas dcadas no es un fenmeno exclusivo de Europa, sino que se est produciendo a una escala mundial. De hecho, Europa, por sus especiales caractersticas polticas, se podra considerar como un laboratorio en el que poner a prueba los desarrollos necesarios en el sistema financiero global para lograr compaginar con xito, de un lado, las soberanas nacionales, y de otro, el funcionamiento eficiente de los mercados financieros y de las entidades que operan en ellos. En segundo lugar, porque los dos grandes desarrollos regulatorios que impulsan el inters en las posibilidades de la tecnologa XBRL en Europa son dos fenmenos cuyo mbito es global. Es decir, Basilea II y las Normas Internacionales de Informacin Financiera tienen un alcance universal y, en este sentido, afectan tambin a esta regin. En tercer lugar, porque las crecientes demandas de informacin por parte de los supervisores y de los mercados suponen una mayor complejidad, tanto para los generadores de la informacin, es decir, para las entidades, como para los usuarios de la misma. Es decir, an obviando los procesos de globalizacin a los que me he referido, XBRL tiene sentido como un mecanismo de racionalizacin de la gestin de la informacin financiera. En este sentido, si finalmente el estndar XBRL solo se aplicara en Espaa para la informacin que las entidades bancarias remiten al Banco de Espaa, no les quepa duda de que an as, se tratara de una enorme mejora para nuestras entidades y para la institucin que yo represento. XBRL en Espaa y proyectos del Banco de Espaa al respecto Permtanme que aborde, brevemente, el ltimo de los aspectos que querra tratar en el da de hoy, que no es otro que compartir con ustedes la experiencia espaola. Espaa se convirti en una jurisdiccin XBRL en el ao 2004, crendose la asociacin XBRL Espaa. Comenc mi intervencin constatando y motivando el empeo que el Banco de Espaa est poniendo en fomentar el lenguaje XBRL. Buena prueba de ello, en la medida en la que se considera que su adopcin es de inters pblico, es que esta asociacin est presidida, precisamente, por el Banco de Espaa. El principal objetivo de la asociacin es promover la introduccin, adopcin y desarrollo, tanto a nivel nacional como internacional, del lenguaje XBRL, con el propsito que ya les he venido exponiendo: unificar los principios aplicables en la informacin financiera. Detrs de este objetivo se sita el que podra considerarse objetivo primordial de todo este proceso, y del que sin duda se esperan importantes beneficios para quienes participen de l: facilitar la integracin de los mercados financieros tanto espaoles como europeos. Desde que se cre XBRL Espaa hemos experimentado un fuerte crecimiento en el nmero de miembros, hasta totalizar hoy en da unos 40. Las actividades de la asociacin han estado, y estn, relacionadas con la cooperacin entre las distintas agencias regulatorias, lo que se ha establecido como un objetivo principal. Asimismo, se trabaja en el desarrollo de una serie de taxonomas, adems de la decidida e intensa cooperacin que se ha llevado a cabo con las internacionales (por ejemplo, en el mbito de los ya mencionados proyectos de COREP y FINREP). De hecho, XBRL ha sido implementado y est ahora en uso. Por su parte, el Banco de Espaa ha iniciado una serie de proyectos en el terreno de la aplicacin del lenguaje XBRL. El primero de ellos est relacionado con la informacin prudencial que las entidades han de remitir al Banco de Espaa y, en particular, consiste en recibir las declaraciones de aquellas cotizadas en lenguaje XBRL. En su fase inicial, el proyecto se circunscribe a los principales grupos bancarios, pero el objetivo es que progresivamente el resto de grupos bancarios acaben unindose al proyecto. Las entidades que participan en el mismo, y esto es un ejemplo de los ahorros de costes que supone la adopcin de XBRL, pueden reutilizar la informacin para informar a otras agencias como, por ejemplo, la Comisin Nacional del Mercado de Valores. El segundo de los proyectos al que querra hacer referencia tiene que ver con la recepcin de la informacin que en el mbito de la solvencia es requerida por la Directiva comunitaria que implementa Basilea II. Este es un proyecto que ha estado, desde sus orgenes, liderado por XBRL, y la intencin es materializar su desarrollo a lo largo de este ao para, en el siguiente, comenzar a recibir informacin aplicando ya este estndar. Por incidir en los beneficios que aportar este nuevo enfoque, piensen que las entidades espaolas transfronterizas podrn reportar la misma informacin a otros supervisores de la Unin Europea, con el consiguiente ahorro de costes que ello supone. Finalmente, el tercer proyecto que desarrollar el Banco de Espaa est encaminado a recibir la informacin contable supervisora en XBRL, en la medida en la que se est implementando un marco de informacin financiera armonizada en la Unin Europea. En este sentido, y como ya les he mencionado, se est participando activamente en la creacin de la taxonoma FINREP y el proyecto espera desarrollarse a lo largo de 2007. Conclusiones En definitiva, y como pueden observar, la implicacin del Banco de Espaa en este mbito est siendo muy relevante y ello por los motivos que, a lo largo de mi intervencin, he tratado de trasladarles. XBRL es una herramienta, como ya he dicho, que aporta precisin, fiabilidad y rapidez en la transmisin de la informacin financiera, caractersticas que, sin duda, contribuirn a promover un funcionamiento ms eficiente de los mercados financieros. Es ms, XBRL aporta ventajas operativas muy importantes ya que, una de sus grandes virtudes, es que slo necesita una pequea masa crtica para que su implementacin merezca la pena. Es por ello tambin que el Banco de Espaa ha mostrado su inters por este estndar. Es decir, desde la perspectiva espaola, simplemente el xito en los proyectos iniciados por mi institucin respecto del modo en el que las entidades nos comunican la informacin supondr un gran paso adelante. Ahora bien, no es menos cierto que si pensamos en el conjunto de iniciativas que se estn desarrollando en este mbito  en Espaa, en la Unin Europea a travs de CEBS o en otros lugares, como las iniciativas de la SEC- tenemos una herramienta de enorme potencia que, estoy seguro, aportar importantes beneficios a quienes decidamos emplearla. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Speech: Inauguration of the extension building of the Banco de Espaa and the exhibition "150 Years of History of the Bank of Spain"
text: Vigo, 7 February 2006 Conference at the Business Meeting of the Financial Club of Vigo Jaime Caruana Governor of the Bank of Spain First of all, I would like to thank the Financial Club of Vigo for the invitation to participate in one of its business meetings, which have become, on their own merit, a prestigious forum for the dissemination of ideas and debate. I will take this unique opportunity, which coincides with the recent publication of our Quarterly Economic Outlook Report, to reflect with you on the current situation of the Spanish economy within the euro area. I will begin with a very brief reference to the international environment, to continue with a more detailed analysis of the situation of the euro area and some of its structural problems that will serve to establish the framework of the Spanish conjuncture. In 2005, the world economy returned to great strength, suffering only moderately from the significant rise in oil prices. Thus, it is very likely that the global GDP growth rate has exceeded 4%, driven by the still accommodative tone of the economic policy set, the persistence of favourable financial conditions and the consolidation of corporate balance sheets. In the course of last year, the dynamism shown by the United States, despite the slight stumbling of the National Accounts figures for the fourth quarter - which seem to reflect some temporary distortions - and by the Asian economies (including China and India) was transferred -to some extent- to other regions, such as Japan and Europe. to which I will devote special attention later. Among the reasons why higher oil prices have so far had only a moderate impact on the dynamism of the expansion of global activity are the decrease in the degree of energy dependence of the main economies, compared to previous historical episodes, or the fact that the rise in oil prices has been due to the increase in oil prices. to a large extent, to the strength of demand (reflecting the widespread economic boom). However, the maintenance of the high pressure on the demand for this raw material, in a context in which the crude oil extraction and refining industries are operating in conditions close to their maximum capacity level, removes the possibility that this rise in oil prices constitutes a temporary phenomenon. Nevertheless, this phase of expansion in the world economy is expected to continue in the near future, fuelled by favourable monetary and financial conditions, the absence of underlying inflationary tensions and the dynamism of world trade, driven in turn by demand from oil-producing countries. However, the risks surrounding this scenario are predominantly to the downside and are related to the persistence of high oil prices and the possibility of further increases, as well as to a possible unordered correction of global macroeconomic imbalances that could trigger episodes of exchange rate volatility and, eventually, lead to a sharp increase in long-term interest rates. which are currently at unusually low levels. The European Economic and Monetary Union has been one of the areas of the world that has shown weakest growth in 2005, since its rate of growth has probably not exceeded 1.5%. However, as the year progressed, economic activity became stronger. Thus, in the first half of last year, the accumulated appreciation of the euro exchange rate in previous years and the loss of purchasing power of households as a result of the high price of oil were a brake on the expansion of activity in the area. However, in the second half of 2005, the economy began to show signs of becoming more dynamic as demand from abroad drove corporate spending decisions, also stimulated by very favourable financial conditions and recovery in margins. However, despite recent signs of improving European consumer confidence, the absence of clear signs of strengthening private consumption is an element of uncertainty for the consolidation of an environment of sustained growth in activity in the near future. In any case, the outlook for the first half of 2006 points to a rate of growth in output close to or even somewhat higher than the area's potential growth. As I have already indicated for the international context, this scenario is also surrounded by uncertainties arising from the evolution of energy commodity markets and global macroeconomic imbalances. With regard to inflation, developments in the harmonised index of consumer prices in the euro area have reflected changes in oil prices in recent months. For the first months of 2006, a moderate increase in the inflation rate is expected due to the recent upswing in oil prices and the disappearance of some transitory elements that have affected 2005 and is not expected to fall below 2 per cent until well into the year. Despite this, core inflation, i.e. the trend in the prices of the most stable components of the HICP goods basket, has remained low, at rates close to 1.5%. However, in the course of 2006, the perception that high oil prices could remain for a long time tends to increase the risk of translation of higher production costs to final prices, as well as wage tensions, especially if economic activity and the labour market gradually gain strength. Against this background, the Governing Council of the ECB, at its meeting on 1 December, considered that risks to price stability had increased in the medium term and decided to increase key interest rates by a quarter of a point, to 2.25%, after having kept them unchanged for two and a half years at their historical lows. This measure aims to ensure that the temporary deviations observed in the inflation rate above 2% and the perception that inflationary risks have increased are not consolidated in an upward revision of inflation expectations, so that they remain in line with the objective of price stability. In any case, monetary policy continues to show d0 pending further economic data d0 an accommodative tone that will support the progressive strengthening of domestic demand and job creation. The maintenance of monetary and financial conditions favourable to economic growth in EMU as a whole contrasts, however, with the relatively mediocre results obtained in recent years. This apparent contradiction is a powerful reminder that, despite the progress made, Europe has not, for the time being, done all its homework in removing the obstacles that limit its potential growth. In a world where population ageing or rapid technological progress and the rapid incorporation of new regions onto the global economic scene are shaping an increasingly dynamic environment, the fulfilment of the remaining tasks in this area are becoming more pressing every day. It seems to me that there is little doubt that perseverance in introducing policies aimed at promoting the adaptability of the European economy to these changes is an essential ingredient for increasing the levels of prosperity achieved. Indeed, the rigidities afflicting the euro area economy have recently been a hindrance to improving the living standards of its citizens, as suggested by a comparison of per capita income trends in the euro area and in the United States. Thus, the process of bringing the European standard of living closer to the North American one that had occurred between the end of the Second World War and the decade of the 70s, has not only stopped later, but, since the mid-90s, the gap has deepened. These developments justify pausing myself, even if only for a few minutes, to analyze the phenomenon, examining what have been the contributions to the expansion of the per capita product of the area of its two main determinants: the evolution of the use of the labor factor and productivity. As regards the use of the labour factor, it is estimated that average hours worked per capita of working age in EMU currently account for only 77% of those in the United States. In turn, this variable can be decomposed into the product of hours worked per employee, the proportion of employees within the active population and the activity rate. This decomposition allows us to see how each of these three magnitudes contributes to explaining a part of the gap observed in the hours worked by the working-age population as a whole. Firstly, a very important contribution to this differential comes from the fact that each employed person in the euro area works, on average, 15% fewer hours per year than an American employee, which is mainly due to the fact that in our currency area the number of working days is lower, although it is also due to the greater extension of part-time employment and the shorter duration of the working day. Labour. Secondly, the labour force employment rate in EMU is about three percentage points lower than in the United States, since, despite the fact that unemployment has fallen significantly in Europe over the last decade thanks to reforms in labour markets and social benefit systems, the decline in the unemployment rate has been even greater in the United States. Finally, although the reforms promoted in Europe have also had a positive impact on the participation rate, bringing it closer to the level of the United States, the differential between the two areas still stands at around ten percentage points. Various explanations have been provided to explain this lower use of labour resources in Europe. One of the most frequently heard attributes this fact to individual preferences that prioritize leisure more than in the United States. Without completely denying the validity of this hypothesis, I find more convincing other explanations that associate the phenomenon with the disincentives caused by certain features present in the tax systems, and social benefits, which discourage participation and demand for employment. The evidence in this regard justifies policies aimed at reducing these distortions, in order to tend to reduce the gap between the United States and EMU in the use of the labour factor. As for the level of productivity, which is the second and last element in which the per capita product is decomposed, not only is there also a notable differential between the United States and EMU, but it has registered a substantial expansion since the 90s of the last century. The evolution of productivity can be analyzed from that of its two components, that is, the intensity in the use of the capital factor d0 which is usually measured as the quotient between the capital stock and the number of hours worked d0 and the technological progress or total productivity of the factors. Analysis of such a breakdown provides strong evidence that both components of productivity have in the recent past performed less dynamically in EMU than in the United States. Specifically, on the one hand, the strong growth in employment registered since the mid-90s and the increase in the weight of less qualified workers within the total have resulted in a slowdown in productivity. Moreover, the scarcity of incentives for innovation and the existence of barriers to the diffusion and use of new information and communication technologies, especially in the services sector, have prevented the euro area from taking full advantage of the technological revolution. In conclusion, widening the spread between per capita output in Europe and the United States requires that priority be given to policies aimed at promoting both greater use of labour and increased productivity. Thus, more intense job creation and the increase in the participation rate require the implementation of ambitious reforms in the labour market and social protection systems. For its part, the promotion of productivity requires a very broad set of measures that, without wishing to be exhaustive, include the improvement of education systems - so that they are more in tune with the needs of companies - reforms aimed at increasing the degree of efficiency in the markets for products and services, or the creation of more favourable conditions for innovation and the adoption of new technologies. In 2000, the European Council in Lisbon took up these priorities and set as a strategic objective, I quote, to make Europe 'the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth with more and better jobs and greater cohesion' within ten years. In the spring of last year, the European Council examined the degree of compliance with the objectives of the Agenda outlined five years earlier in the Portuguese capital, concluding that, although progress has been made in the use of the labour factor, the overall balance sheet is not satisfactory. In particular, productivity developments have fallen short of expectations. In this particular area, the European Council judged, in its March 2005 review, that the pace of innovation and adoption of new technologies in Europe has been too low, entrepreneurship has lacked dynamism and the degree of market integration is far from desirable levels. The diagnosis of European leaders pointed out how the excess of simultaneous objectives and the lack of definition of clear priorities between them have contributed adversely to progress in achieving the goals set out in the Agenda. To these causes should be added, in addition, the lack of unequivocal political commitment on the part of the Member States. In the light of this analysis, the Heads of State and Government decided that efforts should be concentrated on areas that have the most favourable impact on economic growth and job creation. In addition, European leaders considered it appropriate to delineate more clearly the division of responsibilities between the Community and national levels. At Community level, the Commission has presented a Programme containing the actions required at EU level to achieve the final objectives. The Programme sets as priorities the creation of a genuine single market for services, the completion of the European energy market, the reduction of the Community regulatory burden, the improvement of the environment for innovation and the effective liberalisation of international trade. For their part, at national level, it was agreed that the authorities of each Member State would agree on the concrete actions they consider necessary to achieve these goals, and translate them into a document called the National Reform Programme. In these programmes, countries have mostly identified a set of five priority areas for reform. These areas include improving the functioning of labour markets, improving the regulatory environment in which enterprises operate, promoting educational reforms aimed at increasing the quality of education and promoting research and development, and achieving sustainability and quality of public finances. After analyzing the contents of the programs, the European Commission has presented on January 25 an Annual Progress Report in which it analyzes the contents of these documents with a double objective. On the one hand, it tries to identify the elements that contribute most to achieving the final objectives, so that they serve as an example for the rest of the countries. On the other hand, the Report puts on the table the areas in which, in the Commission's opinion, countries have shown a lower degree of ambition, proposing concrete actions to correct these deficiencies. To sum up, I am convinced that the process that has been initiated is a promising starting point for the relaunch of the Lisbon Agenda. However, it is difficult to know to what extent these proposals constitute sufficient instruments to achieve the objectives set, since, ultimately, the will of the social partners and, above all, of the political authorities to act decisively will continue to be an essential ingredient for the success of the future prosperity of the European economy. It is therefore essential that the various actors are aware that their well-being depends on the implementation of a wide range of structural reforms, in a context of macroeconomic policies that favour sustained growth. In particular, the cycle of economic expansion that seems to be approaching should not be wasted, since the phases of greater dynamism of activity allow to minimize the possible short-term costs of the reforms. The Spanish economy shares some of the structural features characteristic of the euro area economies that I have just described. Thus, for example, in relation to the various components that explain the behaviour of per capita income, the most recent estimates show that, although Spain has a somewhat more advantageous position than the European one in terms of the use of the labour factor, productivity per hour is at levels below the average of the EMU countries. without any improvements in this ratio in recent years. Therefore, the programme of structural reforms resulting from the Lisbon Agenda is particularly relevant to strengthen and give sustainability to the process of convergence of the Spanish economy. But before turning to this subject, on which I will return at the end of my speech, I would like to take a few minutes to comment on the situation of the economy at the beginning of 2006. Despite the similarities with the euro area, the results of the Spanish economy in terms of growth in recent years have been closer to those of the US economy than to those of the central core of EMU countries. The year 2005 was no exception in this regard. During the past year, the economy achieved a growth of 3.4% of GDP, prolonging the long decade of continuous expansion that began in the mid-nineties. In addition, growth in activity exceeded that recorded in 2004 and showed a certain upward trend throughout the year, which would have stabilised in the last quarter with a year-on-year increase of 3.5%, the same as in the previous quarter. In terms of composition, domestic demand grew by around 5 per cent in 2005, with a significant contribution from consumption and construction expenditure, which also included investment in equipment; On the other hand, external demand partially offset this growth with a negative contribution of 1.8 percentage points. Behind the new growth of the economy in 2005 are the same supply and demand stimuli that, with varying intensity, have been operating since the beginning of the expansionary phase. These stimuli have led, on the one hand, to a high rate of growth in domestic demand, especially that of households, which has intensified in recent years. On the other hand, the growth potential has also expanded, allowing an expansive response of production. Among the factors that have facilitated the increase in the productive capacity of the economy, the most important has been the increase in the supply of labour, in which various phenomena have converged in the last ten years, such as the reduction of structural unemployment, the upward trend in the activity rate - especially of women - and, Finally, the entry of immigrant workers, a phenomenon that has reached great prominence since 2000. In this regard, the latest data from the Labour Force Survey have confirmed that the group of workers active in the labour market increased by 3.2 per cent in 2005, a rate that combines a very strong increase in the foreign population, of more than 20 per cent, albeit within a trend towards moderation, and a further increase in the participation rate of women. The increase in labour supply has made it possible for the boost in demand to have resulted in growth in job-generating activity. Thus, in 2005, it is estimated that the number of jobs rose by 3.1%, prolonging the period of low productivity growth. There is no doubt that the increase in employment has been one of the pillars on which the strength of domestic spending has been based, since it has allowed the growth of household disposable income to remain around 3% in recent years. Along with this stimulus, membership of the Monetary Union has provided an anchor to inflation expectations and has placed interest rates at low levels, set according to the needs of the euro area as a whole, which have given considerable slack to the monetary and financial conditions of the Spanish economy. Only in the final part of 2005 has there been a slight tightening of these conditions, following the recent rate hike implemented by the ECB. During the past year, in addition, the stock markets experienced significant increases, which contributed additionally to maintaining household spending through the revaluation of their financial wealth, although the most powerful effects have continued to have their origin in the increases in house prices, which, despite pointing to a beginning of slowdown, have continued to grow at double-digit rates. As a result of the increase in the value of their wealth and the maintenance of high income expectations, household spending grew similarly to 2004, close to 4.5%. However, in the second half of the year there has been a trend towards moderation in consumption, which has mainly affected some items, such as car purchases. Residential investment, the other component of household spending, also grew at rates close to 6% in 2005, further driven by the low cost of financing, although there are also some signs of slowdown in this case. Even so, everything indicates that households again spent in 2005 above the growth of their resources, so that their financial situation experienced a certain additional stress, characterized by the fall in the savings rate, the increase in their financing needs - when this has traditionally been a sector with the capacity to finance other sectors of the economy - and an increase in indebtedness, which exceeded 110% of disposable income. Although households continue to enjoy a sound financial position, supported by the increase in their net wealth, the sensitivity of their spending decisions to changes in the evolution of crucial variables, such as interest rates or house prices, has increased. In this sense, the slowdown pointed out by house prices in 2005, if confirmed in the coming months, could facilitate an orderly and gradual absorption of the existing overvaluation in this market. This trend would facilitate a progressive adjustment of household spending towards rates compatible with the evolution of their income and, therefore, more sustainable in the medium term and compatible with the necessary change in trend in the expansion of their debt. The remaining components of construction investment also recorded significant increases in 2005. The tender figures point towards a recovery in infrastructure spending. For their part, estimates of non-residential investment, together with the increase in investment in equipment, illustrate the recovery experienced by private productive investment last year - perhaps the most positive development of 2005 - although in the course of it the strong initial rebound tended to lose intensity. In this way, business spending seems to have responded, at least partially, to circumstances, in principle, very favorable to the increase in investment, such as the low cost of financing, the healthy situation of the business accounts and the significant generation of income in the sector. It is very likely that the determining element of this change has been the improvement in demand prospects, although in this sense, there is a risk that these prospects may be affected by the difficulties that Spanish products are having in maintaining their market shares. The most recent confidence indicators also show some signs of hesitation that will need to be closely monitored. As I pointed out earlier, in contrast to the strength of demand from households and firms, the foreign sector made a strongly negative contribution to output growth in 2005. Exports of goods barely experienced positive growth, despite the pull of foreign markets, since they could not overcome the strongly negative results of the first quarter during the year. And, although tourism revenues did show a clearer improvement from the spring, they only partially offset the weakness in goods sales. Imports of goods and services, meanwhile, continued to grow at rates well above those of final demand, particularly with payments for tourism. These trends, which have led to a substantial widening of the trade deficit, have been combined with the deterioration shown by the items corresponding to income and net transfers abroad, so that the nation's need for financing has reached levels close to its historical highs. Although this sharp increase in the external imbalance can be attributed, in part, to factors specific to the economic situation, such as the relatively maturing state of the Spanish economic cycle, the growth in investment in equipment or the increase in energy prices, there are clear indications that the deterioration of the external position goes beyond what these elements would justify. And it is also rooted in accumulated losses of competitiveness. The competitiveness of an economy is a complex concept to measure, which has multiple dimensions, the effects of which are best judged through the overall results achieved. Thus, the loss of competitiveness can be identified through the fall in share in export markets and in the domestic market, the breadth and rapid growth of the external deficit, and the extent to which this deficit corresponds more to a weakening of savings than to an increase in productive investment. Some of these indications are present in the case of Spain. As for the causes that fuel the losses of competitiveness, they are also multiple, from the geographical and productive specialization of exports -which, in the case of Spanish products, makes it difficult to take advantage of the greater dynamism of some sectors and some countries-, to the maintenance of price and cost growth differentials that, On the one hand, they damage the ability of our products to maintain positions in foreign markets and, on the other, they reduce export profitability. The different measures of the inflation differential provide different results, depending on the price index with which they are calculated. In general, those related only to tradable goods tend to result in smaller spreads, reflecting the effects of increased exposure to competition on pricing, while those covering larger parts of the economy are more representative of inflationary tensions as a whole. Among the latter, the inflation differential between Spain and EMU based on consumer prices was 1.2 percentage points in 2005, above the average recorded since the establishment of monetary union, reaching 1.5 points in December. Given the leading price indicator for January, this spread could have widened to an all-time high since the creation of EMU. The most worrying aspect of this high differential is the persistence it shows both in terms of its magnitude and its composition. In particular, the wide differential in the case of services prices stands out, which reflects the importance of the phenomenon of dual inflation in Spain, associated with the lower degree of competition that exists, in general, in some services markets in which there has been a continuous expansion of margins. In fact, when the inflation differential is analysed from the point of view of the contribution of labour costs and business margins, it is found that it is precisely services and construction - which is not represented in the consumer price index - that are the activities where margins have expanded the most. as a result of high demand pressure, combined with uncompetitive market structures. Labour costs have also helped to sustain the inflation differential. The evolution of wages in Spain can be considered moderate when compared with their historical patterns and with increases in producer prices. However, the growth rate of nominal wages has been much higher than those recorded in the countries with which Spain competes, resulting in comparatively high increases in labour costs, which put downward pressure on the margins of companies with a presence in international markets. The wage determination system in our country is characterized by favouring little differentiated increases in remuneration between sectors, systematically fixing them at rates of 3%. To this is added the almost generalized existence of wage review clauses, which tend to prolong the inflationary impact of external shocks, such as the increase in energy price prices, making it difficult for the economy to adjust to this type of phenomenon and favoring the accumulation of losses in competitiveness. There is no doubt that the impact of wage increases on competitiveness depends on the importance of labour productivity gains. In this area, however, the situation is not very rosy either, since, as I mentioned earlier, productivity in Spain is even less dynamic than in the monetary union as a whole, where it is already considerably lower than in the United States. It is true that this is partly the result of a pattern of growth heavily focused on labour-intensive activities, such as construction and services, which is in principle consistent with the large supply of labour and the composition of demand. However, when analyzing the evolution of representative measures of technological progress, such as total factor productivity, it is observed, as in the European case, the low growth of productivity in Spain also reflects the low level of technological and productive innovation, the small size of the sectors dedicated to new information and communication technologies, the low diffusion of these technologies in key sectors, such as services, the persistence of rigidities and inefficiencies in some markets, and the insufficient accumulation of human capital. A series of shortcomings that the economy must alleviate in order to be able to compete in the new international environment and continue to progress in real convergence. In any case, the analysis of the economic situation indicates that the Spanish economy has ended 2005 with a trend of dynamism similar to that which has characterized it since the middle of the previous decade, and that it will very likely remain in a range only slightly lower in 2006, in a context of new increases in the supply of labour - since the flows of immigrants are still very high - and monetary and financial conditions that They will remain expansive. However, in order to achieve a projection of this path of growth in the medium and long term, it is essential to straighten out the imbalances that have begun to materialize and for the composition of expenditure to become more balanced, relying less on household spending and slowing the trend towards enlargement of the external deficit. And for this, it is crucial to reverse the process of continued losses of competitiveness through the combined action of effective wage moderation and policies that favor productivity growth and capitalization of the economy, maintaining the process of job creation. The design of economic policy must face these challenges from the privileged position of belonging to the euro area. The macroeconomic and financial stability that characterises EMU provides the most suitable basis from which to achieve a policy mix that is adapted to the specific conditions of the Spanish economy. In this sense, the rise of a quarter point in the basic intervention rate of the European Central Bank in December, which responds to the requirements to guarantee price stability in the area as a whole, is good for the needs of the Spanish economy. This increase will somewhat alleviate the slack in the monetary conditions in which the Spanish economy operates, although these will continue to be considerably expansionary, which will require that the remaining instruments of economic policy, and in particular fiscal policy, have a stabilizing tone aimed at modulating domestic demand pressures. The Update of the Stability Programme - presented on 30 December - which defines the orientation of budgetary policy for the period 2005-2008, points in this direction. In this Update, the estimates and projections of the balance of the Public Administrations have been revised upwards with respect to the latest official figures, so that the surplus for 2005 is now 1% of GDP and the projected for 2006 increases to 0.9% of GDP. This revision, which corresponds to the strong dynamism that public revenues have maintained throughout 2005 and with its logical translation to the fiscal results of 2006, confirms that the greater growth in collection, in relation to that foreseen in the budgetary programming, has been destined to improve the savings of the Public Administrations. The fiscal projections for 2007 and 2008 assume a slight reduction in the surplus, consistent with a significant decline in the debt ratio, which would stand at 36.6% of GDP in 2008, although it is expected that if the implementation of these plans follows the patterns recorded in 2005, higher surpluses could be achieved, in line with the requirements arising from the need to mitigate the imbalances generated by the pressure of domestic demand. Within monetary union, flexibility is essential to adapt efficiently to adverse economic shocks or emerging external technological and commercial challenges. Therefore, the proper design of supply-side and structural reform policies, aimed at promoting flexibility in pricing and income determination mechanisms, productivity growth and the efficient functioning of markets, are of great importance in order to obtain the expected benefits of EMU membership. This is the National Reform Plan, which the Spanish Government approved in October and which contains a set of measures specifically designed to boost productivity growth and job creation, in order to achieve two specific objectives by 2010: to achieve convergence in per capita income with the EU-25 and to place the employment rate at 66%. one point above the current European average. The plan places special emphasis on complementary action in various fields, over a relatively long horizon, an approach that seems appropriate to encourage changes in the productive structure that are necessary to sustain growth in the medium and long term. It is desirable, therefore, that the proposals included in the Plan be concretized in a decisive government action, following a timetable for its implementation. Nor should we forget, however, that there are other important aspects for the flexibility and improvement of the functioning of the Spanish economy - such as the labour market - that would require progress that goes beyond what is included in this package of actions, relating for example to the field of collective bargaining. In short, for the remarkable process of economic growth that Spain has enjoyed in the last decade to be consolidated, and for the expected benefits of EMU membership to be achieved, economic policy and economic agents, in general, must face important challenges. The pattern of growth, the productive structure and, in general, the functioning of the economy must be reoriented to correct the imbalances that have arisen in the expansionary stage and to adapt to the new needs of the global economy, taking advantage of the advantages provided by the favorable situation.
text_original: Vigo, 7 de febrero de 2006 Conferencia en el Encuentro Empresarial del Club Financiero de Vigo Jaime Caruana Gobernador del Banco de Espaa En primer lugar, quiero agradecer al Club Financiero de Vigo la invitacin a participar en uno de sus encuentros empresariales, que se han convertido, por mrito propio, en un foro prestigioso de difusin de ideas y de debate. Esta descomposicin permite comprobar cmo cada una de estas tres magnitudes contribuye a explicar una parte de la brecha observada en las horas trabajadas por el conjunto de poblacin en edad laboral. En primer lugar, una aportacin muy importante a este diferencial proviene del hecho de que cada ocupado de la zona del euro trabaja, por trmino medio, un 15% menos de horas al ao que uno estadounidense, lo que se debe principalmente a que en nuestra rea monetaria el nmero de das laborables es menor, aunque tambin obedece a la mayor extensin del empleo a tiempo parcial y a la duracin ms reducida de la jornada laboral. En segundo lugar, la tasa de empleados dentro de la poblacin activa de la UEM es unos tres puntos porcentuales inferior a la de los Estados Unidos, ya que, pese a que el paro se ha reducido significativamente en la ltima dcada en Europa gracias a las reformas introducidas en los mercados de trabajo y en los sistemas de prestaciones sociales, el descenso de la tasa de desempleo ha sido an mayor en Estados Unidos. Para explicar esta menor utilizacin de los recursos laborales en Europa se han proporcionado explicaciones diversas. Una de las que se escuchan con mayor frecuencia atribuye este hecho a unas preferencias individuales que priman ms el ocio que en los Estados Unidos. Sin negar completamente la validez de esta hiptesis, me parecen ms convincentes otras explicaciones que asocian el fenmeno a los desincentivos provocados por determinados rasgos presentes en los sistemas impositivos, y de prestaciones sociales, que desalientan la participacin y la demanda de empleo. La evolucin de la productividad se puede analizar a partir de la de sus dos componentes, esto es, la intensidad en el uso del factor capital -que suele medirse como el cociente entre el stock de capital y el nmero de horas trabajadas- y el progreso tecnolgico o productividad total de los factores. El anlisis de tal desglose proporciona evidencia slida de que ambos componentes de la productividad han tenido en el pasado reciente un comportamiento menos dinmico en la UEM que en los Estados Unidos.
