Adems, el bajo coste de la financiacin hipotecaria y los factores demogrficos estn contribuyendo adicionalmente a sostener la inversin en vivienda, que se ha mantenido en tasas del 6% a lo largo de los dos ltimos aos. En conjunto, las familias han seguido reduciendo su tasa de ahorro e intensificando sus necesidades de financiacin, lo que se ha traducido en ritmos importantes de crecimiento del crdito, fundamentalmente hipotecario, y en un nuevo aumento de su ratio de endeudamiento. Este se ha situado en el 110% de la renta disponible en 2005, claramente por encima de la media de la UE, aunque lejos todava de las cotas que alcanza en Estados Unidos. Entre los componentes de la demanda interna, la inversin empresarial ha aportado sin duda uno de los elementos ms positivos al panorama reciente de la economa, al haberse recuperado intensamente. A pesar de que las condiciones financiacin venan siendo favorables desde antes, incluso, de la constitucin de la UEM, la inversin productiva haba mostrado un comportamiento muy moderado hasta bien entrada la dcada actual, afectada por diversos factores, relacionados con el proceso de internacionalizacin de las empresas espaolas, sus necesidades de saneamiento interno y las incertidumbres cclicas y de otro tipo que se han sucedido en el entorno econmico global. Sin embargo, desde mediados de 2004, la inversin productiva ha mejorado significativamente su tono, de forma que el componente de inversin en bienes de equipo se ha incrementado un 9,5% en el conjunto del pasado ao. La perspectiva de continuidad de las favorables condiciones de financiacin, a pesar del reciente aumento de tipos de inters, el saneamiento alcanzado por el sector empresarial y una mejora de las expectativas de demanda son los elementos que ayudan a explicar la recuperacin. Tambin en este caso, el mayor crecimiento del gasto ha venido acompaado de una aceleracin del crdito a las actividades productivas y de un mayor endeudamiento empresarial y de la carga financiera asociada, como avanzan los datos de la Central de Balances Trimestral. En contraste con la demanda interna, la demanda exterior neta ha profundizado ligeramente su contribucin negativa al crecimiento en 2005, hasta una media de 1,9 puntos porcentuales, llegando a superar los dos puntos porcentuales en la primera mitad del ao. Esta aportacin refleja tanto el estancamiento sufrido por las exportaciones de bienes y servicios, que apenas se incrementaron un 1% el ao pasado, como el empuje que conservaron las importaciones. En el caso de las exportaciones, destaca especialmente el mal comportamiento de las ventas de bienes, que registraron incluso un ligera contraccin, frente a un crecimiento relativamente dinmico de los mercados exteriores (cercano al 6%). Este comportamiento denota, al margen de posibles efectos transitorios que hayan podido operar en 2005, el impacto negativo de las prdidas acumuladas de competitividad frente a nuestros principales socios comerciales. Este mismo tipo de efectos estaran impulsando las importaciones, que continan creciendo muy por encima de la demanda final, si bien, en este caso, algunos aspectos, como los elevadsimos ritmos de aumento de los pagos por turismo, pueden estar reflejando otro tipo de procesos, relacionados con la convergencia y la integracin de la economa espaola en el exterior. Como es sabido, la prolongacin de esta etapa de expansin, con caractersticas similares durante un perodo dilatado de tiempo, ha hecho que afloren algunos desequilibrios, cuyo agravamiento en 2005 ha ido parejo con la mayor intensidad que ha alcanzado el crecimiento. De una parte, los notables impulsos expansivos que han incidido sobre el gasto de las empresas y, sobre todo, de las familias les han llevado a elevar su gasto, un ao ms, por encima del crecimiento de sus rentas y a incrementar su endeudamiento, como ya he comentado. Este efecto es particularmente significativo en el caso de las familias, en el que destaca, ms que el nivel alcanzado por la ratio de deuda, el ritmo al que esta se est incrementando, que no parece sostenible de forma prolongada. De hecho, el aumento de los pagos por servicio de la deuda ha hecho que el ahorro no destinado a esta fin sea ya prcticamente nulo. Es importante tener en cuenta que la riqueza de las familias se ha revalorizado con el stock de viviendas y con la subida de las cotizaciones burstiles, de forma que el mayor endeudamiento no ha supuesto una mayor fragilidad de su posicin patrimonial, que sigue siendo muy slida. No obstante, el aumento del endeudamiento s ha elevado la vulnerabilidad de los hogares frente a futuros movimientos en los tipos de inters o en otros determinantes del gasto, que podran tener efectos significativos en los segmentos con mayores niveles de endeudamiento, que suelen coincidir con los de menores niveles de renta y mayor propensin al gasto. De otra parte, la notable presin que la demanda ha ejercido sobre la oferta ha contribuido a generar alzas de precios significativas, a pesar de que la respuesta de la oferta ha sido ms dinmica y flexible de lo que en principio caba esperar. Estas presiones de la demanda estn siendo ms potentes sobre algunas ramas productivas, como la construccin y algunos servicios, que son, de hecho, las que ms han incrementado su ritmo de actividad y en las que se ha concentrado la creacin de empleo. An as, al tratarse de actividades relativamente protegidas de la competencia externa, la magnitud alcanzada por las presiones de la demanda ha determinado que los incrementos de precios de estos productos estn siendo sustanciales y las ampliaciones de mrgenes empresariales muy significativas y persistentes. Adems, estos aumentos de precios se combinan con las inercias existentes en la formacin de salarios, reforzndose mutuamente y transmitiendo las presiones de costes hacia el resto de ramas de actividad. La combinacin de esta situacin interna, propicia a las alzas de precios y costes, con las tensiones procedentes de los mercados exteriores y en particular con el aumento del precio del petrleo y la moderada depreciacin del tipo de cambio ha configurado un panorama desfavorable, desde el punto de vista del comportamiento de los precios, en 2005, que se ha extendido a los primeros meses del ao actual. As, el IPC finaliz el pasado ao con una tasa interanual del 3,7% en diciembre (y un aumento del 3,4% en el conjunto del ao) y ha iniciado 2006 con un incremento medio del 4%, en el primer trimestre. Los principales indicadores de precios y costes relativos han recogido este comportamiento y han reflejado importantes prdidas de competitividad, que se han aadido a las acumuladas en el pasado y han terminado afectando negativamente a los flujos de comercio de bienes y servicios con el exterior, como ya he sealado. La notable ampliacin que ha registrado el dficit exterior en 2005, cuando la necesidad de financiacin ha alcanzado una cota mxima del 6,5% del PIB, resume las consecuencias tanto directas como las canalizadas a travs de las prdidas de competitividad del fuerte movimiento expansivo de la demanda. Aunque hay elementos transitorios que han contribuido a la ampliacin del dficit en 2005 especialmente, el encarecimiento del petrleo parece claro que los elementos asociados al ciclo expansivo de la economa son los que explican fundamentalmente este deterioro. La constatacin de la existencia de estos desequilibrios y de su ampliacin en 2005 abren interrogantes sobre la posibilidad de que sigan amplindose en el futuro, o de que se desencadenen procesos de ajuste ms o menos bruscos que tiendan a corregirlos. En este aspecto, la nueva situacin definida por la pertenencia de Espaa a la UEM nos sita en un terreno novedoso, en el que las experiencias anteriores de correccin de ciclos expansivos ya no proporcionan indicaciones adecuadas sobre la evolucin ms probable en las circunstancias actuales. En cualquier caso, es importante valorar en qu medida las tendencias con las que se ha iniciado el ejercicio actual pueden ayudar a una correccin de estos desequilibrios. A lo largo de los tres primeros trimestres de 2005, el PIB experiment una suave aceleracin, que lo llev a tasas interanuales del 3,5% en los meses de verano. En los meses finales del ao, se observ, sin embargo, una cierta estabilizacin que podra estar apuntando a un posible punto de inflexin en la tendencia ascendente de la actividad. A lo largo del ao, la demanda nacional registr una tenue desaceleracin, que se acentu algo en el ltimo trimestre, en el que se percibi tambin una correccin algo ms fuerte de la aportacin negativa de la demanda exterior. La informacin coyuntural disponible sobre el inicio de 2006 es todava muy escasa y, adems, como es propio de un momento en el que podra estar teniendo lugar un cambio de tendencia, no es unnime en cuanto a las seales que aporta. Algunos datos, como los correspondientes a las encuestas de opinin de los primeros meses del ao o las matriculaciones de ese perodo, parecan apuntar con alguna claridad hacia una posible desaceleracin, especialmente del consumo y aunque, en menor medida, tambin de la inversin que registros posteriores han venido a matizar, en alguna medida, dando una visin ms equilibrada del trimestre. Adems los indicadores disponibles sobre la evolucin del empleo a falta del dato de la EPA apuntan a que este ha tendido a conservar una notable fortaleza. En cualquier caso, existe un cierto consenso entre las instituciones que realizan un seguimiento de la economa espaola de que en 2006 el crecimiento ser algo menor que en 2005. Los motivos que estn detrs de esta proyeccin derivan fundamentalmente de que se espera que los impulsos expansivos por el lado de la demanda se vayan amortiguando y con ellos el gasto. En particular, la desaceleracin del precio de la vivienda, junto con el tono algo menos holgado de las condiciones monetarias, deberan dar lugar a una moderacin del gasto de los hogares, tanto en consumo como en inversin residencial. Sin embargo, como acabo de comentar, la informacin disponible sobre esa desaceleracin es todava tenue. En este contexto, el impulso corrector de los desequilibrios que se deriva de estas tendencias no sera suficiente para contrarrestar las inercias que gestionan los desequilibrios de la economa, sin que pueda descartarse que sigan producindose presiones sobre los precios o que el dficit exterior se ample adicionalmente. En cualquier caso, an cuando la demanda entrase en un proceso de desaceleracin ms marcado, el ajuste de los desequilibrios macroeconmicos por esa sola va resultara posiblemente muy lento. Es por ello por lo que cabe insistir, como he venido haciendo en distintas ocasiones, en la importancia de que las polticas econmicas que quedan bajo soberana nacional asuman su papel estabilizador y contribuyan en la medida de lo posible a reconducir los ritmos de crecimiento de la demanda hacia niveles sostenibles en el medio plazo. De otra parte, las polticas de oferta deben encaminarse a mejorar la respuesta de la economa ante las presiones de la demanda, flexibilizando la oferta y creando las condiciones para un crecimiento basado en el avance de la productividad y no nicamente del empleo. A medio plazo, un funcionamiento ms eficiente y flexible es una condicin necesaria para que la economa espaola alcance todos los beneficios que cabe esperar de su pertenencia a la UEM, en trminos de convergencia real. En el planteamiento de la poltica fiscal es importante tener en cuenta que las condiciones monetarias, ligadas a la situacin de la zona del euro, seguirn siendo relativamente holgadas para las necesidades de la economa durante algn tiempo, an cuando la poltica monetaria se oriente ahora hacia un tono ms neutral. Sin duda, la consecucin de un supervit del 1,1% en 2005 en las cuentas pblicas es un resultado muy positivo y es indicativo de la voluntad de las autoridades fiscales de destinar los recursos impositivos no esperados a mejorar el saldo y no a atender mayores gastos. Es preciso que esta orientacin se mantenga y se refuerce con el objetivo de contribuir en la medida de lo posible al control de las presiones de demanda. Estos saldos superavitarios y el consiguiente descenso de la deuda pblica que conllevan son tambin adecuados para preparar los retos que en el futuro se derivarn del envejecimiento de la poblacin. En el caso de las polticas de oferta, la orientacin adoptada por las acciones emprendidas por el Gobierno, resumidas en el Plan Nacional de Reformas, es adecuada porque parte de un diagnstico acertado de las deficiencias y rigideces estructurales que afectan a la economa, centradas en el bajo crecimiento de la productividad, y establece un marco global para acometer las medias correctoras. No obstante, la ausencia de medidas decididas en el mbito del mercado de trabajo y de la negociacin colectiva es una laguna importante, que sera preciso cubrir.

Title: The Spanish banking system: recent trends and future challenges
text: Santander, 23 June 2006 The Spanish banking system: recent trends and future challenges "The new environment of the financial sector". Association of Economic Information Journalists (APIE) d0 Men8endez Pelayo International University (UIMP) Gonzalo Gil Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain It is a pleasure for me to be here today, one more year, with all of you. As you can imagine, today is probably one of my last public interventions as Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain, and I am especially pleased that the forum in which it is framed is the conference that has been organized annually by the Association of Economic Information Journalists (APIE) at the Men8endez Pelayo International University. Briefly reviewing the conferences I have given in this forum, I have seen that the topics discussed have ranged from the presence of Spanish banks in Latin America, and in general of its internationalization process, to issues related to good corporate governance, through an analysis of recent regulatory changes, such as, for its relevance, the International Financial Reporting Standards or Basel II. These are, in my opinion, areas that have marked the current situation of our banking sector in recent years. Precisely, the objective that I propose today is to assess what has been the evolution of Spanish entities over the last few years that I have shared with you, as well as to outline some of the possible lines of development that, from my point of view, are open for the future. To this end, I shall divide my speech into two parts. A first in which I intend to review what has been the evolution of the sector in its operations and what the main changes in its regulatory framework. In the second part I will try to explore, with the necessary caution, its possible future evolution. Finally, I intend to conclude with some thoughts on the future of banking supervision within the framework of the European Union. I am aware that this is an ambitious goal and that it is impossible to tackle it in its entirety at a conference. That is why I must warn you in advance that I will leave questions, certainly relevant, in the pipeline, and that in others I will not deepen everything that should be. However, I do hope that my reflections will at least outline the main features that have characterized the banking system over the past six years, as well as some of the issues that will have to be addressed sooner rather than later. I. Evolution of the Spanish banking sector and the regulatory framework over the last six years The banking sector In recent years, there has been an increase in financial and banking activity worldwide, which has been more intense than the growth observed in the real sector of the economy. This strong expansion of banking activity is evident in the Spanish case: the total assets of deposit institutions have grown on an annual average, at a consolidated level, by 14.2% between 1999 and 2005, which means that the level recorded in 1999 has multiplied by just over 2 times. Throughout these years, which in general terms can be considered very favourable for the Spanish economy, nominal GDP has grown, on average annually, by 7.7%. Therefore, the greater dynamism of banking activity with respect to GDP intensifies another of the defining characteristics of the Spanish financial system, that is, its high degree of banking. The main protagonist of the significant increase in banking activity has been the credit granted, and in particular, financing to the private sector. Thus, the average growth of this item between 1999 and 2005 is almost 5 percentage points higher than that recorded for total assets. This explains why, in relative terms, the weight of private sector financing on bank balance sheets rose from 51.7 per cent in 1999 to 64.7 per cent in 2005. This expansionary behavior of credit is closely linked to the real estate sector in the broad sense, that is, to that granted both to families for the purchase of housing and to construction and real estate development companies. If the total credit, including that granted to the Public Administrations, is put in relation to GDP, the degree of banking penetration of the Spanish economy is confirmed, since it goes from 94% of GDP in 1999 to 120% in 2004. Compared to other neighbouring countries, in particular the euro area, it can be seen that despite the greater dynamism shown by GDP in Spain, the ratio of credit granted to GDP has evolved more rapidly in our country (growing by 27 percentage points in Spain to 7 percentage points in the euro area). The increased activity, especially for some entities that have intensified their process of geographical expansion outside their traditional scope of action, is related to the increase in the number of offices, which have grown, in cumulative terms, by 6.7% from 1999 to 2005. Thus, some entities, and especially in a context of strong competition and low interest rates, have set as an objective to increase their turnover, considering the extension of their network of offices a relevant tool to do so. However, this strategy based on the expansion of the commercial network in Spain has not been shared by all entities, at least not throughout the analysis period. This is explained, among others, by two factors. First, it is the result of the restructuring processes that have occurred in certain banking groups that have undertaken merger processes during the period. Second, some entities have focused their efforts on its expansion internationally. On the other hand, the increase in the number of employees has been, in general terms, more moderate, presenting a cumulative rate of change of 2.1% between 1999 and 2005. In fact, over the years there have been at least two developments that help explain this evolution: moderation in the increase in the costs of entities, in an attempt to improve operational efficiency, necessary to act successfully in a market as competitive as Spain; and a process of renewal of the workforce, so that the recruitment of new staff has occurred simultaneously with the early retirement processes. The dynamism of the activity of Spanish depository institutions is not, however, limited to credit activity, although this is, as I have already mentioned, a prominent protagonist. Thus, there are two additional lines in which greater activity has been observed in recent years, and which in reality are not exclusive issues of the Spanish banking system: the development of new products and activities other than traditional ones, and the increase in internationalization. The technological developments that have occurred during the last decades, as well as the new habits and financial culture, have contributed to the sophistication of the banking business, which has a greater capacity to offer new products. Thus, for example, beyond their traditional activities, entities today offer a wide range of services related to insurance and wealth management. As for insurance activity, around 37% of the assets of all insurers belong to companies dependent on deposit institutions. With regard to wealth management, assets managed by companies dependent on depository institutions have shown a growing profile since 1999, almost doubling those managed in 2005. The trends pointed out are consistent with the fact that, since the mid-90s, in Spain, as has also happened in many other countries around us, there has been a certain process of financial disintermediation. This process, despite the increase in insurance and pension fund activities, has been led by the boom in collective investment, and in particular investment funds. In Spain it could be said that financial disintermediation has been supervised by deposit institutions, which have found it beneficial to guide certain clients from the most traditional bank liabilities towards collective investment. In this sense, around 80% of the assets of investment funds are controlled by deposit institutions. The greater sophistication of the business is also evident, for example, in the field of asset securitization, a market that in recent years has developed with great intensity in Spain. Thus, the outstanding balance of asset-backed securities in 2005 is almost 10 times higher than in 2000. The securitisation of liabilities of credit institutions, especially mortgage bonds, has proved very relevant, and in 2005 it accounted for 38% of the outstanding balance of securitisation bonds. In fact, the mortgage bond market has grown more strongly, and in 2005 its outstanding balance was almost 14 times higher than five years earlier. The importance of asset securitisation processes can be seen by the fact that their relative weight in the loan portfolio has increased from 2% in 1999 to 7.5% in 2005; while mortgage bonds account for 12.4% of total mortgage loans, almost double that six years earlier. The expansion of the Spanish securitisation market is part of a context in which the European market has also been dynamic, although Spain has been among the top positions by volume of total issues. In our case, this dynamism can be explained based on a set of changes in regulatory matters, as well as by a series of demand factors whose analysis is outside the scope of this conference. However, the strong expansion of this type of activity is not understandable without considering the remarkable growth that, as I have already pointed out, credit activity has experienced in Spain, since through the securitization of assets institutions have found a way to finance it. I mentioned earlier that the changes that have occurred in the Spanish banking system in recent years not only imply the increase in banking activities and the development of new products, but also a process of internationalization of the activity. Largely enhanced by an incessant process of technological advance, which has made it possible to significantly reduce the transaction costs derived from operations at an international level, there has been a process of globalization of financial activity, and in particular, of internationalization of banking entities. These developments, shared by the financial and banking systems of a number of countries, are reflected in Spain in the fact that, of the consolidated balance sheets of Spanish depository institutions, the relative importance of business abroad rose from 19.4% in 1999 to 23.8% in 2005. I do not discover anything new if I tell you that the main destination of the international expansion of Spanish banking was, initially, Latin America. Although the presence in the region continues to be very relevant, as evidenced by the fact that the financial assets of Spanish depository institutions in Latin America accounted for 28% of the total in 2005, there has recently been a significant change in the composition of financial assets abroad, increasing the relative importance of the European Union (from 41% in 1999 to 64% in 2005). This change in orientation, and the good performance of Latin American economies in recent years, explain why the risk profile of financial assets abroad shows a downward trend. This trend has been observed since 2001, when this risk profile reached its maximum in the period in relation to the problems experienced by the Argentine economy. In any case, it does seem relevant to highlight some aspects that have marked the process of international expansion of Spanish banks, and that have contributed to minimizing the risks assumed, especially in those cases in which investments occurred in regions of greater financial instability. I will simply point out four major areas under which these elements are collected. First, expansion has typically occurred through the acquisition of entities long established in and with extensive experience in local markets. Second, acquisitions, preceded by rigorous market and entity analyses, have been of a permanence nature. Third, the Spanish parent companies have addressed substantial improvements in the information, management and risk control systems of the acquired entities. Fourth, and finally, the Bank of Spain has established specific supervision processes. This set of elements has contributed to limiting the risks assumed in the expansion processes. In summary, from 1999 until today, there has been a strong increase in the activity of Spanish depository institutions. This growth, although it has been led by the increase in credit activity, especially that related to the real estate market in a broad sense, has also been observed, first, in the development of new activities other than those typically banking and, second, in the process of internationalization of Spanish entities. During these years of growth in activity, there have been no major problems for the Spanish financial system. In fact, there has been no bank failure, but only the orderly liquidation of an entity that, moreover, did not result in losses for depositors. The Argentine crisis also had a very limited impact on the affected banks, demonstrating their ability to withstand large-scale adverse shocks. However, from the developments that I have mentioned, elements of attention are derived that the managers of the entities must take into account. The strong growth of credit, particularly that linked to the real estate sector, and the increasing concentration of credit to developers in the portfolios of banks are two particularly relevant examples. However, and before analyzing in the second part of my speech the changes that banks are facing, I would like to emphasize that the solidity shown in general terms by the Spanish banking sector is confirmed when analyzing its profitability and solvency. Thus, the return on equity has risen from 15.2% in 1999 to 16.1% in 2005, always showing a level substantially higher than the yield on Spanish public debt. For its part, the result before tax on average total assets has remained stable at levels close to 1.2%. The strength shown in terms of ROE occurs despite the narrowing of operating margins (intermediation, ordinary and operational) that entities have been experiencing, basically as a result of low interest rates and the strong competitive pressure existing in the Spanish market. In fact, the good profitability situation of Spanish banks is partly explained by the aforementioned expansionary behaviour of activity. However, this is not the only explanatory factor and the managers of the entities have become fully aware that operating successfully in such a competitive market requires doing so from an efficient behavior. Although this is a challenge that remains open for the future, operating expenses on total assets show a decreasing profile, from 2.5% in 1999 to 1.65% in 2005. As a result, the efficiency ratio of depository institutions, at consolidated level, reached 53.6%, some 12 percentage points less than in 1999. Compared to other neighbouring countries, and in particular with the euro area average (MU12), the ROE of Spanish banks is around 5 percentage points higher, being 3.3 percentage points higher than for the average of the enlarged EU (EU25). In terms of the efficiency ratio, the comparison is also favourable for Spanish banks, which improve the average ratio for euro area countries by almost 10 points, and by 5.5 for those in the enlarged EU. For its part, the solvency ratio of Spanish depository institutions is well above the regulatory minimum: 3.1 percentage points in 1999 and 2.8 percentage points in 2005. This slack is extended if the solvency ratio is calculated using the Basel regulations, less demanding than the Spanish one, reaching 4.1 percentage points in 2005 over the minimum required. The soundness of the solvency of Spanish banks is confirmed by an analysis of the basic ratio, well above the minimum 4% required, although it nevertheless goes from 9.1% in 1999 to 7.9% in 2005. As can be seen from the above data, over the years there has been a slight downward trend in the solvency ratios of Spanish deposit institutions, since, in a context of strong credit growth, capital requirements have put pressure on the ratio. An element to which I will refer later in a little more detail and which is related to the above, is the need to maintain a high quality of capital, both total and first category, since it is not only enough to guarantee its slack with respect to the regulatory minimum. Compared to the euro area average, the situation for Spanish banks is favourable, but not as clearly as in the case of profitability. Thus, the total coefficient in 2005 was 0.7 percentage points above that recorded for the euro area average and only 0.3 percentage points higher than the average figure for the enlarged EU. Moreover, the basic solvency ratio is slightly below that for both the euro area average (0.45 percentage points) and the enlarged EU (0.5 percentage points). In any case, it should not be forgotten that the solvency of Spanish depository institutions is reinforced by a solid system of provisions for insolvencies. In this sense, in Spain provisions have always been part of the prudential regulation framework, since experience has shown that, in a situation of generalized default crisis, the problems could be reflected in those entities that, despite having a solid solvency ratio, did not have their assets well valued. The provision system has changed several times since 1999, first to incorporate what became known as statistical provision, and second to comply with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). These changes have been compatible with the maintenance of a macro-prudential element within our system. Changes to the regulatory framework The changes that we have addressed during this stage in the area of provisions are part of a broader context of reform of the accounting regulations in force to date. In fact, IFRS, together with Basel II, constitute the main changes in regulatory matters that have taken place not only in Spain, but internationally, in recent years. The Banco de Espa96a has participated very actively in both processes of which, for just a few minutes, I would like to recall their main characteristics. In the context of the development of measures that can enhance and promote the European single market, last year the European Union approved a Regulation by which all companies with securities listed on a regulated market in the Union, including therefore credit institutions, had to prepare their financial information on a consolidated basis following IFRS. For its part, the Bank of Spain developed Accounting Circular 4/2004, which entered into force on January 1, 2005, and whose main objective is to modify the accounting framework in force in Spain until that date, and which had not been substantially altered in the last 14 years, to adapt it to these International Financial Reporting Standards. It is not my intention to address now what modifications have been introduced, let alone go into the technical aspects of the new Circular. However, I would like to give you some idea of the magnitude of the change from a conceptual point of view, while indicating that the data available to the Bank of Spain show that, in quantitative terms, the impact has been very limited. As I say, from a qualitative point of view, Circular 4/2004 does introduce relevant modifications. Without wishing to be exhaustive, let me point out four that I consider particularly important. First, we move from an accounting model in which the rules emphasized the protection of the funds that were entrusted to the entities, to a new approach that emphasizes information to the market, since it is considered that if investors have adequate information, it will also be useful for other users of it. Second, progress is being made from a model that gave more importance to the development of detailed rules, to a more flexible one, which is based on the development of principles, and which therefore transfers greater responsibility to the administrators of the entities in the preparation of financial information. Third, the use of fair value for the preparation of financial information is deepened, although it has been limited to cases in which there are liquid and deep markets. Finally, Circular 4/2004 has given greater weight to the economic fund of operations over and above their specific legal form. These conceptual modifications, which only reflect a part of the existing ones, have required significant efforts to adapt to the entities and to the Bank of Spain itself. Recognizing that common accounting standards are essential for Europe and its single market project, the Bank drew up the above-mentioned Circular with several objectives in mind. First, try to provide certainty to Spanish entities during the adaptation process. Second, to encourage the adoption of the most prudent accounting approach when accounting standards offered several options. Finally, and without prejudice to the EU Regulation, extend the scope of these rules, as regards the preparation of their prudential statements, to all credit institutions and to annual accounts at individual level. Behind this decision is the intention to ensure that the playing field in which Spanish entities compete is not altered by the application of one or another accounting option. In short, Circular 4/2004 not only allows compliance with the European Union Regulation, which, as you can imagine, is an essential requirement, but also ensures that the Spanish accounting framework remains consistent with best practices in risk management. The reform of provisions, to which I have already referred, is a good example of this. The second of the regulatory changes to which, due to its magnitude, I would like to refer is the process of reforming the framework related to the international convergence of capital measures and rules, better known as Basel II. As you all know, it is now about six years since the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision began a process of reform of the 1988 Capital Agreement, which is currently in force. The 1988 Agreement, which essentially sought to capitalise banks while promoting a competitive playing field, has been unquestionably successful. In fact, it has been adopted by more than 100 countries and has become an essential reference. However, since 1988 the process of change in the financial markets has been remarkable. This very market dynamic is what justifies that Basel I has become obsolete, widening the gap between regulatory capital and the risk incurred by entities. The need to modify this framework was not only recognized by the Basel Committee, but there was a high degree of consensus on this issue. Basel II seeks a greater link between the regulatory capital that institutions must maintain and their level of risk. To promote better risk management, institutions that wish to do so have been allowed, subject to compliance with certain minimum requirements, to develop their own risk measurement models. The new Agreement also introduces incentives for proper performance in areas as important as operations based on long time horizons or based on the best standards in the field of corporate governance, among others. These incentives are reinforced by the promotion of more qualitative supervision, based on what is known as the risk approach, and by the discipline introduced by the action of financial market participants. The approach adopted by Basel II is comprehensive, insofar as it calls for joint action by the three pillars. That is, the initial and primary responsibility of institutions for the correct management and measurement of risks is reinforced, in the first instance, by the action of the supervisor, and complemented by the discipline introduced by the markets. The comprehensiveness of Basel II can be seen in other elements, such as the consideration of a broad set of risks, the inclusion of new risk mitigation techniques or the development of highly complex issues, such as asset securitization. It should be noted that Basel II was not born with the vocation of being an immutable and generic rule that pretends to be applied by everyone without more. On the contrary, it is an evolutionary and flexible approach. Evolutionary because it cannot be considered as a closed framework, but as additional issues arise that must be incorporated into the framework of capital, it will be done. We are talking about the regulation of a sector that, in essence, is dynamic, and therefore this characteristic is very relevant. As far as flexibility is concerned, this is also an issue that I believe will contribute to its success, because it is difficult to imagine that, not only at international level, but even within each country, the whole set of credit institutions can be treated in exactly the same way. An example of the flexibility provided by Basel II is in relation to the use of internal models, as alternatively a less sophisticated approach, called the standard approach, has been proposed, which is likely to be sufficient for a good number of entities. Finally, although this is not in itself a feature of Basel II, I would like to mention the fact that the new agreement both requires international cooperation between the various banking supervisors. Indeed, this is an area in which the Basel Committee has been, and continues to do, work. I will return to this issue in a few minutes, but allow me to turn now to the second block of my speech, in which I intend to identify some of the challenges that entities will have to consider. II. Looking to the future The elements I have just mentioned, the rate of credit growth and regulatory change, are those that will most imminently entail, in fact they are already doing, changes and adaptations in the operations of Spanish entities. Credit growth and real estate sector Firstly, as I have already pointed out, recent years have been characterised by a strong rate of expansion of lending activity in Spain, especially that related to the financing of activities linked to the real estate sector. Processes of strong credit growth sometimes occur in overly optimistic contexts or encouraged by strong competitive pressures. It is likely that in the Spanish case, both factors have recently been mixed. The risk may arise to the extent that, with the intention of offsetting declining operating margins, institutions have sought to increase volume at the cost of a relaxation in the admission criteria for borrowers. If this were the case, historical experience and empirical studies show us that these expansionary processes usually lead to significant increases in non-performing loans, causing problems for entities when the conditions of the economic environment become less benign. In this regard, therefore, institutions must pay special attention to their credit policies, including the admission and risk management processes. For this, a very relevant complement is stress exercises. There is a growing consensus every day that proper risk management requires assessing the resilience of institutions to the occurrence of different adverse shocks. This is how they can be correctly prepared to face these eventualities with guarantees. The growth of credit, which in itself, as I say, implies potential risks to be monitored, has significantly increased the exposure of Spanish entities to the real estate sector. Thus, on the one hand, financing to families for the purchase of housing has been increased. Although the equity position of households is solid, it cannot be forgotten that their level of indebtedness is at increasingly high levels, making the sector more sensitive to possible adverse changes in the economic environment. This sensitivity is increased by the fact that most of the financing granted is at variable interest rates, which quickly conveys to households the impact of potential changes in interest rates. On the other hand, the concentration in the real estate market is also observed in the increase in the relative weight of the financing granted, within the productive activities, to construction companies, and in particular, to those of real estate development. The concentration of loan portfolios is a worrying element from the supervisory point of view, especially when this concentration occurs in a sector that has shown delinquency rates considerably above the average of the rest of productive activities in previous recessionary phases of the Spanish economy. Moreover, to the extent that banks participate in the capital of real estate development companies, additional risks may arise. Thus, a business such as real estate development, which has a strong cyclical component, would require entities to establish an adequate risk premium to cover the greater potential losses associated. However, the ownership of these companies can generate conflicts of interest that relax the necessary rigor in the establishment of credit policies. I will return to the issue of industrial holdings later, an issue which has often raised some concern among banking supervisors. In short, and as I have pointed out, banks must strengthen their credit policies, as well as their own resources, since these become a fundamental line of defence when problems materialise. The strength of the solvency ratio not only means that equity must grow sufficiently to compensate for the increase in capital requirements resulting from the strong expansion of credit, but that banks must pay particular attention to their quality. In fact, in the face of the materialization of the problems, own resources must not only be sufficient, but also of quality. This quality requires at least two conditions: permanence capacity and loss absorption capacity. Adapting to regulatory changes I have previously pointed out the need for entities to adapt to recent regulatory changes. Indeed, it can be considered that this adaptation process is already being faced by the entities. Basel II, as I have already mentioned, is a sufficiently significant change for some to have described it as a revolution in the field of risk management and measurement. The Basel Committee has sought to promote a real improvement in risk management. As you can imagine, promoting a true risk culture requires an adaptation effort on the part of institutions, which must invest resources in the development of quantitative models for measuring risks. The resources to be invested are both of a technical nature, for example, computer equipment, information management systems or databases; and of a human nature, to the extent that it is necessary to incorporate sufficiently qualified personnel. This effort in terms of resources must also be compatible with the need to contain operating costs, since competing successfully in a market such as Spain, which at the same time is open to international competition, will continue to require doing so from efficiency. However, the changes necessary for the adaptation to Basel II are not only at the quantitative level, but from the qualitative point of view the entities must also deepen in several lines. On the one hand, the bank's senior management must play an increasingly leading role in assuming its responsibilities for risk measurement and management systems. As established in pillar 2 of the new Agreement, it is the senior management of the institutions that is primarily responsible for developing a plan to assess whether the capital is adequate in relation to the risk assumed, as well as for the design of a strategy to maintain it. This requires, among many other considerations, that policies and procedures be defined to manage risks, that a target capital to be maintained be determined and that an adequate internal control structure be established. On the other hand, the senior management of the entities must ensure that all this development does not remain merely formal, but must permeate the daily practice of the entities, making that culture of risk management and control flow throughout the organization. This is a complex task, in which staff training processes must play an important role. The measurement models developed by institutions should not be mere more or less complex statistical developments, which are not used in the daily course of banking activity, but must be incorporated into the business models of institutions. The changes related to Basel II not only affect institutions, but banking supervisors also have important efforts to undertake. These efforts are not only related to the need to understand, check and finally accept the validity of the internal models developed by institutions, but pillar 2 requires us to determine the risk incurred by institutions and, from there, establish the level of solvency with which they should operate. In this sense, and as I have already mentioned, Basel II introduces incentives for a more qualitative supervision that complements the more traditional one based on the revision of the accounting data included in the financial statements of the entities. The need for adaptation requires at least two additional issues, both related to transparency. First, the greater transparency with which we supervisors themselves must act, avoiding that our actions can be interpreted as arbitrary. Secondly, the effort that must be made to fully assimilate that, today, the transparency of institutions, and ultimately market discipline, is an essential complement to developing effective banking supervision. International Financial Reporting Standards pose similar challenges for both institutions and supervisors. In general terms, it can be said that, being a regulation more based on the establishment of general principles than detailed rules, it is sought that the accounting standard ceases to be used as a control mechanism for entities. This implies, therefore, that the responsibility of managers and owners of entities is increased. While Basel II has not entered into force, IFRS has already done so just over a year ago. I believe that throughout this time, both the entities and the Bank of Spain itself have been able to respond reasonably well, rising to the occasion. Thus, apart from the specific problems that may have arisen, as a logical consequence of the implementation of any complex system, from the Bank of Spain we have not detected special tensions in the sector. I would therefore like to take this opportunity to recognise the effort made by Spanish entities. I have no doubt that the response to the implementation of Basel II will be equally fluid. However, having said that, I believe that now is the time to start what has sometimes been called a regulatory pause. That is, the magnitude of the changes advises that we all take time to adapt and digest them properly. Corporate governance I have mentioned on several occasions that the regulatory changes that have occurred in recent years imply for the administrators of financial institutions the assumption of greater responsibilities. In this sense, from the point of view of the good governance of the entities, an issue to which I would like to dedicate a few words, the responsibility and professionalism of bank managers must be the fundamental criteria that, above any other consideration, guide their actions. Good corporate governance has been an area that has captured the attention of regulators and supervisors in different markets in different countries, as well as the industry itself, over the last few years. Unfortunately, well-known cases in which there has been a breach of the basic principles of good governance have contributed to this. These developments, together with the dynamics of the markets themselves, have recently led to the emergence of new initiatives, both internationally and domestically. In the area of banks, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has not only shown its concern about these issues in the development of Basel II, but in February this year updated its recommendations in this area. In Spain, I think everyone is aware that barely a month ago a document was published that, apart from other more or less novel issues, unified the previous codes of good governance existing in our country: the Olivencia code and the Aldama Report. The Banco de Espa96a has actively participated in both initiatives, forming part of the working groups that, in each case, have developed the respective projects. The difficulties that have occurred recently, and which have affected large companies in both the United States and Europe, have not involved financial institutions. I would like to think that, in addition to the good work of the banks themselves, the development of prudential regulation over the last decades has contributed positively to this circumstance. However, despite the above, we must not lose sight of the fact that good corporate governance is very relevant for credit institutions, since the banking business is based on trust. If that principle is broken, the bank will most likely have to stop working. Strengthening trust requires, in the first instance and above other issues, that the managers of the entities act responsibly and professionally, establishing the strategic objectives and corporate values of the entity, and transmitting them throughout the organization. The responsibility of the directors of the entities also requires that they establish effective supervisory mechanisms, using both internal and external auditors, to limit potential conflicts of interest, to establish remuneration policies consistent with the long-term objectives of the entity, to increase due diligence when acting through structures or in jurisdictions that may limit transparency and to communicate to the market all relevant information that is needed so that the discipline can be exercised effectively. The above are just some of the elements, in my view the most important, that must be strengthened to achieve good corporate governance. Among them, today there is a broad consensus on the importance of strengthening information transparency, and therefore, market discipline. In a world like today's, the action of the markets must be understood as an essential complement, to the extent that they have the capacity to reward well-managed entities and punish those that are not. In line with the above, the application of these rules should take into account the specific circumstances (ownership or other) of each type of entity, so that the final result in terms of transparency and market discipline is equivalent. Industrial holdings Allow me to take just a few minutes to raise some ideas about industrial holdings, bearing in mind that, from the point of view of prudential supervision, it is not intended to alter the freedom of choice with regard to the business strategies to be developed, provided that the soundness and solvency of the banking groups is guaranteed. Maintaining industrial participations raises, beyond the diversification of the business itself, positive aspects that should not be disregarded. Thus, if the participation in a certain non-financial company allows entities to obtain first-hand information about the financial situation of the company, its future prospects and the projects it intends to undertake. In relation to the above, and to the extent that there is a capacity to influence the decisions of the company, the entity will be better able to defend its interests as a creditor. However, as I have already pointed out, shareholdings pose management problems, and risks, for banks. Apart from the greater volatility that equity investing may induce in the profit and loss accounts and in banks' capital, in certain circumstances institutions may remain captive by the company's managers. In other words, managers can review the relationship maintained with the entity in response to a potential sanctioning action for their conduct by the entity, when it acts as a shareholder. On the other hand, the entity could have incentives to help the company beyond what would be justifiable in terms of operating in a competitive and efficient market. For example, in adverse cyclical times, when the company may be in difficulty, the bank could be driven to engage in support of the company beyond what a prudent credit policy would advise. In any case, and as I have already said, from the point of view of prudential regulation, what is relevant is the sound and prudent action of institutions, without this affecting, at least in principle, their freedom of choice in terms of their investment policy. However, what is required, among other things, is that an adequate level of capital be maintained in terms of the risks assumed. Basel II, with its more demanding treatment in terms of capital for company holdings (requirements can range from the current 8% to 36%, or even above), will give supervisors more room for manoeuvre. Finally, from the point of view of the possibilities open to institutions, given the fact that they maintain, in some cases, large shares in industrial companies, it is worth asking to what extent there is no risk of distortion of the banking business, traditionally based on the granting of financing based on deposits raised. Again, as was the case with corporate governance rules, this risk, which exists for all institutions, has different characteristics depending on the nature of the entities holding the shares. Medium-long term changes in the banking business: risk transfer From a broader perspective, it is worth considering the extent to which the banking business is changing, and will change in the future. As I have already pointed out in my speech, in recent years we have witnessed a strong process of change in the sector that, driven by technological progress, has allowed institutions to develop and offer new and more sophisticated products, while deepening the development of new risk management techniques. These changes have different implications, but I will focus on two of them. On the one hand, to what extent is the role of banks changing in the development of their financial intermediation work? On the other hand, and in some way related to the above, if the banking business is increasingly sophisticated, what implications does this have from the point of view of the responsibility of the entities and the consumers themselves? With regard to the first of the two issues, let me recall that banks have traditionally been acting not only as financial intermediaries, but also in transforming maturities and amounts, while assuming, among others, the credit risk implicit in operations. In other words, in the development of their traditional work, banks take deposits, typically from their retail clients, to, modifying terms and amounts, grant loans to third parties. In the development of this task, the bank assumes the risk that the borrower does not satisfy, in the form and in time, the contract agreed with the entity. Therefore, a basic function that entities have been playing is to evaluate and control borrowers, contributing significantly to reducing market imperfections arising from the existence of information asymmetries, as well as moral hazard. In many highly developed financial markets, mainly in the United States, thanks to new technologies and risk management models, the profile and business strategy of some entities is changing: risk transfers are taking place thanks to the emergence of products such as credit derivatives or asset securitization processes. In the latter case, it is possible, on the one hand, to transfer the risk to a third party, while the entities obtain funds to finance their activities. From what has been said so far, I would like to influence two ideas: first, the traditional business changes, since the bank becomes a channel that sends funds from financial investors (typically institutional) to other real investors (families and companies) getting rid of traditional risks (basically credit). Second, and related to the above, the transfer process does not imply that risks disappear, but that they are transformed, and entities must face operational or business risks, for example. Therefore, credit risk undergoes a process of transformation, while dispersing among a greater number of investors, ceasing to accumulate on bank balance sheets. From the point of view of financial stability, the greater dispersion of risks, and their lower concentration in the banking sector, has positive effects. However, problems may also arise, which have to do with a possible overconcentration of trading in a few financial intermediaries. Likewise, when risks are transferred, they can end up in unregulated entities, favoring the accumulation of imbalances and making it difficult to find solutions to crisis situations. In this sense, situations of regulatory arbitrage may occur, in which banks have incentives to transfer their riskiest assets, so that it is these types of unregulated entities that end up assuming them. Recently, some concern has arisen around hedge funds, which can act as investors interested in this type of risk transfer processes. Although these are institutions that promote the efficiency of markets, since they provide greater liquidity and act with different points of view than those maintained by the rest of the market, there are some elements of their actions that justify the growing attention they are receiving in different international forums. In particular, they typically operate with a high degree of leverage, while often concentrating their strategies on certain markets with low degree of liquidity. These two circumstances, together with the fact that these are generally non-transparent institutions, can pose a danger to financial stability in the face of an adverse scenario. Although it is not a strategy only followed by hedge funds, in a context of reduced volatility some investors have developed riskier investment strategies, to the point that on different occasions this greater risk-taking has been considered excessive. The causes for a scenario of reduced volatility such as the one we have experienced in recent years are several, ranging from structural issues, related to the improvements that have occurred in the functioning of financial markets; to others with a more circumstantial profile. Therefore, the degree of permanence of a scenario of reduced volatility depends, to a large extent, on the relevance of the cyclical factors. Its reversal, if it occurs very abruptly, could imply difficulties from the point of view of financial stability, for example through the losses that investors with large exposures would incur. Additional responsibilities derived from the increased sophistication of the business: no zero-risk If you remember, the second question I have raised has to do with the degree of responsibility that, in the face of the greater offer of sophisticated products, not only financial institutions, but also consumers, must assume. Financial institutions, on the other hand, not only have to worry about knowing their customers properly, which seems an elementary rule for the success of any business. They can be expected to provide advice to clients by offering their services, so that they sell them the product that best suits their needs and their risk profile. For their part, consumers can be expected to assume a certain degree of responsibility, insofar as they have to try to understand the product they are purchasing or, in other words, the risks they are taking. This need is not only increased by the greater sophistication of the products offered, but also because recent economic and demographic changes, including the gradual aging of the population, are causing consumers to make more and more financial decisions that will significantly affect their future well-being. Undoubtedly, demographic changes offer additional business opportunities to entities, for example through the enablement of new markets, but they also require them to keep up with the times. From the point of view of consumers' greater responsibilities in financial decision-making, not only should the collaboration of entities be expected, but public policy makers must also play a role. In this sense, the Bank of Spain has developed, among other initiatives, an Internet site, called the Banking Customer Portal, which aims to guide customers on some practical elements. Likewise, and with a more educational and formative intention, a project is also being developed through the Internet, called Virtual Classroom, which aims to contribute to promoting a greater financial culture. The role of technology In this whole process of changing the banking business, of which I am only outlining some ideas, technology has played a very relevant role. Will this continue to be the case in the future? Technological advances have been an engine of change in recent years and, in my opinion, will continue to play an important role in the future. In fact, this will be the case, at least, in two aspects: the way in which entities distribute their products and, therefore, relate to customers; and the way in which they develop their daily operations. On the one hand, distribution channels will continue to evolve towards what has come to be called electronic banking, which includes everything from telephone banking services to those carried out through the Internet. In fact, ATMs, nowadays implemented throughout the territory, progressively allow more operations, assimilating, saving distances, to virtual offices. It seems reasonable to think that these trends will be reinforced in the medium term. On the other hand, technology has allowed entities to substantially modify their internal processes, in terms of the amount of information they process, the speed with which they do so and the complexity of the operating procedures available today. This has not only allowed the development of more sophisticated products, but also, very importantly, to deepen the improvement of risk measurement and management models. The progress in this direction has been very relevant and, in my opinion, in the coming years we will see how everything related to the quantification of risks is deepened. Obviously technology is not the only cause, but it does offer possibilities only a few years ago difficult to imagine. One of the opportunities open for entities in this field is to take advantage of technological developments to add value to their customers, and ultimately, to be able to compete in better conditions. The difficulty of this increases if one takes into account that this must be compatible with cost containment processes, which, in some way, forces entities to prioritize some operating expenses over others. A recent trend in this regard is the hiring of external technology providers (outsourcing), which provides advantages for entities. It is a formula that allows access to knowledge in certain areas, while being cost-efficient and providing flexibility. However, these processes can entail certain risks for institutions, including inconsistency with their strategic plans and a certain loss of control over outsourced processes. Entities must ensure that this is not the case, while applying measures to limit other types of risks that may arise, for example those related to security issues, integrity of the systems used, confidentiality of information and even compliance with applicable rules and regulations. In this sense, the fact of contracting certain services with third parties does not exempt the entities from their responsibility. Therefore, entities must clearly define the services to be outsourced, properly choose the company that will be responsible for providing them and implement the necessary controls to reduce the associated risks. For our part, supervisors must be attentive to the potential risks that may arise and ensure that the transfer of these services will not reduce the entity's ability to comply with regulatory requirements. * * * * * In short, risk transfer processes, demographic developments and technological innovation are some of the elements that will contribute to changing the panorama of the banking sector in the medium term. I am aware that, as I already mentioned in my introduction, I leave many things in the pipeline, but I would not want to forget the growing process of internationalization of the banking sector, both globally and within the European Union. In my view, this process, largely encouraged after the introduction of the euro, will continue in Europe over the coming years, posing additional challenges for institutions. Thus, competition, to an increasing extent, is acquiring a more international dimension. What is the response that entities have to offer? The phenomenon of the internationalization of our financial system should not be seen as an isolated or specific development of our country. On the contrary, our banks have only joined a global trend, although it is true that they have done so with particular success and, why not recognize it, courage. It is not my intention to reflect on the positive aspects of financial globalization, which has them and are well known, but to focus on what it implies for the framework of regulation and supervision. Indeed, we have global banks, managed from the parent company, with centralized functions such as operational risk control or liquidity management, and local regulations and supervisors, that is, with legal powers and obligations that do not fit with the operations of these global banks. A single management corresponds to a multiplicity of regulators. Problems arise not only from the point of view of the manager. The supervisor must also be convinced that all activities and risks are being adequately supervised and this is true for both the source and destination supervisors. Finally, the very nature of new regulations, such as Basel II, partly facilitates the work by providing a globally homogeneous regulatory base. But the very nature of those rules, which are intended to be applied at a consolidated level, makes it difficult to apply them on the basis of the legal entity, that is, at the level of the individual subsidiary. In the following paragraphs I will concentrate on analysing this problem at European Union level. Globally, solutions to this problem are even more complex, and only initiatives such as those of the Basel Committee (through the AIG, or Accord Implementation Group) can succeed. Only through intensive dialogue between banks, parent supervisors and destination supervisors can the complexities introduced by the global management of the financial system with its supervision carried out at local level be alleviated. The European Union has unique characteristics, not only economic, but also political and institutional, which on this point focus on a reinforced interest in achieving a deepening and full integration of the European financial market, which is already bearing fruit in areas such as money and interbank markets, securitization, as well as encouraging the realization of large cross-border bank acquisition operations. In fact, if one looks at the changes experienced by the EU financial market over the last six years, it can only be described as a revolution: creation of a single currency in part of the EU, full integration of money and interbank markets, deepening of the markets for securitised assets and financing of large companies, emergence of new large truly pan-European banks, emergence of cooperation bodies between supervisors, creation of political structures in the European Council dedicated exclusively to promoting the creation of the single financial market (The Financial Services Committee), analysis of crisis management with pan-European impact (crisis management MOUs between Ministries, Central Banks and Supervisors and crisis simulation exercises at EU and EU level Eurosystem), etc. But the main revolution is, perhaps, that for the first time since the constitution of the EU, the financial area has been identified as one of the keys to closing the EU's productivity gap compared to other economic areas. The question, largely unresolved, is what supervisory structures the EU must have in place to meet the growing demands of this single market, while at the same time neglecting the needs of financial markets that also remain local in nature (think, for example, of retail banking). I would like to clear up two options which seem to me to be impossible at the current juncture of the internal market. The first to reject is the option of inaction: the single market is changing and with it must our regulatory and supervisory scheme. The second, that of creating a supervisor at European level, is equally unlikely because of the practical impossibility of carrying it out given the current institutional infrastructures. Let us therefore move to a pragmatic solution, designed in the light of current needs, and also capable of adapting to the evolution of those needs and to the evolution of the single financial market. The elements of such a pragmatic solution would be several. The first of these, due to its importance, is that of legal certainty, for supervisors and for entities, of any solution that is adopted, whether centralized or decentralized. In other words, in supervision the middle ground does not represent a compromise, but no man's land. The second element of the pragmatic solution is that it must take into account the diversity of realities within this single market, with pan-European entities present in almost all EU countries but also with small entities, and with a few employees. For all of them, it is essential to ensure a balance of the playing field. The third element is, perhaps, of limited theoretical importance, but of very important practical relevance. Given the diversity of the organisation of supervision in the EU, with single supervisors in some countries, central banks supervising banking in others and twin peaks in the rest, the solution designed must respect that diversity which is based on a set of factors, commercial, institutional, market structure, etc. And not because of some sacrosanct principle, but because if national institutional homogeneity were a prerequisite for the organisation of single market supervision, we would have to wait no less than a decade. But diversity in national oversight is not only reflected in the organization, but is also reflected in issues such as the use of on-site supervision, the role of external auditors, etc. Neutrality with respect to the organizational and management models of national supervision therefore appears as an aspect to be guaranteed. The fourth prerequisite is only a version of the previous one: the need to respect subsidiarity as much as possible (solutions must be national as far as possible) and proportionality (simple institutions must not be subjected to complex and costly solutions). The new Basel II directive already marks some interesting directions. The concept of multilateral cooperation is introduced, with the creation of the college of supervisors (i.e. the presence of all supervisors, home and destination), and the recognition of the leading role of the supervisor on a consolidated basis. To these changes, of a legal nature (and, therefore, of obligatory compliance), is added the growing role being played by the European Committee of Banking Supervisors, known as CEBS. Indeed, this committee, in its first two and a half years of life, has carried out important supervisory cooperation work that will allow a more homogeneous application of Basel II in the EU. But where it really needs to deliver is in achieving convergence of supervisory practices in EU countries. Or, in plainer language, to achieve a common culture of supervision where so far there have been 25. The process can be long and complicated but, at the same time, inevitable. In fact, the profound transformation of the supervisory model so far in force has already begun. III. Conclusions I will conclude my speech by emphasizing the two great ideas that I have tried to convey to you today. First, that during the last six years the Spanish banking sector has consolidated, in terms of its efficiency, profitability and solvency, in the leading group of European countries. This achievement undoubtedly contributes to the stability of our financial system, and therefore favors the proper functioning of the economy. Second, building on what has been achieved so far requires not complacency, but requires daily action to cope with the changes that are to come. My experience as Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain during these years tells me that between this institution and Spanish credit institutions there has been a fluid relationship and, in general terms, absent of special tensions. Moreover, and regardless of the possible discrepancies of opinion that, occasionally, may have existed, I believe that the relationship has been based on mutual trust and close collaboration. Successfully facing the challenges of the future will require maintaining this spirit of mutual collaboration, assuming with professionalism, each from the exercise of his functions, the tasks that correspond to him. Taking the opportunity offered by this forum to address economic journalists, I would like to remind you that you also play an active and very important role, insofar as you contribute to information transparency. Preserving this task, intensifying the professionalism with which they have been developing it, will have a positive impact on the better functioning of our financial system. I have no doubt that this will be the case in the future and that each of us will responsibly assume our task. From that conviction I reaffirm the belief that the Spanish banking system will successfully address the transformations that the future will bring. Thank you very much for your attention.
