Tercero, desde las matrices espalas se han impulsado notables mejoras en los sistemas de informaci, gesti y control de los riesgos de las filiales adquiridas. Finalmente, el Banco de Espa ha establecido procesos de supervisi especficos, con el fin de seguir mejor la evoluci de dichas actividades en Amrica Latina. Este conjunto de elementos han contribuido a acotar los riesgos asumidos en los procesos de expansi. Es ms, los timos movimientos importantes hacia una a mayor internacionalizaci de las entidades espalas se han producido en Europa y Estados Unidos, lo que ha permitido diversificar los riesgos asumidos. As, el peso de los pases emergentes se ha reducido desde los primeros procesos de expansi internacional, si bien dentro de estos se mantiene la concentraci de la actividad en Latinoamrica. Este cambio en la composici de los activos en el exterior, unido a factores coyunturales relacionados con la mejora experimentada en los timos as por la economa mundial, explican que se haya reducido el perfil de riesgo de los activos financieros en el exterior. Esto me lleva a una reflexi, que tiene que ver con el hecho de que las entidades, algunas de las cuales se han convertido en estos as en competidores globales, mantienen retos de gesti importantes ante los que deben permanecer alerta. As, una actividad cada vez ms internacionalizada implica una gesti ms compleja, en la que conviven mtiples mercados, segmentos de negocio, monedas y marcos regulatorios. Por lo tanto, las entidades embarcadas en estos procesos han de tener en cuenta la necesidad de evaluar de forma permanente los riesgos en los que incurren, sus interrelaciones y co estos pueden trasladarse a lo largo de toda la organizaci. La diversificaci del riesgo de crdito tiene un alcance limitado, y el riesgo de mercado (a travs de la correlaci entre mercados), el riesgo operacional (derivado de una creciente complejidad de las entidades) y el riesgo reputacional (si el problema en un pas se traslada a todo el grupo), son so algunos ejemplos que ilustran la necesidad de, si cabe, intensificar los mecanismos de control y gesti de los riesgos. He selado que la actividad de las entidades a nivel internacional implica la convivencia con diferentes marcos regulatorios. Sin duda, esto supone retos adicionales para los reguladores y supervisores bancarios, que hemos de profundizar en la colaboraci mutua e intercambio de informaci. Orquestar los mecanismos que permitan estos objetivos de forma eficiente no es tarea sencilla, pero se estn haciendo importantes esfuerzos en este terreno. Ya me he referido a los avances que se han logrado en Europa tras la aplicacin del enfoque Lamfalussy y la puesta en marcha del Comit de Supervisores Bancarios Europeos. La experiencia de colaboraci del Banco de Espa con los supervisores de los pases en los que nuestras entidades tienen intereses, es otro ejemplo de ello. No quiero cerrar esta reflexi sin destacar los efectos dinmicos, de futuro, que tiene la internacionalizaci del sistema bancario espal. En efecto, la competencia, en una primera fase, de la banca espala con la extranjera en el mercado espal, junto con la ulterior expansi exterior de nuestras entidades, nos sit en una magnfica posici para aprovechar el impulso que se est produciendo en el mercado financiero europeo. Dicho con otras palabras, el haber hecho los deberes en materia de solvencia, competencia y eficiencia nos sit en una posici muy favorable para aprovechar el crecimiento de los mercados financieros europeos en la prima dcada y las oportunidades que su creciente integraci trae consigo. Todo ello, al margen de que tambin se aprovechen las ocasiones que puedan presentarse fuera de Europa. Conclusiones He iniciado mi intervenci refirindome a los retos derivados de las recientes transformaciones que se viven en los mercados financieros internacionales y la concluyo aludiendo a los que surgen de los procesos de internacionalizaci de la actividad bancaria. La experiencia del sistema bancario espal a lo largo de los timos aos me hace confiar en que sabremos aprovechar las oportunidades que nos ofrecen estos desarrollos y gestionar adecuadamente los riesgos que traen consigo, de forma que todo ello redunde en la eficiencia y solidez de nuestras entidades; algo que, sin duda, servir para seguir impulsando el desarrollo econico y financiero de Espa. Muchas gracias.

Title: "Banking Reforms". Speech delivered at the "High level Seminar on Central Bank Modernization and Banking Reforms" jointly organized by the Banco de Espaa and the IMF (Toledo)
text: Toledo, November 3rd 2006 Banking Reforms High Level Seminar on Central Bank Modernization and Banking Reforms. Banco de Espaa -IMF Jose Vials Deputy Governor of the Banco de Espaa Introduction It is a pleasure for me to take this opportunity to share with you some reflections on a matter as important as banking system reforms. I think that all of us agree that a major challenge for every country is to achieve and sustain high rates of economic growth that can improve the standards of living of their citizens. This is particularly important in the North African and Middle East countries participating in this Seminar, insofar as their past growth performance has proven insufficient both in absolute terms and relative to other comparable regions. What is more, in view of geopolitical risks, rapid growth and improved standards of living are very important to foster social and political stability. In this context, why is the topic of this seminar relevant? Something that we also know, based both on economic theory and international experience, is that the contribution of financial development is very important to achieve economic growth and stability. And banking reform is a key element to promote financial development. Indeed, a sound and smoothly functioning banking system that is capable of channelling saving to its most productive uses contributes to higher economic growth. It is also conducive to macroeconomic stability, for at least three reasons: it provides for the elimination of a direct factor of instability, it allows effective monetary policy transmission and it acts as a factor capable of absorbing both domestic and external shocks. In this respect, experience not only shows that the consequences of a weak financial system may prove very serious for the economy as a whole in the event of a crisis; it also reveals that the inefficient workings of financial markets and of the institutions operating in them considerably stifle economic growth. The design of public policies has to include both elements. However, I shall not be focusing today on matters relating rather to crisis-resolution but on banking reforms conducive to their stable and efficient functioning. One relevant question to be answered here is what have we learned in the past about banking reform from our international experience that may be useful for the developing countries and emerging markets attending this Seminar today? To respond, I will structure my presentation around three major headings. First, I think that it is important to start by reveiwing the general economic context and the key features of the financial systems within which the banking system operates in these countries. Second, I will refer to past experience in banking reform in developed countries. Finally, I will try to identify some areas of consensus regarding banking reform. Let me start with the first issue I referred to, namely the general economic context and key characteristics of these countries. My intention is not to be exhaustive, but to point out some elements that I consider relevant from the perspective of todays talk. Regarding the general economic context, and taking into account that, obviously, there are differences from country to country, I would mention three basic features. First, and in spite of recent progress towards an increase in the degree of openness of these countries, they are still relatively closed economies, both in terms of trade and in relation to their financial systems. Second, and also bearing in mind that we have witnessed significant improvements in this area in recent years, greater efforts are needed to strengthen their institutional framework. In this respect, in the past few years some countries have made tangible progress, but many aspects have still to be improved. Reinforcing their legal systems and institutions, property rights and economic institutions are just some examples of the direction in which to move. Finally, but importantly too, in many countries the size of the public sector in the economy remains large, despite progress having been made in some cases. The financial systems of these countries also evidence particularities that should be taken into account when considering banking reforms. The financial systems of these countries are bank-centered, that is to say, the size and the role of capital markets tend to be, in many cases, marginal. It should be noted that, in a number of these countries, the development of capital markets has received growing attention in the last few years, but in most cases they remain very underdeveloped. At the same time, there is a low degree of banking intermediation, in relation to GDP levels, and there is a high share of bank lending to the public sector. The banking system is often highly concentrated, which frequently entails entry restrictions for prospective new players. All in all, these characteristics result in a financial system with low levels of competition and efficiency, and a wide use of cash as a means of exchange in financial transactions. All this is usually reflected in a scarcity of credit to the private sector, as well as in financial systems with a high level of segmentation, that is to say, where there is low or no access for certain groups of borrowers to the financial markets. Some elements of the banking reform experience of developed countries In short, the financial systems of many emerging economies and developing countries need to be reformed to make them more efficient and, thus, a more useful tool in providing economic growth. Can the international experience of banking reforms over recent decades be useful in this connection? In my view, the answer is yes, so let me briefly review the reform process since the 70s in the financial sectors, and particularly in the banking sectors, of a large number of developed countries. Here, as in other fields, each country's experience is unquestionably unique. This is because of the numerous differences between countries both in the starting position of their economic and Yet I believe the varied experiences over recent decades allow us to identify certain common factors in the different banking reforms enacted in different countries. In many European countries, and as in the United States and Japan, among others, the banking system in the 70s was highly regulated. Such regulation affected many of banks operating areas, curtailing their action notably. There were limits, for example, on the interest rates banks could set; there were obligatory investment ratios; the possibility of holding a stake in non-financial corporations was limited or prohibited; and there were restrictions on opening branch offices on the basis of the commercial criteria established by banks. In sum, the basis of regulation in the 70s was the setting of operating restrictions on existing banks, which posed sizeable obstacles to potential new entrants. These entry barriers were effective not only against foreign banks seeking to enter a particular country's market, but also prevented domestic competition arising. As a result, banking systems were at that time highly inefficient, although they generated high profits for the established banks. Over-regulation had one aspect which we might, if you will allow me, declare as positive from the standpoint of the stability of the system; the exceptional profits obtained by banks acted as a buffer that allowed potential difficulties to be withstood. Yet the cost of the system was very high, for at least two reasons. First was the cost for consumers of financial services, since access to bank financing was very difficult and the latter was very expensive. Second, and stemming from the foregoing, a system less efficient in channelling saving to the most productive uses undoubtedly reins in the possibilities of higher economic growth. As you will recall, I referred to this matter at the beginning of my speech. Accordingly, acknowledgement of the shortcomings of the system in terms of its inefficiencies led to deregulation being undertaken in many countries. However, I believe there are other powerful factors relating more closely to the very dynamics and development of financial markets which exerted pressure geared to freeing up the banking market. On one hand, technological progress and the development of new computational techniques meant that the value added by providing a purely local banking service was lower. On the other, and this was a point of particular importance in countries such as the United States, the restrictions on banks led other financial institutions to emerge, institutions with a lesser regulatory burden and a greater capacity to compete in capturing saving. The growing pressure exerted by these institutions also acted as a stimulus for established banks to demand greater scope for action in taking commercial decisions, such as the opening of branch offices or the unrestricted setting of interest rates. Be that as it may, the fact is that this broad set of factors drove a growing process of deregulation and freeing up of the banking sector in many countries. Liberalisation, as is natural, occurred in different ways in different countries. This was due to the type of measures applied and to the pace at which the process was undertaken. However, the general tendency was to lift the restrictions referred to earlier. on the erosion of the market power of already-established banks. Consequently, the exceptional profits banks had enjoyed until then declined, leading many of them to pursue riskier lending policies. Heightened competitive pressure in the banking industry meant that more than a few banks reacted by taking on greater risks and, more importantly, they did so without extending in parallel their risk selection, control and management systems. The shortcomings of banks' corporate governance mechanisms and their risk control and management systems were one of the main reasons behind the banking crises affecting many countries in the 80s. But other factors also contributed. I should like to highlight two of them. Firstly, the macroeconomic situation. On most occasions, bank crises could be seen not to emerge in full until the country's economic situation deteriorated. This shows that if banks do not implement appropriate lending policies during the good times in the cycle, imbalances will build up, becoming manifest subsequently when the situation of the economy worsens. Secondly, the shortcomings in the regulatory and prudential supervision fields. The elimination of the excessive regulation in place previously was not accompanied by additional measures, which meant, for instance, that there were no capital ratios set on the basis of assets at risk, or that on-site inspections were non-existent or insufficient. What is more, the liberalisation drive sometimes saw the authorities fail to be as scrupulous as they ought to have been in granting banking licences, which allowed entrepreneurs with no experience in banking -and who were occasionally only seeking a means of financing other activities -to gain access to the market. In the wake of banking crises that proved costly to differing degrees in terms of GDP, there was a notable change in the banking sector. The regulatory reforms made prevented succumbing to the potential temptation of returning to a highly regulated system. On the contrary, the banking reforms marked a significant step towards what we know today as prudential regulation. Unquestionably, the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision adopted by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision in 1997, and recently under reform, are an essential reference in this area. Banking reform has also been driven by the sector itself, which has seen notable advances in risk management, control and measurement in the last 15 years. Indeed, banks themselves have understood that in an industry such as theirs, where risk is part and parcel of the business, success cannot be had without setting in place the management mechanisms for proper risk measurement and monitoring. Some areas of consensus of potential relevance for banking reform processes At this point I shall attempt to point out some areas of consensus of potential relevance for banking reform processes. Nevertheless, as regards advice on banking reforms, we must start with an exercise in humility. The reason is that there in no one-size-fits-all strategy, since different countries have different characteristics, meaning it is not possible to offer a valid set of recommendations brooking no exception or qualification. The best that we can thus hope for is to identify those areas where some consensus has emerged over the years and try to come up with some useful ideas. There is a need to adopt a pragmatic approach and recognise that banking reform is not an instant process One initial element for achieving a sound financial system is the need to develop an appropriate institutional framework, building up a set of mercantile and civil laws capable of ensuring agents' property rights, developing institutions that foster monetary and fiscal discipline, improving mechanisms to appropriately disclose information and a set of adequate accounting standards, among others. The idea of the need for an appropriate institutional framework is in fact reflected in the preconditions of the Core Principles which, among other considerations, also point to appropriate macroeconomic policies as a necessary element for the proper functioning of financial markets. In fact, unless there is a sound macro-policy framework, there will be imbalances building up which, sooner or later will lead to banking crises, with very disruptive economic and social consequences. In countries whose economies are subject to a greater degree of volatility, it is particularly important to have an institutional framework and to secure economic fundamentals that are sound and stable. A second issue to be considered when reforming the banking system is that there is a need for appropriately setting priorities and finding the correct sequencing of reforms. The specific path of banking reforms may differ from country to country, but often a gradual step-by-step process may in the long run be useful. I have said before that in these economies banks are most relevant in the financial system. In fact, regarding financial development, there is no clear evidence as to whether a model based on banks is better than one based on markets, or vice versa. In my view, the important thing is that whatever the mix, the overall system performs efficiently and in a sound manner. Nevertheless, if we are pragmatic, given that banks are central to the financial systems of developing countries and emerging markets, I think that a good strategy would be to give priority to developing a sound and effective banking system. What is more, the development of the banking sector is expected to strengthen the performance of the financial system. A third idea regarding banking reforms is the need to liberalise banking activities. As indicated, in many countries there has been a progressive lifting of regulations that had comprised the imposition of various restrictions on banks' business decision-making capacity. That has allowed progress towards a more competitive and efficient system, and one capable, therefore, of boosting economic growth to a greater extent. Nevertheless, and this is very relevant given the numerous bank crises I referred to earlier, it would seem necessary for financial liberalisation to be accompanied by the application of appropriate measures from the standpoint of prudential regulation and supervision. This could be said to be an accompaniment condition of an internal nature, without which the process of banking reform would be seriously affected. These prudential regulation and supervision elements are included in the Core Principles. In fact, these principles, which have become the pivotal reference for progress towards effective banking supervision, include a broad set of factors. These cover, inter alia, the relevance of the independence of the supervisory authority; the need to establish entry requirements based on the suitability of bank managers; the setting of capital ratios relating risks incurred by banks to the minimum capital requirements they must maintain; the need to introduce appropriate risk control systems and to establish suitable supervisory methods combining on-site inspections with remote monitoring; and the need for banks to provide sufficient information and to set in place both appropriate disciplinary measures and the co-operation mechanisms needed for cross-border supervision. In short, the banking reform process should unfold, from my viewpoint, avoiding financial repression but introducing the appropriate mechanisms so as to avoid the opposite extreme. In this respect, the third reflection I would like to make on this matter is that in our present-day capacity as banking supervisors we must work to introduce the appropriate incentives so that banks can function correctly. The action of markets, and of the agents participating in them, must be an essential complement to banking supervision. Furthermore, banks' senior officers have a responsibility for the correct functioning of their institutions. Indeed, the chief responsibility for the sound functioning of banks lies with them. In fact, banks themselves have to make a continuous effort to improve their risk management and control systems, along with their corporate governance structures. In other words, supervision is not confined solely to bank supervisors and regulators. Recent reforms, such as Basel II with the joint operation of its three pillars, are geared in this direction. In my view, Basel II is an important step in the right direction: as it is based on the correct principles, I think that it will help countries to promote financial stability and growth. Regarding the adoption of Basel II by developing countries, this is a widely discussed and relevant topic. I am not going to go into details now, but I think that for many developing countries and emerging markets the adoption of Basel II, even in its simplified approaches, must be a target to be achieved through a gradual process over time. There is a fourth element regarding banking reforms which, in fact, I consider as another accompaniment condition in this process. I refer here to the need to step up the degree of external openness, insofar as liberalisation of the capital account entails significant benefits. Indeed, financial globalisation offers benefits in terms of greater growth potential. Moreover, the financial systems of many emerging economies are small, and this gives rise to negative factors such as those derived from an excessive concentration of risks or from the fewer investment opportunities that such systems offer. Nevertheless, external openness is not free from difficulty, which is why I believe that in this case there is a need to be prepared. Consequently, the process should be gradual and, if it is to be successful, it will first need a sound banking system. A fifth element of this process is related to the bank ownership structure. In this regard allow me just a couple of reflections regarding public-sector banks as well as foreign banks. In relation to the opening-up process, a phenomenon seen in many emerging economies is the entry of foreign banks into local markets. Occasionally, it is believed this can cause a measure of uncertainty and instability in the banking sector of the host country. However, the benefits are very significant, as highlighted by Spain's own experience, to which I shall refer shortly. Foreign banks thus tend to heighten competition and efficiency, contributing to the transfer of technology and of human capital, which increases local banks' capacity. In fact, in certain circumstances the entry of instance if privatisation processes are undertaken. At this juncture I would like briefly to reflect on the role of public-sector banks, whose presence is still very significant in quite a few countries. Firstly, I think a distinction needs to be drawn between public-sector development banks and public-sector commercial banks. Development banks are considered useful if there are market imperfections warranting government action and if they complement private banks, not competing with them. But the growth of public-sector commercial banks, though there is no absolutely conclusive evidence, is usually associated with a lesser degree of financial development, with less protection of borrowers' rights and with bigger spreads. All of this reduces the efficiency of the financial intermediation process and ultimately economic growth. Among other considerations, public-sector commercial banks tend to finance governments more, especially where the budget deficit is greater and the alternatives for seeking alternative sources of financing are fewer. The adverse effects are most considerable, and include most notably crowding out or, what is of substantial relevance for developing countries and emerging economies, greater country-risk exposure, increasing the vulnerability of the financial system. I talked earlier of privatisation via foreign banks. But this is just one of the many existing alternatives with regard to how to pursue this process if it is deemed necessary. I do not intend now to tackle this question, which itself merits a deep analysis. But I would like to point out that the option chosen depends on the particularities of the country involved and that it should be the result of a gradual and progressive process. In any case, regarding foreign and public-sector banks, and other topics, the relevant question is how much and how fast. But often -and in my view this is the major risk -the result is too little, too late. This leads me to the sixth issue I wish to discuss, namely the need to be pro-active in the approach to banking reforms. In that vein, it is preferable not to wait until a major crisis occurs, which is very costly. Practical experience, however, shows that a major crisis has often been a catalyst for reforms. Finally, I would also like to make a reference to the role of central banks. This role concerns the promotion, stemming from the pursuit of its responsibilities, of macroeconomic stability -and of price stability in particular-which, as I indicated, is a necessary condition for achieving a sound and stable financial system. But at the same time, the central bank can and should contribute to strengthening the financial system, assisting in the development of infrastructures, for example, through the development of efficient payment systems. Undoubtedly, a payment system capable of increasing the security with which banks relate to one another, while reducing costs, is of paramount importance for obtaining a sound and stable financial system. The central bank can also contribute to the promotion of a more efficient banking system, and particularly to the development of money markets, by adopting market-orientated monetary policy instruments and procedures. And finally, in those cases where the central bank is entrusted with responsibility for banking regulation and supervision, it is of paramount importance that it should do its job efficiently and in an operationally independent manner. Allow me to conclude with a brief reference to the Spanish case. Although I realise the subsequent panels will be discussing different national experiences in detail, I could not omit a few brief remarks on the Spanish financial system, as I consider its development over the past thirty years is most illustrative of a banking reform process. From a system in which the operations of private banks, existing alongside public-sector banks, was very restricted, we have moved to a highly efficient, solvent and competitive system compared with our peer countries. As can be inferred from the deep-seated banking crisis in the late 70s, the process has perforce been gradual and not free from difficulty. Briefly, and following the progressive elimination of restrictive regulations, it involved the privatisation of public-sector banks, allowing entry to foreign banks, opening up the system to foreign competition and fostering domestic competition. In recent years, as in other countries, we have witnessed a process of banking consolidation along with the sectors growing internationalisation. This entire process of transformation has been accompanied by changes in the regulatory and supervisory framework, geared to making it more effective and robust. To conclude, a final idea by way of summary. The financial system is the engine of economic growth, and financial crises entail very high costs. There are usually three common elements behind these crises: a strong deterioration in macroeconomic conditions; shortcomings in regulation and banking supervision; and deficiencies in corporate governance and in banks' risk management systems. From my viewpoint, pushing through bank reforms involves making headway in these three areas. Thank you.

Title: Opening Remarks at the Third High Level Seminar of the Eurosystem and Latin American Central Banks: Monetary and Financial implications of globalisation
text: Madrid, 4th December 2006 Opening Remarks III High Level Seminar of the Eurosystem and Latin American Central Banks: Monetary and Financial implications of globalisation Miguel Fernandez Ordonez Governor of the Banco de Espana Good morning, Welcome to our Seminar, focused on the Monetary and Financial Implications of Globalisation. The accelerated path of economic and financial integration that we are witnessing at the global level is introducing substantial changes in the behaviour of variables that are crucial for monetary policy and is bearing intensely on the factors and relationships that guide our decisions. The issue of integration was already present in the first edition of the seminar, although from a more parcial perspective, as we then discussed only about regional integration both in Europe and Latin America-. To better understand why globalisation is now at the forefront of the economic debate and what are the challenges for policymakers that it entails, it would be useful to look at the developments in the world economy over the past four years and hint how increased integration has contributed to a period of rather successful economic performance. In 2002 the world economy was recovering from a slowdown driven by a mild recession in the U.S, after the stock markets had experienced a sharp correction. That year the global economy posted a growth rate of 3% and was on its way to reach the growth rates of around 5% that we are experiencing now. The prospects today are supportive for the continuation of this solid global growth, despite the fact that some uncertainties remain regarding the depth of the expected US slowdown driven this time by the adjustment in the housing sector and the extent to which the euro area, Japan and the emerging economies will be resilient to such developments. Once again, the United States has played a leading role as an engine of the global economic expansion over the last years, but the most remarkable aspect has been the key contribution made by emerging market economies. 2006 will be the fourth year in a row in which this group of economies achieves average rates of growth over 6.5%, which is specially telling given the fact that economic performance in emerging markets has been rather volatile in the past. Indeed, their contribution to global growth and their share in global output have been increasing for several years now. Of course, this high average growth masks large differences between countries and areas. When looking at individual performances what really stands out is the consolidation of very high rates of growth in China and, with a certain lag, in India and other smaller Asian economies. The impact of Asia -and of China in particular- on international exchanges has also increased dramatically even though its weight in world trade is still low compared to its potential in terms of output and population. Given this spectacular economic dynamism what is really surprising is the low prominence given to China in the reports on international economy only four years ago. No doubt, the emergence of China as a global player and the efforts made by the international community to come to terms with this new reality have probably been one of the most dramatic transformations in the global economy. When we turn to the performance of the euro area and Latin America in those four years we find instead that for different reasons both regions seem to have been lagging somewhat in the global context. The euro area started a cyclical recovery in 2002 but until very recently it has only shown a rather disappoining growth record. Although there have been some exceptions -Spain would be one- the overall figures have been dragging due to the weakness of the larger economies in the area. Only in 2006 is activity picking up strongly, to around 2.5%. The observed recovery in domestic demand is particularly welcome, since its weakness has been weighting heavily on growth in the last years. In fact, one of the factors identified behind the lacklustre behaviour of domestic consumption have been precisely globalisation forces -acting mainly through the reallocation production and labour and reinforced by the paralel process of European enlargement-. This has contributed to contain wage pressures and labour costs, but has also underlined the need to reinforce the basis for euro area growth. On the other hand, Latin America has been one of the emerging regions which delayed its incorporation to the current expansionary cycle. Between 2001 and 2003 the region underwent strong economic turbulences which slashed growth and even generated deep economic crises in some of the countries which are present here today. The financial vulnerability of the region exacerbated the impact of the financial turbulences, but once the recovery took hold, there has been a sustained effort by the authorities to reduce these vulnerabilities, as we will have time to discuss today in the second session. One element which has contributed to this reduction in vulnerability has been the accumulation of reserves, the topic of the afternoon session. Here, the assessment has experienced a U-turn: four years ago Latin America and other emerging countries were concerned about the depletion of reserves; now, driven in some cases by the rapid increases in commodities prices, the debate focuses on excessive reserves, mainly in Asia, but also in Latin America. Our discussion here today will focus around some of the new developments that have characterised this recent period of economic expansion and globalisation. The favourable behaviour of inflation over the last years has surprised policy makers. Inflation has only slightly increased in the average of industrialised countries from the low levels recorded in 2001 to rates around 2.5%. In most emerging markets inflation has fallen after 2003 and even more markedly in Latin America where it is setting historical lows. But I prefer to put this figure in the context of the parallel and dramatic increase in commodities prices. The price of oil has increased from less than 20 per barrell in 2002 to around 60 today. Jointly with the economic recovery, this was feared to put strong inflationary pressures on the economies and has become a recurrent concern in policy discussions. All in all, I would dare to say that none of us would have thought that these risks to inflation would have been dodged so well. We, central bankers, could be tempted to take the full credit for this remarkable achievement. To be fair, however, we must admit that globalisation, again, has greatly helped through the reduction of the import prices of manufactured goods and the disciplinary effect on domestic production costs. Developments around global imbalances have been less favourable. This issue was already a concern four years ago when US current account deficit was heading towards 5% of GDP-. Today it is even more so as the US external imbalance will be around 6.5% of GDP this year despite the 20% real effective depreciation of the US dollar. Not only have the imbalances widened but their accumulating impact has increased the scope for a disorderly adjustment in the future. It is true that the deeper financial integration associated to globalisation -which, for instance, reduces the home bias of investors- contributes to make current account imbalances more persitent and maybe more sustainable, but their magnitude remains rather worrisome. I do not want to extend further in these opening remarks. I would like to conclude by saying that in the last years the world economy has dealt quite successfully with some important shocks, that in other circumstances could have seriously impaired its dynamism. Globalisation has in certain aspects helped to overcome these risks, but in others it has generated new challenges that we need to face. I think that the open discussion we are having today will contribute to this task. Let me now give the floor to Mr. Trichet to make the introduction to the Seminar. Thank you very much and welcome again to Madrid.

Title: Las cajas de ahorros espaolas
text: Madrid, 18 January 2007 Spanish savings banks Foundation for Financial Studies Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor of the Bank of Spain It is a pleasure for me to be here today with all of you, and I would like my first words to be of thanks to the Fundaci97n de Estudios Financieros, and to its president, Xavier Adser88, for the invitation he has extended to me to participate in this event. The work that the Foundation has been carrying out deserves recognition and, in particular, I would like to welcome initiatives aimed at a deeper understanding of our financial system and the institutions that operate in it, since contributing to the development of a sound and efficient financial system also requires its serious and rigorous analysis. The fact that civil society is actively involved in this field is something that must be positively valued. Let us hope that this work, on which I am not going to pronounce, will be complemented by others, with different points of view, and that the public debate on financial issues will gain in quality and depth. The institution I represent has contributed very significantly, over the years, to the debate on the most relevant economic issues. Historically, greater emphasis has been placed on issues related to the real sector of the economy, but we know that the efficient and stable functioning of the financial system is a necessary condition for promoting economic growth. For this reason, the efforts aimed at enhancing their better knowledge are of great relevance, and this has led the Bank of Spain to be involved, even more intensively, in this task for some years. A good example of this is the publication of both the Review and the Financial Stability Report. In my speech, I would like to take this opportunity to share with you some general reflections on the sector of savings banks, institutions that are the subject of the study presented today. To do this, I will begin by exposing what is the context in which the ideas are framed that I will later transfer to you. Next, I will point out what are, in my opinion, the three basic pillars on which the current model of savings banks is based. Finally, I will raise some elements that I believe should be taken into account in order to strengthen the future model of the savings banks. General framework of reflections Allow me, therefore, to begin by raising three general reflections that have to do with the timeliness of the debate, the definition of the savings bank model and the special need for the generation of recurring profits by these entities. In relation to the timeliness of the debate on the role of savings banks within the Spanish financial system, I have already pointed out that I consider the analysis of financial issues from the seriousness and rigour to be positive. But even more, I think we are at a good time to reflect on what are the parameters that should guide the sector's action in the coming times, since, in the last decade, the financial markets have undergone profound transformations. Technological progress, the internationalization of activity, the development of more sophisticated products and the appearance of new agents in the markets, are some of the elements that have starred in this process of change. Given these developments, and in a context of intense competition with other banking and non-banking intermediaries, savings banks have been able to adapt and have ratified, and even intensified, their relevant position within our financial system. However, the forces of change are still present, and we must all be prepared, each from our own responsibility, to move solidly towards a more efficient, more integrated and more competitive system. Secondly, and in relation to the definition of the savings bank model, I would like to point out something that is no less relevant because it is obvious, and that sometimes seems to be forgotten. The Bank of Spain does not define the model of the savings banks, since this is a matter for the legislator. Only when the legislator considers modifications, the Bank of Spain will express its opinion that, as it could not be otherwise, will be based on its responsibilities as prudential supervisor. Thirdly, the Bank of Spain considers that there are some peculiarities in the current model of savings banks that imply a greater need to appeal to retained profit to strengthen the solidity of this sector. In the event of difficulties, depository institutions must have sufficient financial muscle. This means, in the first place, that the results obtained must be solid, so that they can act as the first line of defense against the potential realization of an adverse scenario. Secondly, depository institutions, with the intention of facing unexpected losses that may materialize, must maintain a sufficient level of capital, and quality, in relation to the risks assumed. However, for savings banks, having sufficient capital means, to a greater extent than for other entities, accumulating reserves, that is, retaining profits. Therefore, the solidity of the profit and loss account, key in any business, becomes an element, if possible, of greater relevance for savings banks. The soundness of the income statement depends, of course, on the business management policies developed by each entity. I do not think it can be said that there is, in this sense, a single valid formula to achieve a recurrence in the results, but I would like to recall two aspects that could be considered common to any strategy that aims to be successful in this area: diversification of risks and flexibility of costs. These elements are necessary to provide the profit and loss account with greater stability and, therefore, more capacity to face the different phases of the economic cycle that will undoubtedly succeed each other. The strength of the result is an issue of particular concern to the prudential supervisor, but I believe that, in this area, there is a full alignment of the interests of all parties, since the savings banks themselves assume as their objective the achievement of a robust profit and loss account. First, because they are the most interested in their own survival. Second, and as a consequence of the above, because that is the best guarantee that savings banks can satisfy their social character, which has been present in their business model since its foundation. Current situation of savings banks Indeed, since their inception savings banks have developed an intense social activity, closely linked to the local area in which the savings bank operated and, together with some banks with a long history, have been providing basic financial services to the whole population that had greater difficulties in accessing commercial banking. Since that initial moment, many things have changed in our economy and in our financial system. The savings banks continue to carry out an important social work, allocating a part of their profits to that end. And, at the same time, in the last two decades they have been established as full deposit institutions, so that their operational capacity is fully comparable to that of banks. During this process of change, the need arose to move from a management model that incorporated an important administrative component to a more modern, and inevitably, more complex one. This challenge, which has also been addressed over a few years of profound changes in the financial markets, also meant notable opportunities for savings banks, opportunities that they have been able to take advantage of, deepening their own strengths and limiting their weaknesses. Its success is the result of a wide range of factors, but I would like to point out three that I consider fundamental: professionalization, ability to compete and market discipline. The increase in professionalization in savings banks has been very relevant in recent years. Today, the management teams of savings banks are highly qualified, having adopted the highest standards of the banking sector. A significant effort has also been made to increase the level of training and competence of the workforce. The professionalization of management teams has contributed to the development of strategic plans in line with the times, and has been key in the process by which these entities have moved to act according to the correct economic and financial criteria, above any other consideration. This does not imply that the savings banks have ceased to be true to themselves, but rather the opposite: it is the greatest guarantee to continue serving the interests of their depositors and society in general. These economic and financial criteria have incorporated two very relevant elements: efficiency and risk management. On the one hand, operational efficiency has been recognized as a key variable to be able to act adequately in a market as competitive as Spain. The rationalization of costs, in addition to the aforementioned flexibility of its structure, are common recommendations for any company, but they have not lost their validity. While acknowledging the remarkable efforts that have been made in this area in recent years, we should not be complacent. In fact, I believe that institutions must bear in mind that, at least in part, the increase in efficiency that has occurred in recent years is the result of the distribution of structural costs among a greater volume of activity, so if the rate of expansion of this were reduced, efficiency could suffer. Cost rationalisation processes pose an additional challenge, as they must be compatible with the second element I mentioned: proper risk management. Institutions have recognized the importance of establishing adequate risk control and management systems, applying significant efforts to introduce best practices in this area. Basel II will be, and indeed is already assuming, an important lever of change to move in the right direction. The savings bank model has also been underpinned by their ability to compete, particularly in the loan and deposit markets. In recent years, these entities have been progressively gaining market share, both in the financing granted and in the collection of deposits. This has happened in their geographical areas of influence, as well as in those market segments in which, traditionally, they have been more present. However, there has also been an increasing expansion into new markets, both geographical and product. This management strategy has helped to diversify activity, and to a large extent responds to the need to obtain higher revenues in an environment in which margins have been progressively pressured downwards. However, the processes of expansion of the activity entail, in most cases, learning costs and others related to the initial difficulties suffered by entities to discriminate adequately between their potential customers. In order to minimize them, the savings banks involved in this process must intensify their risk measurement and control systems. The increasing professionalisation of the sector to which I have referred has undoubtedly contributed to the fact that this is the case in most cases, although further progress must be made. The third element on which the box model has focused is market discipline. Today, and on this I think we will all agree, market discipline is not only an indispensable complement to the exercise of prudential supervision, but has become a basic instrument for introducing the right incentives for the management teams of institutions. Over the last few years, savings banks have been subjected to market discipline to a greater extent through different mechanisms, such as that exercised by rating agencies on their debt securities. However, of the three elements that I have identified as key in the savings bank model, market discipline is the one in which the least progress has been made and which I will address in more detail in the last part of my speech. In any case, the savings bank model has proven successful. Proof of this are the higher market shares achieved, its increasing operational efficiency, and its high levels of both profitability and solvency. The better performance of the entities that make up a financial system has an impact, as it could not be otherwise, on the greater competitiveness, efficiency, solvency and innovation capacity of the system as a whole. The Spanish savings banks, together with the rest of the deposit institutions, have contributed decisively to reinforce these characteristics that are now clearly evident in our financial system. In other words, the Spanish financial system has proven highly effective in the development of its main functions, that is, in channeling savings and transmitting risks, in such a way that it has become a key player in promoting the growth of our economy. Future of savings banks Having analysed the positive evolution of savings banks in recent years, given that the continuous progress of the global financial system must remove any temptation to complacency, I would like to devote the last part of my speech to sharing with you some thoughts on certain aspects of the future of savings banks. My analysis will not focus on the most circumstantial aspects, of which to a large extent the opinion of the Bank of Spain is already known, for example through its Financial Stability Report, but on some others that, without involving regulatory changes, have implications in the medium and long term. To do this, I will make four reflections that revolve around industrial participation, social work, the ability to compete and market discipline. The acquisition of industrial stakes has meant for savings banks, as well as for other entities, new business opportunities and alternative ways to generate income in a context of strong competition. However, business ventures not only offer opportunities, but also incorporate additional risks. To the extent that they are holdings with a vocation for long-term permanence, the risks assumed will also remain, while additional risks related to participation in the shareholding and management arise. On the other hand, a more or less high proportion of income will be generated by the evolution of a business other than banking, and this type of participation could induce greater volatility of the profit and loss accounts. In this sense, it is worth asking to what extent it is worth introducing additional volatility in a business as changing as banking. For our part, prudential supervisors have already recognised the additional risks involved in such activities. Basel II, by introducing a new framework of capital requirements for industrial holdings, is moving in this direction. My second reflection concerns social work. I think we will all agree that the attribution of results to social work can never compromise the future budget of the savings banks. For this reason, there has always been a legitimate concern on the part of the regulator about the percentage of profits destined for this purpose, insofar as the retention of results is the main source of capital for these entities. Recognizing this fact, and to the extent that alternative mechanisms could be developed whereby savings banks would strengthen their capital on market terms, greater convergence with the situation of banks in terms of the proportion of profits to be distributed could be envisaged. The box model, as I said, has also been based on its ability to compete, which, in recent years, has resulted in its incursion into a good number of new markets, both product and geographical. Thus, and despite the fact that there are still differences in specialization with banks, savings banks have increased their financing granted to companies, when traditionally they had focused to a greater extent on the household sector. On the other hand, in the last two decades the boxes have gone from operating locally to doing so throughout the national market. The process of geographical expansion has been progressive, but very intense, and has been supported by the extension of the commercial network through the opening of offices. The general impression is that there is now a certain degree of office saturation in the internal market. This translates into high degrees of density in certain regions, which introduces additional cost pressures, making them less flexible. In an attempt to alleviate this situation, some savings banks have initiated, albeit moderately, processes of presence in international markets through branches. At a time when competition is going to acquire a more European, even global, dimension, entities must be able to adapt to this environment. International expansion is a valid alternative for funds of sufficient size, since it can encourage the diversification of risks and income received, helping to mitigate the business risk to which they could be exposed, but this eventual process must be based on prudence, developing gradually and analyzing case by case, as it has been for other banks in the past. It is also necessary to make an evaluation from a double perspective. On the one hand, verifying whether the fund has the management and financial capacity to undertake the process. On the other hand, evaluating the benefits that it incorporates, net of the additional risks involved. In this sense, managers, from an attitude marked by prudence, must consider that the process should not respond to a mere attempt to gain size, but must be fully consistent with the medium and long-term financial and capital strategy established by the entity. Likewise, it is necessary to take into account how the process has to influence the risk profile of the fund, and ensure that the appropriate measurement and control systems have been put in place, including the evaluation of adverse assumptions regarding the evolution of the business. In short, if international expansion processes are to be undertaken, entities must be aware that this implies more complex risk profiles, which requires strengthening management capacity, as well as the responsibility and quality that can be expected from management. Consequently, institutions should, themselves, adapt solvency levels to the highest level of risks assumed. Are there other alternatives to expansion through offices, or via internationalization processes? Some players in the sector believe that mergers between savings banks could be considered. Logically, this type of operation should be guided by the same parameters of economic and financial rationality as other types of strategies, and to the extent that they meet these criteria and contribute to increasing the degree of efficiency of the system, they should not be ruled out as a strategic option provided that mergers are between savings banks with little geographical and sectoral overlap. Any of the above alternatives implies greater complexity in the set of risks assumed, which is why moving in the direction of greater market discipline becomes even more relevant. Progress in market discipline should be framed by the requirements of international supervisors' best practices. In fact, Basel II, through the third pillar, is already an important opportunity to move in this direction: increasing information transparency to the markets, so that the agents that participate in them have the possibility of assessing key aspects of the entities is an essential step for market discipline to be exercised. As I have already pointed out, in recent years savings banks have advanced to some extent towards greater submission to the rigors of market discipline, for example through which they exercise the rating agencies that value their debt issues or that practiced by the holders of this type of instruments. However, these forms of market surveillance cannot be considered as active as those affecting banks, not least because there is no such close link with the actual evolution of the results obtained by the savings banks. The savings banks have instruments that, in some way, could alleviate this problem to a large extent, significantly increasing the exercise of market discipline on these entities. However, if financial instruments of this type are to be used in order to enhance market discipline, it does not seem logical that their commercialization is carried out massively through the network of offices, placing the majority of retail clients. On the contrary, a significant proportion would have to be placed among institutional clients, since they are the ones who have the necessary capacity to develop a correct evaluation and monitoring of the economic-financial situation of the issuing entity, including, for example, the recurrence of the results or the adequacy of the credit policies developed. Greater market discipline requires greater transparency of information. I have already pointed out that the third pillar of Basel II goes in this direction, and initiatives such as the need to complete a corporate governance report contribute to this. However, the governing bodies of the savings banks need to step up their efforts in terms of transparency of information. In fact, information transparency and the promotion of an adequate culture of risk management by the senior management of entities will be enhanced to the extent that savings banks improve in line with the recommendations for good corporate governance issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. Conclusion In short, the intensification of market discipline mechanisms will result in a strengthening of the other two foundations on which, in my opinion, the model of savings banks has been based in recent years: professionalism and the ability to compete. This model of boxes has to be judged, in historical terms, as successful. However, ensuring that this continues to be the case in the future, in a context of permanent change in the financial markets, means, as I tried to convey to you throughout my speech, to strengthen these three pillars. My personal conviction is that savings banks, as they have shown on other occasions, will rise to the occasion and take the necessary steps in the right direction. Thank you very much for your attention.

En este sentido, los gestores, desde una actitud marcada por la prudencia, han de considerar que el proceso no debe responder a un mero intento de ganar tamao, sino que ha de ser totalmente coherente con la estrategia financiera y de capital de medio y largo plazo establecida por la entidad. Asimismo, ha de tenerse muy presente cmo el proceso ha de influir en el perfil de riesgos de la caja, y asegurar que se han puesto en marcha los sistemas de medicin y control adecuados, incluyendo la evaluacin de hiptesis adversas respecto de la evolucin del negocio. En definitiva, si se han de acometer procesos de expansin internacional, las entidades han de ser conscientes de que ello implica perfiles de riesgo ms complejos, lo que exige afianzar la capacidad de gestin, as como la responsabilidad y la calidad que cabe esperar de la gerencia. En consecuencia, las entidades deberan, por si mismas, adecuar los niveles de solvencia al mayor nivel de los riesgos asumidos. Existen otras alternativas a la expansin a travs de oficinas, o va procesos de internacionalizacin? Algunos agentes del sector consideran que podran plantearse fusiones entre cajas de ahorros. Lgicamente, este tipo de operaciones habran de guiarse por los mismos parmetros de racionalidad econmica y financiera que otro tipo de estrategias, y en la medida en la que cumplan esos criterios y contribuyan a aumentar el grado de eficiencia del sistema, no deberan ser descartadas como opcin estratgica siempre que las fusiones se planteen entre cajas con un escaso solapamiento geogrfico y sectorial. Cualquiera de las alternativas anteriores implica una mayor complejidad en el conjunto de riesgos asumidos, razn por la cul avanzar en la direccin de una mayor disciplina de mercado se hace todava ms relevante. El avance en la disciplina de mercado debera encuadrarse en las exigencias de las mejores prcticas de los supervisores a nivel internacional. De hecho, Basilea II, a travs del tercer pilar, supone ya una importante oportunidad para avanzar en esta direccin: incrementar la transparencia informativa a los mercados, para que los agentes que participan en ellos tengan la posibilidad de valorar aspectos clave de las entidades es un paso imprescindible para que la disciplina de mercado pueda ser ejercida. Como ya he sealado, en los ltimos aos las cajas han avanzado en alguna medida hacia un mayor sometimiento a los rigores de la disciplina de los mercados, por ejemplo a travs de la que ejercen las agencias de calificacin que valoran sus emisiones de deuda o la practicada por los tenedores de este tipo de instrumentos. No obstante, estas formas de vigilancia de los mercados no pueden considerarse tan activas como las que afectan a los bancos, entre otras cuestiones porque no existe un vnculo tan estrecho con la propia evolucin de los resultados obtenidos por las cajas. Las cajas disponen de instrumentos que, de alguna manera, podran paliar en buena medida este problema, incrementando sensiblemente el ejercicio de la disciplina de mercado sobre estas entidades. Ahora bien, si han de emplearse instrumentos financieros de este tipo en aras de potenciar la disciplina de mercado, no parece lgico que su comercializacin se realice de forma masiva a travs de la red de oficinas, colocando su mayora a clientes minoristas. Por el contrario, una proporcin significativa habra de colocarse entre clientes institucionales, ya que son stos los que disponen de la capacidad necesaria para desarrollar una correcta evaluacin y seguimiento de la situacin econmico-financiera de la entidad emisora, incluyendo, por ejemplo, la recurrencia de los resultados o lo adecuado de las polticas crediticias desarrolladas. La mayor disciplina de mercado precisa de una mayor transparencia informativa. Ya he sealado que el tercer pilar de Basilea II va en esta direccin, e iniciativas como la necesidad de cumplimentar un informe de gobierno corporativo contribuyen a ello. No obstante, es preciso que los rganos rectores de las cajas intensifiquen sus esfuerzos en lo que a la transparencia informativa se refiere. De hecho, la transparencia informativa y el impulso de una adecuada cultura de la gestin de los riesgos por parte de la alta administracin de las entidades, se ver potenciada en la medida en la que las cajas mejoren en la lnea de las recomendaciones de buen gobierno corporativo emitidas por el Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea. Conclusin En definitiva, la intensificacin de los mecanismos de disciplina de mercado se traducir en un reforzamiento de los otros dos fundamentos sobre los que, a mi juicio, se ha venido asentando el modelo de cajas en los ltimos aos: profesionalidad y capacidad para competir. Este modelo de cajas ha de juzgarse, en trminos histricos, como exitoso. Ahora bien, garantizar que esto siga siendo as en el futuro, en un contexto de cambio permanente de los mercados financieros, pasa, como he pretendido trasladarles a lo largo de mi intervencin, por afianzar esos tres pilares. Mi convencimiento personal es que las cajas de ahorros, como ya han demostrado en otras ocasiones, sabrn estar a la altura de las circunstancias y darn los pasos necesarios en la direccin correcta. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Reflections on MiFID
text: Madrid, 24 January 2007 Reflections on MiFID CMNV Conference on Investor Protection in MiFID. CNMV Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor of the Bank of Spain I would like to begin my speech by thanking the Chairman of the CNMV, my good friend Manuel Conthe, for his kind invitation to deliver this closing speech at the Conference organised by the CNMV on investor protection in the directive on markets and financial instruments. This gives me the opportunity to share with you my reflections on a matter of great interest to the Bank of Spain, taking into account that more than 80% of the investment services provided in our country are channeled through credit institutions, following a common trend in Continental Europe. As will no doubt have already been pointed out throughout the different presentations that have preceded my speech, MiFID, deepening the principles of the Investment Services Directive of 1993, expands and updates its content following two inspiring criteria: first, the recognition of the current greater complexity of services, financial instruments and trading systems, an area of the economy where innovation occurs with great dynamism; and second, the need to increase investor protection. The first criterion derives from the acceptance of new organised trading systems, in addition to the current regulated markets, which means boosting competition in this field. The second inspiring criterion, investor protection, is specified in two sets of measures required of investment service providers, whether companies specialized in this business or credit institutions: those that establish the list of minimum requirements of organization and internal control that they must have and those that refer to the rules of conduct that they must maintain with customers. These broad and ambitious objectives explain the long gestation process of the directive, until it finally saw the light in 2004. In addition, as a Community framework standard designed under the Lamfalussy criteria, it requires its development through a second level, and it was not until 2006, two years later, when the important and detailed provisions that complete it were approved. From November 2007, the date of its entry into force, entities must be prepared to comply with the new regulation, through an implementation process to which I will refer later. The MiFID framework: Single Market integration To properly assess the importance of this directive, it is worth remembering that it was born within the framework of the Financial Services Action Plan of the European Union, better known as FSAP. As you all know, the FSAP is a programme prepared in 1999 which proposes a whole set of measures and rules with the ultimate goal of promoting a single financial market in the European Union. Therefore, MiFID ultimately aims to promote the fulfillment of this objective. Thus, in assessing its impact, one must not lose sight of the benefits to be expected from a more integrated financial system. Let me say a few words on this issue, because it is important to remember that these benefits have to do with the greater possibilities of diversification that a single market allows, in such a way that its capacity to channel funds to the most productive uses is increased, and the mechanisms of transfer, coverage and, ultimately, risk management. Integration also allows for deeper and more liquid financial markets, where a higher level of competition can be expected. All this results in a more efficient, innovative system capable of providing final consumers with a greater number of possibilities of choice, thus increasing their well-being. Finally, it should not be forgotten that an integrated financial market facilitates the transmission of monetary policy, with the obvious associated benefits. The set of effects I have mentioned is summarized in a very simple idea: financial integration positively affects the growth of our economies, a conclusion supported by the available empirical evidence. The main objective of the FSAP, in which MiFID also participates as one of its elements, is to help these positive effects materialize. Today, the degree of integration achieved in the European Union is significantly higher than it was seven years ago. However, the situation is not uniform across all markets, so any detailed diagnosis will depend substantially on the particular market concerned. Thus, at the extreme of full integration could be placed the money markets of the euro area, which have been greatly favoured by the stimulus of the common monetary policy. The euro is undoubtedly playing an important role in the process of financial integration. At the opposite extreme are the Union's retail markets, where a clear dominance of local activity persists. Between these two points could be placed the rest of the markets. Thus, public debt can be considered with a high level of integration, to which both the disappearance of exchange rate risk and the convergence in inflation expectations between the different Member States have contributed. In the case of corporate debt markets, the level reached is also relatively high. In fact, in recent years it seems that the characteristics of the country of bond issuance are of less marginal importance as an explanatory factor for the performance of securities. This shows that progress is being made along the path outlined by the Financial Services Action Plan. Progress is more limited in equity markets, where important steps still need to be taken. However, to some extent results are already being observed. On the one hand, as in the corporate debt market, events that transcend the local are increasingly important when it comes to explaining the evolution of stock prices, although the relevance of the factors specific to each country is still very important. On the other hand, in recent years there have been rapprochements between the stock exchanges of different countries. Let me elaborate a little more on the situation of the retail markets, which do not currently enjoy the levels of integration that a priori would be expected from a single financial market. A clear example is the retail banking sector, a segment to which the activity of credit institutions in our country is predominantly oriented. Despite the fact that cross-border consolidation movements have begun to be observed in recent years, a trend that could intensify in the future, a low level of integration still persists in this market, which is not necessarily explained by the existence of legal barriers: indeed, it is worth asking to what extent the marked local profile of these activities is not determined, At least in large part, by the very nature of the activity. In the banking business, it has been shown that proximity to the customer and the relationships established with him are very relevant, which helps explain why local entities maintain certain advantages over banks in other countries in their retail activities. It is remarkable that in many European countries, and Spain is no exception, foreign entities that have tried to establish themselves in retail markets, have only been successful if they are efficient and able to understand the needs and peculiarities of the local user. In any case, and regardless of the degree of integration that can be expected in the European Union's retail markets, I am convinced that MiFID will contribute to its achievement and will be a key element in ensuring that the benefits derived from the single financial market also reach consumers. MiFID and protecting investors' interests Focusing on the area that has convened us, MiFID faces the achievement of the objective of improving investor protection through two means: strengthening the organisational and operational requirements of investment service providers; and the improvement of the rules of conduct governing its relations with customers. With regard to the internal structure of institutions, MiFID, which places responsibility for ensuring the proper fulfilment of its mandates at the highest level of the institution, addresses issues relating to control functions and, in particular, regulatory compliance, internal procedures and risk management; clearly sets out the principles for identifying, processing and publicising conflicts of interest; and regulates the minimum conditions for the externalization of activities. More novel are the rules of conduct that should govern relationships with customers, including those of a potential nature. Thus, the first measure, from which the rest is structured, is the necessary prior classification of customers in one of the two basic categories: retail or professional. The former are those that enjoy the highest degree of protection, which translates into a different scope of information and documentation they have to receive. Hence, an evaluation of the characteristics of the investor must be carried out, of different scope depending on the service demanded, but which includes in any case the assessment of the knowledge and experience of the client as a previous step to the decision on whether he understands the risks of the product and it is suitable for him. Another of the most outstanding novelties of MiFID is the concept of "best execution", which was born as a counterweight to the breach of the principle of concentration of orders in regulated markets and which aims to ensure the best possible option for clients when executing their mandates. Implementation of MiFID The improvement of investor protection is not only a legitimate objective in itself, responding to a societal demand increasingly present in the public debate, but is, and should be, fully shared by financial market participants, for at least two reasons: The first, because enhancing the organization and internal control is a requirement of good management that results in an operational improvement with positive effects on the efficiency and credibility of the entity. The second, because from the point of view of comprehensive risk management there is an increasing sensitivity about the importance of reputational risk, especially in the case of credit institutions, whose business is based on trust, so that the impact on reputational risk of aspects related to customer protection is very relevant. How prepared is the sector to comply with MiFID? It should be clarified first of all that we are not starting from scratch. Institutions have already developed organisational structures, registration and control systems, or internal procedures applicable to the provision of investment services, necessary to comply with the regulations still in force in this area and, crucially, to effectively meet their own governance and management needs. The implementation of MiFID does not mean, therefore, building from a plot, but adapting to the new regulations buildings that are already fulfilling their mission, generally satisfactorily, and that are now in the process of improvement to enhance their functionalities. However, we must be aware that this implementation is complex. It should be recalled that the second-level standards have been approved in the year just ended, and that today regulators are still working on the development of guidelines. Along with the assimilation of the new provisions and organizational adaptations, it is necessary to undertake the training of staff and networks of branches, very extensive in the case of Spanish banks; And the date of entry into force, November 2007, is just around the corner. In addition, we are in a period in which the entities operating in our financial system are immersed in a profound process of adaptation to far-reaching regulatory changes and very demanding in terms of organizational, personal and technological resources. First, they had to face the adoption of the new accounting framework of international financial reporting standards. Then, the preparations for the important reform of the solvency regulations, driven by the agreement known as Basel II. And today, almost coinciding in time, the practical implementation of the requirements of MiFID. I think it is fair to recognize that Spanish entities are addressing these processes satisfactorily, with professionalism and diligence, very aware that the complexity of the new regulatory environment is not capricious but derives from principles shared by all, such as the improvement of risk management systems and measurement of the solvency of entities. investor protection mechanisms; And well aware, too, that the nature of the standard and the importance of these objectives influence that the processes of preparing for change have to ensure above all that the inspiring principles of the new rules are met. Given the style of regulation present in Basel II, in MiFID and in its implementing provisions, at the time of its application it is essential to pay attention fundamentally to the spirit and purpose of the standards, to their ratio legis. This is how the Bank of Spain has been judging the work carried out by the entities for the implementation of solvency standards, and will continue to do so, logically, in the case of MiFID. The Directive on markets and financial instruments is, in short, the latest project of a series of major regulatory reforms addressed at Community level, whose implementation cannot be considered closed on a specific date, the date of entry into force, because it aims to ensure a continuous process of reflection and improvement by administrators and managers, for the sake of the effective, and not merely mechanistic, fulfillment of the objectives described above. I am well aware of the high level of demand that these regulatory changes imply for institutions, because supervisors also have to adapt our knowledge, our systems and our resources to the implementation and assimilation of the necessary internal improvements, which we have been facing gradually and in advance, thinking at all times about how best to meet the principles that inspire change.
