Una desaceleraci ms profunda en la economa estadounidense, una correcci desordenada de los desequilibrios globales o de los precios de los activos son algunos de los riesgos que no se han materializado, pero que, si lo hicieran en el futuro, podran llevar a un menor crecimiento, y por tanto a que el ajuste en nuestra economa no se realizara en los trminos tan codos como los que vienen dndose desde el a pasado. Muchas gracias.

Title: Financial Integration in Europe: Facts and Policy Challenges. Speech at the European Conference of the Financial Management Association
text: Barcelona, 30 May 2007 Financial Integration in Europe: Facts and Policy Challenges European Conference of the Financial Management Association (FMA) Jose Vinals Deputy Governor of the Banco de Espana Good afternoon. First of all, I would like to thank IESE and the Financial Management Association for their kind invitation to address such a distinguished audience in this international conference. Conferences like this are doing an excellent job in fostering interaction between academics and practitioners and in disseminating state-of-the art research in finance. I am glad that this year the European Conference of the Financial Management Association is being held at IESE, which is now widely recognised on one of the leading European and international business schools. * * * We are currently living in a period of remarkable institutional changes in Europe, which are particularly visible in the economic sphere. In particular, during the nineties in the previous century we witnessed a period of monetary integration which changed markedly the economic landscape in Europe after the creation of the euro area in 1999. If the nineties was for Europe the monetary integration decade, I believe the current decade could in the future be recalled as a decisive period for financial integration. There is currently ample agreement on the potential benefits of fully developing a single market for financial services in Europe. This is a general claim shared by savers, entrepreneurs and intermediaries. Moreover, although it is not difficult to identify some specific examples of an unjustified pseudo-nationalism, authorities are generally giving proof of growing support for the overall objective, helped by social demand and the traditional peer pressure mechanisms of the European Union. My experience attending meetings of different EU Committees has taught me that these apparently loose coordination mechanisms are frequently much more effective than often thought. I therefore think that this is good opportunity to reflect on the current state, prospects and policy implications of the process of financial integration in Europe. In doing so I will be dealing with an issue of high relevance for the world economy, as Europe represents roughly one-third of the global financial system. For instance, at the end of 2006 the share of European stock exchanges in terms of world market capitalisation was 30%, moderately below the US share of 38%. Europe also represents around 30% -in terms of assets- of the institutional investment industry. Finally, about 27% of the outstanding stock of debt securities and 26% of central banks reserves were denominated in euros at end-2006. In the rest of my talk I will first describe recent developments and discuss the main drivers and achievements of the process of financial integration in Europe. I will then address the remaining steps to attaining a truly single financial area in Europe and summarise some of the most recent public and private initiatives in this domain. Finally, I will comment on the implications of this process for both agents behaviour and public policies, stressing the challenges for monetary and prudential authorities. * * * Arguably, over the last ten years we have already witnessed a remarkable increase in cross-border financial activity. Let me give you some figures to illustrate this. The share of bonds issued by euro area residents and held by euro area residents outside the issuing country rose from 10% in 1997 to more than 55% in 2005. The figures for the equity market show a smaller but still significant increase, from 13% to 27%. This fall in the home country bias has been especially visible in the portfolio of institutional investors and, in particular, investment funds. Also illustrative for me is the increasing use of cross-border collateral used for Eurosystem credit operations, the share of which climbed from 28% in 2002 to 50% in 2006. Another sign of increasing integration is the consolidation process of financial institutions, as illustrated, for example, by the recent rise in cross-border M&A transactions involving financial firms although, as you know, most operations are still at the national level. We have also observed a downward trend in the number of entities operating as a central counterparty, which fell from 13 in 1998 to 7 in 2006, expressing a clear integration of this type of activity within a framework in which national borders progressively lose importance. Finally, traditional measures of financial integration based on prices, which exploit the law of one price, also suggest a growing degree of financial integration. For instance, some empirical research shows that the proportion of the variance of the returns on securities explained by domestic factors has fallen in recent years in Europe. In order to understand the drivers of these developments in European financial activity, we must consider first a number of global factors which are fostering financial integration worldwide. In particular we should focus on at least three main elements: changes in regulation, the institutionalisation of saving and the improvement in information technologies. Let me briefly deal with these in turn. Regulation has progressively shifted to a prudential control system. This has meant the abolition of regulations and restrictions on investment and financing positions in certain instruments, and facilitated cross-border financial operations. No doubt this has contributed to larger international capital flows and to reducing the home country portfolio biases. The second global factor is the institutionalisation of saving. This process means that households tend to invest in financial markets through institutional investors - such as mutual funds, pension funds, insurance companies, private equity firms or hedge funds - rather than taking direct positions in securities. Institutional investors are better equipped, due to their size and better financial knowledge, to reap full benefit from geographical diversification. Finally, improvements in information technologies have fostered cross-border trading in various ways. First, greater connectivity between operating systems and enhanced clearing and settlement systems have reduced the transaction costs associated with cross-border operations. And second, IT improvements have increased the speed of diffusion of information. Beyond those global elements, the European financial environment has been directly influenced by the process of economic integration in Europe. The single financial area was quickly seen as a key component of the single market initiative and became one of the areas which attracted most policy initiatives. In particular, European authorities have already launched a number of initiatives to harmonise financial market legislation in the European Union. The Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP), initiated by the European Commission in 1999 and completed in 2005, was a major step forward in this regard. Another relevant development has been the application of the so-called Lamfalussy framework, which consists, as many of you know, of three levels. The first is the basic regulation containing high-level principles. The second is the technical regulation, which is in the hands of the EU Commission and Regulators Committees. And at the third level are the committees of supervisors, whose aim is to ensure convergence of supervisory practices. This framework was applied in 2000 for securities and extended to banks and insurance in 2003. Still, a major driver of the process of financial integration has been the creation of a monetary union. That acted as a key catalyst for the intensification of cross-border financial flows. In principle, it could be argued that in a frictionless world, the introduction of the euro and the single monetary policy should not have had a positive impact on the internationalisation of portfolios. In particular, the elimination of exchange rate variability and a higher correlation of returns across countries could have reduced the gains from international diversification. Indeed, the empirical evidence shows that co-movements in national stock indices have intensified in the recent past in conformity with the high synchronisation of economic cycles in different euro area countries. However, in practice the introduction of the euro meant the removal of some existing legal barriers to cross-border holdings for certain institutional investors, which were subject to restrictions on investment in assets denominated in foreign currency. Additionally, the design of the operational framework of the single monetary policy and the initiatives by the Eurosystem to facilitate a smooth and homogeneous transmission of monetary policy actions acted as a powerful engine to favour the reduction of costs associated with cross-border financial operations. Specifically, the Eurosystem has contributed to financial integration in various relevant ways, including the adoption of an eligibility criterion for collateral in its monetary policy operations that permitted credit institutions wishing to receive liquidity from the central bank to use a wide range of securities issued in any Member States. The most effective initiative by the Eurosystem in that regard has, however, probably been the establishment of TARGET, introduced at the beginning of Stage Three of EMU, which has permitted the creation of a safe and efficient mechanism to process cross-border payments based on the interconnection of national real-time-gross-settlement systems. As I commented earlier, all these initiatives have already had a noticeable impact on the degree of financial integration in Europe. However, the process is far from complete and progress has not been homogeneous across market segments. More concretely, at the most advanced extreme of the integration scale we can find money markets which are practically fully integrated. Liquidity is currently transferred across banks in the euro zone in virtually identical conditions regardless of the location of the institutions participating in each interbank operation. In the upper-mid reaches of the scale we would locate government and corporate bond markets. Here the degree of integration is high, as illustrated by the sizable proportion of foreign fixed-income instruments in the portfolios of international investors. The lower-mid segment would be for equity markets, where despite the increasing volume of cross-country operations, a significant home country bias remains. For both bonds and stocks a major obstacle to full integration is the lack of integration of security settlement systems, which makes cross-border operations comparatively more expensive than pure domestic operations. In any case, the market segment in which integration seem to be lowest is retail banking markets. As of today, the participation of foreign institutions in domestic markets of regular commercial banking services is still quite low in many Member States. Therefore, despite the progress made, the project to achieve a single financial area has not yet been fully realised in Europe. The only reasonable corollary of this statement is that more needs to be done to further increase the degree of financial integration. Against this background, European authorities have been working over the last few years on new initiatives to further develop the European market for financial services. In December 2005 the European Commission released the White Paper on Financial Services Policy 2005-2010, which contains a clear policy strategy in the field for the short and medium term. The policys main priorities are the completion of unfinished measures, the removal of the remaining economically significant barriers and the enhancement of supervisory co-operation and convergence in the European Union. The full implementation of the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (the so-called MiFID) will be a major step forward for the integration of capital markets in Europe. In particular, by November 2007 the stock exchange monopoly in trading shares will have come to an end and investment firms in one Member State will be able to use the clearing and settlement system of any other Member State. The Eurosystem continues fostering financial integration through various means. Let me mention two recent initiatives. The first is TARGET2. As I said earlier, TARGET was an important step towards integrating the interbank market in Europe. The launch of TARGET2, scheduled for the end of the current year, will introduce an even more uniform wholesale payment infrastructure. In particular, TARGET 2 will provide harmonised services and prices for domestic and cross-border payments, which would de facto imply the abolition of any relevant distinction between the two types of operations. The second initiative is the TARGET2-Securities project, which aims to harmonise and simplify the settlement of securities transactions and, ultimately, to process both securities and cash settlements on a single platform. This will provide for easier and cheaper access by investors to instruments issued in any national securities settlement system participating in the new platform. This process has also been boosted by private-sector initiatives. In particular I should emphasise the European Code of Conduct for Clearing and Settlement signed at the end of 2006 by the European industry associations for exchanges and post-trading. This Code will significantly support public-sector competition-promoting objectives and improve the efficiency of clearing and settlement in the EU. In the retail area the banking community, with the support of European authorities including those of the Eurosystem, is actively working for the creation of the single euro payments area, which could eventually permit people to process payments in other countries under similar conditions to those in their own country. Specifically, the so-called SEPA project aims to bring about a fully integrated market for retail payment services. I believe this initiative is probably that which will be most visible to European citizens, as they will be able to perceive the implications in their everyday life. In particular, starting in 2008, individuals will be able to use payment schemes in particular, for credit transfers, direct debit and credit and debit cards- which will be identical across European countries. Only two years later, all existing infrastructures should be able to process SEPA instruments. * * * I am sure all these initiatives will ultimately allow the euro zone economy to develop a truly single market for financial services, providing important benefits for European society as a whole. In particular, a more integrated financial system broadens the opportunities for investors to diversify their portfolio, thereby improving the risk-return combination and favouring more efficient consumption-savings decisions. Demanders of funds will also benefit from the greater opportunities to raise funds in deeper financial markets. Therefore, these developments contribute to a better intertemporal allocation of financial resources which, by definition, implies higher social welfare. But, in order to allow society to fully grasp the benefits of greater financial integration, public policy must adapt itself to a new environment. Let me devote the last part of my intervention to the implications of this process for policymakers and, in particular, for central banks and prudential authorities. From the monetary policy perspective, a well-integrated financial system facilitates a homogenous and effective transmission of monetary impulses across the euro area. The integration of money markets has been an important achievement in this respect. But, as I said, further progress is needed in banking retail markets, which play an important role in the transmission of the single monetary policy impulses to those interest rates that actually influence private-sector expenditure decisions. Another implication for monetary policy is the upgraded role played by financial developments in the assessment of the macroeconomic outlook. Already evident in several countries is an expansion of financial assets and liabilities of households and firms, largely induced by financial integration and the modernisation of the financial system, that has made consumption and investment decisions much more sensitive to financial shocks. This process is therefore strengthening the links between macroeconomic and financial stability in a policy-relevant way. In that setting, central banks with the help of the academic literature- have identified the limitations of monetary policy strategies that make interest rate decisions depend exclusively on the deviation of predicted inflation from a more or less explicit target. In order to maximise their contribution to safeguarding macroeconomic stability, central banks should also pay attention to abnormal developments in financial markets and the financial sector that may eventually cause abrupt corrections with high potential costs in the medium to longer term. The ECB is well equipped to address these challenges by following a robust monetary policy strategy which embeds not only a standard macroeconomic analysis of future output and inflation prospects but also a careful monitoring of relevant monetary and financial indicators. In the field of prudential policies, financial integration also generates some key implications. As you would agree, financial stability is an elusive concept; as has sometimes been said, you only know what it is when you lack it. While trusting that I will not be suspected of taking any of the central bank policy functions lightly, I can safely confess that, as a central banker, the task of preserving financial stability poses in some respects more challenges than the conduct of monetary policy. For the latter, we have clear, even quantified objectives; we also have at our disposal a rich set of analytical tools to evaluate the future course of the policy-relevant variables, and a relatively wide consensus based on a wealth of knowledge accumulated over many years- on how central banks should normally react to different types of incoming information. But, more importantly, monetary policy has a well-defined set of instruments and, in particular, those helping control short-term interest rates- which have proven effective in achieving and preserving price stability. By contrast, in the domain of financial stability a non-quantifiable concept- authorities have to face the lack of a sufficiently robust understanding of the factors triggering episodes of financial distress and the absence of a universally valid set of tools to prevent and counteract those situations. Although well-designed regulation and supervision no doubt helps reduce the likelihood and the adverse consequences of financial turbulence, it is neither possible nor, probably, desirable to build a prudential shelter that could be effective under any conceivable shock. Moreover, the design of policies for both prevention and resolution must face the singularity of almost all crisis episodes. Finally, although academic research in the field has been making substantial progress in the last few years, there is still a relatively large number of unresolved issues. For example, as you well know, the academic literature provides extensive and convincing evidence on the welfare benefits associated with the international integration of the financial industry, but it is much less unanimous on its implications for financial stability. On one hand, as a result of geographical diversification, national financial systems are increasingly exposed to shocks arising in other parts of the world and, therefore, contagion becomes more likely. But, on the other, greater risk diversification means that financial institutions have a higher capacity to absorb these shocks. Clearly, adequate supervision and regulation should help ensure the positive welfare effects prevail over the less favourable ones. However, identifying the optimal degree of regulatory intervention and the specific form that this should take is open to a debate on which the guidance provided by the academic literature is arguably still scarce. Another controversial area is that of competition policy. In a more integrated system financial institutions can find incentives to grow to fully exploit economies of scale. Users of the services provided by these institutions can potentially benefit from these efficiency gains to the extent they would translate into lower prices. However, this will largely depend on the compatibility of the integration process with the preservation of a satisfactory degree of competition which may not always be the natural market tendency. Public authorities therefore face a difficult task: they should be vigilant to avoid restricting the growth of institutions through mergers and acquisitions on grounds not related to clear supervisory risks but, at the same time, they should avoid the proliferation of dominant players in the different segments of the industry. So far, the risks of excessive public intervention in the industrys development have become more evident than the emergence of natural monopolies. In this respect, initiatives to limit unwarranted protectionism have become more pressing. In particular, the recently agreed directive on mergers and acquisitions is a step forward to ensure that cross-border operations are judged on supervisory grounds by the European supervisory authorities, and goes in the direction of reducing State involvement in national financial systems. From an organisational standpoint, supervisory arrangements should evolve so as to be able to capture the change in the size and nature of the risks faced by financial institutions operating in a more internationally integrated environment. Available information shows that despite the remaining fragmentation in retail banking in the euro area, a number of large and medium-sized banks have significant cross-border activity. According to a survey conducted by the ESCB Banking Supervision Committee, in 2005 there were 33 internationally active banking groups in the euro area whose consolidated group assets accounted for 53% of total euro area banking assets. Their degree of internationalisation, measured as the percentage of consolidated assets held in foreign branches and subsidiaries, varied across home countries but was on average above 30%. Therefore, efforts are needed to avoid excessive duplications and inconsistencies of supervisory rules and practices across Member States as this may damage the activity of institutions which currently conduct cross-border business and, therefore, may act as an implicit barrier to a further expansion of the sectors international integration. To bring this about, in the short to medium term I see no better alternative than further enhancing co-operation between regulators and supervisors and increasing consistency in supervisory practices. In this regard, the Lamfalussy framework, based on a network of Level 3 Committees and convergence instruments, should play a greater role in the immediate future. This role poses a clear challenge for EU public authorities in general and supervisors in particular, because it entails a review and an enhancement of the functioning of the Level 3 committees and the creation of new instruments of cooperation and convergence of supervisory practices. In relation to the functioning of the Committees, two of the issues I believe are worth reviewing are the decision-making mechanisms, which are currently based on consensus of the members, and the enforcement of level three, where compliance with the principles or recommendations agreed are at present voluntary. When dealing with the concrete instruments, it is also worth mentioning that a number of incentives are being studied to enhance compliance with Level three measures. I might just mention here peer reviews, supervisory transparency and mediation mechanisms. On the issue of the organisation of supervision, I have only talked about the short to medium term. What do we want and what can we expect over a longer timespan? I believe that in that horizon we could see a less decentralised organisation of the European supervisory structure. It could be some form of federal system or some kind of common supervision at the EU level, at least for pan-EU banks. Any of these systems raises important and difficult questions related, for example, to the role of the European Central Bank in the framework, supervision by objective versus sectoral supervision, the role of principles-based regulation and the use of risk-based supervision. But to get there, there are first a number of prerequisites that we are far from being able to comply with: today our institutional frameworks have a large number of significant differences in supervisory models, and in civil and company law, that would have to be ironed out. And we also see major differences in our financial system structures and financial cycles. One last thing I wish to mention in this respect is the issue of financial crises. As you know, public authorities and supervisors have been pooling their efforts in the EU on the issue of crisis prevention and crisis resolution. This is a very difficult subject with a number of challenges. If we divide this question into two, that is, into liquidity crises and solvency crises, we could say that National Central Banks have worked together in the European Central Bank and have been able to devise clear and orderly mechanisms of liquidity assistance. The issue of solvency is more complex: crisis-resolution exercises have been developed, MoUs have been signed, and work has been done, and is ongoing, on issues such as the development of similar tools for crisis prevention and resolution, the impact of cross-border crises on the functioning of those instruments, the role, characteristics and differences between Deposit Guarantee Systems in different countries, etc. Nevertheless, even though we are now in a fairly good position to tackle a financial crisis of a cross-border, pan-EU bank, and we are not expecting a crisis to take place, more work has still to be done. Let me recapitulate with a list of the main things I have mentioned and what we expect to be principally dedicating ourselves to in the short, medium and long term, something that I would call, if you will allow me the term, the ten commandments: (1) the integration of payment, clearing and settlement systems; (2) the implementation of MiFID; (3) the implementation of Basel II and Solvency II; (4) the enhancement of cross-border competition; (5) the lifting of obstacles to cross-border retail banking integration; (6) the reduction of State intervention in national financial systems; (7) improved cooperation between EU supervisors, to which I would add the need for a more intense dialogue between European financial authorities and those of other areas; (8) increased convergence of supervisory practices and enhancement of the functioning of the Lamfalussy approach; (9) an adequate structure and distribution of responsibilities of EU supervision that could eventually lead to a federal system of supervisors or some form of unified supervisory body for pan-EU banks; (10) an adequate framework for crisis prevention and resolution geared specially towards cross-border banks. In any event, as the financial system is constantly evolving and posing fresh challenges for policymakers, it is likely that the above list will soon have to be expanded accordingly. For example, one relevant recent development has been the transfer of risks from banks to other financial institutions, a process fostered by the emergence of an active market for credit derivatives and securitised loans. As a result, banks have been able to improve their risk management strategies, becoming less exposed to some specific shocks affecting the solvency of their borrowers. As those risks have now been spread out across a variety of investors, we might expect the financial sector to have become less vulnerable as a whole, in principle. But the concern is that supervisors have a limited knowledge of who is taking up this or that type of risk and we cannot therefore exclude the possibility of some less regulated financial institutions, such as hedge funds, eventually becoming excessively exposed. In a context in which loose monetary conditions are increasing the risk appetite of investors wishing to secure satisfactory returns, this concern has become a major policy issue and has been on the agenda of meetings of all relevant international financial institutions and fora. The challenge for policymakers is twofold. Firstly, to make an effort to identify concrete ways to improve the information on the activities of these institutions that is available for investors and supervisors. Secondly, to assess whether current regulation is sufficient to prevent these institutions from accumulating an amount of risks that could eventually jeopardise the stability of the global financial system. In sum, policymakers are currently facing some key challenges from financial integration in Europe. But as I hope to have made clear in my intervention, there is a need for more analytical and empirical work to provide the right guidance to national and European authorities. I am fully aware of the high analytical complexity of these issues and of the difficulty of designing formal models and empirical exercises that could directly fit policymakers preoccupations. But, in the relatively short history of finance as a scientific discipline, it is not difficult to find examples of highly sophisticated technical work that has effectively helped to improve our financial decisions and to make our financial systems more efficient and safer. With that in mind let me encourage you to address in your research some of the issues I have outlined in my talk. I wish you all success in this International Conference. Thank you very much.

Title: The efficiency of the banking system and the supervision of the Bank of Spain. Closing conference in the course organized by the Association of Economic Information Journalists at the Menndez Pelayo International University
text: Santander, June 22, 2007 The efficiency of the banking system and the supervision of the Bank of Spain Closing Conference of the Course organized by the Association of Economic Information Journalists (APIE) at the Men8endez Pelayo International University (UIMP) Jose Vi96als Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain I would like to begin by thanking the organizers, the Association of Economic Information Journalists and the Men8endez Pelayo International University, for their invitation to deliver this closing conference in a conference that, year after year, has been demonstrating its usefulness as a meeting point and reflection on the situation of the Spanish financial system, its challenges and its perspectives. Certainly, it is a pleasure to be with all of you today in a call raised around a question - Why is the Spanish financial system the most efficient in Europe? - whose very formulation expresses a very positive judgment about the situation of our system, as well as a favorable vision of its ability to face the challenges and take advantage of the opportunities offered by an increasingly integrated and competitive market. Efficiency is, in fact, one of the keys that allow us to weigh the maturity of a financial system: it is not only directly related to profitability and solvency, but it is also a very precise barometer to measure the competitive capacity and adaptation to the dynamism of a sector in continuous search for innovations. The continuity of financial institutions in the medium and long term and their ability to develop business strategies that allow them to opt for leadership positions depend, in large part, on success on the complex path to efficiency. In these days it has undoubtedly been of interest to analyze what degree of truth exists in the question with which the organizers extol the conditions of efficiency of our financial system, in comparison with other European countries, but it is equally interesting to look back and ask ourselves what we could have said about this same issue thirty years ago. at a time when Spain was facing its democratic transition. At the end of the 70s our banking system was weak and outdated, unprepared to face the challenge of economic liberalization after many decades surviving in a very protectionist environment. Similarly, our supervisory system was weak and showed many shortcomings. It is not surprising, therefore, that there was then the most severe banking crisis that Spain has had to face throughout its recent history, in which more than half of private banks went through problems. Fortunately, this black and white photograph has little to do with the one that can be taken today, already in color, by any observer: a modern, solid and efficient system with the capacity for expansion; and a supervisory model equally prepared to meet the objectives of promoting financial stability and protecting depositors. These two snapshots are separated by thirty years of efforts that have been justly rewarded for success. ***** In the first part of my speech, I will make some comments on certain factors that have undoubtedly contributed particularly to the efficiency of our banking system: internal competition, technological development, human capital, the banking model, risk management systems and international expansion. In the second part, I will analyse certain aspects of the exercise of the supervisory function and the regulatory policies applied that are related to the efficiency of institutions. Previously, I would like to review some general figures that reflect how much progress has been made in recent years. The most widely used indicator for the overall assessment of banks' efficiency, the ratio that measures structural costs in relation to ordinary margin, has improved by almost 15 points since 1999 in all Spanish groups of deposit institutions. Starting from an initial value of around 62%, throughout 2006 it broke the 50% barrier, to stand at 47.5% at the end of the year. If we did a separate analysis of banks and savings banks, we would see that the trajectory has been very similar. My first reflection refers precisely to the importance of intense competition between banks and savings banks in the Spanish banking model. The current configuration of our banking system is the result of a historical process in which entities of different commercial nature have demonstrated their ability to serve different segments of the population with specific banking needs, so that neither the geographical location, nor the levels of education and income, nor the productive sector have been decisive conditions for access to the offer of banking products. The legal equalization of the operational possibilities of banks and savings banks was the logical corollary to the accumulated experience, and was a stimulus for the development of two subsectors capable of developing increasingly effective strategies based on customer orientation, innovation and management procedures, generating a competitive environment that has meant a notable boost to efficiency. Another factor that has had a clear influence on improving the behavior of our system is technological development. Investment in technology is a large and relevant investment, hence planning and managing it properly is not a minor issue within the set of strategies of the entities. The key is to know how to translate that volume of investment into profits, via improved efficiency, and opportunities to compete. Without forgetting, also, that the use of more complex technological processes requires managing a new risk: technological risk. A specific aspect that implies its management is the need to develop emergency plans in the event of the possible interruption of the normal operations of an entity. The importance that this aspect of internal control can have has led supervisory authorities to warn about the need for managers to take appropriate control measures. The Bank of Spain, in the Supervisory Report of the last financial year, which is about to be published, will echo these reflections by assuming the high-level principles on business continuity published in August 2006 by the Joint Forum, an international group of which supervisors of the three traditional financial sectors are part: banking, securities and insurance. The third point I would like to comment on concerns human capital. If we look back a decade, we will see that there has been a broad renewal of the management teams of credit institutions and a significant change in the profile of the average bank employee. I will dwell briefly on two factors associated with this process: initial preparation and training. The average academic preparation of bank workers has improved markedly over time; at least, it is what the Bank of Spain has been receiving day by day in the frequent contacts maintained for the exercise of its different functions. I am particularly pleased to be able to make this comment within the framework of a teaching institution, such as the Men8endez Pelayo International University, which hosts this meeting. Undoubtedly, now that we are immersed in the process of adaptation to the European Higher Education Area (Bologna reform), Spanish universities will be able to face with more possibilities of success the challenge of a greater rapprochement between the university world and that of the company, placing more emphasis on training oriented to professional practice. Along with this, the entities have understood that investment in training is one of the most profitable investments they can make and the one that provides a more favorable cost-benefit ratio in terms of efficiency. A fourth point on which I would like to dwell is the typical banking business model of Spanish entities, retail banking, which is no stranger to the levels of efficiency achieved. Firstly, because specialisation in this area has been so intense that it has provided our entities with a clear competitive advantage in the internal market. Secondly, because this specialization has involved the development of business strategies and the formation of highly qualified management teams, which have become an intangible of great value in the expansion decisions of some entities; and, thirdly, because being a business model that promotes recurring results has favored the construction of efficient structures with a vocation for stability. My next thought revolves around the relationship between risk management systems and efficiency. Traditionally, risk management has been the part of a more opaque credit institution to the general public. But, just as the non-visible facilities of a building are essential for its proper functioning, risk management systems constitute a basic infrastructure on which the success of the activity carried out depends to a large extent. It is not surprising, therefore, that the most recent initiatives on transparency obligations d0 corporate governance reports, annual report, Pillar 3 of the new solvency regulations d0 promote increasingly complete information on this matter. Banks and savings banks have a very wide terrain here to explore new paths. It is increasingly notorious that in risk management systems entities have room to obtain competitive advantages. In fact, it has been said that such systems are already part of the hallmarks of a credit institution. But we must not forget that the search for efficiency is also the search for economies of scale. Hence, to conclude these comments dedicated to examining the factors that have driven the efficiency of our banking system, I will briefly stop to review the trajectory that the banking sector has followed in Spain, since the first merger between two large Spanish banks took place at the end of the 80s. In a first phase, there was an intense process of consolidation of entities within Spain, which resulted in the case of banks in mergers between larger entities and, in the case of savings banks, in concentrations within each autonomous area. Subsequently, since the mid-90s, Spanish banks began the process of international expansion that still characterizes it today, mainly targeting the Latin American market. The cultural proximity, the availability of management surpluses as a result of mergers in Spain, and the dedication to markets in which to provide a more relevant retail banking experience, have facilitated this process, despite the risks involved in the presence in markets with a lower level of maturity, has been able to contribute to the improvement of the overall efficiency of Spanish groups with more active expansion policies. And finally, already in this century, these policies have begun to be strongly directed towards our continent, although in the retail banking business there is still a level of integration in the European Union much lower than that achieved in other financial markets, while the presence in other geographic markets begins. A veteran manager of a Spanish entity often said a phrase that can be remembered as a direct and, in my opinion, very wise motto about the banking profession: efficiency is only pursued, never achieved. It is a concise and realistic way of expressing the danger of complacency when you have responsibilities whose exercise has been paid off in a positive way, but which are not exempt from risks and threats. Maintaining the battle for efficiency as a strategic priority is the best way for banks to face a future characterised by a foreseeable increase in external competition in the domestic retail banking market, current regulatory changes or the possible need to manage risks incurred in macroeconomic conditions not as favourable as those of recent years. ***** In the second part of my speech it is my purpose to refer to the role played by the Bank of Spain, as regulator and supervisor, in promoting the efficiency of our banking system. Supervisors have sometimes been criticized as causing some obstacles to the achievement of optimal returns by institutions. I will not shy away from this controversy, but I would like to start from two principles that I am sure are widely shared. Firstly, credit institutions and supervisory authorities, in order to adequately fulfil their purposes, which are private and public in nature respectively, have intermediate objectives that coincide. Thus, the greater efficiency of the entities links perfectly with the legal mandate of the Bank of Spain to help make the banking sector as safe and stable as possible, and that it has ample capacity to offer citizens quality services at competitive prices. Second, the exercise of the supervisory function necessarily entails certain costs for institutions arising from the need to comply with prudential rules, to meet the supervisor's information requirements and to maintain frequent dialogue with him. These costs are real and quantifiable, but an adequate measurement would also lead us to calculate the indirect benefits that, for each participant in the sector, supposes the existence of a public surveillance system, due to the degree of security it provides and the overall confidence in the system it generates. Hence, a good monitoring system is one that generates benefits that far outweigh the costs incurred. From here, the duty of every supervisor is to submit to permanent analysis the initiatives adopted in the field of regulation and supervision to facilitate the path to efficiency for institutions. It would be a misconception and a disservice to the general interest to consider that the status of public authority exempts from the need to carry out such an analysis. In its recent history, the Bank of Spain has experienced three phases in relation to the supervisory approaches applied. Until the early 80s, a highly regulatory legal structure was maintained in terms of the operational possibilities of credit institutions, the prices applied and access to banker status, which determined a formalistic supervisory orientation, which emphasized compliance with provisions in many cases not related to prudential concerns. From the crisis of the late 70s-early 80s the liberalization of the system was accompanied by a change in the supervisory approach, which was aimed at having an updated knowledge of the financial situation of the entities through revisions of the financial statements and own resources. Valuable experience in asset quality verification was then developed, which continues to be an important element of our supervisory model, and which gradually incorporated more qualitative elements. Finally, since the end of the last decade, the Bank of Spain adopted the orientation known as Supervision of Banking Activity under a Risk Approach, in acronym SABER, whose foundation lies in structuring the supervision tasks around the assessment of the risk profile of each entity. In my opinion, the risk approach is the most appropriate to limit the supervisory burden. First, because it brings more added value to institutions, by carrying out an independent review not only of the financial statements, but also of the risk management systems used; secondly, because it allows more selective action in the areas where risks are concentrated; third, because it facilitates dialogue since the risk approach is a common language shared by all; and, finally, because it is better aligned with the current course of solvency regulations and internal management. The supervisors entrusted with monitoring the solvency of the entities are usually designated with the appellation of "prudential". It therefore seems intrinsic to our role the application of criteria of prudence. The lessons learned from the severe crisis to which I referred earlier also taught us the virtues of such criteria. On occasion we have received the criticism of having gone at some point a little beyond what has been traveled by other European countries. Perhaps the issue that has concentrated more comments on this has been that of the regulation of provisions for insolvency. I can announce that the Banco de Espa96a has already initiated preliminary studies to promote a regulatory reform so that entities that have integrated credit risk management systems and a sufficiently extensive experience of historical data can, in the near future, follow the path already pointed out in the last accounting circular, Calculate its provisions for insolvencies according to its own internal models. This reform is in no way intended to reduce the level of demand of the current system of provisions but, rather, to adapt it to the specific circumstances of each entity. I believe that the evolution of the profitability, solvency and efficiency figures of our institutions in recent decades, and their positive comparison with those of other countries in our environment, testify that the competitive capacity of our banking system has not been diminished at all by supervisory policies that have contributed to strengthening the solvency of institutions and increasing public and market confidence. Undoubtedly, the level of prudence of the criteria applied by the Bank of Spain can be modulated according to each historical moment. In the future, the application of internal models for both the calculations of own resources and for provisions, will mean the need for managers to make estimates subject to different types of assumptions, which implies a significant increase in their responsibility, very reasonable considering the maturity that the sector has reached. Administrators, when defining their policies, will undoubtedly have in their sights the need to protect the quality of assets, the solvency of the entity, confidence in the business and its continuity. I would also like to make a few comments on regulation styles. Banking regulation has achieved a high degree of harmonisation within the European Union. A recent trend in the new directives applicable in the financial field is to seek a greater link between how prudential requirements are complied with and how directors and officers manage their institution. I have already mentioned that, with the new general solvency framework, known as Basel II, institutions will be able to calculate their own resources using advanced approaches anchored in their internal management models. To do this, they will need to demonstrate that they have systems in place to improve the estimates provided by standardised compliance methods. This approach undoubtedly has an impact on the efficiency of credit institutions. Firstly, it will allow a more efficient use of capital, contributing to the definition of optimal financing strategies and allocation of own resources. This narrows the gap between the concepts of internal capital and regulatory capital. Second, incentives are created for improved management, as the adoption of more advanced approaches depends on the quality of the risk management systems and procedures used. To emphasize this last aspect of the Basel II rules, the concept of incentive regulation has been coined. In the definition of the reference standards developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, the process of dialogue with representatives of credit institutions is increasingly accentuated to achieve agreements that are more respectful of the real needs of banks. This trend is repeated in the legislative processes of the European Union and Spain. The publication of impact studies also contributes to a better understanding of the standard-setting process. The Bank of Spain, in the ongoing consultation process on the new solvency circular, has begun the practice of publishing such studies, an initiative that will continue in the future. In this move towards flexibility, a new concept is making way, principled regulation, which promotes a regulatory style less supportive of numerous prescriptive rules of detail and more based on the enunciation of more general objectives, which institutions can address in the way that best suits their circumstances. This trend is linked to the provision incorporated into the Bill amending the current Law on Own Resources, recently published in the Bolet92n de las Cortes, according to which the Bank of Spain is empowered to prepare and publish guides, aimed at supervised entities and groups, indicating the criteria, practices or procedures that it considers appropriate to promote a good assessment of risks and better compliance with the rules of ordination and discipline. The impact of supervisory burdens on efficiency is multiplied in the case of multinational groups with a presence in different countries, subject to different legal regimes and supervised by different authorities. In the European Union it is a frequent reflection, because it becomes more relevant as progress is made in the integration of financial systems. Therefore, the current efforts of European supervisors are focused on improving cooperation and convergence in supervisory practices, once an adequate homogenization of national regulations has been achieved. To achieve this, it is a question of strengthening the instruments known as Level 3 in the scheme of Lamfalussy's committees of regulators and supervisors. This is without prejudice to further reflection on the structure of European supervision in the longer-term future, a debate in which one of the important factors to be analysed is the influence that such a structure has on the costs of supervision for groups with a multinational presence. ***** From my words it can be concluded that the issue of the efficiency of credit institutions raises a wide range of issues, which will have to be addressed by bank managers and supervisory authorities. A fundamental aspect to take into account is the need to consider the battle for efficiency a permanent battle. In conclusion, I believe that the success story of the evolution of the Spanish banking system in recent decades has been the result of an unwritten alliance between the private sector and the public sector, which have understood very well that the path they were traveling was a common path and mutual understanding contributed to pave it. At first, the public part had to assume a more relevant role, since it was necessary to manage the exit from an intense crisis, create regulatory infrastructures that allowed the performance of efficient supervision and adopt as many coercive or persuasive measures as were necessary to promote the solvency of the entities, but the private sector has been taking more and more prominence in the task of leading the Spanish banking system to the leading positions that today Holds. Thank you very much for your attention.

Por eso, los esfuerzos actuales de los supervisores europeos se centran en mejorar la cooperacin y la convergencia en prcticas supervisoras, una vez alcanzada una adecuada homogeneizacin de las normativas nacionales. Para lograrlo se trata de potenciar los instrumentos conocidos como de Nivel 3 en el esquema de comits de reguladores y supervisores de Lamfalussy. Ello sin perjuicio de que, de cara al futuro a ms largo plazo, se siga reflexionando sobre la estructura de la supervisin europea, un debate en el que uno de los factores importantes a analizar es la influencia que tal estructura tiene en los costes de la supervisin para los grupos con presencia multinacional. ***** De mis palabras se puede concluir que la cuestin de la eficiencia de las entidades de crdito suscita temas muy variados, que habrn de ser afrontados por los gestores bancarios y por las autoridades de supervisin. Un aspecto fundamental a tener en cuenta es la necesidad de considerar la batalla por la eficiencia una batalla permanente. Como conclusin, creo que la historia de xito en que ha consistido la evolucin del sistema bancario espaol en estas ltimas dcadas ha sido el resultado de una alianza no escrita entre el sector privado y el sector pblico, que han comprendido muy bien que el camino que estaban recorriendo era un camino comn y el entendimiento mutuo contribua a allanarlo. Al principio, la parte pblica debi asumir una funcin ms relevante, ya que fue necesario gestionar la salida de una crisis intensa, crear infraestructuras regulatorias que permitieran el desempeo de una supervisin eficiente y adoptar cuantas medidas coercitivas o persuasivas fueron necesarias para promover la solvencia de las entidades, pero el sector privado ha ido tomando cada vez ms protagonismo en la tarea de conducir al sistema bancario espaol a las posiciones punteras que hoy ostenta. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Appearance before the Committee on Economy and Finance of the Congress
text: Madrid, June 26, 2007 Appearance of the Governor of the Bank of Spain before the Economy and Finance Committee of the Congress Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor Ladies and gentlemen, I wish, first of all, to express my gratitude for the opportunity that this appearance gives me to share with you the vision of the situation of the Spanish economy incorporated in the Annual Report of the Bank of Spain. The publication of this Report constitutes a milestone of deep-rooted tradition that serves to recapitulate on the balance of opportunities and challenges facing our economy. I am particularly pleased to share these reflections with the representatives of popular sovereignty. As you well know, the fabric of our country's economic policies is profoundly conditioned by membership of the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). It seems to me, therefore, that the ideal starting point to address before you, as governor of the Bank of Spain, the current moment and the prospects of the Spanish economy is the analysis of the monetary policy of the European Central Bank. In the last year and a half, the progressive consolidation of the recovery of activity in the area has led to the emergence of risks to price stability in the medium and long term. And faced with this, the ECB has adopted an attitude of alert to the possible materialization of the same, with the intention of preserving the preventive nature of monetary policy, which has led to a progressive change in its tone. Thus, in December 2005 the Governing Council decided to end a two-and-a-half-year period during which key interest rates had remained unchanged at 2%, which was historically very low for all countries in the area, even those with a long tradition of stability. Subsequent successive hikes (up to a total of eight times) have placed the headline rate at 4%, which has made it possible to move towards normalising existing monetary conditions. In recent years, the accommodative tone of monetary policy has been favoured by the maintenance of a notable degree of wage moderation in the euro area d0 albeit with notable differences between countries d0 which has made it possible to limit the inflationary effects of the rise in oil prices. Factors such as relatively low utilization of installed capacity until recently, the growing emergence of new competing countries on the international economic scene and the appreciation of the euro exchange rate have also contributed to the containment of inflationary pressures. However, in recent months, monetary policy has had to ensure that inflationary pressures that could be generated as a result of the impact of greater activity dynamism on the mechanisms for price and wage formation are controlled. In any case, despite the increase in interest rates, monetary conditions continue to be conducive to the expansion of domestic demand, the recovery of which already seems to be in the process of full consolidation. Indeed, for this year, the prospects for economic growth in the area are clearly favourable, given that the information available for the first half of the year points to a dynamism even higher than expected at the beginning of the year. This strength of activity is being led by a high investment dynamism that, despite the increase in the cost of financing, continues to present a very encouraging picture, thanks to the solid financial position of companies, in a context of increased utilization of installed capacity. It is true, however, that the most recent data on household spending continue to indicate that this component of demand lags somewhat behind the global expansionary cycle. In any case, the improvement in employment expectations and the optimism of families reflected in the confidence surveys predict a strengthening of consumption in the course of the coming quarters. On the external side, a continuation of the dynamism of global activity can be expected, so that, in the most likely scenario, the prospects of a slight moderation in activity in some geographical areas should not be an obstacle to maintaining the good tone of euro area exports. These favourable prospects are, however, subject to some downside risks, of predominantly external origin, over the medium and long-term horizon, mainly as a result of the possibility that the slowdown in the US economy will be more intense than currently anticipated, that further increases in oil prices will take place, that the prevailing optimism in global financial markets will be reduced or that there will be a disorderly correction of global imbalances. On the price front, inflation is likely to benefit in the coming months from some transitory effects. In the medium term, which is the relevant horizon for monetary policy decision-making, forecasts point to rates of around 2%, but with upside risks, mainly derived from the possibility that labour factor costs will grow higher than expected. It is therefore important that wage agreements remain on the current path of moderation and reflect a sufficient degree of differentiation according to the specific conditions of each sector and the productivity of each company. Of course, the future course of monetary policy will be marked by the evolution of the risk factors for inflation containment that I have just mentioned. The Governing Council of the ECB shall exercise rigorous and continuous supervision of the factors affecting its priority objective and shall act decisively to maintain inflation expectations at levels consistent with price stability. As in the past, the Governing Council will seek to make its own decisions predictable by regularly indicating how new information confirms or qualifies its assessment of the relevant macroeconomic outlook. At the same time, it will avoid incurring predetermined commitments that limit its capacity to act in the light of new information available. I must say that, for the Spanish economy, the process of normalisation of monetary conditions to which I have just referred is proving particularly appropriate. Firstly, because it contributes to preserving the stability and sustained growth of our trading partners. Secondly, because it is also helping us to achieve a more balanced composition of expenditure, to achieve a certain moderation in the demand for financing and to contain the increases in the price of housing. I will therefore comment on the basic features of the recent evolution of the Spanish economy. As indicated in the Annual Report, in 2006 the expansion phase that has characterized its performance since the middle of the last decade continued. GDP growth amounted to 3.9 per cent, compared with 3.5 per cent in the previous year, once again exceeding the forecasts made at the beginning of the year. On the expenditure side, this upturn in activity was offset by a slight slowdown in domestic demand and a more intense improvement in the contribution of net foreign demand to output growth, thus leading to more balanced growth. These trends have continued in the first quarter of 2007, with GDP growth rising to 4.1 per cent, slightly higher than at the end of 2006, as a result of a further slowdown in domestic demand and a further improvement in the contribution of the foreign sector to output growth. The growth dynamics of the Spanish economy continue to be supported by the stimuli induced by monetary and financial conditions that continue to favour the dynamism of spending and activity, although logically with less intensity than in the past, after the rise in interest rates that has been occurring over the last year and a half. But at the same time, the increase in labor supply has continued, as a result of the magnitude of migratory flows and the advance of female participation. The increasing availability of labour resources has meant that the dynamism of expenditure translates into increases in activity and employment and that cost and price tensions remain relatively contained. All this, in a context of increased flexibility in the mechanisms of adjustment of the economy and macroeconomic stability, despite the intensity reached by the increases in oil prices in the first half of last year. To all these factors was added, in 2006, the good performance of the world economy and, in particular, the recovery of the euro area, which is boosting sales abroad after several years of weakness, allowing to compensate for the strength of imports, in a context of strong final demand and highly competitive imported prices. Thus, the contribution of net foreign demand to output growth is improving, although the nation's need for financing continues to expand, albeit at a slower pace than in recent years. With regard to household spending, private consumption and residential investment maintained a strong tone in 2006, supported by the expansion of disposable income, high levels of confidence d0 possibly encouraged by the good outlook for employment and permanent income d0 and the appreciation of wealth, although to a lesser extent than in previous years due to the gradual slowdown in the price of housing. For its part, the relative tightening of monetary and financial conditions had a limited impact on both expenditure components in 2006, as I pointed out in my last appearance in this Committee. However, both consumption and residential investment in 2006 marked a slight slowdown compared with the high figures reached in previous years that continued in the first months of 2007. In the case of consumption, this trend would mainly reflect the slight slowdown in disposable income and wealth. In residential investment, it would be changes in interest rates and expectations of lower appreciation that have begun to exert a certain modulating effect on housing demand, as the profile of the slowdown in the prices of this asset seems to be indicating. Throughout this period, the household savings rate has continued to fall, which, together with the dynamism of residential investment, has led to an expansion of their financing needs and an increase in their indebtedness. However, the rate of growth of credit to families began to show signs of inflection in the last months of last year, a trend that has continued in the elapsed part of this year and that probably reflects the impact of the rise in the cost of financing. This trend has been determined by the slowdown in loans for the purchase of housing, while the resources allocated to consumption have stabilized their rates of expansion at relatively high rates. Regarding the performance of non-financial corporations, business investment maintained a strong tone throughout last year that has continued in the first months of this year, in response to very robust demand and corporate earnings conditions that are offsetting the effect of the interest rate hike on investment decisions. In fact, in 2006 significant investment plans were launched in equipment while important corporate acquisitions were carried out aimed at the diversification of business areas, given the maturation of certain productive activities, and the internationalization of Spanish companies. On the other hand, the financing needs of the sector were expanded and there was a growing recourse to external financing, which has continued in the first months of this year, causing an increase in the sector's debt ratios. Throughout this process, productive activity, derived from the supply conditions of the economy, is responding with some agility to the expansion of spending, supported, as I have already said, by the strength that employment continued to show. Particular note should be made of the strength of the industrial sector, which picked up strongly over the past year and continues to expand at a high pace, after several years of weakness, as well as the sustained expansion of the construction sector, which shows only slight signs of slowdown after such a strong and widespread boom. Precisely this agility in the response of the supply, together with the improvements in the adjustment capacity of the economy, are helping to ensure that this prolonged phase of boosting demand has been reconciled with a stage in which wage costs have maintained a relatively moderate behavior despite the dynamism shown by wage agreements last year. Despite this, the inflation rate maintained an average growth of 3.5% in 2006, widening the differential with inflation in EMU, and 3.1%, when excluding the energy component, particularly dynamic last year. The behaviour of prices in the first part of 2007 is proving more favourable, although energy prices are once again playing an outstanding role in this development. However, the core inflation rate remains stabilised at 2.5% and some major headings, such as services, stand at 4%, so it is possible that once the favourable effect of the declines in energy prices has been exhausted, inflation will pick up somewhat. The Spanish economy has thus entered 2007 with remarkable dynamism and a more balanced composition of expenditure as the slight slowdown in domestic demand and the improvement in net foreign demand continue, while business investment begins to take over from the push for residential investment. In this scenario of continuity of dynamism in the short term, the sustainability of growth in a longer horizon acquires great importance. In this sense, and as the Bank of Spain has pointed out on multiple occasions, the normalization of spending and indebtedness patterns of Spanish families and companies is considered a necessary condition to ensure the stability of growth. In the new context of less financial slack to which I have just referred, the gradual slowdown in house prices and the mild moderation of credit have made it possible for some progress, albeit limited, to take place in the process of adapting Spanish households to the gradual withdrawal of monetary stimulus. In the field of companies, however, the concurrence of other factors has meant that the normalization of interest rates has hardly been reflected in the behavior of investment and indebtedness in the sector. It is expected that the adjustment of financial conditions will end up generating a moderation of these patterns of indebtedness and spending, which will reduce the financial risks of companies and guarantee the continuity of the investment process in the medium term. But in addition, the Spanish economy must be prepared to face the challenges posed by phenomena such as globalisation or demographic evolution, which shows great dynamism due to the intensity of migratory flows, but which faces a process of marked aging in the long term. It is therefore necessary to improve our ability to compete, through a greater alignment of our costs and prices with those of our main trading partners and a genuine improvement in the quality and functioning of our productive apparatus, which should be reflected in greater productivity gains. The latter is especially relevant to continue the process of real convergence, once the impulses derived from the increase in the employment rate lose strength, as we approach areas of relatively low level of unemployment. Economic policies have an important responsibility to adopt the most appropriate measures to meet these challenges. The monetary policy of the European Central Bank has made it possible, through the gradual increase in benchmark interest rates since the end of 2005, to bring financial conditions closer to levels more in line with the requirements of the Spanish economy, although they are still accommodating. Under these conditions, it is up to the policies that remain in the hands of the national authorities to assume the role of mitigating the risks inherent in a boom cycle as long as the one our country is experiencing and, at the same time, strengthening its growth potential. The reforms needed to expand the economy's potential require time to unleash their full impact, so the opportunity offered by the current economic boom to ambitiously define and implement them quickly should not be missed. Fiscal policy is an important tool for achieving the above-mentioned objectives. In this area, and from a short-term point of view, the strength of revenues in the first months of the year allows us to predict, as has happened in recent years, a growth in collection above budget. Given the cyclical position of the economy, it should be ensured that this dynamism in revenues is used to improve the existing fiscal surplus. A strategy that should be accompanied by an effort to control on the expenditure side, so that higher revenues do not result in additional increases in this item. The implementation of the budget for the remainder of the year and the preparation of the budget for next financial year should be carried out on this basis. Of course, the final result of the fiscal policy orientation in a strongly decentralised State such as Spain depends crucially on the collaboration of all the Administrations and, in particular, of the Autonomous Communities, given that these are responsible for a good part of the spending competences, so they should adopt the previous guidelines as their own. This budgetary strategy is also appropriate from a medium-term perspective. The dynamism of public revenues has a transitory component, linked to the strength of domestic demand and, in particular, of the real estate sector, so that a greater degree of consolidation will allow to expand the room for manoeuvre available to be used in the face of possible deviations from the high growth scenario. Similarly, taking into account that the main challenge facing public finances continues to be that derived from the impact of population ageing on pension and health spending, an additional fiscal consolidation effort would allow this impact to be better addressed, although, in any case, the reform of the pension system should also be deepened. aimed at ensuring its long-term sustainability. Finally, it is necessary that the above-mentioned strategy be carried out in a manner compatible with an improvement in the efficiency and quality of public finances, that generates the appropriate economic incentives in economic agents, eliminates unwanted distortions of public intervention and improves the provision of factors, in particular human and technological capital through education and research. The role of fiscal policy on long-term growth is, however, limited and must be complemented by the implementation of structural policies. These policies should be defined in such a way as to further improve the degree of flexibility and responsiveness of supply to economic conditions and the growth potential of the economy. The response of the supply depends first and foremost on the proper functioning of the labour market. The strong dynamism generated by the high migratory flows and the growing participation of women has provided powerful levers of flexibility to the labour market, but in the long term it is necessary to better adapt the institutional framework that provides more stable bases for an efficient use of labour resources and expand the possibilities of employment and income generation of the entire population. This, as I said in my speech to the Bank's Governing Council, must be done without losing the achievement of social peace. I would like to conclude by pointing out that boosting productivity also requires improving the quality of human capital and strengthening the competitive environment in which companies operate, so as to generate the right incentives for business investment and the development and spread of innovations. And for this, it is necessary to persevere and extend the liberalization processes undertaken in recent years and advance in the definition of a simpler and more transparent regulatory framework. Thanks a lot
text_original: Madrid, 26 de Junio de 2007 Comparecencia del Gobernador del Banco de Espaa ante la Comisin de Economa y Hacienda del Congreso Miguel Fernndez Ordez Gobernador Seoras: Deseo, en primer lugar, expresar mi agradecimiento por la oportunidad que me brinda esta comparecencia de compartir con ustedes la visin de la situacin de la economa espaola incorporada en el Informe Anual del Banco de Espaa. La publicacin de dicho Informe constituye un hito de arraigada tradicin que sirve para recapitular sobre el balance de oportunidades y retos a los que se enfrenta nuestra economa. Me complace particularmente hacer partcipe de estas reflexiones a los representantes de la soberana popular. Como ustedes bien saben, el entramado de las polticas econmicas de nuestro pas est profundamente condicionado por la pertenencia a la Unin Econmica y Monetaria (UEM). Me parece, por tanto, que el punto de partida idneo para abordar ante ustedes, como gobernador del Banco de Espaa, el momento actual y las perspectivas de la economa espaola es el anlisis de la poltica monetaria del Banco Central Europeo. En el ltimo ao y medio, el progresivo afianzamiento de la recuperacin de la actividad del rea ha ido dando lugar a la aparicin de riesgos para la estabilidad de precios en el medio y largo plazo. Y frente a ello, el BCE ha adoptado una actitud de alerta ante la posible materializacin de los mismos, con la intencin de preservar el carcter preventivo de la poltica monetaria, lo que ha conducido a un cambio progresivo en su tono. As, en diciembre de 2005, el Consejo de Gobierno decidi poner fin a un perodo de dos aos y medio de duracin durante el cual los tipos de inters oficiales haban permanecido inalterados en el 2%, que era un nivel histricamente muy reducido para todos los pases del rea, incluso para aquellos con gran tradicin de estabilidad. Las sucesivas elevaciones posteriores (hasta un total de ocho ocasiones) han situado el tipo principal en el 4%, lo que ha permitido avanzar hacia la normalizacin de las condiciones monetarias existentes. En los ltimos aos, el tono acomodante de la poltica monetaria se ha visto favorecido por el mantenimiento de un notable grado de moderacin salarial en el rea del euro -aunque con notables diferencias entre pases-, lo que ha permitido limitar los efectos inflacionistas del alza del precio del petrleo. A la contencin de las presiones inflacionistas han contribuido asimismo factores tales como una utilizacin de la capacidad instalada relativamente reducida hasta hace poco, la creciente irrupcin de nuevos pases competidores en la escena econmica internacional y la apreciacin del tipo de cambio del euro. Sin embargo, en los ltimos meses, la poltica monetaria ha debido asegurar el control de las presiones inflacionistas que pudieran generarse como consecuencia del impacto del mayor dinamismo de la actividad sobre los mecanismos de formacin de precios y salarios. En todo caso, a pesar del aumento de los tipos de inters, las condiciones monetarias continan siendo propicias para la expansin de la demanda interna, cuya recuperacin parece estar ya en vas de plena consolidacin. En efecto, para el presente ejercicio, las perspectivas de crecimiento econmico en el rea son claramente favorables, dado que la informacin disponible correspondiente al primer semestre del ao apunta a un dinamismo incluso superior al que se esperaba al comienzo del mismo. Esta fortaleza de la actividad est siendo liderada por un elevado dinamismo inversor que, a pesar del aumento del coste de financiacin, contina presentando un panorama muy alentador, gracias a la slida posicin financiera de las empresas, en un contexto de aumento de la utilizacin de la capacidad instalada. Es cierto, no obstante, que los datos ms recientes referidos al gasto de las familias continan sealando que este componente de la demanda se encuentra algo rezagado con relacin al ciclo expansivo global. En cualquier caso, la mejora de las expectativas de empleo y el propio optimismo de las familias que reflejan las encuestas de confianza auguran un fortalecimiento del consumo en el curso de los trimestres venideros.
