University of Valencia Jose Vi96als Deputy Governor of the Bank of Spain Dear friends, It is an honor for me to have been invited to participate in this event, which ends the activities carried out in the last twelve months to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the Faculty of Political, Economic and Business Sciences. Therefore, my thanks go to the Dean and the management team of the Faculty for their kind invitation; Thanks that I wish to extend to all those who are part of it. During these four decades of life of the Faculty, many things have changed, both in Spain and in the world. In our country, the political, social and economic changes have been so many and so profound that the Spain of the late 60s is barely recognizable to us; And the world has undergone far-reaching transformations that were unthinkable in those times. Globalization, understood as a process of growing integration worldwide, is undoubtedly one of the most outstanding phenomena and with the greatest capacity for transformation of our environment in recent decades. This process of integration dilutes and makes national borders more permeable, projecting itself in multiple dimensions: social, political, cultural and, of course, economic. In many respects, globalization is a potentially enriching phenomenon. Thus, in the cultural and social sphere, we can consider the globalization of the media, information and knowledge, or the growing generalization of certain patterns of social behavior, which facilitate interrelations and shorten distances. However, problems and other less positive aspects are also globalized. Such is the case of global terrorism, in the political and geostrategic sphere, or of global warming, in the environmental field, problems that require the search for global solutions. But I do not intend to approach globalization today from such a broad perspective. In view of the interest of the audience, and in strict application of the principle of comparative advantage, I will focus my intervention on some aspects of the globalization process linked to the economic and financial level, which seem to me to be particularly relevant. In recent decades d0 and in particular in the last ten or fifteen years d0 the process of globalization has received a unique impulse, supported by two types of factors, which have also characterized other stages of accelerated integration in the history of human progress: technology and political and institutional changes. Technological advances have allowed a profound transformation in crucial aspects for integration. In transport, the widespread use of the container d0 so important, by the way, for the take-off of the port of Valencia d0 and the greater accessibility of air transport have reduced the cost of moving goods and people across the globe. In the area of information technologies, the universalization of computers, the improvement of communications and, in particular, the use of the Internet have reduced the cost of transmitting, obtaining and processing information to unsuspected limits. These technological changes have transformed production processes, allowing their segmentation between different locations, and have revolutionized the functioning of financial markets. In addition, at the institutional level, the recovery of multilateralism, greater trade and regional integration d0 the European Union being a paradigmatic case in this regard d0 and the liberalisation of capital flows have become engines of globalisation. To these we must add, on a more political level, the fall of the "iron curtain", at the end of the eighties, and the collapse of the socialist economic model in Eastern Europe and other countries, which has led to its irruption on the world economic scene. A case in point is that of China, which is designing its own path to a market economy and is already a major economic power. Some figures help to understand the magnitude of the impetus that all these forces have given to the process of globalization. The increasing integration of goods markets has meant that the weight of foreign trade in world GDP has almost tripled in the last thirty years, and now represents close to 30%. Labour markets have also undergone a rapid process of interconnection, which has manifested, on the one hand, in the form of immigration flows. In particular, immigration to OECD countries, mainly from developing areas, measured as a percentage of the resident population, has also tripled in the last 30 years. Spain is one of the most outstanding examples of this evolution, with a ratio of resident foreign population approaching 10% of the total population, compared to figures below 2% at the end of the nineties. On the other hand, the segmentation of production processes and the relocation of labor have also increased the integration of labor markets, by encouraging workers from different countries to participate in different phases of the same production process (a phenomenon known as offshoring). All this has taken place in parallel with the emergence of emerging economies, whose weight in world GDP and trade has risen rapidly. As striking as the figures illustrating economic globalization are, progress in financial integration has been even more intense: for example, in 1970, the foreign assets of developed economies were equivalent to 25 per cent of their GDP; by 1990 this ratio had tripled, and has tripled again since then, reaching 225% of GDP in 2005. The greater speed acquired by financial integration is a reflection of the enormous development that the monetary and financial dimension of economies has acquired, as opposed to the 'real' dimension. For example, in the United States, the value of financial assets is seven times the value of GDP. The magnitude of the transformations that globalization is causing to the real economy and the functioning of the financial system force the authorities to ask what are the consequences for the functioning of the economy and the implications for their economic policy decisions. For this reason, and given my work as a central banker, I want to dedicate the rest of this conference to reflect on the implications of this stage of intense globalization for monetary and financial stability, the main area of responsibility of central banks and a key piece to guarantee sustained economic growth rates that improve the standard of living of citizens. It is important to note that, in recent decades, the confluence of monetary policy objectives of many countries around price stability d0 understood as maintaining low and stable inflation rates d0 has been widespread, in response to the virtually universal consensus that monetary policy can best contribute to macroeconomic stability and growth. This general objective is compatible, however, with different strategies. In some of them, inflation becomes the sole objective of monetary policy d0 as in the case of the Bank of England d0 in others, it is the primary objective d0 as in the ECB d0 or it can also be part of a dual objective, as in the Federal Reserve. With regard to financial stability, this is reflected in some key aspects, such as: (i) the soundness of credit institutions (banks and savings banks) and the efficiency in their task of channelling savings flows towards investment; (ii) the proper functioning of markets; and (iii) the quality of operational infrastructures (payment, contracting, clearing and settlement systems) that support the activity of institutions. Central banks generally have competences in this area, which are translated into different functions: ensuring the proper functioning of payment systems, acting as basic liquidity providers and lenders of last resort d0 a task that has become very important in recent months, in the wake of recent financial turbulence d0 and, in many cases, Among them the Spanish, carry out the supervision and regulation of banking entities. What implications does globalization have on these tasks of central banks? Economic globalization d0 that which refers to the functioning of the real sector of the economy d0 affects, above all, the management of monetary policy (and has some impact on financial stability), while financial globalization directly affects both financial stability and monetary policy. In any case, the experience of recent years suggests that globalisation has not posed major problems for monetary policy in achieving the objective of price stability. On the contrary, it even seems to have facilitated it, as I shall argue later. Overall, globalization appears to have contributed to improving economic growth potential, mainly through its favourable impact on global productivity. Indeed, the increased competition brought about by globalization has fostered innovation in production processes, while access to a global market allows economies of scale to be exploited, all of which tend to lead to greater productivity gains. Overall, the most recent phase of globalization has coincided with a period of remarkable macroeconomic stability, characterized by a high rate of growth d0 in the last five years the highest period of economic growth in the last thirty years has been reached d0 the achievement of low and stable inflation rates, and reduced macroeconomic volatility d0 a phenomenon known as 'the great moderation'. This is not to say, however, that the good results in terms of moderating inflation can be attributed solely to globalization. In fact, the factor that has led, in the first instance, to the moderation of inflation has been the growing consensus on the orientation of monetary policies towards price stability. Not surprisingly, in the long run, inflation is a phenomenon primarily of a monetary nature. The basic elements of this consensus are several: (i) the importance of the institutional framework and, in particular, central bank independence and price stability as a primary medium-term objective; (ii) an understanding of what is considered price stability d0 annual inflation up to 2% or 3%, depending on the structural characteristics of each country (just under 2% in the euro area); (iii) convergence towards strategies of "limited discretion" in decision- making processes, which improves the policy framework; and (iv) predictability, transparency and good communication as key aspects in the management of monetary policy. The implementation of this consensus has allowed inflation expectations to be anchored and has favoured the maintenance of moderate rates of price increase. Along with this, the available evidence suggests that globalization has indeed facilitated the task of central banks in controlling inflation through several avenues. On the one hand, globalization has pushed up the prices of raw materials and downwards those of manufactures. This has largely been a consequence of the positive impact that this process has had on both the demand for raw materials and the supply of manufactured products, in line with the incorporation of emerging economies d0 and in particular, China and India d0 into the global market. It seems clear that these conflicting price movements are, in fact, a significant adjustment of relative prices, but they have also had a net favourable effect on the inflation rate in developed economies, which has been reduced by a few tenths per year. How long this slight favourable impact will last is a different question, since it is expected that, although it may be persistent, it will be transitory. On the other hand, globalization could have had other favourable effects on inflation, by fostering an environment of greater external competition, through international trade and immigration flows, which in turn would have favoured greater discipline of wages and prices. Another important change in the monetary policy environment that has been observed in recent years, in the context of increasing economic integration, has been the flattening of Phillips curves in most economies. This means that, in the short term, changes in the pace of economic activity (or in the trend in unemployment rates) have less impact on inflation than in the past. The observed flattening may be the result, at least in part, of greater flexibility in the economy linked to globalization. Thus, the favourable impact of globalisation on the behaviour of inflation has been added to that resulting from the implementation of decidedly anti-inflationary monetary policies, which have managed to anchor agents' inflation expectations around much lower rates than in the past. This anchoring would also have contributed d0 powerfully d0 to making inflation less sensitive to changes in the pace of economic activity. In other words, while globalisation has strengthened the credibility of monetary policy, reducing the variability of inflation and moderating its response to higher rates of economic activity d0 relative to the past d0 any easing of monetary discipline would lead to a de-anchoring of price expectations and inflation itself. with the negative effects that this entails. If, as I have pointed out before, in the long run inflation is fundamentally a monetary phenomenon, monetary policy must remain vigilant and not let its guard down. Moreover, while economic globalization has contributed to the reduction of inflation and facilitated the task of monetary policy in this regard, it has in other ways complicated it, adding greater uncertainties to the overall environment in which policymakers must make their decisions. Thus, for example, globalization makes it difficult to measure variables that are very relevant to this decision-making process, such as potential output and the output gap. Also, the external dimension gains relevance, so that external variables must be increasingly taken into account. In short, central bankers have to think, more and more, in a global key, although we continue to act in a local key. While economic globalization has, on the whole, facilitated the achievement of low inflation, financial globalization has added complexity, both in terms of the implementation of monetary policy and in the area of financial stability. This introduces new challenges for central banks, which have become particularly apparent from the financial turbulence that began last summer, and in which we are still immersed, to which I will refer later. But first, in order to properly understand the causes and effects of turbulence, I will briefly examine the main characteristics of the process of financial globalization in recent years that, together with innovation, have been shaping a 'new international financial system', whose most salient features are the following: (i) increasing freedom of international capital flows; (ii) rapid collection and dissemination of information on a global scale; (iii) integration of domestic financial markets into truly global markets and the internationalization of banking activity (the global banking phenomenon); (iv) emergence of new financial products, including many increasingly complex 'derivative products'; and v) emergence of new investment agents and instruments (hedge funds, private equity, conduits, structured investment vehicles (SIVs), increasingly opaque in their operations and scarcely subject to prudential regulations. Related to this point, a final feature to mention is the growing importance, especially in Anglo-Saxon countries, of a banking model based on the principle of 'originate to distribute', which, unlike the traditional banking model, does not keep credit on the balance sheet but, after granting it, packages it in the form of bonds and sells it to third parties. All this has taken place in a context of abundant liquidity on a global scale, as a result, not only of relatively low official interest rates in the main areas of the world, but of the growing capacity of the markets, through, precisely, these financial innovations, to multiply liquidity through high levels of indebtedness, or leverage, in chain. This 'new international financial system' has, in my opinion, had a very favourable impact, on the whole of the world economy, although there have been some excesses, which are partly behind the current financial turbulence and which need to be corrected. In other words, a situation of chiaroscuro, but where I believe that the lights clearly prevail over the shadows, both for developed and emerging economies. On the bright spotlight, the new global financial system is made up of more complete, deeper and more liquid markets, allowing for greater efficiency in the allocation of resources, within and between countries. It also promotes greater diversification and dispersion of risks, which tends to generate more resilience to negative shocks. I would like to highlight this point, because in the last decade there has been no shortage of shocks with potential negative impacts on the world economy: remember the explosion of the technological bubble, at the beginning of the current decade, which had a significant impact on advanced economies, but not too deep or persistent; we must also mention, in this regard, the Argentine crisis, the events of September 11, 2001, or the corporate scandals of Enron, Worldcom or d0 here in Europe d0 Parmalat, whose negative effects have been considerably smaller on a global scale than would have been the case in previous times. Another positive aspect that I would like to highlight is the disciplining effect that greater freedom of international capital flows has had on countries' economic policies. The competitive pressures mentioned earlier not only affect companies, but also states and, in this sense, capital mobility has contributed to increasing economic discipline, especially in emerging economies. But there have also been shadows in the process, which have surfaced suddenly in recent months. Thus, the dispersion of risk favored by financial innovation and globalization has not been homogeneous, but pockets of fragility have been generated, as a result of the concentration of risks. In turn, the opacity and complexity of many of the new financial products, and the proliferation of new agents and investment vehicles have shown that problems can accumulate silently and that, sometimes, their true depth and magnitude is only known when they explode. On the other hand, recent financial developments also appear to have generated inappropriate incentives, resulting in insufficient risk surveillance and excessive levels of indebtedness; incentives that the herd behavior that sometimes characterizes financial markets has tended to intensify. Finally, financial globalization d0 and the different degree of development of developed and emerging financial systems, in favour of the former d0 has led to an unusual pattern of global balance-of-payments imbalances and movements in international capital flows, which instead of moving from rich to poor countries (to finance their development, attracted by higher potential returns), they are moving from developing countries to the world's richest economy d0 the United States d0 to finance their high external deficit. Now, having said all this, what challenges does the 'new financial system' that emerged from globalisation pose for monetary policy and financial stability? With regard to monetary policy, the main challenge is undoubtedly to have to be carried out in an environment of greater uncertainty. First, global liquidity conditions, which have been very comfortable in recent years, are increasingly relevant in the determination of long-term interest rates, which has implied a growing disconnect from short-term rates d0 on which national monetary policy decisions have a direct influence. On the other hand, knowledge of the mechanisms of monetary transmission is increasingly uncertain, because we still ignore many things about new financial products and agents. We know a lot more about how traditional agents such as banks, insurance companies and pension funds behave, but, even in these cases, patterns of behavior have changed. In short, although the monetary transmission mechanism does not become a 'black box', it is, at least, a somewhat darker box than in the past. On the other hand, external shocks of a financial nature, which may arise unexpectedly and whose effects may be significant, given the size of global financial markets, constitute an additional source of risk. Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that this environment of greater uncertainty has not, so far, been an insurmountable obstacle for monetary policy to achieve its objective of price stability. However, in the area of financial stability, the 'new financial system' has meant new challenges for central banks, as highlighted in the current episode of turbulence. The source of the financial turbulence lies in the US mortgage market, where, in recent years d0 and in the heat of the expansion of the housing market d0 an increasing proportion of mortgage loans have been granted to clients who did not meet the appropriate collateral (called subprime loans, a term that refers to the reduced capacity of borrowers to service the debt incurred). What factors have led to the excessive development of such loans? Basically, the confidence of debtors d0 and creditors d0 in the possibility of refinancing their loans in the future, in a context of strong revaluation of house prices, an asset that constitutes the guarantee of the loan. In the case of creditors, the 'originate to distribute' banking model has generated perverse incentives. In this scheme the loans, once granted, do not remain in the balance sheet of the originator. On the contrary, profitability derives from the amount of loans granted that are securitized and resold with juicy commissions, regardless of the credit risk, since this is assumed by a third party. In the case of subprime mortgages, these third parties have turned out to be investment vehicles of various kinds and banks in many countries, which had acquired structured bonds, more or less complex, collateralized with this type of mortgage. Apart from the high yield on bonds, an additional element that has facilitated their distribution, despite the valuation difficulties involved, has been that rating agencies have given them high ratings (triple A in many cases). In short, given the complexity and opacity of many of these products, investors have relied on the ratings of the agencies, without considering to what extent they had appropriate valuation models, or even to what extent a good rating constituted a sufficient guarantee. In a way, investors have also sinned, in many cases, of lack of prudence and due diligence. The generation and distribution mechanism I have just described has been working d0 and increasingly intensively d0 until the change of cycle in the US housing market has led to a significant deterioration in underlying mortgage assets, which has become evident in the first half of 2007. Indeed, after the start of an upward cycle of interest rates by the Federal Reserve, the upward trend in house prices in the United States ended up breaking, leading to a very sharp increase in mortgage delinquencies, especially in the subprime segment of this market. This has generated a high level of distrust in structured products based on these mortgages, which has resulted in a revision of the ratings of many of them, from the usual triple-A levels to minimum credit ratings. As a result, the "financial chain" of generation and distribution has broken down and structured commodity markets have come to a standstill, with considerable uncertainty emerging about the ultimate distribution of losses and their true magnitude. To the extent that some major banks, as I have already pointed out, are involved in holding these structured products, there has been a contagion of distrust towards interbank markets, which have also been blocked, except in very short terms. All this has been shaping a panorama of scarcity and increase in the cost of financing, so that the crisis of confidence and the liquidity crisis have gone hand in hand. But what have been the really unexpected aspects in the development of this financial turbulence? The general rise in risk premia for riskier credit assets since July has not, as the risk assessment had been repeatedly acknowledged to be abnormally low. In this respect, the upward correction experienced by these premiums could be considered healthy. On the contrary, the rapidity with which the markets of structured products (based on mortgages) have lost liquidity, the duration of this "drought" and the paralysis of the interbank forward markets during all these months, have been largely unexpected aspects. As the origin of the problems has also been unexpected, given that the current crisis in the US subprime market represents potential losses that barely reach 0.5% of global banking assets. The rapid transmission of turbulence to a large number of geographically dispersed financial markets underscores the importance of loss of confidence for global markets. The reaction of the central banks of the major advanced economies to the financial storm has been, in the first instance, to inject liquidity to calm tensions in interbank markets. These actions were individual until last week when the Federal Reserve, the ECB and three other central banks coordinated their efforts, as the malfunctioning of interbank markets persisted. Some central banks have also reduced their official interest rates, such as the Federal Reserve or the Bank of England, while others, such as the ECB or the Bank of Japan have maintained them, compared to expectations of hikes before the summer. In the United States, there have also been some initiatives involving the private sector (albeit with the support of the authorities) to renegotiate the terms of some poorer quality mortgage loans, bypassing interest rate revisions, in order to avoid further increases in non-performing loans. The regulatory and supervisory authorities have also opened a process of reflection on control mechanisms, to reduce risks to financial stability in the future. This reflection takes place at different levels, although they all have in common their multilateral character: the Financial Stability Forum, the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, the G-7, the G-20 or the European Union itself. The truth is that, despite all these reactions, the tensions in the international financial markets have not subsided, without being able to foresee, today, when calm will return and its operation will normalize. In any case, and in order to make a reasonable assessment of the current situation and the risks, it should not be forgotten that there are certain elements of strength that are helping to limit the impact of the financial storm on an international scale: the good tone of the global economy, where the moderation of US growth is largely offset by the dynamism of other economies. among which emerging and developing countries stand out (such as Asia, Latin America, etc.); the favourable initial position of banks in terms of capitalisation and profits (which provides them with buffers to absorb any losses); and the strength of corporate and household assets (with the exception of the sub-prime segment in the US). Although, as I have mentioned, it is not yet possible to think how much longer the financial storm will last, the current difficulties and uncertainties should not make us lose perspective and arrive at a negative assessment of the process of financial globalization. On the contrary, I believe that the assessment should remain favourable, mainly for two reasons: on the one hand, because financial globalisation has bequeathed us a more efficient and, with some specific segments, more solid international financial system; and, on the other, because financial globalization is the necessary counterpart of economic globalization and because both are mutually reinforcing, with the consequent benefits that this entails in terms of a greater potential for economic growth. What is necessary, in the light of the current tensions, as I mentioned earlier, is to identify the failures that have occurred in the functioning of the new international financial system in order to correct them and avoid a repetition in the future of episodes of financial stress such as the one we are experiencing. Let me conclude by summarizing the main conclusions of my speech. In it, I have examined some of the most important challenges that the globalization process poses for central banks in terms of their two primary functions, maintaining price stability and safeguarding financial stability, both of which are prerequisites for economies to grow at sustained rates, and thus contribute to improving citizens' living standards. So far, it can be concluded that the challenges have been overcome, that the globalization process has facilitated the maintenance of moderate inflation rates and that, despite the current episode of turbulence, financial stability has also been strengthened. It is no coincidence, therefore, that the most recent phase of the globalizing process has coincided with the stage of greatest prosperity of the world economy in recent decades. It has been precisely during all these years when the Faculty of Economics has been growing, becoming increasingly solid and training generations of economists who, from diverse and numerous fields, and in different capacities, have contributed and contribute to the prosperity of the Valencian Community and Spain and to reinforce their role in this globalized world in which we are immersed. Thanks a lot.

En general, la globalizacin parece haber contribuido a mejorar el potencial de crecimiento econmico, a travs principalmente de su impacto favorable sobre la productividad global. En efecto, la mayor competencia que trae consigo la globalizacin ha fomentado la innovacin en los procesos productivos, mientras que el acceso a un mercado global permite el aprovechamiento de las economas de escala, todo lo cual tiende a propiciar un mayor avance de la productividad. En conjunto, la fase de globalizacin ms reciente ha coincidido con un perodo de notable estabilidad macroeconmica, caracterizado por un elevado ritmo de crecimiento en el ltimo lustro se ha alcanzado el perodo de crecimiento econmico ms alto de los ltimos treinta aos, la consecucin de tasas de inflacin bajas y estables, y una reducida volatilidad macroeconmica fenmeno que se conoce como 'la gran moderacin'. Esto no quiere decir, sin embargo, que los buenos resultados en trminos de moderacin de la inflacin puedan ser atribuidos nicamente a la globalizacin. De hecho, el factor que ha propiciado, en primera instancia, la moderacin de la inflacin ha sido el creciente consenso en torno a la orientacin de las polticas monetarias hacia la estabilidad de precios. No en vano, en el largo plazo, la inflacin es un fenmeno primordialmente de carcter monetario. Los elementos bsicos de ese consenso son varios: i) la importancia del marco institucional y, en concreto, de la independencia de los bancos centrales y de la estabilidad de precios como objetivo primordial a medio plazo; ii) un entendimiento en torno a qu se considera estabilidad de precios una inflacin anual hasta el 2%  el 3%, dependiendo de las caractersticas estructurales de cada pas (algo menos del 2% en la zona euro); iii) la convergencia hacia estrategias de discrecionalidad limitada en los procesos de toma de decisiones, lo que mejora el marco de actuacin; y iv) la predicibilidad, transparencia y buena comunicacin como aspectos fundamentales en la gestin de la poltica monetaria. La aplicacin de este consenso ha permitido el anclaje de las expectativas de inflacin y ha favorecido el mantenimiento de tasas moderadas de aumento de los precios. Junto con ello, la evidencia disponible sugiere que la globalizacin, efectivamente, ha facilitado la tarea de los bancos centrales en el control de la inflacin a travs de varias vas. Por una parte, la globalizacin ha impulsado al alza los precios de las materias primas y a la baja los de las manufacturas. Esto ha sido consecuencia, en buena media, del impacto positivo que este proceso ha tenido tanto sobre la demanda de materias primas como sobre la oferta de productos manufacturados, al hilo de la incorporacin de las economas emergentes y en particular, de China y la India- al mercado global. Parece claro que estos movimientos contrapuestos de precios son, en realidad, un importante ajuste de precios relativos, pero han tenido tambin un efecto neto favorable sobre la tasa de inflacin en las economas desarrolladas, que se ha visto reducida en unas pocas dcimas por ao. Cuestin distinta es cuanto durar este ligero impacto favorable, pues cabe esperar que, aunque pueda ser persistente, tenga carcter transitorio. Por otra parte, la globalizacin ha podido tener otros efectos favorables sobre la inflacin, al fomentar un entorno de mayor competencia exterior, a travs del comercio internacional y de los flujos de inmigracin, que habra favorecido, a su vez, una mayor disciplina de salarios y precios. Otro cambio importante en el entorno de la poltica monetaria que se ha observado en los ltimos aos, en el contexto de una creciente integracin econmica, ha sido el aplanamiento de las curvas de Phillips en la mayora de las economas. Esto significa que, a corto plazo, los cambios en el ritmo de actividad econmica (o en la evolucin de las tasas de paro) inciden menos que en el pasado sobre la inflacin. El aplanamiento observado puede ser resultado, al menos en parte, de una mayor flexibilidad de la economa ligada a la globalizacin. As pues, el impacto favorable de la globalizacin sobre el comportamiento de la inflacin ha venido a sumarse al que se deriva de la puesta en prctica de unas polticas monetarias decididamente anti-inflacionistas, que han conseguido anclar las expectativas de inflacin de los agentes en torno a tasas mucho ms reducidas que en el pasado. Este anclaje tambin habra contribuido poderosamente a hacer menos sensible la evolucin de la inflacin a los cambios en el ritmo de actividad econmica. En otras palabras, si bien la globalizacin ha reforzado la credibilidad de la poltica monetaria, reduciendo la variabilidad de la inflacin y moderando su respuesta ante mayores ritmos de actividad econmica en relacin con el pasado, cualquier relajamiento de la disciplina monetaria dara lugar a un desanclaje de las expectativas de precios y de la propia inflacin, con los efectos negativos que ello comporta. Si, como he sealado antes, en el largo plazo la inflacin es fundamentalmente un fenmeno monetario, la poltica monetaria debe mantenerse vigilante y no bajar la guardia. Adems, aunque la globalizacin econmica haya contribuido a la reduccin de la inflacin y haya facilitado, en ese sentido, la tarea de la poltica monetaria, en otros sentidos la ha complicado, al aadir mayores incertidumbres al entorno general en el que las autoridades deben tomar sus decisiones. As, por ejemplo, la globalizacin dificulta la medicin de variables muy relevantes para ese proceso de decisin, como son el producto potencial y la brecha de produccin. Asimismo, la dimensin exterior gana relevancia, de modo que hay que tener cada vez ms en cuenta las variables externas. En definitiva, que los banqueros centrales tenemos que pensar, cada vez ms, en clave global, aunque sigamos actuando en clave local. Si la globalizacin econmica ha facilitado, en conjunto, el logro de una inflacin reducida, la globalizacin financiera ha aadido complejidad, tanto por lo que se refiere a la instrumentacin de la poltica monetaria como en el mbito de la estabilidad financiera. Ello introduce nuevos retos para los bancos centrales, que se han puesto particularmente de manifiesto a raz de la turbulencia financiera que comenz el pasado verano, y en la que seguimos inmersos, a la que me referir ms adelante. Pero antes, para entender adecuadamente las causas y los efectos de la turbulencia, examinar brevemente las principales caractersticas del proceso de globalizacin financiera en estos ltimos aos que, junto con la innovacin, han ido configurando un 'nuevo sistema financiero internacional', cuyos rasgos ms sobresalientes son los siguientes: i) creciente libertad de los flujos internacionales de capitales; ii) rapidez en la obtencin y difusin de informacin a escala global; iii) integracin de los mercados financieros nacionales en mercados verdaderamente globales y la internacionalizacin de la actividad bancaria (el fenmeno de los bancos globales); iv) aparicin de nuevos productos financieros, entre ellos, muchos 'productos derivados' de creciente complejidad; y v) aparicin de nuevos agentes e instrumentos de inversin (hedge funds, private equity, conduits, vehculos de inversin estructurada SIVs, en ingls-), cada vez ms opacos en su operativa y escasamente sometidos a las regulaciones prudenciales. Relacionado con este punto, un timo rasgo a mencionar es la creciente importancia, sobre todo en los pases anglosajones, de un modelo bancario basado en el principio de originar para distribuir, que, a diferencia del modelo de banca tradicional, no mantiene el crdito en el balance sino que, tras concederlo, lo empaqueta en forma de bonos y lo vende a terceros. Todo ello ha tenido lugar en un contexto de abundante liquidez a escala global, como resultado, no slo de tipos de inters oficiales relativamente reducidos en las principales reas del mundo, sino de la creciente capacidad de los mercados, a travs, precisamente, de estas innovaciones financieras, para multiplicar la liquidez mediante elevados niveles de endeudamiento, o apalancamiento, en cadena. Este 'nuevo sistema financiero internacional' ha tenido, a mi juicio, un impacto muy favorable, en conjunto, sobre la economa mundial, si bien ha habido algunos excesos, que en parte estn detrs de la actual turbulencia financiera y que deben ser corregidos. En otras palabras, una situacin de claroscuros, pero donde creo que las luces claramente prevalecen sobre las sombras, tanto para las economas desarrolladas como para las emergentes. Respecto a las luces, el nuevo sistema financiero global se compone de mercados ms completos, profundos y lquidos, lo que permite una mayor eficiencia en la asignacin de los recursos, dentro de los pases y entre pases. Tambin promueve una mayor diversificacin y dispersin de riesgos, lo que tiende a generar ms resistencia ante perturbaciones negativas. Me gustara resaltar este punto, porque en la ltima dcada no han escaseado las perturbaciones con potenciales impactos negativos para la economa mundial: recordemos el estallido de la brbuja tecnolgica, al comienzo de la dcada actual, que tuvo un impacto importante en las economas avanzadas, pero no demasiado profundo o persistente; tambin hay que mencionar, en este sentido, la crisis argentina, los acontecimientos del 11 de septiembre de 2001, o los escndalos corporativos de Enron, Worldcom o aqu en Europa Parmalat, cuyos efectos negativos han sido considerablemente menores a escala global que lo que hubiera sido el caso en pocas previas. Otro aspecto positivo que quiero destacar es el efecto disciplinador que la mayor libertad de flujos internacionales de capitales ha tenido sobre las polticas econmicas de los pases. Las presiones competitivas que mencionaba antes no slo afectan a las empresas, sino tambin a los estados y, en este sentido, la movilidad del capital ha contribuido a incrementar la disciplina econmica, sobre todo en las economas emergentes. Pero tambin han existido sombras en el proceso, que han aflorado de manera sbita en los ltimos meses. As, la dispersin del riesgo favorecida por la innovacin financiera y la globalizacin no ha sido homognea, sino que se han generado bolsas de fragilidad, resultado de la concentracin de riesgos. A su vez, la opacidad y complejidad de muchos de los nuevos productos financieros, y la proliferacin de nuevos agentes y vehculos de inversin han demostrado que los problemas se pueden acumular silenciosamente y que, en ocasiones, solo se conoce su verdadero calado y magnitud cuando estallan. Por otro lado, los desarrollos financieros recientes tambin parecen haber generado incentivos inapropiados, que han derivado en una vigilancia insuficiente de los riesgos y en niveles excesivos de endeudamiento; incentivos que el comportamiento gregario que a veces caracteriza a los mercados financieros, ha tendido a intensificar. Por ltimo, la globalizacin financiera y el diferente grado de desarrollo de los sistemas financieros desarrollados y emergentes, a favor de los primeros ha propiciado un patrn poco comn de desequilibrios globales de balanza de pagos y de movimientos de los flujos internacionales de capitales, que en lugar de ir desde los pases ricos hacia los pobres (para financiar el desarrollo de stos, atrados por una mayor rentabilidad potencial), estn yendo desde los pases en desarrollo hacia la economa ms rica del mundo -los Estados Unidos-, para financiar su elevado dficit exterior. Ahora bien, dicho todo esto, qu retos entraa el 'nuevo sistema financiero' surgido de la globalizacin para la poltica monetaria y para la estabilidad financiera? Respecto a la poltica monetaria el principal reto es, sin duda, tenerse que llevar a cabo en un entorno de mayor incertidumbre. En primer lugar, las condiciones globales de liquidez, que en los ltimos aos han sido muy holgadas, son cada vez ms relevantes en la determinacin de los tipos de inters a largo plazo, lo que ha implicado una creciente desconexin respecto de los tipos a corto plazo sobre los que tienen influencia directa las decisiones de poltica monetaria nacionales. Por otro lado, el conocimiento de los mecanismos de transmisin monetaria es cada vez ms incierto, porque ignoramos an muchas cosas sobre los nuevos productos y agentes financieros. Sabemos bastante ms acerca de cmo se comportan los agentes tradicionales como los bancos, compaas de seguros y los fondos de pensiones, pero, incluso en estos casos, los patrones de comportamiento han cambiado. En definitiva, aunque el mecanismo de transmisin monetaria no llega a ser una 'caja negra', s es, al menos, una caja algo ms oscura que en el pasado. Por otra parte, las perturbaciones exteriores de carcter financiero, que pueden surgir inesperadamente y cuyos efectos pueden ser importantes, dado el tamao de los mercados financieros globales, constituyen una fuente adicional de riesgo. A pesar de todo, hay que reconocer que este entorno de mayor incertidumbre no ha sido, hasta el momento, un obstculo insalvable para que la poltica monetaria alcanzara su objetivo de estabilidad de precios. Sin embargo, en el mbito de la estabilidad financiera el 'nuevo sistema financiero' ha significado nuevos retos para los bancos centrales, como se ha puesto de relieve en el actual episodio de turbulencias. El origen de las turbulencias financieras se halla en el mercado hipotecario de Estados Unidos, donde, en los ltimos aos -y al calor de la expansin del mercado inmobiliario-, se ha venido concediendo una proporcin creciente de prstamos hipotecarios a clientes que no reunan las garantas apropiadas (denominados prstamos subprime, trmino que se refiere a la reducida capacidad de los prestatarios para hacer frente al servicio de la deuda contraida). Qu factores han dado lugar a un desarrollo excesivo de ese tipo de prstamos? Bsicamente la confianza de los deudores y de los acreedores en la posibilidad de refinanciar sus prstamos en el futuro, en un contexto de fuerte revalorizacin de los precios de la vivienda, activo que constituye la garanta del prstamo. En el caso de los acreedores, el modelo bancario de 'originar para distribuir' ha generado incentivos perversos. En este esquema los prstamos, una vez concedidos , no permanecen en el balance del originador. Bien al contrario, la rentabilidad deriva de la cantidad de crditos concedidos que son titulizados y revendidos con jugosas comisiones, sin importar, en principio, el riesgo de crdito, ya que este es asumido por un tercero. En el caso de las hipotecas subprime, estos terceros han resultado ser vehculos de inversin de diversa ndole y bancos de numerosos pases, que haban adquirido bonos estructurados, ms o menos complejos, colateralizados con ese tipo de hipotecas. Aparte de la elevada rentabilidad de los bonos, un elemento adicional que ha facilitado su distribucin, a pesar de las dificultades de valoracin que entraan, ha sido que las agencias de calificacin les han otorgado ratings elevados (triple A en muchos casos). En definitiva, ante la complejidad y opacidad de muchos de estos productos, los inversores han confiado en los ratings de las agencias, sin plantearse en qu medida estas disponan de modelos de valoracin apropiados, o, incluso, en qu medida un buen rating constitua una garanta suficiente. En cierto modo, los inversores han pecado tambin, en muchos casos, de falta de prudencia y de la diligencia debida. El mecanismo de generacin y distribucin que acabo de describir ha venido funcionando y de forma cada vez ms intensa hasta que el cambio de ciclo en el mercado inmobiliario de Estados Unidos ha producido un deterioro importante de los activos hipotecarios subyacentes, que se ha ido haciendo evidente en el primer semestre de 2007. En efecto, tras el inicio de un ciclo alcista de tipos de inters por parte de la Reserva Federal, la trayectoria ascendente de los precios de la vivienda en Estados Unidos termin por quebrarse, propiciando un incremento muy acusado de la morosidad hipotecaria, especialmente en el segmento subprime de este mercado. Se ha generado as una elevada desconfianza en los productos estructurados basados en esas hipotecas, que se ha traducido en una revisin de los ratings de muchos de ellos, desde los niveles de triple A que eran habituales hasta calificaciones crediticias mnimas. En consecuencia, la cadena financiera de generacin y distribucin se ha roto y los mercados de productos estructurados se han paralizado, aflorando una notable incertidumbre sobre la distribucin ltima de las prdidas y su verdadera magnitud. En la medida en que algunos bancos importantes, como ya he sealado, estn implicados en la tenencia de estos productos estructurados, se ha producido un contagio de la desconfianza hacia los mercados interbancarios, que tambin se han bloqueado, salvo en plazos muy cortos. Todo ello ha ido perfilando un panorama de escasez y encarecimiento de la financiacin, de forma que la crisis de confianza y la crisis de liquidez han ido de la mano. Pero cules han sido los aspectos realmente inesperados en el desarrollo de esta turbulencia financiera? No lo ha sido la elevacin generalizada de las primas de riesgo que registraron los activos crediticios ms arriesgados a partir del mes de julio, puesto que se haba reconocido repetidamente que la valoracin de los riesgos era anormalmente baja. En este sentido, cabra considerar que la correccin al alza experimentada por estas primas ha sido saludable. Por el contrario, la rapidez con que los mercados de productos estructurados (basados en hipotecas) han perdido liquidez, la duracin de esta sequa y la paralizacin de los mercados interbancarios a plazo durante todos estos meses, s han sido aspectos en gran medida inesperados. Como tambin ha sido inesperado el origen de los problemas, dado que la crisis actual del mercado subprime de Estados Unidos supone unas prdidas potenciales que apenas alcanzan el 0,5% de los activos bancarios globales. La rpida transmisin de la turbulencia hacia un nmero elevado de mercados financieros, dispersos en trminos geogrficos, subraya la importancia que la prdida de confianza tiene para los mercados a escala global. La reaccin de los bancos centrales de las principales economas avanzadas ante la tormenta financiera ha sido, en primera instancia, la de inyectar liquidez para calmar las tensiones en los mercados interbancarios. Estas acciones fueron individuales hasta que la semana pasada la Reserva Federal, el BCE y otros tres bancos centrales coordinaron sus esfuerzos, en vista de que el mal funcionamiento de los mercados interbancarios persista. Algunos bancos centrales tambin han reducido sus tipos de inters oficiales, como la Reserva Federal o el Banco de Inglaterra, mientras que otros, como el BCE o el Banco de Japn los han mantenido, frente a las expectativas de subida que haba antes del verano. En Estados Unidos, han habido tambin algunas iniciativas que implican al sector privado (aunque con el apoyo de las autoridades) para renegociar los trminos de algunos prstamos hipotecarios de peor calidad, soslayando las revisiones de los tipos de inters, con objeto de evitar nuevos incrementos de la morosidad. Las autoridades regulatorias y supervisoras hemos abierto tambin un proceso de reflexin sobre los mecanismos de control, para reducir los riesgos sobre la estabilidad financiera en el futuro. Esta reflexin se desarrolla a distintos niveles, aunque todos tienen en comn su carcter multilateral: el Foro de Estabilidad Financiera, el Banco de Pagos Internacionales de Basilea, el G-7, el G-20 o la propia Unin Europea. Lo cierto es que, a pesar de todas estas reacciones, las tensiones en los mercados financieros internacionales no ha remitido, sin que pueda preverse, hoy por hoy, cundo retornar la calma y se normalizar su funcionamiento. En cualquier caso, y para hacer una valoracin razonable de la situacin actual y de los riesgos, no debe olvidarse que existen determinados elementos de fortaleza que estn ayudando a limitar el impacto de la tormenta financiera a escala internacional: el buen tono de la economa global, donde la moderacin del crecimiento norteamericano viene compensada en buena parte por el dinamismo de otras economas, entre las que destacan los pases emergentes y en desarrollo (como Asia, Amrica Latina, etc.); la favorable situacin inicial de los bancos en trminos de capitalizacin y beneficios (que les proporciona colchones para absorber eventuales prdidas); y la solidez patrimonial de las empresas y las familias (con la excepcin del segmento sub-prime en los EEUU). Aunque, segn he mencionado, no resulta posible pensar an cunto ms va a durar la tormenta financiera, las dificultades e incertidumbres actuales no deben hacernos perder la perspectiva y llegar a una valoracin negativa del proceso de globalizacin financiera. Por el contrario, creo que la valoracin debe seguir siendo favorable, principalmente por dos razones: de una parte, porque la globalizacin financiera nos ha legado un sistema financiero internacional ms eficiente y, salvo algn segmento concreto, ms slido; y, de otra, porque la globalizacin financiera es la contrapartida necesaria de la globalizacin econmica y porque ambas se refuerzan mutuamente, con los consiguientes beneficios que ello supone en trminos de un mayor potencial de crecimiento econmico. Lo que s resulta necesario, a la luz de las tensiones actuales, como he mencionado anteriormente, es identificar los fallos que han habido en el funcionamiento del nuevo sistema financiero internacional para corregirlos y evitar que, en el futuro, se repitan episodios de tensin financiera como el que estamos viviendo. Permtanme que termine resumiendo las conclusiones principales de mi intervencin. En ella, he examinado algunos de los desafos ms importantes que el proceso de globalizacin entraa para los bancos centrales en lo que respecta a sus dos funciones primordiales, mantener la estabilidad de precios y salvaguardar la estabilidad financiera, por ser ambas requisitos imprescindibles para que las economas crezcan a ritmos sostenidos y, de esta forma, contribuyan a mejorar los niveles de vida de los ciudadanos. Hasta ahora, cabe concluir que los desafos se han superado, que el proceso de globalizacin ha facilitado el sostenimiento de tasas de inflacin moderadas y que, a pesar del actual episodio de turbulencia, la estabilidad financiera tambin ha salido reforzada. No es casualidad, por lo tanto, que la fase ms reciente del proceso globalizador haya coincidido con la etapa de mayor prosperidad de la economa mundial en las ltimas dcadas. Ha sido precisamente durante todos estos aos cuando la Facultad de Econmicas ha ido creciendo, vertebrndose de forma cada vez ms slida y formando generaciones de economistas que, desde diversos y numerosos mbitos, y en diferentes capacidades, han contribuido y contribuyen a la prosperidad de la Comunidad Valenciana y de Espaa y a reforzar su papel en este mundo globalizado en el que estamos inmersos. Muchas gracias.

Title: The role of the Banco de Espaa in Spanish Banking. Speech at the Meeting between Harvard Business School and IESE on the occasion of the celebration of the anniversary of both institutions
text: Madrid, 11th January 2008 The role of the Banco de Espa in Spanish Banking IESE and Harvard Business School Jose Vils Deputy Governor of the Banco de Espa First of all, I would like to thank both IESE and Harvard Business School for the opportunity to address such a distinguished audience on the occasion of this anniversary. It is a great pleasure to be here to join in the celebrations. My sincere congratulations to IESE on its 50th anniversary and to the HBS on its centenary. Both institutions have so much to be proud of and some of their students are here as witnesses of their success in paving the way forward for international business schools. In this panel devoted to banking, I want to talk about the contribution that the regulatory and supervisory authorities can make to the successful development of the banking system. For this reason I will touch on the Spanish experience, which I think provides a very clear example of the above. I will divide my talk into two parts. The first will be backward-looking and will focus on how banking regulation and supervision have contributed to the modernisation and success of Spanish banks. The second will be forward-looking and will examine how well-placed our banks are to cope with the challenges posed by the "new global financial system" that has evolved in recent years, and which is now under tension as a result of the turmoil that started in the summer on the back of the US sub-prime problems. Spanish banking: a success story But before I go on to address specific issues, let me briefly recall that having a sound and efficient banking system is key for achieving sustained economic growth and for minimising the intensity of cyclical fluctuations, both of which favourably influence economic well-being. As far as growth is concerned, a soundly functioning banking system which efficiently performs its role of intermediating between savers and investors helps to achieve a better allocation of resources in the overall economy and ultimately fosters total factor productivity and growth. As for cyclical fluctuations, a solid banking system is by definition less crisis-prone. On the one hand, it reduces the likelihood and potential costs associated with financial shocks; and, on the other, it helps to reduce the overall economic costs arising from real shocks insofar as it acts as a buffer. For all these reasons, a sound and efficient banking system is an important source of economic growth and stability. In fact, Spain's very successful overall economic performance over the past twenty years cannot be explained without taking into account the significant contribution made by the financial sector and, in particular, by the banking system. To be sure, the transformation of our banking system in this period has been remarkable. Much like the mythical Phoenix, it rose from the ashes after the very severe crisis that hit our credit institutions in the late 70s and early 80s to become a most successful banking system. This is evidenced, for example, by its very good performance in terms of profitability, efficiency and solvency both on an absolute basis and by comparison to other countries. In the light of the above, a key question is what were the factors behind this success story. Although it is by no means easy to answer this question in such a short time, let me nevertheless mention some of the main drivers. One initial driver is that both banks and the authorities learned the right lessons from the crisis and took measures to avoid the mistakes that led to it in the first place. In the run-up to the crisis our banking system was weak and old-fashioned. It had got used to living in a closed environment and taking advantage of protectionist policies. In fact, it was not well-prepared to face liberalisation, with no good professional teams or systems to adequately identify and manage risk. At the same time, our regulatory and supervisory framework was weak and outdated. What the authorities did In the years after the crisis, a number of initiatives were launched by the authorities to foster both efficiency and soundness. As a result, regulatory changes were made to promote a freer and more competitive banking environment. To name just the most significant ones, public-sector commercial banks were privatised and barriers to potential entrants were gradually dismantled, letting foreign banks come in and allowing saving banks to engage in the full range of banking activities. Over time, and as a result of the new rules of the game, which led to a more open, competitive environment, banks embarked first upon processes of consolidation to better exploit economies of scale and scope and, later, significantly internationalised their activities. It was also clearly recognised that a freer, more competitive banking system needed a significant overhaul of the regulatory and supervisory framework in order to preserve the soundness of the system and to avoid new systemic crises. Banking regulators and supervisors encouraged banks to adopt better risk management systems, to be more transparent vis-a-vis clients and markets, and to provide more complete and frequent information to the supervisor: Banco de Espa. The establishment of a strong, professional and independent team of supervisors conducting frequent on-site inspections and the reinforcement of the legal powers of the Banco de Espaa to enforce banking norms and regulations was also of paramount importance. So too was the creation of a central credit registry, the establishment of tougher-than-Basel I solvency requirements and, since 2000, the introduction of a system of counter-cyclical provisions. Finally, and also to keep pace with the internationalisation of the banking system in recent years, the supervision of banking groups is carried out on a consolidated basis and coordination with other national supervisors has been strengthened through the signing of bilateral MoUs. Another distinctive feature of our framework is that Banco de Espaa is also the accounting regulator for banks. This has allowed our accounting rules to take into account supervisory goals, thus fostering prudential objectives. This allows, for example, for the application of conservative asset valuation principles to enhance asset quality. Needless to say, since 2004 our norms have also been consistent with the new international financial reporting standards. Beyond these regulatory and supervisory changes, Banco de Espaa has also directly contributed towards financial modernisation through the development of bond market and clearing and settlement payment system infrastructures. As I mentioned earlier, the regulatory and supervisory framework has established the rules of the game. At the same time, banks have, by sticking to these rules, made most significant progress in terms of modernisation. What banks did In Spain, banks learned the lessons from the banking crisis and learned, too, how to cope with the challenges of competing in a liberalised environment so as to better seize their opportunities. In fact, banks realised that they have to make continuous efforts to retain adequate internal risk control methods and to invest in technology and human capital. Furthermore, banks have constantly to maintain the capacity to adapt to and take advantage of a changing environment. At present, our banking system is expanding abroad. Our two main banks are leaders in many Latin-American countries and recently their presence in the US, in other European countries and in Asia has also been relevant. Such internationalisation which is now also being pursued by other Spanish banks has widened their scope and activities and thus fostered diversification. Another issue to be considered when talking about the features of the present Spanish banking system is its business model. This has retail banking and traditional banking intermediation as its core activity, far removed from the originate to distribute model so widespread and well-known today. At this point I shall attempt to draw the two main lessons learned through this twenty-year process of modernisation. Firstly, the regulator and banks have formed a joint partnership, prompting a fruitful virtuous cycle and matching goals and efforts in order to attain efficiency and soundness. Close communication and constant exchanges of views are the principles currently governing this relationship. And secondly, as the Spanish case clearly shows, there has not been any adverse trade-off between profitability and soundness over the medium-term. Indeed, the competitive capacity of Spanish banks has not been dented in the least by supervisory policies, which have been oriented towards enhancing the solvency of banks, and to increasing the confidence of the public and of markets in banks. New challenges in a global banking system So far, the story has been one of success. But the global banking system is continuously evolving within what is known as the "new global financial landscape". This is characterised by several features: free international capital flows, global financial markets and global banks, faster transmission of risks from one area to another, and potential cross border contagion effects. In this context, some new products of increasing complexity, many of them derivatives, are being introduced. We are also observing new players such as hedge funds, private equity funds, conduits, SIVs, etc., whose actions are less and less transparent and subject to little or no regulation. In certain countries the use of an originate to distribute strategy has been widespread. Along with this new financial situation, the forthcoming Basel II package will have to accommodate these new risks. Banks will be able to calculate their capital requirements using internal riskassessment methods and, at the same time, they will have incentives to better manage their risks. Overall, the benefits from the new global financial landscape are considerable in terms of efficiency, by making national and international financial markets more complete, and also in terms of resilience, allowing for a wider dispersion of risks. However, as the recent financial turmoil is showing, problems caused by certain excesses linked to the inappropriate incentives of various agents have also arisen. In fact, there is not as much risk dispersion as was thought, since it has been discovered that there were pockets of fragility where risks were being concentrated. Another point of concern is the increasing opacity of the financial system, with problems building up without their true scale being known until they finally explode. Moreover, some agents may have relaxed their oversight of risks (lenders, rating agencies, investors, and even some regulators and supervisors). Finally, the potential cross border contagion effects of globalized markets and intermediaries is also a point of concern. And what about Spanish banks? I believe that the Spanish banking system is well-placed to meet the fresh challenges arising from the new financial landscape while continuing to exploit the opportunities this entails. Their successful performance in recent years is the best proof of it. However, are Spanish banks well-positioned to withstand the current financial turmoil? Undoubtedly, the current tensions in global financial markets, originated by the US sub-prime problems, have increased overall uncertainty in markets, particularly in markets for complex structured products and in interbank markets. Yet I think that there are a number of features in the Spanish banking system that puts it in a relatively favourable position to cope with current tensions. In particular, banks in Spain are characterised by: retail rather than investment banking; not adhering to an originate-to-distribute model; having resorted to securitisation of (high-quality) mortgages to raise funds and not as a business model itself; not being directly or indirectly exposed to US sub-prime loans; having sound systems for credit risk assessment and management; and, finally, having important cushions in terms of profitability, provisions and solvency. In turn, the regulatory and supervisory framework has established: a wide supervisory perimeter not leaving any SIV or conduits outside of it; tough criteria applied to the credit risk transfer mechanism; and, since 2000, counter-cyclical provisioning. At present, one of the main effects of the turbulence is the drying-up of market liquidity, with access to financing from capital markets proving more difficult and expensive for banks on a global basis. In principle, one should expect the Spanish banking system to be less vulnerable given its heavy reliance on deposits to finance credit, but if the turmoil lasts for a very long time all banking systems in the world will be tested. Let me conclude with a couple of comments. First, globalization and the financial innovation that in many cases is related to it, are, as I have already said, essentially positive developments. Nevertheless, the increasing complexity of certain operations we have witnessed can have a downside. As any instrument, they can be put to good and less good use. The present turmoil is providing us with what we could call a reality check that can give rise to a kind of Darwinist natural selection. In fact, this can be a positive development: those instruments whose characteristics and utilization are basically sound will strive and survive; those instruments, business strategies and, potentially, institutions whose raison detre was exclusively the loose conditions of markets and trades experienced in recent years are bound to disappear. And second, as you know, regulators and supervisors around the globe are analysing the present situation to obtain lessons and make the necessary adjustments. This analysis should be a calm one, making sure that we do not overreact and find ourselves lamenting in the near future rushed decisions taken today. Also, we must make sure that we strike the right balance between rules that enhance financial stability and the need to preserve an international level playing field. Let me just end by saying that one of the lessons that has clearly come up is the increased need to coordinate these analysis and the corresponding actions among supervisors worldwide. It is true that we have a good and long lasting cooperation in many international committees and bodies. But it is also true that there is room for improvement in that cooperation to assure convergent and consistent reactions internationally. I am convinced that the close cooperation and continuous feedback between supervisors and institutions, that give rise to the virtuous cycle I have mentioned, will allow us to respond adequately to the present circumstances and to get things back on track potentially on a healthier level that up to now. Thank you.

Title: Presentation of the book: "Strategies for effective government". Intervention in the presentation organized by PriceWaterhouseCoopers Foundation and Instituto de Empresa
text: Madrid, 18 February 2008 Closing Conference Presentation of the book: "Strategies for effective government" Instituto de Empresa Jose Vils Deputy Governor of Banco de Espa Good afternoon. First of all, I would like to thank the heads of PriceWaterhouseCoopers and Instituto de Empresa, Carlos Mas and Diego del Alc87zar, and Julio Gez-Pomar, Director of the PriceWaterhouseCoopers Center - Instituto de Empresa del Sector Plico and Coordinator of the book "Strategies for an effective government", together with Professor Francisco Cabrillo and Dr. Fitzpatrick, for their kind invitation to participate in this event. In this sense, I would like to convey to all of you that this is an invitation that I find particularly pleasant, not because I come from two institutions as relevant in the professional and academic field of our country, as are those represented here, or because the coordinators of the book are people with a trajectory of professional and academic excellence fully contrasted and recognized, but also because this work, which comes to light today, addresses a topic of singular importance, such as the improvement of procedures, strategies and tools of public management, and because it does so in a rigorous and well-founded way, at the same time original, practical and suggestive. That is why I would also like to congratulate PriceWaterhouse and Instituto de Empresa on having undertaken such a thorough and thorough examination of one of the issues which, fortunately and increasingly, is receiving greater attention: the improvement in the provision of services by the entities through the use of management mechanisms typical of the private sector. You will agree with me that since the publication of Adam Smith's "The Wealth of Nations" and the characterization of the market as the "invisible hand," in contrast to the "visible hand" of the state, few issues have been the subject of such intense and ongoing debate as the role of the state in the economy and, in general, in society. leading to the question of what the State should and should not do, and how the State should do those functions that correspond to it. Well, the splendid book that we are presenting today focuses precisely on exploring how efficiency can be improved in the decision-making areas, and, in particular, on identifying which strategies are most appropriate for this, analyzing the contribution that can be derived from the incorporation in the public sector of procedures, tools and strategies of the private sector. In my view, the search for "effective government" is not an option, but an obligation of those responsible for public administration in a democratic society. Responsibility that emanates from the need to ensure that the money collected from taxpayers through the tax system is managed to achieve maximum efficiency in satisfying the needs of society, in conditions of transparency, and with an adequate framework of accountability to citizens. But I believe that the basis for "effective government" is not only the natural corollary of the "principle of responsibility" which must imbue any manager in a democratic society, but that efficiency in management is something that is particularly important, in practice, because of two developments that are particularly important today: globalization and technological advances. Globalization has not only been and constitutes a powerful factor of discipline for state policies (such as tax policies), but also penalizes those countries that do not have an "effective government". Technological advances, in turn, allow a greater division of tasks and production processes, and facilitate their contracting in numerous areas outside the state sphere, giving greater prominence to the market in the production of goods and services that are then supplied by the public sector. Finally, technological advances have also allowed what was previously considered "natural monopolies in certain industries" to cease to be so, thus disprising the presumption that their direct administration by the state is most advisable. Consequently, although it is true that the comparison between the objectives and the functioning of the public and private sectors may suggest a distance in terms of their fields of action and even with respect to the components that make them up; And although it is also true that any process of adaptation to the public sector of techniques and practices already established in the private sphere will not, in principle, be automatic, this should not lead us to discard that idea, but to continue deepening it, to the extent that any improvement, any new approach, any possible line of action in this regard, Although it is novel, it can ultimately lead to positive results for governments, which will be contributing to the COM good and to the placid self-interest. For this reason, I consider this book, "Strategies for Effective Government", to be a magnificent example of certain processes already fully experienced in the private sphere. They can encourage, through concrete mechanisms or proposals, a more efficient management than I know. I understand that one of the successes of this work is to raise this dynamic of confluence between the plico and the private not from a theoretical point of view, but also from a double prism: on the one hand, from the dissemination of specific tools, with a high degree of detail, in order to escape from that feeling that sometimes good ideas do not have practical examples; and on the other, through the contribution of already accredited experiences, models of transfer of the form of management from the private to the public that have already worked in certain situations, which makes them an extremely useful reference for analysis and reflection. It is from this perspective that I believe we must face some of the initiatives that are proposed and developed in this work and that it is followed below, such as, for example: the adoption of market principles and the decentralization of competences as a new form of public management; the use of strategic tools in the public sector, such as activity-based accounting, user surveys or different budgeting; the implementation of performance measurement and performance evaluation systems, in their possible role as instruments for improving the performance of this sector; external contracting and public-private partnerships as increasingly common methods of providing public services; or, finally, the use of advances in information and communication technologies as elements of the conversion towards the so-called electronic administration. All these tools in the field of action in the public sector are intended to contribute to the achievement of various objectives, such as the promotion of competition, the improvement of productivity, the reduction of costs or the promotion of efficiency and, in the same instance, also seek to move towards a progressive modernization of public entities, In such a way that the optimization of resources and efficiency in their management are not elements alien to their strategy. I share many of these ideas and also those that refer to the need to have an entrepreneurial public sector that tries to improve society and that includes among its strategies all those that go through innovation and technological development. The above therefore serves to convey my conviction of the usefulness of trying to transpose d0 with the necessary adaptations d0 private management methods to certain Areas of action in the public sector and, above all, how appropriate it is to continue working, from the analysis and detailed examination, on initiatives such as those addressed in this book and which constitute the necessary seed for the subsequent and possible implementation of these ideas. And I will conclude now. Since, as we all know, there are books and books, I have tried to convey to you my conviction that the work presented today is a product of considerable added value, since it contains novel and suggestive ideas, articulated in a pedagogical and practical way. I believe that the proposals contained in the book deserve to be studied, both for their intrinsic value and on the basis of the conviction that achieving an "effective government" is not, as I have already mentioned, an intrinsic obligation for public administration in any democratic society, but because if a government, an effective state is also the necessary catalyst for more market and better market. Thanks a lot.

Title: The International Economy: Recent Developments and Prospects
text: Las Palmas, 31 March 2008 The international economy: recent developments and prospects The economy at the crossroads: medium and long-term perspectives. Royal Economic Society of Friends of the Country Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor of the Bank of Spain The world economy is going through times of uncertainty and concern in which policymakers are having to face a situation of rapid financial deterioration d0 to limits that were almost unthinkable a short time ago d0 in a context of increasing complexity of global economic and financial relations. These are also times of accelerated learning for those of us who are closely following these developments and are committed to facilitating the least costly way out of the challenges facing the global economy. An old and ambiguous Chinese curse reads: 'May you live in interesting times', implying that comfort is boring but interesting is always risky. These are undoubtedly difficult times but also interesting ones. Until the outbreak of the financial turbulence last August, the world economy experienced a period of little interest d0 in the sense I have just outlined d0 characterized by high growth, moderate inflation developments and a very favourable behaviour of the financial markets. The results of 2007 are proof of this. Indeed, global growth returned to high rates, at around 5%, completing the four-year period of highest average global growth since the decade of the 60s: 4.8%, a mixture of 2.9% growth in advanced economies and 7.5% in emerging economies. Moreover, this phase of growth has been widespread, with the vast majority of countries improving their per capita income levels, many of them substantially. It is difficult to find a period in recent economic history when a similar situation has occurred. The radical change in the international economic and financial landscape since last summer has resulted not so much from the natural maturation of the business cycle in advanced economies, and in particular in the United States d0 which would have been reasonable to expect d0 but from the unleashing of turbulence in financial markets, which have reached a depth and significance difficult to foresee. regardless of its specific origin. However, although this disruption has placed the global economy at a delicate moment, the exposure of the different economic areas to its effects has not been the same, at least at the starting point, and will surely also be different in the future development of the crisis. In particular, the fate of the Spanish economy in such a situation marked by global events is linked, even more than in quiet times, to its membership of the euro area and the role that this area is having in the development of global turbulence. And the way out of this crisis will be determined to a large extent by the economic policy decisions taken at the global level and at European level in particular. For this reason, I thought it appropriate to devote my speech today to analysing the impact of the financial turmoil on the growth conditions and prospects of the different economic areas, paying particular attention to the developed economies, where their epicentre has been located, but without forgetting the emerging economies, which today represent almost 50% of world GDP.
