OF THE MATURATION OF THE CYCLE... Industrialized economies contributed more than expected at the beginning of the year to the dynamism of the global economy in 2007, given the advanced cyclical position in which some of them found themselves. This is particularly the case in the United States, where the adjustment in the real estate sector, which began in 2006, was expected to begin to weigh on the rest of the activity, mainly through wealth effects. However, the impact of this adjustment on employment and consumption did not begin to be observed until the last quarter of last year. From that moment on, there was a downward trend in growth rates, which was also helped by the fall in confidence that was affecting economic agents d0 companies and households d0 as a result of the turbulence. For their part, emerging economies continued to grow in 2007 at very high rates, similar to those of the previous year and also above expectations, supported by increasingly robust domestic demand, while consolidating the improvement in their economic fundamentals. Moreover, the impact of the turbulence on these economies has so far been limited, so that together they were responsible for 70% of global growth in 2007. On the inflation front, the moderate behaviour of consumer prices in recent years has been threatened by the continuous increase in the prices of both energy and, most notably, food raw materials in 2007. Price pressures became particularly evident from the second half of the year onwards and quite widely. However, despite the pick-up in headline inflation rates, core inflation remained stable and inflation expectations anchored. Only in the most recent months has there been a rise in expectations in those countries that, like the United States, have adopted a very aggressive monetary policy to deal with the economic slowdown. During the first part of 2007, despite the maturation of the global economic cycle and the fact that the correction in the US housing market represented an obvious risk to the evolution of this economy and its mortgage market, the world financial markets maintained a very favourable performance. Financing conditions remained accommodative in virtually all segments and capital flows continued to flow, in previously unrecorded amounts, to emerging economies: in 2007, they exceeded 600 billion, almost triple the previous year. Even global imbalances, which had been widening in the previous years of the expansionary phase, pointed to a moderate correction, supported by lower relative growth in the United States and the depreciation of the dollar. ... TO FINANCIAL TURBULENCE The turbulence that emerged from August onwards abruptly broke the favourable behaviour of the financial markets in the first part of the year, revealing substantial risks to the prolongation of the expansionary cycle globally and, especially, in developed economies. However, the abrupt unleashing of this episode of financial turmoil does not mean that it was totally unexpected, since the seeds of this adjustment had been sown during the boom years. Over the past five years, the low volatility that characterised the evolution of the main economic magnitudes (growth and inflation), the abundance of liquidity and the ample financing conditions that prevailed in the markets, led to a generalised search for yield and a significant increase in risk appetite, which were manifested in the compression of risk premia and the also generalised appreciation of real assets and Financial. In turn, financial innovation processes, stimulated by this search for profitability, led to the development of new markets and products, allowing a more active and sophisticated management of risks and greater diversification of these. Diversification and improvements in risk management should, in principle, have led to a better allocation of financial resources at global level. However, the ample liquidity conditions of recent years meant that, in the context of the economic expansion, there was a certain relaxation of investor caution and incentives were generated towards unwise behaviour on the part of some of them, leading to an inadequate assessment of the risks assumed in the financial markets. Since 2004 in the United States and since 2005 in the euro zone, the monetary authorities have been responding to this situation of financial slack, abundant liquidity and maturation of the economic cycle with the progressive withdrawal of monetary stimulus to the different economies, while different international forums warned of the tensions and risks that were accumulating. The perception that risk premia did not reflect the underlying fundamentals of the assets or the ease with which liquidity was raised, despite the tightening of monetary conditions, were indications of a mismatch that could eventually lead to a more or less intense correction. In practice, however, it is not easy to contain possible excesses in financial markets without seriously disrupting their functioning, especially in situations where financial innovation makes diagnosis particularly imprecise. It was in this context of financial exuberance that the crisis of low-quality mortgages (known as subprime) in the US triggered the process of serious financial turmoil that we are currently going through. The fact that the subprime segment of the US mortgage market barely represents a minimal percentage of the volume traded in global financial markets contrasts with the depth, persistence and generalization of the turbulence, and shows that this episode is the result of imbalances that go far beyond the difficulties of the US mortgage market. Thus, the translation of the problems of this market to the rest of the financial system, not only American but worldwide, has been produced by the interweaving of subprime mortgages in a series of complex financial instruments that have developed exponentially in recent years and that have been distributed through global financial markets. Uncertainty about the valuation of these instruments, which incorporated the risks associated with subprime mortgages in a non-transparent manner, the spread of risk through the global financial system and the exposure of financial institutions to these risks generated a sudden shortage of liquidity in credit markets, which quickly spread to money markets. The central banks of the major developed economies reacted by injecting liquidity into interbank markets d0 sometimes in a coordinated manner d0 and there was gradually a change in the monetary policy outlook. However, despite these measures, the deterioration of the financial situation has persisted and even intensified. Given the origin of the turbulence, the change in the tone of monetary policy has been particularly marked in the United States, although credit constraints to the productive sector and prolonged uncertainty have begun to take their toll on the indicators of the real sector of this economy, particularly evident in the first months of 2008. The impact and implications of this episode of financial turbulence on the global economic outlook and on the prospects of the different economic areas are, logically, the main points of discussion in international economic debates. The interconnectedness of developed countries' financial markets and their increasing exposure to structured credit instruments soon dispelled the illusion that they could be kept insulated from financial turbulence. On the contrary, the impact on emerging economies has been limited for the time being. The resilience of these economies to global turmoil and their growing weight in the global context have meant that, so far, they are behaving as an alternative engine of the global economy, which is cushioning the global slowdown and could even facilitate the economic reactivation of industrialized economies. PERSPECTIVES Given these circumstances, how does the world economy face 2008? The central scenario foresees a slowdown in world GDP towards growth rates of around 4%, almost one percentage point below that recorded in 2007, but still above the average growth of recent decades and, without a doubt, far from a situation that could be considered a recession on a global scale. However, this average growth masks a very different behavior of the different economic areas. On the one hand, the United States, where the central scenario incorporates a notable but short slowdown, with expected growth of less than 1.5%, compared with 2.2% in 2007; on the other hand, the rest of the developed economies, for which a significant reduction in growth is expected, to around 2%, about three tenths less than the previous year. In any case, it should be stressed that these average growth rates expected in developed economies hide a profile of sharp slowdown throughout the year. A third pole is formed by emerging economies, where growth would remain somewhat below previous years, but still very robust, with rates of 7%, compared to 7.8% in 2007. In this last group of countries, we must highlight the leadership of China, which, despite slowing down, would continue to grow at rates of around 10%. This central scenario d0 which, despite its robustness, is continuously being subjected to downward revisions d0 presupposes that there are a series of turbulence containment barriers that would limit its extension between different sectors (real and financial) and geographical areas, [what has come to be called 'decoupling', which we could translate in Spanish as 'unmatching' or 'divorce']. We are, however, in a situation in which the chances of breaking these barriers are high, which means that particularly downward biased risks weigh on the central scenario, which can be summarized mainly in three: The most immediate risk, which, according to recent evidence, seems to be rapidly being verified, is the possibility of a recession in the US. But the main risk is undoubtedly that severe financial turbulence will lead to severe and widespread credit tightening on a global scale. This risk, which is still considered an unlikely event, would have major repercussions on global activity, since it would short-circuit the financial intermediation channels that sustain the development of economic activity. The last risk to take into account is the evolution of the price of oil and other raw materials, which has two dimensions: the negative impact on activity, which may be greater in the current context of slowdown, and the pressure on inflation. This combination of slowing activity and maintaining inflationary pressures is already creating important monetary policy dilemmas and limiting central banks' ability to support the recovery in economic activity. I will now go on to detail the prospects for the various economic areas. 1.1 United States In the United States, the outlook for this year points to a continuation of the adjustment of the real estate sector and its greater impact on activity, which, together with the effects of financial turbulence on the availability of credit, would end up generating a sharp slowdown in the first quarters of the year, perhaps with negative growth rates in some of them. However, the strong activism shown by both monetary and fiscal policy should support the recovery in demand as the year progresses. But this scenario is subject to significant risks, especially as the United States is the epicenter of financial turbulence. The first and foremost is that funding constraints are more severe, extended and durable than expected, to the extent that banks cannot rebuild the capital needed to maintain the supply of credit and capital markets remain sluggish. Even if this credit crunch does not materialize, the decline in activity could deepen beyond expectations, due to a more intense and lasting fall in the real estate market in that country or a substantial adjustment in employment, which already shows undoubted signs of weakness. It should be borne in mind that housing and the labour market have been the two pillars on which the dynamism of domestic demand has been based in the US over the last five years. The loss of these supports could cause a strong adjustment in consumption. 1.2 Other developed countries The second pole of the world economy is the rest of the developed economies, among which the United Kingdom, the euro area and Japan deserve to be highlighted due to their global weight. It is interesting to note that the close transatlantic financial links have had a relatively high impact on economic activity in the former, while Japan has remained relatively little directly affected. 1.2.1 United Kingdom In the United Kingdom, the country that has experienced one of the greatest impacts of the turbulence apart from the United States, a sharp slowdown in growth is expected, probably even below 2% for the whole of 2008. This development is based on the delayed effects of the withdrawal of monetary stimulus in the first part of 2007, the effect of credit restrictions and the ongoing correction in the real estate market, three factors that have begun to weigh on the dynamism of domestic demand. As in the case of the United States, the main risk is also the possible intensification of the shocks, especially relevant for the British due to the strong weight that the financial sector has in the economic activity of that country. Likewise, a sharp and severe correction in the housing market could weigh on household wealth and lead to an intense adjustment in consumption. All this, in a context in which inflation is expected to pick up significantly. 1.2.2 Japan On the contrary, in Japan the impact has been little on the financial and real sector, due to the low exposure of its banking sector to the subprime segment in the US. However, the outlook for 2008 also points to a certain slowdown in activity, judging by the deterioration in consumer and business confidence. This deterioration occurs in an environment in which the Japanese economy has not just left behind deflation and the long period of low economic growth of recent decades, due to the persistent weakness of domestic demand. Therefore, perhaps the main risk in the short and medium term is the slowdown observed in the process of structural reforms. 1.2.3 Euro Area With regard to the outlook for the euro area, which is our closest economic environment, some of the risks previously identified have gradually materialised over the last few months, such as a larger-than-expected slowdown in the US economy, the appreciation of the euro or the rise in oil and other raw materials. as well as the impact on confidence and financing conditions resulting from financial stress. In this way, towards the end of the year the first symptoms of slowdown began to be confirmed and a scenario of less dynamism also began to take shape, after two years growing above 2.5%. In any case, the euro area economy has solid fundamentals to face the change in the economic outlook in the medium term, which derive from the favourable equity situation of companies, the high rate of job creation and the greater weight of trade with areas less exposed to the financial crisis. Both domestic and external demand are expected to support continued euro area real GDP growth, albeit at significantly lower rates than in 2007. However, as in other developed countries, uncertainty remains high, for similar reasons. Because of its importance for monetary policy decisions affecting our country, I would like to emphasise the evolution of prices, which stood at 3.5% in January 2008, the highest rate in recent years in the euro zone. This figure reflects the existence of strong upward pressures on inflation in the short term, the origin of which must be placed mainly in the increases in energy and food prices in recent months. Consistent with the transitory nature of this pick-up, no significant second-round effects on wages and prices have been observed so far, and long-term inflation expectations remain anchored at levels consistent with the price stability objective. It is foreseeable, therefore, that although inflation will remain high for some months, a phase of gradual renewal towards the level of 2% will begin in the second half of 2008, although there are obvious upside risks. These include uncertain developments in commodity prices, rising corporate margins in markets with a low degree of competition and, above all, the possibility of widespread second-round effects on wage and price setting. 1.3 Emerging economies As for emerging economies, one of the most striking features of this episode of turbulence has been the relatively little that has affected the financial assets of these economies, which in the past had been extremely prone to accuse the swings of appetite and risk aversion in international financial markets. It is also possible that this limited transmission of shocks through the "financial channel" to the emerging economies as a whole may explain why economic growth in most of these economies has so far remained immune to a situation of deep global instability. It is also significant that growth forecasts have hardly been lowered and, even more, that monetary and financial policies have not been subordinated to responding to turbulence, as was usual in the past, in order to prevent capital flight. That said, it seems difficult to think that, if a scenario of strong adjustment in growth materializes in developed countries, emerging economies will not be substantially affected. The good news, given the precedents, is that the most likely impact, at least for now, would be through the commercial channel, which probably operates in these countries with certain delays and in a less virulent way than the financial channel. However, the situation of the different emerging economies is not homogeneous either, given that they show different vulnerabilities. In any case, China d0 which although it represents only 10% of global GDP is the country that contributes most to global growth d0 plays a key role, both for emerging countries and for the global economy as a whole. 1.3.1 China and Emerging Asia Therefore, it is crucial to assess China's prospects. The strength shown by domestic demand in China in recent years, its relative financial isolation (due to the existence of extensive capital controls) and the specificity of still being a heavily intervened economy are factors that suggest that it could remain relatively immune to a slowdown in the American economy. In fact, at this point is the consensus of the forecasts for next year, which has barely lowered its growth by half a point, to around 10%. With this rate of growth, the main risk is to avoid overheating the economy and entrenching inflation. The economic slowdown could be somewhat more noticeable in the rest of the economies of the area, given that they are (with the exception of India and, to a certain extent, South Korea) small and open economies, with a relatively high exposure to the transmission of the American slowdown through the commercial channel. 1.3.2 Latin America Growth prospects for Latin America in 2008, meanwhile, remain favourable, in a context of significant dynamism in domestic demand and the maintenance of commodity prices. Only in countries that are very open and have important trade ties with the United States, such as Mexico and Central America, have the outlook deteriorated more sharply. In fact, the comparatively favourable evolution of Latin American financial markets to financial turbulence reflects the perception of reduced vulnerability to external shocks resulting from the improvement in macroeconomic fundamentals and their comfortable external position in recent years, which is a situation practically unprecedented in its recent history. However, since Latin America is an emerging region particularly integrated into global financial markets, a substantial deterioration in the economic situation in the United States could affect this region through the financial channel, feed back through the commercial channel, and even affect other flows that in recent years have acquired great importance. such as remittances from emigrants. Also key for many countries in the region (Chile, Peru, Venezuela, or Argentina) is the evolution of commodity prices, which could register significant declines in the event that the economic adjustment were to acquire a global scale. 1.3.3 Eastern Europe Finally, in the case of Eastern Europe, many of whose countries are already our partners in the European Union, growth prospects for 2008 point to a slowdown of just over one percentage point compared to 2007 to around 5%. This outlook is supported both by an expected moderation in growth in the euro area, its main export market, and by tighter conditions for access to international credit. Vulnerabilities in the financial sector are precisely the main risk to the region's growth, given the high financing needs arising from the region's large external deficits, in contrast to the rest of the emerging areas. In particular, a sudden reversal of capital flows to the region could trigger a severe and prolonged credit crunch in these economies, which would break their process of nominal and real convergence with the rest of the members of the European Union. THE ROLE OF ECONOMIC POLICIES This review of the global economy and the different areas highlights the uncertainty of the current situation, and therefore, the difficulties of economic policies to face it. A key priority is to facilitate the return to normal functioning of financial markets and overcoming turbulence, but this should not make us lose sight of the importance of safeguarding the framework of economic stability and discipline achieved in recent years. In the United States, the epicenter of the turbulence and where financial difficulties are more palpable, more serious and more widespread, economic authorities have reacted quickly and from multiple fronts to try to mitigate the impact of financial instability on activity. Thus, the Federal Reserve d0 which has the dual objective of keeping growth and inflation stable d0 has expanded, through a sequence of new facilities, the mechanisms for providing liquidity to the financial system and has supported the purchase of financial institutions in difficulty for more solid ones. It has also cut interest rates sharply since August last year, by almost three percentage points, even though inflationary pressures have increased in this period. The US Treasury, for its part, has already approved a fiscal stimulus package of a high magnitude, around one percentage point of GDP, and there is speculation about new fiscal measures. Finally, both institutions, in conjunction with other financial regulators, have implemented a series of measures to moderate the adjustment in the real estate and mortgage sector, such as initiatives to favor the review of mortgages or others to increase the capacity of some public entities to support the mortgage market through a relaxation of regulatory criteria. Undoubtedly, these are decisive and far-reaching actions, which could exert a strong expansionary impact if economic conditions were normal. However, financial and liquidity difficulties and the uncertainty and lack of confidence of agents will surely moderate their impact on activity, which also explains the intensity of the measures implemented. In any case, economic policy activism in the United States, and of the Fed in particular, is explained as a preventive action to prevent turbulence from leading to a serious financial crisis. This is a low-probability event with unpredictable consequences for the U.S. and global economy, so it may be reasonable to act decisively. This activism contrasts with the actions of economic authorities in Europe, where there is no economic emergency. As regards the Eurosystem's monetary policy performance, the months since last summer clearly demonstrate that the monetary policy strategy has been particularly appropriate in these uncertain times. First, the Eurosystem's operational framework has proved sufficiently agile and flexible to respond to the liquidity difficulties experienced by financial institutions during the turbulence, contributing to the maintenance of financial stability. Also in the area of maintaining price stability, monetary policy offers a robust anchor. On the one hand, because it is the objective set out in its mandate and, on the other, because the time reference of that mandate d0 the medium term d0 provides the necessary room for manoeuvre to avoid hasty responses to the shocks that have affected the global economy and the euro area in recent times. The Governing Council of the ECB has maintained its emphasis on the existence of risks to the achievement of the price stability objective and has unequivocally demonstrated its determination to prevent these from materialising and that, as a result, medium- and long-term inflation expectations could be de-anchored. Undoubtedly, the current stance of monetary policy should favour the achievement of these objectives in a context in which the situation of financial fragility has resulted, also in the euro area, in a de facto tightening of the financing conditions of the agents. At the same time, the level of uncertainty about the economic outlook remains high and, at the current juncture, circumstances may change rapidly, requiring close monitoring of all developments over the coming weeks and months. With regard to fiscal policies, all countries must avoid the temptation to squander progress in consolidating public accounts in recent years. The improvement in public accounts in recent years has been determined, in many countries of the world, by an increase in tax collection above what economic activity predicted. This increase in elasticities, and the fact that we are uncertain about their nature, temporary or structural, feeds doubts about the fiscal room for manoeuvre that actually exists in the event of a sharp slowdown in activity. Therefore, at a time when the situation can be considered as one of cyclical slowdown, the automatic stabilizers that moderate it should be allowed to act. CONCLUSION The global economic situation does not invite optimism. However, despite the uncertainty about the immediate future of the global economy, some resilient factors can be identified that can make us look ahead with some confidence. To end this speech on a positive note, I would like to review them briefly. First, the favourable economic situation at the outset, with robust global economic growth, a healthy situation in corporate balance sheets, contained inflation and strong growth and reduced vulnerability in emerging economies, which may limit the effects of financial turbulence on the real sector. Second, the economic slowdown in the US and the depreciation of the dollar may contribute to the correction of global imbalances. The third and final element of resistance, the process of globalization, is paradoxical. While globalization implies greater integration and interconnectedness between countries and thus increases exposure to economic shocks, it also reduces the vulnerability of the system and of individual economies. This is because globalization reinforces the fabric on which the world economy is based. On the one hand, by configuring a multipolar world d0 with more than one locomotive d0 in which emerging economies have more and more weight. On the other hand, by making all economies more flexible, they have had to adapt to the competitive pressures arising from globalization. Thus, although it is difficult to think that, if global economic conditions deteriorate for a long time, some economies can be kept on the sidelines, it is also true that, in a less negative scenario, continued dynamism in emerging economies could help sustain global demand and, in addition, we would expect the global economy to cope with negative shocks. with lower costs in terms of activity or employment. Finally, although the process of globalization and financial innovation has encouraged some excesses derived from unwise behavior, it has also made the global financial system more flexible and efficient, and has given it a greater capacity to react to situations of this type. In this sense, the current episode of turbulence could correct the excesses accumulated in the previous phase and lead to a normalization of financial conditions and a more stable global financial system in the future. Thanks a lot
text_original: Las Palmas, 31 de marzo de 2008 La economa internacional: evolucin reciente y perspectivas La economa en la encrucijada: perspectivas a medio y largo plazo. Real Sociedad Econmica de Amigos del Pas Miguel Fernndez Ordez Gobernador del Banco de Espaa La economa mundial atraviesa tiempos de incertidumbre y preocupacin en los que las autoridades econmicas estn teniendo que hacer frente a una situacin de rpido deterioro financiero hasta lmites que hace poco tiempo eran casi impensables, en un contexto de creciente complejidad de las relaciones econmicas y financieras globales. Son tambin tiempos de aprendizaje acelerado para los que seguimos de cerca estos acontecimientos y estamos implicados en facilitar una salida lo menos costosa posible a los desafos que tiene planteados la economa mundial. Una vieja y ambigua maldicin china reza: Ojal vivas tiempos interesantes, dando a entender que lo cmodo es aburrido pero lo interesante es siempre arriesgado. Estos son, sin duda, tiempos difciles pero tambin interesantes. Hasta el desencadenamiento de la turbulencia financiera de agosto pasado, la economa mundial vivi un perodo de poco inters en el sentido que acabo de sealar, caracterizado por un elevado crecimiento, una evolucin moderada de la inflacin y un comportamiento muy favorable de los mercados financieros. Los resultados del ao 2007 son buena prueba de ello. En efecto, el crecimiento global volvi a situarse en tasas elevadas, en el entorno del 5%, completando el perodo de cuatro aos de crecimiento mundial medio ms elevado desde la dcada de los aos 60: un 4,8%, mezcla de un avance del 2,9% en las economas avanzadas y del 7,5% en las economas emergentes. Adems, esta fase de crecimiento ha sido generalizada, de modo que la inmensa mayora de los pases han mejorado sus niveles de renta per cpita, muchos de ellos de manera sustancial. Es difcil encontrar un perodo en la historia econmica reciente en que se haya dado una situacin similar. El cambio radical producido en el panorama econmico y financiero internacional a partir del verano pasado no se ha derivado tanto de la maduracin natural del ciclo econmico en las economas avanzadas, y, en particular, en Estados Unidos,- lo que hubiera sido razonable esperar-, sino del desencadenamiento de unas turbulencias en los mercados financieros, que han alcanzado una profundidad y una trascendencia difciles de prever, ms all de cul haya sido su origen concreto. Sin embargo, aunque esta perturbacin ha colocado a la economa global en un momento delicado, la exposicin de las distintas reas econmicas a sus efectos no ha sido la misma, al menos en el punto de partida, y seguramente ser tambin distinta en el desarrollo futuro de la crisis. En concreto, la suerte de la economa espaola en una coyuntura tan marcada por los acontecimientos globales est ligada, incluso ms que en tiempos tranquilos, a su pertenencia a la zona del euro y al papel que esta zona est teniendo en el desarrollo de la turbulencia a nivel mundial. Y la salida de esta crisis vendr determinada en buena medida por las decisiones de poltica econmica que se adopten en el plano mundial y en el europeo, en particular. Por ello, me ha parecido oportuno dedicar mi intervencin de hoy a analizar el impacto de la perturbacin financiera sobre las condiciones de crecimiento y las perspectivas de las diferentes reas econmicas, dedicando especial atencin a las economas desarrolladas, donde se ha situado su epicentro, pero sin olvidar a las economas emergentes, que hoy en da representan casi el 50% del PIB mundial. DE LA MADURACION DEL CICLO Las economas industrializadas contribuyeron al dinamismo de la economa global en 2007 por encima de lo que se esperaba al comienzo del ao, dada la avanzada posicin cclica en la que se encontraban algunas de ellas. Este es particularmente el caso de Estados Unidos, dnde se esperaba que el ajuste en el sector inmobiliario, iniciado en 2006, comenzara a lastrar al resto de la actividad, principalmente a travs de los efectos riqueza. Sin embargo, el impacto de ese ajuste sobre el empleo y el consumo no comenz a observarse hasta el ltimo trimestre del ao pasado. A partir de ese momento, se produjo una flexin a la baja en las tasas de crecimiento, a la que contribuy tambin la cada de la confianza que estaba afectando a los agentes econmicos empresas y familias- como consecuencia de la turbulencia. Por su parte, las economas emergentes siguieron creciendo en 2007 a tasas muy elevadas, similares a las del ao anterior y tambin por encima de las esperadas, con el apoyo de una demanda interna cada vez ms robusta, al tiempo que consolidaban la mejora de sus fundamentos econmicos. Adems, el impacto de la turbulencia sobre estas economas ha sido, hasta ahora, limitado, de forma que, en conjunto, fueron responsables de un 70% del crecimiento mundial en 2007. En el frente de la inflacin, el comportamiento moderado de los precios de consumo durante los ltimos aos se ha visto amenazado por el continuo incremento de los precios de las materias primas tanto energticas, como, de modo muy destacado en 2007, alimenticias. Las presiones sobre los precios se hicieron especialmente evidentes a partir de la segunda mitad del ao y de modo bastante generalizado. No obstante, a pesar del repunte en las tasas generales de inflacin, la inflacin subyacente se mantuvo estable y las expectativas de inflacin ancladas. Slo en los meses ms recientes se ha observado un alza en las expectativas en aquellos pases que, como Estados Unidos, han adoptado una poltica monetaria muy agresiva para hacer frente a la desaceleracin econmica. Durante la primera parte de 2007, a pesar de la maduracin del ciclo econmico global y de que la correccin en el mercado inmobiliario norteamericano representaba un riesgo evidente para la evolucin de esta economa y su mercado hipotecario, los mercados financieros mundiales mantuvieron un comportamiento muy favorable. Las condiciones de financiacin continuaron siendo acomodaticias en prcticamente todos los segmentos y los flujos de capitales siguieron fluyendo, en cuantas no registradas con anterioridad, hacia las economas emergentes: en 2007, superaron los 600.000 millones de dlares casi el triple que el ao anterior. Incluso los desequilibrios globales, que se haban venido ampliando en los aos previos de la fase expansiva, apuntaban una correccin moderada, apoyada en el menor crecimiento relativo de Estados Unidos y en la depreciacin del dlar.  A LA TURBULENCIA FINANCIERA Las turbulencias que surgieron a partir de agosto quebraron de forma brusca el comportamiento tan favorable de los mercados financieros en la primera parte del ao, poniendo de manifiesto riesgos sustanciales sobre la prolongacin del ciclo expansivo a nivel mundial y, especialmente, en las economas desarrolladas. No obstante, el desencadenamiento abrupto de este episodio de perturbaciones financieras no significa que fuera totalmente inesperado, pues las semillas de este ajuste se haban sembrado durante los aos de bonanza. En los ltimos cinco aos, la reducida volatilidad que caracteriz la evolucin de las principales magnitudes econmicas crecimiento e inflacin, la abundancia de liquidez y las condiciones holgadas de financiacin que prevalecieron en los mercados, dieron lugar a una bsqueda generalizada de rentabilidad y a un aumento notable del apetito por el riesgo, que se manifestaron en la compresin de las primas de riesgo y en la revalorizacin tambin generalizada de los activos reales y financieros. A su vez, los procesos de innovacin financiera, estimulados por esa bsqueda de rentabilidad, dieron lugar al desarrollo de nuevos mercados y productos, permitiendo una gestin ms activa y sofisticada de los riesgos y una mayor diversificacin de stos. La diversificacin y las mejoras en la gestin del riesgo deberan haber propiciado, en principio, una mejor asignacin de los recursos financieros a escala global. Sin embargo, las holgadas condiciones de liquidez de los ltimos aos hicieron que, en el contexto de la expansin econmica, se produjera una cierta relajacin de la cautela de los inversores y se generaran incentivos hacia comportamientos poco prudentes por parte de algunos de ellos, llevando a una valoracin inadecuada de los riesgos asumidos en los mercados financieros. Desde 2004 en Estados Unidos y desde 2005 en la zona euro, las autoridades monetarias fueron respondiendo a esta situacin de holgura financiera, abundante liquidez y maduracin del ciclo econmico con la retirada progresiva del estmulo monetario a las distintas economas, al tiempo que desde distintos foros internacionales se adverta de las tensiones y los riesgos que se estaban acumulando. La percepcin de que las primas de riesgo no reflejaban los fundamentos subyacentes de los activos o la facilidad con la que se captaba liquidez, a pesar del endurecimiento de las condiciones monetarias, eran indicios de un desajuste que podra terminar abocando a una correccin ms o menos intensa. Sin embargo, en la prctica no es fcil contener los posibles excesos de los mercados financieros sin perturbar gravemente su funcionamiento, especialmente en situaciones en las que la innovacin financiera hace particularmente impreciso el diagnstico. Fue en este contexto de exuberancia financiera cuando la crisis de las hipotecas de baja calidad (conocidas como subprime) en EEUU desencaden el proceso de graves perturbaciones financieras que estamos atravesando en la actualidad. El hecho de que el segmento subprime del mercado hipotecario estadounidense apenas represente un porcentaje mnimo del volumen negociado en los mercados financieros mundiales contrasta con la profundidad, persistencia y generalizacin de las turbulencias, y pone en evidencia que este episodio es resultado de desajustes que trascienden, con mucho, las dificultades del mercado hipotecario norteamericano. As, la traslacin de los problemas de este mercado al resto del sistema financiero, no slo estadounidense sino mundial, se ha producido por la imbricacin de las hipotecas subprime en una serie de instrumentos financieros complejos que se han desarrollado exponencialmente en los ltimos aos y que se han distribuido a travs de los mercados financieros globales. La incertidumbre sobre la valoracin de estos instrumentos, que incorporaban los riesgos asociados a las hipotecas subprime de un modo poco transparente, la difusin del riesgo a travs del sistema financiero global y la exposicin de entidades financieras a estos riesgos generaron una sbita escasez de liquidez en los mercados de crdito, que se extendi rpidamente a los mercados monetarios. Los bancos centrales de las principales economas desarrolladas reaccionaron inyectando liquidez en los mercados interbancarios en ocasiones de forma coordinada y, paulatinamente, se produjo un cambio de signo en las perspectivas de poltica monetaria. No obstante, a pesar de estas medidas, el deterioro de la situacin financiera ha persistido e, incluso, se ha intensificado. Dado el origen de la turbulencia, el cambio en el tono de la poltica monetaria ha sido particularmente marcado en Estados Unidos, aunque las restricciones crediticias al sector productivo y la incertidumbre prolongada han empezado a hacer mella en los indicadores del sector real de esta economa, de forma particularmente evidente en los primeros meses de 2008. La incidencia y las implicaciones de este episodio de turbulencias financieras sobre el panorama econmico global y sobre las perspectivas de las distintas reas econmicas estn siendo, lgicamente, los principales puntos de discusin en los debates de economa internacional. La interconexin de los mercados financieros de los pases desarrollados y su exposicin creciente a los instrumentos estructurados de crdito disip muy pronto la ilusin de que se pudieran mantener aislados de la turbulencia financiera. Por el contrario, el impacto sobre las economas emergentes ha sido, por el momento, limitado. La resistencia de estas economas ante la perturbacin global y su peso creciente en el contexto mundial han hecho que, hasta el momento, se estn comportando como un motor alternativo de la economa global, que est amortiguando la desaceleracin global e incluso podra facilitar la reactivacin econmica de las economas industrializadas. PERSPECTIVAS Dadas estas circunstancias, cmo afronta el ao 2008 la economa mundial? El escenario central prev una desaceleracin del PIB mundial hacia tasas de crecimiento en torno al 4%, casi un punto porcentual por debajo del registrado en 2007, pero todava por encima del crecimiento promedio de las ltimas dcadas y, sin duda, muy alejado de una situacin que pudiera considerarse de recesin a escala global. No obstante, este crecimiento medio encubre un comportamiento muy diferente de las distintas reas econmicas. Por una parte, Estados Unidos, donde el escenario central incorpora una desaceleracin notable, pero corta, con un crecimiento esperado inferior al 1,5%, frente al 2,2% de 2007; por otra el resto de economas desarrolladas, para las que se prev una reduccin significativa del crecimiento, hasta el entorno del 2%, unas tres dcimas menos que el ao anterior. En cualquier caso, cabe subrayar que estas tasas medias de crecimiento previsto en las economas desarrolladas esconden un perfil de acusada desaceleracin a lo largo del ejercicio. Un tercer polo lo forman las economas emergentes, donde el crecimiento se mantendra algo por debajo de los aos anteriores, pero an as muy robusto, con tasas del 7%, frente al 7,8% de 2007. En este ltimo grupo de pases hay que destacar el liderazgo de China que, a pesar de desacelerarse, seguira creciendo a tasas en torno al 10%. Este escenario central que, a pesar de su robustez, est siendo sometido continuamente a revisiones a la baja presupone que hay una serie de barreras de contencin de la turbulencia que permitiran limitar su extensin entre diferentes sectores el real y el financiero y reas geogrficas, [lo que se ha venido a denominar 'decoupling' en ingls, que podramos traducir en espaol por desemparejamiento o divorcio]. Nos encontramos, no obstante, en una situacin en la que las posibilidades de ruptura de estas barreras son elevadas, lo que significa que sobre el escenario central gravitan unos riesgos particularmente sesgados a la baja, y que se pueden sintetizar principalmente en tres: El riesgo ms inmediato, y que, de acuerdo con la evidencia reciente, parece que se est verificando con celeridad, es la posibilidad de una recesin en EEUU. Pero el riesgo principal es, sin duda, que las graves turbulencias financieras desemboquen en una restriccin severa y generalizada del crdito de escala global. Este riesgo que se considera, todava, un evento poco probable, tendra repercusiones de primer orden sobre la actividad mundial, pues cortocircuitara los canales de intermediacin financiera que sustentan el desarrollo de la actividad econmica. El ltimo riesgo a tener en cuenta es la evolucin del precio del petrleo y del resto de las materias primas, que tiene dos dimensiones: el impacto negativo sobre la actividad, que puede ser mayor en el actual contexto de desaceleracin, y la presin sobre la inflacin. Esta combinacin de desaceleracin de la actividad con mantenimiento de presiones inflacionistas est ya generando importantes dilemas de poltica monetaria y limitando la capacidad de los bancos centrales para apoyar la recuperacin de la actividad econmica. Pasar ahora a detallar las perspectivas de las distintas reas econmicas. 1.1 Estados Unidos En Estados Unidos, las perspectivas para este ao apuntan a una continuacin del ajuste del sector inmobiliario y un mayor impacto de ste sobre la actividad, lo que, unido a los efectos de las turbulencias financieras sobre la disponibilidad de crdito, terminara por generar una fuerte desaceleracin en los primeros trimestres del ao, quizs con tasas negativas de crecimiento en alguno de ellos. No obstante, el marcado activismo mostrado, tanto por parte de la poltica monetaria como de la poltica fiscal, debera apoyar la recuperacin de la demanda a medida que avance el ao. Pero este escenario est sujeto a riesgos importantes, sobre todo al ser Estados Unidos el epicentro de las turbulencias financieras. El primero y principal es que las restricciones de financiacin sean ms severas, extendidas y duraderas que lo esperado, en la medida que los bancos no puedan reconstituir el capital necesario que les permita mantener la oferta de crdito y que los mercados de capitales mantengan su atona. Incluso si no se materializase esta contraccin del crdito, el descenso de la actividad podra profundizarse ms all de lo esperado, por una cada ms intensa y duradera del mercado inmobiliario en ese pas o por un sustancial ajuste del empleo, que ya da muestras indudables de debilidad. Hay que tener en cuenta que vivienda y mercado de trabajo han sido los dos pilares sobre los que se ha asentado en EE.UU. el dinamismo de la demanda interna en los ltimos cinco aos. La prdida de estos soportes podra provocar un fuerte ajuste del consumo. 1.2 El Resto de pases desarrollados El segundo polo de la economa mundial lo constituye el resto de economas desarrolladas, entre las que merece destacar, por su peso global, el Reino Unido, el rea del euro y Japn. Es interesante constatar que los estrechos vnculos financieros transatlnticos ha provocado un impacto relativamente elevado sobre la actividad econmica en los primeros, mientras que Japn se ha mantenido relativamente poco afectado de una forma directa. 1.2.1 Reino Unido En el Reino Unido, el pas que ha experimentado uno de los mayores impactos de las turbulencias aparte de Estados Unidos, se espera una fuerte desaceleracin del crecimiento, probablemente incluso por debajo del 2% para el conjunto de 2008. Esta evolucin se fundamenta en los efectos retrasados de la retirada del estmulo monetario en la primera parte de 2007, el efecto de las restricciones crediticias y la correccin en marcha en el mercado inmobiliario, tres factores que han empezado a lastrar el dinamismo de la demanda interna. Como en el caso de Estados Unidos, el principal riesgo lo constituye tambin la posible intensificacin de las perturbaciones, especialmente relevante para los britnicos por el fuerte peso que tiene el sector financiero en la actividad econmica de ese pas. Asimismo, una correccin brusca y severa del mercado inmobiliario podra pesar en la riqueza de las familias y producir un ajuste intenso del consumo. Todo ello, en un contexto en el que la inflacin se prev que repunte notablemente. 1.2.2 Japn Por el contrario, en Japn el impacto ha sido escaso sobre el sector financiero y real, debido la baja exposicin de su sector bancario al segmento subprime en EEUU. Sin embargo, las perspectivas para 2008 tambin apuntan a una cierta ralentizacin de la actividad, a juzgar por el deterioro de la confianza de los consumidores y empresarios. Este deterioro se produce en un entorno en el que la economa japonesa no acaba de dejar atrs la deflacin ni el largo perodo de bajo crecimiento econmico de las ltimas dcadas, debido a la persistente atona de la demanda interna. Por eso, quiz el principal riesgo a corto y medio plazo lo constituye el freno observado en el proceso de reformas estructurales. 1.2.3 rea del Euro En cuanto a las perspectivas de la zona del euro, que es nuestro entorno econmico ms prximo, a lo largo de los ltimos meses se han ido materializando de manera progresiva algunos de los riesgos identificados previamente, como una desaceleracin mayor de la esperada de la economa americana, la apreciacin del euro o el encarecimiento del petrleo y de otras materias primas, adems de la incidencia sobre la confianza y sobre las condiciones de financiacin derivada de las tensiones financieras. De este modo, hacia el final del ao comenzaron a confirmarse los primeros sntomas de desaceleracin y empez tambin a configurarse un escenario de menor dinamismo, tras dos aos creciendo por encima del 2,5%. En cualquier caso, la economa de la zona euro cuenta con unos fundamentos slidos para afrontar a medio plazo el cambio en el panorama econmico, que se derivan de la favorable situacin patrimonial de las empresas, del elevado ritmo de creacin de empleo y del mayor peso del comercio con las reas menos expuestas a la crisis financiera. Cabe esperar que tanto la demanda interna como la externa respalden la continuacin del crecimiento del PIB real de la zona del euro, aunque a tasas sensiblemente inferiores a las del 2007. Sin embargo, como en el resto de pases desarrollados, la incertidumbre sigue siendo elevada, por razones similares. Por la importancia que tiene para las decisiones de poltica monetaria que afectan a nuestro pas, quiero hacer nfasis en la evolucin de los precios, que se ha situado en el 3,5% en enero del 2008, la tasa ms elevada de los ltimos aos en la zona euro. Este dato refleja la existencia de fuertes presiones alcistas a corto plazo sobre la inflacin, cuyo origen hay que situar, principalmente, en los incrementos de los precios de la energa y de los alimentos durante los ltimos meses. De manera coherente con el carcter transitorio de este repunte, no se han observado hasta ahora efectos significativos de segunda ronda sobre los salarios y los precios y las expectativas de inflacin a largo plazo permanecen ancladas en niveles compatibles con el objetivo de estabilidad de precios. Es previsible, por tanto, que aunque la inflacin permanezca en tasas elevadas durante algunos meses, en la segunda mitad de 2008 comience una fase de progresiva reconduccin hacia el nivel del 2%, si bien existen evidentes riesgos al alza. Entre ellos destacan la evolucin incierta de los precios de las materias primas, el aumento de los mrgenes empresariales en mercados con un reducido grado de competencia y, sobre todo, la posibilidad de que emerjan efectos generalizados de segunda vuelta en la fijacin de salarios y precios. 1.3 Las economas emergentes En cuanto a las economas emergentes, uno de los rasgos ms llamativos de este episodio de turbulencias ha sido lo relativamente poco que han afectado a los activos financieros de estas economas, que en el pasado haban sido extremadamente proclives a acusar los vaivenes del apetito y la aversin al riesgo en los mercados financieros internacionales. Es posible tambin que esa limitada transmisin de las perturbaciones a travs del canal financiero hacia el conjunto de las economas emergentes pueda explicar que el crecimiento econmico en la mayor parte de estas economas se haya mantenido hasta ahora inmune a una situacin de profunda inestabilidad a nivel global. Tambin es significativo que las previsiones de crecimiento no hayan sido apenas rebajadas y, an ms, que las polticas monetarias y financieras no hayan sido subordinadas a responder a las turbulencias, como era habitual en el pasado, para evitar fugas de capitales. Dicho esto, parece difcil pensar que, si se materializa un escenario de fuerte ajuste en el crecimiento en los pases desarrollados, las economas emergentes no se vean sustancialmente afectadas. La buena noticia, dados los precedentes, es que el impacto ms probable, al menos por ahora, sera a travs del canal comercial, que probablemente opera en estos pases con ciertos retardos y de forma menos virulenta que el canal financiero. Con todo, la situacin de las distintas economas emergentes tampoco es homognea, dado que muestran vulnerabilidades diferentes. En cualquier caso, China que aunque representa slo el 10% del PIB global es el pas que ms contribuye al crecimiento mundial juega un papel clave, tanto para los pases emergentes como para la economa global en su conjunto. 1.3.1 China y Asia Emergente Por todo ello, es crucial evaluar las perspectivas de China. La fortaleza mostrada por la demanda interna en China en los ltimos aos, su relativo aislamiento financiero (por la existencia de amplios controles de capital) y la especificidad de ser an una economa fuertemente intervenida son factores que permiten pensar que podra mantenerse relativamente inmune a una desaceleracin de la economa americana. De hecho, en este punto se sita el consenso de las previsiones para el ao prximo, que apenas se ha rebajado su crecimiento en medio punto, hasta el entorno del 10%. Con este ritmo de crecimiento, el riesgo principal es evitar el sobrecalentamiento de la economa y el arraigo de la inflacin. La desaceleracin econmica podra notarse algo ms en el resto de las economas del rea, dado que se trata (con la excepcin de India y, en cierto modo, Corea del Sur) de economas pequeas y abiertas, con una exposicin relativamente elevada a la transmisin de la desaceleracin americana por el canal comercial. 1.3.2 Amrica Latina Las perspectivas de crecimiento para Amrica Latina en 2008, por su lado, se mantienen favorables, en un contexto de importante dinamismo de la demanda interna y de mantenimiento del precio de las materias primas. Slo en los pases muy abiertos y que mantienen importantes vnculos comerciales con EEUU, -como Mxico y Centroamrica-, las perspectivas se han deteriorado de modo ms acusado. De hecho, la evolucin comparativamente favorable de los mercados financieros latinoamericanos a la turbulencia financiera refleja la percepcin de menor vulnerabilidad ante shocks externos que se deriva de la mejora de los fundamentos macroeconmicos y de su holgada posicin exterior en los ltimos aos, lo que es una situacin prcticamente indita en su historia reciente. Sin embargo, siendo Amrica Latina una regin emergente particularmente integrada en los mercados financieros globales, un deterioro sustancial de la situacin econmica en Estados Unidos podra afectar a esta regin a travs del canal financiero, retroalimentarse a travs del canal comercial, e, incluso, afectar a otros flujos que en los ltimos aos han adquirido una gran importancia, como las remesas de emigrantes. Tambin resulta clave para muchos pases de la regin (Chile, Per, Venezuela, o Argentina) la evolucin de los precios de las materias primas, que podran registrar importantes descensos en el caso de que el ajuste econmico adquiriera escala global. 1.3.3 Europa del Este Por ltimo, en el caso de Europa del Este, muchos de cuyos pases son ya nuestros socios en la Unin Europea, las perspectivas de crecimiento para 2008 apuntan a una desaceleracin, de algo ms de un punto porcentual respecto a 2007, hasta alrededor del 5%. Esta perspectiva se apoya tanto en una prevista moderacin del crecimiento en el rea del euro, su principal mercado de exportacin, como en unas condiciones de acceso al crdito internacional ms restrictivas. Precisamente el riesgo principal para el crecimiento de la regin lo constituyen las vulnerabilidades en el sector financiero, dadas las elevadas necesidades de financiacin que se derivan de los amplios dficits externos en la regin, en contraste con el resto de reas emergentes. En particular, una sbita reversin de los flujos de capitales a la regin podra desencadenar una severa y prolongada restriccin de crdito en estas economas, que quebrara su proceso de convergencia nominal y real con el resto de miembros de la Unin Europea. EL PAPEL DE LA POLITICAS ECONOMICAS Este repaso a la economa global y de las diferentes reas pone de manifiesto la incertidumbre de la situacin actual, y por lo tanto, las dificultades de las polticas econmicas para afrontarla. Una prioridad fundamental est siendo la de facilitar la vuelta al normal funcionamiento de los mercados financieros y la superacin de las turbulencias, pero ello no debera hacer perder de vista la importancia de salvaguardar el marco de estabilidad y disciplina econmica alcanzado en los ltimos aos. En Estados Unidos, epicentro de la turbulencia y donde las dificultades financieras son ms palpables, ms graves y ms extendidas, las autoridades econmicas han reaccionado rpidamente y desde mltiples frentes para intentar mitigar el impacto de la inestabilidad financiera sobre la actividad. As, la Reserva Federalque tiene el objetivo dual de mantener el crecimiento y la inflacin estables ha ampliado, a travs de una secuencia de nuevas facilidades, los mecanismos de provisin de liquidez al sistema financiero y ha apoyado la compra de entidades financieras en dificultades por otras ms slidas. Tambin ha recortado notablemente los tipos de inters desde agosto del ao pasado, en casi tres puntos porcentuales, a pesar de que las presiones inflacionistas se han incrementado en este perodo. El Tesoro estadounidense, por su parte, ya ha aprobado un paquete de estmulo fiscal de una magnitud elevada, en torno a un punto porcentual del PIB, y se especula con nuevas medidas fiscales. Por ltimo, ambas instituciones, en conjuncin con otros reguladores financieros, han instrumentado una serie de medidas para moderar el ajuste en el sector inmobiliario e hipotecario, como las iniciativas para favorecer la revisin de las hipotecas u otras para incrementar la capacidad de algunas entidades pblicas para apoyar el mercado hipotecario a travs de una relajacin de los criterios regulatorios. Sin duda stas son actuaciones decididas y de amplio calado, que podran ejercer un fuerte impacto expansivo si las condiciones econmicas fueran normales. Sin embargo, las dificultades financieras y de liquidez y la incertidumbre y falta de confianza de los agentes seguramente van a moderar su impacto sobre la actividad, lo que explica tambin la intensidad de las medidas implementadas. En cualquier caso, el activismo de poltica econmica en Estados Unidos, y de la Fed en particular, se explica como una actuacin preventiva para evitar que la turbulencias deriven en una grave crisis financiera. Este es un evento de baja probabilidad pero de consecuencias imprevisibles para la economa estadounidense y global, por lo que puede resultar razonable actuar con decisin. Este activismo contrasta con la actuacin de las autoridades econmicas en Europa, donde no hay una situacin de emergencia econmica. Por lo que respecta a la actuacin de la poltica monetaria del Eurosistema, los meses transcurridos desde el verano pasado demuestran claramente que la estrategia de poltica monetaria ha sido particularmente adecuada en estos momentos de incertidumbres. En primer lugar, el marco operativo del Eurosistema se ha revelado lo suficientemente gil y flexible para dar respuesta a las dificultades de liquidez que han atravesado las instituciones financieras durante la turbulencia, contribuyendo al mantenimiento de la estabilidad financiera. Tambin en el mbito del mantenimiento de la estabilidad de precios, la poltica monetaria ofrece un anclaje robusto. Por un lado, porque es el objetivo que recoge su mandato y, por otro, porque la referencia temporal de ese mandato el medio plazo proporciona el margen de maniobra necesario para evitar respuestas apresuradas a las perturbaciones que han afectado a la economa global y a la zona del euro en los ltimos tiempos. El Consejo de Gobierno del BCE ha mantenido el nfasis en la existencia de riesgos para la consecucin de objetivo de estabilidad de precios y ha mostrado de forma inequvoca su determinacin para prevenir que estos se materialicen y que, como resultado, las expectativas de inflacin a medio y largo plazo pudieran quedar desancladas. Sin duda, la orientacin actual de la poltica monetaria ha de favorecer la consecucin de estos objetivos en un contexto en que la situacin de fragilidad financiera se ha traducido, tambin en el rea del euro, en un endurecimiento de facto de las condiciones de financiacin de los agentes. Al mismo tiempo, el nivel de incertidumbre sobre las perspectivas econmicas sigue siendo elevado y, en la actual coyuntura, las circunstancias pueden cambiar rpidamente, lo cual exige un seguimiento muy atento de todos los factores durante las prximas semanas y meses. Por lo que respecta a las polticas fiscales, todos los pases deben huir de la tentacin de dilapidar los progresos en la consolidacin de las cuentas pblicas durante los ltimos aos. La mejora de las cuentas pblicas en estos aos ha venido determinada, en muchos pases del mundo, por un aumento de la recaudacin fiscal por encima de lo que la actividad econmica haca presagiar. Este incremento en las elasticidades, y el hecho de no estar seguro sobre su carcter, temporal o estructural, alimenta las dudas sobre el margen de maniobra fiscal realmente existente en caso de una desaceleracin brusca de la actividad. Por ello, en un momento en el que la situacin puede ser considerada como de desaceleracin cclica, debe dejarse actuar a los estabilizadores automticos que la moderen. CONCLUSIN La situacin econmica global no invita al optimismo. No obstante, a pesar de la incertidumbre sobre el futuro inmediato de la economa global, pueden identificarse algunos factores de resistencia que nos pueden hacer mirar hacia delante con cierta confianza. Me gustara, para acabar esta intervencin con un tono positivo, repasarlos brevemente. En primer lugar, la favorable situacin econmica de partida, con un crecimiento econmico global robusto, una situacin saneada en los balances de las empresas, una inflacin contenida y el fuerte crecimiento y reduccin de la vulnerabilidad de las economas emergentes, lo que puede limitar los efectos de las turbulencias financieras sobre el sector real. En segundo lugar, la desaceleracin econmica en EEUU y la depreciacin del dlar pueden contribuir a la correccin de los desequilibrios globales. El tercer y ltimo elemento de resistencia, el proceso de globalizacin, no deja de resultar algo paradjico. Aunque la globalizacin supone una mayor integracin e interconexin entre pases y, por lo tanto, aumenta la exposicin a las perturbaciones econmicas, tambin reduce la vulnerabilidad del sistema y de cada una de las economas. Esto es as porque la globalizacin refuerza el entramado sobre el que se sostiene la economa mundial. Por un lado, al configurar un mundo multipolar con ms de una locomotora- en la que las economas emergentes tienen cada vez ms peso. Por otro lado, al hacer todas las economas ms flexibles pues se han tenido que adaptar a las presiones competitivas derivadas de la globalizacin. De este modo, aunque es difcil pensar que, si las condiciones econmicas globales sufren un prolongado deterioro, se puedan mantener al margen algunas economas, tambin es cierto que, en un escenario menos negativo, la continuidad del dinamismo en las economas emergentes podra contribuir a sostener la demanda global y, adems, cabra esperar una mayor capacidad de la economa global para hacer frente a perturbaciones negativas, con menores costes en trminos de actividad o empleo. Finalmente, aunque el proceso de globalizacin e innovacin financiera ha fomentado algunos excesos derivados de comportamientos poco prudentes, tambin ha vuelto al sistema financiero global ms flexible y eficiente, y le ha dotado de una mayor capacidad de reaccin ante situaciones de este tipo. En este sentido, el actual episodio de turbulencia podra corregir los excesos acumulados en la fase anterior y propiciar una normalizacin de las condiciones financieras y un sistema financiero global ms estable en el futuro. Muchas gracias

Title: Presentation of "Asian Development Outlook 2008". Intervention in the presentation of the report prepared by the Asian Development Bank.
text: Madrid, 4 April 2008 Presentation of Asian Development Outlook 2008 Introductory Remarks Jose Vinals Deputy Governor Thank you angel and good morning to everyone. It is for me a great pleasure to be here today at the presentation of the Asian Development Outlook for 2008: An excellent piece of work that the Asian Development Bank has once again put together, this year with a special focus on the topic Work and Workers in Developing Asia. As in previous editions, the report that the ADB is presenting today provides a state-of-the-art analysis and a thorough assessment of the economic situation in Asia. It addresses issues so topical in the current policy debate as the resiliency of Asia to a potential US recession, the increase in inflation, and the risks and policy trade-offs that such complex combination of events (slower growth and higher inflation) might entail. The report also deals with the challenges facing Chinese authorities when trying to cool an overheating economy and gearing it into a more sustainable growth trend. And finally, a number of other very relevant subjects in the labour markets sphere, such as the importance of improving the employment prospects for young people, the skills gap and labour mobility are also addressed, all of them key challenges to the economic policymaking in Asia. There is thus a lot of ground to cover this morning, and do not want to overextend my intervention. Therefore, I will focus my remarks on the first topic of the long list I just referred to--the ability of emerging market economies (not only Asia, but also Latin America and Emerging Europe) to weather the turbulence still unfolding in global financial markets. Few would question the fact that over the past decades Asia has taken the centre stage in the world economy along many dimensions (growth, trade, FDI flows, official reserves) but as I will argue, the economic performance of Asia has recently become specially relevant, since its ability to weather some of the potential spillovers from the global financial turbulence might be key to cushion the negative effects of the US downturn on the world economy, and more specifically, the effect on other emerging market economies, like those in Latin America. In fact, for many observers including myself, possibly one of the most striking features in the performance of the world economy since the subprime event hit global markets, in the early summer of 2007, has been the outstanding resilience of most emerging market economies to the unravelling of the global turbulence. If we look at their recent performance, IMF figures show that the emerging market economies grew 7.5% in 2007, accounting for around 45% of the world production and contributing close to 70% to world growth. Developing Asia grew almost 9% and more specifically China expanded over 11%. These rates of growth and the subsequent per capita increase they entail are truly outstanding achievements by themselves, let alone in times of considerable stress. They also illustrate clearly how important Asia is to sustaining global growth. On the financial side, it is also encouraging that basic financial market indicators of risk, such as sovereign spreads, exchange rates or equity markets behaved, on the whole, significantly better than comparative asset classes in the industrial economies over the past six months. In addition, credit has generally continued to be available in these economies, and creditworthy emerging market borrowers have not been shut out from international markets, contrary to developments in the past. The question that quickly comes to mind is whether this resilience is bound to last, or whether the turbulence that has spread, swiftly in some cases, from the US to other industrial economies, will end up affecting the emerging economies too, if only with a lag. In other words, is this remarkable resilience just temporary or will it be persistent? Let me just say that, on this, the jury is still out, what makes me even more eager to learn about the conclusions of todays presentation. Let me just explain why I think this is such a difficult and complex issue. On the one hand, it is widely shared that emerging markets show today considerable strengths as compared to the past. Growth has become more broad-based, with a stronger contribution of domestic demand, south-south trade linkages and intra-regional trade linkages among emerging economies have increased and, very importantly, economic policies have been generally sound. How shielded these economies would be in the case of a severe downturn in their external demand from industrial countries remains an open question though. In addition some emerging economies have greatly benefited from the tail winds of record high commodity prices, which are in turn partly explained by the industrialization processes of countries like China or India, a process which is undeniably long-lasting. Moreover, there has also been an important reduction of the financial vulnerabilities in emerging markets that were widespread in the past, and which led to costly crises with important output losses and poverty, as the Asian crises ten years ago crudely demonstrated. So, all in all, there is little question about the improvement of macro fundamentals in emerging economies that has taken place over the last decade or so, coincidentally since the Asian crises erupted. On the other hand, it goes without saying that vulnerabilities and risks remain. Despite decades of diversification efforts, Latin America, a major commodity producer and exporter, would still be vulnerable to a terms-of-trade shock, given its high dependence on commodity prices, which in turn correlate with the world business cycle. Eastern Europe has become very capital-dependent to finance its convergence process, and capital, lets face it, has become more scarce. Globalization the tremendous increase in economic and financial integration that has happened over the past decades means that spillovers may always take place. The good news so far is that the most visible spillovers into emerging markets have been confined to the trade channel, that operates with longer lags and in a less virulent way than the financial channel, through the gradual weakening of export demand. In most cases, the financial channel, which so many times in the past quickly changed the economic outlook for emerging economies, has remained largely off in this occasion. The bad news may be however that there is no guarantee that this channel will continue to be so well behaved if global financial tensions persist. I would like to end my intervention on a cautiously positive note. Asia has become increasingly relevant for the world economy over the past few decades, and all indications are that going forward it will continue to be so. Increasingly Asia and specifically China have become some kind of second pillar to world growth and particularly to other emerging market economies, a very positive development in a world where the US economy continues to have the leading role. But in the short term, as economic and financial risks are tilted to the downside, the months ahead could be challenging times, reinforcing the need for policy cooperation from different areas and countries. The Asian Development Bank and the Asian Development Outlook make an outstanding contribution not only to better understanding the Asian economies and their role in an increasingly integrated world, but also to analyzing the scope and impact of different policy responses. And I believe that the capacity to understand well the nature and essence of underlying economic problems to form good judgement and provide adequate policy responses can truly make a difference in the challenging times we are living today. Thank you.

Title: Presentation of the Annual Report
text: 2007 PRESENTATION OF THE ANNUAL REPORT Speech by the Governor to the Governing Council of Banco de Espa SPEECH PRESENTING THE ANNUAL REPORT TO THE GOVERNING COUNCIL OF THE BANCO DE ESPA84A Miguel Fernandez Ordez GOVERNOR Legal depito: M. 30334-2008 Imprenta del Banco de Espa Presentation speech of the Annual Report to the Governing Council of Banco de Espa Ladies and Gentlemen Councillors: I am presenting to this Council today the Annual Report for 2007, in a national and international economic climate very different from that of the scams. The world economy, which had been showing remarkable dynamism in the face of scams, has been affected almost simultaneously by three far-reaching shocks, which have affected its growth already during the second half of last year, but which, above all, will condition its future evolution. I am referring, of course, to the upward behaviour of the prices of crude oil and other raw materials and foodstuffs, the deterioration of the cyclical situation of the US economy and the serious turbulence that has arisen in the international financial markets. The economic history of the last century contains enough examples to illustrate how any of these three shocks alone could have led the world economy to a situation of weakness and placed economic authorities in front of major dilemmas. It is not surprising, therefore, that their coincidence in time has led to the downward revision of global growth prospects, nor that it has also revived old debates about the use that, in situations such as this, should be made of the different economic policy tools available. All this is also surrounded by some unique challenges that the new tensions have raised from the point of view of maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability. These shocks have reached the European economy at a time of buoyant activity and heightened risks to price stability. In our country, on the other hand, the economy was already beginning to enter a phase of slowdown, after an exceptionally long period in which GDP had been showing remarkably high rates of expansion. Given this variety and complexity of topics, allow me to subordinate its overall description to a somewhat more detailed treatment of those that are most relevant. Thus, in the obligatory reference to the international context, I will concentrate on the analysis of the two factors that, in my opinion, constitute the main source of uncertainty at the moment: the evolution of the elements of financial instability and the extent of the recent resurgence of inflationary tensions. The figures for the whole of 2007 show a world economy that maintained the strong dynamism registered in previous years. The growth rate is around 5%, for the fourth to consecutive period, and, although this behavior was quite widespread among the different areas, it was the emerging economies that once again stood out from the rest, contributing almost 70% of the advance of world GDP. These figures, however, mask important differences between the first and second half of the year, once the international financial turbulence broke out. It should come as no surprise that, in the first instance, their impact has been particularly pronounced in the United States, a country where, as is well known, its epicentre is situated. Certainly, the American economy had been suffering the drag of adjustment in its housing market since at least one year before. However, GDP had remained at growth rates close to potential until the first half of 2007, when delinquency problems emerged in its subprime mortgage markets, which spread to the rest of the financial system, accentuating the intensity of real estate adjustment and leading the economy to a path of sharp slowdown. The rest of the world has not been immune to either the slowdown in the United States or the financial turbulence in that country, although so far the effects appear to have been more pronounced in industrialized economies. The remarkable resilience shown by emerging economies is, in fact, one of the most unique elements of this stage. This is not the reason to enter the debate that has opened up on the reasons for this apparent decoupling, but I would not want to fail to say that its future evolution will end up significantly conditioning the world growth figures in the as cousins. In this respect, the outlook for the global economy in 2008 has been unanimously and substantially revised downwards. This review has also been accompanied by the recognition of greater than usual uncertainty, attributable to the accumulation of various risk factors. The behavior of the industrialized economies d1 and, in particular, that of the U.S. economy d1 is now much more uncertain than a few months ago, as evidenced by the debate on the pattern of exit from the crisis in the United States. Nor are there greater certainties about the behaviour of exchange rates and their influence on global imbalances that are far from being corrected. But, at the moment, the main source of uncertainty still lies in the possible trajectory and outcome of serious international financial tensions. I shall now refer to this from an exclusively international perspective, leaving the situation of our financial system for later. A local financial shock such as the one affecting the US subprime mortgage market last summer cannot become a phenomenon with the current size and severity, if it is not as a result of the existence of other structural failures in the framework through which international financial flows are channeled. It is important to note that some of the possible weaknesses were noticed some time ago by the main ones responsible for ensuring the integrity of the system. Virtually all international financial stability reports dated before the turbulence warned of a more than likely general underestimation of the risks embodied in the main financial assets, the most evident manifestation of which was found in the too low premiums that were being traded in the markets. The existence of a favourable macroeconomic context, with strong growth rates and then moderate risks to price stability, is likely to contribute to exaggerated optimism in the markets and to mute the warnings made, while encouraging the growth of corporate and household debt levels globally. The progressive leverage at the international level, which subsequent events have revealed to be excessive in some cases, was also facilitated by the emergence of new financial products and vehicles that made it easier for banks to raise the necessary resources to meet the growing demand for loans. In particular, financial innovation in the area of securitisation has played a major role in this process. All these factors contributed to generate a climate of financial exuberance that came to cover up the structural deficiencies that were accumulating. When the events of last summer abruptly altered investor confidence, the underlying problems were laid bare. In my opinion, there are three main fronts on which these problems arise on a global scale. The first of these fronts can be located in the line of confluence between the processes of financial innovation and the regulation of markets and financial intermediaries. Recent events have shown an insufficient capacity to adapt the regulatory framework of some countries to the appearance of increasingly sophisticated products and vehicles outside the consolidation perimeters of entities. When financial innovation processes are based precisely on the existence of opportunities for regulatory arbitrage, it is clear that regulation is not well conceived. Nor do those products that, like some of those that have emerged in these times in the field of credit securitization, reach a degree of complexity and, why not say it, opacity that hinders the correct assessment of the risks assumed when acquiring them, have no real added value for investors.
