This is the second of the fronts to which the financial authorities of many countries and the competent international organizations will have to pay special attention to prevent situations like the current one from recurring. The third and third of the fronts on which I believe it will be necessary to concentrate efforts at international level is that of cooperation between supervisors. While it is clear that there has been a breeding ground for widespread turbulence, it cannot be denied that the increasing internationalization of flows and financial intermediaries themselves has also played an important role in the rapid spread of the same countries. Where market operators acquire an overall dimension, the authorities responsible for supervising their actions should also acquire the same dimension. There are several possible ways forward to achieve this objective, but I am convinced, for many reasons, that the one that currently offers the greatest guarantees is the one that runs through greater cooperation between the current national supervisors, based on a smooth exchange of relevant information. Let me turn now to the other risk factor for global growth and, above all, inflation which, in my view, deserves special attention: the continued rise in the price of raw materials, particularly energy, and food. In general, the strong upswing in these prices has been mainly associated with the strong increase in demand from, above all, emerging economies. The energy needs of a clearly expanding industrial sector and changes in consumption and food patterns, generally derived from a higher level of wealth, are probably the main factors underlying this dynamism in demand. But the pressures have also exposed the constraints to expanding supply, at least in the short term. The low spare capacity of production and refining is undoubtedly behind the sharp increase in the price of crude oil since the beginning of 2007. Similarly, behind the acceleration of food prices there are also supply factors linked, in some cases, to particularly adverse weather conditions. In the medium term, it is possible that the very strength of demand will stimulate the search for more efficient production processes that allow expanding supply capacity. But it is unlikely that in the immediate future we will see significant corrections in energy and food prices, which are sure to remain high. Even the risk of continuing recent trends cannot be ruled out, with consequent expansionary effects on aggregate inflation rates. Nor should we underestimate the possibility that the adjustment of relative prices will be perceived as a permanent, and not temporary, increase in inflation that contaminates wage bargaining and margin formation, triggering dangerous spirals between wages and prices of well-known effects. This has created a particularly complex situation for most central banks, combining inflationary tensions with a marked tendency towards a slowdown in activity and significant risks to financial stability. Let me address the dilemmas posed by this situation from the more specific perspective of the Eurosystem's monetary policy, whose decisions have a much more direct impact on the Spanish economy. In 2007, GDP growth in EMU again exceeded 2.5% for the second consecutive period, although activity showed a high degree of volatility throughout the year. In fact, the effects of the various international shocks mentioned and the appreciation of the euro began to be felt in the last quarter. However, both then and in the first months of this year, the euro area is showing a significant capacity for resilience, whose points of support are found, externally, in the strength maintained by emerging economies and, internally, in the dynamism that has characterized the behavior of the labour market. In the medium term, however, there is considerable uncertainty about how the European economy will behave. In recent months, private institutions and international bodies have revised downwards their growth forecasts for EMU, to rates of around 1.5% for this year and the next, and the Eurosystem itself has made its forecasts, according to which the area's GDP could grow by around 1.8% in 2008 and 1.5% in 2009. with predominantly downside risks. Price developments in the euro area have inevitably been influenced by developments in international commodity and food markets. Inflation has ended up above 3%, a figure virtually unknown since the start of EMU. In the first few months it is foreseeable that inflation will still remain high and that it will be from the beginning of the thumous section of the year when it begins to experience a gradual decline that lasts throughout 2009. But even this scenario is subject to upside risks. Especially since, when unemployment falls and the level of utilization of productive capacity is high, there is a danger that the levels of inflation recorded will give rise to second-round effects on wage-setting, margins and prices. The expected slowdown in economic growth in the area could mitigate, albeit only in part, these risks. In these circumstances, the difficulties faced by the Eurosystem have been evident and have not been limited to the choice of the most appropriate tone for monetary policy. Financial tensions particularly affected European interbank markets, where there was a sudden loss of liquidity and an increase in risk premia. As is well known, the interbank market is a fundamental piece in the implementation and transmission of monetary policy. The Eurosystem therefore attaches the highest priority to the objective of helping to restore its proper functioning as soon as possible and, in view of developments elsewhere, the operational framework of the Eurosystem's monetary policy should prove adequate. However, the increase in risk premia in the money market, the rise in corporate bond spreads, the tightening of loan supply conditions revealed by the results of the Bank Lending Survey and the appreciation of the euro have meant, for the same level of official interest rates, a tightening of the financing conditions of the area. In any event, the Governing Council of the ECB continues to analyse developments in the utmost care, while remaining firmly committed to acting to prevent risks to price stability from materialising. This is, in short, the international framework in which the analysis of the situation of the Spanish economy must be contextualized, to which I will devote the rest of my intervention. The Spanish economy has begun a phase of slowdown and adjustment that is mainly due to the confluence of two factors: on the one hand, the maturation of the prolonged expansionary cycle that has lasted more than a decade and, on the other, the disturbances that have affected the world economy and especially the international financial markets. The growth phase that began in the mid-nineties has led to the creation of almost six million jobs, and has allowed an average annual growth of 3.5% of GDP and considerable progress in convergence. A period in which Spain has reaped the results of the establishment of a macroeconomic stability regime, the fiscal consolidation effort made, and the structural transformations carried out. Throughout this period, the dynamism was mainly nourished by the strong boost in domestic spending, with an intense advance in residential investment, although the efforts of companies to expand their productive capacity and strengthen their international expansion were also notable. This continued boost in demand led to the emergence of some imbalances, which tended to gradually reduce the capacity to expand spending and required a redirection of spending towards more sustainable patterns. Indeed, following the change in the Eurosystem's monetary policy stance in December 2005, domestic demand is beginning to slow down as early as 2006. In the first half of 2007, this process intensified as a result of the effects of the gradual normalisation of monetary conditions and, above all, the beginning of the correction in the real estate sector. The intensity and prolongation of the expansionary period of this sector had led the nero of houses under construction and the increases in their prices to levels that made a certain adjustment inevitable and necessary. It is in this framework of the beginning of the process of moderation and recomposition of the growth of the Spanish economy, with high rates of expansion still, that the impact of the deterioration of the international climate and the financial turbulence that arose last summer must be inscribed. Despite the limited nature of the direct impact on Spanish banks, these turbulences have undoubtedly had an impact on our economy, causing an increase in financial costs, in particular due to the tightening of interbank rates, as well as by inducing a tightening of the criteria used by institutions in granting credit. However, the channel that has probably been most relevant has been the deterioration of the confidence of economic agents, as a result of the increase in global financial instability and uncertainty at a time when they had already begun to correct their spending patterns. If we focus on the results for the Spanish economy in 2007, we can see that, on average, there is still high dynamism, with GDP growth of 3.8%, an annual rate only one tenth lower than the previous one. It is clear from my previous comments that these annual data mask a declining profile over the years. Thus, compared with GDP growth rates of around 4% in the first half of 2007, activity slowed to 3.5% in the quarter of 2007. In 2008, this pattern of lower output strength has become more evident, with a GDP expansion rate of 2.7% in the first quarter, which reveals that the intensity of the adjustment is being more pronounced than initially expected. There is no doubt that, apart from the slowdown in private consumption, the slowdown in residential investment and the adjustment in the real estate sector are having a special impact on the rest of the economy, since it is a very intensive sector in the use of employment and has knock-on effects on other productive branches. by demanding large intermediate consumption of industry and services. This is an aspect that underlines the enormous importance of the degree of flexibility of the economy in mitigating as far as possible the effects of the real estate adjustment, both to facilitate the reallocation of resources towards other activities that can take over from construction, and to prevent an excessive fall in employment from acting as an amplifying channel for such adjustment. On the other hand, one of the most positive elements of the Spanish economy in 2007 has been the dynamism that has maintained productive investment, with growth rates even higher than those of the previous one, above 10%, in the case of investment in capital goods. This boost in capital investment, which began more intensively in 2005, is an essential ingredient in the recovery of demand growth and favours the expansion of potential output, as it lays the foundations for an increase in productivity in the future. The comfortable situation of the business fabric, reflected in high rates of return, together with the strength still shown by national demand and international markets in 2007 as a whole, drives the need to expand the productive capacity of our economy. Certainly, this component is sensitive to cyclical conditions, and, in fact, its expansion has moderated in the second half of 2007 and in the first months of this year, although it continues to remain the most dynamic component of demand. As usual in cyclical downturns, net foreign demand cushions the impact of lower domestic demand growth on output. Indeed, in the case of Spain, the moderation in domestic demand in 2007 was offset by the improvement in the contribution of external demand to GDP. Although the lower growth in imports explains much of this effect, the good performance of our exports should also be highlighted, as they maintained an appreciable growth rate of over 5%, despite the strong appreciation of the euro. Within the framework of this pattern of adjustment, particularly visible in the evolution of domestic demand and in the higher costs of financing, the credit raised by households, which had already begun to moderate in the previous year, continued to accelerate, as did that for enterprises, whose modulation had begun somewhat later. This slowdown also responded to greater caution on the part of banks when granting loans, since, although their capacity to finance new investments was not significantly reduced as a result of the turbulence in international financial markets, they did carry out a review of the risk parameters of these operations. Although at the end of 2007 financing to the private sector was still growing, in year-on-year terms, at rates higher than those of nominal growth in the economy, the shortest growth rates of this aggregate already pointed to values closer to nominal GDP growth, a trend that the data for the first months of 2008 have tended to confirm and that should materialize. Finally, in a reduction in the debt ratios of the private sector. A very relevant ingredient to explain the recent evolution of our economy and analyze its prospects is the considerable upswing in inflation that has taken place since last summer. It has indeed been unfortunate that, in addition to the impact of the turbulence on the financial markets, strong upward pressures have been added to the international commodity markets, which have led to a substantial increase in the price of both oil and many foods. Inflation, as measured by the year-on-year rate of the CPI, which had reached 2.2% in Spain in August 2007, increased rapidly to 4.2% at the end of that year, and to 4.6% in May 2008. There is no doubt that the intensification of inflationary pressures at this point in the cycle is particularly unfavourable. Inflation rates above 4%, such as those recorded in recent months, represent a sharp decline in the purchasing power of a large part of the population, discourage current consumption and induce a negative effect on the confidence of agents, by increasing uncertainty about real income in the future, which depresses, Also, spending plans. It is true that the bulk of the upswing in inflation has an external origin. The prices of energy and processed food have increased the most in recent months, mainly as a result of the increase in the price of raw materials on international markets, while the rate of growth in the prices of services has generally remained stabilised, and that of non-energy industrial goods has even slowed. The fact that the price differential with the euro area has widened over this period is partly due to the fact that some of the most expensive products, such as fuel and some food (in particular bread and milk), have a greater relative weight in the basket of consumer goods in Spain. All this, however, should not lead us to consider this evolution of inflation as inevitable and outside the sphere of influence of the authorities. In this sense, the persistent maintenance of Spain's price differential with EMU is something that has long required a correction, which becomes particularly urgent when the Spanish economy enters the necessary adjustment of the imbalances accumulated during the expansion. If we examine the components of the CPI, it is probably the prices of services d0 which have grown by about 4% in 2007 d0 that represent the main obstacle for the Spanish inflation rate to converge to the European average, although recently food prices have also shown a more bullish behavior than in other European countries. As is well known, in Spain the increase in inflation tends to be passed on to labour costs as a result of revision clauses, a feature that, if in an environment of economic prosperity can be accommodated without great friction, in a context of slowdown in demand can be more harmful. It does not seem reasonable that, when the increase in inflation has its origin in an increase in the import prices of various raw materials, the existing indiciaci mechanisms try to avoid the inescapable loss of real income that this increase implies. But, above all, the application of these clauses implies a lower incentive for job creation, which means that, in an environment of slowdown, it is on this variable that the fundamental adjustment mechanism of the economy rests, which can act as an amplifying factor for this adjustment. It should be borne in mind that unit labour costs in Spain have grown at a faster rate than in the euro area, both due to higher wage increases and higher wage increases. I eat for the weakest productivity records. Part of the wage growth will have to be offset by an improvement in productivity, which in the last decade has shown very low rates of growth, linked, to some extent, to the type of growth followed. However, it is not expected that productivity can recover significantly in the short term, so efforts to maintain a path of wage moderation and corporate margins are essential to preserve the competitiveness of our production and limit the scope of the current phase of slowdown. In a situation such as the current one, in which the main destination countries of our exports are also immersed in a phase of slowdown, the performance of competitiveness is a crucial element for the contribution of the external sector to counteract the loss of vigor of domestic demand and facilitate the return to a path of sustainable growth in the medium term. With all these ingredients, the outlook for the Spanish economy points, in the immediate horizon, to a stage of adjustment in which growth is lower than its potential pace. A scenario that, in any case, has some supports, which will help cushion the decline in activity in the short term and open the way to a sustainable recovery in the medium term. In this sense, although it is foreseeable that the population will show lower growth rates in the future, these will probably remain relatively high, which would mean maintaining a dynamic labor supply and also supporting the creation of households and the demand of the economy, both in consumption and housing. Furthermore, despite the persistence of some rigidities in our economy, we are facing this phase of slowdown with a more flexible productive, institutional and market structure than existed, for example, in the early nineties, which allows us to have reasonable expectations about the economy's capacity to absorb the imbalances and shocks recently recorded. It should be remembered, however, that membership of EMU, by limiting the use of certain economic policy instruments, makes it essential to deepen flexibility if the costs of macroeconomic adjustment are to be softened. Budgetary policy, for its part, represents a significant support factor in this cyclical phase, since, as I will discuss later, the fiscal surplus achieved allows the full potential of the free operation of automatic stabilisers to be realised. And, finally, the soundness of our financial system is, as I have already highlighted, a major asset to cushion the impact that international financial instability may have on the financial conditions of families and companies. Obviously, the prospects I have just described are not without risk. Some of them are beyond our control, such as those that come from a more pronounced deterioration of the international con-text, either by a greater slowdown in the US economy or by greater contagion to emerging countries, hitherto little affected by the turbulence. Further pressures in oil and, in general, commodity markets could also deteriorate global growth forecasts. In the case of Spain, the evolution of tensions in international capital markets is essential, given our dependence on foreign savings. Slow or inadequate progress in resolving these tensions could make the financing of activity in our country more expensive and hinder and could interfere with the adjustment path, amplifying contractionary trends. In a situation such as the one described, with challenges of considerable magnitude for the Spanish economy, it is up to economic policies to ensure that the aforementioned supports can unfold all their effects and limit the possibility of materializing the risks to which I have just referred, so as to limit the impact of macroeconomic adjustment on employment and activity. In addition, an adequate design of the direction of economic policy in the present situation may allow that, once the cyclical slowdown phase is over, the Spanish economy is in a better position to resume a path of high growth, commensurate with its potential for expansion. In any case, the intensity of the adjustment and the time needed for the economy to return to its long-term growth path will depend not only on the extent of the external shocks, but also on the efforts made by all the administrations d1 in particular the autonomous communities, given the high powers they have acquired in the scams d1 and all the social partners, each in its field of action. The main message of my Annual Report is that, at a time like the present, when we are facing a period of adjustment in a context of financial instability, deteriorating expectations and greater uncertainty, and in which employment behaviour plays a decisive role, economic policies must continue to be firmly based on the guidelines that have guided the authorities' action in these situations. We must therefore continue to achieve macroeconomic stability and to adopt measures to improve the degree of competition, the mobility of factors of production and the flexibility of costing and pricing mechanisms. And we must avoid approaches that are too short-term oriented and that may delay the necessary adjustments or that may even become counterproductive. Under these premises, the scope for the application of expansionary demand policies is certainly limited. As is well known, monetary policy has as its main objective to ensure price stability in the euro area over the medium term, which has led the Eurosystem to keep key interest rates unchanged since June last year. This decision, together with the increase in risk premia that is accompanying the episode of financial turbulence, has led to a tightening of monetary and financial conditions, which is in line with the need to contain inflationary tensions in the Spanish economy, but which, as is smooth, is less favourable to spending. On the contrary, fiscal policy has some scope to counteract the cyclical slowdown, starting from a relatively favourable situation in fiscal finances, as reflected in the figures summarizing its performance in 2007. The balance of the account of the Plicas Administrations shows a surplus equivalent to 2.2% of GDP, and the debt ratio is 36.2% of GDP, in the same year. In a phase of adjustment such as the one we are experiencing, and when starting from a healthy situation, it makes perfect sense that automatic stabilizers can act freely, exercise the countercyclical role for which they have been designed and serve, finally, as an important support factor. Being willing to use these mechanisms is, in fact, a differentiating feature that puts the economy in a better position to face the slowdown than in the past. On the other hand, discretionary actions to increase flat expenditure or to reduce taxes which could lead to a permanent deterioration in the flat balance should be avoided. And this, in the first place, because the good fiscal results of the scams contain a cyclical component, difficult to estimate but that can be of high magnitude, especially if one takes into account the strong positive impact that the real estate dynamism of the tima decade generates on tax revenues. This component will tend to disappear in a stage of lower growth. In fact, a weakening of tax revenues has already been observed in recent months, particularly for the figures most dependent on the evolution of the real estate market. It should also be borne in mind that discretionary measures may exhaust the room for manoeuvre that might be needed if the risks of prolonged financial turbulence and a deeper slowdown in the world economy materialise. Therefore, the measures adopted must be selective and must be accompanied, in any case, by efforts to contain other budgetary areas that are likely to reduce costs. At this point, special mention should be made of the effort to rationalize spending that the autonomous communities have to make in this new stage, especially in view of the notable slowdown observed in the collection of assigned taxes and which is expected to continue in the first few months. All these considerations lead me, in short, to reiterate the importance that must be attached to maintaining budgetary stability in the design of economic policy at this juncture. And along with this, the other crucial component is the strengthening of flexibility and efficiency in the functioning of factor and product markets, which will be fundamental to facilitate the necessary transfer of resources from the sectors in the process of adjustment to those that can take over. Given the effect that employment behavior will have, both for the magnitude and duration of the adjustment and to activate the levers of recovery, the efficient functioning of the labour market is of particular importance. Measures should be taken to avoid the adjustment falling predominantly on employment, because this would have negative multiplier effects on demand and activity through disposable income and future income expectations, while facilitating labour mobility between firms and sectors. The Annual Report explains that there have been changes in the labour market that are better able to cope with the cyclical slowdown than in the past. At this point, however, I would like to underline the tasks that remain. In particular, the existing systems of temporary recruitment and collective bargaining still suffer from rigidities that hinder the adequate response in terms of wage moderation and tend to offload most of the adjustment through temporary employment, where the greatest margins of flexibility are concentrated. In fact, the data on the behaviour of the labour market in the final months of 2007 and in the first months of 2007 point to a rapid loss of dynamism in employment, located in certain sectors and highly concentrated in temporary employment, as well as a rebound in labour costs that may have a negative impact on both firms' hiring decisions and inflation. at a time of deterioration of it. Priority is therefore given to finding ways to recover the trajectory of wage moderation which, with the support of the social partners, reap such good results in terms of job creation in scams. In particular, the current indiciaci systems, which tend to prolong the incidence of inflationary resurgence episodes, should be modified, avoiding that the transitory upswing in inflation generates a lasting deviation from the pattern of wage moderaci. It would also be desirable to undertake changes in the framework of collective bargaining that facilitate the adaptation of wages to the productivity and economic conditions of sectors and enterprises. Labour recruitment systems should also be reformed in such a way as to stimulate the creation of stable employment and increase incentives to actively seek employment, without sectoral or localisation changes constituting a serious obstacle to the reallocation of jobs. In any case, the measures adopted in the labour market must be framed within a set of more general actions that make the markets for goods and services more flexible and liberalise and, in particular, that increase their level of competition and eliminate the obstacles that may hinder the creation of companies that will have to generate new activity in the expanding sectors. Progress in liberalization will give rise to new profitable and job-generating niches of activity, particularly in the services sector, where the path to achieving efficiency and productivity improvements is potentially very high, as recent international experience shows. It is therefore essential to transpose the Services Directive swiftly and ambitiously and to remove restrictions on retail trade, given the crucial role played by distribution channels in productivity behaviour and price formation processes. Improvements in the functioning of network industries also generate important multiplier effects on economic growth and welfare, so it is necessary that their regulation promotes competition. With regard to these improvements, I would like to make particular mention of the energy sector, where the events of the months in the international oil markets and the environmental challenges that arise in the medium term recommend rapid progress in extending competition to all businesses, which, by triggering innovative processes and improving efficiency, It will help to meet the environmental commitments assumed. It is also essential to introduce competition in port and rail freight services, to strengthen the competitiveness of industrial and export sectors. This economy also needs a sufficiently deep rental housing market to meet households' demand for residential services, complement the home ownership market and facilitate regional mobility of workers. The reform of some of the restrictions that hinder the development of the rental market is all the more important at the present time, as it would serve to mitigate the magnitude of the adjustment in the real estate sector, facilitating the reabsorption of excess supply and providing affordable solutions to the demand for accommodation. Improving the legal certainty of the supply of rental housing and removing restrictions on the duration of contracts may introduce doses of flexibility which are particularly necessary during this adjustment phase. Finally, I would like to draw attention to the importance of the measures being implemented being guided by the objective of increasing growth in the long term. In this sense, increases in physical, technological and human capital d0 through improvements in training and education d0 and the promotion of innovation are essential. Allow me to devote part of my speech to delving into the state of our banking system. During the long period of prosperity enjoyed by the Spanish economy, the Spanish banking system was strengthened in terms of business expansion and consolidation, accumulation of own resources and accounting provisions, technological investment, improvements in efficiency and progress in risk management and control. Therefore, when the turbulence in the financial markets appeared in the summer of 2007, banks were reasonably prepared to deal with the situation. I will highlight four elements that have made it possible for the system not to be directly affected by this disturbance. In the first place, the fundamental weight of its activity pivots on traditional financial intermediation, consisting of the collection of deposits and the granting of credit to families and companies, with which the main source of financing is recurrent, stable and based on the opening of offices in the national territory. In the case of our most international banks, with presence in other countries through subsidiaries, the business they carry out is also characterized by the same banking model. This entails a recurrent flow of margins that has powerful elements of inertia, especially opportune in times of difficulty. Secondly, the process of securitization of Spanish banks, certainly intense in scams, especially if the issuance of mortgage bonds is included, has been characterized by its simplicity. The banking system has not developed particularly complex and difficult-to-value products, and securitisations have been carried out using relatively simple and transparent instruments, based mainly on mortgages, without resorting to complex instruments such as CDOs. Banks have segregated a pool of assets and financed them with the highest quality obligations by prioritizing the fund's liabilities and concentrating credit risk on a tranche of "capital" that has usually remained on the balance sheet. The bonds have also been placed directly on institutional investors, without promoting "vehicles" that transform long-term instruments into very short-term bonds. Given the links between the institutions and the management of investments and their participation in risks, operations have been managed professionally and have been subject to accounting, solvency and internal control rules for the activity as a whole. In other words, something similar to the model called "originate to distribute" has not been registered in Spain, and the absence of "ad hoc vehicles" has prevented contagion and the spread of problems. Finally, the management of credit institutions, supported by demanding accounting and solvency regulations and by supervision attentive to the evolution of risks, has made it possible to accumulate significant pockets of provisions to cover losses, not specifically identified in good times, but which manifest themselves when the business cycle changes. In general, it can be said that the assets of Spanish institutions are valued with a degree of prudence that makes the sector's comfortable solvency levels reliable. While it is true that this episode did not entail direct losses, it should be argued that the resulting blockade of the euro area money and private bond markets has had a significant impact on banks and savings banks. The process of intense growth and the consequent expansion of the demand for credit observed during the ten years has led to a notable appeal to the wholesale private fixed income markets, mainly through the placement of securitization bonds and mortgage bonds with an average maturity of approximately four years. With the markets closed down, although banks had been maintaining reasonable liquidity slack and broad diversification of maturities and financing segments, the collapse of issuances has generated intense disruption. In this difficult environment, banks and savings banks have modulated their different lines of business. On the one hand, they have perceived a lower demand for credit as a result of the rapid slowdown in the economy. On the other hand, they have adapted their sources of financing, struggling to capture traditional liabilities and, until the end of last year, raising resources from the Eurosystem. However, it is important to note that banks and savings banks have been demanding liquidity in a much lower proportion than the weight of our economy in the euro area, and have now placed their participation at a level equivalent to the Bank of Spain's 'key' in the ECB's capital. Since mid-April 2008, the primary market for simple bank bonds and mortgage bonds has been reactivated, but securitisation placements among institutional investors continue to be blocked. The Spanish entities have managed to place in the medium-term market d0 mortgage bonds, "senior" bonds and convertible bonds d0 a volume of issues of around 20,000 million euros in a very short time. As expected, the terms are shorter d0 two, three aces d0 the price conditions are more demanding, as the credit and liquidity risk premiums have increased, and the volumes are tighter. But what is relevant is that the generalized blockade has been overcome and private bond markets are beginning to express their preferences by quoting prices and not limiting the amounts indiscriminately. In this environment, banks and savings banks must increase their presence in the market, so that the expansion of their assets responds to the situation of international markets. It is unlikely that the conditions under which the financial system has operated in the fourteen-year scams will be repeated. The long shock wave of the Spanish economy has already given way to a phase of adjustment, the vigorous growth of residential construction has declined, which has dragged credit to the promotion, construction and acquisition of housing, and the almost unlimited availability of financial resources in the international markets of the euro with extraordinarily low credit risk premiums and illiquidity will not return. Banks and savings banks have to get used to a significant decline in business growth rates, which will be in the national GDP environment, to an exhaustion of the process of reintermediating liabilities for reabsorption of pension and investment funds, and to higher differentials in the interest rates of their liabilities placed in institutional markets. That is why the balance and diversification of masses and terms of its balance sheet and the care of the second lines of liquidity are so relevant. The expansion of their sources of financing, the establishment of permanent schemes for the promotion and marketing of their products in the international markets of the euro, the search for new "business niches", especially in those entities that have specialized in the financing of residential investment, and the rationalization of their cost structure and their network of branches are urgent tasks for banks and savings banks. The slowdown in the economy will not allow the higher financing costs to be transferred mechanically to customers, and this will mean pressure on margins and profits at a time when NPL ratios will increase. In this less comfortable environment, where there is an accentuation of competition in the internal banking market, it will not be possible to pass on to credit claimants the possible inefficiencies in the organization, imposing a tighter management of costs. In conclusion, it seems necessary to make a reference to the work of supervision. Our modes of continuous inspection, in close relationship with the entities, have worked reasonably well and have allowed the surprises of the summer of 2007 to be confined to the external environment. Banco de Espa has increased reporting requirements on financing structures and liquidity conditions, and will continue to insist on their proper management, including stress tests and contingency plans that take into account market uncertainties. And it will continue to monitor innovative businesses to promote rigorous implementation and demand adequate control and treatment of asset securitisations or the use of complex products. In terms of accounting provisions, a current of opinion is becoming evident in favour of maintaining a preventive scheme compatible with international accounting standards and with the acceptance of the internal models of the most advanced entities. This scheme is allowing banks to gradually apply the accumulated generic provisions to the new specific provisions for non-performing loans that are manifesting themselves in a more pronounced way in 2008. The first months will also be marked by the implementation in Spain of the new solvency regulations, known as Basel II, whose Circular approved by the Governing Council on May 22. The improvements it is already bringing to the management of banks are proving useful in the face of the current financial turbulence, and the new tools will expand the capacity for supervisory action if necessary. I would also like to point out that, if Parliament approves the introduction in Spain of a new financial supervisory structure based on the twin peak model, the Bank will help this transformation by taking on the task of safeguarding the solvency of all financial intermediaries, including securities firms and insurance intermediaries. By this time, I cannot fail to express my gratitude for the support I have always found during this year from this Governing Council, the Executive Committee, the Deputy Governor, the Directors-General and all the staff of the Bank. Thanks to the joint effort of all, we have been able to satisfactorily carry out the tasks entrusted to this institution one by more. I am confident that this same spirit of working together will enable us to successfully meet the important challenges that lie ahead.

En lneas generales, el fuerte repunte de estos precios ha estado asociado principalmente al fuerte incremento de su demanda por parte, sobre todo, de las economas emergentes. Las necesidades energticas de un sector industrial en clara expansi y los cambios en los patrones de consumo y de alimentaci, derivados, en general, de un mayor nivel de riqueza, son, probablemente, los principales factores que subyacen a este dinamismo de la demanda. Pero las presiones han puesto tambin al descubierto las limitaciones existentes para expandir la oferta, al menos en el corto plazo. Del mismo modo, tras la aceleraci de los precios de los alimentos se encuentran tambin factores de oferta ligados, en alg caso, a condiciones meteorolicas particularmente adversas. Aunque a finales de 2007 la financiaci al sector privado todava avanzaba, en trminos interanuales, a tasas superiores a las del crecimiento nominal de la economa, las tasas de crecimiento ms cortas de este agregado apuntaban ya valores ms cercanos al avance nominal del PIB, una tendencia que los datos de los primeros meses de 2008 han tendido a confirmar y que deber materializarse, finalmente, en una reducci de las ratios de endeudamiento del sector privado. Un ingrediente muy relevante para explicar la evoluci reciente de nuestra economa y analizar sus perspectivas es el considerable repunte de la inflaci que ha tenido lugar desde el pasado verano. Ha resultado, en efecto, desafortunado que, al impacto de las turbulencias en los mercados financieros, se hayan adido fuertes presiones alcistas en los mercados internacionales de materias primas, que han originado un encarecimiento sustancial tanto del petreo como de numerosos alimentos. Es indudable que la intensificaci de las presiones inflacionistas en este momento del ciclo resulta particularmente desfavorable.
