No es difcil identificar ya alguno de esos peligros en las voces y en las propuestas que se elevan en determinados pases a favor del nacionalismo econico y el proteccionismo, basadas en la falsa creencia de que la vuelta a la defensa de los intereses nacionales puede proteger a cada economa de los efectos de una espiral contractiva global. Los resultados de esa estrategia son bien conocidos: cuando cada pas se embarca en una dinmica de protegerse a s mismo, el resultado es una amplificaci de los impulsos recesivos globales. Esa fue la fuerza ms destructiva de la Gran Depresi. Esa es una leccin que no conviene olvidar. El alivio de las tensiones pasa necesariamente por una accin concertada y coordinada entre el mayor nmero posible de pases, que sea capaz de devolver la confianza a los mercados financieros, de impulsar una dinmica de saneamiento de las instituciones financieras y de propulsar el dinamismo del gasto. En un marco de libertad de comercio y de transacciones financieras, la coordinaci de las polticas nacionales refuerza y multiplica sus efectos, amplificando as los impulsos expansivos que de ellas se derivan. El corolario evidente de este razonamiento es que cualquier plan de accin que se emprenda debe, necesariamente, articularse y encontrar su acomodo en el marco de los acuerdos adoptados internacionalmente. Y tampoco podemos cometer la equivocacin de deslindar la trayectoria del crdito en nuestro pas del resto de los factores que confluyen en el severo ajuste por el que est atravesando la economa espaola. Nada sera ms contraproducente que caer en la simplificaci errea de que la salida de la crisis depende exclusivamente de la existencia de una disponibilidad abundante de financiacin crediticia. Antes de que anglicismos como subprime, conduit y otros tantos pasaran a formar parte de nuestro vocabulario comn, la economa espala acumulaba una serie de desequilibrios internos que haban ido socavando su dinamismo y que hacan inevitable un ajuste que habra podido ser gradual si las circunstancias internacionales no hubiesen cambiado tan dramticamente. En cualquier caso, en una tesitura en la que se da la desafortunada coincidencia del ajuste interno con unas condiciones externas extraordinariamente adversas, la recuperacin de la confianza, adicionalmente dada por los acontecimientos excepcionales que se estn viviendo a escala mundial, y la reanimacin del gasto, sobre el que se han acumulado numerosos factores contractivos, no sern posibles si no se abre camino la perspectiva de una absorcin de los desequilibrios acumulados. La reanimacin del crdito forma parte, sin duda, de la soluci, pero esta no es posible si no se dan las condiciones adecuadas para que las empresas y las familias recuperan la confianza en sus rentas futuras y dispongan de bases slidas sobre las que asentar sus planes de gasto de consumo o inversi, o de generaci de empleo en el caso de las empresas. En ocasiones anteriores me he referido a los fenmenos que estamos viviendo como resultado de la confluencia de una serie de crculos viciosos que se realimentan entre s. Los consumidores gastan menos porque temen por el futuro de sus rentas. Las empresas invierten menos y contratan menos trabajadores porque esperan menos demanda y se enfrentan a mayores dificultades financieras. Los bancos y cajas prestan menos porque captan menos recursos y temen por la solvencia de los prestatarios. Son crculos viciosos que difcilmente se pueden romper por un solo punto. El estado de la confianza y el tono de las expectativas son determinantes no slo de las decisiones de gasto y de la demanda de financiacin sino tambin de la percepci del riesgo y de los requisitos exigibles en la concesi del crdito. Y la recuperaci de la confianza y la mejora de las expectativas, aunque no sern independientes de la evoluci de la crisis internacional, dependern en gran medida de la capacidad que vaya mostrando la economa para enfrentarse a las adversas circunstancias existentes y superar los retos presentes. Hay que ser conscientes, adems, de que en cualquiera de los escenarios posibles de superacin de esta crisis, las condiciones crediticias habrn de ser necesariamente ms limitadas y ms restrictivas que antes de la misma. Durante la larga fase de expansi, el endeudamiento de las familias y las empresas espaolas crecia un ritmo que, repetidamente el Banco de Espaa calificcomo insostenible. Es muy difcil, a mi juicio, que esta economa pueda reencontrar una senda de reactivacin sida y sostenida del gasto sin que, previamente, haya avanzado el proceso de saneamiento de la posicin patrimonial del sector privado que ya est en marcha. El sistema financiero espal tendr tambin que adaptarse a estas nuevas condiciones. Su buena salud global es un activo de primer orden para la economa espaola, pero debemos velar para que esa solidez se preserve en las condiciones de tensi financiera y deterioro macroeconmico que estamos viviendo. No resulta verosmil pensar en escenarios de reanimaci de los flujos de financiacin si no se asientan en un sistema de intermediarios sido y rentable. Si el sistema financiero espal se debilitara severamente, como ha ocurrido en otros pases, la financiaci de la economa se hara a ms difcil y el crecimiento se resentira en mayor medida. Por otra parte, el restablecimiento de bases adecuadas para la recuperaci de la confianza y la reanimaci de los planes de gasto del sector privado descansa en buena medida en que el ajuste de la economa se traduzca en una mejora de la competitividad y de las condiciones del mercado de trabajo. Tras varios as de vigorosa generaci de empleo, hemos entrado en un proceso de destrucci de puestos de trabajo y de aumento del desempleo de una intensidad superior a la de recesiones anteriores. Ello refleja la persistencia de algunos rasgos estructurales de nuestro mercado de trabajo que no resultan problemticos cuando la economa se expande, pero que tienden a descargar el peso del ajuste de manera excesiva sobre el empleo cuando cambia el ciclo. Y ello contribuye a que el consumo se contraiga de manera ms acusada que la renta disponible y a que la contracci de la inversin no se limite al componente residencial, donde la necesidad de un ajuste es evidente, sino que tambin afecte de manera intensa al resto de la inversi productiva. El efecto propagador de las tendencias contractivas que ejerce el aumento del desempleo tambin se transmite a la morosidad, a la calidad de los activos bancarios y, en definitiva, repercute sobre el endurecimiento de las condiciones en la concesi de crditos. Y en estas condiciones es muy probable que una parte importante de los posibles impulsos expansivos que se puedan generar vea frenada su traslacin efectiva al gasto. Todo ello es suficientemente ilustrativo de la complejidad que subyace a la contracci econica y financiera que estamos viviendo, en el marco de la primera crisis crediticia global de la historia econica reciente. Espero haber sido capaz de transmitirles la imposibilidad de tratar las tensiones crediticias como si de un fenmeno aislado se tratara. El corolario de ello, y con esto termino Seoras, es que cualquier programa de acci efectivo debe contemplar acciones coordinadas en diversos frentes que permitan abordar de manera conjunta los no pocos retos a los que se enfrenta la economa espaola en estos momentos. Este es el enfoque adoptado a nivel internacional, que tambin nosotros hemos de seguir, adaptndolo a las particularidades del proceso de ajuste emprendido y de la situacin diferenciada de nuestro sistema financiero. Muchas gracias.

Title: Introduction to the IV High Level Seminar of Central Banks of the Eurosystem and Latin America. Intervention at the Seminar jointly organized by the Bank of Mexico, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Spain. English only
text: Mexico, 23 March 2009 Introduction to the IV High Level Seminar of the Eurosystem and Latin American Central Banks Banco de Mexico, Banco Central Europeo and Banco de Espaa Jose Vials Deputy Governor Good morning, First of all, I would like to thank you, Governor Ortiz, for your warm hospitality today (and for the delicious dinner yesterday), and the staff of Banco de Mexico and the ECB for such fluid collaboration in organising this important event. It is a source of great satisfaction to introduce the fourth edition of the Eurosystem and Latin American High-Level Seminar, an initiative that started in Madrid, in 2002, and was repeated in Brazil (2004) and again in Madrid (2006). I also want to join Governor Ortiz and President Trichet in welcoming you all, and in thanking you for making the effort to attend this meeting in such difficult circumstances. In introducing the Seminar, I will try to share with you some reflections along the lines of the topics envisaged in the programme. In fact, the changes in the planning of this Seminar mirror the radical transformation that the world economy has undergone in less than a year. When the letters of invitation were sent out, last July, one of the main concerns for central bankers was the impact of high increases in commodity prices on inflation and on general economic performance and indeed, this was intended to be the main topic for our discussions today-. At present, however, commodity prices have retreated by more than one-third from their record highs last summer, and the overriding concerns are now the rapid spread of the financial crisis, the deep economic recession and the policy response to both of them. I should stress that the sharp correction in commodity prices is a challenging development for a large number of Latin American economies, which are net exporters of primary products. As a matter of fact, this sudden change of scenario could lead to the reversal of some of the improvements achieved in the region in recent years in terms of reduced vulnerabilities, an issue that we will discuss in the second session of the Seminar. Let me focus now on the financial crisis and its implications. The world economy is in the middle of a profound and generalised adjustment in financial and real terms. Downward revisions to growth forecasts are becoming bolder as the crisis unravels and negative feedback effects between real and financial sectors intensify. Since October, the IMF has cut the forecast for world growth in 2009 by almost 5 p.p. (to a global recession), and revisions for both the euro area and Latin America are of the order of -3 p.p.. After more than a year of dire economic and financial difficulties the end of the current troubles is not yet in sight rather the recovery is being continuously postponed-. The factors that are at the origin of this situation have to be traced back to the protracted period of expansion that started in the aftermath of the ICT revolution, underpinned by a process of rapid financial innovation and increasing economic and financial integration. Economic policies, in general, were excessively supportive of this process in many parts of the world and were not able to a large extent-to take into account the accumulation of internal and global imbalances. Regulatory frameworks, in turn, were not sufficiently alert to indentify the problems building up in the financial sector and did not address them in time. Consequently, the major financial technology shock that supported innovation and financial globalisation had weak foundations. Now we are witnessing the reversal of this process which is equivalent to a negative supply shock to the real economy. In the medium to long run, as the severe adjustment of the financial sector is factored in, potential output growth, which was probably overestimated in the boom years, will be lower for a certain period of time. In the short run, the consequence of this negative financial shock has been the shrinking of the financial systems of many advanced economies. Furthermore, the serious trouble of the financial system is having two major consequences. On the one hand, it is damaging financing flows worldwide and, on the other, it is fuelling a negative feedback between the financial and real sectors. I will tackle these two issues briefly. The financial market freeze is a direct consequence of the dramatic shift from the search for yield process that characterised the global situation before August 2007, to the flight to safety induced by unprecedented uncertainty and lack of confidence prevailing after that date. From an external perspective, crises usually prompt a retrenchment of capital flows towards the domestic base in advanced countries. Indeed, the change in market sentiment has led in these countries to significant amounts of capital being repatriated. In contrast, in emerging markets  including some Latin American countries-capitals have flown out in spite of the progress made in recent years in developing local financial markets. Indeed, despite the reduction of financial vulnerabilities Latin America and other emerging markets are facing difficulties in achieving a sustained flow of external financing. We may wonder whether the countries in the region could have taken greater advantage of the good times to strengthen their economic and financial position even further. In any case, if we compare Latin America with other emerging regions we see that the efforts to reduce financial and economic vulnerabilities are paying off. For instance, some Eastern European countries are facing now some of the problems that affected Latin America in the past: large foreign currency financing needs, large currentaccount deficits, excessive credit growth and major currency mismatches. Turning to the feedback effects between the financial and real sectors, the prevailing direction is changing at the global level. During the initial stages of the crisis, the direction of the impact was from the financial to the real sector as the process of deleveraging unfolded, and liquidity preference and counterparty risk contributed to the contraction in credit markets. The deterioration of the financial situation was channelled to the real sector through the tightening of financing conditions, a sharp contraction of financial wealth and the erosion of confidence, all of which constrained consumption and investment decisions. The collapse of Lehman Brothers came as another huge financial shock, which hit the economy with unprecedented severity. As a result, global growth plunged dramatically to negative rates of -6% in 4Q08 and very few countries were spared from this sharp overturn. At present, while the financial sector is still undergoing a severe adjustment the reverse feedback is gaining strength and the worsening economic situation is having an increasingly negative impact on the financial system. The intensified adjustment in the housing sector, growing difficulties in the corporate sector and the rise in unemployment are damaging previously healthy, traditional bank assets and non-performing loans are thus increasing. One particular example of the close linkages between finance and activity is trade. The current recession has seen the sharp drop in global trade in the last quarter of 2008. While this can be explained to a large extent by the contraction in global demand, severe disruptions in trade finance, after last September, may have also played a part in the collapse of trade. These disruptions have a larger direct impact on emerging economies, where export firms may have no other source of finance. The policy response to the crisis has been stepped up since October. Monetary policy easing, financial support plans and fiscal packages were implemented urgently in order to prevent financial panic and stabilise the markets, put a floor on the foreseeable fall in activity, and most of all stop the loss of confidence that had spread through the real and financial sectors. Central banks have responded decisively to the changing outlook for price stability brought about by the escalation of the crisis by changing the monetary policy stance through substantial cuts in official interest rates and by an unprecedented increase in liquidity provision. Since October, the ECB has reduced its interest rate by 275 bp; and in Latin America large cuts have also recently been made, with a lag of some months. An additional challenge for Central Banks -one which is less pressing in Latin America for the moment-is the need to conduct policy in an environment where official interest rates have become very low. These considerations have led an increasing number of major central banks to implement unconventional measures to support the flow of credit, which have induced a substantial expansion of central banks balance sheets. In Latin America, in addition to interest rate cuts, there was also ample liquidity support, with a strong bias towards foreign currency provision, and foreign exchange reserves were used to limit exchange rate fluctuations. Regarding financial support packages, there have been common elements capital injections, guarantees, asset purchases-but with very different mixes and sizes from one area to another. The contrast between the committed amounts in advanced economies (almost 50% of GDP) and emerging markets (around 2%) is most significant. Finally, fiscal stimuli have been widespread, amounting to an estimated 2.7% of GDP for the G20 countries between 2008 and 2010. Here the divergence between advanced and emerging countries is less marked, due to the weight of the measures applied by Russia and China. Some Latin American countries such as Argentina and Chile-have also announced sizeable packages. The ammunition spent in sustaining the financial system and cushioning the decline in growth in advanced economies leads in my view to two main considerations: The first is that although the three types of policies monetary, financial and fiscal-have been adopted, the stabilisation of the financial sector is a precondition for macro policies to work fully and effectively in pulling the economies out of the recession; from that perspective the emphasis given to the recovery of the financial sector seems to be totally justified. The second is that given the extraordinary nature of the measures introduced in all three policy dimensions, and the negative consequences that would result from maintaining them beyond what is reasonable, the design of exit strategies over the medium term that continue to ensure price stability, the sustainability of public finances and an efficient and sound financial system is necessary to sustain confidence and reduce uncertainties on how our economies and financial systems will look like in the aftermath of the crisis. Something that will condition our future potential growth rates. In this respect, it is particularly important to take into account that public finances in a number of advanced economies are becoming dangerously overstretched. In principle, part of the funds invested or committed to supporting the financial system will be recovered. However, Treasuries and even some Central Banks are incorporating ever-greater risks into their balance sheets, and fiscal positions will worsen substantially. Likewise, debt-to-GDP ratios will increase, partly induced by the huge support to the financial sector. The cost of financing now subdued in advanced economies as their public debt is considered a safe haven-may shoot up in the future, reflecting an increased perception of risk and the massive issuance of public debt. If we factor in subdued growth for several years, debt dynamics can turn very negative. So even if the swift and strong policy reaction is largely warranted in the present circumstances, it should be followed by a timely and decisive withdrawal of the stimulus when the situation stabilises, as I pointed before. A further consideration in view of the large financial and fiscal packages introduced in advanced economies regards emerging markets, which may suffer lasting financing constraints. On the one hand, sovereign spreads have widened substantially; and on the other, the increasing supply of sovereign issues by advanced economies increases the competition that emerging economies face in financing themselves in the markets. I would like to make a last point, on the need for international policy cooperation, before leaving the floor. There is a risk that national responses lead to a reversal in globalisation which, in spite of possible excesses, has been the driving force behind the increased growth potential in recent decades. The case of trade I mentioned earlier is just one aspect of the possible impact of the crisis on the globalisation process, but I should stress that the risk of financial de-globalisation is also high. As I suggested, the natural reaction to a crisis in advanced economies is retrenchment, back to the domestic base. But on top of it, the national financial policy options in particular, those aimed at keeping domestic credit flowing-may exacerbate this retrenchment through the segmentation of markets. Contrary to protectionism, which is an explicit policy option, financial de-globalisation may be the unintended outcome of domestic policies. This risk and the synergies that joint coherent action may provide highlight the need for international policy cooperation. The efforts within the G-20 and the European Union go in the right direction, although they are far from complete. At present, the outlook for the global economy remains highly uncertain. On the positive side, a fair amount of stimulus is in the pipeline and the framework for financial support is slowly settling down. On the negative side, the unfavourable effects of the perverse real-financial interactions have not been fully felt yet. These counteracting forces and their impact on confidence will determine the scope for the recovery of the global economy. But as mentioned, such recovery will not take hold until the policy efforts succeed in sorting out the deep-seated problems of the financial system. Let me conclude. We have a very busy day ahead to discuss these topics, but to end on a positive note I just hope that in our next meeting two years from now we will have succeeded in leaving the crisis behind and our economies once again enjoy growth, but this time based on really sound economic and financial foundations. Thank you.

Title: The future of supervision. Implementation of the Larosire Report. Closing conference in the course organized by the APIE at the Menndez Pelayo International University
text: Santander, 19 June 2009 The future of oversight. Implementation of the Larosi8fre Report APIE Course at Men8endez Pelayo International University Francisco Javier Ar92ztegui Deputy governor Introduction I would like to begin my speech by thanking the Men8endez Pelayo International University and the Association of Journalists of Informacin Econica for their opportunity to close these conferences on the impact of the crisis on the financial sector and other sectors of the economy. In these minutes that I am going to share with you, I will try to point out how financial supervision will be organized from today in the European Union. Today is a key day for financial supervisors in Europe, as the Heads of State and Government are endorsing the implementation of new proposals in this area. I will begin with a brief reference to the origin of the changes and describe the two pillars on which the new structure will be based: what in specialist jargon is called "macroprudential supervision" and "microprudential supervision". Subsequently, I will highlight the importance of the interrelations between both pillars that are, without a doubt, a key piece of this reform. Finally, I will refer to its implementation and the need for it to be done in an orderly manner. The origin of the changes We are experiencing an unprecedented situation in the financial markets. What began as a problem in the U.S. market for low-quality mortgages has morphed into a global financial crisis, which has spread to economic activity and employment, and generated a global recession. States have intervened to support financial systems in ways that no one would have imagined a few years ago. And from the beginning we have wondered how we may have arrived at this situation and what we can do to reduce the likelihood of such events being recorded again. The debate in academic forums and international decision-making centres on the causes of the crisis tends to opt for two lines of argument, sometimes operating independently and sometimes in a coordinated manner. One line of debate suggests that there have been serious failures in the public regulation of markets, financial institutions and their ancillary industry. Part of the conviction that the ordination Of all these institutions it was poorly designed and that, therefore, burdened in a situation of tension, tended to collapse. Another line of argument posits that the biggest problems arose not from particularly inadequate regulation but, rather, from a lack of enforcement and poor supervision of institutions and financial markets. Going deeper into this second line of explanation, Europe will emerge from the Larosi8fre Report which will focus my presentation today. Indeed, in October 2008, the President of the European Commission, Jos8e Manuel Barroso, asked Jacques de Larosi8fre to chair a group of experts to advise the European Commission on the future of Community financial legislation and supervision. Its recommendations were published on February 25, 2009, in the now famous, at least among those of us who dedicate ourselves to this, Larosi8fre report. The Report makes a diagnosis of the causes of the crisis and insists that it is necessary to require credit institutions to have more own and better quality resources, that prudential rules and accounting schemes must establish "buffers" of reserve capital and provisions that allow to cushion the tensions generated by the business cycle, and that the governance and management criteria of financial institutions must provide a framework where medium-term strategies and risk control prevail. Following these regulatory considerations, the Report focuses on the changes required for financial supervision in Europe. And in this area, it proposes two blocks of reforms that we can frame in what has been called "macroprudential financial supervision" and "microprudential supervision" Macroprudencial supervision The first pillar of the reform, and probably the most novel, is the so-called "macroprudential supervision". There is no simple way to define this concept, nor will I try to do it precisely. A general approach, however, would lead us to point out that it is a framework of analysis that allows detecting weaknesses or potential risks in financial systems considered as a whole and not institution to institution. It would also include the management of the means that serve to avoid, or at least attenuate, contagion. It seems clear, for example, that the sharp drop in interest rates promoted by the Federal Reserve at the beginning of this decade has had to do with the climate of euphoria that permeates the investor sentiment from 2003 to 2006. Another example of potential risk can be widespread "bubbles" in housing markets or commodity prices spreading to the extent that, although overall inflation rates do not detect worrying warming, there may be indications that a potentially dangerous inflation process is brewing. "Macroprudential supervision" would be dedicated to detecting these processes and proposing measures to avoid them. In a world such as the one we live in, this function cannot be limited to the sphere of national authorities, but must, by its very nature, have a global approach. It is not surprising, therefore, that practically all the international forums working to draw lessons from this crisis point out as a key and urgent factor the implementation of a "macroprudential" approach in financial supervision. The incorrect identification and measurement of the exposure of financial systems to complex and interconnected systemic risks, and the lack of reaction to those that were identified, have been one of the main weaknesses highlighted by the current crisis. I will return to this later, which is fundamental to understanding what underlies these new proposals. Is this task going to be tackled in Europe? To address this problem, and following one of the recommendations of the Larosi8fre group, the Heads of State and Government are today discussing the creation of a new, independent and high-level oversight gain for all financial sectors, to be called the European Systemic Risk Council (ESRB). This new body will be responsible for "macroprudential" supervision in Europe and will have four functions: 1. Design, collect and analyze all the information needed to identify the global risks of the financial sector. This information shall include macroeconomic data and financial statements of individual entities treated in aggregate form. 2. Assess the significance of these risks 3. Issue alerts and recommendations on them 4. Ensure that these recommendations are met In addition, it will maintain close contact with the International Monetary Fund and other international organizations, to incorporate possible alerts on global risks into their analysis. The recommendations issued by this new Council may affect the whole of Europe or specific countries. Their alerts and warnings must be attended by the public powers or they must state the reasons that lead them not to comply with them. The new European Systemic Risk Council will have wide-ranging governance, although, as is the case, the key role will be played by the central banks integrated into the European System of Central Banks. It will meet in Frankfurt, receive technical and logistical support from the European Central Bank and coordinate with the authorities responsible for the day-to-day supervision of individual financial institutions. Microprudencial supervision The reform of microprudential supervision in the European Union is the second pillar of the proposal. The change consists of the creation of three microprudential supervisory authorities to be built on the basis of the existing European committees of supervisors (CEBS, CSAR, CEIOPS). At the outset, it should be clarified that a European "ICO supervisor" is not created in the sense that it has responsibility for the day-to-day supervision of all the entities of the Uni, not even of the large transnational banks. The day-to-day supervision of institutions will continue to be a national responsibility, not only because national supervisors know their banks and their markets best, but also because it is the Treasury Offices and national taxpayers who would pay for the resolution of crises in their country's institutions. The aim of the creation of these three new Community authorities is to achieve greater convergence, cooperation and coordination between national supervisors. So far, the European committees of supervisors have promoted the same objective. And I can assure you that very important progress has been made in the five years. However, the cooperation and voluntary convergence d0 that is, full consensus d0 on which these committees are based has limits, and national interests have prevailed in many cases. This has indicated that the current structure is insufficient to achieve the desired objective. To achieve this, it has been decided to create an integrated network of supervisors called the European System of Financial Supervisors (ESFS). This network will consist of two blocks: -One will be the current sectoral supervisory committees, now converted into European authorities. In principle, there will be a European supervisory authority for banking, another for insurance and another for securities and markets. -The other block will be the national supervisors This dual structure aims to combine the daily and detailed knowledge that each national supervisor has of its markets and entities, with a European vision independent of the new authorities. National supervisors are closest to their countries' markets and institutions. Therefore, they are the ones who can best carry out the day-to-day supervision of their national entities and will continue to do so. However, the three new independent authorities (ESAs) will have effective powers to take some decisions above the criteria of national supervisors. For example, until now, the guidelines of the European committees were voluntary for national supervisors. With this reform, the new authorities will be able to draw up technical rules on co-carrying out inspections, which national supervisors will have to comply with. These authorities will also have databases that will accumulate the individualized financial information of all the European institutions and ensure a common supervisory culture throughout the area. Another example is the power of mediation assigned to the new authorities in cases where there are disagreements between supervisors in different countries. Although I have to point out that, at least so far and in the banking sector, European supervisors have reached agreements without the need for external arbitration. The same can be said, in the case of Spain, of relations with supervisors in third countries, especially, in our case, with our counterparts in the Americas with whom we have had excellent relations and have achieved extensive voluntary agreements. It should be noted, however, that in this dual network, in addition to national supervisors and the new European authorities, "colleges of supervisors" d0 one for each supranational bank, with participation limited to supervisors in the countries where the entity is established d0 will also play a prominent role in this dual network, which will strengthen the exchange of information and mutual trust between inspectors from different countries. As you can see, the new proposals are not simply a change of organization, but involve major reforms. Macro-micro prudential link Even if the two pillars I have just described are sufficiently serious, we will not be able to achieve strong supervision in UNIN if the links between the two levels do not work properly. Although the relationship between the two pillars may seem obvious d0 and it is easy to see that one complements the other d0 you will not be surprised if I tell you that its implementation is not going to be easy. Among other factors, it is difficult to specify the specific way of operating of the Systemic Risk Council, which, as I have already indicated, is a novelty in the new structure. For supervision of this type to be effective, it must be able to develop an accurate diagnosis of the weaknesses and risks of the system; It must be able to issue recommendations using that diagnosis, and it must establish a mechanism to ensure that those recommendations are addressed. Therefore, the "macroprudential" supervisor must be equipped with sufficient instruments and must have the support of the "microprudential" supervisor. In order to carry out the diagnosis, the Council must have at its disposal all the relevant information on the European markets and financial institutions. In this framework, the new "microprudential" authorities will be responsible for centralizing the detailed financial statements of the different banks and insurance companies managed by national supervisors and transmitting them in aggregate form to the Systemic Risk Council. The Board should rely on the support of the supervisors of institutions to properly interpret the information collected and to gauge the risks identified. And, in addition, the three "microprudential" authorities will participate in the Council's governing gains. These interrelationships are also articulated in the reverse direction. Thus, the "microprudential supervision" of institutions (that is, "the one of a lifetime", if I may use it) cannot be conceived as a supervision in which the global weaknesses and risks detected by the Systemic Risk Board are not taken into account. It is worth mentioning another aspect that I mentioned a moment ago and that is, in my opinion, more relevant. This is the need to put in place effective mechanisms to ensure that the recommendations of the macroprudential supervisor are translated into concrete actions and actions by the different national supervisors of institutions and by the three new "microprudential" authorities. We must be aware that, even if we manage to properly identify and manage the future risks faced by financial systems, if there are no pressure mechanisms and incentives to act accordingly, all our efforts will be a dead letter. This is precisely one of the main conclusions of the Larosi8fre report. First steps in the implementation of the reform To conclude my speech, I would like briefly to see how this reform is going to be implemented and where we stand. As I said at the beginning, today is a key day for European supervision. The Council of Heads of State and Government must decide whether to "give the green light" to these new proposals. The aim is for the new European supervisory framework to be operational by 2010. As you can imagine, this is going to be a great challenge for all of us involved in the project. The proposals on the table are feasible, although there are still many details to be specified. They do not represent a sudden change, and they are the natural evolution of a system whose weaknesses the current crisis has revealed. In addition, there is a broad consensus among the Member States and there is a political moment conducive to its implementation. In this sense, the words of the President of the European Commission, Jos8e Manuel Barroso, capture the importance of the moment: "It has to be now or never. If we can't reform the financial sector and financial supervision when we have a real crisis, when will we reform it?" However, I would like to highlight some potential risks which, if they materialise, would result in the failure of the progress made. Three are, in my opinion, the most relevant. The first has to do with the design of new structures. In the world, there has been a clear tendency in Europe and globally to create complex and multiple structures to discuss issues related to financial regulation and supervision. An overly complicated organization, composed of too many forums and groups, in which responsibilities are not clearly defined, or in which responsibilities overlap with those of other existing bodies, would jeopardize the effectiveness of reform. There must therefore be clear lines of responsibility. Secondly, even if adequate structures with defined responsibilities are developed, if they are not provided with the necessary resources, it will not be possible to achieve the desired goals. One of the weaknesses of the current supervisory committees has been the lack of powers and resources to carry out their functions effectively. Third, the urgency and timing of the moment should not make us make hasty decisions. It is important that the implementation of the reform be done in an orderly manner. In any case, the implementation of these new proposals is not the end of the process. And they probably won't be enough to solve all the future challenges that supervisors will have to face. What is certain is that it is a step in the right direction. The debate continues and the reform that we all hope will be adopted today will be reviewed in three years' time. Time will tell if we were able to adequately meet the challenge before us. Thanks a lot.
text_original: Santander, 19 de junio de 2009 El futuro de la supervisi. Implementaci del Informe Larosire Curso de la APIE en la Universidad Internacional Menndez Pelayo Francisco Javier Arztegui Subgobernador Introducci Quisiera comenzar mi intervenci agradeciendo la oportunidad que me brinda la Universidad Internacional Menndez Pelayo y la Asociacin de Periodistas de Informacin Econica de clausurar estas jornadas sobre la repercusi de la crisis en el sector financiero y otros sectores de la economa. En estos minutos que voy a compartir con Ustedes, intentar apuntar co va a organizarse a partir de hoy la supervisin financiera en la Unin Europea. Precisamente hoy es un da clave para los supervisores financieros en Europa, ya que los Jefes de Estado y de Gobierno estn dando su respaldo a la puesta en funcionamiento de nuevas propuestas en este rea. Comenzar con una breve referencia al origen de los cambios y describir los dos pilares sobre los que se asentar la nueva estructura: lo que en jerga de especialistas se denomina la supervisi macroprudencial y la supervisi microprudencial. Posteriormente, resaltar la importancia de las interrelaciones entre ambos pilares que son, sin duda, una pieza clave de esta reforma. Para finalizar me referir a su implantaci y a la necesidad de que sta se haga de una manera ordenada. El origen de los cambios Estamos viviendo una situaci sin precedentes en los mercados financieros. Lo que empezsiendo un problema en el mercado estadounidense de hipotecas de baja calidad, se ha transformado en una crisis financiera mundial, que se ha contagiado a la actividad econica y al empleo, y ha generado una recesin mundial. Los Estados han intervenido para apoyar a los sistemas financieros de una manera que hace unos as nadie se hubiera imaginado. Y desde el comienzo nos hemos preguntado co es posible que hayamos llegado a esta situacin y qu podemos hacer para reducir la probabilidad de que este tipo de sucesos vuelvan a registrarse. El debate en los foros acadmicos y en los centros de decisi internacionales sobre las causas de la crisis tiende a decantarse en dos lneas de argumentaci que, en ocasiones, operan de manera independiente y, en otras, de modo coordinado. Una lnea de debate sugiere que ha habido fallos graves en la regulaci pblica de los mercados, de las instituciones financieras y de su industria auxiliar. Parte de la convicci que la ordenaci de todas estas instituciones estaba mal diseda y que, por ello, agobiadas en una situaci de tensin, tendieron a colapsar. Otra lnea de argumentacin postula que los mayores problemas no surgieron por una normativa especialmente inadecuada sino, ms bien, por una falta de exigencia de su cumplimiento y por una mala supervisin de las instituciones y de los mercados financieros. Ahondando en esta segunda lnea de explicaci, surgien Europa el Informe Larosire que hoy centrar mi exposici. En efecto, en octubre de 2008, el Presidente de la Comisi Europea, Jos Manuel Barroso, pidia Jacques de Larosire que presidiera un grupo de expertos que deban prestar asesoramiento a la Comisin Europea sobre el futuro de la legislacin y la supervisi comunitarias en materia financiera. Sus recomendaciones se publicaron el pasado 25 de febrero de 2009, en el ya famoso, al menos entre los que nos dedicamos a esto, informe Larosire. El Informe realiza un diagnstico de las causas de la crisis e insiste en que es necesario exigir a las entidades de crdito ms recursos propios y de mejor calidad, que las normas de prudencia y los esquemas contables deben establecer unos colchones de capital de reservas y provisiones que permitan amortiguar las tensiones que genera el ciclo de los negocios, y que los criterios de gobierno y gesti de las entidades financieras han de proporcionar un marco donde primen estrategias a medio plazo y el control de los riesgos. Despus de estas consideraciones sobre regulaci, el Informe centra su atencin en los cambios que precisa la supervisin financiera en Europa. Y en este mbito, plantea dos bloques de reformas que podemos encuadrar en lo que se ha llamado la supervisi financiera macroprudencial y la supervisi microprudencial Supervisi macroprudencial El primer pilar de la reforma, y probablemente el ms novedoso, es la denominada supervisin macroprudencial. No existe una manera sencilla de definir este concepto, ni yo voy a tratar de hacerlo con precisin. Una aproximacin general, no obstante, nos llevara a apuntar que es un marco de anlisis que permite detectar debilidades o riesgos potenciales en los sistemas financieros considerados en su conjunto y no instituci a institucin. Comprendera, tambin, el manejo de los medios que sirvan para evitar, o al menos atenuar, el contagio. Parece evidente, por ejemplo, que la intensa bajada de los tipos de inters que impuls la Reserva Federal a comienzos de esta dcada ha tenido que ver con el clima de euforia que impregnla actitud de los inversores desde 2003 a 2006. Otro ejemplo de riesgo potencial pueden ser las burbujas generalizadas en los mercados inmobiliarios o en los precios de las materias primas que difunden seles de que, a pesar de que los ndices generales de inflacin no detecten un calentamiento preocupante, puede haber indicios de que est incubndose un proceso de inflacin potencialmente peligroso. A detectar estos procesos y a proponer medidas para evitarlos estara dedicada la supervisin macroprudencial. En un mundo como el que vivimos, esta funcin no puede limitarse al mbito de las autoridades nacionales, sino que, por su propia naturaleza, ha de tener un enfoque global. No es extrao, pues, que la prctica totalidad de los foros internacionales que trabajan en extraer lecciones de esta crisis sealen como un factor clave y urgente la instrumentaci de un enfoque macroprudencial en la supervisi financiera. La incorrecta identificaci y medicin de la exposici de los sistemas financieros a riesgos sistmicos complejos e interconectados, y la falta de reaccin ante los que s se identificaron, han sido una de las principales debilidades que ha puesto de manifiesto la actual crisis. Ms adelante volver sobre este tema, que es fundamental para entender lo que subyace a estas nuevas propuestas. Co va a abordarse esta tarea en Europa? Para afrontar este problema, y siguiendo una de las recomendaciones del grupo Larosire, los jefes de Estado y de Gobierno debaten hoy la creaci de un nuevo gano de vigilancia para todos los sectores financieros, independiente y de alto nivel, que se denominar Consejo Europeo de Riesgo Sistmico (ESRB). Este nuevo rgano ser el encargado de la supervisin macroprudencial en Europa y desarrollar cuatro funciones: 1. Diser, recopilar y analizar toda la informaci precisa para identificar los riesgos globales del sector financiero. Esta informacin comprender datos macroeconicos y estados financieros de entidades individuales tratados de una manea agregada 2. Evaluar la importancia de dichos riesgos 3. Emitir alertas y recomendaciones sobre los mismos 4. Asegurarse que se cumplen dichas recomendaciones Adems, mantendr un estrecho contacto con el Fondo Monetario Internacional y otros organismos internacionales, para incorporar a sus anlisis posibles alertas sobre riesgos globales. Las recomendaciones que emita este nuevo Consejo podrn afectar a toda Europa o a pases concretos. Sus alertas y avisos debern ser atendidos por los poderes pblicos o stos debern exponer las razones que les llevan a no cumplir los mismos. El nuevo Consejo Europeo de Riesgo Sistmico tendr una gobernanza de amplio espectro, aunque, como es lico, el papel fundamental lo desempearn los bancos centrales integrados en el Sistema Europeo de Bancos Centrales. Se reunir en Frankfurt, recibir el apoyo tcnico y logstico del Banco Central Europeo y deber coordinarse con las autoridades encargadas de la supervisin diaria de las entidades financieras individuales. Supervisi microprudencial La reforma de la supervisi microprudencial en la Unin Europea es el segundo pilar de la propuesta. El cambio consiste en la creacin de tres autoridades supervisoras microprudenciales que debern construirse a partir de los comits europeos de supervisores, ya existentes (CEBS, CSAR, CEIOPS). De entrada hay que aclarar que no se crea un supervisor ico europeo en el sentido de que tenga la responsabilidad de la supervisin diaria de todas las entidades de la Uni, ni siquiera de los grandes bancos transnacionales. La supervisin da a da de las entidades continuar siendo una responsabilidad nacional, no so porque los supervisores nacionales son los que mejor conocen a sus entidades bancarias y a sus mercados, sino tambin porque las Haciendas Plicas y los contribuyentes nacionales son los que pagaran la resolucin de las crisis de las entidades de su pas. Lo que se busca con la creacin de estas tres nuevas autoridades comunitarias es conseguir una mayor convergencia, cooperacin y coordinaci entre los supervisores nacionales. Hasta ahora los comits europeos de supervisores han promovido este mismo objetivo. Y les puedo asegurar que se han registrado avances muy importantes en los timos cinco aos. Sin embargo, la cooperacin y la convergencia voluntaria es decir, el pleno consenso- en la que se basan estos comits tiene lmites, y los intereses nacionales han prevalecido en muchos casos. Esto ha indicado que la estructura actual es insuficiente para alcanzar el objetivo deseado. Para lograrlo se ha decidido crear una red integrada de supervisores denominada Sistema Europeo de Supervisores Financieros (ESFS). Esta red estar formada por dos bloques: -Uno sern los actuales comits supervisores sectoriales, convertidos ahora en autoridades europeas. En principio, habr una autoridad supervisora europea para la banca, otra para seguros y otra para valores y mercados -El otro bloque sern los supervisores nacionales Esta estructura dual tiene por objeto combinar el conocimiento diario y detallado que cada supervisor nacional tiene de sus mercados y entidades, con una visi europea e independiente de las nuevas autoridades. Los supervisores nacionales son los que ms cercanos se encuentran a los mercados e instituciones de sus pases. Por ello, son los que mejor pueden realizar la supervisi da a da de sus entidades nacionales y seguirn hacindolo. No obstante, las tres nuevas autoridades independientes (ESAs) tendrn poderes efectivos para tomar algunas decisiones por encima de los criterios de los supervisores nacionales. Por ejemplo, hasta ahora, las guas de los comits europeos eran de voluntario cumplimiento para los supervisores nacionales. Con esta reforma, las nuevas autoridades podrn elaborar normas tcnicas sobre co realizar las inspecciones, que los supervisores nacionales tendremos que cumplir. Estas autoridades, asimismo, dispondrn de bancos de datos que acumularn la informacin financiera individualizada de todas las instituciones europeas y asegurarn una cultura supervisora comn en toda el rea. Otro ejemplo es el poder de mediaci asignado a las nuevas autoridades para aquellos casos en que existan desacuerdos entre supervisores de distintos pases. Aunque tengo que sealar que, por lo menos hasta ahora y en el sector bancario, los supervisores europeos hemos llegado a acuerdos sin necesidad de arbitraje externo. Y lo mismo se puede decir, en el caso de Espaa, de las relaciones con supervisores de terceros pases, especialmente, en nuestro caso, con nuestros homlogos de Amrica con los que hemos mantenido magnficas relaciones y hemos conseguido amplios acuerdos voluntarios. Cabe selar, por timo, que en esta red dual, adems de los supervisores nacionales y de las nuevas autoridades europeas, tambin tendrn un papel destacado los colegios de supervisores uno para cada banco supranacional, con la participaci limitada a los supervisores de los pases donde la entidad est implantada que permitirn reforzar el intercambio de informacin y la confianza mutua entre los inspectores de los distintos pases. Como pueden apreciar, las nuevas propuestas no son simplemente un cambio de organizaci, sino que implican reformas de importante calado. Vnculo macro-micro prudencial Aunque los dos pilares que les acabo de describir sean suficientemente sidos, no podremos lograr una supervisi potente en la Unin si los vnculos entre ambos niveles no funcionan correctamente. Aunque la relaci existente entre ambos pilares puede parecer obvia -y es fcil ver que uno complementa al otro-, no les sorprender si les digo que su implantaci no va a ser sencilla. Entre otros factores, pesa la dificultad de precisar el modo concreto de operar del Consejo de Riesgo Sistmico que, como ya he indicado, constituye una novedad en la nueva estructura. Para que una supervisin de este tipo sea efectiva, tiene que ser capaz de elaborar un diagntico preciso de las debilidades y riesgos del sistema; ha de poder emitir recomendaciones utilizando dicho diagnstico, y tiene que establecer un mecanismo que asegure que se atienden dichas recomendaciones. Por todo ello, el supervisor macroprudencial debe estar dotado de instrumentos suficientes y ha de contar con el apoyo del supervisor microprudencial. En efecto, para efectuar el diagntico, el Consejo deber disponer de toda la informacin relevante de los mercados y de las instituciones financieras europeas. En este armazn, las nuevas autoridades microprudenciales sern las encargadas de centralizar los estados financieros detallados de los distintos bancos y compaas de seguros que manejan los supervisores nacionales y transmitirlos de manera agregada al Consejo de Riesgo Sistmico. El Consejo habr de contar con el apoyo de los supervisores de las entidades para interpretar adecuadamente la informacin recopilada y calibrar los riesgos detectados. Y, adems, las tres autoridades microprudenciales participarn en los ganos de gobierno del Consejo. Estas interrelaciones tambin se articulan en direcci inversa. As, no puede concebirse la supervisi microprudencial de las entidades (esto es, la de toda la vida, si se me permite la expresi) como una supervisi en la que no se tengan en cuenta las debilidades y riesgos globales detectados por el Consejo de Riesgo Sistmico. Cabe selar otro aspecto que he mencionado hace un momento y que es, a mi juicio, a ms relevante. Se trata de la necesidad de que se establezcan mecanismos efectivos que aseguren que las recomendaciones del supervisor macroprudencial se materializan en acciones y actuaciones concretas por parte de los distintos supervisores nacionales de las entidades y por parte de las tres nuevas autoridades microprudenciales. Debemos ser conscientes de que, aunque logremos identificar y ordenar adecuadamente los riesgos futuros a los que se enfrentan los sistemas financieros, si no existen mecanismos de presin e incentivos para actuar en consecuencia, todos nuestros esfuerzos sern papel mojado. Esta es precisamente una de las principales conclusiones del informe Larosire. Primos pasos en la implantaci de la reforma Para finalizar mi intervencin, querra selar brevemente co va a ponerse en prctica esta reforma y en qu punto nos encontramos. Como he dicho al comienzo, hoy es un da clave para la supervisin europea. El Consejo de Jefes de Estado y de Gobierno debe decidir si da luz verde a estas nuevas propuestas. El objetivo es que el nuevo marco de supervisin europea pueda comenzar a funcionar en el a 2010. Como podrn imaginarse, esto va a ser un gran reto para todos los que estamos involucrados en el proyecto. Las propuestas que estn encima de la mesa son factibles, aunque todava existen numerosos detalles por concretar. No suponen un cambio brusco, y son la evoluci natural de un sistema cuyas debilidades ha puesto de manifiesto la actual crisis. Adems, existe un amplio consenso entre los Estados miembros y se registra un momento poltico propicio para su implantacin. En este sentido, las palabras del Presidente de la Comisin Europea, Jos Manuel Barroso, captan la importancia del momento: Tiene que ser ahora o nunca. Si no podemos reformar el sector financiero y la supervisi financiera cuando tenemos una autntica crisis, cundo lo reformaremos?. Sin embargo, me gustara sealar algunos riesgos potenciales que, si se materializaran, supondran el fracaso de los avances conseguidos. Tres son, a mi entender, los ms relevantes. El primero tiene que ver con el dise de las nuevas estructuras. En los timos as ha existido, en Europa y a nivel global, una clara tendencia a crear estructuras complejas y mtiples para discutir temas relacionados con la regulaci y la supervisin financiera. Una organizacin excesivamente complicada, integrada por demasiados foros y grupos, en la que no queden claramente definidas las responsabilidades, o en la que stas se solapen con las de otros organismos existentes, pondra en peligro la efectividad de la reforma. Por tanto, debe haber lneas claras de responsabilidad. En segundo lugar, aunque se desarrollen estructuras adecuadas y con responsabilidades definidas, si no se les dota de los recursos necesarios, no ser posible alcanzar las metas deseadas. Una de las debilidades de los actuales comits supervisores ha sido la falta de poderes y recursos para cumplir eficazmente sus funciones. En tercer lugar, la urgencia y oportunidad del momento no deben hacernos tomar decisiones precipitadas. Es importante que la implantacin de la reforma se haga de manera ordenada. En cualquier caso, la instrumentaci de estas nuevas propuestas no es el fin del proceso. Y probablemente no sern suficientes para solucionar todos los retos futuros a los que los supervisores nos tendremos que enfrentar. Lo que s es seguro es que es un paso en la direccin correcta. El debate contin y la reforma que todos esperamos que hoy se apruebe se revisar dentro de tres aos. El tiempo nos dir si supimos afrontar adecuadamente el reto al que tenemos ante nosotros. Muchas gracias.

Title: Appearance before the Economy and Finance Committee of Congress
text: Madrid, 23 June 2009 Appearance of the Governor of the Bank of Spain before the Committee of Economy and Finance of the Congress Miguel Fernandez Ordez Governor Seoriah: The evolution of the Spanish economy referred to in the Annual Report of the Bank of Spain that motivates this appearance is framed, as you know, in the context of a financial and economic crisis of global scope and unprecedented for many decades. The origin of the crisis d0 which dates back to the summer of 2007 d0 was eminently financial and the globalization of financial activity led to its rapid spread. The activity of the international financial markets suffered, reaching its practical paralysis in some of them. The degree of financial stress peaked in October 2008 and, although it has declined in recent months, it still remains at relatively high levels. The severity of the financial shocks leads to a deep real crisis, which affects the world economy with unprecedented intensity and simultaneity, placing most developed countries in a recessionary situation at the end of 2008. From the fourth quarter of 2008 onwards, contractions were observed both in activity in many countries and in world trade, which sharpened in the first quarter of this year. However, in that period it may have already reached the minimum in the decline in activity, since the most recent indicators show that, although output is likely to continue to fall, it will do so at a more contained pace, which seems to remove the risk of a recessionary spiral in the world economy. The dimension that this crisis has reached and the multiplicity of its ramifications raise the need to react on various fronts to prevent its recurrence. It is clear that the financial crisis has exposed many gaps in financial regulation that need to be addressed promptly. It is also necessary to analyse why structural weaknesses in economies and financial systems were not detected or corrected in time, allowing the spread of knock-on effects of considerable magnitude. With the advantage of now looking back, it seems clear that the economic policies adopted in recent years were, in general, too permissive during this period of high growth with respect to the imbalances generated by the growing indebtedness. It is therefore essential that policymakers critically examine the institutional and regulatory frameworks of their economies and financial systems and diffuse them. mechanisms to strengthen them, so that the recurrence of a crisis such as the current one can be prevented. This review should cover a number of key areas. I will leave for later those referring to financial regulation and supervision policies, to focus now on the need to reflect on the role of macroeconomic policies, which will ensure their role in the management of the crisis and analyze their most appropriate design to correct imbalances such as those observed in recent years. In fiscal policy, a stronger stabilising role has been lacking in high-growth years, which would have balanced the momentum of private spending and helped keep public finances on a more sustainable path over the medium and long term. With regard to monetary policy, the role of central banks in stability strategies should be deepened. Many of the measures adopted in recent months by the economic and monetary authorities were based on common principles jointly agreed in the framework of various international forums. In the case of the European Central Bank, unprecedented expansionary measures have been put in place, aimed at alleviating the contractionary tendencies that have been perceived both at the real and financial levels. The liquidity provision became more flexible since the summer of 2007, although it was from October 2008 when the changes were more substantial, as the liquidity requests of the entities began to be satisfied in their entirety and the set of financial assets admitted as collateral for these operations was expanded. Since the summer of 2008, the official intervention rate has been reduced by 325 basis points to a record low of 1% after last May's meeting. In the field of exceptional measures, it should be mentioned, among others, the extension of the terms to which liquidity is injected, which now covers up to twelve months, and the recent decision to acquire mortgage bonds firmly. Governments have also taken numerous measures to address the financial crisis, which can be grouped into two broad blocks: those aimed at supporting financial systems and those aimed at boosting spending. In the first group, it has acted with a wide range of instruments, ranging from the extension of bank guarantees, to the granting of state guarantees to bank issues, injections of public capital in some entities and the purchase of problematic assets that were in the portfolios of banks. Among the measures to stimulate demand, we should highlight both the action of automatic fiscal stabilizers, which are very relevant in European economies, and specific measures aimed at supporting through increases in public spending or tax reductions for groups or sectors most affected by the crisis. The measures taken by the Spanish authorities generally follow the same approach. Thus, in our country the guarantee of the depitos is extended; a Fund for the Acquisition of Financial Assets is created to purchase high-quality assets from Spanish entities; guarantees are being granted for the issuance of bank bonds; the opening of various lines of special financing through the ICO was approved; new deductions were introduced in the IRPF and the so-called Local Investment State Fund and the Special State Fund for the revitalization of the economy were launched. More recently, new measures to boost demand have been announced (such as aid for the acquisition of automiles), while the details for the establishment of a Bank Restructuring and Management Fund (FROB) are being finalized to serve as a tool for the remodeling of our financial system. Let me now turn my attention to the state of the Spanish economy. The international crisis came at a particularly delicate time for Spain, as the economy was already entering a process of adjustment of some imbalances that had accumulated during the long period of high growth that took place since the mid-nineties. Some imbalances that had some points in common with those detected globally, but also showed specific features. As in other countries, the dynamism of private sector spending in Spain will establish a rapid increase in the indebtedness of households and companies, encouraged by the low levels of debt from which it was based and by favorable financial conditions, propitiated by a tone of monetary policy that during that period was too lax for the conditions of our economy. Financial slack also facilitates an excessive concentration of economic and financial resources in the real estate sector, which should add severity to the adjustment phase. Fiscal policy, for its part, faces a significant consolidation process, but its contribution to the moderation of domestic demand was not sufficient to offset the effects of monetary laxity. As you well know, the Spanish economy experienced a very severe adjustment in the second half of 2008: GDP showed negative quarter-on-quarter growth from the third quarter, which became more intense until the first quarter of 2009, in which activity fell by 1.9% compared to the previous quarter, which adds to the decline of 1% observed in the last three months of last year. This contraction resulted in a year-on-year fall in GDP of 3% in the first quarter of 2009. The short-term data for the second quarter are still inconclusive, but suggest, in any case, that the rate of contraction in activity is less pronounced than in the previous quarter. In the Spanish recession, the strong impact of the international financial crisis came to overlap the real estate adjustment, which had already begun to unfold its effects before. The magnitude of the resulting disruption has been substantial and has profoundly affected agent confidence and depressed spending decisions and employment behaviour. Throughout 2008, the sharp decline in household spending stood out, both in consumption and in residential investment. But the deepening of the financial crisis since the summer and the deterioration of macroeconomic expectations caused other items to be affected as well, such as business investment. This sharp fall in domestic demand resulted in a substantial decline in imports, so that the contribution of net foreign demand to GDP better cushioned the decline in activity. The contraction in private spending allowed some of the imbalances accumulated in previous years to begin to adjust. The financing capacity of households has increased, with a notable increase in the savings rate, and the need for financing of companies has been reduced, all reflected in a decrease in the financing needs of the nation, which has been gradually becoming more intense in recent quarters. The weakening of activity was gradually transferred to all branches of production, with declines in employment, initially in construction, which later affected industry and, finally, services. In this way, there was a generalized process of job destruction, which reached great intensity in the final months of 2008 and in the first months of 2009, and a very substantial increase in the unemployment rate, up to 17.4% in the first quarter of this year. While the extent of the recession in Spain, in terms of GDP growth, is even lower than that afflicting other European countries, the sharp increase in the unemployment rate is a particularly damaging feature of our evolution and reveals one of the fundamental weaknesses of our institutional framework that needs to be corrected. One of the problems in the functioning of the labour market is related to the low sensitivity of labour costs to the particular conditions of each firm or to cyclical developments. In particular, labour costs showed high increases in 2008, reflecting the deterioration caused by the sharp rise in oil prices in the inflationary situation in the first part of the year. Although it seems that the pressure on wage costs has begun to subside in 2009, its evolution is insufficient in relation to the trajectory of inflation and the recession that the economy is experiencing, so that the resulting real wage growth will not be conducive to job creation. In recent months it has been observed that the current recession, which is intensely affecting household consumption, is also causing downward revisions in prices and margins. Thus, in May the year-on-year rate of the CPI stood at -0.9%, the lowest level since the middle of the last century, nine tenths below the inflation rate in the euro area. Although these year-on-year rates are expected to return to positive values at the end of the year, once the statistical effect linked to higher oil prices in the initial months of 2008 disappears, the fact that in May there were year-on-year declines in the prices of food and industrial goods is still remarkable. Also in services, which constitute the traditionally most inflationary component of the Spanish economy, there is a gradual moderation. This price behaviour is in line with the appropriate way to improve the competitiveness of the economy, reduce the costs of the recession and initiate a recovery. The outlook for the Spanish economy suggests that GDP could continue to contract in the remainder of the year, so that in 2009 as a whole its fall will be very substantial, although probably lower than that shown by other European countries, more affected by the collapse of world trade in recent months. Although GDP could continue to fall in 2010 on an annual average, it would do so at a less pronounced rate, since the wide range of measures implemented should gradually moderate the intensity of the restrictive impulses on activity. However, given the intensity of the adjustments to employment, the unemployment rate may still continue to rise. It is true that some imbalances accumulated during the expansion are being corrected. As I have just mentioned, the inflation differential vis-88-vis the euro area is now favourable to Spain, while the external deficit is narrowing sharply, and it is expected to continue on this trajectory, so that its ratio to GDP will fall in 2010 to less than half of what it was in 2007. Although we should deepen the reabsorption of these imbalances, it is undeniable that the improvements obtained are linked to a very sharp contraction in demand, with very negative effects on the unemployment rate and the productive fabric. Therefore, it is essential to review some elements of our institutional framework to prevent these losses of employment and productive capacity from becoming entrenched and hindering the recovery, as well as to prevent the reappearance of imbalances similar to those detected in recent years when demand begins to grow again. In the recovery of the Spanish economy, as in the case of the world economy, the contribution of the exceptional measures adopted both in the field of demand policies d0 monetary and fiscal d0 and in support of the financial system will be very relevant. But, in Spain, with national demand very affected by the need to clean up the equity position of the private sector and the impact of the high unemployment rate, it will be essential to have the recovery of external demand as the main support to boost spending. Taking advantage of the improvement in external demand when it occurs will require companies to be able to offer competitive products and for this they will have to increase their productivity and adjust their costs, margins and prices flexibly. Substantial declines in key central bank rates around the world over the last year have led to a significant decline in the cost of financing. In Spain, its expansionary stimulus is particularly powerful as a result of the predominance of variable-rate financing. This boost will be especially relevant in some sectors, such as residential construction, where the combination of lower interest rates and price adjustments will make it more accessible for families to buy a home. As in other countries, fiscal policy in Spain has also helped to cushion the decline in activity, through both the operation of automatic stabilisers and the adoption of various discretionary measures. The magnitude of this fiscal effort is being very important and greater than in the countries of our environment. In addition, in the case of Spain, the loss of revenue linked to the weakness of spending has been joined by the disappearance of the extraordinary income that the real estate boom had allowed to obtain in the last decade. For all these reasons, the deterioration in the balance of public administrations has been considerable, going from a surplus of more than 2% of GDP in 2007 to a deficit that, according to the figures announced by the Government, could be close to 10% of GDP this year. With this evolution, the possibilities for expansionary action of fiscal policy have been exhausted. The fiscal imbalance has reached a level that requires a correction strategy, which must be credible, in order for actors to have confidence in maintaining budgetary stability over the medium term. In this regard, the Government has just announced the budgetary stability objectives for the period 2010-2012, which commit an enormous effort to fiscal consolidation, since they aim to cut the deficit from almost 10% of GDP that could reach in 2009 to 3% in 2012, thus complying with the guidelines established for Spain by the European Council in relation to compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact. The magnitude of the correction envisaged in such a short space of time requires very strict budgetary implementation and vigorous action. The recent increase in some indirect taxes is a first step in this direction, although past experience shows that for fiscal consolidation processes to be successful they must focus on cuts in public spending and, in particular, in unproductive spending. In this sense, the autonomous communities, given their participation in public spending, should actively contribute to the recovery of the path of fiscal consolidation and budgetary stability. In any case, although monetary and fiscal policies have played a very important role in compensating for the tremendous contractionary impulses that economies have suffered, we cannot continue to rely on these supports when the recovery begins. Governments and central banks must prepare the design of "exit strategies" from the current framework of extraordinary fiscal and monetary policy action, in order to prevent future processes of economic instability from germinating. It is therefore imperative that policy efforts focus on reforms that can help improve productivity and the performance of factor and product markets. Unlike in the field of demand-side policies, here the scope for action is wide and, moreover, its potential effects are very significant. In the Spanish case, as I recalled earlier, one of the main problems of our economy lies in the labour market. The current crisis has once again generated a very strong increase in the unemployment rate, which reminds us that the adjustment in this economy occurs mainly through the destruction of jobs. Action is needed to prevent the increase in the number of unemployed from becoming entrenched and their employability from falling rapidly. And also to allow a rapid reallocation of resources between sectors, which facilitates the replacement of real estate activity by other productive branches. The labor reform is unavoidable and should address various areas. In the field of collective bargaining, it seems necessary that working conditions and remuneration be adjusted more flexibly to the economic situation, especially that of specific companies or productive sectors. It is also vital to introduce changes in recruitment systems and an improvement in labour market intermediary systems and in the mobility and training of the unemployed, so that workers who have lost their jobs find new opportunities soon. These reforms would not only improve the medium-term growth prospects of this economy, but would also help to prevent the deterioration of the productive fabric. Obviously, the labour market, while important, is not the only area that should deserve the reforming attention of our authorities. Closely linked to the labour market is the issue of human capital and education, where it must be reiterated that, although the returns are, above all, in the medium term, the implementation of reforms is urgent. Finally, it is essential that Spain equips itself with a much more serious competitive environment, in which our companies can operate more efficiently and on equal terms with companies from other countries. Within this environment, the role of services is fundamental, given their growing overlap with industrial activities. In addition, the lack of liberalization of some segments may be limiting their expansion, which is especially pernicious given that this is a sector that encompasses some of the most dynamic activities and with the greatest capacity to generate employment. In this sense, the initiative recently proposed by the Government to implement the Services Directive through a bill that ree actions in numerous areas, should be applied decisively, for which it is necessary that the Autonomous Communities and Local Corporations collaborate in their areas of responsibility. Also advancing in the promotion of competition in network industries would allow inputs to be supplied to the rest of productive activities in more competitive conditions. To conclude this speech, allow me to briefly review the situation of the Spanish banking system. A differentiating feature of the Spanish situation is that it was able to face this crisis with a relatively strong position from its banks. The business model that these have been following has been the traditional one, focused on the retail segment, so that we have been oblivious to the development of those more sophisticated models that have deeply given to entities in other countries d0 and even to financial systems completely d0 which explains why the weight of Costa Rican assets in the balance sheets of Spanish entities is irrelevant. The Bank of Spain's action also helps to make the starting position of the entities more relaxed in the face of the crisis, by requiring the constitution of countercyclical provisions, which could cushion the pressure in the negative stages, and by defining sufficiently broad consolidation perimeters for the banking groups, which would allow a correct assessment of the risks assumed. These good starting conditions allowed the Spanish financial system to withstand the first wave of the financial crisis and continue to channel the necessary inflow of foreign savings although in different ways, since the paralysis of securitized asset markets requires recourse to alternative sources, such as short-term paper issues and ECB loans. The depitos, on the other hand, also gained relative weight during this first phase of tensions. However, the transformation of the financial crisis into recession has led to a second wave of risks to financial stability, the nature of which is, this time, eminently macroeconomic. Although our financial system faces this second wave with the relative advantage of having been less damaged by the first, there is no doubt that the deterioration of the Spanish economy puts pressure, in different ways, on the income statements of banks and savings banks. In particular, the destruction of employment is worsening the ability of some families to pay, while the decline in activity is being particularly pronounced in the real estate sector, which required abundant financing and had acquired a high relative weight in the balance sheets of some entities. Thus, after a long period of economic expansion, in which NPL ratios reached historically low levels, since 2008 they have been showing significant upswings and it is expected that the pressure has not yet been exhausted.
