En el contexto actual, lo verdaderamente importante es que el grueso de nuestro sistema financiero, esa amplia mayora de entidades bien gestionadas, eficientes y rentables, comprendan que para lograr resultados como los del pasado probablemente sern necesarias nuevas estrategias y un esfuerzo por redimensionar y racionalizar el sector bancario de nuestro pas. En este sentido, ms all de las responsabilidades individuales a las que me he referido, existe tambin una responsabilidad colectiva de todo el sector, que debe contribuir a la resolucin de los problemas existentes minimizando los costes para el conjunto de la sociedad. Del xito en esta tarea depender en gran medida que dentro de unos pocos as nuestro pas siga contando con un sistema financiero sido que pueda seguir apoyando el crecimiento econmico. En definitiva, debemos aspirar a que nuestro sistema bancario salga fortalecido de la complicada situaci econica y financiera en la que el mundo desarrollado est inmerso, con plena capacidad para seguir prestando eficientemente sus servicios a la comunidad y a la economa. Pero el futuro primo no est exento de riesgos. Por eso es imprescindible que todos, entidades y autoridades, afrontemos el desafo de los primos meses aunando esfuerzos, desarrollando nuestras responsabilidades con diligencia, aceptando los sacrificios que sean necesarios. En estos momentos en los que los niveles de incertidumbre siguen siendo muy altos, alguien ha recordado lo que dijo Cervantes y que parece especialmente oportuno al preguntarnos sobre el futuro de nuestro sistema financiero: no hay ms cierta astrologa que la prudencia. Muchas gracias.

Title: Speech at the Conference "Challenges and Strategies for Promoting Economic Growth", organized by the Bank of Mexico. "Growth, stability and monetary policy"
text: Mexico, 19 October 2009 Growth, stability and monetary policy Sesin sobre d2Price Stability, Financial Development and Economic Growthd3 en la Conferencia d2Challenges and Strategies for Promoting Economic Growthd3/Banco de M8exico Miguel Fernandez Ordez Governor Good afternoon. First of all, I would like to thank the Bank of Mexico for its kind invitation to participate in this Conference, which gives me the opportunity to share with you some reflections on the role of monetary and other economic policies in achieving macroeconomic and financial stability. I will begin my speech by reading you a quote: "Deep economic depressions are no longer a problem. Globalization, financial innovation and more efficient economic policies have tempered the breadth of economic cycles that we will soon consider history." Do not try to guess the author, although many of you already have more than one candidate in mind, because it is a collective quote, built with different statements from various economists. Just two years ago, the visi of that meeting was shared mostly both among economic authorities and in academic circles. And the dissonant voices, those who warned of the risks hidden behind the growing accumulation of so-called global imbalances, the evolution of private indebtedness or the minimum levels reached by risk premiums in all markets, were minority voices. We lived then in a world characterized by high and stable growth rates and moderate and low volatile inflation rates. This bonanza had a global character, since both the most developed and emerging economies enjoyed it. This idyllic situation was thought to be the result not only of globalisation, but also of appropriate economic policies. These included monetary policies firmly geared towards achieving price stability in the medium term, and implemented by independent central banks, and financial regulation policies - the so-called "light hand regulation" - which had directed their efforts towards promoting self-regulatory mechanisms in the markets themselves, favouring, among other things, significant progress in the field of risk diversification. And, sbitably, we went from that almost paradise to experiencing the most serious financial and real crisis since World War II. More time must pass to fully understand the process that explains this abrupt turn in the economy, but some of the main issues of debate are already quite well defined. Prominent among these is the role played in recent years by excessive reliance on the so-called principle of efficiency in financial markets. In the heat of this vision, important processes of financial innovation were generated that, although they had positive effects for the well-being of citizens, were also accompanied, unfortunately, by other more spurious, materialized in instruments of increasing complexity and decreasing added value. Products, moreover, whose complicated ramifications interconnected the fate of multiple markets to unknown limits. On the other hand, the mistake was made of believing that all financial products had liquid markets. The course of the crisis left no market references to many new financial products, especially the most complex ones, and has shown that the importance of liquidity risk had been underestimated. In this context, the regulatory and prudential supervisory policies of most countries lacked the necessary tools to detect these processes and even to be able to react to them with the required speed and intensity. But the debate on the role of economic policies is not being confined to regulatory and supervisory policies. The performance of other policies, such as monetary, is also subject to scrutiny. As a matter of principle, I have no doubt that price stability must remain the primary objective of monetary policy. Stable prices stimulate growth and thus employment, while helping to reduce fluctuations in output, thereby raising the welfare of agents who are, by nature, averse to the variability of their incomes. Furthermore, I do not think anyone disputes that price stability, being a fundamental component of macroeconomic stability, also contributes to a greater degree of financial stability. Precisely, we are in a country, Mexico, and in a region, Latin America, where the contribution of monetary policy to the development and consolidation of the financial system has been evident in the last decade. The economic policy factors behind this development have been diverse, but they stem from price stability. The reduction of inflation through pragmatically implemented inflation targeting regimes has catalyzed a strong impetus to the development of capital and banking markets in recent years in Latin America. Thus, lower inflation has made it possible to reduce the tendency to borrow in foreign currency and abroad, and has led to a change in the financing model, more oriented to domestic markets and in local currency; Greater price stability d0 and good supervisory practices d0 have also favoured an accelerated process of banking in most countries, where intense credit growth has kept pace with the expansion of the slowdown. As a result, Latin America has swum against the tide in the years prior to the crisis: while in the world the domestic bias of investors was reduced, in Latin America it increased. The development of domestic markets, financing through banks with a retail vocation and adequately capitalized and macroeconomic stability allow us to explain to a large extent the resistance to the crisis d0 unthinkable a few years ago d0 that the region's financial systems have shown. However, returning to a more general geographical context, the current crisis is proving to be a painful reminder of two realities whose implications, at the time, were perhaps not fully assessed. The first is that although price stability is a necessary condition for financial stability, it is by no means a sufficient condition. Second, episodes of financial instability can entail significant risks to price stability. It is not surprising, therefore, that one of the first open debates on the role of monetary policy took place between proponents and opponents of extending the mandate of central banks to explicitly include the achievement of financial stability among their objectives. It is not clear that this enlargement is currently the best alternative. It is true that in recent years there has been considerable convincing empirical evidence that the level of interest rates influences investors' attitudes to risk. What is not obvious is that interest rates are the most ideal instrument for achieving financial stability, since perhaps the same objective could be achieved at a lower cost if it is pursued, for example, through prudential regulatory and supervisory policies. The crisis, in any case, has intensified the debate on the role to be assigned to financial stability issues in the design and exercise of monetary policy, regardless of whether it is primarily aimed at maintaining price stability. As everyone will remember, before the summer of 2007 the thesis of those who argued that, in this area, central banks should limit themselves to cushioning the effects on the economy of episodes of instability once they materialized had prevailed. Without going into the details, the fundamental arguments on which this position was based can be summarized in the difficulties in identifying a financial crisis ex-ante and even, once anticipated, the problems in gauging the timing and magnitude of the response. The very success of controlling inflation and economic stability during this period contributed to the perception that monetary policy was successfully fulfilling its mission and that no change was necessary. Recent events, however, give air to those who doubt that monetary policy should continue to act asymmetrically in the future in the face of such imbalances: ignoring them while they accumulate, but reacting strongly when the critical point at which they explode is reached. On the one hand, because the data can be too large and too difficult to absorb. Suffice it to say that at the moment there are many central banks that have been forced to resort to the implementation of extraordinary measures in view of the inadequacy of ordinary instruments. On the other, because, as Bill White recently asked, perhaps "the reaction to successive sets of difficulties lays the foundation for the next and, what is worse (...) detract from the credibility of available instruments." Defining and articulating policies to prevent the growth of financial imbalances is certainly a difficult task, but the general perception of our ability to anticipate such events may be beginning to change. Some economists have warned that the fact that crises tend to be decades apart creates the false illusion that "this time is different." However, it is also possible to identify certain common patterns that can be very useful in the detection and eventual prevention of the next one. But exploiting these patterns to cement a more symmetrical monetary policy attitude to financial stability requires reconsidering some of the factors that have inspired the monetary policy practice of some central banks. Thus, for example, the BIS economists, who have probably been the most active on this front, have argued for the need to make progress in three areas: first, to increase the attention paid by central banks to the evolution of credit and the prices of some assets in their analyses; secondly, to set the time horizon for the objective of price stability in longer maturities than the two typical years of inflation targeting regimes; Finally, pay greater attention to the balance of risks in the decision-making process. The challenge of incorporating the lessons and new sensitivity that stems from what happened during the crisis is not the same for all central banks. In the case of the Eurosystem, for example, the coexistence of an economic and a monetary analysis should facilitate the shift to pay more attention to variables such as credit developments, indebtedness or asset prices. Similarly, the absence of inflation targets with an explicit time horizon creates a relatively favourable framework for a renewed monetary policy. However, neither the Eurosystem nor any other central bank has macroeconomic models with a sufficiently large and rich financial portfolio, meaning one in which the main financial variables play a role that is not merely residual. This is an aspect in which it would be convenient to advance but, given its complexity, we should avoid that the absence of models paralyzes our thinking. In the meantime, we can and must continue to reflect on the role of economic policies in avoiding serious financial imbalances. The design of monetary policy should make it possible to pay greater attention to financial stability risks, without jeopardising the effectiveness and credibility achieved in meeting an objective in which it has so far achieved remarkable success: the achievement of price stability. And in any case, the framework of independence of central banks remains a fundamental requirement to perform the entrusted functions with an adequate medium and long-term perspective, which allows consistent behavior over time. In fact, the requirement of independence will be more necessary in the new context in which the responsibilities of central banks are being extended and in which the weakness of economic growth on a global scale can generate tensions between the demands of expansion in the short term and the goals of macroeconomic and financial stability in the medium term. In parallel with the changes in the monetary sphere, it is essential to deepen the articulation of a financial stability strategy based primarily on prudential regulation and supervision policies aimed at preventing the emergence and growth of imbalances in the financial markets. The crisis has taught us that this strategy should not be conceived in isolation, but seeking the greatest possible coherence with the rest of economic policies, both with domestic policies among themselves and with those adopted by other countries. In forums such as the Financial Stability Board or the G-20, whose prominence has been strengthened, work is being done on developing internationally adopted responses and their agreements cover a wide spectrum of macroeconomic and financial policies. Along the same lines, important developments in the regulatory and supervisory structure are being promoted in Europe, such as the creation of three new supervisory authorities at European level or the creation of the European Systemic Risk Board, which will allow monitoring systemic risks from a supranational perspective, and in which, in addition to central banks, Market, banking and insurance supervisory bodies will participate. These developments suggest that the idea that achieving economic and financial stability requires a more comprehensive response, involving all countries and all spheres of economic policy, is gaining ground. This movement to open dialogue and cooperation between countries and between policies is unstoppable and, in my opinion, positive. Care must be taken to ensure that, in the area of monetary policy, this new stance does not erode the two most valuable assets achieved in recent decades: the maintenance of price stability as a priority objective and the independence of central banks as a necessary instrument. At the same time, however, monetary policy must operate from an open perspective, aware of the importance of its interaction with other macroeconomic and financial policies. The past can give us some clues for future action. Perhaps the most traditional example of interaction is the dialogue between monetary and fiscal policy, which, incidentally, will become more prominent as the economic recovery takes hold and extraordinary demand stimuli begin to withdraw. I mentioned earlier the importance of interaction with prudential regulatory and supervisory policies on which the greatest effort of international consultation has focused, aimed at strengthening the global financial system and preventing future crises. The list of what has been achieved and the work under way in this area is well described in the Pittsburgh communiqu8e and, although well known and extensive, there is no point in reiterating it here. Less developed is macroprudential surveillance policy, both domestically and globally, aimed at identifying and controlling systemic risks beyond the scope of the microprudential approach. In this area we are only beginning to create the institutions to which this mission will be entrusted, but there is still much progress to be made in defining its contents. However, the role of central banks in achieving financial stability objectives has been strengthened, not only in the articulation of monetary policy, but also through a greater role in the field of macroprudential supervision policies specifically aimed at achieving this objective. A good example of this is the weight that has been given to the European Central Bank and the national central banks in the European Systemic Risk Board. This movement can also be seen in the proposals that are appearing in some countries to give their central banks responsibility for microprudential supervision. Finally, if we think about the type of economy that will emerge after the crisis, it seems clear that central banks will not be able to worry exclusively, as until now, about dialogue to achieve adequate wage or fiscal policies for stability or, as the crisis has shown, about establishing the necessary interaction with regulators and supervisors. They must also ensure that the necessary structural measures are taken to improve expectations for growth and job creation. Monetary policy may well have to operate in the future in an economic and financial environment very different from that of the pre-crisis years. Lower leverage, a smaller and less expansive financial sector and a lower generation of innovations must lead, caeteris paribus, to a world that is perhaps more stable, but also of lower growth. And that will have consequences. We should recognize that if the performance of central banks was highly praised in the past, it was on its own merits, but also because it occurred in a context of exceptional and lasting expansion in which also d0 remember d0 the actions of private businessmen and bankers, as well as the economic policies of almost all governments, were highly praised. However, without major changes in structural policies, in this new scenario of low growth and weak employment generation, the most correct monetary policy will be difficult for public opinion to accept, and this could jeopardise the two assets I mentioned earlier. In short, the financial crisis has opened an intense debate about the objectives and adoption of economic policies. This is a positive debate, which should help us avoid repeating mistakes in the future. For this to happen, it is essential that we are able to preserve the elements of the hitherto existing economic model that have proved most valuable, such as the liberalisation and integration of markets, fiscal consolidation or, what interests us today, the maintenance of price stability. At the same time, however, the successful overcoming of the current crisis will also require new responses from the different areas of economic policy, which must also be more coherent with each other than they have been in the past. Living in an ivory tower was never advisable. From now on it will be impossible. Only by being aware that we will have to act in a new environment, we will know how to defend and save the best of what has been achieved so far.
text_original: Mxico, 19 de octubre de 2009 Crecimiento, estabilidad y poltica monetaria Sesin sobre Price Stability, Financial Development and Economic Growth en la Conferencia Challenges and Strategies for Promoting Economic Growth/Banco de Mxico Miguel Fernndez Ordez Gobernador Buenas tardes. En primer lugar, quiero agradecer al Banco de Mxico su amable invitaci para participar en esta Conferencia, que me brinda la oportunidad de compartir con ustedes algunas reflexiones acerca del papel de la poltica monetaria y otras polticas econicas para conseguir la estabilidad macroeconmica y financiera. Comenzar mi intervenci leyndoles una cita: Las depresiones econmicas profundas ya no son un problema. La globalizaci, la innovaci financiera y unas polticas econicas ms eficientes han atemperado la amplitud de unos ciclos econicos que pronto consideraremos historia. No intenten adivinar el autor, aunque muchos de ustedes tendran ya ms de un candidato en mente, porque es una cita colectiva, construida con distintas declaraciones de varios economistas. Hace apenas dos aos, la visi de esa cita era compartida mayoritariamente tanto entre las autoridades econmicas como en los crculos acadmicos. Y las voces disonantes, las que alertaban de los riesgos que se escondan tras la creciente acumulaci de los llamados desequilibrios globales, la evoluci del endeudamiento privado o los niveles mnimos alcanzados por las primas de riesgo en todos los mercados, eran voces minoritarias. Vivamos entonces en un mundo caracterizado por tasas de crecimiento elevadas y estables y por tasas de inflaci moderadas y poco voltiles. Esta bonanza tena un carcter global, pues tanto las economas ms desarrolladas como las emergentes disfrutaron de ella. Se pensaba que esta situaci idlica era el resultado no so de la globalizaci, sino tambin de unas polticas econmicas adecuadas. Entre ellas, unas polticas monetarias firmemente orientadas al logro de la estabilidad de precios en el medio plazo, e instrumentadas por bancos centrales independientes, y unas polticas de regulaci financiera -la denominada light hand regulation-que haban dirigido sus esfuerzos hacia el fomento de mecanismos de autorregulaci de los propios mercados, favoreciendo, entre otras cosas, importantes avances en el terreno de la diversificaci de los riesgos. Y, sbitamente, pasamos de ese casi paraso a experimentar la crisis financiera y real ms grave desde la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Debe pasar ms tiempo para comprender bien el proceso que explica este abrupto giro de la economa, pero alguna de las principales cuestiones de debate estn ya bastante bien perfiladas. Entre ellas, ocupa un lugar destacado el papel que ha desempeado en los ltimos aos una confianza excesiva en el llamado principio de eficiencia de los mercados financieros. Al calor de esta visi, se generaron importantes procesos de innovaci financiera que, aunque tuvieron efectos positivos para el bienestar de los ciudadanos, vinieron tambin acompaados, lamentablemente, de otros ms espurios, materializados en instrumentos de creciente complejidad y de decreciente valor aadido. Productos, adems, cuyas complicadas ramificaciones interconectaban entre s hasta lmites desconocidos la suerte de mltiples mercados. Por otra parte, se cometiel error de creer que todos los productos financieros contaban con mercados lquidos. El transcurso de la crisis dejsin referencias de mercado a buena parte de los nuevos productos financieros, en especial los ms complejos, y ha demostrado que se haba infravalorado la importancia del riesgo de liquidez. En este contexto, las polticas de regulaci y de supervisi prudencial de la mayora de los pases carecan de los instrumentos necesarios para detectar estos procesos e, incluso, para poder reaccionar ante ellos con la rapidez y la intensidad requeridas. Pero el debate sobre el papel de las polticas econicas no se est circunscribiendo a las polticas de regulaci y supervisi. La actuaci de otras polticas, como la monetaria, est igualmente sujeta a escrutinio. Vaya por delante que no me cabe ninguna duda de que la estabilidad de precios debe seguir siendo objetivo primordial de la poltica monetaria. Unos precios estables estimulan el crecimiento y, por tanto, el empleo, al tiempo que contribuyen a reducir las fluctuaciones del producto, elevando de este modo el bienestar de los agentes que son, por naturaleza, aversos a la variabilidad de sus rentas. Asimismo, no creo que nadie cuestione que la estabilidad de precios, al ser un componente fundamental de la estabilidad macroeconmica, contribuye tambin a propiciar un mayor grado de estabilidad financiera. Precisamente, nos encontramos en un pas, Mxico, y en una regi, Amrica Latina, donde la contribuci de la poltica monetaria al desarrollo y consolidaci del sistema financiero ha sido evidente en la ltima dcada. Los factores de poltica econica detrs de este desarrollo han sido diversos, pero tienen como origen la estabilidad de precios. La reducci de la inflaci a travs de regmenes de objetivos de inflaci -inflation targeting-, instrumentados de un modo pragmtico, ha catalizado un fuerte impulso al desarrollo de los mercados de capitales y bancarios en los ltimos aos en Amrica Latina. As, la menor inflaci ha permitido reducir la propensin a endeudarse en moneda extranjera y en el exterior, y han propiciado un cambio en el modelo de financiaci, ms orientado a los mercados domsticos y en moneda local; la mayor estabilidad de precios y unas buenas prcticas supervisoras-tambin ha favorecido un acelerado proceso de bancarizaci en la mayora de los pases, en los que el intenso crecimiento del crdito ha ido acompasado a la expansi de los depitos. Como consecuencia de todo ello, Amrica Latina ha nadado a contracorriente en los aos previos a la crisis: mientras en el mundo se reduca el sesgo domstico -home bias-de los inversores, en Amrica Latina se incrementaba. El desarrollo de los mercados domsticos, la financiaci a travs de bancos con vocaci minorista y adecuadamente capitalizados y la estabilidad macroeconica permiten explicar en buena medida la resistencia a la crisis impensable hace unos aos-que han mostrado los sistemas financieros de la regi. No obstante, volviendo a un contexto geogrfico ms general, la crisis actual est resultando un doloroso recordatorio de dos realidades cuyas implicaciones, en su momento, quizs no se valoraron en su justa medida. La primera es que aunque la estabilidad de precios es una condici necesaria para la estabilidad financiera, no es en absoluto una condici suficiente. La segunda, que los episodios de inestabilidad financiera pueden conllevar importantes riesgos para la estabilidad de precios. No es de extrar, por tanto, que uno de los primeros debates abiertos en torno al papel de la poltica monetaria haya tenido lugar entre los defensores y los detractores de ampliar el mandato de los bancos centrales para incluir explcitamente entre sus objetivos el logro de la estabilidad financiera. No est claro que esta ampliaci sea, hoy por hoy, la mejor alternativa. Es cierto que en estos ltimos aos se han acumulado pruebas empricas bastante convincentes de que el nivel de los tipos de inters influye sobre la actitud de los inversores ante al riesgo. Lo que no es obvio es que los tipos de inters sean el instrumento ms ideo para lograr la estabilidad financiera, en la medida que quizs el mismo objetivo se podra alcanzar con un coste menor si se persigue, por ejemplo, mediante polticas de regulaci y supervisi prudencial. La crisis, en todo caso, ha intensificado el debate sobre el papel que debe asignarse a los temas de estabilidad financiera en el diseo y el ejercicio de la poltica monetaria, independientemente de que sta se oriente primordialmente al mantenimiento de la estabilidad de precios. Como todos recordarn, antes del verano de 2007 se haban impuesto las tesis de quienes defendan que, en este terreno, los bancos centrales deban limitarse a amortiguar los efectos sobre la economa de los episodios de inestabilidad una vez se materializaban. Sin entrar en los detalles, los argumentos fundamentales en los que se sustentaba esta posici pueden resumirse en las dificultades para identificar ex-ante una crisis financiera e incluso, una vez anticipada, los problemas para calibrar el momento y la magnitud de la respuesta. El propio xito en el control de la inflaci y la estabilidad econica de este perodo contribuyeron a la percepci de que la poltica monetaria estaba cumpliendo satisfactoriamente su misi y que no era necesario plantearse cambios. Los sucesos recientes, sin embargo, dan aire a quienes dudan de que la poltica monetaria deba seguir actuando en el futuro de manera asimtrica ante este tipo de desequilibrios: ignorndolos mientras se acumulan, pero reaccionando fuertemente cuando se alcanza el punto crtico en el que estallan. Por un lado, porque los daos pueden ser demasiado grandes y demasiado difciles de absorber. Baste sealar que en estos momentos son muchos los bancos centrales que se han visto obligados a acudir a la instrumentaci de medidas de carcter extraordinario ante la insuficiencia de los instrumentos ordinarios. Por otro, porque, como recientemente se preguntaba Bill White, quiz la reacci ante los sucesivos conjuntos de dificultades siente las bases para el siguiente y, lo que es peor () reste credibilidad a los instrumentos disponibles. Definir y articular polticas para evitar el crecimiento de desequilibrios financieros es sin duda una tarea difcil, pero la percepci general sobre nuestra capacidad para anticiparnos a este tipo de eventos podra estar comenzando a cambiar. Algunos economistas han advertido que el hecho de que las crisis tiendan a estar separadas por dcadas crea la falsa ilusin de que esta vez es diferente. Sin embargo, es posible tambin identificar determinados patrones comunes que pueden resultar de gran utilidad en la detecci y eventual prevenci del siguiente. Pero explotar estos patrones para cimentar una actitud ms simtrica de la poltica monetaria respecto a la estabilidad financiera requiere reconsiderar algunos de los factores que han inspirado la prctica de poltica monetaria de algunos bancos centrales. As, por ejemplo, los economistas del BIS, que son probablemente quienes se han mostrado ms activos en este frente, han defendido la necesidad de avanzar en tres reas: en primer lugar, incrementar la atenci que prestan los bancos centrales a la evoluci del crdito y de los precios de algunos activos en sus anlisis; en segundo lugar, fijar el horizonte temporal para el objetivo de la estabilidad de precios en plazos ms largos que los dos aos tpicos de los regmenes de inflation targeting; por ltimo, prestar mayor atenci al balance de riesgos en el proceso de toma de decisiones. El reto que supone incorporar las lecciones y la nueva sensibilidad que se deriva de lo sucedido durante la crisis no es igual para todos los bancos centrales. En el caso del Eurosistema, por ejemplo, la coexistencia de un anlisis econico y otro monetario debera facilitar el giro a prestar ms atenci a variables como la evoluci del crdito, el endeudamiento o los precios de los activos. Igualmente, la ausencia de los objetivos de inflaci con un horizonte temporal explcito configura un marco relativamente propicio para una renovada poltica monetaria. No obstante, ni el Eurosistema ni ningn otro banco central cuenta con modelos macroeconicos con un mdulo financiero suficientemente sido y rico, entendiendo por tal uno en el que las principales variables financieras desempeen un papel que no sea meramente residual. Este es un aspecto en el que convendra avanzar pero, dada su complejidad, habra que evitar que la ausencia de modelos nos paralice el pensamiento. Mientras tanto, podemos y debemos seguir reflexionando sobre el papel de las polticas econicas para evitar serios desequilibrios financieros. El diseo de la poltica monetaria debera permitir prestar una mayor atenci a los riesgos sobre la estabilidad financiera, sin poner en peligro la efectividad y la credibilidad alcanzadas en el cumplimiento de un objetivo en el que hasta ahora ha cosechado un notable xito: la consecuci de la estabilidad de precios. Y en todo caso, el marco de independencia de los bancos centrales sigue siendo un requisito fundamental para desempear las funciones encomendadas con una perspectiva adecuada de medio y largo plazo, que permita una conducta consistente a lo largo del tiempo. De hecho, el requisito de la independencia va a ser ms necesario en el nuevo contexto en el que las responsabilidades de los bancos centrales se estn viendo ampliadas y en el que la debilidad del crecimiento econmico a escala global puede generar tensiones entre las exigencias de expansi en el corto plazo y las metas de estabilidad macroeconmica y financiera en el medio plazo. En paralelo a los cambios en el plano monetario, es imprescindible profundizar en la articulaci de una estrategia de estabilidad financiera que se base primordialmente en unas polticas de regulaci y supervisi prudencial orientadas a evitar la aparici y el crecimiento de desequilibrios en los mercados financieros. La crisis nos ha enseado que esta estrategia no debe concebirse de manera aislada, sino buscando la mayor coherencia posible con el resto de polticas econmicas, tanto con las domesticas entre s como con las adoptadas por otros pases. En foros como el Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera o el G-20, cuyo protagonismo se ha visto reforzado, se est trabajando en la elaboraci de respuestas adoptadas internacionalmente y sus acuerdos abarcan un amplio espectro de polticas macroeconmicas y financieras. En esta misma lnea, en Europa se estn impulsando importantes novedades en la estructura de regulaci y supervisi, como la creaci de tres nuevas autoridades supervisoras a nivel europeo o la creaci del European Systemic Risk Board, que permitir vigilar los riesgos sistmicos desde una perspectiva supranacional, y en el que, adems de los bancos centrales, participarn los organismos supervisores de mercados, banca y seguros. Estos desarrollos parecen indicar que est ganando terreno la idea de que la consecuci de la estabilidad econica y financiera exige una respuesta ms global, en la que deben implicarse todos los pases y todas las esferas de la poltica econmica. Este movimiento de apertura del dilogo y cooperaci entre pases y entre polticas es imparable y, en mi opini, positivo. Hay que estar atentos a que, en el mbito de la poltica monetaria, esta nueva orientaci no erosione los dos activos ms valiosos conseguidos en las ltimas dcadas: el mantenimiento de la estabilidad de precios como objetivo prioritario y la independencia de los bancos centrales como instrumento necesario. Pero, al mismo tiempo, la poltica monetaria deber actuar desde una perspectiva abierta, consciente la importancia de su interacci con otras polticas macroeconmicas y financieras. El pasado nos puede dar algunas pistas de actuacin para el futuro. Quizs el ejemplo ms tradicional de interacci sea el dilogo entre la poltica monetaria y la fiscal, que, por cierto, cobrar an ms protagonismo a medida que se afiance la recuperaci econica y comiencen a retirarse los estmulos extraordinarios de demanda. Antes he mencionado la importancia de la interacci con las polticas de regulacin y supervisi prudencial en las que se ha centrado el mayor esfuerzo de concertacin internacional, encaminado a fortalecer el sistema financiero global y a prevenir crisis futuras. La lista de lo conseguido y de los trabajos en marcha en este mbito est bien descrita en el comunicado de Pittsburg y, por sobradamente conocida y extensa, no tiene sentido reiterarla aqu. Menos desarrollada est la poltica de vigilancia o supervisi macroprudencial, tanto a nivel domstico como global, dirigida a identificar y controlar los riesgos sistmicos que escapan del mbito del enfoque microprudencial. En este mbito estamos solo empezando a crear las instituciones a las que se les va a encargar esa misi, pero todava queda mucho por avanzar en la definici de sus contenidos. Nese que el papel de los bancos centrales en el logro de los objetivos de estabilidad financiera se ha visto reforzado, no solo en la articulaci de la poltica monetaria, sino tambin a travs de un mayor protagonismo en el mbito de las polticas de supervisi macroprudencial orientadas especficamente a la consecuci de este objetivo. Una buena muestra de ello es el peso que se ha concedido al Banco Central Europeo y a los bancos centrales nacionales en el European Systemic Risk Board. Este movimiento se puede percibir tambin en las propuestas que estn apareciendo en algunos pases para dotar a sus bancos centrales de responsabilidad en la supervisi microprudencial. Finalmente, si pensamos en el tipo de la economa que surgir despus de la crisis, parece claro que los bancos centrales no podrn preocuparse exclusivamente, como hasta ahora, de dialogar para conseguir unas polticas salariales o fiscales adecuadas para la estabilidad o, como ha mostrado la crisis, de establecer la necesaria interacci con reguladores y supervisores, sino que tambin debern preocuparse de que se adopten las medidas estructurales que sean necesarias para mejorar las expectativas de crecimiento y generaci de empleo. Es muy posible que la poltica monetaria tenga que actuar en el futuro en un entorno econmico y financiero muy distinto al de los aos previos a la crisis. Un menor apalancamiento, un sector financiero ms reducido y en menor expansi y una menor generaci de innovaciones deben llevar, caeteris paribus, a un mundo quizs ms estable, pero tambin de menor crecimiento. Y ello tendr consecuencias. Deberamos reconocer que si la actuaci de los bancos centrales fue muy elogiada en el pasado, lo fue por sus propios mritos, pero tambin debido a que se produjo en un contexto de expansi excepcional y duradera en el que tambin  recuerden ustedes  fueron muy elogiadas las actuaciones de empresarios y banqueros privados, as como las polticas econicas de casi todos los gobiernos. Sin embargo, si no se adoptan cambios importantes en las polticas estructurales, en ese nuevo escenario de bajo crecimiento y dbil generaci de empleo la poltica monetaria ms correcta ser difcil de aceptar por la opini pblica, y ello podra poner en peligro los dos activos que he mencionado anteriormente. En resumen, la crisis financiera ha abierto un intenso debate acerca de los objetivos y la adopci de las polticas econicas. Se trata de un debate positivo, que debe ayudarnos a evitar la repetici de errores en el futuro. Para que as sea, es fundamental que seamos capaces de preservar los elementos del modelo econico hasta ahora vigente que han demostrado ser ms valiosos, como la liberalizaci e integraci de los mercados, la consolidaci fiscal o, lo que nos interesa hoy, el mantenimiento de la estabilidad de precios. Pero a la vez, la superaci exitosa de la crisis actual exigir tambin nuevas respuestas desde los diferentes mbitos de la poltica econica, que adems debern ser ms coherentes entre s de lo que han sido en el pasado. Vivir en una torre de marfil nunca fue aconsejable. A partir de ahora ser imposible. Solo siendo conscientes de que tendremos que actuar en un nuevo entorno, sabremos defender y salvar lo mejor de lo conseguido hasta ahora.

Title: The New International Financial Architecture. Conference at the XVIII National Audit Congress
text: Seville, 26 November 2009 The New International Financial Architecture XVIII National Congress of Audit Javier Ar92ztegui Deputy Governor of Banco de Espa I would like to begin this conference by thanking you for the invitation to participate in this eighteenth National Audit Congress. It is always a pleasure to be able to attend these events where you can share useful experiences from our respective areas of action. In this regard, I would like to highlight the good collaboration between the audit firms and Banco de Espa. Although with different objectives, it is obvious that there is a mutual interest in the proper conduct of an external and independent review of credit institutions. In our country, the supervision system is very intense, with on-site inspections, which are carried out with our own resources. Therefore, the work of the auditors is very useful for Banco de Espa, since they complement our work. We are users of the auditors' opinions, both the audit report of the annual accounts, and the special report that has been issued since the late 80s to provide the supervisor with specific information of interest. These reports, however, do not exhaust the collaboration between the auditors and the supervisor, but there are other cases where the exchange of information or the performance of review tasks of specific areas prevail. I would therefore like to thank the profession for the loyal collaboration that the Bank of Spain has always found in its tasks. That said, the issue that brings us here today is different: the new international financial architecture. I think it is an issue that has its appeal, especially for those, including myself, who have been working within the financial system for many years. However, it is a difficult issue to address, with many edges to polish and, unfortunately, still with numerous uncertainties in its concrete development. This explains why my intervention deliberately falls short in specifying the details of many measures that are still to be defined. To begin, I would like to make a brief review of the topics that I am going to develop. In the first place, it seems relevant to me to raise some reflections on the adequacy of the supervisory structure in the face of the challenges arising in scams, and to analyse the influence that this may have on the design of a new international financial architecture. Subsequently, I will summarize how the previous reflections are reflected in practice, and for this I will address a brief summary of the international initiatives underway, especially in the field of the European Union. By this reason, and in addition to the debate on the new international financial architecture, I will gloss some of the contributions that, from the experience acquired by the Bank of Spain in these timas decades, are being considered for the improvement of supervisory practices worldwide. Firstly, we must ask ourselves whether the reaction to the crisis by financial supervisors has been as expected. In this sense, I believe that it should generally be considered "neat", demonstrating that the current structure of the supervisory function is a good foundation on which to build in the future. But it is also true that we have not always been able to respond fully to certain challenges arising from the evolution of the financial system of scams. What challenges do I mean? Without wanting to be exhaustive, I think we can mention three points: 1. First of all, and although it begins to sound like a too hackneyed concept, we must emphasize the importance of economic globalization, especially the financial business. This factor is in contrast to the current organization of financial supervision, which is eminently national. If we remember the triggers of the current financial crisis, its origin can be traced to the absence of serious credit risk management criteria in certain areas of the mortgage market in the United States. Without ignoring the influence of other variables, the effect caused by the deterioration in these subprime securities quickly crosses borders and plunges global financial markets into a high tension, if not in an absolute disappearance of liquidity. This shows us that it is not realistic to assume that national supervisors live in their particular bubble, isolated from the outside world, but that cooperation and the exchange of information between them must be increased, without this implying a change in supervisory powers. 2. But globalization "per se" does not provide a complete explanation of the speed of change we have faced. The liberalization in capital movements and the processes of financial deregulation have also led to the emergence of new business opportunities, which have modified banking activity itself, through financial innovation. In this sense, phenomena such as the securitization of assets or the issuance of new financial instruments with hybrid characteristics have altered the basis of the banking business itself, giving priority to an activity of packaging of credit assets and subsequent sale. Was this new paradigm more suitable? Allow me to question this in the light of the experience gained during these two years. Probably the market-based model is inevitable when developed companies with high management costs operate a "mature" business, such as banking and this induces them to seek a more lucrative activity such as intermediation as opposed to the more traditional generation of an asset and subsequent administration of it on the balance sheet. But, obviously, this transformation of the banking business to make it more efficient has not been done carefully and has demonstrated its risks. The values of a traditional model, focused on the retail business and self-sufficient of the rest of the group, have been revealed by the shock experienced in the models dependent on the financial markets. In my opinion, this allows us to draw several lessons: that financial markets are not always liquid (although it seems obvious, it was a factor that was easily forgotten) and that they generate volatility in the business that, if not managed rigorously, can be counterproductive for the long-term stability of institutions. In addition, these new business models "originate to distribute" have caused the appearance of new risks that many entities have not been able to manage in an adequate way. But this does not mean that the traditional model is risk-free, as unfortunately demonstrated by the current situation of the real estate market in Spain. 3. Accordingly, it is appropriate to consider the scope of prudential supervision, especially whether it should be extended to a macro-prudential approach. This scenario has been assumed by the Bank of Spain in its Financial Stability Report, allowing to analyze the evolution of the solvency and profitability of the sector and identify potential future risks, such as concentrations of risks in specific sectors. Therefore, we have to try that this critical vision of the environment where the business of a specific entity is developed is incorporated into the process of individual supervision. Having said that, I think it is right to ask how all this affects the design of the new international financial architecture. At this point I will limit my presentation to the scope of the European Union. In Europe, full consensus has been reached on the need to broaden the supervisor's horizon to introduce a macro-prudential approach, and to improve coordination between different supervisors. This is the so-called Larosi8fre process, in reference to the report issued by the group of experts chaired by Jacques de Larosi8fre in February 2009, which inspires these reforms. Two blocks of changes have been proposed that, using the usual jargon, we can fit into "macroprudential supervision" and "microprudential supervision". In the area of macro supervision, it has been agreed to set up a committee responsible for analysing potential weaknesses or risks in financial systems as a whole (and not institution to institution). This committee will be the European Systemic Risk Council (ESRB) and will have the technical and logistical support of the European Central Bank. As you can easily deduce, it tries to strengthen macroeconomic analysis, through the issuance of alerts and recommendations on the risks to the solvency of the European banking system that it is able to identify. The addressees of the recommendations will be obliged to take action or, otherwise, notify their possible lack of action ("act or explain" in Anglo-Saxon terminology). On the other hand, the supervision of individual institutions forms the second block of the proposal of the "Larosi8fre Report", and consists of the creation of three sectoral supervisory authorities that will be constituted from existing European committees of supervisors. Together, they will constitute the so-called "European System of Financial Supervisors" (ESFS). It should be noted that these new authorities will not have the responsibility for the day-to-day supervision of entities, not even large transnational groups. That work will continue to be a national responsibility. There is an exception to this rule in the securities sector, with rating agencies, but I am not the most appropriate person at this table to talk about it. The idea is to seek a better balance between national supervision and common regulation applied in a homogeneous manner. To this end, according to the European Commission's proposal, the new authorities should have three new powers: a5 Powers to develop mandatory technical standards, for a series of areas in supervision, clearly identified and bounded. a5 Power of mediation in certain cases of disagreement between supervisors from different countries. a5 Powers to act in emergency situations; This aspect is currently being discussed and which is not easy to define and delimit. The legislative proposals to implement these innovations, both in the macro and micro part, are now running through the legislative procedures of the European Union. It is not an easy negotiation, but we hope that an agreement will be reached as soon as possible, to get the new approach in motion. The reform of the supervisory architecture does not exhaust the possible improvements of the supervisory system at international level, and numerous proposals for regulatory reform are being discussed in areas such as the regulatory definition of own resources, or the establishment of a new "leverage ratio" to be applied to banks. In my opinion, the Bank of Spain can provide some proposals whose origin is in the lessons learned from the experience accumulated in the forty years, and especially from the Spanish banking crisis of the early 80s. It gives characteristic features to the Spanish ways of carrying out the prudential inspection when compared with the practice of other supervisors. What contributions do I mean? I am thinking in particular of the following aspects: 1. The countercyclical approach in prudential and accounting regulation. The inherent procyclicality of the financial business should be mitigated as far as possible through various instruments such as, for example, dynamic provisions. These provisions, in the application of which Banco de Espa has been a pioneer, allow the financial statements of the entities to recognize as a loss the risk incurred by the entities in a transparent manner, without having to wait until the explicit manifestation of the loss incurred. 2. In addition, we must highlight the importance of intensive supervisory activity. If you allow me the license to use an accounting term, this is a very valuable "intangible asset" of the Espal supervisory model, since it allows to know first-hand and more deeply the management strategies, internal control and risk profile of the entity. Some may consider that this characteristic generates high regulatory costs in the banking sector; Without underestimating this criticism, I would like to emphasise that the benefits to be gained from this approach in the form of mutual knowledge and avoiding much more intrusive concrete actions far outweigh these costs. 3. By scam, I do not want to forget our way of doing in the crisis management of individual entities. In this regard, I would like to highlight the role of the Guarantee Funds for Espales. Compared to the traditional approach, focused on the protection of the depitos, these funds were created with broader powers, ranging from the liquidation of the entities to the possibility of recapitalization, and with this greater capacity to act have been used in the problems of two savings banks in this a. This greater flexibility gives advantages in the adaptation of the measures to the specific moment and environment, although always with the objective of the stability of the banking system and of minimizing the public cost, since these institutions are financed only by the banking sector. Finally, I would like to end with a thought: I am sure that everyone here misses any more concrete proposal, capable of increasing the quality of the supervisory system. Without ignoring the obvious possibility of improvements, let me quote the old Spanish saying that "perfection is sometimes the enemy of the good". In this regard, I am sure that the progress I have mentioned, little by little and with parsimony, will allow banking supervisors to continue to perform our "boring" main function, which is to maintain the stability and solvency of the banking system. Thanks a lot.

Este comit ser el Consejo Europeo de Riesgos Sistmicos (ESRB) y contar con el apoyo tcnico y logstico del Banco Central Europeo. Poder de mediacin en determinados casos de desacuerdo entre supervisores de distintos pases. En mi opini, el Banco de Espa puede aportar algunas propuestas cuyo origen est en las lecciones aprendidas de la experiencia acumulada en los timos cuarenta aos, y en especial de la crisis bancaria espala de principios de los aos 80. sta otorg unos rasgos caractersticos a los modos espaoles de realizar la inspecci prudencial si se compara con la prctica de otros supervisores.
