Finalmente, me gustara terminar con una reflexin: estoy seguro que todos los presentes echan de menos alguna propuesta ms concreta, capaz de incrementar la calidad del sistema supervisor. Sin desconocer la evidente posibilidad de mejoras, permtanme citar el viejo refrn espal que sela que la perfeccin a veces es enemiga de lo bueno. En este sentido, estoy seguro que los avances que he mencionado, poco a poco y con parsimonia, permitirn que los supervisores bancarios podamos continuar realizando nuestra aburrida funcin principal, que es el mantenimiento de la estabilidad y solvencia del sistema bancario. Muchas gracias.

Title: Closing conference at the XXXI Conference of the State Attorney General
text: LOGO_3_Negro_300 Madrid, 27 November 2009 Closing Conference XXXI Conference of the General Advocacy of the State Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor Throughout these days you have had the opportunity to review the main issues that make up banking regulation. Indeed, both the principles of international banking regulation and the various models of supervision have been discussed in depth, and special attention has been devoted to such topical problems as the treatment and resolution of banking crises and the incipient reform of the European Union's institutions in this area. I am going to take advantage of this closing event to convey my reflections on three issues that seem to me to be of interest: firstly, I will refer to how the crisis has affected financial integration in Europe; I will now elaborate on the role of Eurosystem central banks in banking crisis resolution processes; And finally, I will spend the last few minutes describing the initiatives that are being taken in the international context to resolve the financial crisis and avoid its repetition, initiatives that will require the contribution of lawyers when implementing them. Financial integration in the European Union According to a report prepared by the European Central Bank (ECB)1, from 2000 to the end of 2007 there were 20 major mergers or acquisitions between European banks. The growing cross-border presence of European banks in recent years has thus focused more on the acquisition of existing domestic institutions than on the establishment of subsidiary companies. During the aforementioned period, there was also a significant increase in the percentage of banking assets managed by European groups with the greatest international presence. In this regard, it is noteworthy that the 16 main cross-border players identified by the ECB as those groups with a presence in at least 6 EU countries and that had 25% or more of their assets outside their country of origin, owned in 2005 a third of all banking assets in the European Union. 1 The data handled under this heading have been obtained from the publication "Review of the Lamfalussy framework, Eurosystem contribution, ECB, November 2007" Regarding the structure of European banking groups, the report showed a growing centralization of business management, regardless of the legal form adopted in the different countries in which they are present (subsidiaries or branches). In this regard, the most frequently centralized functions included: (i) strategic planning, (ii) treasury, (iii) market risk management, and (iv) the wholesale market, in addition to the areas of communication and information systems. This report reflected that new developments introduced or to be implemented in the area of wholesale payment systems, retail payment systems or securities settlement systems should contribute to further increasing the centralisation of operational functions. Therefore, in the moment immediately prior to the outbreak of the current financial crisis, the European banking market was characterized by a slow but growing trend towards integration, which rested, essentially, on certain group structures with strong operational or functional centralization. However, the widespread crisis in the sector since mid-2007, and especially since the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, has had negative effects on the integration of European financial markets. The euro interbank market, a paradigm of financial integration before the crisis, has suffered significantly, with a decline in confidence among participating banks leading to a decrease in traded volumes and the concentration of transactions between well-known counterparties, which are often from the same country. On the other hand, in the securitisation market, investors disappeared for much of the crisis period, which has affected the ability of many domestic entities to obtain funds from abroad. Previously, entities placed these financial instruments mostly among foreign investors who, with the crisis, have disappeared, which has contributed to the re-nationalization of financial markets. Also, on a global scale, there has been an increase in the domestic bias of financial markets. In fact, the most recent information from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) points to how exposure to foreign assets of domestic banking systems has been significantly reduced in the last year. These movements of disintegration have only highlighted something we knew before the crisis began, and that is that although markets were increasingly global, regulation and, above all, supervision, rested on national levels. Even before the crisis, the structures of financial groups posed considerable difficulties in coordinating the efforts of national authorities to supervise them efficiently. But the questions are even greater when we consider the treatment that should be given to them in episodes of crisis such as the current one. The range of measures and tools with which different states approach the management of banking crises is usually the product of a delicate balance generally linked to the financial history of the country in question. And, as I said, regardless of how such measures are legally articulated, they were developed at strictly national levels. Therefore, no one should be surprised that solutions to the crisis have been sought mainly with national solutions, even in those cases in which the entity in difficulty could genuinely qualify as cross-border. It is true that, in some isolated cases, the States involved have been able to find coordinated solutions, but the absence of a genuine European framework has revealed the shortcomings of the current model, based on lukewarm regulatory harmonisation. As you know, in the case of Spain, the crisis has not affected large banks, but smaller entities operating within the country, but the fact of being part of the Eurosystem has forced important changes in our legal system in order to solve the problems in this new environment. That is why I thought it appropriate to focus most of my speech on the regulatory changes made in Spain. In all countries, the financial crisis has required a rapid response from the authorities, and in particular from central banks and supervisors, who have had to equip themselves with tools to deal with situations of a gravity that just over two years ago seemed unimaginable. In the case of our country, the Bank of Spain had action mechanisms that in the past proved useful and effective. However, there were some elements that distinguished the current crisis from previous episodes, which advised the creation of a new instrument better adapted to these new requirements: the Fund for Orderly Bank Restructuring (FROB). With the approval of the FROB, a restructuring process has been established for those cases in which a certain entity is unable to find a private solution to its viability problems, eliminating some of the obstacles that could have hindered this process if the previous regulatory framework had been maintained. One of the main differences between the current situation and previous financial crises is that, contrary to what happened in the past, this time savings banks have not been immune to difficulties. For this reason, the Royal Decree-Law creating the FROB incorporates measures of an exceptional nature in relation to the restructuring processes of savings banks, such as the provision that the FROB holds voting rights in its governing bodies through the acquisition of participatory quotas or the one that unifies in the Bank of Spain the regime of administrative authorizations to which merger operations are subject or Disposal of assets and liabilities of such entities. Another reason that led the Spanish authorities to approve the creation of the FROB was the need to have a mechanism to temporarily provide the financial support that an entity with serious viability problems may need while the corresponding restructuring plan is approved, an essential task within any restructuring scheme and that, given our membership of the Eurosystem, today it could no longer take over the Bank of Spain, If the tasks of the supervisor for the prevention of banking crises are easily identifiable, and are limited to the control of the conditions of access to and exercise of financial activity through administrative measures, the role of central banks in this area resists a precise legal classification. However, the dependence of banks on central bank financing illustrates their importance in preventing or alleviating the occurrence of pathological phenomena in the system. The provision of financing is, under normal conditions, the ordinary instrument used by central banks to implement their monetary policies, thus regulating the liquidity and interest rate variables of the financial system. In the case of the Eurosystem, the various refinancing or liquidity drain-down operations are structured through classic contractual tools (pledged loans, simultaneous transactions, currency swaps) to which banks access through the ordinary procedure of periodic auctions or the permanent facilities available at any time at the respective central bank at a penalised interest rate. Central bank funding, however, becomes decisive in sharp and sudden cases of illiquidity. In these cases, the combination of the functions of supervisor and central bank in a single institution can adequately assess the need for a possible injection of funds, in view of the financial institution's equity situation and the effects that its hypothetical collapse would transmit to the system. Obviously, those countries that opt for the express decoupling of both functions in separate institutions do so considering that the existence of a single body lacks the advantages described above and that, on the contrary, it can lead to a direct conflict of interest when dealing with financing operations in a context in which there are serious liquidity problems. The function of the central bank as "lender of last resort" - which, on the other hand, is the norm in the vast majority of credit systems - lacks concrete legislative expression in Spain, except for some specific precedent, such as article 18 of the old Banking Regulation Law of December 31, 1946, in which it was indicated textually as "own mission" of the Bank of Spain "when the general interest so advises, that of offering credit institutions that, having accommodated their actions to good banking practices, find themselves, in the event of a general crisis or other circumstances, with cash flow difficulties, the possible contest within their orbit of action and compatible with the security of their operations". The Law on the Autonomy of the Bank of Spain refers indirectly to financing operations presumably extraordinary when it establishes in its article 4.2. that the report accompanying the balance sheet and accounts for each financial year shall detail in particular "loans or other operations ... which have not been concluded on market terms or which otherwise entail loss of profit or loss for the Bank". Using the language of the ECB, we can today define these emergency liquidity provision (ELA) operations as those that consist of "providing liquidity, in extraordinary circumstances, to a credit institution with temporary liquidity problems that cannot obtain it in the market by participating in monetary policy operations"2. 2, See ECB Monthly Bulletin, February 2007, "EU mechanisms for financial crisis management", pp. 86-87. However, the subjection to the Eurosystem's regulatory framework has introduced certain legal conditions that represent a significant change with respect to the previous situation in terms of the capacity of the national central banks, and therefore of the Bank of Spain, to formalize the aforementioned operations in emergency situations. One of these conditions is precisely the so-called principle prohibiting monetary financing, enshrined in Article 101 of the Treaty establishing the European Community, which was introduced at Maastricht as one of the essential pillars guaranteeing the primary objective of monetary policy of maintaining price stability and improving the budgetary discipline of governments. This prohibition is still a reflection of the financial independence of the central bank and is one of the techniques that guarantee the autonomy of central banks. As you all know, Article 101 expressly prohibits the authorisation of overdraft facilities or the granting of any other type of credit by the European Central Bank and the National Central Banks in favour of Community institutions or bodies, central governments, regional, local and other public authorities, bodies governed by public law or public undertakings of the Member States, as well as the acquisition of debt instruments issued by them. And in Community regulation this concept of "other types of credits" is a very broad term, which encompasses any type of financing of public sector obligations vis-88-vis third parties. The Treaty does, however, contain an exception to the prohibition, since it does not apply to public banks, which, in the context of the provision of liquidity by central banks, were given the same treatment as private banks. As is well known, the generalisation of the liquidity crisis from the second half of 2007 forced the ECB to adapt the framework of monetary policy operations to the new situation, making it more flexible and extending its concession periods. In addition, and to the extent that the crisis led to the granting of emergency financing by various central banks, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, as an auditor of compliance with the principle of prohibition of monetary financing3, had to analyze and determine the scope of this principle in relation to the aforementioned operations. 3 See Article 237(d) of the Treaty. The general position of the European Central Bank on Article 101 of the Treaty and its application to emergency liquidity assistance operations has been made public in the so-called Convergence Reports since 2006, as well as in the various opinions in response to consultations made by Member States on draft legal provisions in accordance with their duty under Article 105 of the Treaty. Treaty. According to the ECB's interpretation, the key element in determining whether a given emergency provision of liquidity constitutes a central bank's own operation or, on the contrary, must be considered monetary financing, rests on the solvency criterion of the receiving credit institution. According to that reasoning, the provision of liquidity in cases of insolvency as part of a rescue operation by the public authorities would be outside the functions of a central bank, so that such financing would be a case prohibited by Article 101 of the Treaty. The determination of whether a particular entity is insolvent or merely illiquid is particularly complex in the vast majority of cases where an immediate injection of funds is required. Given this difficulty, one of the few options that allow us a certain degree of action is the one that replaces the assessment of solvency with a judgment on the viability of the entity, to be issued by the supervisor. Moreover, emergency financing, like all refinancing operations by the Eurosystem central banks, should be backed by adequate guarantees, which, together with the requirement of logically penalised remuneration, helps to mitigate the risk of considering that such financing is being granted to an insolvent institution. In this respect, the public nature of certain guarantees has introduced a new element in the analysis of compatibility with the principle of prohibition of monetary financing, since the need to resort to them in the absence of other "ordinary" collateral could lead to doubts as to the true situation of the entity receiving the financing. To avoid them, the European Central Bank has pointed out that emergency financing to a troubled entity by providing a State guarantee is only compatible with the principle of monetary financing if the strict conditions made public by the European monetary authority in its opinions on European legislation in the context of the financial crisis since 2008 are metfinancial since 2008financial since 2008 4 Opinions CON/2008/42 (Luxembourg), CON/2008/46 (Belgium), CON/2008/48 (Ireland), CON/2008/58 (Italy) and CON/2008/80 (Poland). (i) Funding must be short-term. (ii) The State guarantee must be valid, without there being any doubt about its legal and economic validity, as well as its execution under national legislation. (iii) It must be considered that there is a systemic risk, in the sense of assessing that the operation is critical to maintain the stability of the financial system. Finally, in addition to the variables to which I have just referred, another element to be taken into account when judging emergency financing in the light of Article 101 would undoubtedly be the degree of independence of the Central Bank in granting it. The European monetary authority establishes that the independence in the granting of an ELA must be at least comparable to that exercised by central banks in their capacity as members of the European System of Central Banks. Consequently, any imposition by the public authorities on the central bank concerned during the granting of a particular credit transaction would immediately place that credit operation within the scope of Article 101. The circumstances to which I have just referred illustrate well the differences in the scope for manoeuvre of the national central banks that are part of the Eurosystem for the resolution of banking crises before and after Maastricht. And one of its immediate consequences has been the creation of the FROB, which will now be responsible for the urgent provision of liquidity to those entities that are prohibited from accessing financing from the Bank of Spain in view of their viability problems. I do not want, however, to conclude this closing speech without making some reference to the problems that have arisen with the current global crisis and to the solution formulas that are beginning to be pointed out in various international forums, such as the Financial Stability Board, the Basel Supervisory Committee or the European Commission itself. From now on, the agreements that are being adopted will have to materialize in new rules and changes to the pre-existing regulation, in a process that will undoubtedly require a great effort on the part of legal professionals. Efforts are focusing on diagnosing the causes that led us to the financial crisis and arbitrating the appropriate reforms to avoid its repetition, while optimizing the surgical instruments necessary to face in an agile, efficient and safe way the specific episodes of crisis that may occur in the future. With regard to diagnosis, it seems clear that the model that had been developed in recent years, characterized by a growing degree of globalization and a continuous process of financial innovation, did not lead, as was believed, to a more efficient financial system. We now know that this model had many weaknesses and that regulation and supervision in many countries did not adapt flexibly enough to these new realities; the abundance of liquidity generated by broadly expansionary monetary policies contributed to rapid credit growth and increased indebtedness; The regulation did not incorporate mechanisms to prevent the actions of agents operating in the financial sector from contributing to exacerbating the economic cycle; Securitization markets developed rapidly, often based on the originate-to-distribute model, which encouraged lax lending policies and which, instead of helping to manage risks more efficiently and flexibly, helped spread risks to the rest of the system, masking their location and nature. Finally, the importance of liquidity risk was not sufficiently taken into account, nor was the necessary attention paid to so-called systemic risks, the existence of which reminds us that individual institutions may not be exposed to a certain risk, but the system as a whole is. Given all these shortcomings, there is a broad consensus, endorsed in successive G20 communiqu8es, on the need for far-reaching changes in the architecture and functioning of regulation and supervision that contribute to financial stability. To move in this direction, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) is discussing a broad set of measures, which aim to correct the errors detected, improve international coherence and coordination in the areas of regulation and supervision and introduce a new macroprudential perspective into these policies, which does not only take into account the sum of individual risks, but it also makes it possible to assess the risk borne by the financial system as a whole. In Europe, moreover, all these reforms will be accompanied by the creation of new Community bodies responsible for monitoring the formation of hazards at the macro level, such as the European Systemic Risk Board, and for strengthening and guiding the process of regulatory integration, a role that the future European Banking Authority will assume. Among the concrete measures currently being discussed in the main international for a are: the establishment of stricter capital requirements in terms of both volume and quality; mitigating the procyclicality of the financial system through capital buffers and provisioning systems that help smooth the cycle; reviewing clearing practices to prevent managers from focusing excessively on the short term; improving the functioning of derivatives markets, especially those that are not traded on organised markets; revision and standardisation of accounting standards; or the establishment of measures to ensure compliance with international standards of regulation and supervision in all jurisdictions. Various measures are also being discussed to reduce the probability and impact of crises in institutions that, due to their complexity, may affect the financial system as a whole, including the possible requirement of specific capital requirements or the establishment of restrictions on its legal and operational structure. In relation to this last aspect, the revision of the tools to minimize the impact of bank failures is a major challenge from the legal perspective. As you have already had the opportunity to hear during these Days, the ways of improvement in this area are basically proposed in two directions: on the one hand, the aim of reducing the harmful effects of a possible crisis through measures such as the simplification of structures and functions in financial groups and, on the other hand, the preparation by them of authentic corporate wills (called by some living wills) intended to facilitate their total or partial liquidation in case of need. Along with these measures, the improvements currently under consideration are the harmonisation (or even unification, if we are talking about the European Union) of the legal tools available to the public authorities to ensure the rapid resolution of any episode of crisis without affecting basic banking services. In short, it is a question of being able to transfer the banking business "with an open heart", either through operations of coercive assignment of assets and liabilities or of taking and subsequent disposal of a controlling interest in the intervened entity. The approach to reforms in this regard raises, as is logical, the difficulty of reconciling the protection of the public interest derived from an orderly bank liquidation process with the rights of shareholders and institutional creditors. We are therefore faced with a difficult task, which will only be possible if we combine the necessary political will with the efforts of industry and the decisive contribution of better legal reasoning. It has therefore come "the time of the jurists" who are those who in modern societies have, if necessary, the experience in the management of disputes, since the disaggregation of "bank property" in cases where the resolution of an entity proceeds, must be based on the search for legal formulas that reconcile the most efficient management of the assets of the financial system with the most scrupulous respect for rights. of the various agents involved, giving harmony to the banking regulatory system as a whole. This work will undoubtedly be multidisciplinary, but the contribution of legal experts acquires a relevant tone. Therefore, we must congratulate the State Attorney's Office d0 always attentive and always aware of the needs of the public authorities d0 for devoting special attention to these phenomena, as evidenced by the celebration of these days at this opportune moment. And with these reflections aloud, let me conclude by congratulating the organizers and speakers for these Days, undoubtedly of great interest, and thanking everyone for their attendance and intervention in them. Thank you very much for your attention.
text_original: LOGO_3_Negro_300 Madrid, 27 de noviembre de 2009 Conferencia de clausura XXXI Jornadas de la Abogaca General del Estado Miguel Fernndez Ordez Gobernador A lo largo de estas jornadas han tenido ustedes ocasin de recorrer los principales asuntos que componen la regulacin bancaria. En efecto, se han tratado aqu en profundidad tanto los principios de la ordenacin bancaria internacional como los distintos modelos de supervisin, y se ha dedicado una especial atencin a problemas tan actuales como el tratamiento y resolucin de las crisis bancarias y la incipiente reforma de las instituciones de la Unin Europea en este mbito. Voy a aprovechar este acto de clausura para trasladarles mis reflexiones sobre tres asuntos que me parecen de inters: en primer lugar, me referir a cmo la crisis ha afectado a la integracin financiera en Europa; a continuacin, me extender sobre el papel de los bancos centrales del Eurosistema en los procesos de resolucin de crisis bancarias; y finalmente, dedicar los ltimos minutos a describir las iniciativas que se estn adoptando en el contexto internacional para resolver la crisis financiera y evitar su repeticin, iniciativas que van a demandar la aportacin de los juristas a la hora de implementarlas. La integracin financiera en la Unin Europea Segn un informe elaborado por el Banco Central Europeo (BCE)1, desde el ao 2000 hasta finales de 2007 se registraron 20 grandes operaciones de fusin o adquisicin entre entidades bancarias europeas. La creciente presencia transfronteriza de los bancos europeos en los ltimos aos se centr pues, ms en la adquisicin de entidades ya existentes a nivel domstico, que en el establecimiento de sociedades filiales. Durante el perodo citado se registr, asimismo, un incremento significativo en el porcentaje de activos bancarios gestionados por los grupos europeos con mayor presencia internacional. En este sentido, es de destacar que los 16 principales grupos transfronterizos (Key cross-border players) identificados por el BCE como aquellos grupos con presencia en al menos 6 pases comunitarios y que tenan el 25% o ms de sus activos fuera de su pas de origen, posean en 2005 un tercio de todos los activos bancarios en la Unin Europea. 1 Los datos manejados en este epgrafe han sido obtenidos de la publicacin Review of the Lamfalussy framework, Eurosystem contribution, ECB, november 2007 En cuanto a la estructura de los grupos bancarios europeos, el informe mostraba una creciente centralizacin de la gestin del negocio, con independencia de la forma jurdica adoptada en los distintos pases en los que aquellos estn presentes (filiales o sucursales). En este orden de cosas, las funciones ms frecuentemente centralizadas incluan: (i) la planificacin estratgica, (ii) la tesorera, (iii) la gestin del riesgo de mercado, y (iv) el mercado mayorista, adems de las reas de comunicacin y sistemas de informacin. Este informe reflejaba que los nuevos desarrollos implantados o por implantar en el rea de sistemas de pago mayoristas, en los sistemas de pago minoristas o en los de liquidacin de valores deberan contribuir a incrementar an ms la centralizacin de funciones operativas. Por lo tanto, en el momento inmediatamente anterior al desencadenamiento de la actual crisis financiera, el mercado bancario europeo se caracterizaba por una lenta pero creciente tendencia a la integracin, que descansaba, esencialmente, en determinadas estructuras de grupo con una fuerte centralizacin operativa o funcional. Sin embargo, la crisis generalizada que sufri el sector desde mediados de 2007, y muy especialmente desde la cada de Lehman Brothers en septiembre de 2008, ha tenido efectos negativos sobre la integracin de los mercados financieros europeos. El mercado interbancario en euros, paradigma de la integracin financiera antes de la crisis, se ha resentido significativamente, con una disminucin de la confianza entre los bancos participantes que ha llevado a una disminucin de los volmenes intercambiados y a la concentracin de las operaciones entre contrapartes que se conocen en profundidad, que con frecuencia son de un mismo pas. Por otra parte, en el mercado de titulizaciones, los inversores desaparecieron durante buena parte del perodo de crisis, lo que ha afectado a la capacidad de numerosas entidades nacionales para obtener fondos del exterior. Anteriormente, las entidades colocaban estos instrumentos financieros mayoritariamente entre inversores extranjeros que, con la crisis, han desaparecido, lo que ha contribuido a la re-nacionalizacin de los mercados financieros. Asimismo, a escala global, se ha producido un aumento del sesgo domstico de los mercados financieros. De hecho, la informacin ms reciente del Banco de Pagos Internacionales (BIS) seala cmo la exposicin a los activos exteriores de los sistemas bancarios nacionales se ha reducido en el ltimo ao de forma significativa. Estos movimientos de des-integracin, no han hecho sino poner ms de manifiesto algo que sabamos antes de que se iniciara la crisis, y es que aunque los mercados eran cada vez ms globales, la regulacin y, sobre todo la supervisin, descansaba en mbitos nacionales. Ya antes de la crisis, las estructuras de los grupos financieros planteaban bastantes dificultades a la hora de coordinar los esfuerzos de las autoridades nacionales para supervisarlos eficientemente. Pero los interrogantes son an mucho mayores cuando nos planteamos el tratamiento que se les debe dar en episodios de crisis como la actual. El abanico de medidas y herramientas con las que los distintos estados afrontan la gestin de las crisis bancarias es usualmente el producto de un delicado equilibrio generalmente ligado a la propia historia financiera del pas en cuestin. Y, como he dicho, con independencia de cmo se articulen jurdicamente tales medidas, las mismas se desarrollaron en mbitos estrictamente nacionales. Por eso, a nadie debe extraarle que se hayan buscado las salidas a la crisis fundamentalmente con soluciones nacionales, incluso en aquellos casos en los que la entidad en dificultades poda calificarse genuinamente como transfronteriza. Es cierto que, en algn caso aislado, los Estados involucrados han sido capaces de arbitrar soluciones coordinadas, pero la ausencia de un autntico marco europeo ha puesto de manifiesto las carencias del actual modelo, basado en una tibia armonizacin normativa. Como saben ustedes, en el caso de Espaa, la crisis no ha afectado a las entidades grandes, sino a entidades de menor tamao que operan dentro del pas, pero el hecho de formar parte del Eurosistema ha obligado a cambios importantes en nuestro ordenamiento para poder resolver los problemas en este nuevo entorno. Por ello me ha parecido conveniente centrar la mayor parte de mi intervencin en los cambios normativos realizados en Espaa. En todos los pases la crisis financiera ha exigido una rpida respuesta de las autoridades, y en particular de los bancos centrales y los supervisores, que se han tenido que dotar de herramientas para hacer frente a situaciones de una gravedad que hace poco ms de dos aos pareca inimaginable. En el caso de nuestro pas, el Banco de Espaa dispona de mecanismos de actuacin que en el pasado demostraron ser tiles y efectivos. Sin embargo, haba algunos elementos que distinguan la crisis actual de episodios anteriores, que aconsejaron la creacin de un nuevo instrumento mejor adaptado a estas nuevas exigencias: el Fondo de Reestructuracin Ordenada Bancaria (FROB). Con la aprobacin del FROB se ha establecido un proceso de reestructuracin para aquellos casos en que una determinada entidad sea incapaz de encontrar una solucin privada a sus problemas de viabilidad, eliminando algunos de los obstculos que habran podido dificultar este proceso de haberse mantenido el marco normativo anterior. Una de las principales diferencias entre la situacin actual y crisis financieras anteriores es que, al contrario de lo ocurrido en el pasado, esta vez las cajas de ahorros no han sido inmunes a las dificultades. Por eso, el Real Decreto-Ley por el que se crea el FROB incorpora medidas de naturaleza excepcional con relacin a los procesos de reestructuracin de cajas de ahorro, como la previsin de que el FROB ostente derechos de voto en sus rganos de gobierno mediante la adquisicin de cuotas participativas o la que unifica en el Banco de Espaa el rgimen de autorizaciones administrativas a las que se encuentran sujetas las operaciones de fusin o cesin de activos y pasivos de dichas entidades. Otra de las razones que llevaron a las autoridades espaolas a aprobar la creacin del FROB fue la necesidad de disponer de un mecanismo para suministrar temporalmente los apoyos financieros que pueda precisar una entidad con problemas graves de viabilidad en tanto se aprueba el correspondiente plan de reestructuracin, tarea esencial dentro de todo esquema de saneamiento y que, dada nuestra pertenencia al Eurosistema, hoy por hoy ya no podra asumir el Banco de Espaa, Si las funciones del supervisor para la prevencin de crisis bancarias son fcilmente identificables, y se cien al control de las condiciones de acceso y ejercicio de la actividad financiera mediante medidas de carcter administrativo, el papel de los bancos centrales en este terreno se resiste a una calificacin jurdica precisa. Sin embargo, la dependencia de las entidades respecto a la financiacin del banco central ilustra su importancia a la hora de prevenir o aliviar la aparicin de fenmenos patolgicos en el sistema. El suministro de financiacin es, en condiciones normales, el instrumento ordinario de que se sirven los bancos centrales para ejecutar sus polticas monetarias, regulando as las variables de liquidez y tipo de inters del sistema financiero. En el caso del Eurosistema, las distintas operaciones de financiacin o de drenaje de liquidez se articulan a travs de clsicas herramientas de carcter contractual (prstamos con garanta pignoraticia, operaciones simultneas, swaps de divisas) a las que las entidades acceden a travs del procedimiento ordinario de subastas peridicas o de las facilidades permanentes disponibles en todo momento en el respectivo banco central a un tipo de inters penalizado. La financiacin procedente del banco central, sin embargo, se vuelve decisiva en supuestos agudos y repentinos de falta de liquidez. En estos casos, la conjuncin de las funciones de supervisor y banco central en una sola institucin puede permitir evaluar adecuadamente la necesidad de una eventual inyeccin de fondos, a la vista de la situacin patrimonial de la entidad financiera y de los efectos que su hipottico colapso transmitira al sistema. Como es obvio, aquellos pases que optan por la disociacin expresa de ambas funciones en instituciones separadas lo hacen considerando que la existencia de un nico organismo carece de las ventajas antes descritas y que, por el contrario, puede desembocar en un conflicto de intereses directo a la hora de abordar operaciones de financiacin en un contexto en el que existen problemas graves de liquidez. La funcin del banco central como "prestamista de ltima instancia" -que, por otra parte, es norma en la gran mayora de los ordenamientos crediticios- carece en Espaa de expresin legislativa concreta, salvo algn precedente especfico, como el artculo 18 de la vieja Ley de Ordenacin Bancaria de 31 de diciembre de 1946, en el que se indicaba textualmente como "misin propia" del Banco de Espaa "cuando as lo aconseje el inters general, la de ofrecer a las instituciones de crdito que, habiendo acomodado su actuacin a las buenas prcticas bancarias, se encuentren, en caso de crisis general o por otras circunstancias, con dificultades de tesorera, el concurso posible dentro de su rbita de accin y compatible con la seguridad de sus operaciones". La Ley de Autonoma del Banco de Espaa se refiere indirectamente a operaciones de financiacin presumiblemente extraordinarias cuando establece en su artculo 4.2. que en el informe que acompae al balance y cuentas de cada ejercicio se detallarn especialmente "los prstamos u otras operaciones... que no se hubieran concertado en condiciones de mercado o que, de cualquier otra forma, entraen lucro cesante o quebranto para el Banco". Utilizando el lenguaje del BCE, podemos definir hoy en da estas operaciones de provisin urgente de liquidez (ELA, en sus siglas en ingls) como aquellas que consisten en proporcionar liquidez, en circunstancias extraordinarias a una entidad de crdito con problemas temporales de liquidez que no puede obtenerla en el mercado participando en operaciones de poltica monetaria2. 2, Vid. Boletn Mensual del BCE, febrero 2007, Mecanismos de la UE para la gestin de crisis financieras, pgs. 86-87. Ahora bien, la sujecin al marco regulador del Eurosistema ha introducido determinados condicionantes legales que suponen un cambio significativo respecto a la situacin anterior en lo que se refiere a la capacidad de los bancos centrales nacionales, y por tanto del Banco de Espaa, para formalizar las citadas operaciones en situaciones de emergencia. Uno de dichos condicionantes es, precisamente, el llamado principio de prohibicin de financiacin monetaria, recogido en el artculo 101 del Tratado de la Comunidad Europea, y que fue introducido en Maastricht como uno de los pilares esenciales que garantizan el objetivo primordial de la poltica monetaria de mantener la estabilidad de precios y mejorar la disciplina presupuestaria de los Gobiernos. Esta prohibicin no deja de ser el reflejo de la independencia financiera del banco central y es una de las tcnicas que permiten garantizar la autonoma de los bancos centrales. Como todos ustedes conocen, dicho artculo 101 prohbe expresamente la autorizacin de descubiertos o la concesin de cualquier otro tipo de crditos por el Banco Central Europeo y los Bancos Centrales Nacionales en favor de instituciones u organismos comunitarios, gobiernos centrales, autoridades regionales, locales y otras autoridades pblicas, organismos de Derecho pblico o empresas pblicas de los Estados miembros, as como la adquisicin de instrumentos de deuda emitidos por aquellos. Y en la regulacin comunitaria ese concepto de otro tipo de crditos es un trmino muy amplio, que engloba cualquier tipo financiacin de las obligaciones del sector pblico con respecto a terceros. El Tratado, no obstante, contiene una excepcin a la prohibicin, ya que esta no se aplica a los bancos pblicos, a los que, en el marco del suministro de liquidez de los bancos centrales, se decidi dar el mismo trato que a los bancos privados. Como es notorio, la generalizacin de la crisis de liquidez a partir del segundo semestre de 2007 oblig al BCE a adecuar el marco de las operaciones de la poltica monetaria a la nueva situacin, flexibilizndolo y ampliando sus plazos de concesin. Adicionalmente, y en la medida en que la crisis determin la concesin de financiaciones de emergencia por parte de diversos bancos centrales, el Consejo de Gobierno del Banco Central Europeo, en cuanto fiscalizador del cumplimiento del principio de prohibicin de la financiacin monetaria3, hubo de analizar y determinar el alcance de este principio con relacin a las citadas operaciones. 3 Vid. art. 237 d) del Tratado. La posicin general del Banco Central Europeo ante el citado artculo 101 del Tratado y su aplicacin a las operaciones de ayuda de emergencia de liquidez se ha hecho pblica en los llamados Informes de convergencia desde el ao 2006, as como en los distintos dictmenes en respuesta a consultas formuladas por los Estados Miembros sobre proyectos de disposiciones legales de conformidad con el deber que a tal efecto les impone el artculo 105 del Tratado. De acuerdo con la interpretacin del BCE, el elemento clave a la hora de deslindar si una determinada provisin urgente de liquidez constituye una operacin propia de banco central o, por el contrario, debe ser considerada financiacin monetaria, descansa en el criterio de solvencia de la entidad de crdito receptora. De acuerdo con ese razonamiento, el suministro de liquidez en casos de insolvencia como parte de una operacin de rescate a cargo de los poderes pblicos quedara fuera de las funciones propias de un banco central, por lo que esta financiacin sera un supuesto de los prohibidos en el artculo 101 del Tratado. La determinacin de si una entidad concreta resulta insolvente o meramente ilquida resulta particularmente compleja en la inmensa mayora de los casos en los que se precisa una inyeccin inmediata de fondos. Ante esa dificultad, una de las pocas opciones que nos permiten cierto grado de actuacin es la que sustituye la valoracin de la solvencia por un juicio sobre la viabilidad de la entidad, a emitir por el supervisor. Por otra parte, las financiaciones de emergencia, como todas las operaciones de financiacin a cargo de los bancos centrales del Eurosistema, deben estar respaldadas por garantas adecuadas, lo que, unido a la exigencia de una remuneracin lgicamente penalizada, contribuye a mitigar el riesgo de considerar que dicha financiacin se est concediendo a una entidad insolvente. A este respecto, la naturaleza pblica de determinadas garantas ha introducido un nuevo elemento en el anlisis de compatibilidad con el principio de prohibicin de financiacin monetaria, ya que la necesidad de acudir a las mismas ante la ausencia de otros activos de garanta ordinarios podra llegar a suscitar dudas sobre la autntica situacin de la entidad receptora de la financiacin. Para evitarlas, el Banco Central Europeo ha puntualizado que una financiacin de emergencia a una entidad con problemas terciando una garanta del Estado slo es compatible con el principio de financiacin monetaria si se cumplen las estrictas condiciones hechas pblicas por la autoridad monetaria europea en sus dictmenes sobre la legislacin europea en el contexto de la crisis financiera desde 2008financiera desde 2008financiera desde 2008 4 Dictmenes CON/2008/42 (Luxemburgo), CON/2008/46 (Blgica), CON/2008/48 (Irlanda), CON/2008/58 (Italia) y CON/2008/80 (Polonia). (i) La financiacin debe ser a corto plazo. (ii) La garanta estatal debe ser vlida, sin que puedan existir dudas sobre su validez legal y econmica, as como de su ejecucin bajo la legislacin nacional. (iii) Debe estimarse que existe un riesgo sistmico, en el sentido de valorar que la operacin es crtica para mantener la estabilidad del sistema financiero. Finalmente, junto a las variables a las que acabo de referirme, otro elemento a tener en cuenta a la hora de juzgar una financiacin de emergencia a la luz del artculo 101 sera, indudablemente, el del grado de independencia del Banco Central para concederla. La autoridad monetaria europea establece que la independencia en la concesin de un ELA debe ser como mnimo equiparable a la que ejercen los bancos centrales en su condicin de miembros del Sistema Europeo de Bancos Centrales. En consecuencia, cualquier imposicin de los poderes pblicos sobre el respectivo banco central durante la concesin de una determinada operacin crediticia colocara a esta inmediatamente dentro del mbito del artculo 101. Las circunstancias a las que me acabo de referir ilustran bien las diferencias en el margen de actuacin de los bancos centrales nacionales que son parte del Eurosistema para la resolucin de las crisis bancarias antes y despus de Maastricht. Y una de sus consecuencias inmediatas ha sido la creacin del FROB, al que corresponder ahora la provisin urgente de liquidez a aquellas entidades que tengan vedado el acceso a la financiacin del Banco de Espaa en atencin a sus problemas de viabilidad. No quiero, sin embargo, concluir esta intervencin de clausura sin hacer alguna referencia a los problemas que han surgido con la actual crisis global y a las frmulas de solucin que comienzan a apuntarse en distintos foros internacionales, como el Financial Stability Board, el Comit de Supervisin de Basilea o la propia Comisin Europea. De ahora en adelante, los acuerdos que se estn adoptando debern concretarse en nuevas normas y en cambios de la regulacin preexistente, en un proceso que sin duda exigir un gran esfuerzo por parte de los profesionales del derecho. Los esfuerzos se estn centrando en diagnosticar las causas que nos llevaron a la crisis financiera y arbitrar las reformas adecuadas para evitar su repeticin, optimizando al mismo tiempo el instrumental quirrgico necesario para enfrentarnos de forma gil, eficiente y segura a los episodios concretos de crisis que puedan producirse en el futuro. Por lo que refiere a la diagnosis, parece evidente que el modelo que se haba desarrollado en los ltimos aos, caracterizado por un creciente grado de globalizacin y un continuo proceso de innovacin financiera, no dio lugar, como se crea, a un sistema financiero ms eficiente. Ahora sabemos que este modelo tena muchos puntos dbiles y que la regulacin y la supervisin en muchos pases no se adaptaron con la suficiente flexibilidad a estas nuevas realidades; la abundancia de liquidez generada por unas polticas monetarias globalmente expansivas contribuy al rpido crecimiento del crdito y al aumento del endeudamiento; la regulacin no incorpor mecanismos para evitar que las acciones de los agentes que operan en el sector financiero contribuyeran a exacerbar el ciclo econmico; se desarrollaron rpidamente los mercados de titulizacin, con frecuencia basados en el modelo de originar para distribuir, que incentiv polticas de concesin de crditos poco rigurosas y que, en vez de ayudar a una gestin de los riesgos ms eficiente y flexible, contribuy a diseminarlos hacia el resto del sistema, enmascarando su ubicacin y su naturaleza. Por ltimo, tampoco se tuvo suficientemente en cuenta la importancia del riesgo de liquidez, ni se prest la atencin necesaria a los denominados riesgos sistmicos, cuya existencia nos recuerda que es posible que las entidades consideradas individualmente no estn expuestas a un determinado riesgo, pero el conjunto del sistema s lo est. Ante todas estas deficiencias, existe un amplio consenso, refrendado en los sucesivos comunicados del G-20, sobre la necesidad de introducir cambios de calado en la arquitectura y en el funcionamiento de la regulacin y la supervisin que contribuyan a la estabilidad financiera. Para avanzar en esta direccin, en el Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera (FSB) se est discutiendo un amplio conjunto de medidas, que persiguen corregir los errores detectados, mejorar la coherencia y la coordinacin internacional en los mbitos de la regulacin y la supervisin e introducir en estas polticas una nueva perspectiva macroprudencial, que no slo tenga en cuenta la suma de los riesgos individuales, sino que tambin permita evaluar el riesgo que soporta el sistema financiero en su conjunto. En Europa, adems, todas estas reformas irn acompaadas de la creacin de nuevos organismos comunitarios encargados de vigilar la formacin de peligros a nivel macro, como el Consejo Europeo de Riesgo Sistmico o European Systemic Risk Board, y de reforzar y guiar el proceso de integracin regulatoria, papel que asumir la futura Autoridad Bancaria Europea. Entre las medidas concretas que se estn discutiendo en estos momentos en los principales foros internacionales se encuentran: el establecimiento de unos requerimientos de capital ms estrictos tanto en volumen como en calidad; la mitigacin de la prociclicidad del sistema financiero a travs de colchones de capital y de sistemas de provisiones que contribuyan a suavizar el ciclo; la revisin de las prcticas de compensacin para evitar que los gestores se centren excesivamente en el corto plazo; la mejora del funcionamiento de los mercados de activos derivados, especialmente de aquellos que no se negocian en mercados organizados; la revisin y la homogenizacin de las normas contables; o el establecimiento de medidas para asegurar la observancia de los estndares internacionales de regulacin y supervisin en todas las jurisdicciones. Tambin se estn discutiendo distintas medidas para reducir la probabilidad y el impacto de crisis en instituciones que, por su complejidad, pueden afectar al sistema financiero en su conjunto, entre las que se incluye la posible exigencia de requerimientos de capital especficos o el establecimiento de restricciones sobre su estructura legal y operativa. En relacin con este ltimo aspecto, la revisin de las herramientas para minimizar el impacto de las quiebras bancarias supone un importante desafo desde la perspectiva jurdica. Como ya han tenido ustedes oportunidad de escuchar a lo largo de estas Jornadas, las vas de mejora en este terreno se plantean bsicamente en dos direcciones: por un lado, la tendente a disminuir los efectos nocivos de una eventual crisis mediante medidas tales como la simplificacin de estructuras y funciones en los grupos financieros y, por otra, la elaboracin por estos de autnticos testamentos corporativos (denominados por algunos testamentos vitales) destinados a facilitar su liquidacin total o parcial en caso de necesidad. Junto a dichas medidas, las mejoras actualmente en estudio se concretan en la armonizacin (o incluso en la unificacin, si hablamos de la Unin Europea) de las herramientas jurdicas a disposicin de los poderes pblicos para asegurar la rpida resolucin de cualquier episodio de crisis sin que los servicios bancarios bsicos resulten afectados. Se trata, en definitiva, de poder transferir el negocio bancario a corazn abierto, ya sea mediante operaciones de cesin coactiva de activos y pasivos o de toma y posterior enajenacin de una participacin de control en la entidad intervenida. El planteamiento de reformas en este sentido suscita, como es lgico, la dificultad de conciliar la proteccin del inters pblico derivado de un proceso de liquidacin ordenada bancaria con los derechos de accionistas y acreedores institucionales. Nos enfrentamos, en consecuencia, a una tarea difcil, que solo ser posible si aunamos la necesaria voluntad poltica con el esfuerzo de la industria y la decisiva contribucin del mejor razonamiento jurdico. Ha llegado por tanto la hora de los juristas que son quienes en las sociedades modernas tienen, llegado el caso, la experiencia en la gestin de las controversias, pues la desagregacin de la propiedad bancaria en los casos en que proceda la resolucin de una entidad, debe estar basada en la bsqueda de frmulas legales que compatibilicen la gestin ms eficiente de los activos del sistema financiero con el ms escrupuloso respeto a los derechos de los diversos agentes implicados, dando armona al sistema regulatorio bancario en su conjunto. Esta labor ser, qu duda cabe, multidisciplinar, pero la aportacin de los expertos jurdicos adquiere un tono relevante. Por tanto, debemos felicitar a la Abogaca del Estado siempre atenta y siempre conocedora de las necesidades de los poderes pblicos- por dedicar una especial atencin a estos fenmenos, como lo evidencia la propia celebracin de estas jornadas en este oportuno momento. Y con estas reflexiones en voz alta, permtanme finalizar felicitando a los organizadores y ponentes por estas Jornadas, sin duda de gran inters, y agradeciendo a todos su asistencia e intervencin en las mismas. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Conference at the luncheon-colloquium organized by the Financial Club of Vigo. "Perspectivas de la economa espaola"
text: Vigo, 26 January 2010 Outlook for the Spanish economy Conference at the Financial Club of Vigo Miguel Fern87ndez Ord9796ez Governor Good morning, and a special thanks to the Financial Club of Vigo, for giving me the opportunity to share with you some reflections on the perspectives of the economy and the financial system of our country. The first thing I want to tell you is that I look to the future with optimism. Some will not understand this optimism at a time when we receive very negative news about unemployment and the situation of companies, or when there is an abundance of criticism, more or less well-founded, that is being made beyond our borders about the Spanish economy. But I am convinced that if we adopt some profound structural reforms as soon as possible, we can restart another path of growth and job creation which, as has happened in the last 30 years, will continue to bring us closer to the levels of income, wealth and well-being of our main European partners. It is also true that if these reforms are not adopted promptly, or are not ambitious enough, a period of serious difficulties could open up before us. A year ago, in Zaragoza, I explained in detail the specific challenges facing our economy after 14 years of almost spectacular, but also unbalanced, growth. I am not going to repeat here everything that, incidentally, is still in force, but I do want to remind you of something because, although it is clear that the international crisis has caused us to go through difficulties similar to those suffered by most developed economies, it would be dangerous to fall into the temptation of thinking that our main problems have arisen only as a result of that crisis and not because of our own imbalances accumulated during that stage of the crisis. growth. What, in short, are the problems facing our economy? In addition to an excessive concentration of resources in the real estate sector, during those years of expansion, the Spanish economy accumulated a substantial loss of competitiveness in relation to our European partners. It is true that this also happened other times in the past, and yet we moved forward. It's true, but now there are some differences. This time we have to add to this loss of competitiveness the exceptional increase in indebtedness to which both families and, above all, companies have resorted. This time we must also add the challenge of dealing with a public deficit of historic dimensions. But what is more important is that in the past we were not part of a currency area and then there was devaluation, which almost automatically impoverished workers, or inflation, which reduced their wages but made it easier for the state to improve its income. Today you will thank me if I did not talk to you in detail about all this. In the reports of the Bank of Spain and in my appearances before Parliament you will find an extensive analysis of the causes that have led us to where we are, the different possible scenarios or the inescapable reforms. There are very important reforms d0 such as education or pensions d0 that I will not even mention today. Today I will only talk about the reforms which, in my opinion, do not allow for further delay. Since the turbulence began in the summer of 2007, enough time has passed to know what we have to do and, therefore, the only thing that is involved is to encourage us to do it as soon as possible. Unemployment and the state of public accounts are our two major challenges. The labor reform and the policy of budgetary consolidation are the two most necessary and urgent reforms. Unemployment, because it is closely related to all the other challenges we have in the Spanish economy: growth, the need to recover a level of public income that maintains the welfare state or the situation of the financial system. Therefore, the reform of our labor institutions is absolutely essential to get out of the situation in which we find ourselves. It is a more than evident fact that Spain stands out in the developed world for the uniqueness of its labor institutions and for the pernicious effects that this singularity produces. The evidence is overwhelming if we review what in school they called "Geography and History". If we look at what our history says, it is the third time that Spain reaches unemployment levels of the order of 20%, rates unknown in any developed country. It is true that in mid-2007 we achieved the lowest unemployment rate in the last 30 years: 8%. But, if we take a look now at the Geography, we will see that other countries have not even reached that unemployment rate now, after having suffered during these two years the biggest crisis since the thirties. Whether we look to the past, then, or look at what happens in other countries, we know that we have to change what does not work. Nor should we underestimate the magnitude of our problem of imbalance in public accounts. Although our country had a relatively low level of public debt at the beginning of the crisis, it is very possible that 2009 will close with a public deficit that can be described as "historic". And if we move from History to Geography, we will see that the current Spanish deficit is one of the largest in developed countries. Therefore, bringing our labor institutions closer to those of other developed countries and now facing a budgetary consolidation that saves us in the future more painful cuts in public spending, are the two most urgent measures to recover growth. The immediate adoption of ambitious measures to help resolve unemployment and the fiscal situation is an essential step to achieve what, in the end, is the key to getting out of the crisis: recovering confidence. If the future is not trusted, the country will remain idle, or with mediocre growth. Consumers need to be sure that their future will not be marked by unemployment. Investment will continue not to contribute to growth as long as companies do not see clear the future of their sales, that is, that of consumers. And banks and savings banks will only be more active than now in granting loans if they trust that the future of workers and companies will allow them to repay those loans. The State itself will be able to meet its financing needs with lower costs if investors in our securities are confident that we will soon return to sustained growth. Regaining trust is therefore essential. And after two years of crisis we know very well that waiting for our problems to disappear when the international crisis ends, without having made the necessary reforms, does not lead us to regain confidence. Only if all consumers, entrepreneurs, investors, etc., perceive that we are willing to reform whatever is necessary to restore growth, confidence will return. The labor reform involves reviewing a large set of institutions (hiring, negotiation, employment services, training, administrative intervention, etc.) in which we deviate much from what other countries do. Today, for the sake of brevity, I will talk about only one, collective bargaining. Of the reform of contracting, which is undoubtedly important, I think that some proposals known in recent months, such as the document published by 100 of the best economists in the country, have served to clearly expose the deficiencies and have put on the table some interesting ideas about what can be done. But at the moment the most urgent reform is that of collective bargaining because it can help a lot to stop the bleeding of unemployment, recover some competitiveness and improve productivity and, in this way, take advantage of the recovery that is beginning in the world economy. This reform is particularly necessary for medium-sized and small enterprises, which are particularly affected by the lack of flexibility in the current system. These companies often do not have the capacity and tools to take advantage of complicated labour systems. For SMEs it is very important that the reforms that are carried out lead to simple and easy to implement solutions. It would be necessary to ensure that, without major complications, the workers of any company could agree with their employers what best suits them. In the current situation this is not possible as a result of sectoral and regional agreements, which impose a significant degree of rigidity both in the setting of wages and in all those aspects that have to do with the internal organization of work in companies. As a result of this lack of flexibility, in circumstances as adverse as those of recent quarters, many companies are forced to do just the opposite of what their workers would like, such as reducing the workforce or even ending up closing and laying off 100% of their employees. To change this, it would not be necessary to abolish sectoral or regional agreements agreed by trade unions and employers. These agreements could serve as a reference or safety net for all those workers and employers who fail to reach an agreement at company level. The key is to find a simple legal mechanism that allows Spanish workers to reach agreements with their employers to keep their jobs. In addition, for those companies that are not in difficulty, collective bargaining at company level is a capital instrument to enable productivity gains, which, let us not forget, is what allows wages to be increased on a lasting basis. Some structural reforms bring improvements for everyone. Thus, both the reform of collective bargaining and the reform of hiring, if implemented without altering the conditions of dismissal of workers currently hired, would favor all workers, both unemployed and employed. Unfortunately, this does not happen with the public spending reform policies necessary to return to healthy public accounts, which are much more difficult to design and which will require an exceptional effort from everyone, and especially from the autonomous communities and municipalities, because they are the entities that concentrate most public spending and the largest number of civil servants. Of course, the central administration also has an inexcusable responsibility because many of the expenses of the autonomous communities themselves are determined by state regulation. We know the enormous difficulty of the parliaments of centralised countries in deciding where to reduce expenditure. But in countries with a budgetary decentralization as intense as Spain, the difficulties increase and this should lead us to increase the exercise of responsibility of both to achieve the resolution of a problem that affects us all. As has been said, bringing our deficit back to sustainable levels is still feasible, but the usual plans, however ambitious, of pure reduction of budget items will not suffice, but it will be essential to undertake, in each of the expenditure headings, profound structural reforms. Other countries, such as the Nordic countries, which suffered a similar fiscal crisis in the nineties, managed to maintain the essence of the welfare state thanks to the adoption of bold reforms throughout the range of public spending. I think we could learn something from them. I will also take advantage of this speech to comment on the outlook for the banking system. At the beginning of the crisis, in all my lectures I stressed that Spain faced it with two very firm supports, which other countries did not have. On the one hand, we had healthy public accounts, a budget surplus unknown in the large countries and a level of public debt that was among the lowest in developed countries. The other support was the banking system, which, well regulated by the governments and the Courts, well supervised by the Bank of Spain and well managed by most of our banks and savings banks, allowed us to face the beginning of the turbulence and the crisis on a solid foundation that, as we have been able to verify amply, did not exist in other countries. Well, unfortunately, now the situation of the public accounts has gone from being a support to being a burden that will hinder our recovery. Is the same thing going to happen with our banking system? I don't think so. Most banks and savings banks continue to show a solidity that should give us great confidence. In fact, only a minority of entities have difficulties. But we cannot forget that the relationship between the economy and the banking system is very close. In the same way that the solidity of our financial system has helped us to move through these two years of crisis, it is equally true that if we do not adopt urgent reforms that allow us to recover growth within a reasonable time, we could see more entities with high NPL ratios, which would prevent them from actively contributing to sustaining the economy and supporting the recovery. It would be regrettable if, by not doing now what is essential to improve confidence and change the growth expectations of our economy, what to date has been a support ends up being an additional burden. This would hinder the provision of credit and also increase public spending aimed at helping banks, aggravating the imbalance in public accounts. It is very interesting to understand the importance of unemployment and labour reform for the supervisor of the banking system, because both the public deficit and the situation of our financial system depend to a large extent on the evolution of unemployment. If unemployment continues to rise, we will have more problems. If, on the other hand, reforms aimed at rapidly improving the employment situation are adopted, banks and savings banks will be able to contribute, as they should, to the recovery of the economy. And by the way, I take this opportunity, as I always do, to call on all credit institutions to be responsible so that, of course, they never give credit to those who are not going to return it, but also to remind them that, if they stop lending a single euro to those who are solvent, they are throwing stones on their own roof. With regard to the regulation of the banking system aimed at dealing with the consequences of the crisis, I believe that the government and the opposition that has supported it by supporting the various laws have done what was required and in my opinion we now have legislation which, given the constitutional distribution of powers, It is the best possible. When serious difficulties arose for the financing of our entities, we reacted quickly by approving the fund for the acquisition of financial assets and the issues guaranteed by the State. Although now the most solid savings banks and banks can now go without public aid to the stock markets, we should not forget that in the first half of last year the lack of financing could have caused a serious strangulation in the Spanish economy and this was avoided thanks to the legislation approved by a broad consensus in Parliament. On the other hand, the use of the ICO, which, like everything, can experience improvements, is in the right line of helping to correct the exaggerated increase in risk aversion brought about by the crisis, concentrating on helping, above all, medium and small companies. Finally, the FROB is an appropriate instrument to manage the necessary restructuring of our banking system. Parliament has provided the Bank of Spain with the necessary instruments to manage the crisis of any entity, with the maximum possible powers to restructure entities whose viability is in serious danger. Until now, the exceptional measure of intervention and replacement of directors has only been justified on one occasion but, if unfortunately it is necessary to approve any other, let no one doubt that the Bank of Spain will intervene promptly these entities, will issue their managers and directors, and will adopt the resolutions aimed at the fastest sale or, where appropriate, liquidation of the entity. But, fortunately, that moment has not arrived and precisely another positive aspect of the FROB law is that the legislator not only took care of providing the Bank of Spain with the appropriate instruments to act when there are serious problems of viability, but also wanted to anticipate, in my opinion correctly, the appearance of these problems. With the FROB, a message was sent to those entities that in the future could have difficulties and that wanted to avoid intervention, the file to directors and administrators and also the negative impact that a traumatic restructuring derived from an intervention can have on the territories, so that they get down to work to save their future. Although this legal provision is giving enormous work to the Supervision of the Bank of Spain, I still think that Parliament was right when it gave entities the possibility of having public resources as long as they address integration and restructuring, which allows them to move forward. In these "preventive" cases of the FROB, the task entrusted to the Bank of Spain is to ensure that these operations give rise to solid entities and use the least possible public resources. Unlike cases of intervention and change of directors whose decision corresponds to the Bank of Spain, the power to use this other instrument designed to avoid subsequent traumatic solutions is in the hands of credit institutions and, in the particular case of savings banks, the authorization of the autonomous communities. My assessment of how this second possibility opened by the FROB Law is being used so far is mixed. On the one hand, although the work is immense, it has been very satisfying to see that, as soon as the FROB was approved, a good number of savings banks have started looking for integration and restructuring solutions. On the other hand, some of these processes are taking longer than they should. Therefore, I consider it essential to appeal to the responsibility of all those who in one way or another are involved in these operations so that they do not unnecessarily delay their conclusion, since that lost time could end up harming the flow of credit to companies and families in their area. What is the role of the Bank of Spain in this "preventive" phase? To ensure that integration projects are viable and result in strong entities. And why are only the conclusions of the Bank of Spain accepted against those that can be expressed by the managers of the savings banks, or the authorities, or associations, or consultants, or economic institutes, or any other organization? Because the legislator has decided that, when State resources are going to be used, the authority that supervises the solvency of the banking system is responsible for judging, with exclusively professional criteria and without any other interest, personal or collective, interfering whether an integration project is sufficiently solid or not. The Bank of Spain is obliged to analyse projects in order to approve only those that give rise to new solid entities, a solidity that is required for two reasons that the Spanish Parliament has clearly transmitted. On the one hand, because taxpayers throughout Spain are going to put very considerable resources at risk, so it is necessary to ensure that the resulting entities will be able to return them. Taxpayers would not understand if their taxes were then used to pay for projects that fail and cannot return the public money provided. But also for another reason, which is now even more important if possible, and that is that, if the entities with problems are replaced by new entities that are not sufficiently solid, they would not be able to comfortably meet the demand for credit in the area in which they operate and, therefore, we would not have made any progress in supporting families and companies in this delicate economic moment that the country. It is said that time is money and certainly in this case it is for taxpayers who have the right to have the entities that made a mistake cost them as little as possible, and it is clear that the longer the process is prolonged that cost will be greater. But time is also money for those who need credit because, while the integration processes are not closed, the decisions in these entities are delayed and, although they are few, in these times of crisis what their clients least need is to delay in resolving their affairs. The regulatory changes adopted so far by Parliament have addressed the most urgent problem, which was to facilitate the restructuring of credit institutions and especially savings banks which, due to their unique characteristics, have forced the modification of legislation that seemed to mean that only banks could experience difficulties. But it is also necessary, as the Government has announced, to continue advancing in other regulatory changes, for example, with regard to the own resources of the savings banks. Although this is not as urgent as restructuring, it is clear that the sooner it is adopted, the sooner it can be used. To face the new regulatory requirements, both the savings banks that have had or may have viability problems, and, above all, the savings banks that are well, will need to have new instruments that allow them to grow and continue serving the Spanish economy and society as they have done in the past. While it is true that the regulatory changes we are agreeing to in Basel will only come into force when the crisis has subsided, these new rules will require increases not only in the quantity but also in the quality of banks' capital. If Spain did not have equity formulas that, adapted to the nature of the savings banks, are equivalent to capital, our best savings banks could not grow or develop in the same way as banks. This regulatory modification would be in line with the reforms adopted over the last decades: to continue freeing savings banks from those obstacles that prevent them from competing on an equal footing with banks. This is an objective that must be maintained because, as has been demonstrated in our country, competition between entities is something very positive. Let me finish by going back to macroeconomics. As is happening in neighbouring countries, the most recent data indicate that the most acute phase of the contraction of the Spanish economy has already passed. The outlook suggests that a phase of gradual growth could begin this year, based on maintaining a positive contribution from external demand. This is to be celebrated because it means that our companies will no longer experience the free fall in sales that occurred last year. However, what is relevant to solving our two main problems d0 unemployment and the public deficit d0 is to increase the growth potential with which our economy will face the new expansionary cycle. As I have explained on numerous occasions and I will not repeat here, there are many reasons that justify that Spain can grow more than other European countries. But it escapes no one that the optimism I have proclaimed is conditional optimism. We are at one of those historic moments when, if we do what we have to do, we can increase our growth potential and get back on the path of development and convergence. On the contrary, if reforms come late or are insufficient, our future is undoubtedly worrying. But I am confident that we will undertake the reforms. My confidence lies mainly in the Spanish population, which for the last 30 years has been favourable to reforms and knows that this is the real secret of the continued rise in welfare. I am convinced that the majority of the Spanish people are aware that our progress has been based on changing, reforming, adapting our most outdated institutions to those more modern that prevail in countries richer than ours. The indisputable success of these last 30 years has not come from the sky but from a continuous process of reforms. And I don't see the reason why now, all of a sudden, we stop and accept that without doing anything substantial we will move forward. What I do want to emphasize is that the tasks before us are of such an entity that they do not correspond to one or more of the actors or those responsible for the country. It is a task that corresponds to all of us: central government, autonomous communities, local corporations, regulators and supervisors, workers and employers, unions and employers, governing parties and parties that are in opposition to the different parliaments, etc. It is true that some should propose and others should support. That some should lead and others should help with their ideas, that some should lead and others collaborate. But I do not believe that in the current situation no one can escape the responsibility of solving problems that today are only economic but that - we cannot close our eyes - if we do not tackle them soon, could at some point go beyond that terrain. Thanks a lot.

Mi valoracin de cmo se est utilizando hasta el momento esta segunda posibilidad abierta por la Ley del FROB es mixta. El Banco de Espaa est obligado a analizar los proyectos para aprobar slo aqullos que den lugar a nuevas entidades slidas, solidez que viene exigida por dos razones que el Parlamento espaol ha transmitido claramente. Los cambios normativos adoptados hasta el momento por el Parlamento han atendido al problema ms urgente, que era el de facilitar la reestructuracin de las entidades de crdito y en especial de las cajas de ahorro que, por sus caractersticas singulares, han obligado a modificar una legislacin que pareca suponer que slo los bancos pudieran atravesar dificultades. Pero tambin es necesario, tal como ha anunciado el Gobierno, seguir avanzando en otros cambios normativos, por ejemplo, en lo que se refiere a los recursos propios de las cajas. Aunque esto no es tan urgente como la reestructuracin, es evidente que cuanto antes se adopte, antes podr ser utilizado. Para afrontar las nuevas exigencias regulatorias, tanto las cajas que han tenido o que pueden tener problemas de viabilidad, como, sobre todo, las cajas que estn bien, van a necesitar disponer de nuevos instrumentos que les permitan poder crecer y seguir sirviendo a la economa y la sociedad espaola como lo han hecho en el pasado. Aunque es cierto que los cambios regulatorios que estamos acordando en Basilea slo entrarn en vigor cuando la crisis haya remitido, esas nuevas reglas van a exigir aumentos no solo en la cantidad sino tambin en la calidad del capital de las entidades de crdito. Si Espaa no contara con frmulas de recursos propios que, adaptadas a la naturaleza de las cajas, sean equivalentes al capital, nuestras mejores cajas no podran crecer ni desarrollarse de la misma forma que los bancos. Esta modificacin normativa ira en la lnea de las reformas adoptadas a lo largo de las ltimas dcadas: continuar liberando a las cajas de aquellos obstculos que les impiden competir en igualdad con los bancos.
