The cited figure is the simple average of the two-year average share of countries with systemic banking crises. 5See Laeven and Valencia (2018). 6See International Monetary Fund (2018). 7See International Monetary Fund, ibid. 8See Carstens (2019). 9See eg Thorndike (1914) and Underwood (1957). These reforms are a testament to the strong willingness of Basel Committee members to cooperate on global financial stability issues. At a time of growing strains on multilateralism, the Committees accomplishments over the past decade highlight the determination of central banks and supervisory authorities to work constructively towards finding global solutions to enhance the resilience of the global banking system. My speech today focuses on the future path of the Basel Committee. After a few months on the job, and having chaired my first meeting of the Committee in June, I want to outline a set of guiding principles that will help me steer the work of the Committee. These principles are high-level in nature. These will be complemented by a set of longer-term strategic priorities, which the Committee will set out in due course. Principle 1: Remembering the lessons of the past The history of banking crises is rich and deep. Since 1920, the average share of countries around the world experiencing a systemic banking crisis in any given year is about 7%.4 There have been over 150 systemic banking crises around the globe since 1970.5 The Basel Committee itself was established in the aftermath of a series of banking crises in 1974, the most notable being the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in then West Germany. Systemic banking crises have a profound impact on our economies and social welfare. The scars of the Great Financial Crisis (GFC) of 200709 are still raw. The IMF estimates that output levels remain below pre-crisis trends in more than 60% of economies.6 These deviations reflect profound structural changes in economic activity, including lower capital stock investments and diminished total factor productivity. The broader societal impact of the global financial crisis is no less jarring: the crisis has had a significant impact on migration flows and fertility rates.7 We have yet to feel the full impact of such changes. And yet, despite the painful experiences of the many occurrences of banking crises, history suggests that the lessons from such events can sometimes be forgotten as part of a so-called regulatory cycle.8 Memories of banking crises fade over time, whether because of the mere passage of time (decay theory) or due to succeeding events (interference theory).9 Vested interests start to gain momentum, and the fallacy of this time is different reoccurs. It tests our will to persevere with the implementation of post-crisis reforms. We convince ourselves that some reforms may no longer be needed or warranted, or even that rolling back reforms may be the key to achieving other short-term economic objectives. This is not a path that I intend to embark on with the Basel Committee. The Committees work will be guided by a medium-term perspective and will avoid the temptation of falling into a regulatory cycle. I will be relying on three core safeguards to ensure that we do not deviate from this medium-term perspective. First, the Committee will resolutely pursue its mandate of strengthening the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. This will define the scope and nature of our work. And the Committees outputs should be judged against such an outcome. Second, the Committee will continue its Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) to promote full, timely and consistent implementation of its reforms. It has delivered tangible benefits to date: a substantial number of deviations from globally agreed standards have been identified and rectified by members thus far. But there is scope to further enhance the timeliness and consistency of implementation, particularly in the light of signs of delays in the implementation of some of the agreed post-crisis reforms. The Committee will further assess the causes of such delays and review whether the existing RCAP toolkit and measures are sufficient to meet the G20 Leaders recurring commitment to implementing the Basel III framework in full, on time and consistently. Third, the Committees policy work will be anchored by rigorous empirical analysis, including a comprehensive evaluation work programme. The Basel III reforms are wide-ranging and unprecedented in their numbers and impact. To that end, the Committee has set up an ambitious work programme to carefully evaluate the impact of its reforms in achieving their intended objectives, and whether the reforms have had any unexpected outcomes, while also remaining mindful of any regulatory gaps in the light of ongoing changes in financial markets. This includes evaluations related to whether individual reforms have achieved their objectives, the interactions and coherence across different reforms, and the broader impact of the Committees post-crisis reforms. In parallel, the Committee is assessing banks behavioural responses to post-crisis reforms, including signs of regulatory arbitrage or transactions that do not meet the spirit of the intended reforms. This evaluation work programme will assist the Committee in filtering out the noise emanating from the regulatory cycle and to have grounded discussions on whether its reforms are achieving their objectives. Principle 2: Global engagement and transparency The Committee has a long and well established history of engaging with external stakeholders. This includes an extensive and transparent consultation process: a permanent forum for deepening engagement with central banks and supervisors around the world through the Basel Consultative Group (BCG), the biennial International Conference for Banking Supervisors, and regular speeches and discussions with interested parties on the Committees work. Our role as the global standard setter for banks demands nothing short of this. I intend to build on this commitment to engage transparently with a wide range of stakeholders as part of the Committees future work and its evaluation of post-crisis reforms. We will continue to seek the views of all stakeholders on the relevant aspects of our work, including academics, analysts, central banks and supervisory authorities, international organisations and public bodies, market participants and the general public. Banking crises affect all of society, so it is important that society as a whole can provide input into the work of the Committee. Global financial stability also requires effective collaboration and cooperation among different authorities. This includes close coordination between micro- and macroprudential policy authorities, where the Committee provides a natural forum to consider both perspectives when assessing vulnerabilities and designing policy and supervisory measures. In addition, cross-sectoral financial stability issues, such as the recent developments related to so-called stablecoins require effective coordination across a number of authorities, including those with responsibilities for consumer protection, anti-money laundering and data privacy, to name just a few. I will ensure that the Committee effectively coordinates its work with the relevant authorities on cross-cutting issues. I also intend to keep an open mind regarding the Committees global footprint. The Basel III reforms are often cited as the major post-crisis accomplishment by the Committee. But I believe that an equally important post-crisis development was the expansion of the Committees membership, resulting in the current 45 members from 28 jurisdictions and nine observers. For example, the BCG has gradually expanded as well over time. Principle 3: A disciplined focus on global financial stability issues My third guiding principle is to focus on financial stability issues that require global responses, and to consider the full spectrum of possible policy and/or supervisory responses to such issues. Financial stability is a global public good. The cross-border spillovers of financial distress can result in an under-investment in financial stability by individual jurisdictions.10 So an open global financial system requires global prudential standards. Just like how monetary policy may face a macroeconomic trilemma, one can think of a financial trilemma, whereby any two of global financial stability, financial integration and national financial policies can be achieved, but not all three.11 If we want to achieve the first two of these objectives, then this calls for a minimum set of global standards. Failure on this count could result in regulatory fragmentation, regulatory arbitrage and an uneven playing field for internationally active banks. 10 See Eichengreen (2006). 11 See Obstfeld and Taylor (1998); and Schoenmaker (2011). Accordingly, the Committee will continue to focus its work on those areas that require a global and coordinated response. This is how the Committee adds value and complements the work of its individual members. Indeed, the need for global standards is not incompatible with additional financial stability measures at the national or regional level. The Committee sets minimum standards to provide a common financial stability baseline across jurisdictions. Jurisdictions are, of course, free and in fact encouraged to go beyond this baseline if the size and structure of their banking system and the associated risks warrant additional measures. Such measures only reinforce global financial stability. More generally, the Basel Framework provides authorities with the possibility of designing a proportional domestic prudential regulatory regime. As you know, the Basel Framework is expected to be implemented in full by Basel Committee member jurisdictions for internationally active banks. The Committee recognises that non-Committee jurisdictions may wish to implement some or all of the Basel III framework for a number of reasons. And Committee jurisdictions may also wish to adapt a proportionate regime for non-internationally active banks. The Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision  which are relevant for all banks and jurisdictions around the world  embed the role of proportionality. In practice, this means that jurisdictions could implement the most appropriate approaches among those available in the Basel Framework (ie among the range of standardised and internally modelled approaches) for internationally active banks in member jurisdictions. There is no expectation that banks must use internally modelled approaches. And, for non-internationally active banks, and for non-member jurisdictions, this could also mean implementing standards that are broadly consistent with the principles of the applicable Basel standards. Moreover, in considering how to respond to global financial stability issues, the Committee will consider the full suite of its toolkit. This includes both policy and supervisory measures. Indeed, supervision is an integral aspect of the Committees work and complements our policy standards. Indeed, the Basel III reforms will only truly be successful if supervisors actively and continuously ensure that banks are complying with both the letter and spirit of the standards. Principle 4: Adopting a forward-looking approach My fourth and final principle relates to the need to adopt a forward-looking approach to our work. Consider the following excerpt of a Basel Committee publication: continuing technological innovation and competition among existing banking organisations and new entrants have allowed for a much wider array of banking products and services to become accessible and delivered You may be forgiven for thinking that this quote comes from a recent publication. In fact, it was published more than 18 years ago as part of the Committees risk management principles for electronic banking. The fact that these points are still relevant today highlights the constant evolution of the financial system. As was the case 18 years ago, we are witnessing rapid developments in financial innovation and changes to the structure of the financial system. Some of these changes may contribute positively to financial stability, while others may be more dubious in nature. In the face of such developments, regulation and supervision must keep pace. Put simply: standing still means going backwards. I occasionally hear the assertion that policymakers are forever fighting the last war, and that the next financial crisis will be different from the previous one. This framing of the issue entails a false dichotomy, suggesting that one can either look back and respond to a previous crisis or look ahead and mitigate future risks. In fact, both of these courses of action can, and must, be pursued. The Basel III reforms have indeed been mainly shaped in response to the material weaknesses in the banking system exposed by the GFC. But these reforms are complemented with an active forward-looking approach to the Committees current policy and supervisory work. There is no shortage of risks affecting the banking system today. Banks are navigating in a river filled with conjunctural risks, including low or negative interest rates, and increasing corporate and government debt levels. More fundamentally, the landscape itself is being reshaped in response to structural risks such as cyber attacks, the growth of financial technology and crypto-assets, and the transition towards new benchmark rates. These examples underline the importance to the Committee of continuously scanning the horizon and assessing emerging vulnerabilities in the banking system as well as, where relevant, mitigating such risks. Conclusion The Basel Committees post-crisis reforms have helped enhance financial stability by strengthening the resilience of the banking system, and improving the capacity and sustainability of the provision of financial services to the real economy. Looking ahead, the Committee will continue to be guided by its mandate of strengthening the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide. In this endeavour, we will not forget the lessons of the past. We will continue to engage actively with all interested stakeholders in a transparent manner. We will focus on global financial stability issues that require a global response. And we will adopt a forward-looking approach to assessing emerging vulnerabilities. Title: Opening speech at the First Conference on Sustainable Finance, organized by ABANCA, Association of Spanish Issuers, and finReg360
text: October 18, 2019 Keynote address I Conference on Sustainable Finance / ABANCA, Association of Spanish Issuers and finReg360 Margarita Delgado Subgobernadora Good morning and many thanks to ABANCA, Spanish Issuers and finReg360 for their kind invitation to open this first conference on sustainable finance. The fact that, as the title indicates, it is the first day leads us to conclude two things. Firstly, the relatively novel nature of this topic; Secondly, that there is a clear intention to organize successive editions, which means that sustainable finance is not a passing fad and is here to stay. I fully agree with both conclusions. Introduction Climate change and public opinion You only have to review the news of this summer to see that concern about climate change in public opinion is growing. Fortunately, a majority of citizens are gradually becoming aware of the importance of this issue. The number of people convinced of the problem and its magnitude is growing, while the group of 'climate skeptics' is decreasing. According to a recent survey by the Elcano Royal Institute1, 97% of Spaniards agree that climate change exists, and 92% believe that humans are primarily responsible. 1 ? WCM_GLOBAL_CONTEXT/elcano/elcano_es/zonas_es/encuesta-espanoles-ante-cambio-climatico-sep-2019 For 56% it is the greatest threat facing the world, followed by armed conflicts, which are reported by only 20%. If I may, I wanted to take advantage of the fact that I open this event to verify a couple of truisms before another does. The first would be that climate change is a global issue, both in its consequences and its causes. It is clear that a potential Rising temperatures affect the entire planet as a whole. It is also clear that air pollution does not stop when it reaches a border. The second obvious would be that, being a global problem, the rise in temperatures affects some countries differently and others. Studies indicate that global warming may be economically and socially beneficial for rich countries, especially colder ones such as Sweden or Norway, negatively affecting poorer countries2. 2 Global warming has increased global economic inequality - Noah S. Diffenbaugh and Marshall Burke 3 As reflected in the work of Gonz87lez and N9c96ez (2019) The problem is also seen differently depending on the distance to the sea. For the inhabitants of the Maldives, the threat of sea level rise is a problem that is beginning to be pressing, given that more than 80% of its surface is less than 1 meter above sea level, with 2.3 meters being the maximum height reached in any of its 1,200 islands and atolls. Impact and adaptability If we focus on the European continent and analyze the type of climate prevailing in each region, we see that Spain is one of the potentially most affected countries in Europe. According to the report prepared by ESPON Climate (2011)3, Spain is among the countries where the potential aggregate impact of climate change will be of great intensity. Unfortunately, in some regions of our country there is a risk of endemic drought, which would affect agriculture and even tourism in these areas. According to the same report, Spain would currently be among the countries with the least capacity to adapt to this change. Additionally, we must not forget that Europe is at the gates of the African continent, which can be greatly affected by the effect of climate change, since heat waves cause crop production to plummet, which can cause a humanitarian or even migratory crisis. All this leads us to underline the urgency of providing a response, which must necessarily be global, given the dimension of the problem. Climate change and public opinion Normally, when talking about seeking global solutions to global problems, the citizen usually agrees. This kind of language makes everything seem very far away. However, in this case it seems clear that citizens are willing to take more concrete actions. For example, according to the aforementioned survey, 94% agree to dedicate part of the State Budget to alleviate and compensate for the damages of heat waves, drought and fires. Naturally, support goes down when we talk about concrete measures that may affect the pocketbook. The percentage of support drops to 57% when asked if you would be willing to pay more for car road tax. There is also a tendency to dilute individual responsibility, so the percentages of people who believe that companies, governments or other countries are responsible for climate change are around 70%, while only 47% of men (compared to 61% of women, much more aware) think that each of us is responsible. Despite these nuances, it can be concluded that the degree of personal involvement of citizens is high; in fact, it is even in those countries that are theoretical winners of global warming, such as Norway and Sweden. This awareness in countries that, on paper, may be favored by a rise in temperatures shows the degree of international commitment. Banking and climate change As I have already pointed out, sustainable finance is a recent development but, in reality, the fight against climate change is not such a new issue, but has been a recurring objective of international institutions at least since the United Nations Summit held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. For a long time, however, the involvement of the financial sector in this struggle has been very limited. Until very recently, climate risk has not begun to be an element that is considered in the risk management of some entities, if anything it was something contemplated tangentially in their areas of social responsibility. Of course, we must admit that it was not an area evaluated by prudential supervision either, as it was considered something outside our competences. This has changed radically, or perhaps it is more accurate to say that it is changing at great speed, since the process has not finished. Banks, regulators and supervisors are incorporating the environmental dimension into the banking management and supervision framework. It is worth considering 2 things: the reason for this change and how it will be carried out. I believe that the origin of this change would lie in the Paris agreement of 2015. After this agreement, the objective of combating climate change has acquired greater specificity and momentum, to which has been added the setting of a deadline for compliance in the so-called 2030 agenda of the United Nations. As is known, the ultimate goal of all measures is to avoid an increase in average temperature beyond two degrees Celsius from pre-industrial levels. This process should lead us towards a fully decarbonized society. But, in addition to setting a specific objective and timetable, it is in the Paris agreement where the importance of the financial system to channel, in an efficient way, the necessary resources to transform the economy towards a sustainable model is recognized for the first time. National and international actions in relation to the ecological transition Consequently, the role that finance can play in the ecological transition has also gained visibility and importance in the agenda of international financial organizations. There are a large number of initiatives, whether at the level of the G20, the United Nations, the Financial Stability Board, or the OECD. In the field of central banks, the work of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) undoubtedly stands out. International Initiatives - NGFS The NGFS is a network of supervisors and central banks created in December 2017, in which the Bank of Spain actively participates. The brief history of NGFS illustrates the exponential growth in the world of sustainable finance. Originally, the NGFS had 8 members, but today, less than two years after its creation, it has 46 full members and 9 observers, representing the five continents. Another example of the relevance of the work of the NGFS can be seen in the work plan for 2019-2020 of the Basel Committee (BCBS), which includes for the first time the intention to evaluate the NGFS report published in April of this year. This report includes in 6 recommendations, addressed to central banks, supervisors, regulators and financial institutions, the best practices to boost the role of the financial sector in compliance with the Paris agreement. In addition to these international initiatives, in the closest area of the EU it is worth noting the relevance of the European Commission's action plan on sustainable finance, to which I will refer later, and in our country the draft draft Climate Change Law, which will affect us directly. Role of banking The ultimate goal of the Paris agreement, and the consequent evolution towards a decarbonized economy, implies the need for us to change our production model. Almost by definition, a change of production model has systemic implications, so we must carry out this process in a careful and gradual way if we want to avoid unwanted economic and social consequences. The objective is to achieve what has come to be called just transition, paying due attention and support to those groups or geographical areas most severely affected by this transition. In any case, it is clear that, to be successful, any transition that implies a change in the production model must include measures and instruments of very broad scope, which affect practically all economic agents. In fact, it is worth considering how banks can contribute to this collective challenge; After all, when we think of climate change, particularly polluting activities immediately come to mind, certainly not the bank. The reality is that, despite being a 'low emissions' sector, banking has a very important role to play in achieving this transition. In addition, investors are also called to be essential actors in this change. Precisely, the role of banks and investors will be discussed in the two panels that will take place after my speech. My intention is not to 'advance' any debate, nor to detract one iota of interest from the discussions of the two panels, but I did want to highlight some ideas regarding the contribution of banks and investors. In relation to banking, I wanted to highlight two elements. Firstly, it is clear that any change affecting economic operators also directly affects banks, so it is essential to properly measure the risks arising from the transition process towards a more sustainable economic model. Secondly, I wanted to stress that, in addition to measuring and controlling risks, both banks and investors can and should play an active role in this transition. Risk measurement Physical and transition risk Starting with the measurement and control of risk, in the process of ecological transition two types of risks are distinguished: (i) on the one hand there are the so-called physical risks, caused by the direct effects of climate change, either by the gradual increase in temperature or by a greater frequency or severity of events such as storms, floods or natural disasters, (ii) on the other hand there would be the so-called risks of transition, referring to the effect that, on certain bank borrowers, regulatory measures aimed at sustainably transforming the economy, technological changes, as well as the evolution in the behavior and preferences of customers motivated by greater environmental awareness may have. Relationship between physical and transition risk Physical risks can manifest themselves gradually, for example the gradual rise in sea level, or suddenly, through occasional storms or floods. Transition risks can also be gradual, and have less impact, if the transition is made in a progressive and planned manner, but they can also be abrupt, if policies are introduced late. In addition, both risks are clearly related: the greater the ambition of climate change regulation, there will be a greater risk of transition, but a lower physical risk and vice versa. Environmental risk has its own nature, although its impact is materialized through 'traditional' banking risks. To cite a few examples, an insolvency caused by a change in customer behaviour with respect to the use of a certain polluting technology would be treated as a credit risk, while a significant loss in the market value of oil or certain collateral would be imputed as market risk. Finally, damage to own buildings caused by floods would be considered operational risk. In any case, measuring and quantifying physical and transition risks presents significant challenges. There are obvious methodological difficulties in incorporating these factors into banks' internal risk models. To give a few examples, the horizon over which the effects of physical risk are observed may be much higher than that generally used in the assessment of credit risk, let alone market risk. On the other hand, the risk of environmental transition, by its very definition, is not found in the historical record of events, so it would be difficult to estimate and validate this risk in a 'traditional' way, that is, looking at our past. However, the latter statement should be qualified. It is true that there is no record for this type of transition, but it does exist for other types of transitions. Institutions have historically been subject to transition risk, although they may have called it something else. If we look at the recent past, it is easy to find numerous examples of solvent and strong companies, many of them international leaders, that have lost their leadership position or even disappeared, in a short period of years because they have not been able to adapt to a change in technology or consumer behavior. The conclusion I wanted to emphasize today would be that the analysis of potential changes in the environment, in order to assess the possibility of business failure, is an essential part of the assessment and management of risks in the financial system, regardless of whether such change in the environment has a technological origin, customer behavior, regulatory or environmental. Banking as a facilitator of the change of production model This brings me to the second essential element to which I referred earlier. In addition to measuring risks, banks must encourage a change in the production model. In reality, this second element is a logical consequence of the first. It is known that the banking sector, through its work of analysis and evaluation of risk prior to the granting of financing, acts as an essential filter for the functioning of the economy, allowing the correct allocation of available financial resources by discriminating those projects with a high probability of success from those that are not viable in the medium term. As we have had the misfortune to see during the crisis, if the filter does not work properly, or does so in an excessively relaxed way during the expansionary stage, the negative social and economic consequences will increase during the crisis. Similarly, if banks identify, quantify and pass on climate risks in price and capital, it becomes a 'facilitator' of change, by making financing cheaper for those activities that contribute most to the sustainable transformation of the economy, while discouraging the most polluting activities. Risk governance As many of you know, in my speeches I like to refer to the issue of governance, as an essential aspect without which adequate control and prudent risk management are impossible. In this regard, I wanted to stress the importance of supervisors engaging in dialogue with banks to analyse how they are dealing with environmental risks. Many entities that already explicitly consider this risk have tended to include it within their areas of social responsibility. We must verify that the entities are incorporating it, in addition, in their strategies and analysis and monitoring of risks, and that the information generated internally reaches the Board itself. The supervisory expectation in the short and medium term would be that institutions understand the implications of this risk and are able to identify and measure it, always in proportion to its size and complexity. Two aspects should be highlighted: first, banks must be able to assess how risk may affect their business model; Second, they must integrate it into their risk appetite framework. Role of investors Green bonds Let me say a few words about the role that investors must also play in facilitating this transition. Every day in the economic press we can read news regarding the growing issuance of so-called 'green bonds', placed among investors with a higher demand and costs, in general, lower than those of equivalent standard issues. The history of 'green bonds' began in 2007, with the first issue by the European Investment Bank. A green bond should be used to finance projects that are directly related to sustainability, the preservation of natural environments and the transition to a low-carbon economy. To receive green bond certification, it is necessary that the bond complies with principles, such as the Green Bond Principles (GBP) issued by ICMA in 2014, and that such compliance is certified by an external evaluator. The market has been particularly active in recent years, especially since the publication of GBP in 2014, with issues from both financial and non-financial institutions and even treasuries. As of June 2019, the live volume of this instrument is 630 billion dollars. It is clear that the attractiveness of green bond issues among investors is an indication of growing concern about the effects of climate change, but it could also reflect lower underlying risk. In any case, the change in attitude and public awareness of climate change, and its effect on the type of financial investments most in demand, is an element that should also act as a catalyst for change towards more sustainable activities. Taxonomy International initiatives d0 European Commission Action Plan However, in order to ensure the proper functioning of these markets and improve transparency, initiatives developed within the framework of the European Commission are essential. The Commission, within its action plan presented in May 2018, includes a proposal for three regulations that affect the need to provide greater transparency and homogeneity to this type of investment. In particular, the regulations concern the disclosure of information, the creation of low-carbon benchmarks and, finally, the creation of a 'taxonomy', i.e. a technically sound classification system that provides clarity on what is 'green' or 'sustainable' (green activities) as opposed to 'polluting' activities (also known as brown activities). As I have already mentioned, several 'green' principles have been published, such as GBPs, which have enabled the initial development of the market, but there is still no commonly accepted taxonomy4. A shared taxonomy is important for several reasons. 4 The Green Bond Principles are generally updated once a year in order to reflect the latest developments on the market. There are other standards established by the Climate Bond Initiative and rating agencies have also developed criteria to assess the "green" degree of emissions destined for certain projects. Some jurisdictions, such as China, have set their own standards. First, it will allow us to perform a much more consistent analysis of the delinquency, price, or price differential between green or brown assets. Secondly, the taxonomy will enable the risk analysis in an aggregate way by the supervisor, as well as the development of macroeconomic models, necessary to evaluate medium and long-term effects on the economy or for the consistent articulation of stress exercises. Finally, a common taxonomy is needed to provide clear and homogeneous information to investors and public opinion in general, as will be required, for all listed companies, in the Spanish law on ecological transition. Role of supervisors Central bank involvement So far I have basically described a list of duties for banking, which I usually do, as the representatives of the entities present will be able to confirm. However, in this case, supervisors also have a fairly long list of duties to attend to. As I said at the beginning of my speech, the transition to a more sustainable economy has a potentially systemic dimension, so as a micro and macro supervisor Prudentially, we must be able to assess and quantify these risks, both for each individual institution and for the financial sector as a whole. Among other tasks, we must be able to assess the exposures of financial institutions to high-carbon activities, perform stress exercises for the system as a whole or define scenarios and methodologies that institutions must apply individually. Obviously, we supervisors are, like institutions, at an early stage. In particular, we are building internal governance methodologies and structures, also promoting a cultural change in the supervisory model. Of course, we are also assessing the information and data needs we need to meet this challenge. In relation to the data, for any centralized analysis we need to have sufficiently detailed information and disaggregated by type of activity, sector or geographical location of the credit. In this sense, the Bank of Spain has for decades had a Risk Information Centre (CIR) widely used in supervision, statistics and remote monitoring; In addition, the recent implementation of the SSM project known as 'Anacredit', will provide a greater level of detail of exposures to companies. Despite this, the information available will not be sufficient to cover all the objectives set, although we are exploiting it to carry out limited studies. With regard to methodologies, we must still advance in the development of models that contemplate the macroeconomic effects of different ecological transition scenarios, in order to know the potential impacts of climate change on certain economic sectors, industries or even companies, as well as on variables of a more aggregated nature, such as growth or inflation. Of course, as knowledge about these risks increases, so does the integration of these risks into the supervisory culture. I already said that we are in an initial phase, but you can see how this risk is being explicitly incorporated into our actions, yes, with a different level of progress. To cite a few examples, already in 2018 the Bank of the Netherlands conducted a stress test for its entire banking sector5 in the face of an energy transition scenario; the Bank of England has recently announced that it will use climate scenarios within its next endurance test, while the EBA6 is investigating the appropriateness of its incorporation. 5 6 With regard to the Single Monitoring Mechanism, in which we are, we can point out that it has included for the first time the risks linked to climate change as an element to be considered among its priorities for 2019. Role of central banks as investors Finally, I wanted to make a brief reference to the role of central banks as investors, both in the field of monetary policy and reserve management. Although we have not yet incorporated environmental risk assessment, we are working to correct this situation. The consideration of these criteria is very novel, and their application as well. In fact, very recently, on September 26 to be exact, we announced participation in a fund launched by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) that invests entirely in green bonds. This type of initiative aims to incorporate environmental sustainability objectives into reserve management, in line with NGFS membership. Another proof of the novelty of these initiatives is that just yesterday afternoon, just in time for this day, the NGFS published a guide on the application of criteria called 'Sustainable and Responsible Investment' (SRI) for the portfolios of central banks. This guide reflects the results of a survey conducted among NGFS members and responds to the implementation of the second recommendation of the report published in April of this year. An intensive review of risk assessment processes is under way within the Eurosystem to ensure that all relevant factors, such as environmental factors, are taken into account for the prudent management of portfolios held by central banks. Clearly, a common taxonomy would contribute to the development of more robust and robust rating methodologies. Conclusions Let me conclude by reiterating the global challenge we face. The consequences of climate change affect us all and the transition from our current production model to a more sustainable one also concerns us all: citizens, companies, governments and public authorities. However, I believe that both banks and financial authorities share an outstanding responsibility. Despite methodological difficulties, the absence of a taxonomy and the lack of granularity in the available data, both banking and supervisor, we must increase efforts to develop methodologies, controls and governance structures that allow us to assess, manage and adequately mitigate the risks associated with climate change. This challenge must be faced with realism but, above all, with sufficient ambition to achieve the objectives set out in the Paris agreement. In this sense, in the field of the numerous international initiatives that seek to comply with this agreement, I believe the developments in Europe will be an international reference and I hope that Spain stands out within this global commitment. Thanks a lot.

Cambio climtico y opinin pblica Normalmente, cuando se habla de buscar soluciones globales a problemas globales, el ciudadano suele estar de acuerdo. Banca y cambio climtico Como ya he sealado, las finanzas sostenibles son un desarrollo reciente pero, en realidad, la lucha contra el cambio climtico no es un tema tan novedoso, sino que lleva siendo un objetivo recurrente de las instituciones internacionales al menos desde la Cumbre de Naciones Unidas celebrada en Ro de Janeiro en 1992. No obstante, durante mucho tiempo la involucracin del sector financiero en esta lucha ha sido muy reducida. Hasta hace muy poco, el riesgo climtico no ha empezado a ser un elemento que se considere en la gestin de riesgos de algunas entidades, si acaso era algo contemplado tangencialmente en sus reas de responsabilidad social. Por supuesto, debemos admitir que tampoco era un rea evaluada por la supervisin prudencial, al considerarse algo ajeno a nuestras competencias. Esto ha cambiado radicalmente, o quiz sea ms preciso decir que est cambiando a gran velocidad, dado que el proceso no ha finalizado. Las entidades, los reguladores y los supervisores estamos incorporando la dimensin medioambiental al marco de gestin y supervisin bancaria. Cabe plantearse 2 cosas: el porqu de este cambio y el cmo se va llevar a cabo. Creo que el origen de este cambio se encontrara en el acuerdo de Pars de 2015. Tras este acuerdo, el objetivo de lucha contra el cambio climtico ha adquirido una mayor concrecin e impulso, a lo que se ha aadido la fijacin de un plazo de cumplimiento en la denominada agenda 2030 de Naciones Unidas. Como es conocido, el objetivo final de todas las medidas es evitar un aumento de la temperatura media ms all de dos grados centgrados desde los niveles preindustriales. Este proceso debera conducirnos hacia una sociedad totalmente descarbonizada. Pero, adems de fijar un objetivo y calendario concretos, es en el acuerdo de Pars donde se reconoce por primera vez la importancia del sistema financiero para canalizar, de un modo eficiente, los recursos necesarios para transformar la economa hacia un modelo sostenible. Actuaciones nacionales e internacionales en relacin a la transicin ecolgica En consecuencia, el papel que las finanzas pueden jugar en la transicin ecolgica ha ganado tambin en visibilidad e importancia en la agenda de los organismos financieros internacionales. Existen gran nmero de iniciativas, ya sea en el mbito del G20, de Naciones Unidas, del Financial Stability Board, o de la OCDE. En el mbito de los bancos centrales, destacan sin duda los trabajos de la Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS). Iniciativas internacionales - NGFS El NGFS es una red de supervisores y bancos centrales creada en diciembre de 2017, en la que participa activamente el Banco de Espaa. La breve historia del NGFS ilustra el crecimiento exponencial en el mundo de las finanzas sostenibles. En origen, el NGFS contaba con 8 miembros, pero hoy, menos de dos aos despus de su creacin, cuenta con 46 miembros plenos y 9 observadores, representando a los cinco continentes. Otra muestra de la relevancia del trabajo del NGFS la podemos observar en el plan de trabajo para 2019-2020 del Comit de Basilea (BCBS), en el que se incluye por primera vez la intencin de evaluar el informe del NGFS publicado en abril de este ao. Este informe recoge en 6 recomendaciones, dirigidas a bancos centrales, supervisores, reguladores e instituciones financieras, las mejores prcticas para impulsar el papel del sector financiero en el cumplimiento del acuerdo de Pars. Adems de estas iniciativas internacionales, en el mbito ms cercano de la UE cabe sealar la relevancia del plan de accin de la Comisin Europea sobre finanzas sostenibles, al que me referir ms tarde, y en nuestro pas el borrador de anteproyecto de Ley de Cambio Climtico, que nos afectar de modo directo. Papel de la banca El objetivo final del acuerdo de Pars, y la consiguiente evolucin hacia una economa descarbonizada, implica la necesidad de que cambiemos nuestro modelo productivo. Casi por definicin, un cambio de modelo productivo tiene implicaciones sistmicas, por lo que debemos llevar a cabo este proceso de un modo cuidadoso y gradual si queremos evitar consecuencias econmicas y sociales indeseadas. El objetivo es lograr lo que se ha venido en llamar como transicin justa, prestando la debida atencin y apoyo a aquellos colectivos o zonas geogrficas ms severamente afectados por esta transicin. En todo caso, es evidente que, para tener xito, cualquier transicin que implique un cambio de modelo productivo debe incluir medidas e instrumentos de muy amplio alcance, que afectan prcticamente a todos los agentes econmicos. De hecho, cabe plantearse cmo pueden contribuir las entidades bancarias a este reto colectivo; a fin de cuentas, cuando pensamos en el cambio climtico, nos vienen a la mente inmediatamente actividades especialmente contaminantes, entre las que desde luego no se encuentra la banca. La realidad es que, pese a ser un sector de bajas emisiones, la banca tiene un papel muy importante que jugar para lograr esta transicin. Adems, los inversores tambin estn llamados a ser actores esenciales en este cambio. Precisamente, el papel de la banca y de los inversores ser objeto de discusin en los dos paneles que tendrn lugar despus de mi intervencin. Mi intencin no es adelantar ningn debate, ni restar un pice de inters a las discusiones de los dos paneles, pero s quera destacar algunas ideas respecto a la contribucin de la banca y los inversores. En relacin a la banca quera subrayar dos elementos. En primer lugar, es evidente que todo cambio que afecte a los agentes econmicos afecta tambin de modo directo a los bancos, por lo que resulta fundamental medir adecuadamente los riesgos derivados del proceso de transicin hacia un modelo econmico ms sostenible. En segundo lugar, quera destacar que, adems de medir y controlar los riesgos, tanto la banca como los inversores pueden y deben jugar un papel activo en dicha transicin. Medicin de riesgos Riesgo fsico y de transicin Comenzando por la medicin y control del riesgo, en el proceso de transicin ecolgica se distinguen dos tipos de riesgos: (i) por un lado estn los llamados riesgos fsicos, provocados por los efectos directos del cambio climtico, bien por el aumento gradual de la temperatura o bien por una mayor frecuencia o severidad de eventos como tormentas, inundaciones o catstrofes naturales, (ii) por otro lado estaran los llamados riesgos de transicin, referidos al efecto que, sobre determinados acreditados bancarios, puedan tener las medidas regulatorias encaminadas a transformar de modo sostenible la economa, los cambios tecnolgicos, as como la evolucin en el comportamiento y preferencias de la clientela motivados por una mayor concienciacin medioambiental. Relacin entre riesgo fsico y de transicin Los riesgos fsicos pueden manifestarse de modo gradual, por ejemplo la paulatina subida del nivel del mar, o de modo sbito, a travs de tormentas o inundaciones puntuales. Los riesgos de transicin pueden ser tambin graduales, y tener un menor impacto, si la transicin se hace de una manera progresiva y planificada, pero pueden ser tambin abruptos, si las polticas se introducen tardamente. Adems, ambos riesgos estn claramente relacionados: a mayor ambicin de la regulacin contra el cambio climtico existir un mayor riesgo de transicin, pero un menor riesgo fsico y viceversa. El riesgo medioambiental tiene naturaleza propia, aunque su impacto se materializa a travs de los riesgos tradicionales bancarios. Por citar unos ejemplos, una insolvencia causada por un cambio en el comportamiento de la clientela respecto al uso de determinada tecnologa contaminante se tratara como riesgo de crdito, mientras que una prdida significativa en el valor de mercado del petrleo o de determinados colaterales se imputara como riesgo de mercado. Por ltimo, daos en inmuebles propios causados por inundaciones tendran la consideracin de riesgo operacional. En todo caso, la medicin y cuantificacin de los riesgos fsicos y de transicin presenta retos significativos. Existen evidentes dificultades metodolgicas a la hora de incorporar estos factores en los modelos internos de riesgos de las entidades. Por poner unos ejemplos, el horizonte en el que se observan los efectos del riesgo fsico puede ser muy superior al que se emplea de modo general en la evaluacin del riesgo de crdito, no digamos ya del de mercado. Por su parte, el riesgo de transicin medioambiental, por su propia definicin, no se encuentra en el registro histrico de eventos, por lo que resultara complicado estimar y validar dicho riesgo de modo tradicional, es decir, mirando nuestro pasado. No obstante, cabe matizar esta ltima afirmacin. Es cierto que no existe registro para este tipo de transicin, pero s que existe para otro tipo de transiciones. Las entidades han estado histricamente sometidas al riesgo de transicin, aunque posiblemente lo hayan denominado de otro modo. Si miramos al pasado reciente, es fcil encontrar numerosos ejemplos de compaas solventes y fuertes, muchas de ellas lderes internacionales, que han perdido su posicin de liderazgo o incluso desaparecido, en un plazo escaso de aos al no haberse sabido adaptar a un cambio tecnolgico o de comportamiento del consumidor. La conclusin que quera recalcar hoy sera que el anlisis de potenciales cambios en el entorno, con objeto de evaluar la posibilidad del fracaso empresarial, es una parte esencial de la evaluacin y gestin de riesgos en el sistema financiero, con independencia de que dicho cambio en el entorno tenga un origen tecnolgico, de comportamiento del cliente, regulatorio o medioambiental. La banca como facilitador del cambio de modelo productivo Esto me lleva al segundo elemento esencial al que me he referido antes. Adems de medir los riesgos, la banca debe favorecer el cambio de modelo productivo. En realidad, este segundo elemento es consecuencia lgica del primero. Es sabido que el sector bancario, a travs de su labor de anlisis y evaluacin del riesgo previo a la concesin de financiacin, acta como un filtro esencial para el funcionamiento de la economa, permitiendo la correcta asignacin de los recursos financieros disponibles al discriminar aquellos proyectos con alta probabilidad de xito de aquellos que no son viables a medio plazo. Como hemos tenido la desgracia de comprobar durante la crisis, si el filtro no funciona adecuadamente, o lo hace de un modo excesivamente relajado durante la etapa expansiva, las consecuencias negativas sociales y econmicas se acrecentarn durante la crisis. De igual modo, si la banca identifica, cuantifica y repercute en precio y capital los riesgos climticos, se convierte en un facilitador del cambio, al abaratar la financiacin de aquellas actividades que contribuyen ms a la transformacin sostenible de la economa, a la vez que se desincentivan las actividades ms contaminantes. Gobernanza del riesgo Como muchos de ustedes saben, en mis intervenciones me gusta referirme al tema de la Gobernanza, como un aspecto esencial sin el que es imposible un control adecuado y una gestin prudente de los riesgos. En este sentido, quera resaltar la importancia de que los supervisores entablemos un dilogo con las entidades para analizar cmo estn tratando los riesgos medioambientales. Muchas entidades que ya contemplan este riesgo de un modo explcito han tendido a incluirlo dentro de sus reas de responsabilidad social. Debemos verificar que las entidades lo estn incorporando, adems, en sus estrategias y anlisis y seguimiento de riesgos, y que la informacin que se genera internamente llega hasta el propio Consejo. La expectativa supervisora a corto y medio plazo sera que las entidades entiendan las implicaciones de este riesgo y sean capaces de identificarlo y medirlo, siempre de modo proporcional a su tamao y complejidad. Cabra destacar dos aspectos: en primer lugar, los bancos deben ser capaces de evaluar cmo el riesgo puede afectar a su modelo de negocio; en segundo lugar, deben integrarlo dentro de su marco de apetito al riesgo. Papel de los inversores Bonos verdes Permtanme que me refiera brevemente al papel que los inversores deben jugar tambin como facilitadores de esta transicin. A diario en la prensa econmica podemos leer noticias en relacin a la emisin creciente de los llamados bonos verdes, colocados entre inversores con una demanda superior y a unos costes, en general, inferiores a los de emisiones estndar equivalentes. La historia de los bonos verdes se inicia en 2007, con la primera emisin por parte del Banco Europeo de Inversiones. Un bono verde debe destinarse a financiar proyectos que guarden una relacin directa con la sostenibilidad, la preservacin de los medios naturales y la transicin hacia una economa de bajo carbono. Para recibir la certificacin de bono verde, es necesario que el bono cumpla con unos principios, como los Green Bond Principles (GBP) emitidos por ICMA en 2014, y que dicho cumplimiento lo certifique un evaluador externo. El mercado ha sido especialmente activo en los ltimos aos, sobre todo desde la publicacin de los GBP en 2014, con emisiones tanto de instituciones financieras como no financieras e, incluso, tesoros. A junio de 2019, el volumen vivo de este instrumento es de 630 mm de dlares. Es evidente que el atractivo entre los inversores de las emisiones de bonos verdes es un indicio de la creciente preocupacin que existe por los efectos del cambio climtico, pero tambin podra ser reflejo de un menor riesgo subyacente. En todo caso, el cambio de actitud y la concienciacin en la opinin pblica respecto al cambio climtico, y su efecto en el tipo de inversiones financieras ms demandadas, es un elemento que debera actuar tambin como catalizador del cambio hacia actividades ms sostenibles. Taxonoma Iniciativas internacionales  Plan de accin de la Comisin Europea No obstante, para lograr un correcto funcionamiento de estos mercados y mejorar la transparencia resultan fundamentales las iniciativas desarrolladas en el mbito de la Comisin Europea. La Comisin, dentro de su plan de accin presentado en mayo de 2018, incluye una propuesta de tres reglamentos que inciden en la necesidad de dotar de una mayor transparencia y homogeneidad a este tipo de inversiones. En concreto, los reglamentos se refieren a la divulgacin de informacin, a la creacin de ndices de referencia de bajo carbono y, por ltimo, a la creacin de una taxonoma, es decir, un sistema de clasificacin tcnicamente slido que aporte claridad sobre qu es ecolgico o sostenible (actividades verdes) en contraposicin con aquellas actividades contaminantes (tambin conocidos como actividades marrones). Como ya he citado, se han publicado diversos principios verdes, como los GBP, que han posibilitado el desarrollo inicial del mercado, pero no existe todava una taxonoma comnmente aceptada4. Una taxonoma compartida es importante por varios motivos. 4 Los Green Bond Principles se actualizan, generalmente, una vez al ao con objeto de recoger los ltimos desarrollos del mercado. Existen otros estndares establecidos por Climate Bond Initiative y las agencias de rating tambin han elaborado criterios para valorar el grado verde de emisiones destinadas a determinados proyectos. Algunas jurisdicciones, como China, han establecido sus propios estndares. En primer lugar, nos permitir realizar un anlisis mucho ms consistente del diferencial de morosidad, precio, o cotizacin entre activos verdes o marrones. En segundo lugar, la taxonoma posibilitar el anlisis de riesgo de modo agregado por parte del supervisor, as como el desarrollo de modelos macroeconmicos, necesarios para para evaluar efectos a medio y largo plazo sobre la economa o para la articulacin consistente de los ejercicios de estrs. Por ltimo, se precisa una taxonoma comn para proporcionar una informacin clara y homognea a los inversores y la opinin pblica en general, tal y como se exigir, para todas las sociedades cotizadas, en la ley espaola de transicin ecolgica. Papel de los supervisores Involucracin de los bancos centrales Hasta ahora he descrito fundamentalmente una lista de deberes para la banca, cosa que hago habitualmente, como podrn confirmar los representantes de las entidades presentes. No obstante, en este caso, los supervisores tenemos tambin una lista bastante larga de deberes que atender. Como dije al inicio de mi intervencin, la transicin hacia una economa ms sostenible tiene una dimensin potencialmente sistmica por lo que, como supervisor micro y macro prudencial, debemos ser capaces de valorar y cuantificar estos riesgos, tanto para cada entidad individual como para el sector financiero en su conjunto. Entre otras tareas, debemos ser capaces de evaluar las exposiciones de las instituciones financieras a las actividades con altas emisiones de carbono, realizar ejercicios de estrs para el sistema en su conjunto o definir escenarios y metodologas que deban aplicar las entidades de modo individual. Evidentemente los supervisores estamos, al igual que las entidades, en una fase inicial. En concreto estamos construyendo las metodologas y las estructuras de gobernanza interna, promoviendo tambin un cambio cultural en el modelo de supervisin. Por supuesto, estamos tambin evaluando las necesidades de informacin y datos que precisamos obtener para afrontar este desafo. En relacin a los datos, para cualquier anlisis centralizado precisamos contar con informacin suficientemente detallada y desagregada por tipo de actividad, sector o ubicacin geogrfica del crdito. En este sentido, el Banco de Espaa cuenta desde hace dcadas con una Central de Informacin de Riesgos (CIR) ampliamente usada en labores de supervisin, estadstica y seguimiento a distancia; adems, la reciente implantacin del proyecto del SSM conocido como Anacredit, proporcionar un mayor nivel de detalle de las exposiciones a empresas. Pese a ello, la informacin disponible no ser suficiente para cubrir todos los objetivos planteados, aunque estamos explotndola para realizar estudios limitados. Por lo que respecta a las metodologas, debemos todava avanzar en el desarrollo de modelos que contemplen los efectos macroeconmicos ante distintos escenarios de transicin ecolgica, con objeto de conocer los potenciales impactos del cambio climtico en determinados sectores econmicos, industrias o incluso empresas, as como en variables de carcter ms agregado, como el crecimiento o la inflacin. Por supuesto, a medida que los conocimientos sobre estos riesgos aumentan, tambin tiene que evolucionar la integracin de estos riesgos en la cultura supervisora. Ya digo que estamos en una fase inicial, pero se puede observar cmo este riesgo se va incorporando de modo explcito a nuestras actuaciones, eso s, con un diverso nivel de avance. Por citar algunos ejemplos, ya en 2018 el Banco de Holanda condujo una prueba de resistencia para todo su sector bancario5 ante un escenario de transicin energtica; el Banco de Inglaterra ha anunciado recientemente que utilizar escenarios climticos dentro de su prxima prueba se resistencia, mientras que la EBA6 est investigando la conveniencia de su incorporacin. 5 https://www.dnb.nl/binaries/OS_Transition%20risk%20stress%20test%20versie_web_tcm46-379397.pdf 6https://eba.europa.eu/documents/10180/2647097/2019+EBA+POLICY+RESEARCH+WORKSHOP+-+Call+for+Papers.pdf Por lo que respecta al Mecanismo nico de Supervisin, en el que nos encontramos, podemos sealar que ha incluido por primera vez los riesgos ligados al cambio climtico como un elemento a contemplar entre sus prioridades para 2019. Papel de los bancos centrales como inversores Finalmente, quera hacer una breve referencia al papel de los bancos centrales como inversores, tanto en el mbito de la poltica monetaria como de gestin de las reservas. Aunque an no hemos incorporado todava la evaluacin del riesgo medio ambiental, estamos trabajando para corregir esta situacin. La consideracin de estos criterios es muy novedosa, y su aplicacin tambin. De hecho, muy recientemente, el 26 de septiembre para ser exactos, anunciamos la participacin en un fondo lanzado por el Banco de Pagos Internacionales (BPI) que invierte ntegramente en bonos verdes. Con este tipo de iniciativas se pretende incorporar objetivos de sostenibilidad medioambiental en la gestin de reservas, en lnea con la pertenencia al NGFS. Otra prueba de lo novedoso de estas iniciativas es que ayer mismo por la tarde, justo a tiempo para esta jornada, el NGFS public una gua relativa a la aplicacin de criterios denominados Sustainable and Responsible Investment (SRI) para las carteras propias de los bancos centrales. Esta gua refleja los resultados de una encuesta realizada entre los miembros del NGFS y responde a la implementacin de la recomendacin segunda del informe publicado en abril de este ao. En el marco del Eurosistema se est realizando una intensa revisin de los procesos de valoracin de riesgos, con objeto de asegurar que se tienen en cuenta todos los factores relevantes, como los medioambientales, para la gestin prudente de las carteras mantenidas por los bancos centrales. Evidentemente, una taxonoma comn contribuira al desarrollo de metodologas de calificacin ms slidas y robustas. Conclusiones Permtanme concluir reiterando la globalidad del reto al que nos enfrentamos. Las consecuencias del cambio climtico nos afectan a todos y la transicin de nuestro modelo productivo actual hacia otro ms sostenible, nos incumbe tambin a todos: ciudadanos, empresas, gobiernos y autoridades pblicas. No obstante, creo que tanto la banca como las autoridades financieras compartimos una responsabilidad destacada. Pese a las dificultades metodolgicas, la ausencia de una taxonoma y la falta de granularidad en los datos disponibles, ambos, banca y supervisor, debemos acrecentar los esfuerzos para desarrollar las metodologas, controles y estructuras de gobernanza que nos permitan valorar, gestionar y mitigar adecuadamente los riesgos asociados al cambio climtico. Este reto tiene que afrontarse con realismo pero, sobre todo, con la ambicin suficiente para alcanzar los objetivos marcados en el acuerdo de Pars. En este sentido, en el mbito de las numerosas iniciativas internacionales que persiguen cumplir con este acuerdo, creo los desarrollos en Europa sern una referencia internacional y espero que Espaa destaque dentro de este compromiso global. Muchas gracias.

Title: Post-Basel III: time for evaluation
text: Post-Basel III: time for evaluation Speech by Pablo Hernandez de Cos Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain Keynote address at the 14th ASBA-BCBS-FSI High-level Meeting on Global and Regional Supervisory Priorities Lima, 1 October 2019 Introduction Good morning, and welcome to the 14th high-level meeting jointly organised by the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas, the Basel Committee and the Financial Stability Institute. Let me start by thanking our friends at the Superintendency of Banking, Insurance and Private Pension Funds of Peru for hosting this years event. It is a pleasure to be in Lima. The Basel Committee places great weight on its outreach programme with external stakeholders. Events organised by the FSI are a key channel for the Committee to engage directly with counterparts at central banks and supervisory authorities around the world to discuss financial stability issues with the aim of improving and strengthening their financial systems, and I am sure that this weeks meeting will contribute to this objective. As you probably know, the Committees current work programme covers three broad themes: first, ensuring full, timely and consistent implementation of the Basel III reforms; second, assessing emerging risks and initiating targeted policy and supervisory developments; and third, evaluating and monitoring the impact of the post-crisis reforms. Allow me to focus my initial remarks on this latter issue. Evaluating post-crisis reforms is one of the core safeguards to ensure that the Committees work is guided by a medium-term perspective. But perhaps the goals and content of this evaluation work are not sufficiently known. So allow me to take this opportunity to describe this key component of our current work programme related to evaluating post-crisis reforms. In addition, I will try to cover very briefly two of the topics included in todays agenda. First, one of our sessions will discuss coordination and cooperation among financial authorities, and I would like to comment on one aspect that affects the macro- and microprudential policy authorities. And, second, I will briefly comment on the issue of proportionality, which is the focus of another session and is another topical issue on the Basel Committees agenda. Evaluation of post-crisis reforms: an imperative for standard-setting bodies Before I get into the specifics of the Committees work programme on the evaluation of post-crisis reforms, I think it is helpful to take a step back and remind ourselves why the Committee is conducting these evaluations. Let me start by emphasising what we are not doing: we are not re-opening previously agreed standards, rolling back or watering down reforms, or undertaking a rubber stamping exercise. Rather, this is a genuine, evidence-based analysis of the reforms, their impact and their interactions. Our evaluation work programme is motivated by three broad necessities. First, it is an imperative for standard-setting bodies  and indeed, any policymaking body  to evaluate the impact and effectiveness of any measure or reform it introduces. This is an integral part of the policymaking process. It enhances the intellectual rigour of standard setting by providing an ex post appraisal of the degree of success in attaining a policy objective, which complements the range of ex ante assessments conducted during the design stage. And such evaluation strengthens the accountability and credibility of policymakers by providing a transparent judgment on the impact of their reforms. Second, the evaluation of post-crisis reforms is not being conducted in a vacuum. We will actively encourage and seek input from a broad range of stakeholders. Indeed, this is consistent with our approach to designing standards, which was recently described as one of the most procedurally sophisticated processes.1 1 A Viterbo, The European Union in the transnational financial regulatory arena: the case of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Journal of International Economic Law, vol 1, no 24, June 2019. Third, the work on evaluating post-crisis reforms is agnostic to the outcome. Our sole requirement is that any inputs to the evaluation be based on rigorous empirical analyses. As a result, I remain open-minded about our findings and any potential policy responses. Indeed, there may be as much a case to pursue additional measures or to address regulatory gaps as there may be a need to fine-tune aspects of our post-crisis framework. Framework for evaluating post-crisis reforms The Basel Committee approved a work programme for evaluating its post-crisis reforms towards the end of 2017. The programme covers three types of evaluations: (i) Whether individual reforms, or a subset of reforms, have achieved their intended objectives. For example, to what extent has a specific reform delivered its intended outcome of, say, enhancing risk sensitivity, or have a subset of reforms been effective in reducing excessive variability of banks risk-weighted assets (RWAs)? (ii) An evaluation of the interaction and coherence across different reforms. For example, are different measures mutually reinforcing or conflicting? Do different measures treat similar risks in a similar way? In principle, these could also include cross-sectoral interactions, ie interactions between the Committees reforms and other post-crisis reforms. (iii) An assessment of any broader impact of the Committees reforms, in aggregate or for a subset of reforms. For example, are there any structural impacts arising from the reforms? To what extent are these impacts desirable or undesirable? The Committee also agreed to an initial set of evaluations which relate to all three of these cases (Table 1). In addition, it is actively involved in cross-sectoral thematic evaluations alongside other standard-setting bodies and international forums such as the Financial Stability Board. This has included evaluations related to the effects of reforms on: (i) incentives to centrally clear over-the-counter derivatives; and (ii) infrastructure finance; while evaluations are ongoing in relation to (iii) small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) financing; and (iv) ending too big to fail.2 2 See the final evaluation reports on the incentives to centrally clear over-the-counter derivatives and on infrastructure finance; the consultation paper on SME financing, and the terms of reference for the evaluation of too-big-to-fail reforms. An important feature of the Committees evaluation work programme is its ex post nature. Put simply, we cannot fully evaluate the extent to which our standards have achieved their objectives until they are implemented. So our work on evaluating post-crisis reforms should not be seen as a reason to delay the implementation of Basel III among member jurisdictions. More than ever, it is important that Committee members adhere to the G20 Leaders continued commitment for full, timely and consistent implementation of Basel III. Given this ex post nature, our evaluation work programme is a multi-year initiative. For some of the topics  such as the Basel III definition of capital  the standards have been implemented and so our evaluation work is well under way. In other instances, such as the more recent Basel III standards  with an implementation date of January 2022, or January 2027 for some aspects of the framework  we are currently conducting preparatory analysis, including the design of our evaluation methodologies and the required data to support our empirical analysis. There will be plenty of opportunities for the Committee to provide additional information on its evaluations as the work progresses. And we will be actively seeking input from all stakeholders to assist us. Let me now briefly turn to the agenda for our high-level meeting this week, which includes a number of topics that could also benefit from additional analysis. I would like to offer a few personal reflections on a couple of them. Macro- and microprudential policy: two sides of the same coin? One of our sessions will cover coordination and cooperation among financial authorities, including the interactions between macro- and microprudential policy. During the session we will have the opportunity to discuss institutional and cooperation arrangements among different authorities, but let me say a few words about some of the potential dynamics of macro- and microprudential policy in the Basel Framework. One of the most important elements of Basel III is the introduction of macroprudential instruments. These instruments seek to reduce the build-up of aggregate credit imbalances (eg the countercyclical capital buffer) and to ensure that loss-absorbing resources match the systemic risk profile of banks (eg the buffers for systemically important banks). They build on, and complement, the microprudential framework in Basel III. A common feature of the Basel III macroprudential instruments is that they take the form of buffers: an additional layer of loss-absorbing resources above the regulatory minimum. Banks operating at levels below the buffers are subject to automatic restrictions on capital distributions, such as dividends and bonuses. When the restrictions are in effect, they limit the proportion of earnings that may be paid out. The rationale for designing the macroprudential instruments as buffers is threefold. First, it gives banks flexibility to absorb losses in times of stress, thus enhancing their resilience. Second, it mitigates negative macroprudential externalities (eg related to fire sales or deleveraging). And third, it prevents imprudent depletion of capital resources, by setting constraints on the amount of capital distributions. These interrelated objectives seek to directly address the outcome experienced during the Great Financial Crisis. Banks sharply cut back their lending to the real economy (Graph 1) due to a number of factors, one of which could have been to avoid breaching their capital requirements (although other factors, such as weak loan demand and funding difficulties, also played an important role). The incentive to deleverage should arguably be less pronounced in a situation where banks have a usable extra layer of capital resources  in the form of buffers  above minimum requirements. At the same time, some banks that incurred losses during the Great Financial Crisis continued to pay out dividends and even bonuses, with some of these payments increasing relative to the pre-crisis period (Graph 2). The automatic distribution restrictions in the buffer framework seek to prevent the imprudent outlay of capital resources and ensure that banks rebuild their capital strength in a timely and organic manner. But will these macroprudential buffers operate as intended in practice, or could there be tensions between the macroprudential and microprudential objectives of the Basel Framework? These buffers have been largely untested in practice, especially in time of systemic stress, so it is not possible to provide a definitive answer at this stage. However, one could envisage examples of potential conflicts between macro- and microprudential policy. For example, at a turning point in the credit cycle, the macroprudential perspective could call for distressed banks to draw down their capital buffers to absorb losses without abruptly cutting back on lending to the real economy. At the same time, the microprudential perspective may be more concerned with the resilience of distressed banks and the need for such banks to shore up their capital buffers. Both perspectives are understandable and legitimate, and highlight the importance of jurisdictions coordinating their macro- and microprudential policy regardless of their institutional setup. More generally, the usability of capital buffers may also depend on the way in which banks perceive or anticipate any market reaction to a buffer drawdown. This also highlights the importance of an effective and coordinated communication strategy by macro- and microprudential authorities. The Basel Committee will continue to monitor such developments and provide a forum for members to exchange their experiences in coordinating macro- and microprudential policy. Proportionality and the Basel Framework Another session for our meeting this week discusses the role of proportionality, which is another topical issue on the Basel Committees agenda. Over the past decade, the Committee has pursued a comprehensive and wide-ranging set of post-crisis reforms. While these reforms have strengthened the resilience of banks and enhanced global financial stability, they have also resulted in an increasingly voluminous and complex framework (Graph 3). This, in turn, could pose challenges for some banks and supervisory authorities in implementing and overseeing the Basel Framework. And it has raised questions about adequately balancing simplicity, comparability and risk sensitivity. As you know, the Basel Framework is expected to be implemented in by Basel Committee member jurisdictions for internationally active banks. But the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision  which are relevant for all banks and jurisdictions around the world  embed the role of proportionality, including that supervisory practices should be commensurate with the risk profile and systemic importance of the banks being supervised. But the Committee also recognises that non-Committee jurisdictions may wish to implement some or all of the Basel III framework for a number of reasons. For example, they may wish to comply with the latest global banking standards which address fault lines in previous regulatory frameworks. In some instances, stakeholders such as market participants or credit rating agencies may also call for jurisdictions to implement the latest global standards. The Committee recently conducted a stocktake of proportionality measures in place across jurisdictions, which highlighted that a majority of jurisdictions apply such measures.3 3 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2019): Proportionality in bank regulation and supervision  a survey on current practices), March. Yet how easy is it for such jurisdictions to implement Basel III in practice? On the one hand, the Basel Framework includes a number of standardised approaches in addition to internally modelled approaches. The former are in principle meant to be simpler to operate and implement than the latter, with both sets of approaches deemed to be equally acceptable options. On the other hand, are the standardised approaches simple enough to be used in a proportionate regime for non-Basel Committee member jurisdictions? Or are there instances where some of the standardised approaches are too complex for both banks and supervisors to implement and oversee? This is a genuinely open question, and I look forward to hearing your views on this matter. Conclusion In conclusion, the Basel Committee will be devoting a substantive part of its agenda over the next few years to carefully evaluating the impact and effectiveness of its post-crisis reforms. This work will be grounded in rigorous empirical analysis, and will require the full implementation of our standards in order to arrive at an accurate assessment. We will be actively seeking stakeholders views to support us in this work, and I am certain that our high-level meeting this week will serve as an important input.
