En el ltimo ao las perspectivas de crecimiento global se han deteriorado y se han vuelto ms inciertas; y, en consecuencia, los tipos de inters probablemente se mantengan en niveles reducidos durante ms tiempo en un gran nmero de pases. Adems, el endeudamiento a nivel global se encuentra en mximos histricos. Este contexto macrofinanciero introduce riesgos de distinta naturaleza para la estabilidad financiera. Por un lado, el entorno macro-financiero al que me acabo de referir, junto con la presin adicional que imponen algunos de los cambios estructurales antes sealados y la existencia todava de algunos legados de la crisis, est provocando que el sector bancario est encontrando en muchas jurisdicciones dificultades para generar unos niveles de rentabilidad que superen el coste de capital. Hay que recordar que la capacidad de generacin de resultados no solo es la primera lnea de defensa de las instituciones financieras ante la materializacin de riesgos, sino que unos niveles de rentabilidad insuficientes dificultan el reforzamiento de su solvencia. En este contexto, se hace preciso que las entidades sigan trabajando en mejorar la calidad de sus balances y aumentando su eficiencia, considerando para ello la adaptacin de sus modelos de negocios al cambio tecnolgico, entre otros factores. Por otro lado, la coyuntura actual de bajos tipos de inters y las presiones sobre la rentabilidad bancaria pueden incentivar a la asuncin de mayores riesgos por parte de las entidades. As, los elevados niveles de la deuda empresarial de alta rentabilidad, y la participacin de los bancos y otros intermediarios financieros en la financiacin de este segmento de mercado a nivel mundial, puede ser un ejemplo paradigmtico de este tipo de tendencias hacia la asuncin de mayores riesgos. En concreto, la informacin disponible apunta a que el volumen de deuda de alto riesgo materializada en prstamos apalancados (leverage loans) y sus titulizaciones (CLO) se mantiene en niveles elevados a nivel internacional y las vulnerabilidades en este segmento de mercado han aumentado en los ltimos aos, al incorporar estos productos unos menores niveles de proteccin crediticia y al haberse producido cambios en la estructura del mercado que lo han hecho ms complejo y opaco. Adems, la informacin disponible tambin apunta a que los bancos se sitan entre los principales tenedores directos de este tipo de productos. Estos desarrollos globales deben ser analizados en mayor profundidad para comprender definitivamente sus potenciales implicaciones sistmicas. En todo caso, en el entorno que he descrito, los requisitos de capital y liquidez del marco de Basilea III contribuyen a prevenir y contener los efectos de una asuncin excesiva de riesgo. Asimismo, los supervisores microprudenciales tienen un importante papel que jugar. En este sentido, el Comit de Basilea es un foro en el que poder potenciar la cooperacin transfronteriza en el mbito de la supervisin microprudencial mediante el intercambio de enfoques y tcnicas supervisoras. Por su parte, los instrumentos macroprudenciales tambin deben contribuir a mitigar la potencial acumulacin de riesgos para la estabilidad financiera en un contexto macro-financiero mundial como el actual. Riesgos para la estabilidad financiera que son compartidos por la economa espaola Permtanme que termine mi intervencin con una mencin a la valoracin que hacemos en el Banco de Espaa sobre los riesgos para la estabilidad financiera en nuestro pas. Como saben, publicamos nuestro Informe de Estabilidad Financiera de otoo el pasado 31 de octubre. En el informe se destaca, de forma coherente con lo que acabo de mencionar para la economa global, un cierto deterioro del balance de riesgos para la estabilidad financiera en nuestro pas. Las fuentes de los riesgos identificados para la estabilidad financiera en Espaa tambin son similares a los identificados a escala global. Por una parte, se identifican los riesgos derivados de la ralentizacin econmica global y la incertidumbre geopoltica, que est afectando ms intensamente a Europa y a las economas emergentes. Un menor dinamismo econmico y una eventual materializacin de los riesgos geopolticos pueden tener implicaciones para la estabilidad financiera en Espaa a travs de distintos canales. En primer lugar, puede llevar a que los participantes de los mercados financieros revalen su percepcin del riesgo. Esto hara que las primas de riesgo de los instrumentos financieros, actualmente muy comprimidas, aumentaran, lo que reducira la valoracin de los activos y, por tanto, la riqueza y el valor de los colaterales. Estos desarrollos podran afectar en mayor medida a los segmentos ms vulnerables como el de la deuda con peor calidad crediticia y a los mercados con valoraciones elevadas, y podran extenderse a otros activos. En segundo lugar, puede afectar a los flujos de renta de los agentes, con implicaciones sobre sus decisiones de gasto en consumo y en inversin. En el caso de los hogares, podran reducir la creacin de empleo y el crecimiento salarial. En el de las empresas no financieras, disminuira el avance de sus beneficios. El sector pblico tambin vera afectado su saldo de ingresos y gastos no financiero por la operativa de los estabilizadores automticos. Todo ello conllevara que los niveles de endeudamiento tanto privados como pblicos podran terminar siendo ms elevados de lo esperado, con implicaciones adicionales tanto en las decisiones de gasto como en la percepcin de los mercados financieros sobre la senda de sostenibilidad de la deuda. Lgicamente, un eventual deterioro del contexto macroeconmico tambin afectara a las entidades de depsito. A la disminucin del valor de algunos de sus activos se unira una demanda de crdito menor. Adems, la calidad del activo podra empeorar, dado que la capacidad de pago de sus acreditados se vera negativamente afectada. Encontraran asimismo ms dificultades para continuar desprendindose de sus activos improductivos. Como resultado, sus cuentas de prdidas y ganancias se veran sometidas a presiones a la baja. Esto es especialmente relevante en un contexto, como el actual, en el que la rentabilidad de los bancos presenta unos registros reducidos. Este es, de hecho, el segundo riesgo para la estabilidad financiera identificado en nuestro informe. De nuevo, tampoco es algo especfico del sistema financiero espaol. Si bien la rentabilidad de las entidades espaolas es superior a la media europea, esta sigue siendo inferior al coste del capital lo que, como he mencionado, dificulta el reforzamiento de su solvencia. Precisamente, una forma de evaluar la adecuacin de los niveles de solvencia de las entidades consiste en someterles a pruebas de estrs. El Banco de Espaa realiza este tipo de ejercicios anualmente para todas las entidades espaolas. Para ello toma como punto de partida datos muy granulares del balance de las entidades al cierre del ao anterior y define un escenario macroeconmico central, que coincide con las previsiones del Banco de Espaa disponibles en el momento de la realizacin del ejercicio, y otro estresado, que trata de recoger el efecto de la materializacin de los riesgos identificados previamente. La diferencia entre ambos escenarios recoge el grado de estrs del ejercicio, que, en el realizado este ao, es ligeramente superior al del ao anterior debido a la intensificacin de los riesgos a la que me he referido. Los resultados obtenidos en relacin con la capacidad de resistencia del conjunto de las entidades espaolas resultan, en general, positivos. Las necesidades de capital que se producen en el escenario adverso son moderadas a nivel agregado, aunque existe bastante heterogeneidad entre entidades. En concreto, la reduccin de la ratio de capital CET1 para las entidades grandes con actividad internacional significativa es de 0,4 puntos porcentuales (pp), de 2,7 pp para el resto de las entidades supervisadas por el MUS y de 0,6 pp para las entidades menos significativas. Estos resultados son, en general, ms favorables que el ao pasado, ya que las entidades han aprovechado el ltimo ao para reducir su exposicin a las variaciones en los precios de algunos activos, como son los activos adjudicados. En concreto, los bancos se han desprendido de importantes paquetes de activos adjudicados durante 2018 y lo que va de 2019. La ltima fuente de riesgo identificada en el informe tiene que ver con el riesgo operacional de las instituciones financieras. El riesgo operacional representa un 9,3 % del volumen de activos ponderados por riesgo de las entidades de depsito espaolas, ligeramente por debajo de la media europea (10,5%). En todo caso, el deterioro de la solvencia asociado a un evento de riesgo operacional puede ser elevado de acuerdo con la experiencia histrica. En el caso espaol, la potencial materializacin de costes asociados a riesgos legales contina contribuyendo al riesgo operacional de las entidades de depsito. Los procesos vinculados a litigios pasados tales como el de las clausulas suelo han tenido un coste estimado para el sector de ms de 2.200 millones de euros hasta junio de 2019. Adems, existen otros procesos legales relevantes pendientes de resolucin. En cualquier caso, el riesgo legal y algunos otros factores relacionados con la conducta de las entidades han tenido un impacto relevante en la reputacin del sector bancario, y no solo en Espaa. En este sentido, conviene recordar que la reputacin y la confianza de los clientes son los elementos fundamentales en los que se basa el negocio bancario. Por tanto, las entidades deben esforzarse en revertir esta tendencia proporcionando a sus clientes los productos y servicios financieros adecuados a sus necesidades y capacidades, as como suministrando la informacin relevante de manera clara y transparente. que sern objeto de seguimiento estricto por el Banco de Espaa En este contexto de potenciales riesgos, y tras un anlisis tcnico que combina indicadores cuantitativos con informacin cualitativa, el Banco de Espaa ha mantenido en el cuarto trimestre de 2019 el porcentaje del Colchn de Capital Anticclico (CCA) en el 0 %. En concreto, el conjunto de indicadores cuantitativos que guan las decisiones sobre el CCA comprende indicadores que tratan de recoger la evolucin del ciclo crediticio del sector privado no financiero y su crecimiento excesivo, la posicin del ciclo econmico, la potencial sobrevaloracin de los precios de la vivienda, el esfuerzo que representa el pago de los inters y la devolucin del principal de los prstamos para hogares y empresas (servicio de la deuda), el desequilibrio exterior, y el entorno macroeconmico. El anlisis tcnico valora la evolucin reciente de los indicadores, su situacin actual y tambin su comportamiento esperado en los prximos trimestres consistente con las previsiones macroeconmicas que elabora trimestralmente el Banco de Espaa. El anlisis prospectivo es particularmente relevante en este contexto, ya que, en caso de activarse el CCA, las entidades cuentan con doce meses para cumplir con el requerimiento. En concreto, el indicador de ciclo crediticio contina mostrando valores por debajo de los umbrales de activacin (atendiendo a la ratio crdito-PIB, que sigue por debajo de su valor tendencial de largo plazo), aunque est convergiendo progresivamente al equilibrio. Por otro lado, la brecha de produccin se encuentra desde principios del ao en valores positivos, y las previsiones sobre su evolucin futura mantienen una perspectiva creciente. Algunos indicadores cuantitativos complementarios tambin apuntan una evolucin creciente durante los prximos dos aos. En conjunto, el anlisis realizado ampara el mantenimiento del CCA en el 0 %, si bien seala la necesidad de continuar un seguimiento estricto tanto de los riesgos de corto plazo como de la evolucin y las proyecciones de los indicadores. Conclusin En resumen, volviendo a la pregunta legtima que muchos se hacen sobre si podemos dar por concluido el proceso de reforma financiera, la respuesta ms adecuada que puedo dar a modo de conclusin es que, una vez finalizado el marco regulatorio de Basilea III, el principal reto es llevar a cabo una implementacin plena y a tiempo del mismo en todas las jurisdicciones, al mismo tiempo que resulta necesario evaluar sus efectos. En paralelo, deberemos seguir alerta y reaccionar a los nuevos riesgos a los que se enfrenta el sistema bancario, tales como los asociados a la creciente desintermediacin financiera, la disrupcin tecnolgica, el cambio climtico, o los derivados del entorno macro-financiero y sus consecuencias sobre los modelos de negocio y el apetito por el riesgo de las entidades. El objetivo de nuestra labor debe seguir siendo el mismo: salvaguardar y reforzar la estabilidad financiera con el uso de instrumentos macro y microprudenciales en un marco de cooperacin y coordinacin entre las autoridades supervisoras a nivel nacional e internacional. Muchas gracias.

Title: Financial technology: the 150-year revolution
text: Financial technology: the 150-year revolution Embargo Not to be released before 20:00 Central European Time on Tuesday 19 November 2019 Speech by Pablo Hernandez de Cos Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain Keynote speech at the 22nd Euro Finance Week 19 November 2019, Frankfurt Introduction Good evening, and thank you for inviting me to speak at this years Euro Finance Week. As many of you know, I was appointed Chairman of the Basel Committee earlier this year. Over the past few months, I have delivered a few speeches that provide an overview of the future path of the Committee, including a set of guiding principles to steer the work of the Committee.1 These consist of the following: 1 See Hernandez de Cos (2019a) for more on the guiding principles; and Hernandez de Cos (2019b) for more on the Committees evaluation work programme. (i) Remembering the lessons of the past, including the profound impact of systemic banking crises. (ii) Proactively engaging with a wide range of stakeholders in a global and transparent manner. (iii) Focusing the work of the Committee on global financial stability issues. (iv) Adopting a forward-looking approach to our work. I will focus my remarks today on this last principle by discussing the Committees work on the growing role played by technology in finance, and its implications for banks and supervisors. Finance and technology: a brief history The past few years have seen growing interest in technology-driven innovation in financial services (Graph 1). This interest in financial technology, or fintech, is not driven solely by intellectual curiosity but is also backed by hard money: in 2018, total investment activity in fintech amounted to 120 billion, spanning about 2,600 deals. Since 2014, there have been over 11,000 fintech investments totalling about 380 billion (Graph 2). In parallel, we have also seen global technology firms increasing their foray into financial services. Collectively, the total volume of new credit provided by fintech and big tech in 2017 exceeded 500 billion, a tenfold increase from 2014 (Graph 3). Against that backdrop, it is perhaps not surprising to have seen fintech discussed at nearly every bank-related conference over the past few years, including this one! A number of observers have concluded that we are witnessing nothing short a paradigm shift in banking.2 Indeed, technological innovation has the potential to affect a wide range of banking product sectors and market support services (Graph 4). 2 See eg Gupta and Xia (2018). 3 See Wilde (2019). 4 Arner et al (2015). 5 Kuhn (1962). 6 See Blosch and Fenn (2018). 7 See Turrin (2019). 8 See Brynjolfsson and MacAfee (2014). Yet finance and technology have a long and symbiotic relationship. Finance has always shaped technological developments. For example, the Industrial Revolution was facilitated by the provision of capital provided by financial intermediaries in the 18th and 19th centuries.3 And technology has been used in finance for over 150 years. As Douglas Arner of the University of Hong Kong and his colleagues have catalogued, one can think of three waves of technological disruptions in finance.4 The first wave of technology (fintech 1.0) was prompted by the completion of the first transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866 and saw finance gradually shift from analogue to digital. This was followed by a second wave of technological innovations in financial services, starting with the advent of the automated teller machine (ATM) in 1967 (fintech 2.0). Fast forward and we are now witnessing a third wave of increasing technological pervasiveness in finance, coupled with the emergence of new actors and channels for the provision of finance (fintech 3.0). So, when put in a historical context, fintech is not necessarily a new phenomenon or an abrupt Kuhnian transformation.5 Whats more, the recent burst of activity in the fintech space has inevitably raised questions about whether we have reached peak fintech, only for it to be followed by a steep trough of disillusionment as part of a hype cycle (Graph 5).6 Some have asked whether we are spectators at an innovation theatre that promotes the impression of innovation and the future value that it brings with concrete tangible improvements.7 And, more generally, regardless of the advancements made in technology, the role of human judgment is an essential element in banking and supervision. Despite the growth in fintech activity over the past few years, the total amount of new credit provided by fintech and big tech companies is relatively small, standing at just 0.5% of total credit at the end of 2017 (Graph 3), although in certain jurisdictions fintech companies account for a much more significant share of banking services. But even if there may be a degree of hype about fintech, there are at least three good reasons to believe that the recent technological developments may have a lasting effect on the banking sector. First, the current pace of innovation is faster than in previous decades, with the rate of adoption increasing commensurately.8 The adoption of ATMs occurred over two decades, while internet banking and mobile banking have taken centre stage over progressively shorter intervals. Second, a generation of digital natives is growing up with a technological proficiency that is at the heart of fintech innovation. Indeed, one of the triggers of the recent fintech wave is precisely changing customer behaviour and demand for digital financial services. Third, fintech has been at the forefront in advances in financial inclusion, with large potential growth opportunities. Given the faster pace of change resulting from technological innovation, the Committee is taking a proactive and forward-looking approach to assessing the potential impact of such developments on banks and supervisors. I will discuss three concrete areas of work by the Committee that touch on the nexus of finance and technology. Technology and banking First, on fintech, the Committee conducted a comprehensive assessment of the risks and opportunities for banks and supervisors. The Committee published its analysis last year as part of a set of Sound Practices on the implications of fintech for banks and supervisors.9 The report considers five stylised and non-mutually exclusive scenarios in which fintech could impact banks, with a particular focus on: (i) who manages the customer relationship or interface; and (ii) who provides the services and takes the risk (Graph 6). These comprise the following: 9 BCBS (2018).  Scenario 1  Better bank: Incumbent banks digitise and modernise themselves to retain the customer relationship and core banking services, leveraging enabling technologies to change their current business models. For example, new technologies such as biometry, chatbots or artificial intelligence could help banks maintain a value added remote customer relationship. Banks could further innovate payment services and digitise the lending process through more efficient interfaces and processing tools.  Scenario 2  New bank: In this scenario, incumbents are unable to survive the wave of technology-enabled disruption, and are replaced by new technology-driven banks (eg neo-banks), with full-service built-for-digital banking platforms. We have seen examples of such banks around the world, such as Atom Bank in the United Kingdom, Bunq in the Netherlands, WeBank in China, and Varo Money in the United States.  Scenario 3  Distributed bank: A third scenario considers the possibility of financial services becoming increasingly modularised. Incumbents are able to carve out enough of a niche to survive, but other financial service providers plug and play on the digital customer interface. A large number of new businesses emerge to provide specialised financial services. For example, the adoption by consumers of mobile wallets developed by third-party technology companies, such as Android Pay, Apple Pay or Samsung Pay, is an example of the distributed bank scenario.  Scenario 4  Relegated bank: Incumbent banks become commoditised service providers, and cede the direct customer relationship to other financial service providers. Fintech and big tech companies use front-end customer platforms to offer a variety of financial services from a diverse group of providers. In contrast, banks would be relegated to providing only commoditised functions such as operational processes and risk management, while other service providers would own the customer relationship.  Scenario 5  Disintermediated bank: The final scenario would see incumbent banks becoming irrelevant because there is no longer a need for balance sheet intermediation, as customers interact directly with individual financial service providers. In this scenario, customers may have a more direct say in choosing the services and the provider, rather than sourcing such services through an intermediary bank. One example is peer-to-peer lending platforms, where individual customers can directly take on the role of the lender or the borrower. There are also further considerations regarding the potential impact of big tech on banks business models. As noted by the Bank for International Settlements, the key features of big techs business models are data analytics, network externalities and interwoven activities.10 These three elements reinforce each other: network externalities beget more users and more value for users, which in turn allows big techs to generate more data, which helps enhance existing services and attract further users. In contrast, while large banks have many customers and offer a wide range of services, they have thus far not been as effective as big techs in harnessing the feedback loop between data, network externalities and interwoven activities. More broadly, the increasing growth of big tech could have a more profound impact on the industrial organisation of financial services. The financial hierarchy could be reversed, with banks relegated from being in the centre of the financial system to a subordinated player to payment services provided by big tech companies (Graph 7).11 10 BIS (2019). 11 Brunnermeier et al (2019). 12 BCBS (2019). While these are clearly hypothetical scenarios at this stage, it is important that banks and supervisors anticipate the risks and opportunities arising from financial technologies and innovation (Graph 8). Accordingly, the Committee has identified 10 key implications and considerations on the following supervisory issues: (1) The overarching need to ensure safety and soundness and high compliance standards without inhibiting beneficial innovation in the banking sector. (2) The key risks for banks related to fintech developments, including strategic/profitability risks and operational, cyber and compliance risks. (3) The implications for banks of the use of innovative enabling technologies. (4) The implications for banks of the growing use of third parties, via outsourcing and/or partnerships. (5) Cross-sectoral cooperation between bank supervisors and other relevant authorities. (6) International cooperation between bank supervisors. (7) The need to adapt the supervisory skill set. (8) Potential opportunities for supervisors to use innovative technologies (suptech). (9) The relevance of existing regulatory frameworks for new innovative business models. (10) Key features of regulatory initiatives set up to facilitate fintech innovation. Building on these Sound Practices, the Committee is now conducting a set of deep dive thematic assessments on selected fintech issues. It will shortly publish a report on open banking and application programing interfaces (APIs).12 Going forward, the Committee will assess the banking and supervisory implications related to: (i) the risk management challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial services; (ii) banks dependencies on unregulated third parties and the implications for outsourcing supervisory regimes; and (iii) supervisory challenges related to data governance and management as well as data security, portability and recovery. Technology and operational resilience The second area of work by the Committee on technology focuses on the risks for banks operational resilience. The proliferation of innovative products and services may increase the complexity of financial service delivery, making it more difficult for banks to manage and control operational risk. Legacy bank IT systems may not be sufficiently adaptable, or banks change management vis-a-vis such innovation may be inadequate. The greater use of third parties, either through outsourcing or other fintech partnerships, increases risks surrounding data security, privacy, money laundering and customer protection. At the system-wide level, the rise of technology in finance could lead to more technological interdependencies among market players and infrastructures, which could cause an IT risk event to escalate into a systemic crisis, particularly where services are concentrated in one or a few dominant players. And, regardless of which financial technology scenario prevails, cyber risk is likely to only grow in magnitude. New technologies and business models can increase cyber risk if controls do not keep pace with change. Heavier reliance on APIs, cloud computing and other new technologies facilitating increased interconnectivity with actors or sectors not subject to equivalent regulatory expectations could potentially make the banking system more vulnerable to cyber threats, and expose large volumes of sensitive data to potential breaches. To that end, the Committee is reviewing and updating its existing principles and guidelines related to operational resilience to reflect and anticipate the risks associated with technological innovations. I expect that the Committee will be consulting on a revised set of principles next year. Technology and money The third area of work by the Committee on technology and finance is on cryptoassets, a field which has been recently and amusingly described as everything you dont understand about money combined with everything you dont understand about computers.13 At this stage, cryptoassets remain small relative to overall assets in the global financial system, and banks currently have very limited direct exposures to them. Nevertheless, the Committee is of the view that the continued growth of cryptoasset trading platforms and new financial products related to cryptoassets have the potential to raise financial stability concerns and increase risks faced by banks. 13 Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (2018). 14 In this regard, cryptoassets differ from central bank digital currencies; see CPMI-MC (2018). While cryptoassets are at times referred to as cryptocurrencies, the Committee believes that such assets do not reliably perform the standard functions of money and are unsafe to rely on as a medium of exchange or store of value. Cryptoassets are not legal tender, nor are they backed by any government or public authority.14 There have been more recent initiatives related to other types of cryptoassets. For example, some initiatives seek to reduce volatility by anchoring cryptoassets to a reference asset. These cryptoassets are sometimes referred to as stablecoins, although the stability of such assets has yet to be tested in practice. The scope of stablecoin initiatives varies, with some focusing on intragroup or interbank payment systems, while others seek to target a broader audience, including consumers globally. While many of these types of cryptoassets have yet to be operational, they have the potential to become systemically important.while others seek to target a broader audience, including consumers globally. While many of these types of cryptoassets have yet to be operational, they have the potential to become systemically important.while others seek to target a broader audience, including consumers globally. While many of these types of cryptoassets have yet to be operational, they have the potential to become systemically important. 15 See G7 Working Group on Stablecoins (2019). 16 Libra Association (2019). As part of its forward-looking approach to emerging risks, the Committee is conducting two initiatives on cryptoassets. First, the Committee will publish a discussion paper to seek the views of stakeholders on a wide range of issues related to the prudential treatment of banks exposures to cryptoassets. Second, the Committee is assessing the implications for banks and supervisors of a sudden increase in the role and use of cryptoassets, including stablecoins. For example, what role would banks play in a stablecoin ecosystem? What are the risks that such cryptoassets could pose to banks? Do supervisors have adequate resources to oversee such risks, and do the current supervisory frameworks enable them to conduct the necessary supervisory oversight? These important questions are being discussed among Committee members. For example, in a world where private sector stablecoin initiatives, such as the proposal by the Libra Association, prevail, banks could play different and non-mutually exclusive roles.16 Such roles could include: (i) the direct participation in the stablecoin ecosystem (for example, acting as custodians of assets that back the stablecoin, or managing those assets); (ii) the facilitation of the functioning of the ecosystem (for instance, by reselling the stablecoin); and/or; (iii) offering broader services to final users (for example, acting as digital wallet providers). Depending on their role, banks could be subject to a wide range of both financial risks (liquidity, market and credit risks) and non-financial risks (such as cybersecurity and data integrity or legal risks, among others). Separately, bank supervisors should consider whether supervisory frameworks and resources would enable them or other supervisory authorities to conduct the necessary supervisory oversight. There are also broader questions about banks business models Consider, for example, the impact on banks profitability and customer relationship base. The emergence of stablecoins as a source of instant payments will compete for commissions on payment transfers, which could dilute banks fee-based revenue stream. And even if banks become active players within a stablecoins ecosystem, they may find it difficult to adapt to the proliferation of innovative products and services offered by fintech and big tech companies. This corresponds to the distributed bank and relegated bank scenarios I outlined earlier. Conclusion In conclusion, with Basel III now finalised, the Committee is increasingly focusing its attention on scanning the horizon and assessing emerging vulnerabilities and structural change in the banking system. The growing and evolving role of technology has the potential to further alter the financial landscape. We are carefully assessing the risks and opportunities of such developments for banks and supervisors, and will take any appropriate policy and/or supervisory measures to mitigate such risks, with a view to enhancing global financial stability. Title: The banking sector at the crossroads: challenges and perspectives. VIII Diario Vasco Business Forum, organized by Diario Vasco, Laboral Kutxa, and EY
text: 22.11.2019 The banking sector at the crossroads: challenges and perspectives VIII Business Forum/Diario Vasco, Laboral Kutxa and EY Margarita Delgado Subgobernadora I would like to thank El Diario Vasco for its kind invitation to speak today at this rostrum of the Business Forum, before such a distinguished audience in which, for a change, there are many more businessmen than bankers. On the other hand, I am delighted to escape from Madrid for a day, especially if it is to visit a city as special as San Sebastian. I wanted to take this opportunity to share with you some reflections on the past and future of the financial sector in our country. I will try to draw some lessons from the severe financial crisis we have endured and the profound regulatory and social changes it has brought about. Finally, I will refer to the type of reforms that, in my opinion, institutions must introduce into their business model in order to be able to face the current environment, which is increasingly competitive and difficult. Crises and restructuring Crises are periods of radical change, in which almost everything is called into question, but I think we will all share that, if they are resolved in an appropriate way, they allow us to transform reality to face the future from a situation of strength. A good example is the process of industrial reconversion, which began in the early 80s of the last century. The reconversion painfully affected the old industrial productive fabric of our country. As you know better than I do, the restructuring also particularly affected certain areas of the Basque Country, forcing, for example, the closure of industries of the importance of Altos Hornos de Vizcaya, which, for much of the last century, was the largest company in Spain. As a testimony of that period, the Blast Furnace No. 1 of Sestao, declared a cultural asset in 1995, still stands today. The process of reconversion was undoubtedly traumatic and left behind unintended social and economic consequences. It is important that society does not forget the past, but always without ceasing to look to the future. In this sense, it is clear that, despite the painful initial consequences, the reconversion served to positively transform the economy. If we look back now, I think few of those present will doubt that the current industrial fabric of the Basque Country is much more sustainable than the one that existed 40 years ago. Not only that; Looking at the average growth figures of the Basque Country since the 90s of the last century and the latest unemployment figures available, I believe that this transformation of the economy can only be described as a success story. In fact, according to data from the latest Active Population Survey, Guip9czcoa is today the province in Spain with the lowest unemployment rate. Part of the credit for this success will undoubtedly lie with the public authorities, which must establish the conditions conducive to healthy economic growth. The banking sector also has a very important role to play in the good performance of the economy, by favoring the rational allocation of financial resources. But, undoubtedly, most of this success must be attributed to entrepreneurial activity. I believe that today we have representatives of the three groups I have just mentioned, but there is a majority of entrepreneurs, so you will possibly agree with me on that economic development, wealth creation and quality employment necessarily come hand in hand with entrepreneurship. The work of the public authorities and the financial sector is undoubtedly important, but nothing can be achieved without companies and individual entrepreneurs committing their resources, effort and work, often risking their reputation and assets, to create the wealth from which society as a whole benefits. Therefore, from a public body such as the Bank of Spain, I can only thank them for the work they do every day. If we analyse the recent evolution of the banking sector, I believe that the transformation it has undergone in the last decade can only be described as a real reconversion, certainly not industrial, but reconversion after all. After the outbreak of the crisis, Spanish banks have carried out an intense process of consolidation, recapitalization and restructuring. All this has occurred in a context of correction of the structural imbalances that had accumulated in bank balance sheets during the expansionary phase prior to the crisis. The importance of the adjustment produced, both in volume of activity and in the amount of credit to the resident private sector, is enormous. Since the peaks of June 2009, in which the stock of credit touched 1.8 trillion euros, there has been a reduction of more than 600,000 million. After the period of unbridled growth that preceded the crisis, the indebtedness of households and non-financial companies has become in line with the European average, also correcting the excessive dependence on external financing1. 1 In particular, the net debt position of the economy has increased from 100% of GDP in 2014 to 77.1% in 2018. 2 Only 2 savings banks have survived, transforming another 7 into banks. Logically, the reduction in credit has resulted in a lower banking business that has also been reflected in a drastic process of bank consolidation. To give some figures, since 2009 there has been a reduction of more than 30% in the number of entities, the most striking impact being that occurred in the old savings banks2, and the number of bank branches has decreased by more than 40% (about 20,000) while the number of employees has decreased by more than 30% (about 90,000 less). Although the effort has been evident, the consolidation process may not yet be complete. In any case, it should be stressed that, in comparative terms, our degree of progress is much higher than that of neighbouring countries. On the other hand, in parallel to this process, during the last five years the sector has managed to significantly improve its situation in basic parameters such as the quality of its assets or its levels of profitability and solvency. I am convinced that the representatives of the entities will agree with me that the environment in which the banking business is developed is increasingly complicated. The need to continue with the reduction of non-performing assets is compounded by the pressure to improve solvency levels. All this in an environment of persistence of interest rates negative, which pressure margins, and in an increasingly competitive context, with the emergence of new non-bank actors. In addition, the sector continues to drag problems of the past in the form of litigation and loss of reputation for certain past actions. All these challenges and difficulties make up a very complicated and competitive environment to which banks must respond. In the second part of my speech I will talk about the changes that, in my opinion, should be introduced in the banking business model in response to this difficult environment. But allow me, before I talk about the future, to share with you some thoughts on the past. Lessons from the banking crisis I have already pointed out the key role of entrepreneurship in achieving wealth creation. However, it is also true that, in order to develop, business activity needs financing, and that it depends on banking, at least in the absence of deep capital markets3. 3 In the EU, efforts are being made to develop the so-called united capital market (CMU) but we are still far from having a truly alternative financing channel to banking, except for large companies. Why is the role of banking still very relevant to achieve healthy and sustainable economic development? Because by analyzing and evaluating the risk before granting financing, the banking sector acts as an essential filter for the functioning of the economy, allowing the correct allocation of available financial resources by discriminating those projects with a high probability of success from those that are not viable in the medium term. Of course, errors can occur in that risk assessment. In fact, it is inevitable that they will occur, even in those entities that best manage credit risk. Overly strict concession standards can act as a brake on innovation and growth, but we must recognise that supervisors tend to be more concerned about the opposite case; When concession standards are excessively relaxed, too many unviable projects end up being financed. In this sense, the crisis has reminded us again of some lesson that we should never have forgotten. The financing of projects of dubious viability is, in the medium term, a terrible business for everyone: it is for the client, who sees his future compromised by a bad personal or business decision. Of course, it is also true for the bank, which has to bear the losses of a doubtful loan. The judicial system also suffers the consequences, as its workload increases, making it difficult to function. Finally, it is for society as a whole, leaving painful consequences in the form of dismissals and evictions. You may be thinking that this lesson is basic. Well, it certainly is, but it is also true that in full economic expansion, particularly when this expansion is prolonged over time, it is easy to forget about it. On the other hand, we must not underestimate the pressure exerted by competition and market expectations. The application of strict standards implies the obligation to say "no" on many occasions to requests for financing, which in peak moments of growth has very bad press and is difficult to assume by the entity that It says "no," particularly if competition is being lax in granting risk. On the other hand, the runaway growth of credit and the consequent accumulation of imbalances does not have apparent negative consequences during an expansionary period, but allows institutions to improve profitability, feeding back risk-taking. Sometimes, the supervisor himself can fall into that false sense of security, growth and profit that would only be leading us to disaster. I would like to underline this point: we must avoid falling into this trap at all costs. Both supervisors and regulators must always look at things in the negative. That said, it seems a little sad; In life it is almost obligatory to be optimistic and, from an economic point of view, without optimism activity slows down and investments stop; The business confidence index is a key variable of the economy. But this being true, regulation must be drafted without ever losing sight of what happens in times of crisis. For example: the evaluation of certain intangible assets, or the amount of capital needed, must be done in a stressed context. Obviously, supervision must be carried out in a similar light. It is therefore worth considering what changes have been made to prudential regulation and to the institutional framework for supervision and resolution, in order to prevent situations from the past from happening again. New regulatory framework Starting with regulation and, more specifically, solvency regulations, the Basel capital framework has been almost entirely reformulated to incorporate the lessons of the crisis. Regulatory changes have affected all the elements that make up the well-known capital ratio: (i) the definition of capital in the numerator is much more demanding, increasing its quality and loss-absorbing capacity while hardening deductions for intangible assets; (ii) the denominator has strengthened the way in which bank risks are translated into weighted assets, including caution regarding the use of internal models; Finally, (iii) the required level of the ratio itself has risen considerably, including additional "buffers" to, inter alia, cover the risks presented by systemic institutions. Almost the entire prudential framework has traditionally revolved around this ratio. However, the crisis has shown that focusing on just one metric can backfire. Other complementary elements to the classic solvency related to liquidity or the degree of leverage of institutions have been introduced. Limits and restrictions have also been implemented on the remuneration policy of credit institutions, with the aim of correcting or, at least, mitigating certain perverse incentives. New institutional oversight framework In addition to regulation, supervision has also changed radically. From an institutional point of view, we have embraced truly European supervision, as a fundamental step towards a Banking Union that provides greater security for the The European financial system as a whole, thereby promoting sustainable growth of the economy. As I have said on other occasions, we still have some way to go to complete the Banking Union; We have two pillars already established: the common supervisory and resolution mechanisms, but we still lack the third: a truly European deposit guarantee fund. In any case, the direction of the project is clear and it seems that steps could be taken to reach an agreement that unlocks this third basic pillar of the Union4. 4 Also important is the promotion of the so-called Capital Markets Union, which would complement the Banking Union in promoting the integration and development of a truly European financial market. Micro and macroprudential supervision Despite all these institutional changes, I believe that the basic role of supervision remains essentially the same. Banking supervision has been, and continues to be, eminently preventive. Our capacity for action as supervisors is very limited once the banking crisis has erupted. At the beginning of my speech, I referred to the process of restructuring and resizing that the banking sector has carried out in the last 10 years. This process has been necessary due to failures in the management of many of the entities as well as in the economic forecasts that were handled. Unfortunately, however, it also reflects a failure of the supervisor to assess risks and the lack of adequate instruments. Something that is particularly disturbing is the fact that banks did not breach solvency regulations at any time during the formation of our real estate bubble. As I have just pointed out, the regulations have changed in order to correct and avoid certain incentives, but it is by no means ruled out that structural imbalances in banks' balance sheets may accumulate again, as happened during the period prior to the outbreak of the crisis. In this context, the so-called macroprudential policy emerges, which complements traditional supervision, also called microprudential. Macroprudential policy aims to enhance financial stability by preventing and mitigating so-called systemic risks and vulnerabilities, also assessing the existence of potential imbalances or overvaluations that may affect a given sector. Therefore, risks are assessed in an aggregate way. Since 2014, the Bank of Spain has been carrying out these tasks of identifying and monitoring vulnerabilities in the financial system and also has the possibility of introducing countercyclical capital buffers. However, we have recently acquired the possibility of using additional tools to the mere activation of capital buffers. These tools are much more specific, and should allow targeted action in the credit segment where imbalances can be concentrated. Of course two questions arise: - How to detect the excessive accumulation of imbalances? - When should we act to correct them? I want to emphasize that this type of measures are very novel, it could even be said that their application is still in its infancy. The methodologies to detect overvaluations or imbalances are still under development, along with the criteria to be followed when activating and deactivating these measures. However, this should not be an excuse for not acting. We have been provided with tools that would have been very useful to correct or alleviate the crisis we have suffered. Obviously, we must act responsibly, but also prudently. Changes to the resolution framework Something that the crisis has also reminded us of is that, despite all efforts, crises of specific entities can continue to occur. Particularly, in an environment as complicated as the current one, so we must have the appropriate mechanisms to avoid transmission or contagion to the rest of the system, while minimizing the risk of having to use public funds. As a result, the framework for the resolution and winding-up of institutions has also been radically modified. Resolution planning by the entities themselves is a key element of this new framework. It seems clear that a crisis environment is not the most conducive to improvisation. Although each crisis is different and it is almost impossible to anticipate all the circumstances that may occur, everything that has been worked on beforehand will help in the process of managing each individual crisis. The other key element concerns the shift in the resolution paradigm, moving from "external" bail-out, largely through the use of public funds (bail-out) to "internal" bail-out, supported by the bank's shareholders and creditors (bail-in). This last element has involved the introduction of the new requirements of "eligible liabilities", known as MREL for its acronym in English. Obviously, the issuance of these eligible liabilities is difficult for entities with limited access to markets, while adding pressure to the income statement. In this sense, it seems that the increasing solvency of the institutions could reduce this pressure somewhat, since the higher the CET1 capital ratio, the lower the debt issuance costs. Changes to be introduced by entities Having covered all the transformations that have occurred in the regulatory, supervisory and resolution frameworks, let me briefly refer to the changes that do not depend on the official sector, but can only be undertaken by the banks themselves. I believe that both supervisors and supervisees operate with a common goal: we both want the entities to remain open, serving their customers and contributing economic development. In any case, the keys to the sustainability of the banking business in the long term are in the hands of the entities themselves. I would like to talk about some of those internal keys. In particular, I will refer to governance, as well as those aspects that must be influenced when rethinking the banking business model. Governance As banks know, governance is an issue that is receiving increasing attention from the supervisor. This is not something new at all. However, it has become crucially important in the wake of the crisis. At a difficult time from a point of view of the traditional banking business, with great pressure on margins and entry of non-bank competitors, it is relatively easy for the improvement of governance to be seen as something secondary; Perhaps desirable, but not a priority. Clearly, improved governance does not contribute in the short term to broadening revenues or controlling costs; On the contrary, it may imply the need to hire staff with a certain profile or undertake reforms that may involve additional costs. Why then this supervisory fixation? Governance is one of those fundamental keys to which I referred earlier that allow to ensure the viability of the business in the long term. It is, of course, not a sufficient condition for such viability, but I firmly believe that it is a necessary condition. Without proper governance, banks cannot manage the conflicts of interest inherent in banking. The most obvious of these would be the one that occurs between the search for short-term profit and the sustainability and viability of the entity in the long term. A sad example is the unbridled growth of credit that occurred, together with the weakening of concession standards, before the outbreak of the crisis. Business model and relationship with customers In this same context of long-term business sustainability, I would like to reflect on the reputation of entities and the customer relationship model. Banks, as much or more than supervisors, face the challenge of recovering their image in the eyes of public opinion and their reputation with customers, which is complicated while cases of the past surface. In recent years, customer protection regulations have changed significantly, in parallel with the evolution of society. Both elements imply a clear increase in the level of demand in terms of transparency, diligence, rigor and honesty expected of banks. A good reflection of this new way of acting is found in the recent Real Estate Credit Law. We could say that we have moved from the regulation of formal transparency to the regulation of conduct, which implies that practices considered appropriate in the past they have ceased to be. A very positive aspect of this approach is the improvement of legal certainty, which makes it possible to cement the future reputation of the sector. As in the case of governance, it is an element that will be key in the medium and long term, although in the short term it implies giving up a certain type of business. Of course, for it to be implemented successfully, it is essential that there is a cultural change in the organization as a whole, for which it must have the decisive support of senior management and the management teams of the entities. Again, we talk about governance as a precondition for change to occur. To be positive, I believe that there is a change in attitude in the entities, although much remains to be done. In this sense, last year there was a fall in the claims filed. According to the 2018 Claims Report of the Bank of Spain, the number of claims processed last year has fallen by more than 50% compared to 2017. Sustainable finance Another obvious change in society is the so-called environmental challenge. It is evident that there is a growing social awareness in relation to pollution and its potential effects on the climate. In fact, according to a recent survey by the Elcano Royal Institute, 97% of Spaniards agree that climate change exists and 92% believe that humans are primarily responsible. From a regulatory point of view, the ecological transition is gaining visibility and importance on the agenda of international financial organizations. There are many official initiatives at the moment. At the EU level, the action plan on sustainable finance stands out and in our country, we must refer to the draft Law on Climate Change. In the environment of central banks, the work of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) stands out, whose fundamental objective is to promote the role of the financial sector in compliance with the Paris Agreements. Obviously, the fulfillment of these objectives necessarily implies very substantial changes in our production model, which will affect practically all economic agents. I think that, once again, we should use the word conversion here. Despite not being part of the sectors with high polluting emissions, the banking sector can and must play an important role to succeed in the challenge of the ecological transition. At the beginning of my speech I spoke about the fundamental role of banking as a necessary filter to discriminate against viable economic projects. In the same way, if entities incorporate into their analysis the risks derived from the ecological transition, they become the engine of change by favoring the arrival of financing to those activities that, in addition to being economically profitable, contribute to the sustainable transformation of the economy. The consideration of sustainability factors in investments is a very relevant change that is already happening. More and more entities are joining ethical or responsible banking initiatives, adhering to international principles. The development of so-called "sustainable bonds", which are highly demanded by investors, is also being encouraged. It should not be forgotten that, according to the above-mentioned EU action plan, achieving the climate and energy objectives is estimated to require an annual investment of around db180 billion over the period 2021-2030. As is often pointed out, the ecological transition will entail risks that the sector will have to control and manage, but also opportunities that banks must take advantage of. Technological change Let me briefly refer to an element that comes up every time the future of the banking business model is discussed. Of course, I'm talking about technology. Technological change is a fundamental issue to face the future but, at the same time, it is an issue that is already fully present. We must be aware that technological adaptation requires significant investments in systems, which is difficult in a context of cost reduction. However, these investments today will be key to the future income statement. Most banking transactions in our country are still carried out through ATMs and windows, but the percentage of online users grows every year. In line with this trend, the potential for cost savings is significant. Regardless of these potential cost savings, the truth is that technology must be an essential part of the reflection on the business model of entities and their sustainability in the long term. Entities have a very significant strength in this new digital era. Naturally, I am talking about customer data, the basic raw material of this fourth industrial revolution. There is often a lot of talk about the transactional part, the quality of the apps and the customer experience, but, without denying its importance, I want to emphasize that it is even more important to focus efforts on "internal" technological change. It is essential that entities are able to extract, exploit and analyze their customer data. Obviously, this information should be used in risk-granting decisions and pricing. In today's competitive environment, institutions must discriminate against each transaction in terms of risk and cost. It is clear that banks need to pass on the costs and risks assumed in each new operation, so pricing policy must incorporate this information. It is also essential to analyze the joint profitability for each client. In this field there is a lot of potential for improvement. In fact, it is not fully demonstrated that information is being properly exploited to transfer the underlying risk to the price. This management deficiency seems to be common for many banks. of the eurozone, so, to make a positive reading, I would say that we would have a clear "lever" to improve banking efficiency. In conclusion, I would like to stress that having the information is not the same as being able to exploit it. The latter issue will be critical in the future. If banks do not take advantage of this advantage today, other new competitors will do so tomorrow. Conclusions Let me conclude. Since 2009, the banking sector has gone through a drastic process of restructuring and adjustment, a real restructuring that has made it possible to reduce its overcapacity and to purge, to a large extent, the excesses committed in the period of accumulation of imbalances that preceded the outbreak of the crisis. Bank regulation, supervision and resolution have also gone through another process of radical transformation, incorporating lessons and becoming truly European in scope. We supervisors have been provided with macroprudential tools, which we will have to use responsibly and prudently. We must not forget the past if we want to build a better future. The industrial reconversion was traumatic and left deep traces in the Basque Country, some of which are still visible, but it allowed to lay the foundations on which its current economy has developed. Similarly, the traumatic process that the financial sector has gone through must serve as a "base camp" to climb into the future. The new environment, extremely competitive and difficult, requires a review of the banking business model to respond to the new economic, technological, environmental and social reality. Only in this way can a solid foundation for the future be laid. Thank you very much, thank you.

En este sentido, es evidente que, pese a las dolorosas consecuencias iniciales, la reconversin sirvi para transformar positivamente la economa. Pero, indudablemente, la mayor parte de este xito se debe atribuir a la actividad empresarial. La labor de los poderes pblicos y del sector financiero es, sin duda, importante, pero nada se puede lograr sin que compaas y empresarios individuales empeen sus recursos, esfuerzo y trabajo, arriesgando en muchas ocasiones su reputacin y patrimonio, para crear la riqueza de la que se beneficia el conjunto de la sociedad. Lgicamente, la reduccin del crdito se ha traducido en un menor negocio bancario que tambin ha tenido como reflejo un drstico proceso de consolidacin bancaria.
