Title: Covid-19 and banking supervision: where do we go from here?
text: Covid-19 and banking supervision: where do we go from here? Speech by Pablo Hernandez de Cos Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain Keynote speech at the 21st International Conference of Banking Supervisors 19 October 2020 Introduction Good morning, good afternoon and good evening. Welcome to the 21st International Conference of Banking Supervisors (ICBS). This is my first ICBS, following my appointment as Chairman of the Committee in March of last year. But Ihad long heard about its reputation as thepremier global bankingconferencefor centralbanks and supervisory authorities. For over 40 years since its inception, the ICBS has been a key forum for senior central bankers and bank supervisors from more than 100 countries to discuss topical supervisory issues. Its enduring success is a testament to the ongoing importance that we all attach to cross-border cooperation, a theme which I will return to. While this years ICBS is being held in a somewhat different format, I have no doubt that it will continue to build on its historical achievements. I would like to start by thanking Governor Macklem, Superintendent Rudin and their teams at theBank of Canada and the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions for hosting this years ICBS virtually. I am sure that I speak on behalf of all participants in saying that we would have loved to be in Vancouver, the vibrant heart of beautiful British Columbia. But we can still recognise the fitting choice of this virtual venue. Vancouver has long been the financial centre of British Columbias resource economy. A recent history of this role vividly depicts how stock brokers, financial agents and bankers played essential roles as intermediaries in the fluid commercial life of early twentieth-century Vancouver.1 Whats more, the Vancouver Stock Exchange was incorporated in 1907  almost 30 years before the Bank of Canada was founded! Tiff and Jeremy, while we may be physically distanced around the world at this years ICBS, you and your organisations have done an excellent job at ensuring that we remain socially together this week. Thank you. The overarching theme for this years ICBS -the future of supervision in a changing world  is perhaps more relevant than ever before. The world has changed profoundly since the outbreak of Covid19 seven months ago. The uniqueness ofthe sudden stop to the global economy in response to the tragichealth crisis is only matched by the sheeruncertainty about the outlook. To borrow a sports metaphor, westill do not know if we are in the first inning, quarter or half of this crisis. Uncertainty is the only certainty there is.2 1 Poitras (2019). 2 Paulos, J (2003). So what isthefuture of supervision in thischanging world, and whatcanwe learn from the current crisis? When the former Chinese premier Zhou Enlai was asked in 1972 about the impact of the French Revolution of 1789  or, as is now generally accepted, the civil unrest of May 1968  he famously replied that it was too early to say.3 Given that weve yet to reach the four year mark since the start of the pandemic  let alone the 184th anniversary!  it would be premature to provide a definitive discourse at this stage. Yet we have already seen fundamental changes to the way we live and work. For example, we witnessed a tremendously rapid shift to remote working arrangements across many sectors. Professor Prithwiraj Choudhury will discuss the implications of the working from anywhere geographic flexibility in more detail on Wednesday, and we will have the opportunity to discuss what this means for supervision. These changes, whether temporary or permanent, offer some clues about the future landscape. So there is merit in starting a discussion about what we have learned to date and, more importantly,the futureand changesthatwe wanttosee in banking supervision. Allow me to outline some personal thoughts on these issues, which may not necessarily represent the view of the Basel Committee. The supervisory response to a global pandemic: a lesson in global cooperation Let me start by briefly reviewing the Committees response to Covid-19. At its last physical meeting in February of this year, the Committee discussed the financial stability implications of the coronavirus outbreak for the banking system and underlined the importance of effective cross-border cooperation in dealing with the ensuing crisis.4 Since then, it has demonstrated its unwavering commitment to such cooperation, with no fewer than 16 virtual meetings. In March, the Committee quickly developed a comprehensive strategy to respond to the pandemic underpinned by three objectives. First, safeguarding the financial and operational resilience of the global banking system. Second, ensuring that banks continue to lend to creditworthy households and businesses. And third, ensuring that authorities and banks have sufficient operational capacity to address short-term financial stability priorities. To that end, we agreed on a range of measures to help meet these objectives.5 To amplify theeffect of the range of government support measuresand paymentmoratoria programmes, theCommittee issued technical guidance to ensure that these risk-reducing measures are reflected in banks capital requirements. To avoid the potential for excessively procyclical dynamics, the Committee set out expectations that banks use the flexibility inherent in expected credit loss (ECL) accounting frameworks to take account of the mitigating effect of Covid-19 support measures. It also provided jurisdictions with greater flexibility indeciding whether and how tophase inthe impact of ECL on banks regulatory capital..6 And the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS) endorsed the Committees decision to defer the implementation of the outstanding Basel III standards by one year.7 Importantly, all 3 Cowen, T (2011). 4 BCBS (2020a). 5 BCBS (2020c). 6 BCBS (2020e). 7 BCBS (2020b). GHOS members unanimouslyreaffirmed their expectation of full, timely and consistent implementation ofall Basel III standards based on the revised timeline. The degree of collaboration demonstrated by the Committee in its response to Covid-19 is truly remarkable. It is a testament to the strong willingness of our members to cooperate on global financial stability, building on the long and strong track record of dispassionate dialogue and collaboration by the Committee. History has shown that collective measures to tackle global problems reinforce individual countries efforts. This time is not different: ongoing global cooperation is key to ensuring a safe banking system that supports the economic recovery. Combatting infectious diseases and safeguarding financialstability are both global public goods which know no borders and require collaboration among countries. We must avoid fragmented and disjointed measures. The path of splintered measures will neither stop this virus nor provide the bedrock of safe and sound banking system. Initial observations from the pandemic So what are some of my initial observations about what Covid-19 has taught us about bank supervision and regulation to date? I will sum them up in the form of a resilience anaphora. First, resilience matters before a crisis emerges. The banking system has thus far been the dog that has not barked (loudly) in this crisis. This is largely thanks to the enhanced resilience of banks emanating from Basel III and related post-Great Financial Crisis (GFC) reforms, and the unprecedented degree of fiscal and monetary support provided by authorities in response to the pandemic. Covid-19 serves as a reminder to all on the importance of having a resilient banking system, underpinned by global and prudent standards. Let us not forget this lesson. Second, resilience matters during a crisis. Looking ahead, there is no shortage of risks facing the banking system. While the themeof our conferenceis rightly focused on the future, we are still very much in the depth of the current crisis. The umbilical cord tying banks to the real economy means that banks cannot remain immune from deteriorating macroeconomic conditions. Many adverse stresstest scenarios conducted before the pandemic could become the baseline today. It is a question of when, not if, banks asset quality will deteriorate in this crisis. A resurgence in Covid-19 cases coupled with the unwinding of support measures could further magnify the crystallisation of bank losses. The mutation of this crisis into a banking one would be devastating. A decade after the global financial crisis, output levels remained below pre-crisis trends for 60% of economies.8 Importantly, banks now have tools in their hands to navigate the choppy waters and ensure that they do not become part of the problem. Most notably, the Basel III capital and liquidity buffers could be a powerful lever for banks to absorb shocks and maintain lending. Since the start of this crisis, the Committee has publicly reiterated its position that a measured drawdown of buffers to meet these objectives is appropriate, and that supervisors will provide sufficient time for banks to restore these buffers.9 Using these resources to absorb shocks and support households and businesses should take priority at present over discretionary distributions. 8 IMF (2018). 9 BCBS (2020d). In addition to mitigating financial risks to the global banking system, another ongoing area of focus for the Committee is to safeguard banks ability to deliver criticaloperations through disruption. To that end, the Committee is consulting on a set of principles to improve operational resilience.10 More generally, Committee members are closely cooperating in monitoring the risks and vulnerabilities to global banking system as the crisis continues to unfold. The Committee will pursue additional measures if needed. Third, resilience matters after a crisis. Safeguarding global financial stability requires us to ensure that the regulatory framework remains robust to arbitrage and erosion over time. This is why the Committee has a comprehensive work programme to evaluate its post-crisis reforms.11 The Committee is conducting a range of empirical analyses based on the experience over the past decade and the current crisis to evaluate the extent to which our reforms have achieved their objectives, the interactions among the reforms, and whether there are any gaps or significant unintended effects. This evaluation work is agnostic to the final outcome and driven only by rigorous empirical analyses on the Basel III reforms that have already been implemented. Far too often, terms such as unintended outcomes are regrettably misinterpreted as an invitation to re-open previously-agreed reforms or as pointing to a unidirectional path towards a weakening of standards. This is far from the casewith our evaluation work. In principle, any identified gaps in our framework could require additional, not fewer, regulatory measures. In the spirit of stimulating some of our discussions over the next four days, let me set out a few questions in three areas about our current framework which may warrant further reflection. These should in nowaybeconstrued asprejudging theCommittees own evaluationorhinting towardsfutureinitiatives. First, is there a need to have a greater layer of usable buffers in steady statethatcan bepromptlydrawn down in times of stress? There has been an active debate inmonetary policy recently onthe neutral rateof interest, whichis neither accommodative nor restrictive.12A clear analogy inbank supervision would be about the role and calibration of the countercyclical capital buffer or a similar buffer at different points of the cycle. Is there a need for a positive cycle-neutral buffer rate, and, if so, how should such a rate be determined? Second, should more be done to simplify the regulatory framework? The Committee has madegreat progress over the past years in seeking to rebalance the degree of simplicity, comparability and risk sensitivity inthe Baselframework.But are there aspects oftheframework that arestill unduly complex andtherefore hindering the resilience of the banking system? Are there merits in further exploring the role of proportionality in the Basel framework? Examples could include promoting further exchanges of information on the use of proportionality across jurisdictions, the development of high-level principles or a set of simplified approaches that could serve as a starting point for designing a proportionate approach. Third, have we struck the right balance between regulation and supervision? Most of the Committees reforms over the past decade have focused on the former. Yet supervision is an integral aspect of the Committees work. Indeed, many of the responses taken by members at the domestic level to Covid-19 are examples of supervision in action. The impact of the low-interest rate environment during the past decade on banks business models and risk appetite has been exacerbated by the current crisis. In addition to overseeing and mitigating risks to banks, supervision will also need to ensure that banks 10 BCBS (2020e). 11 Hernandez de Cos (2019b). 12 See, for example, Powell (2018). businessmodels remain viable. To that end,should more be done to further promoteeffective supervisory practices and coordination across jurisdictions? Covid-19: A catalyst for change.... Throughout history, many have rallied behind the Churchillian call to never let a good crisis go to waste.We have the opportunity during this years ICBS to rethink the world of banking supervision and shape it in a way to be fit for purpose in the new normal environment after the pandemic. Let me outline some examples of possible areas that could warrant further discussions. First, as the financial system continues to evolve, what role will banks play in the future? Hardly aday goes by without a mention about the rise and rise of non-bank financial intermediation, the disruptive nature of financial technology, the promises of big data, ever-greater automation and even cyborgsupervision.13Thecurrent pace of innovation anddigitalisation is faster than in previous decades, with the rate of adoption increasing commensurately.14 Fintech promises a lot, whether with regards to more tailored, efficient and faster banking services, lower transaction costs or financial inclusion. The ongoing digitalisation of finance also presents risks and challenges to the banking system,which Covid-19 has further magnified. This includes the evolving nature of cyber-attacks to banks and the growing reliance on third-party service providers. The technology-enabled disruption could result in a fundamental change in the value-chain of banking services, with an increasing role played by new technology-driven banks, financial technology companies and big tech. In addition, existential debates are underway about the role of money, whether in the form of private crypto-assets or central bank digital currencies, which could also impact the bankingsystem.15 Will we see a paradigmatic change in the world of banking as we know it? Or are the rumours about the imminent death of banking greatly exaggerated? One thing is certain: banking has always evolved throughout history and will continue to do so. Ive previously discussed the 150-year symbiotic relationship between finance and technology.16 And moneyhas continuously taken different forms throughout history. To give just one example related to our virtual venuethis week, the Indigenous Kwakwakawakw peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast made useof wool blankets as a form of currency  a far cry from todays discussions about smart contracts and distributed ledger technology!17 The implications of these developments for supervisors are threefold. First, proactive supervision must be the primary response to these changes, as the traditional regulatory framework may not be sufficient. Second, greater consideration should be given to the regulatory perimeter to ensure that theoft-cited mantra of same activities, same risks, same rules is actually operationalised. And third, cooperation among different authorities  spanning both monetary and regulatory authorities  will be even more important, given the cross-sectoral and cross-cutting natureof the policy issues raisedby these technological innovations. 13 Proudman (2018). 14 Hernandez de Cos (2019c). 15 See, for example, BIS (2018). 16 Hernandez de Cos (2019c). 17 Hawthorn (1988). So while there has rightly been a greater focus on the non-bank corridors of the financial system, it is imperative that we continue to vigilantly oversee the resilience of the banking system. True, banks business models may evolve over time and the provision of financial services may be offered by a broader array of entities and channels in the future. But banks will remain interconnected with other parts of the evolving financial system through far-reaching tentacles. Supervisors will need to proactively identify andmap these interconnections. More than ever, they will need to apply a holistic approach to assessing andmitigating the risks to the banking system from these channels, including through the development and use of additional macroprudential tools, if needed. Second, should there be a greater prudential focus on bank conduct, ethics and incentives? Is there scope for greater collaboration among different types of authorities on cross-cutting issues? The GFC exposed serious deficiencies in these areas. In some instances, misconduct by a few rotten apples in the system threatened to undermine the robustness of the barrel. In response, international bodies and authorities in charge of conduct and market integrity have rightly led the efforts to address these fault lines.18 Yet episodes of malpractice and related behaviours have clear prudential implications too. They may point towards broader deficiencies in banks governance and risk management standards. Conductrelated fines to banks over the past decade totalled hundreds of billions of euros, and proved to be a significant driver of provisions and at times a source of risk to banks capital strength.19 And, even more importantly, ongoing misconduct practices erodes trust between the banking system and the public. A moral run on the bank would have significant prudential implications. Third, what more can supervisors do to anticipate longer-term systemic risks stemming from outside the financial system? Traditionally, our focus on safeguarding the safety and soundness of banks has centred primarily around the dynamics of the financial cycle. But Covid-19 is a reminder that exogenous low-probability, high-impactshocks caninevitably findtheir way to the banking system as well. And slow-moving but longer-term structural trends in our societies can also have financial stability implications. How often can we continue to write-off such incidents as a once in a lifetime or one-off events that could not be foreseen? Examples of such shocks abound. Perhaps most notably, climate change has clear financial stability implications.20 This is why the Committee set up a high-level Task Force on Climate-related Financial Risks, which is developing a set of analytical reports on the transmission channels and measurement methodologies of such risks, and will subsequently develop effective supervisory practices. Other examples of longer-term structural dynamics and shocks that could impact the banking system include changing demographics, income inequality, and space weather.21 To what extent should, and can, central banks and supervisors anticipate and mitigate the impact of these different shocks and longerterm trends on the banking system? How can we delineate the relative roles of different possible responses, be they fiscal, monetary, structural or regulatory in nature? I wont attempt to provide the answers to these questions, but I hope that they provide some stimulus in thinking through the potential catalysts for change in bank supervision. 18 See, for example, FSB (2015). 19 See, for example, Koster and Pelster (2018). 20 See, for example, Bolton et al (2020). 21 See, for example, Goodhart and Pradhan (2017), Mian et al (2020), and Krausmann et al (2014). or more of the same? A critical pre-condition to catalysing any changes we want to see in banking supervision is ensuring thatwe collectively lock-in the benefitsfrom Basel III througha full, timely and consistent implementation. This is essential to ensuring that we do not revert to business-as-normal once the crisis abates. Even though the crisis significantly disrupted global economic activity, with a soaring in unemployment and distress, the gravity of the situation quickly paved way to the bathos of lobbying pressures to dilute global standards and weaken the resilience of the banking crisis. You would be forgiven for wondering whether I am referring to the current crisis or the GFC. The answer is both. As was the case during the past decade, when it comes to Basel III implementation, we areonce again seeing the regrettable re-emergence of the regulatory cycle, characterised by signs of amnesia and the fallacy of this time is different.22 Symptoms include market fragmentations due to deviations and non-implementation of global standards. Its effects were detected in multiple regions around the world before Covid-19, and are starting to re-emerge again. The Basel III framework is a central element of the international communitys response to the GFC. It was developed address the glaring fault-lines in the banking system. These fault-lines include unsustainable growth in leverage and credit, inadequate loss-absorbing capital, and excessive exposure to liquidity risk. The importance of safeguarding against these shortcomings is as important today as it was a decade ago. There is vast empirical evidence on the benefits of prudent regulation for lending and growth.23 It falls to all of us to help ensuring that we secure the real economic benefits from implementing the Basel III framework in a full, timely and consistent manner Conclusion In conclusion, the Committees timely and comprehensive response to Covid-19 is another chapter of its long and successful history of global cooperation. As supervision adapts to the challenges of the future, global cooperation should be inclusive in nature andinvolve a widerange of stakeholders. We must avoid the silo effect of listening only to a subset of our stakeholders, which is a recipe for tunnel vision and regulatory capture. The work of the Committee benefits from an extensive outreach with other global standard setters and international fora, including the G20 and Financial Stability Board, academics, market participants, and the general public. This outreach is integral to the way in which we meet our mandate.24 Over the coming days, we will have the opportunity to discuss and help shape the future of banking supervision. A critical catalyst to see through these changes is the implementation of all aspects of the Basel framework by our members. Title: Challenges and policies for financial stability in the face of the pandemic. Closing speech of the governor at the XI Meeting of the Expansion-KPMG Financial Sector
text: 20.10.2020 Challenges and policies for financial stability in the face of the pandemic Closing of the XI Expansi Financial Sector Meeting - KPMG Pablo Hern87ndez de Cos Governor You will be and be, very good morning: I would like to begin my intervention by thanking the organizers for inviting them to participate, once again, in this annual meeting on the financial sector. It is a pleasure for me to close an event in which, as always, great connoisseurs of the Spanish and global financial system have discussed some of the challenges facing the sector. The serious and rigorous debate that is fostered in this meeting is especially relevant in a situation such as the one we are facing, in which the economic crisis generated by the pandemic is already causing undeniable repercussions also for the financial system. At this point in the year, it is clear to everyone that the health crisis and the measures needed to contain it have had a profound macroeconomic impact around the world. It is also clear that the degree of persistence of this disturbance, which in principle should be considered as temporary, is also very high, as a result of the fact that the outbreaks of the disease are forcing to maintain - and even to increase again - the restrictions on the activity and movement and interaction of people. This persistence makes it more likely that unwanted structural damage will occur, beyond the structural changes that we are beginning to perceive will occur as a result of this crisis. As evident is also the enormous degree of heterogeneity in its effects, both by geographical areas and by sectors and companies, and by population groups, being the Spanish economy one of the most affected so far. But perhaps the most relevant characteristic, from the economic point of view, is the enormous degree of uncertainty that remains about the evolution of the pandemic itself and, of course, about its economic effects, both cyclical and structural. A degree of uncertainty that will continue to make it difficult to make consumption and investment decisions and that, therefore, will continue to negatively affect economic activity and employment. The main message I would like to convey is that, in an environment as complex and uncertain as the current one, the main contribution of economic policy must be to provide certainty to environmental actors. And that applies to both European and national economic policy, in the monetary, financial and fiscal fields. This certainly requires supporting the recovery, but also facilitating the structural adaptation of the economy, and, above all, addressing the long-term challenges now, decisively. Such a long-term orientation should provide guidance and stability for environmental agents, which in turn would increase the effectiveness of the stimulus measures that are still needed in the short term. The credibility of this long-term orientation requires broad consensus among the different actors (political, economic and social), based on a stable and well-established institutional and governance framework. Additionally, in the financial sphere, in the context of the current crisis, the shared objective must focus on preventing the health and economic crisis from becoming a financial crisis. We all know the harshness and persistence of crises that in the past had a relevant financial component. In this context, I would like to focus my intervention today on analysing the main risks that this crisis is creating for financial stability, as well as on the economic policy measures that, in my view, have been and will be necessary to mitigate them. 1 Risks to financial stability The unprecedented impact that the pandemic has had on economic activity has led to a very significant increase in risks to global financial stability. The strong response of economic policy and the effect of the profound international financial reform implemented in the last decade are helping to mitigate and manage these risks. In fact, so far, the financial system is acting as a mitigating factor d0 and not amplifying d0 of the impact of this crisis. But this should not lead us to complacency, because, as I have just stressed, the magnitude of the disturbance is very high and its duration uncertain. Next, I will review the recent evolution of the main risks in this area based on the analysis of the effects of the crisis on the different agents of the economy non-financial companies, households, financial sector and Public Administrations (Public Administrations). For non-financial corporations, they faced disruption with a more favourable financial position than before the global financial crisis. In particular, they had substantially reduced their debt levels, which were below the European average at the end of 2019, and had higher liquidity buffers. Moreover, the sectoral distribution of activity was more balanced than in the situation prior to the previous crisis. However, the information for the first half of the year shows that they have seen their profitability fall sharply. Specifically, the average ordinary return on assets (ROA) was halved, from 4% to 2%, and the percentage of companies with low profitability increased. The percentage of companies with losses also increased by 11 points, to 37%. The simulations carried out by Banco de Espa point to a strong contraction in the profitability of companies in 2020 as a whole, with more than half of the companies with expectations of losses in the whole year and a more unfavorable evolution in SMEs, and especially in the companies of the hospitality branches, catering and leisure, motor vehicles, commerce, and transport and storage. For its part, the simulations carried out by the Bank of Spain on the evolution of corporate liquidity also allow us to anticipate that the percentage of companies with liquidity needs from the second to the fourth quarter of this year would increase as a result of the pandemic by almost 10 percentage points (pp), to 70%. The information on bank credit shows that companies would be resorting to this source of financing to cover a significant part of their liquidity needs. In fact, the balance of credit of non- financial corporations with national credit institutions went from a year-on-year contraction of 1.1% in February to a year-on-year expansion of 8.1% in June, although in July and August this growth moderated One of the most relevant factors in the increase in credit in these months has been the progressive activation of the line of plastic guarantees to non-financial companies and individual entrepreneurs managed by the Official Credit Institute. Of the total new credit granted between December 2019 and June 2020 to non-financial companies, 41% corresponded to operations with guarantees, and this percentage was higher than 60% in SMEs and companies that concentrate their activity in the sectors most affected by the crisis. Equally important is the fact that the conditions for granting these guaranteed loans have been more favourable, in terms of both the interest rates applied and the maturity period, which will also help to reduce future refinancing risks. At the same time, the sector's aggregate debt ratio in terms of GDP has risen for the first time since 2010, to 82% in the second quarter of the year (the highest level since 2017), as a result of both the increase in debt and the fall in GDP. Although the intensity of these upswings will be corrected to some extent when GDP data for the first quarters are incorporated, the simulations carried out by the Bank of Spain also point to a deterioration in the equity situation. Indeed, the percentage of companies with a high debt-to-asset level, approximated by a ratio above 0.75, will increase, according to these simulations, by 7 pps. This percentage is, in any case, modest in relation to the magnitude of the shock, including as a result of the intense pre-crisis deleveraging process. This increase will, however, be much higher (by more than 20 pp in some cases) in companies in the sectors most affected by the crisis. In terms of the debt-to-income ratio, the increase will be higher, due to the fall in the denominator. Specifically, the weight of companies with a level of net debt ten times higher than their income, or with positive net debt and negative revenues, will increase by more than 15 pps, which could reach 40 pps in the sectors most affected by the crisis. It is true that this ratio tends to overestimate the impairment of assets, since, obviously, the level of income for this year cannot be taken as representative of future income. In addition, low interest rates and longer loans during the crisis will also act as mitigating factors. However, this set of indicators serves to illustrate the solvency risks of the non-financial companies we face. In the case of households, after the last global financial crisis, their equity situation also improved significantly, while the conditions for granting mortgage loans have been much more prudent, although consumer credit has been growing at high rates in the scams and groups of households in a situation of vulnerability persisted. However, household incomes have also experienced a significant cut in the current crisis, due to the decrease in hours worked and rising unemployment. Specifically, households' gross disposable income (GDI) fell by 8.8% in the first half of 2020, in year-on-year terms. At the same time, the credit obtained by households has fallen during the months as a result of the fall in new credit operations. The reduction has been more pronounced in the consumer credit segment, while new financing for the purchase of housing decreased with less intensity. Overall, although loan moratoriums, which affect 7% of the outstanding balance of credit to households, have slowed the fall in credit to this sector by reducing the volume of repayments, its year-on-year growth rate fell to d00.9% in August compared with 0.3% in February. This evolution has led to an increase in the financial burden borne by households. Thus, for the household sector as a whole, the debt-to-GDI ratio increased by almost 4 pps in the first half of the year and reached 95%. Again, the intensity of this increase in debt is expected to moderate to some extent with the RBD data for the third quarter. For its part, the increase in household savings not destined to debt service, as a result of the sharp fall in consumption, seems to have been channelled towards bank deposits, which showed a year-on-year increase of 7.1% in July. However, there is no up-to-date information on the distribution of these savings within the household sector, so it is difficult to assess to what extent this development has a mitigating effect on the greater degree of financial pressure for certain groups of households. In this sense, from the point of view of financial stability, the heterogeneity in the financial situation of households is very relevant. If the Bank of Spain's Household Financial Survey is used, it is found that the industries hardest hit by the pandemic employed proportionally more girls and women than the other sectors, and in a higher percentage workers with low wages. These lower wages would be partially offset by the fact that the employees concerned lived with other household members with higher incomes. In terms of wealth, 28% of workers in sectors based on greater social interaction lived in 2017 in households whose financial assets represented less than one month's income, and around 8% had bank debts whose payments exceeded 40% of gross household income. Therefore, the labour income and the patrimonial situation of the households of these workers were in 2017 more fragile than those of those employed in the rest of the branches of activity. Overall, therefore, the financial position of the non-financial private sector has deteriorated. The consequences of this deterioration on the results of credit institutions will be fully manifested in the first quarters. It is also clear that the improvements experienced by the Spanish banking sector in the quality of its balance sheet and in its solvency levels in the last decade have placed it in a better position to absorb this crisis and to continue providing the financing that the economy needs. And the risks to the financial stability of the sector have been mitigated by the various economic policy measures adopted. In any case, banks' income statements have already been adversely affected. Specifically, in the first half of 2020 the consolidated net result of the Spanish banking system as a whole was negative for an amount of around 9,500 million euros, which represents a decline of almost 20,000 million compared to the profits recorded in June 2019, which translates into an ROA of .0, 5% (1.1 pp less than in June 2019) and a return on equity (ROE) of .7.3% (15 pps less than a year earlier). This negative evolution is due (in particular, in the case of the two largest entities) to the deterioration of the goodwill of their subsidiaries abroad, which illustrates that, in the event of a global crisis such as the current one, the international diversification of the business of the Spanish banks will foreseeably be less decisive than in past crises for the containment and mitigation of its effects. In fact, the net result for the Spanish banking system as a whole would have been positive (0.14%) if this impairment of goodwill and other extraordinary adjustments were not taken into account. In any case, the deterioration in profitability is also due to the greater provision of provisions in anticipation of future impairments, so that impairment losses doubled compared to 2019, which explains that, for the rest of the banks without an international presence, the reduction in profits was, on average, 60 %. With this, the profitability of the sector has been well below that demanded by investors. As a result, the evolution of the price-to-book ratio d0 which compares the market capitalization of listed banks with their book value d0 shows Spain, as in the rest of the European countries, a marked contraction in March, falling to levels of around 0.4, although they subsequently recover to some extent. As a selab, one aspect that must be assessed in recent developments is that much of the adjustment in results is due to the anticipation of provisions for credit impairment that has not materialized, but will do so in the first quarters, which allows these provisions to be properly distributed over time. Indeed, the deterioration in economic activity generated by the pandemic has only moderately translated, for the time being, to the evolution of NPLs, and there has been a slight upswing in the second quarter, which, given the high growth in credit, has allowed for further reductions in the NPL ratio. Recurring revenues, meanwhile, have already begun to suffer, but for the time being, expenses have also been adjusted downwards. For now, this deterioration in the profitability of banks has not translated into a reduction in the solvency of institutions. In fact, in the first half of the year it has increased slightly, which highlights the relevance of the measures taken by those responsible for economic policy in their various areas. In particular, the recommendation not to distribute dividends has allowed institutions to add these resources to their capital buffers, the numerator of the solvency ratio. In addition, risk-weighted assets - the denominator of the solvency ratio - have been reduced both by the use of the guarantee programme and by the rapid changes introduced in the European capital regulation at the end of June, changes known as Quick Fix, to which I will refer later. For their part, the ECB's decisions have made it possible to maintain very comfortable financing conditions for banks. However, we should not be complacent about this situation, since, as I said earlier, the foreseeable deterioration of assets will, according to our analyses, have a significant impact on the solvency of institutions. In addition, this impact will affect each other differently, depending on both their starting point and their different exposure to the sectors most affected by this crisis. In this regard, the ECB has recently carried out a vulnerability analysis of the banks under its supervision, to predictively check the resilience of banks to the disruption generated by the pandemic. The results of this exercise, which I will refer to you below, are not qualitatively different from the interim results obtained at Banco de Espa in the FLESB stress test exercise, the final results of which will be published in our Financial Stability Report in the autumn. On the one hand, in the central scenario posed by the vulnerability exercise, which incorporated the most likely effects of the crisis on macroeconomic variables, with cumulative falls in GDP in the euro area in this area and in the two cousins of around 1%, the reduction in the solvency of all European entities was estimated at 2 pp, to stand at 12.6% on average, above the established prudential requirements. Although there is heterogeneity between banks, these results show, on the one hand, that banks have faced this crisis with greater safety margins, partly as a result of the regulatory changes introduced after the international financial crisis. On the other hand, the results also show the effectiveness of the measures that have been implemented to date to mitigate the impact of the crisis, among which, in this area, the guarantee programs, the extraordinary financing measures of the ECB and the recommendation to banks not to distribute dividends, thus strengthening their resilience. In the most severe scenario, in which euro area GDP accumulates a fall of 6% until 2022, the reduction in the solvency ratio is much greater (of 5.8 pps), which would leave the average CET1 at 8.8% of risk-weighted assets. In addition, in this scenario a significant percentage of banks would fall short of the minimum prudential requirements. As you know, the probability of this scenario occurring is low, but not undeniable, so if it materializes, it would be necessary to adopt additional measures to those already implemented. Then I will return to this question. On the other hand, the most recent evolution of public finances in Spain reflects the impact of the pandemic and the measures adopted to contain it, which has resulted in a significant increase in the deficit and public debt, as well as in the contingent obligations assumed by the different administrations. Specifically, the debt of the Public Administrations rose in June to 110% of GDP (14.6 pps more than in December 2019). For its part, the Banco de Espa's macroeconomic projections anticipate a very marked deterioration in the balance of the Public Administrations for 2020 as a whole and a partial correction in the following two years. Specifically, the debt ratio would grow by more than 20 pps in scenario 1 and around 25 pps in scenario 2, reaching 116.8% and 120.6% of GDP respectively. High debt is also vulnerable to the future. In the short term, this risk has been mitigated, firstly, by the ECB's actions, which have prevented the fragmentation of sovereign debt markets in the euro area, and, secondly, by the European response, by putting in place mechanisms to jointly face the costs of the pandemic. However, maintaining such a high level of debt over time would expose the Spanish economy to a situation of increasing vulnerability to changes in investor sentiment in financial markets. The Spanish economy's net external debt position and external indebtedness have risen, in terms of GDP, as a result of valuation effects and the fall in output. Specifically, in the second quarter of 2020 the position of net debtor international investment stood at 77.4% of GDP, 6.5 pp more than in the previous quarter, conditioned by the strong contraction of output. The gross external debt of the nation rose 56,800 million in the second quarter of 2020, due only to the valuation effects, to 188.1% of GDP, its historical maximum. The high debt position of the Spanish economy also remains an element of vulnerability, especially in the current context of high uncertainty about future economic developments. Let me conclude this review of recent developments in financial stability risks by making a brief reference to the most recent performance of financial markets and, in particular, their relationship with the deterioration in the credit quality of non-financial corporations that I mentioned earlier. It is clear that this crisis is also having a strong impact on the valuation of many financial assets, as well as on their volatility. Initially, stock markets tightened sharply and equity and bond volatilities increased sharply. Subsequently, after the reaction of global monetary and fiscal policies, the stock markets began to recover, and the volatilities, to decline. Indeed, in both the United States and the euro area, some market valuation indicators, such as the ratio of stock prices to earnings, have returned to record highs, which could suggest some disconnect between the recent rapid and significant recovery in financial markets and the more dovish developments in macroeconomic data and concerns about corporate sector weakness. In this sense, although there has been a slowdown in the pace of credit rating downgrades in recent months, after the sharp increase experienced between March and May, corporate spreads on debt classified as speculative or high yield (that is, external rating below BBB) saw their improvement interrupted in June in both Europe and the United States, thus preventing them from reaching pre-crisis levels again, unlike investment-grade corporate debt (external rating BBB or higher). This deterioration in corporate credit quality is an additional vulnerability factor for financial stability. Past experiences show that widespread downgrades of corporate sector ratings can generate adverse side effects that feed back into crises. A recent analysis by the European Systemic Risk Board illustrates the importance of this vulnerability. Specifically, it is estimated that investment funds and insurers account for most of the BBB corporate debt holdings, a third of which is associated with sectors considered sensitive to Covid-19. A massive downgrade of the ratings of these companies that would cause them to lose the investment grade condition would imply significant potential losses for the entire financial system of the European Union (EU). The role of rating agencies in this process is fundamental. Therefore, these institutions should take into account the long-term prospects of companies in their assessments and avoid excessively procyclical behaviour. In fact, ratings agencies have apparently been more cautious than in the global financial crisis and, to date, there have been no phenomena comparable to those of the past. In any case, the results of this exercise serve to show the systemic relevance of this vulnerability and the need to be prepared to provide a sufficient and coordinated response on an international scale, depending on how the pandemic evolves globally. 2 The reaction of economic policy Let me concentrate the remainder of my speech on analysing the response of economic policy during this crisis, and in this response must now be adapted to the most recent developments related to the pandemic and its economic effects. In the area of monetary policy, almost seven months have passed since the ECB began rolling out a comprehensive package of measures aimed at mitigating the impact of the pandemic on the euro area economy. In particular, the ECB has adopted a series of measures that can be grouped into two large blocks. In the first place, those aimed at favoring the provision of bank credit to the real economy. Specifically, the ECB approved a battery of measures to provide liquidity to banks, so that they, in turn, preserve access to credit for families and companies. Secondly, the ECB approved a second set of measures, relating to asset purchase programmes. Specifically, we announced in March the launch of a new financial asset purchase program (PEPP), with an initial volume of purchases for the whole of 2020 of 750,000 million euros, which will be extended in June both in term (until at least June 2021) and in volume (with 600,000 million additional euros, thus reaching 1.35 billion euros). In addition, the programme gives the ECB the necessary flexibility to concentrate its purchases at certain points in time or on the bonds issued by certain jurisdictions, in order to avoid fragmentation in the transmission of monetary policy. Today, we can say that the PEPP has been clearly successful in halting the deterioration of financial markets in all countries in the area. This is particularly visible in the evolution of sovereign bond yields, which are now close to pre-crisis levels, but can also be seen in other market segments, such as corporate issuers. This fall in the cost of sovereign debt has expanded the margin of action of the fiscal authorities of all the countries of the area, which has allowed them to deploy unprecedented actions to sustain household and corporate incomes. And this is particularly important because, as I have said on several occasions, budgetary policy is the main way of defending that, from the point of view of economic policy, we have for the fight against the consequences of Covid-19. This instrument has been used decisively since the outbreak of the crisis, in Spain and in other countries. On the one hand, it has been used to increase the budget allocation in the health field to deal with the pandemic. On the other hand, since the beginning of the period of induced hibernation of the economy, different actions have been deployed aimed at making up for the loss of labor income and business income. Particular mention should be made of the temporary adjustment programmes for employment and the granting of guarantees for financing granted by credit institutions to undertakings, to which I referred earlier. As you well know, these actions are aimed at facilitating the maintenance of employment relations once the measures restricting activity and personal mobility have been withdrawn, and to promote the viability of non- financial companies which, although solvent, have seen their liquidity position deteriorate as a result of the crisis. This is a response to fiscal policy which, on this occasion, has not been exclusively national, but also European, with the approval, in particular, of the European reconstruction fund. This European action is particularly relevant in the context of the Monetary Union, given the level of integration between all the economies of the area, which makes joint action much more effective in combating the effects of the crisis. The approval of the reconstruction fund has made it possible, at least temporarily, to make up for the absence of a European macroeconomic stabilisation instrument. The third dimension of action during the crisis is that carried out by the various authorities with prudential financial powers, which have also taken numerous decisions with the main objective of helping the financial system to overcome this crisis. First, supervisory processes have been adapted to free up operational resources for institutions. In this regard, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has decided to delay the implementation of Basel III by one year. Secondly, aspects of the current accounting rules for the calculation of credit risk have been clarified, with the aim of preventing excessive procyclicality. The authorities have also released most of the macroprudential capital buffers they had created, in many cases in response to the development of systemic risk in their economies. It has also been announced that the entities will have a long time for the subsequent reconstruction of these in case they are used. The financial authorities have recommended to the institutions the temporary elimination of the distribution of dividends and the application of prudent criteria in the variable remuneration to employees, with the aim of channeling the resources generated by the entities towards the reinforcement of their capital positions. Finally, a reform of the regulation of capital requirements called "Quick Fix" has been carried out, which includes permanent measures, such as the adaptation of the support factor for SMEs in the calculation of risk-weighted assets, and also transitory measures, such as the application of a prudential filter on changes in the value of sovereign debt instruments. In this way, the capacity of absorption of this shock by the entities has been improved, while financing is favored to the companies and investments that may potentially be most affected. One aspect I would like to highlight about the economic policy response so far is the high degree of complementarity that has existed between the actions of the various authorities. While the ECB's response and the decisions of the European Council have increased the fiscal space for government action, the action of governments and the ECB itself has been crucial to ensure liquidity and reduce the risk of non-financial corporations, which, together with the decisions of the micro- and macroprudential authorities and the ECB, They have allowed credit to continue to flow to economic agents. It is very important that this degree of complementarity be maintained in the future. 3 An economic policy to manage current and future challenges The current macroeconomic context, as I said at the beginning of this intervention, is characterized by a partial, heterogeneous, fragile and uncertain recovery, in which the persistence of the crisis is becoming more evident than initially anticipated. At the same time, some structural problems are already being perceived, among which the increase in the indebtedness of the public and private sector stands out, a certain destruction of the productive fabric d0 as shown by the fact that the number of companies registered with Social Security has been reduced very significantly since the beginning of the crisis. With a decrease of almost 84,000 companies between the end of February and the end of September (-6.1%, year-on-year), the loss of effective employment and the risk that the persistence of the crisis will turn it into long-term unemployment, and, finally, the increase in inequality derived from the fact that the recession is affecting to a greater extent workers with low wages and a more fragile patrimonial situation. Likewise, there are already indications that the pandemic is generating some structural changes in consumption and activity patterns, such as those derived from the increase in teleworking and, in general, the intensification of the use of new technologies in multiple areas. In the same vein, this crisis has already revealed some vulnerabilities associated, for example, with the process of global fragmentation of production, which can generate significant changes in trade relations between countries in the mains. In this context, the relevant question is what the economic policy response should be, particularly in a context of increasingly scarce plastic resources. This response involves a combination of short-term measures with a long-term strategy that provides certainty and urgently addresses the structural challenges that existed before the pandemic, as well as those generated by it. This strategy is also relevant in all monetary, financial and fiscal areas and applies to both European and national policy. Firstly, it seems appropriate to maintain - and even extend, if necessary - the support measures. Their premature withdrawal would cause damage that exceeds the possible costs of maintaining them until recovery shows sufficient strength. This affects both the budgetary policy to support household and corporate incomes as well as the financial and monetary policy. Secondly, in the area of fiscal policy, measures must now be much more targeted at the most affected sectors and population groups. This is the case, for example, of the recent pact between the Government and the social partners for the renewal of the ERTE until January 31, 2021. Third, early identification of structural changes is crucial. Economic policy cannot sustain indefinitely a sector that will structurally reduce its level of activity. In the face of these structural changes, economic policy must be aimed at facilitating and supporting the adaptation of the productive fabric and workers to the new realities, and the efficient reallocation of resources between sectors and companies. This implies that, in the case of companies with non-viable business models, their orderly exit from the market should be facilitated, while, in the case of those facing structural reductions in demand, the correct functioning of the different flexibility mechanisms available to companies in the current labour framework should also be ensured. And, of course, emphasis must be placed on training policies for workers to facilitate the relocation of workers in the sectors of the future. Fourthly, it is necessary to face the structural damages generated by the pandemic. In the case, for example, of the increase in corporate indebtedness, it would make sense to modify the instruments of support for companies, so that these do not imply an increase in financial obligations. Direct aid or temporary capital injections may now be more effective instruments for viable enterprises. And, in parallel, for these viable companies that face difficulties in meeting their financial obligations, a more agile functioning of debt restructuring procedures should be facilitated. To achieve these objectives, improvements in the functioning of judicial and out-of-court insolvency procedures would be desirable to result in greater efficiency and agility. Fifthly, it is urgently necessary to define an ambitious agenda of structural reforms, aimed at increasing the potential growth of the economy, which was already low before this crisis. The typology of the challenges of our economy is very broad and requires addressing the low dynamics of productivity, the duality of the labor market, high unemployment, population aging, inequality, the fight against climate change, changes in the globalization model and the acceleration of the digitalization of the economy. Sixthly, it must be ensured that the use of European funds is earmarked for projects and structural reforms with the potential potential to improve the growth potential of our economy. And European action must also be aimed at filling the existing institutional gaps (in particular, the creation of a permanent macroeconomic stabilisation mechanism, the deepening of the Capital Market Union and, as I will emphasise later, the completion of the Uni Banking process). Seventh, it is necessary to devise a credible strategy of gradual but sustained reduction of fiscal imbalances, for its implementation once the pandemic has been overcome and the economic recovery is firmly established. This strategy is particularly relevant and appropriate for a country, such as Spain, which has faced this crisis from a position of its finances more vulnerable than that of other economies in our environment. This strategy would bring significant benefits through increased potential growth in the economy generated by the reforms and improved credibility on the sustainability of finance over the medium term, which in turn would widen the existing fiscal space and enhance the expansionary effects of current fiscal actions. In short, in order to provide ourselves with the necessary fiscal space to be able to increase measures to support the economy in the event that the evolution of the pandemic so requires, it would be necessary to decisively execute the reform agenda, plan the fiscal consolidation process and reform the support instruments to make them more flexible and focused. In the financial field, as I said, the objective must be that, in no case, the health crisis that has become an economic crisis ends up generating a financial crisis. In this sense, as is already the case in the monetary field and incipient in the fiscal field, in the banking context the response to the possible materialization of these risks can only be European, given the commitment to Uni Bancaria. In any case, at European level, the response to the current scenario must include the completion of the Uni Bancaria, with the approval of a fully mutualised European guarantee fund, since it would make a decisive contribution to ensuring financial stability in the euro area. In addition, it is a priority to analyse the adequacy of European resolution regulations in the face of a hypothetical systemic crisis or the possible role of asset management companies in conditions of serious deterioration of the balance sheets of European financial institutions. EU Member States should also move swiftly towards an agreement to create a European COM procedure for the administrative winding-up of credit institutions. In Spain, recent experience shows the inefficiency, in terms of terms of terms of terms and value recovered, of the current insolvency proceedings for credit institutions. From the point of view of institutions, in the event of a prolongation of the crisis, institutions should, first, ensure adequate and timely recognition of the effective deterioration in the quality of credit exposures through compliance with supervisory guidance. In addition, its dividend distribution and remuneration policies will have to remain very cautious until the current uncertainty dissipates and an economic AIDS recovery is consolidated. Likewise, institutions must deepen the improvement of their efficiency and the realization of the necessary investments in digitization and exploitation of information, while expanding more profitable activities while maintaining strict control over the risks assumed. This is particularly important in a context where an environment of low interest rates is expected for a very long period and bearing in mind that the current crisis may accentuate the advantages of some technological competitors. Consolidation processes in the sector, for which there is still room, can favour the strengthening of entities and the system as a whole. But they must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis and properly executed, so that the gains from potential synergies are realized. Our role as banking supervisors is to analyze the viability and monitor the execution of the fusi projects that are presented to us, from the point of view of the viability of the business and, therefore, the solvency of the resulting entity, as well as financial stability as a whole. On an international scale, the anchor provided by the financial regulation approved in the last decade must be maintained. In particular, as recently agreed within the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, all jurisdictions will need to fully transpose the new Basel III timetable in a full, consistent and timely manner. With regard to monetary policy, the fragility and heterogeneity of the euro area's recovery, expected medium-term inflation well below our target and an evolution of the nominal effective exchange rate, which has offset much of our stimulus over the past few months, lead to the conclusion that there is no room for complacency. We will need to maintain significant monetary stimulus until we achieve an AIDS recovery. In addition, it is not ruled out that it is necessary to recalibrate the previous measures, or introduce new ones if necessary, to comply with our mandate of price stability, always understood in a symmetrical way. In this regard, we must make it clear that inflation of 1.3%, such as that predicted by the ECB in 2022, is not compatible with the ECB's inflation mandate. It is also crucial to maintain flexibility in the execution of our asset purchase programmes to avoid problems of financial fragmentation. Beyond the short-term reaction, we at the ECB have initiated a review of our monetary policy strategy in order to meet the challenges we face; In particular, those derived from the low inflation environment, the reduction of the margin of conventional instruments and the structural role of non-conventional instruments. Given that it is an ongoing process, I cannot anticipate what its conclusions will be, but I can anticipate that it is an open process. Both the ECB and the Eurosystem's national central banks are conducting a great deal of analysis and gathering the views of civil society, academic economists and other professional and social groups. I can also anticipate that one of the key aspects of this review will be the definition of price stability. The current inflation target, consisting of a rate below - but close - to 2%, can be reformulated. On the one hand, it may be necessary to clarify the specific level of inflation to be achieved, in order to facilitate its understanding by economic agents. On the other hand, in line with my previous comments, it would be possible to give this objective a more symmetrical nature, which makes it clear that the degree of tolerance towards deviations of inflation above the target will be the same as when such deviations occur below. Furthermore, in the current context of low inflation and interest rates close to their lower level, the inflation target will have to take into account the need to allow a sufficiently high buffer above zero, which gives more room for manoeuvre to conventional interest rate policy. Ultimately, the objective of this revision of monetary policy strategy should be to strengthen the effectiveness of monetary policy in the euro area and its ability to achieve its objectives in the decade-long macroeconomic environment. 4 Completed To conclude my speech today, I would like to underline what, in my view, must be the main contribution of economic policy in an environment as complex as the one we are experiencing. This contribution must consist of providing certainty to economic actors, supporting recovery, but also facilitating the structural adaptation of the economy and adopting a long-term vision. In the case of our country, this objective requires, beyond short-term measures, the urgent implementation of the necessary structural reforms that increase the potential growth of our economy and the early design of a fiscal consolidation program, for its gradual application from the moment in which the recovery is aided. to ensure the sustainability of the finances. That this strategy is credible and truly provides certainty also requires a consensus between the different actors (political, economic and social) that guarantees the effectiveness of the necessary actions and their durability over time. Thank you very much for your attention.
