Title: Appearance at the Congress of Deputies: presentation of the 2020 Annual Report of the Bank of Spain
text: 19.05.2021 Appearance at the Congress of Deputies: presentation of the 2020 Annual Report of the Bank of Spain Committee on Economic Affairs and Digital Transformation Pablo Hernandez de Cos Governor Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, I appear before this committee in order to present the 2020 Annual Report of the Bank of Spain. As usual, the Report reviews the developments, prospects and challenges facing our economy, as well as our economic policy recommendations. I would also like to share with honourable Members the main messages of the latest Financial Stability Report, in particular those associated with the banking sector. In my speech, I shall first make a diagnosis of the economic situation. Secondly, I will assess the reaction of economic policy during the crisis. Thirdly, I will develop the main economic policy measures that, in the opinion of the Bank of Spain, it would be desirable to take into account in order to promote recovery and, in turn, raise growth potential. Finally, I will address the situation and challenges of the banking system. 1 Diagnosis of the economic situation Graph. Real GDP, level (IV TR 2019100) After a year marked by the enormous cost in both human lives and in economic terms derived from the pandemic, the Annual Report is presented in a context characterized by the change in expectations generated by the progressive administration of vaccines to citizens, which allows us to glimpse a vigorous economic recovery on a global scale in the coming quarters. Restrictions on mobility have already been significantly relaxed in countries where the process is more advanced, such as China, the United Kingdom and the United States, which has resulted in a more favourable evolution of their activity indicators. Spain and the rest of the euro area countries are less advanced in the vaccination process. But their acceleration in recent weeks suggests that they will take the path of recovery in this second quarter, a path that, as restrictions on activity are eliminated, could accelerate in the second part of the year. This evolution is the one that reflects the central scenario of the macroeconomic projections of the Bank of Spain last March. Thus, GDP would grow by 6% in 2021. The greater dynamism of activity from the summer would lead to a carry-over effect in 2022 which, together with the expected impact of the Next Generation EU (NGEU) funds, would bring GDP growth in 2022 to 5.3%, to moderate to 1.7% in 2023. Graphs on cFMI (April), GDP levels in Latin America, Euro area GDP level and Economic impact and contributions (differences from EMU in 2020) This recovery has to be placed in the context of an impact of the crisis on the Spanish economy that has been very intense and greater than that of other developed countries. And in which the effects are being very persistent. The level of GDP was, at the end of the first quarter of 2021, still 9.4 percentage points (pp) below its pre-crisis level and the unemployment rate stood at 16% in the first quarter (21.3% if we add the employees who still remained in temporary employment regulation files -ERTE- and the self-employed in suspension of activity). In addition, the effects of the pandemic may last for several years. In our central scenario, the recovery in the level of pre-pandemic activity would not occur in Spain until 2023, while in the euro area as a whole it would be anticipated to 2022. Graphs on the evolution of employment (discounting the average by sector) by company size and by type of contract; of Evolution of Gross Value Added in the first quarter of 2021 and Economic estimation of the fall in GDP in 2020, by provinces On the other hand, the impact of the crisis is being very uneven. By sector, it has concentrated particularly on hospitality, leisure, commerce and transport, whose gross value added was more than 20 pp below the pre-pandemic level in the first quarter. By geographical area, we observe a greater fall in the island provinces and on the Mediterranean coast, with declines in their product that exceeded 20% in 2020. By groups of workers, they have been affected, above all, young people, with temporary contracts and low incomes; In particular, the youth unemployment rate stood above 30% in the first quarter. As for companies, the smallest are those that have suffered a greater decline in their turnover figures, of around 20%. Diagram showing the factors that will determine the evolution of the Spanish economy in the coming quarters On the other hand, there are still different elements of uncertainty that condition the materialization and intensity of the recovery. First, it will continue to depend on the evolution of the pandemic, including the speed of administration of vaccines and their effectiveness against possible new variants of the virus. Our central scenario assumes that widespread administration of vaccines will allow restrictions to disappear by the end of the year. Secondly, there are doubts about the rate of recovery of tourism, which will be crucial for Spain, given the high weight of the sector in the economy (12.4%) and, in particular, the high weight of international tourism in total tourism expenditure (60.2%). In the central scenario, we assume that these flows will not reach a high degree of normalization until 2022. Thirdly, the intensity of the recovery will depend on the use that households make of the savings they have accumulated during the pandemic, which, in 2020, was almost 6 pp of GDP higher than the average of the previous five years and, according to estimates by the Bank of Spain, the forced nature could have reached 2.5% of GDP until the third quarter of 2020. A part of this saving will go to consumption and would invigorate the recovery. As an example, in China, consumption has already recovered to pre-pandemic levels. However, some elements may limit this standardization. On the one hand, a part of the unsatisfied consumption during the pandemic is attributable to spending on services, which, in general, cannot be postponed. On the other hand, households may decide to maintain a high level of savings out of caution or even because they anticipate tax increases in response to the increase in public debt. The fact that higher-income households, which tend to consume a smaller proportion of their income, have contributed most to the increase in savings, could also limit this effect. Our baseline assumes that the savings rate will decline progressively, but in 2023, it would remain somewhat above the pre-pandemic level. Fourthly, there is uncertainty about the damage to the productive fabric. The number of companies registered with Social Security decreased by 3.7% between February 2020 and March 2021, a figure comparable to that of the 2012 crisis, despite the fact that the fall in activity was much greater last year. Behind this reduction is the decline in business creation, and not a rebound in declines, which could be explained by the support measures adopted, including the bankruptcy moratorium. But future developments are uncertain. Bank of Spain estimates show that the proportion of companies at risk of becoming unviable would have increased between 2 pps and 3 pps. And the percentage of companies that, although viable, would have problems of over-indebtedness could increase between 3 pps and 5 pps. However, our central scenario assumes a moderate destruction of the productive fabric. Fifth, there are doubts about the time distribution and use of NGEU funds. The historical average multiplier of the European Structural and Investment Funds would be around 1. However, the multipliers associated with those funds depend on their specific destination and also on the flexibility of the product and factor markets (they are lower in those countries with greater rigidities). Therefore, its economic impact will depend both on the selection of projects, and on whether it is accompanied by reforms that reduce regulatory rigidity. Our central scenario rests on a degree of absorption in line with historical evidence and multipliers around unity. Specifically, the projections incorporate an impact of 1% on GDP in 2021, which would be extended to 1.9% in 2022. Finally, the intensity and persistence of the recovery depend on the implementation of appropriate economic policies. I will come back to this later. Reflecting this uncertainty, our baseline scenario is accompanied by two additional scenarios, offering GDP growth in 2021 of 3.2% under the most pessimistic assumptions and 7.5% under the most positive scenarios. 2 Lessons for economic policy after a year of crisis The experience of the last year allows us to draw some lessons, even preliminary ones, that may be relevant in order to face the management of the crisis in the coming quarters and also with a medium and long-term perspective. 1 Speed and forcefulness of the response 2 Comprehensiveness of the response 3 Flexibility and adaptability to the evolution of the pandemic 4 Complementarity of the measures of the different authorities 5 Need for concerted and internationally coordinated action 6 Importance of maintaining a balanced and resilient economic position at all times: -In the banking sector -In the patrimonial position of companies and families -In public finances First, the importance of the speed and forcefulness of that response must be stressed. The brutal disruption caused by the pandemic has had an unusual economic policy reaction that has alleviated short-term costs, avoided even more extreme negative scenarios and is likely to reduce damage in the medium and long term. The International Monetary Fund estimates that the fall in global activity in 2020 could have been three times greater without the measures implemented. And countries where the response has been strongest have tended to see less pronounced recessions. The ECB's reaction has been very strong: the emergency pandemic programme (PEPP) allowed asset purchases equivalent to 6.7% of euro area GDP in 2020. As has the reaction of fiscal policy: the public deficit increased by more than 6.5 points of GDP in the euro area, which includes the impact of discretionary measures and automatic stabilisers. Secondly, the comprehensive nature of the response has been crucial, which has made it possible to cover a large part of the transmission channels of a crisis with very specific characteristics and that has affected both supply and demand. Monetary policy has covered the main financing channels for the euro area economy. Fiscal policy has focused on mitigating the impact of the crisis on households and firms. And prudential financial policy has facilitated the improvement of the solvency of financial institutions and the granting of solvent credit. Thirdly, the adaptability of economic policy has been very remarkable, allowing it to adapt to the evolution of the pandemic and its heterogeneous effects. The successive extensions of the measures to support the incomes of the families and the most affected companies are a clear example of this flexibility. So are the various temporary extensions of the PEPP. And its design, which has allowed asset purchases to be concentrated in the most critical months and in those countries that, at each moment, have suffered greater financial tensions, which has allowed to preserve favorable financing conditions for all agents in all countries. Fourthly, the role played by the high complementarity of the measures of the various authorities d1 monetary, fiscal and financial d1 each in fulfilling its mandates, should be underlined. Monetary policy decisions have been particularly relevant from this perspective, as they have given fiscal authorities leeway. During 2020, net purchases of the PEPP amounted to more than 90% of the net public financing needs of euro area countries (and almost 30% of gross needs). This has been particularly important in countries such as Spain, which has been particularly affected by the crisis and was based on high levels of deficit and public debt. The ECB's action is avoiding an increase in funding costs, which would have limited the ability of fiscal authorities to support the economy. The complementarity of the ECB's measures and those taken by both national governments and prudential authorities has also been instrumental in maintaining the solvency of the banking sector and facilitating the flow of funding to the economy. Fifthly, the crisis has shown that, in a highly globalised environment, coordinated action at international level is mandatory. And this is particularly the case in Europe, given our high degree of integration. On this occasion, there has been a genuinely European common response, in which the creation of the NGEU fund stands out. A fund that introduces important elements to share the effort of the economic recovery, some of them unprecedented, such as the large-scale issuance of supranational European public debt to finance reforms and investments in Member States. A final necessary reflection is that this crisis has once again highlighted the importance of maintaining a balanced and resilient economic position at all times. Economic shocks can have very different origins. In this case, it has been a completely unexpected factor and alien to productive activity. But its effects depend on our starting position. In this sense, the improvements in the solvency of the banking sector or in the equity position of companies and households, after the deleveraging process of the last decade in Spain, have allowed us to weather the crisis better. On the contrary, the high public debt and structural deficit at the outset has conditioned the capacity to react during the crisis and has caused its impact to generate a significant increase in the vulnerability of our economy. 3 An economic policy for recovery The expectation of recovery is real, but its speed and scope are subject to high uncertainty and depend on the action of economic policy. In this context, it is crucial to incorporate the lessons of the crisis into crisis management in the coming quarters. In particular, it is necessary to combine simultaneously the management of short-term challenges with those in the long term and that the crisis has exacerbated. In particular, the policy response should combine three objectives: (i) sustain support until the recovery is strong; (ii), facilitating the structural adjustments caused by the pandemic, and (iii), decisively addressing the structural problems that limit our capacity for growth. And this applies to all economic policies, both at global, European and national level. 3.1 Global policies At the global level, concerted action in the short term remains essential. In a context in which the recovery is being heterogeneous by country, this will require a certain coordination in the exit strategies from the crisis and, in parallel, support for the most vulnerable countries. International cooperation is particularly important to accelerate the production of vaccines and facilitate their affordable and equitable distribution for all. Many of the challenges facing our economies are global and require a global response. Therefore, it is very opportune to give a new impetus to multilateralism with the triple objective of acting together to establish economic recovery, counteract the setbacks in inequality and poverty that have occurred due to the pandemic and face the challenges associated with digitalization processes, international taxation or the fight against climate change, among others. All this without forgetting the need to strengthen common prevention and response instruments to systemic crises. In this respect, the agreements reached in the G20 framework to respond to the impact of the crisis on low-income economies. But consensus is needed to address the situation of middle-income countries, some of which are coping with this crisis with limited room for manoeuvre in their domestic policies. 3.2 Monetary policy Graphs on the evolution of long-term interest rates on government bonds in the euro area and on the Eurosystem Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) forecasts (2020-2023) In the case of monetary policy, we must avoid a premature tightening of financing conditions. To this end, the ECB has underlined that purchases under the PEPP will be adjusted to counteract a deterioration in financing conditions that is not accompanied by a return of the medium-term inflation projection to its pre-pandemic level. The increase in the volume of monthly purchases agreed in March this year was precisely for that, in a context in which there had been an increase in long-term interest rates and the increases in inflation observed in 2021 were estimated to be essentially transitory, so that the ECB's medium-term inflation forecasts (1.4% in 2023) remained well below our target and also below the pre-pandemic inflation path. This is the policy framework d0 combining the joint assessment at each point in time of financing conditions and the expected path of inflation d0 that we will follow in the coming months in determining the pace of purchases in the context of the PEPP, including its possible extension. Monetary policy also faces significant structural challenges, arising from an environment of persistently below-target inflation, with very low estimates of the "natural real interest rate" and widespread non-standard measures. That is why we at the ECB have initiated a review of our strategy, which will be completed in the second half of this year. The recent experience of the US Federal Reserve is, in my opinion, important. The review of its strategy shows the benefits of allowing the inflation target to be exceeded moderately and temporarily in an environment where inflation is persistently below target and nominal interest rates are close to their lower bound. That is the environment that has characterised the euro area in recent years. However, a clear numerical inflation target needs to be a prerequisite for a hypothetical strategy of allowing inflation to rise gradually and temporarily above that target to be effective. The ECB's current target d0 an inflation rate below, but close to, 2% d0 does not indicate a specific numerical target. A rate of 2%, understood symmetrically, would be a good option. The US experience also illustrates the role of fiscal policy in the current context, and also in relation to monetary policy challenges. In a double sense: a fiscal stimulus would exert upward pressure on prices and, if the stimulus is properly designed, could raise the potential growth rate and, therefore, the natural real interest rate. This would narrow the gap between effective and natural interest rates, providing additional support to aggregate demand and inflation. 3.3 European policies Outline on medium-term actions at European level (Fonfos Next Generation EU and Multiannual Financial Framework for 2021-2027) The NGEU programme has been a substantial step forward in European policies. Its short-term impact and long-term transformative capacity would be maximised if rapid availability to Member States were accompanied by governance that effectively links the use of funds either to those expenditure items most likely to increase growth potential or to structural reforms geared towards the same objective. However, the NGEU cannot be seen as the cyclical stabilisation mechanism needed by the euro area as a complement to the single monetary policy. We must address the design of a genuine stabilization mechanism that has a permanent character, sufficient endowment and tax and debt capacity. This ties in with the debate on reforming fiscal rules to adapt them to the transformations that have taken place since they were formulated. On the one hand, the secular fall in interest rates makes it possible to maintain higher debt levels without compromising public finances in the long term, provided that potential growth has not been reduced in parallel. On the other hand, the international financial crisis and the pandemic have shown that tail risks are not always manageable exclusively at the national level. Indeed, most of the larger countries in the euro area may lack the fiscal cushion needed to face a recession over the next decade, even if they follow the rules of the Stability and Growth Pact. A new framework is therefore needed in which national and supranational authorities complement each other. National countries should focus on meeting medium-term budgetary objectives, with public debt sustainability as the main benchmark, and addressing asymmetric shocks. Supranationals should respond to tail events and adjust the fiscal policy stance at euro area level to complement monetary policy. There is also a need to simplify the current framework and to improve its hitherto weak capacity to ensure that countries build up fiscal buffers in good times that can be used in future crises. And, of course, we cannot forget that we still do not have a full banking union, which would require the approval of a common and fully mutualised deposit insurance fund. Nor should we lose sight of the fact that capital markets in Europe remain underdeveloped and integrated, which motivates the need to move forward with determination in the adoption of the measures included in the capital markets union project. 3.4 National policies Short-term stimulus measures should continue to target the most affected sectors, enterprises and groups of workers, while maintaining the necessary flexibility to meet the challenges created by this new phase of the crisis. In particular, an extension of ERTEs, in force until the end of May 2021, seems advisable with a design that responds to the dual objective of maintaining a relatively generalized level of protection and, at the same time, favouring the eventual reallocation between sectors and companies. In this phase of the crisis, economic policies must also focus on minimizing damage to the productive fabric. The aim should be to avoid the closure of those companies in difficulty, but which remain viable. Left graph: Increase, due to the Covid19 crisis, in the percentage of over-indebted and viable companies, and their weight in employment and debt Right graph: Unsustainable debt of companies that would become over-indebted, but would remain viable. Sectoral breakdown. In this sense, a package of aid to the business sector and the self-employed has recently been approved. The analysis presented in the 2020 Annual Report shows that, given that the eligibility requirements are based on criteria of belonging to certain sectors and falling turnover, there is a risk that such aid will not reach all companies that, being viable, are in a situation of excess indebtedness. This risk stems from two facts: (i) that even in sectors not most affected by the crisis there would have been an increase in insolvency problems, although less widespread, and (ii) that the insolvency situation also depends on the starting position before the crisis in relation to profitability and debt levels. The flexibility of the aid program in its application by the autonomous communities approved in April could mitigate this risk. In short: for this tool to be useful, its execution must be fast and homogeneous and the distribution mechanisms must allow aid to be focused on viable companies with solvency problems. Flexibility in the volume of funds is also necessary to adapt to the evolution of the pandemic and the eventual materialisation of risks. The analysis presented in this Report also detects risks derived from the pandemic on the health and education of citizens, which must be adequately addressed. In particular, there is an increase in the incidence of mental health problems, especially among women, and delays in access to health care, with possible long-term health consequences. On the other hand, the closures of educational centers during the last school term of 2020 and the consequent change to an education by digital means could have had adverse effects on academic results, especially in the most disadvantaged groups, although different measures have been adopted to mitigate them. At the same time, it is crucial to facilitate the adaptation of the economy to the new realities that have emerged after the pandemic, derived, for example, from the advance of digitalization processes, the use of electronic commerce and teleworking. This necessarily involves allowing the use of the flexibility mechanisms established by the legislation d1 in particular, labord1so that the necessary reallocation of resources between sectors and companies takes place. The functioning of debt restructuring and company liquidation mechanisms should also be improved, especially for business projects that are not viable in the medium term. At the same time, training policies for workers and the unemployed must be strengthened to facilitate retraining for future activities and thus prevent an increase in structural unemployment. This reinforcement is particularly important in a context of continuous and intense process of technological change and gradual aging of the workforce. Outline with the main medium-term challenges and the fundamental levers for a structural transformation In any case, the medium-term outlook is conditioned by a series of structural challenges that already existed before the crisis, some of which could worsen after the pandemic. These challenges include: (i) low productivity growth; (ii) labour market dysfunctions; and iii) the challenges arising from population aging, climate change, and rising inequality. And, at the same time, it is necessary to redirect the deterioration of public accounts. Addressing these structural challenges requires the design of a comprehensive strategy. To this end, three fundamental levers must be considered: the design and approval of an ambitious agenda of structural reforms; the implementation of those public investment projects with greater long-term driving capacity within the framework of the NGEU programme, and the definition and execution of a budgetary plan that allows fiscal action margins to be recovered once the crisis is over. As regards the structural reform agenda, I will not dwell on each of the priorities, as I already detailed them in this very House last June1. However, I would like to briefly mention some fundamental lines of action. Diagram on the structural reform strategy 1 See P. Hern87ndez de Cos (2020), c7The main challenges of the Spanish economy after Covid-19. Appearance at the Commission for the Social and Economic Reconstruction of Spain after Covid-19 / Congress of Deputies, on June 23, 2020", Occasional Documents, n.bc 2024, Bank of Spain. To increase productivity, it would be appropriate, on the one hand, to carry out a review of the regulatory framework, in order to promote business dynamics and growth, increase the degree of sectoral competition and reduce the current obstacles to market unity, and, on the other, develop policies that stimulate the accumulation of human capital, an area in which Spain has serious deficiencies compared to the rest of the countries in our environment. Hence the advisability of rethinking the institutional design of the education system, as well as the content of the curriculum and the learning system itself, and strengthening the mechanisms of continuous training of workers. Technological capital is another fundamental pillar on which the increase in productivity must rest. Beyond the budgetary allocations that may come from the NGEU funds, modifications in the promotion and research career system would be desirable to favor the entry and development of researchers with high potential. Incentives to encourage business investment in this area should also be redesigned and the role of venture capital firms in financing them should be enhanced. In the labour field, reducing the high duality between permanent and temporary workers would make it possible to reduce some of the main structural deficiencies of the labour market, which disproportionately make the costs of adjustments fall on temporary workers and cause structural unemployment to be higher than in neighbouring countries. Improvements in productivity and the functioning of the labour market will reduce existing high levels of inequality. However, the recent evolution of inequality in our country has different dimensions that also require different instruments to address them. And the crisis would have increased levels of inequality, including that associated with uncertainty about future incomes, which especially affects young people. Actions in this area should be based on an analysis of the efficiency of the different existing redistributive schemes. This is the case, as provided for by law, of the minimum vital income program, in which it would be desirable to analyze its effects on labor participation or its degree of coverage, given that, in its initial design, some groups are not eligible that, however, could be at risk of extreme poverty. Additionally, measures aimed at increasing the supply of rental housing would be appropriate. One of the dimensions of inequality that has been gaining ground in the public debate is that related to the disparities in the demographic dynamics of the regions of our country. The 2020 Annual Report devotes a chapter to studying this phenomenon. It is concluded that the concentration of the population in Spain is very high in European perspective, both in urban and rural areas, and that Spain has an exceptionally high percentage of uninhabited territory. In addition, a risk of depopulation is identified for 42% of municipalities. Migration from smaller cities to large cities has contributed to the lower dynamism of rural municipalities around smaller cities; The wage premium is the main determinant of these migrations, especially for skilled workers. In fact, larger cities lost lower-skilled workers between 2005 and 2018. Digitalisation, population ageing and the energy transition pose new challenges, but also opportunities for the development of the rural world. In this context, it is important to consider policies to mitigate depopulation, which seek to halt demographic decline and promote the development of rural areas in the medium term, and adaptation to depopulation, with the aim of maintaining a minimum level of services that guarantees the well-being of rural inhabitants. From the review of some international experiences, it can be concluded that there is a need for a comprehensive strategy with a vocation for permanence, a clear delimitation of competences, financial autonomy and mechanisms for collaboration between municipalities, and a specification of ex-ante measurable objectives, with ex-post evaluation of effectiveness. In addition, the reform agenda must address the challenge of population ageing, which requires action in different areas, such as improving the reconciliation of work and family life d0 in particular, for young women with children d0 adapting migration policy to the needs of the labour market and measures that favour the prolongation of working life. And, of course, it requires addressing its implications for the financial sustainability of the public pension system. Demographic dynamics imply a notable increase of pension expenditure in the coming years, and the return to an inflation-compliant revaluation system and the suspension of the application of the sustainability factor put additional pressure on them. System reform should strengthen the link between contributions made and benefits received d0 ensuring a level of adequacy for those most vulnerable households d0 increase the transparency and predictability of the system, and incorporate considerations of intergenerational equity. It would also be advisable to introduce automatic mechanisms that adapt some parameters of the system to demographic and economic dynamics to ensure sustainability, give certainty to citizens and promote prudent saving, work and retirement decision-making. Finally, moving towards a more sustainable growth model will require a profound economic and technological transformation to mitigate the effects of climate change, in which public policies must play a fundamental role, in particular through environmental taxation, seeking the highest possible degree of international coordination. Outline on the best possible use of the European funds programme in our country The second lever for the structural transformation of the economy is the one provided, given its high size and structural approach, by the NGEU programme, especially in the digital and environmental fields. However, maximizing its effect on long-term growth poses significant challenges. On the one hand, the ex ante selection of projects should be based on an appropriate scheme of public procurement procedures. In addition, there should be an appropriate design of methodologies for real-time monitoring of initiatives, which allow possible deviations to be corrected, as well as a robust framework for ex-post evaluations. Likewise, it must be ensured that there are no obstacles that hinder the process of reallocation of resources between companies and sectors that structural change in the economy would require. Structural transformation necessarily requires economic flexibility. Finally, in order to promote the implementation of structural reforms, part of the resources could be used to mitigate the costs that these sometimes entail for some groups in the short term, in pursuit of the benefits they would generate for society as a whole in the medium and long term. As an illustration, the 2020 Annual Report describes a calibrated mechanism for the Spanish economy to combat the duality of our labour market, based on the accumulation of rights in individual workers' funds and on the reform of dismissal costs, the implementation of which could be favoured by the use of European funds to cover transition costs. The example is calibrated so that companies, as a whole, continue to assume the same aggregate amount of compensation that they assume under the current scheme. What is sought under this scheme is a more equitable distribution of severance pay among workers than the current one. This reform is just one example among many possible to address the problem of duality. It would be desirable to evaluate the different alternatives, particularly at a time when part of the European funds could be used to promote this type of reform. Graph: simulated paths of public debt in the central scenario and under certain assumptions. The third lever is the definition and implementation of a budgetary plan to rebuild fiscal policy space and reduce the vulnerability of high public debt to changes in financing conditions and investor sentiment. It should be borne in mind that the ratio of public debt to GDP has increased by almost 30 pps from 95.5% in December 2019 to 125.3% in March 2021, and the structural public deficit, which already exceeded 3% of GDP in 2019, could reach figures close to 5% after the crisis. Given this initial situation, it is clear that the effort required is considerable and will have to last for several years. To strengthen the credibility of this plan, an early definition and communication of its main characteristics would be desirable, as well as the active participation of all Public Administrations. Combined with the above-mentioned structural reforms would alleviate adjustment needs to the extent that they are capable of increasing the economy's potential growth. For its part, the decision on how to distribute the adjustment among the different items has to be taken in the political sphere, although it must be based on a review of all budget chapters that evaluates the degree of efficiency with which expenditure is executed and public resources are captured. The implications of any fiscal intervention, in terms of both economic growth and redistribution, should also be analysed. 4 Situation and challenges of the banking sector Following the financial crisis, the implementation of global regulatory reform and the restructuring process led banks to increase their solvency and resilience, which has allowed them to better cope with this crisis. In fact, banks have been a key player in the transmission of monetary policy decisions and in the implementation of some of the financial and fiscal measures. Graphs on capital ratios and credit volume and rates of change of business in Spain These measures have made it possible, in parallel, to mitigate the effects of the crisis on the sector. Despite the severe economic deterioration, its solvency ratio (CET1) increased by 71 basis points (bps) to 13.3% at the end of 2020. In parallel, bank credit to the private sector in Spain increased by 3.5% in 2020, breaking the previous trend. The role of the measures implemented has once again been very important. Thus, credit disposed of in transactions related to ICO's guarantee lines represented 18% of total new credit and 34% of credit to non-financial corporations and individual entrepreneurs. In addition, available evidence reveals that banks have used the funding received from the Eurosystem to lend to the and that entities that did not distribute dividends were more active in granting loans. Graphs on the evolution of doubtful loans and the NPL ratio of the resident private sector and on the signs of early deterioration in the credit to the resident private sector. At the same time, non-performing loans continued to fall, albeit at a slower pace than in previous years. However, in the last quarter of 2020 there were some signs of deterioration in credit quality, such as the increase in NPLs in some segments (such as consumer credit), a slowdown in the decline in refinanced credit or a sharp increase in credit under special surveillance. Graphs on the distribution of the ROA and the decomposition of the variation of the result. For its part, the consolidated net result of the banking system was negative in 2020, which meant that the return on assets (ROA) was .0.21%, which represented a fall of 72 bps compared to 2019. A significant part of this decline is explained by extraordinary negative factors in three of the main entities. If the main extraordinary items were excluded, the CEOS would have stood at 0,3%. In any In this case, the downward pressure on profitability was generalised by banks and was due, in particular, to the increase in impairment provisions, of more than 50%. The prospects for economic recovery translate into an improvement in the sector's expectations. In fact, in the first quarter of 2021, return on equity (excluding extraordinary impacts) for listed Spanish banks stood at 8%, still below estimates for the cost of capital (8.9%). But risks to financial stability persist and vulnerabilities have increased, emanating from the reduction of margins and the capital-generating capacity of institutions, as well as the weakening of the financial situation of households and companies. For the management of these risks, supervisory authorities have continued to stress that the use of capital buffers is appropriate to recognise credit deterioration and continue to provide creditworthiness. Banks will have sufficient time to return to meeting capital requirements and the process will not start before the main effects of the pandemic have dissipated. At the same time, due to the fact that uncertainty still persists, because the impact of the pandemic has not been fully manifested on banks' balance sheets and because they continue to benefit from various public support measures, we have recommended that they exercise extreme caution in dividend distribution and variable remuneration policies. At the same time, institutions should maintain a policy of anticipating the recognition of impairments, ensuring that this is adequate and timely, as set out in the supervisory guidelines. In this regard, in the first quarter of 2021 the NPL ratio in the hotel, catering and leisure sectors increased by 1.1 pp and the volume of loans under special surveillance continued to increase at a rate of 8.1% quarter-on-quarter. Also, as might be expected, the signs of deterioration in the portfolios of guaranteed and defaulted loans are higher than those of the rest. Overall, the provisioning effort is likely to be sustained over the next few years. At the same time, we will need to ensure that the resilience of the banking sector remains relative to emerging new risks. In particular, the implementation of the latest global reforms of Basel III is pending. The objective, which remains fully in force, is to standardize the calculation of risk-weighted assets. To achieve this, a key element is the so-called output floor, which establishes a floor to the reductions that banks can obtain with the use of internal models to calculate the minimum capital requirements with respect to the standard method. In addition, the Bank of Spain is in the process of amending Circular 2/2016, to operationalize the new macroprudential instruments conferred in national legislation. These instruments, which include requirements for granting credit, They will improve our ability to act against possible episodes of excessive or inadequate credit growth. It would also be appropriate to reflect on our institutional financial architecture. Some countries have evolved towards more integrated models with a greater role for central banks. Among these, the separation of the responsibilities of preserving the patrimonial soundness of all financial institutions (banking, insurance, securities, etc.), from those of monitoring the conduct in relations with their clients and their assignment to differentiated authorities (the Bank of Spain and the National Securities Market Commission, respectively) represent, in my opinion, an optimal institutional framework for managing potential conflicts between the two responsibilities and for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of supervisory activity. This reflection should include the resolution functions of institutions, which in Spain are separated between those related to prevention and execution, carried out by the Bank of Spain and the FROB, respectively, within the framework of the European Single Resolution Mechanism. This is a more complex scheme than that of other countries, where the two functions are generally unified under the body responsible for banking supervision (in the Spanish case, the Bank of Spain), which is justified by arguments of information economy, costs and coherence in the assessment of the implications for financial stability. Among the new risks that are emerging, the need for the financial sector to incorporate those associated with climate change stands out. Financial supervisors must ensure that institutions correctly assess these risks and incorporate them into their management, and we must encourage the development of information standards and databases suitable for their measurement. As for those derived from technological developments, in addition to those associated with cyberattacks, the possibility that competition from technology companies (bigtech) could become a disruptive way stands out. It will be necessary for the different authorities to adopt a proactive stance to question the regulatory perimeter, so as to guarantee the maximum of "same activity, same risks, same rules". In addition, technological competition could put additional pressure on the profitability of the banking sector, making it essential that banks continue to deepen efficiency gains, reduce costs and use new technologies more intensively. Central banks and financial supervisors must also adapt to new technologies. In the Eurosystem, we are in the process of setting targets and deadlines for a possible digital euro project, which is conceived as a tool to stimulate innovation and act as a catalyst for competitiveness and growth. It would also support the safeguarding of our monetary sovereignty and could also increase the external role of our currency and, by extension, the ability to influence beyond our borders. It is an ambitious approach that forces you to approach your design with an open mind, while taking the necessary precautions to ensure that all relevant dimensions (such as relating to financial stability, monetary policy or the configuration and role of the financial industry) are adequately taken into account. 5 Conclusion I end this hearing by reiterating one of the main messages that I wanted to convey to Spanish society since the beginning of this unprecedented crisis. The challenges facing the Spanish economy are structural in nature, and structural challenges require structural responses. The design and implementation of this response must be based on broad, political and social consensus so that they can have a vocation of permanence and be credible. A consensus that must be fully compatible with the ambition and urgency demanded by the magnitude of the challenges facing our economy. Our future prosperity will depend, to a large extent, on the promptness, ambition and permanence of the decisions we make to meet these challenges. Thanks a lot.

Nuestro escenario central asume que la tasa de ahorro disminuir progresivamente, pero, en 2023, se mantendra algo por encima del nivel previo a la pandemia. Detrs de esta reduccin se encuentra el descenso en la creacin de empresas, y no un repunte de las bajas, lo que podra explicarse por las medidas de apoyo adoptadas, incluida la moratoria concursal. Pero la evolucin futura es incierta. Las estimaciones del Banco de Espaa muestran que la proporcin de empresas en riesgo de convertirse en inviables habra aumentado entre 2 pp y 3 pp. Y el porcentaje de empresas que, aun siendo viables, tendran problemas de sobreendeudamiento podra aumentar entre 3 pp y 5 pp. Con todo, nuestro escenario central asume una destruccin moderada de tejido productivo.
