Title: Basel III implementation in the European Union. Introductory remarks
text: Basel III implementation in the European Union Introductory remarks by Pablo Hernandez de Cos Chair of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain Eurofi panel on Basel III implementation in the EU Ljubljana, 10 September 2021 Check against delivery Good morning and welcome to this panel on implementing Basel III in the EU. When I was asked to chair this panel (in my capacity as Chair of the Basel Committee), I must confess that I had somewhat mixed feelings. On the one hand, I was pleased to see that Eurofi was organising this one-hour panel to discuss what is a crucially important topic. As you know, following the Great Financial Crisis (GFC), the Basel Committee undertook a range of reforms to address material regulatory fault lines in the banking system. The benefits of the initial set of reforms  which were aimed at addressing the unsustainable levels of leverage in the banking system, insufficient high-quality capital, excessive maturity transformation and lack of a macroprudential overlay  were clear to all of us during this pandemic.1 The global banking system has remained broadly resilient to date, and, unlike during the GFC, banks have not exacerbated the economic crisis by sharply cutting back lending. The initial Basel III reforms, alongside an unprecedented range of public support measures, are the main explanations for this outcome.2 1 For a summary of the Basel III reforms, see C Borio, M Farag and N Tarashev (2020): Post-crisis international financial regulatory reforms: a primer, BIS Working Papers, no 859, April. 2 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2021): Early lessons from the Covid-19 pandemic on the Basel reforms, July. 3 P Hernandez de Cos (2021): Crossing the Basel III implementation line, speech given at the Eurofi High-level Virtual Seminar, 15 April. In many ways, Covid-19 has provided clear and tangible evidence of the benefits to society in having a well-capitalised banking system. We saw that jurisdictions with banks that had the largest capital buffers experienced a less severe impact on their expected GDP growth and better-capitalised banks increased their lending more during the pandemic relative to their peers.3 Yet the job of safeguarding global financial stability is far from finished. The outstanding Basel III reforms, which were finalised in 2017, are aimed at addressing significant fault lines in the global banking system. Addressing these fault lines remains as important today as it was pre-pandemic. Indeed, the primary objective of these reforms is to restore credibility in the risk-weighted capital framework. This is to be achieved by reducing excessive variability in banks modelled capital requirements and developing robust risk-sensitive standardised approaches which would also serve as the basis of the output floor. Recall how at the peak of the GFC investors lost faith in banks published ratios and placed more weight on other indicators of bank solvency. Whether due to a lack of robustness in banks models or an excessive degree of discretion in determining key regulatory inputs, the shortcomings in the risk-weighted asset (RWA) framework underlined the need for a complete overhaul. Let me just give one example to underline how these fault lines continue to remain a major concern today. In 2013, the Committees first report on the variability of banks risk-weighted assets highlighted a worrying degree of variation.4 When banks were asked to model their credit risk capital requirements for the same hypothetical portfolio, the reported capital ratios varied by 400 basis points. Fast-forward to 2021  eight years later  and despite repeated claims by some stakeholders that banks have already fixed this problem, the latest report by the European Banking Authority on banks modelled capital requirements points to a significant level of capital dispersion that needs to be monitored.5 4 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) (2013): Regulatory consistency assessment programme (RCAP)  analysis of risk-weighted assets for market risk, 31 January. 5 European Banking Authority (2021): EBA report result from the 2020 market risk benchmarking exercise, EBA Papers, no 5, March. 6 K Budnik, I Dimitrov, J Gross, M Lampe and M Volk (2021): Macroeconomic impact of Basel III finalisation on the euro area, European Central Bank Macroprudential Bulletin, issue 14, July. 7 Viterbo, A (2019): The European Union in the transnational financial regulatory arena: the case of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Journal of International Economic Law, vol 1, no 24, June. Importantly, these Basel III reforms are not an exercise to increase overall capital requirements at a global level. But equally, to successfully meet our primary objective, outlier banks, such as those with particularly aggressive modelling techniques, will rightly face higher requirements. Given the exogenous nature of the Covid-19 shock, these vulnerabilities were not tested during this pandemic. However, it is clear that, if left unaddressed, they will expose material shortcomings in the banking system in future financial crises. So I am pleased that we will have the opportunity this morning to discuss the implementation of these reforms in the EU. On the other hand, I remain concerned about the potential to focus the discussion on whether or how to implement Basel III in the EU in the current juncture! These reforms were finalised in 2017, with a globally agreed (revised) implementation date of 1 January 2023. G20 Leaders have repeatedly called for their full, timely and consistent implementation. Now is therefore the time for action. It is increasingly clear that the outstanding Basel III reforms will complement the previous ones in having a positive net impact on the economy. For example, a recent analysis by the ECB suggests that the GDP costs of implementing these reforms in Europe are modest and temporary, whereas their benefits will help to permanently strengthen the resilience of the economy to adverse shocks.6 It also finds that potential deviations from the globally agreed Basel III reforms  for example, with regard to the output floor  would significantly dilute the benefits to the real economy. Importantly, the reforms also benefited from an extensive consultation process with a wide range of stakeholders. Indeed, a recent academic study described the Committees consultation approach as one of the most procedurally sophisticated processes among policymaking bodies.7 The Committee published no fewer than 10 consultation papers as part of these reforms, with an accompanying consultation period that spanned the equivalent of almost three years! So the finalised standards agreed at the global level are already a compromise by their very nature, and reflect the different views of Committee members and external stakeholders. Over 35 key adjustments were made to the reforms during this period, with the majority of these reflecting the views of different European stakeholders. Financial stability is a global public good. It knows no geographic boundaries  the adage that no one is safe until everyone is safe applies as much to the pandemic as it does to safeguarding global financial stability. This is why the Committee designed and calibrated Basel III at a global level, and incorporated enough flexibility through national discretions within the framework. Approaching these reforms from a different perspective  for example by giving undue attention to the impact on individual banks, jurisdictions or regions  risks missing the forest for the trees. To be clear: the domestic and democratic transposition of global standards is a very important process and one that should be fully respected. But the focus should now primarily be on the action side of things, which means demonstrating how the EUs commitment to multilateralism and to globally agreed decisions endorsed by the Group of Governors and Heads of Supervision, and to which G20 Leaders have repeatedly committed to implementing in a full, timely and consistent manner. So I hope that our panel discussion today and the active participation of the audience will provide a constructive discussion on these important issues, building on the broad landscape that I have just set out.

Title: Governance and conduct of institutions. Keys to the reputation and sustainability of banking business models in Spain
text: 16.09.2021 Governance and conduct of institutions. Keys to the reputation and sustainability of banking business models in Spain Financial meeting point Finanza Pablo Hernandez de Cos Governor Mr. Delegate of the Government, Ladies and Gentlemen, other authorities, ladies and gentlemen, good morning, I want to start by thanking Elkargi and, in particular, its president, Josu S87nchez, and its general director, Zen97n V87zquez, for organizing this meeting and the opportunity they give me to participate in it. On this occasion, I will share with you some reflections on two qualitative elements of the culture and ways of doing things in banking d0 the quality of governance and the conduct of banks d0 which, in my opinion, have a great influence on the medium and long-term sustainability of banking business models and on the reputation of the sector. The international financial crisis showed how banking malpractice can undermine the foundations of the financial system. Hence the emphasis of legislators, regulators and supervisors on improving this practice, with the development of an extensive body of regulations in these matters and a reinforcement in their supervision. In a context where reputational enhancement remains one of the main challenges facing the banking sector, I would like to review progress in these two areas and the main challenges we face. The importance of governance in credit institutions 'Governance' means the set of rules, principles and procedures governing the structure and functioning of an undertaking's governing bodies and enabling decision-making. This mechanism is divided into two aspects: an internal one, which determines the management of the activity itself, and an external one, which defines the framework of the entity's relationship with the various market agents (analysts, customers, shareholders, investors, supervisors and regulators). Given this definition, it is clear that governance is an essential determinant of institutions' ability to respond successfully to new challenges and risks in a changing environment, and thus of the strength of institutions. Assessing governance is a difficult task. In the first place, because it involves analyzing a large number of aspects, of a very diverse nature, at the theoretical level and in their practical effectiveness as lines of defense. Secondly, because, due to the different legal nature of supervised entities and their status as listed or not, there are heterogeneous structures and forms of management, so it has been necessary to design open supervisory models that allow all these situations to be assessed. And, thirdly, perhaps the most relevant, because it is not easily objectifiable or directly measurable, unlike other risks, but it can be calibrated. However, although there is no minimum ratio or level that institutions must achieve in this area, there are factors that determine adequate governance d0 such as transparency in the market, sound and prudent risk management or an appropriate organizational structure. Indeed, in the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) the Governance is one of the four basic elements that we analyze within our annual evaluation of credit institutions, and conditions the minimum capital requirements that we demand and, therefore, the maximum amount distributable to shareholders. The depth, scale and economic and social impact of the 2007 financial crisis, as well as the weak governance structures of some of the banks that suffered most from that crisis, highlighted the need to analyse this aspect of banks in detail and to substantially expand their regulatory framework. Thus, on a global scale, weaknesses were detected in relation to the composition and independence of the boards of directors, outdated organizational structures or a lack of rigor in controls, which prevented correct decision-making on some occasions. In addition, the entities had short-term remuneration schemes that encouraged excessive risk-taking and did not take into account their long-term viability. In Europe, and in Spain in particular, regulatory activity in the field of governance and transparency has been of great importance1. In terms of remuneration, current European regulations impose variable remuneration structures on institutions aligned with their risk profile, to prevent them from leading to excessive risk-taking. In addition, a complete and detailed suitability regime has been established for members of the boards of directors and the regime of incompatibilities and limitations of senior positions has been strengthened. With regard to the functioning of the administrative bodies, it has been mandatory for there to be four committees (appointments, remuneration, audit and risks). 1 In Spain, the reform of the corporate governance of credit institutions has resulted in important substantive rules, such as Law 10/2014, Royal Decree 84/2015 and Circular 2/2016, which transpose and develop the European Capital Directive and affect all credit institutions, regardless of their size/volume of assets or their unique characteristics. In addition, the specific guidelines developed by the European Banking Authority, adopted as its own by the Bank of Spain and by the European Central Bank, which since 2014 has been the consolidated supervisor of significant banking institutions, also apply. In terms of transparency, in the so-called Prudential Relevance Report, institutions must publish information on their decision-making processes, the composition and functioning of their governing bodies, and the remuneration systems of both their directors and senior managers. These increased demands of the regulator, the market and society, together with the need and difficulty to face increasingly important and complex risks, such as conduct and technology, have also led to a significant increase in supervisory intensity and the definition of new processes to determine the suitability of both directors and CEOs or people who manage key areas of banks, who are increasingly demanding with their reputation and knowledge. As a result, there has been an improvement in the quality of governance structures, which have evolved towards more professional models adapted to society, abandoning personalistic management structures, impervious to diversity, technological development and collegial decisions. However, since its creation in 2014, the SSM has carried out numerous supervisory actions on this matter, which have shown the need for improvements both in Spain and in the rest of Europe. These improvements revolve around three fundamental aspects: providing evidence on the quality of the debate in the highest decision-making bodies and the ability to question the decisions taken for approval; improve the knowledge and independence of boards, as well as the allocation of their responsibilities, and necessarily develop more robust and detailed risk appetite frameworks. In Spain, due to national corporate regulations, the governance model of credit institutions has some singularities, compared to other systems implemented in Europe, which must be taken into account when assessing them. The first is the so-called one-tier model, in which the board of directors, or the governing board in the case of credit unions, brings together both the management function of the entity and the supervisory function, compared to the dualist model of other European countries, in which both functions are distributed between two governing bodies. In this case, the mandatory creation of both the delegated committees of the board and those of audit, appointments, remuneration and risks strengthens the supervisory function of the governing bodies through the examination and permanent monitoring of some areas of special relevance. Crucially, such committees should consist entirely of non-executive directors and include a minimum number of independent directors, one of whom will be the chairman. The second is the existence, on many occasions, of an executive chairman. In these cases, Spanish legislation for public limited companies requires, on the one hand, a reinforced majority of two-thirds of the board for their appointment and, on the other, the appointment of a coordinating director from among the independents to serve as a counterweight to the executive directors to ensure that the oversight function is carried out in a full and effective manner. Although international standards advocate a non-executive chairman to facilitate the division of duties, one of the main lessons from the SSM reviews is that there is no perfect governance structure, because, in practice, all governance structures pose similar problems with regard to the effectiveness of management and oversight functions. In fact, in those entities in which the president is not executive, regardless of their legal nature, it is also essential that there is the necessary balance and distribution of functions between the president d0 whose functions should be more focused on strategic aspects d0 and the first executive of the entity, in charge of purely business functions and whose direct report to the board serves to mitigate the excessive concentration of power in the figure. of the President. Within the European context, the governance of Spanish entities currently shows a dual reality. On the one hand, there are those that, although they still have some room for improvement, have made substantial progress in recent years in their governance structures, combining more agile decision-making mechanisms with more robust control processes. This group is mainly included in the largest entities. size with the nature of public limited companies and those with securities admitted to trading, which are more directly subject to market discipline. On the other hand, there is a second group of entities that still have a way to fully comply with both regulation and supervisory expectations in the field of their governance. This group mainly includes some entities that are not public limited companies or that are smaller in size, although the latter aspect is tempered by the application of the principle of proportionality. However, it should be stressed that both aspects (legal nature and size) are not absolute factors that determine the quality of governance, although, in general, the difficulties of small institutions in implementing an adequate separation of internal governance functions and the important value of market discipline for the governance of those entities active in listed markets have been verified. As examples of this duality in progress, it is worth mentioning that in the first group of entities the weight of independent directors has gradually increased in order to improve the supervisory function within the board, in addition to guaranteeing the defense of the rights of all shareholders, partners or participants. At the other extreme, there are still entities with a small share of independents (less than 50%) or even none in their governing bodies. In addition, another deficiency to highlight is that there are entities whose directors have a high seniority in their positions. Secondly, in terms of the professionalism and diversity of the boards, it has been observed that, the larger the entity, the greater the diversity of the board in all dimensions (gender, age, specialization in relevant knowledge, international profiles, etc.). Likewise, in those entities that have made the most progress in the two previous points, a clear improvement has been observed in the collective functioning of the administrative bodies. Thirdly, with regard to the independence of control functions (second line of defence and internal audit), many entities have established a clear separation between these functions and the management units, avoiding any conflict of interest that may arise, while ensuring direct access for their managers to the board and providing them with greater resources. Other entities need to move further down this path to ensure that their governing bodies can oversee and control the management performed, which the smaller the entity, the more it tends to focus on a single person (usually the chief executive), which is a risk to good governance. In summary, although improvements in governance models have been important in the last decade, we cannot ignore the need to continue advancing in this area, which is a fundamental pillar to guarantee the solidity and sustainability of institutions. The conduct of institutions in the framework of financial regulation Regulation of the banking sector, as well as its supervision by public authorities, is based on two fundamental pillars. The first consists of the requirements and the prudential supervision, essentially by imposing levels of own resources linked to the risks they assume and requiring robust procedures for the knowledge and management of those risks. The second relates to the adequate protection of the financial customer through detailed regulation of the relations between institutions and their clients, and the supervision of their compliance. The relationship between these two pillars is very close. Banks and the banking business are based on the trust that customers place in the entities and that generated by the entities among themselves. And this trust is based not only on their financial strength, but also on banks' compliance with values and principles d0 what is called a "banking culture" d0 that promote correct behaviour at all levels and, in particular, towards their customers. Inappropriate conduct, in addition to undermining this trust, also ends up generating direct financial costs in the form of litigation, reimbursement of amounts to customers, compensation, etc. In Spain, these costs materialized most notably in the years following the international financial crisis2. In turn, the accumulation of these events may end up affecting the calculation of the operational risk incurred by the entities and, therefore, their future prudential requirements. 2 By way of illustration, it should be noted that between 2014 and 2020 the cumulative amount of losses due to operational risk of Spanish credit institutions associated with failures in the fulfillment of obligations to customers or the design of products has exceeded 19,000 million euros at a consolidated level. 3 In the regulatory field, in addition to the legislation emanating from the Parliament (national or European), the Banco de Espa96a also issues, through circulars, the precise provisions for the development of those rules that expressly authorize it to do so. 4 The concept of annual percentage rate (APR) appears, a basic piece of information for customers on the cost or profitability of banking products and a key tool for comparing the offers of different entities, which remains fully valid today. From the public sphere, we have tried to encourage and ensure the appropriate behavior of entities in relation to their clients through four instruments essentially: regulation, supervision of entities, resolution of complaints and customer queries, and promotion of financial education of the population. The regulation of the conduct of entities has undergone an important transformation in recent decades. The process of liberalisation of the financial sector in the eighties of the last century, which culminated in 1989 with freedom of pricing for all credit institutions, was followed by an increase in both national and European standards3. From that moment on, transparency and information to customers acquire great relevance, as well as advertising and adequate commercial promotion of banking services. In addition, regulation is beginning to require certain pieces of pre-contractual information that institutions must offer to their customers in order to allow borrowers to make their decisions based on the real risk of the products4. Subsequently, in the context of the lessons of the international financial crisis, there was an evolution towards a more advanced model of conduct, regulating for the first time the figure of responsible credit, which obliges credit institutions to assess the solvency of their customers and the suitability of products for them. Thereafter, With the impetus of a set of European directives5, the general regulatory framework is built, which, with some modifications and additions, is still in force today. 5 Mainly those relating to consumer credit, mortgage credit, payment services, distance marketing and basic payment account. 6 The Banco de Espa96a is responsible for supervising the conduct of entities that market banking or payment products and services 7 In particular, it involves: (i) verification of revolving card marketing, financing for the purchase of motor vehicles and credit granted in the form of overdraft possibilities in demand deposits; (ii) the review of responsible lending practices for consumer finance; 8 Recently, we have also focused on the direct verification of transparency obligations in bank branches, in order to assess whether the information and documentation provided to customers comply with transparency regulations; in the supervision of the advertising of banking products and services, in order to verify and promote that it is truthful, clear and concise, and in the supervision of the activity of the customer services of the entities. At the same time, the Banco de Espa96a has been adapting and strengthening its supervisory activity in this area6 and adapting its own internal organisation to maximise its effectiveness. As an illustration, the Department of Conduct of Entities of the Bank of Spain was created in 2013 with 38 people and today has 107. Given the importance of the mortgage segment for Spanish families, which accounts for just over 74% of the credit granted by the banking system to Spanish households, the priority areas of attention have been the supervision of transparency in the contracting of mortgage loans and the protection of mortgage debtors in economic difficulties. Subsequently, the focus has turned to consumer financing, which in the quarters prior to the onset of the pandemic was growing at significant rates7, 8. And, more recently, during the pandemic, special attention has been paid to the correct implementation by supervised entities of the different debt relief measures approved by the Government d0 moratoriums on mortgage and consumer loans. Let me recall here that supervisory actions in the area of conduct can lead to corrective action. In this sense, the Bank of Spain dictates mandatory requirements for the affected entities and, if necessary, can impose different types of sanctions, including economic ones. Thus, between 2016 and 2020, 26 disciplinary proceedings for infractions in the field of conduct have been resolved, which have resulted in sanctions worth 52 million euros, actions to which should be added the 982 requirements approved by the Executive Committee during the same period, many of which have involved the return of relevant amounts to affected customers. Beyond supervision, the Bank of Spain focuses its action on banking customers in three other major areas. In the first place, the attention of the consultations on their rights in terms of transparency and protection of the clientele or on the legal channels for the exercise of their rights. As an illustration, in 2020 more than 6,200 written queries and more than 40,000 calls were answered; It highlights the reinforcement of attention to address the doubts that are generated in relation to debt payment moratoriums and other measures established due to the COVID-199 crisis. 9 This number of written and telephone consultations represents an increase of more than 50% in relation to those attended in the previous year and, in any case, even cleaning up the specific incidence derived from COVID-19, the figure has remained above those of the previous year throughout 2020. 10 We understand good banking practices as those that, without being imposed by contractual or supervisory regulations or constituting a financial use, are reasonably required for responsible, diligent and respectful management of financial business customers. 11 A good example of this update is the criterion relating to the passing-on to clients of expenses for claiming debtor positions, which in 2020 has become more demanding as regards the justification to be made by institutions on the reality and amount of that expense as a condition for its passing on to customers. Secondly, and closely linked to the attention of queries, the resolution of conflicts that may arise between users and financial institutions appears here. The complaints process d0 identical to that followed by other financial supervisors in the areas of securities and insurance d0 is limited to the analysis of the performance of supervised entities in terms of the correct application of transparency and customer protection regulations and good banking practices10. Throughout its more than 33 years of existence, the Complaints Service of the Bank of Spain has analyzed tens of thousands of cases raised by citizens. This extensive activity has generated a valuable doctrine on good banking practices, which is reviewed and updated every year with the publication of the Claims Report, whose edition corresponding to 2020 was published last July11. The crucial contribution of complaints activity to conduct and transparency oversight processes should be highlighted, as disputes can often reveal regulatory breaches by supervised entities. This has been the case, for example, with the marketing of revolving cards. The value of the complaints system in identifying gaps in citizens' knowledge and possible problems in understanding the products and services offered by banking and payment intermediaries is also important. Hence the reinforcement that we intend to achieve with the recent supervisory guide on the criteria for the organization and operation of the customer services of the entities supervised by the Bank of Spain. Thirdly, we must stress that promoting financial stability requires a comprehensive approach, which also requires fostering society's financial literacy. Indeed, improving this knowledge has become a long-term priority for central banks and supervisors. The starting point is not good. As an example, the results of the Financial Skills Survey, which measures the financial knowledge of the population, showed that, for example, 42% of the Spanish population did not understand what inflation is. Financial education is a fundamental tool to make it easier for citizens to understand the characteristics, risks and opportunities of product contracting financial, as well as the rights and obligations in such procurement. In this way, financial education is a complement to the regulation and supervision of conduct, and, in general, to the promotion of the stability of the financial system. The main action of the Bank of Spain in the field of financial education is mainly channeled through the Financial Education Plan, which was born in 2008 with a collaboration agreement between the Bank of Spain and the National Securities Market Commission (CNMV), promoters of this plan. The main activity of the Plan is developed through a network of collaborators in which the competent administrations in the financial, educational and consumer fields participate, as well as private actors, such as professional associations, training and research institutes, consumer associations, the financial industry, educational associations and social and third sector organizations. Thus, it constitutes a paradigm of the public-private collaboration model that endows it with a high geographical and social capillarity. In this area, the School Programme, which is developed in collaboration with the education authorities, offers manuals for students and teachers, and training and teaching and support materials for the latter, is complemented by competitions and prizes and has been a catalyst for the progressive inclusion of financial education in the school curriculum. The Bank of Spain also feeds the so-called Banking Customer Portal, which, with very accessible formats, provides information, warnings and practical resources on the management of domestic finances and the relationship of customers with banks, and allows access to a consultation system.12 12 During 2020, the Banking Customer Portal reached 5.5 million visits; Especially noteworthy are those made to mortgage or personal loan simulators and APR, and to the table of interest rates, assets and liabilities, applied by the entities. What are the main challenges we face right now in the field of behavior? The first responsibility for improvement in the field of behavior lies with the entities themselves. In this sense, the entities have increased their organizational and resource efforts in this area and have located, in general, their customer service in more prominent places in their organizational structure. In any case, in 2020 the Bank of Spain analysed 21,320 claims, a figure in the average of the last ten years but with an increase of 46% compared to 2019. And, so far in 2021, with almost 13,000 claims in the first quarter, it is not ruled out that the annual figure is very close to the historical highs of 2013, 2014 and 2017. It is true that the figures of claims are highly conditioned by factors such as the announcement or implementation of new regulations, the expansion of news about banking products or about circumstances that occurred in the financial market and the existence of judicial actions or pronouncements that affect the practices of Marketing of financial institutions. In any case, the high number of complaints is also illustrative of the road that still remains to be traveled. In this regard, I would like to stress that the adaptation of entities to a new, more demanding regulatory framework, from both a prudential and conduct point of view, is a necessary condition for maintaining confidence in the industry, but I believe that it is no longer a sufficient condition. An appropriate culture, effectively transmitted from the management bodies of the entities to their entire organization and, in particular, to their commercial network, as well as a continuous effort to reinforce these values for all employees, is essential. In this sense, in terms of claims, in a high percentage of cases, around 70%, the entities comply with the criteria of the Bank of Spain and rectify their conduct. However, the percentage of complaints that, according to the criteria of the Bank of Spain, agree with customers but that some entities do not resolve in their favor remains, in my opinion, very high. Beyond the fact that, in accordance with the current regulations, the reports of the Bank of Spain are not binding on the entities, a circumstance that undoubtedly limits the effectiveness of the claims system and that should be the subject of reflection in a possible modification of the aforementioned regulation, I consider that it would be important from the reputational point of view and of improving relations with their clients that the entities accepted with a generalized character the resolutions of the Bank of Spain. Moreover, institutions should strengthen internal procedures relating to product design, marketing and governance, precisely so that they allow for the development and establishment of compliance behaviours and aimed at making customers at the centre of the institution's strategy. In addition, the management of institutions must be actively involved in aspects such as the governance of the products they market and the adaptation of their design to the needs of their customers, as well as in training and incentive mechanisms for sales personnel. Increased competition d0 with the threat even of new players in the market, such as the so-called fintech and bigtech d0 should, in fact, force entities to take more account of the needs of their customers. The challenges also reach the regulators and supervisors themselves. Thus, the constant evolution of banks' business models, the entry of new operators (such as real estate lenders, real estate credit intermediaries or certain types of payment service providers), who sometimes develop cross-border operations and who largely provide their services in a digital environment, implies a considerable challenge for the regulation and supervision of conduct. We must be able to adapt regulation early and appropriately, so as to ensure the protection of customers in the face of these new developments and, in parallel, a competitive balance between all market players. In supervisory matters, this has acquired a complexity that requires the provision of new tools and new knowledge by supervisors. Thus, in the case of the Bank of Spain, we are going to incorporate a new reporting model for entities Specially designed for the monitoring of the behavior that we estimate will allow us to improve the knowledge of the model of your business and the trends of the market of banking products and services. We will also add machine learning and computer vision techniques to the supervisory process, with the aim of increasing the efficiency of our supervision. Further reflection could also be given to the adequacy of our current institutional oversight architecture, based on a sectoral model. Some countries have evolved towards more integrated models with a greater role for central banks. Among these, separating the prudential supervision responsibilities of all financial institutions (banking, insurance, securities, etc.) from those of monitoring conduct in relations with their customers and assigning them to differentiated authorities (the Bank of Spain and the CNMV, respectively) represents, in my opinion, an optimal institutional scheme to manage possible conflicts between both responsibilities and to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the activity. supervisor as a whole. On the other hand, in terms of financial education, it is necessary to continue focusing on incorporating financial skills into compulsory education. Currently, the Financial Education Plan focuses on secondary school students, but there are already concepts and behaviors that can be learned in primary school. The expert guidelines, which are promoted by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development and followed in most countries, indicate that financial education should be included in the academic curriculum and addressed as a transversal competence. It should also be borne in mind that this new environment in which the way services are provided has changed d1 which, in general, implies a possibility of access to products and services in a more agile, competitive and lower cost manner d1 may also pose difficulties in access to banking services for certain groups and the need for new skills, in addition to the financial ones, such as digital. As a result, risks of financial exclusion as well as fraud could arise. In this context, we must pay special attention to vulnerable groups and the elderly. In conclusion, changes in the ways of relating between entities and their customers are still another manifestation of the response to the new technological and competitive environment in which they operate. This new environment demands new skills, knowledge and procedures among those leading this transformation: bank managers who, supported by solid governance, understand and manage the opportunities and risks presented by technological innovation for banks and their customers, and experts who guide the new analysis tools that make their way in the processes of evaluation and marketing of financial products towards the principles and values of organizations. New legal, risk assessment and compliance competencies will also be needed to drive and drive this new culture from its design in central services to sales networks. And, of course, supervisors and regulators cannot be left behind in understanding and adapting to these transformations. Thank you very much for your attention.

La importancia de la gobernanza en las entidades de crdito Por gobernanza se entiende el conjunto de normas, principios y procedimientos que regulan la estructura y el funcionamiento de los rganos de gobierno de una empresa y que permiten la toma de decisiones. La conducta de las entidades en el marco de la regulacin financiera La regulacin del sector bancario, as como su supervisin por parte de las autoridades pblicas, se basa en dos pilares fundamentales. Al proceso de liberalizacin del sector financiero de la dcada de los ochenta del siglo pasado que culmin en 1989 con la libertad de fijacin de precios para todas las entidades de crdito le sigui un incremento de las normas tanto nacionales como europeas3. Asimismo, la regulacin empieza a exigir determinadas piezas de informacin precontractual que las entidades deben ofrecer a sus clientes con el objetivo de permitir a los prestatarios tomar sus decisiones en funcin del riesgo real de los productos4. Posteriormente, en el contexto de las lecciones de la crisis financiera internacional se produjo una evolucin hacia un modelo ms avanzado de conducta, al regular por primera vez la figura del crdito responsable, que obliga a las entidades de crdito a evaluar la solvencia de sus clientes y la conveniencia de los productos para ellos. A partir de entonces, con el impulso de un conjunto de directivas europeas5, se construye el marco regulatorio general, que, con algunas modificaciones y adiciones, sigue hoy vigente. 5 Principalmente, las relativas a crdito al consumo, crdito hipotecario, servicios de pago, comercializacin a distancia y cuenta de pago bsica. 6 El Banco de Espaa es el responsable de la supervisin de la conducta de las entidades que comercializan productos y servicios bancarios o de pago 7 En concreto, hacia: i) la verificacin de la actividad de comercializacin de tarjetas revolving, de la financiacin para la adquisicin de automviles y del crdito concedido en forma de posibilidad de descubierto en depsitos a la vista; ii) la revisin de las prcticas de concesin responsable de financiacin al consumo, y iii) las prcticas de comercializacin del prstamo al consumo a travs de operadores no bancarios grandes superficies, cadenas comerciales, etc.. 8 Recientemente, tambin hemos puesto el foco supervisor en la verificacin directa de las obligaciones de transparencia en las oficinas bancarias, al objeto de evaluar si la informacin y la documentacin proporcionadas a la clientela satisfacen la normativa de transparencia; en la supervisin de la publicidad de productos y servicios bancarios, a fin de comprobar y promover que sea veraz, clara y concisa, y en la supervisin de la actividad de los servicios de atencin al cliente de las entidades. En paralelo, el Banco de Espaa ha venido adaptando y reforzando su actividad supervisora en esta materia6 y adecuando su propia organizacin interna para maximizar su eficacia. Como ilustracin, el Departamento de Conducta de Entidades del Banco de Espaa fue creado en 2013 con 38 personas y hoy cuenta con 107. Dada la importancia del segmento hipotecario para las familias espaolas, que supone algo ms del 74 % del crdito concedido por el sistema bancario a los hogares espaoles, las reas prioritarias de atencin han sido la supervisin de la transparencia en la contratacin de crdito hipotecario y la proteccin de los deudores hipotecarios en dificultades econmicas. Con posterioridad, el foco ha girado hacia la financiacin al consumo, que en los trimestres previos a la aparicin de la pandemia estaba creciendo a tasas significativas7, 8. Permtanme aqu recordar que las actuaciones supervisoras en el mbito de la conducta pueden derivar en la adopcin de medidas correctivas. En este sentido, el Banco de Espaa dicta requerimientos de obligado cumplimiento para las entidades afectadas y, llegado el caso, puede imponer diferentes tipos de sanciones, entre ellas las econmicas. As, entre 2016 y 2020 se han resuelto 26 expedientes sancionadores por infracciones en materia de conducta, que han dado como resultado sanciones por valor de 52 millones de euros, actuaciones a las que habra que sumar los 982 requerimientos aprobados por la Comisin Ejecutiva durante el mismo perodo, muchos de los cuales han supuesto la devolucin de cantidades relevantes a los clientes afectados. Ms all de la supervisin, el Banco de Espaa centra su actuacin sobre la clientela bancaria en otras tres grandes reas. En primer lugar, la atencin de las consultas sobre sus derechos en materia de transparencia y proteccin de la clientela o sobre los cauces legales para el ejercicio de sus derechos. Como ilustracin, en 2020 se respondieron ms de 6.200 consultas escritas y ms de 40.000 llamadas; destaca el refuerzo de la atencin para atender las dudas que se generaron en relacin con las moratorias de pago de deuda y otras medidas establecidas a causa de la crisis del COVID-199. 9 Esta cifra de consultas escritas y telefnicas supone un aumento superior al 50 % en relacin con las atendidas en el ao anterior y, en todo caso, incluso depurando la incidencia puntual derivada del COVID-19, la cifra se ha mantenido a lo largo de todo el ao 2020 por encima de las del precedente. 10 Entendemos por buenas prcticas bancarias aquellas que, sin venir impuestas por la normativa contractual o de supervisin ni constituir un uso financiero, son razonablemente exigibles para la gestin responsable, diligente y respetuosa con la clientela de los negocios financieros. 11 Un buen ejemplo de esta actualizacin lo constituye el criterio relativo a la repercusin a clientes de los gastos por reclamacin de posiciones deudoras, que en 2020 se ha hecho ms exigente en cuanto a la justificacin que deben hacer las entidades sobre la realidad y la cuanta de dicho gasto como requisito para su repercusin a los clientes. En segundo lugar, e ntimamente ligada a la atencin de consultas, aparece aqu la resolucin de conflictos que pueden surgir entre los usuarios y las entidades financieras. El proceso de reclamaciones idntico al que siguen otros supervisores financieros en las reas de valores y seguros se circunscribe al anlisis de la actuacin de las entidades supervisadas en cuanto a la correcta aplicacin de la normativa de transparencia y proteccin de la clientela y a las buenas prcticas bancarias10. A lo largo de sus ms de 33 aos de andadura, el Servicio de Reclamaciones del Banco de Espaa ha analizado decenas de miles de casos planteados por los ciudadanos. Esta prolija actividad ha generado una valiosa doctrina sobre buenas prcticas bancarias, que se revisa y actualiza cada ao con la publicacin de la Memoria de Reclamaciones, cuya edicin correspondiente a 2020 se public el pasado mes de julio11. Hay que destacar la contribucin crucial que supone la actividad de reclamaciones a los procesos de supervisin de conducta y transparencia, en la medida en que, con frecuencia, las disputas pueden revelar la existencia de incumplimientos normativos por parte de las entidades supervisadas. Este ha sido el caso, por ejemplo, de la comercializacin de tarjetas revolving. Es importante tambin el valor que aporta el sistema de reclamaciones para detectar lagunas en los conocimientos de los ciudadanos y eventuales problemas de comprensin de los productos y servicios que ofrecen los intermediarios bancarios y de pagos. De ah el refuerzo que pretendemos alcanzar con la reciente gua supervisora sobre los criterios de organizacin y funcionamiento de los servicios de atencin al cliente de las entidades supervisadas por el Banco de Espaa. En tercer lugar, debemos subrayar que promover la estabilidad financiera requiere un enfoque global, lo que exige tambin fomentar los conocimientos financieros de la sociedad. De hecho, mejorar estos conocimientos se ha convertido en una cuestin prioritaria a largo plazo para los bancos centrales y los supervisores. El punto de partida no es bueno. Como ejemplo, los resultados de la Encuesta de Competencias Financieras, que mide el conocimiento financiero de la poblacin, pusieron de manifiesto que, por ejemplo, el 42 % de la poblacin espaola no entenda lo que es la inflacin. La educacin financiera es una herramienta fundamental para facilitar que los ciudadanos entienda las caractersticas, los riesgos y las oportunidades de la contratacin de productos financieros, as como los derechos y las obligaciones en dicha contratacin. De esta manera, la educacin financiera es un complemento a la regulacin y a la supervisin de conducta, y, en general, a la promocin de la estabilidad del sistema financiero. La accin principal del Banco de Espaa en materia de educacin financiera se canaliza fundamentalmente a travs del Plan de Educacin Financiera, que naci en 2008 con un convenio de colaboracin entre el Banco de Espaa y la Comisin Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV), promotores de dicho plan. La actividad principal del Plan se desarrolla a travs de una red de colaboradores en la que participan las Administraciones competentes en los mbitos financiero, educativo y de consumo, y tambin actores privados, como asociaciones profesionales, institutos de formacin e investigacin, asociaciones de consumidores, la industria financiera, asociaciones educativas y organizaciones sociales y del tercer sector. As pues, constituye un paradigma del modelo de colaboracin pblico-privada que lo dota de una elevada capilaridad tanto geogrfica como social. Destaca en este mbito el Programa Escolar, que se desarrolla en colaboracin con las administraciones educativas, ofrece manuales para alumnos y profesores, y formacin y materiales didcticos y de apoyo para los segundos, se complementa con concursos y premios y ha sido un catalizador para la progresiva inclusin de la educacin financiera en el currculo escolar. El Banco de Espaa alimenta tambin el denominado Portal del Cliente Bancario, que, con unos formatos muy accesibles, aporta informacin, advertencias y recursos prcticos sobre el manejo de las finanzas domsticas y la relacin de los clientes con las entidades bancarias, y permite el acceso a un sistema de consultas.12 12 Durante 2020, el Portal del Cliente Bancario alcanz 5,5 millones de visitas; destacan en especial las realizadas a los simuladores de prstamo hipotecario o personal y de TAE, y a la tabla de tipos de inters, activos y pasivos, aplicados por las entidades. Cules son los principales desafos a los que nos enfrentamos en este momento en el mbito de la conducta? La primera responsabilidad para la mejora en el mbito de la conducta recae en las propias entidades. En este sentido, las entidades han aumentado sus esfuerzos organizativos y de recursos en esta materia y han situado, con carcter general, sus servicios de atencin al cliente en lugares ms preminentes de su estructura organizativa. En todo caso, en 2020 el Banco de Espaa analiz 21.320 reclamaciones, cifra en el promedio de los ltimos diez aos pero con un aumento del 46 % con respecto a 2019. Y, en lo que llevamos de 2021, con casi 13.000 reclamaciones en el primer cuatrimestre, no es descartable que la cifra anual quede muy cerca de los mximos histricos de 2013, 2014 y 2017. Es cierto que las cifras de reclamaciones estn muy condicionadas por factores como el anuncio o la implementacin de nuevas regulaciones, la expansin de noticias sobre productos bancarios o sobre circunstancias acaecidas en el mercado financiero y la existencia de actuaciones o pronunciamientos judiciales que afectan a las prcticas de comercializacin de las entidades financieras. De cualquier manera, el elevado nmero de reclamaciones es tambin ilustrativo del camino que todava queda por recorrer. En este sentido, me gustara subrayar que la adaptacin de las entidades a un nuevo marco regulatorio ms exigente, desde el punto de vista tanto prudencial como de conducta, es condicin necesaria para mantener la confianza en la industria, pero creo que no es ya condicin suficiente. Una cultura adecuada, transmitida de manera eficaz desde los rganos de administracin de las entidades a toda su organizacin y, en especial, a su red comercial, as como un esfuerzo continuado en el reforzamiento de esos valores para todos los empleados, resulta esencial. En este sentido, en materia de reclamaciones, en un alto porcentaje de casos, en torno al 70 %, las entidades acatan el criterio del Banco de Espaa y rectifican su conducta. Sin embargo, el porcentaje de reclamaciones que, segn el criterio del Banco de Espaa, dan la razn a los clientes pero que algunas entidades no resuelven a su favor sigue siendo, en mi opinin, muy elevado. Ms all de que, de acuerdo con la regulacin vigente, los informes del Banco de Espaa no son vinculantes para las entidades, circunstancia que, sin duda, limita la eficacia del sistema de reclamaciones y que debera ser objeto de reflexin en una eventual modificacin de la referida regulacin, considero que sera importante desde el punto de vista reputacional y de mejora de las relaciones con sus clientes que las entidades aceptaran con carcter generalizado las resoluciones del Banco de Espaa. Por otra parte, las entidades deben reforzar los procedimientos internos relativos al diseo, la comercializacin y la gobernanza de productos, precisamente para que permitan el desarrollo y el asentamiento de conductas de cumplimiento y orientadas a que los clientes se conviertan en el centro de la estrategia de la entidad. Adems, la direccin de las entidades debe implicarse activamente en aspectos como la gobernanza de los productos que comercializan y la adecuacin de su diseo a las necesidades de sus clientes, as como en la formacin y en los mecanismos de incentivos al personal de ventas. La eleva competencia con la amenaza incluso de nuevos actores en el mercado, como las denominadas fintech y bigtech debera obligar, de hecho, a las entidades a tener ms presentes las necesidades de sus clientes. Los retos tambin alcanzan a los propios reguladores y supervisores. As, la constante evolucin de los modelos de negocio de las entidades, la entrada de nuevos operadores (como los prestamistas inmobiliarios, los intermediarios de crdito inmobiliario o determinadas tipologas de prestadores de servicios de pago), que en ocasiones desarrollan una operativa transfronteriza y que prestan en gran parte sus servicios en un entorno digital, implica un reto considerable para la regulacin y la supervisin de conducta. Debemos ser capaces de adaptar la regulacin de manera temprana y adecuada, de modo que se garanticen la proteccin de los clientes antes estos nuevos desarrollos y, en paralelo, un equilibrio competitivo entre todos los actores del mercado. En materia supervisora, esta ha adquirido una complejidad que requiere la dotacin de nuevas herramientas y nuevos conocimientos por parte de los supervisores. As, en el caso del Banco de Espaa, vamos a incorporar un nuevo modelo de reporte para las entidades especialmente diseado para el seguimiento de la conducta que estimamos que nos permitir mejorar el conocimiento del modelo de su negocio y de las tendencias del mercado de productos y servicios bancarios. Asimismo, vamos a aadir al proceso supervisor tcnicas de machine learning y de computer vision, con el objetivo de incrementar la eficiencia de nuestra supervisin. Cabra hacer tambin una reflexin ms a fondo sobre la idoneidad de nuestra actual arquitectura institucional de supervisin, basada en un modelo sectorial. Algunos pases han evolucionado hacia modelos ms integrados y con un mayor papel de los bancos centrales. Entre estos, separar las responsabilidades de supervisin prudencial de todas las entidades financieras (bancarias, de seguros, valores, etc.) de las de la vigilancia de la conducta en las relaciones con sus clientes y asignarlas a autoridades diferenciadas (al Banco de Espaa y a la CNMV, respectivamente) representa, en mi opinin, un esquema institucional ptimo para gestionar los posibles conflictos entre ambas responsabilidades y para mejorar la eficiencia y la eficacia de la actividad supervisora en su conjunto. Por su parte, en materia de educacin financiera se hace necesario seguir poniendo el foco en incorporar las competencias financieras en la educacin obligatoria. En la actualidad, el Plan de Educacin Financiera se enfoca en los alumnos de secundaria, pero hay ya conceptos y comportamientos que se pueden aprender en primaria. Las orientaciones de los expertos, que son promovidas por la Organizacin para la Cooperacin y el Desarrollo Econmicos y seguidas en la mayor parte de los pases, sealan que la educacin financiera debe incluirse en el currculo acadmico y abordarse como una competencia transversal. Hay que tener en cuenta asimismo que ese nuevo entorno en el que la forma de prestar los servicios ha cambiado que, en general, supone una posibilidad de acceso a productos y servicios de manera ms gil, competitiva y con menos costes puede plantear tambin dificultades en el acceso a los servicios bancarios para determinados colectivos y la necesidad de contar con competencias nuevas, adems de las financieras, como son las digitales. Como resultado, podran generarse riesgos de exclusin financiera, as como de fraude. En este contexto, debemos prestar especial atencin a los colectivos vulnerables y a las personas mayores. En conclusin, los cambios en las formas de relacionarse de las entidades con sus clientes no dejan de ser una manifestacin ms de la respuesta ante el nuevo entorno tecnolgico y competitivo en el que se desenvuelven. Este nuevo entorno reclama nuevas capacidades, conocimientos y procedimientos entre aquellos que lideren esta transformacin: gestores bancarios que, apoyados por una slida gobernanza, entiendan y gestionen las oportunidades y los riesgos que presenta la innovacin tecnolgica para las entidades y sus clientes, y expertos que orienten las nuevas herramientas de anlisis que se abren camino en los procesos de evaluacin y comercializacin de productos financieros hacia los principios y valores de las organizaciones. Se necesitarn tambin nuevas competencias en las reas legal, de evaluacin de riesgos y de cumplimiento normativo que impulsen e irriguen esta nueva cultura desde su diseo en los servicios centrales hasta las redes de venta. Y, por supuesto, los supervisores y reguladores no nos podemos quedar atrs en la comprensin y la adaptacin a estas transformaciones. Muchas gracias por su atencin.

Title: Annual meeting of the Latin American Federation of Banks
text: 21.09.2021 COVID-19 and the Basel framework: first conclusions Annual meeting of the Latin American Federation of Banks (FELABAN) Pablo Hernandez de Cos Governor Good afternoon: I want to begin by thanking the Latin American Federation of Banks and the Spanish Banking Association for their invitation to participate in this meeting. I will take this opportunity to share with you the first lessons we have learned in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision on how global banking standards, known as Basel III, work in the context of the COVID-19 crisis. As you know, in response to the great financial crisis of 2007-2009, the Committee introduced profound changes in banking regulatory standards on a global scale1. The objective d0 in response to the weaknesses revealed by the crisis d0 was to strengthen the regulation, supervision and risk management of banks. Following the publication of this new regulatory framework, Basel III, the Committee agreed to assess its impact on the resilience and performance of the banking system. Let me emphasize that the evaluation of the effectiveness of regulatory standards is an integral part of the regulatory policy cycle, since, on the one hand, it allows to know the degree of success and completeness of the standards and, on the other, favors the consistent implementation of these standards. 1 See Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, "Basel III: international regulatory framework for banks" and "Minimum capital requirements for market risk". 2 See Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (July 2021), "Early lessons from the Covid-19 pandemic on the Basel reforms". The committee is approaching this assessment based on conceptual and, to the extent possible, empirical, robust and rigorous analyses, without prior constraints supported by a desire to recalibrate or modify the globally agreed framework. The Committee's agenda is ambitious and is expected to develop over the next few years. However, COVID-19 has undoubtedly represented the first major shock to the financial system since the end of the Basel III framework, and the Committee has seen fit to undertake a preliminary analysis of what could be considered the first lessons about Basel III in a crisis context. The truth is that the pandemic and its effects have not yet ended and that the nature of this shock, of an exogenous nature, is not the same as the trigger for the Basel III reforms, derived, as I mentioned earlier, from the necessary response to the weaknesses of the system that the crisis of 2007-2009 revealed. In any case, bearing these precautions in mind, the Committee has carried out this first assessment of the Basel III reforms already implemented, in a report published in July2. What are the first conclusions observed so far? First, and unlike what happened in the previous great financial crisis, in which banks originated and spread instability, in this one the banking system has remained resilient and has continued to provide fundamental financial services, which have helped cushion the impact of the pandemic on the economy in general. There are two factors that are important and have contributed to this positive outcome: . On the one hand, the unprecedented scope and scale of the measures taken by the public sector in the fiscal, monetary and regulatory fields to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 crisis has been decisive, measures that have so far protected banks from losses. . In addition, Basel III reforms have significantly strengthened the resilience of the global banking system, enabling banks to cope with the effects of the pandemic with higher levels of solvency and liquidity and with an improved capacity to absorb losses. Indeed, the study shows that banks have faced the pandemic with substantially higher capital and liquidity ratios. No internationally active bank has failed or needed public sector financing. Market-based resilience measures, such as CDS spreads, show that some banks experienced tensions at the start of the pandemic, but increases in CDS spreads were smaller for those banks with higher levels of capital. Moreover, the results of the study indicate that better-capitalized banks increased their financing to households and non-financial corporations to a greater extent. Therefore, a first conclusion would be that the global banking sector has been able to complement and reinforce the measures taken by the public authorities to which I referred earlier. The second conclusion I will highlight is that, while the results show that to date the Basel III framework has met its objectives, there are also some aspects that may require further evaluation. Among them, I would highlight three: the functioning of capital and liquidity buffers, the degree of countercyclicality offered by prudential standards, and the treatment of reserves in central banks in the prudential leverage ratio. The conclusions are not clear, at the moment, for a number of reasons, including the difficulty of empirically isolating precisely how certain variables would have behaved in the absence of the effect of measures taken by public authorities. In order not to overextend, I will give just one example. There is an intense debate about the degree of usability of capital buffers. The restrictions on the distribution of dividends and share buybacks adopted by different authorities and, more generally, the public measures taken to combat the economic effects of COVID-19 make it difficult to draw definitive empirical conclusions about the willingness of institutions to use buffers, since, in general, they have maintained comfortable capital positions above the minimum requirements and buffers. Moreover, in this case, although the first results obtained suggest that institutions may have been reluctant to use capital buffers even if necessary, it is not possible to determine what causes this reluctance. In particular, it is not clear whether this unwillingness to use mattresses stems from a precautionary measure against possible losses at a time of uncertainty, or from the desire to avoid the stigma effect that could result from reducing capital levels. In any case, or precisely because of this, the Committee will continue to evaluate these aspects in the coming years, in addition to carrying out a broader evaluation of the impact of the initial Basel III reforms in the last decade. A third conclusion we can draw from recent, and not-so-recent, experiences is that the resilience of the global banking system cannot be taken for granted. In The extent to which the pandemic continues to have effects and at the same time public support measures are withdrawn, additional losses could arise for banks. In addition, rising levels of public and corporate debt could increase structural weaknesses in banks' balance sheets over the long term. In addition, recent vulnerabilities in non-bank intermediation have highlighted its high level of interconnectedness with banks, so the risk of contagion cannot be excluded. Allow me, in this second part of my speech, to convey to you various aspects of a reflection made following the conclusions I have mentioned: . First, the implementation of the initial Basel III reforms has produced a clear net benefit for the global economy and, in general, for society. During the pandemic we have collectively reaped these benefits. In this regard, it should be recalled that different academic studies indicate that the Basel III reforms have resulted in capital requirements that are within the range of estimates that point to positive net macroeconomic benefits, derived from greater financial stability and the better capacity to absorb shocks provided by such requirements3. 3 V8ease Comit8e de Supervisi97n Bancaria de Basilea (junio de 2019): d2The costs and benefits of bank capital d0 a review of the literatured3. The benefits of Basel III implementation are not limited to the economies and financial systems of Basel Committee member countries, but are also relevant to other jurisdictions. Among them, Latin America, both for the effect on banking systems at the local level and for the influence of internationally active banks operating in the region and also influencing the financial cycle in a global way. Basel III will help reduce the likelihood of future crises and, if any, minimize their impact. Without wishing to be comprehensive, reforms of the capital framework, new liquidity requirements and the introduction of a macroprudential approach will help increase the responsiveness and resilience of the region's banking sectors, while also contributing to a more level playing field. . Secondly, we must be aware that regulatory reform is not finalised: there are still crucial aspects to be completed in the implementation of Basel III. The agreed reforms that are still to be implemented, and which contain a series of standards aimed at enhancing the robustness and credibility of the risk-weighted asset framework, address defects that remain as important today as they were before the pandemic. In particular, to the extent that they strengthen comparability between institutions, which has a clear effect on the competitive playing field, and limit the variability of capital requirements. It is increasingly clear that the pending Basel reforms will complement the current regulatory framework and its net positive impact on the real economy. For example, recent analyses by the European Central Bank show that the costs of implementing reforms in Europe in terms of Gross domestic product is modest and transitory, while its benefits will help strengthen economic resilience to future shocks. In addition, the development of these standards benefited from a thorough consultative process. Failure to implement these measures in a comprehensive, timely and consistent manner, as agreed by G20 leaders on several occasions, would leave the remaining structural weaknesses and fragilities unaddressed, entailing a significant cost to the global economy and financial stability. COVID-19 has highlighted the vital importance of having the necessary mechanisms in place before the emergence of a shock; This also applies, no doubt, to prudential standards and to the security and robustness of the banking system. Let me recall, at this point, that the objective of complete, consistent and timely implementation for internationally active banks is not incompatible with the application of a proportionate framework in line with the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision, which states that supervisory practices should be commensurate with the risk profile and systemic importance of supervised banks4. Beyond that, the Committee has ongoing initiatives to promote the role of proportionality in banking regulation and supervision, including the development of practical guidelines on the use and design of a proportional regulatory and supervisory framework, which will be available to jurisdictions for use on a voluntary basis5. 4 See Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2012), "Core Principles for effective banking supervision". 5 Comit8e de Supervisi97n Bancaria de Basilea, d2Basel Committee work programme and strategic priorities for 2021/22d3. . Third, and in parallel with the Committee's ongoing assessment programme, a forward-looking supervisory approach is essential to identify, assess and mitigate emerging risks and structural trends impacting the global banking system. Some of these risks and trends d0 including the digitalisation of finance, climate-related financial risks, and the evolution and sustainability of banking business models d0 had already been identified before the pandemic, and COVID-19 has further underlined the importance of addressing them. I shall conclude now. The implementation of Basel III responds to a global and collective interest. Both the fight against infectious diseases and safeguarding financial stability are global public goods that know no borders and require collaboration between countries. The pandemic won't end until each of us is safe. Similarly, the overall benefits of Basel III will not be achieved without respecting the commitment to complete, consistent and time-bound implementation reached in the G20 and the Group of Governors and Heads of Oversight.
text_original: 21.09.2021 El COVID-19 y el marco de Basilea: primeras conclusiones Encuentro anual de la Federacin Latinoamericana de Bancos (FELABAN) Pablo Hernndez de Cos Gobernador Buenas tardes: Quiero comenzar agradeciendo a la Federacin Latinoamericana de Bancos y a la Asociacin Bancaria Espaola su invitacin a participar en este encuentro. Aprovechar la oportunidad que me bridan para compartir con ustedes cules son las primeras lecciones que hemos aprendido en el Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea sobre el funcionamiento de los estndares bancarios globales, conocidos como Basilea III, en el contexto de la crisis derivada del COVID-19. Como saben, en respuesta a la gran crisis financiera de 2007-2009, el Comit introdujo profundos cambios en los estndares regulatorios bancarios a escala global1. El objetivo en respuesta a las debilidades que la crisis haba puesto de manifiesto era reforzar la regulacin, supervisin y gestin del riesgo de las entidades bancarias. Tras la publicacin de ese nuevo marco regulatorio Basilea III, el Comit acord evaluar su impacto sobre la resistencia y el comportamiento del sistema bancario. Permtanme enfatizar que la evaluacin de la efectividad de los estndares regulatorios es parte integral del ciclo de la poltica regulatoria, ya que, por una parte, permite conocer el grado de xito y completitud de los estndares y, por otra, favorece la implementacin consistente de dichos estndares. 1 Vase Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea, Basel III: international regulatory framework for banks y Minimum capital requirements for market risk. 2 Vase Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea (julio de 2021), Early lessons from the Covid-19 pandemic on the Basel reforms. El comit est abordando esta evaluacin basndose en anlisis conceptuales y, en la medida de lo posible, empricos, slidos y rigurosos, sin condicionantes previos sustentados en deseos de recalibrar o modificar el marco acordado globalmente. El programa del Comit es ambicioso y se desarrollar previsiblemente a lo largo de los prximos aos. Sin embargo, el COVID-19 ha representado, sin duda, el primer gran shock para el sistema financiero desde la finalizacin del marco de Basilea III, y el Comit ha juzgado conveniente realizar un anlisis preliminar de lo que se podran considerar las primeras lecciones acerca de Basilea III en un contexto de crisis. Lo cierto es que la pandemia y sus efectos todava no han finalizado y que la naturaleza de este shock, de carcter exgeno, no es la misma que el detonante de las reformas de Basilea III, derivadas, como me he referido antes, de la necesaria respuesta a las debilidades del sistema que la crisis de 2007-2009 puso de manifiesto. En todo caso, teniendo presentes esas cautelas, el Comit ha llevado a cabo esta primera evaluacin de las reformas de Basilea III ya implementadas, en un informe que ha publicado en julio2. Cules son las primeras conclusiones observadas hasta ahora? En primer lugar, y a diferencia de lo que sucedi en la anterior gran crisis financiera, en la que la banca origin y propag la inestabilidad, en esta el sistema bancario se ha mantenido resiliente y ha continuado prestando servicios financieros fundamentales, que han ayudado a amortiguar el impacto de la pandemia sobre la economa en general. Hay dos factores que son importantes y que han contribuido a este resultado positivo:  Por una parte, ha sido determinante el alcance y la escala, sin precedentes, de las medidas adoptadas por el sector pblico en los mbitos fiscal, monetario y regulatorio para mitigar el impacto de la crisis derivada del COVID-19, medidas que por el momento han protegido a los bancos de las prdidas.  Por otra parte, las reformas de Basilea III han fortalecido de forma considerable la resiliencia del sistema bancario global, permitiendo a las entidades afrontar los efectos de la pandemia con niveles ms altos de solvencia y liquidez y con una capacidad mejorada para absorber prdidas. En efecto, el estudio muestra que los bancos han afrontado la pandemia con ratios de capital y liquidez sustancialmente mayores. Ningn banco internacionalmente activo ha quebrado o ha necesitado financiacin del sector pblico. Las medidas de resiliencia basadas en indicadores de mercado, como los diferenciales de los CDS, muestran que algunos bancos sufrieron tensiones al inicio de la pandemia, pero los incrementos de los diferenciales de los CDS fueron menores para aquellas entidades con mayores niveles de capital. Ms an, los resultados del estudio sealan que los bancos mejor capitalizados aumentaron su financiacin a hogares y sociedades no financieras en mayor medida. Por lo tanto, una primera conclusin sera que el sector bancario global ha sido capaz de complementar y reforzar las medidas adoptadas por las autoridades pblicas a las que antes me he referido. La segunda conclusin que destacar es que, si bien los resultados muestran que hasta la fecha el marco de Basilea III ha cumplido con sus objetivos, tambin existen algunos aspectos que pueden requerir profundizar en su evaluacin. Entre ellos, destacara tres: el funcionamiento de los colchones de capital y de liquidez, el grado de contraciclicidad ofrecido por los estndares prudenciales, y el tratamiento de las reservas en bancos centrales en la ratio de apalancamiento prudencial. Las conclusiones no son claras, de momento, por diversos motivos, incluyendo la dificultad de aislar empricamente con precisin el modo en que se hubieran comportado determinadas variables en ausencia del efecto de las medidas tomadas por las autoridades pblicas. Para no extenderme en exceso, pondr solo un ejemplo. Hay un intenso debate acerca del grado de usabilidad de los colchones de capital. Las restricciones al reparto de dividendos y a la recompra de acciones adoptadas por diferentes autoridades y, ms en general, las medidas pblicas tomadas para combatir los efectos econmicos del COVID-19 dificultan extraer conclusiones empricas definitivas sobre la disposicin de las entidades a usar los colchones, ya que, en general, estas han mantenido posiciones de capital holgadas sobre los mnimos exigidos y los buffers. Adems, en este caso, aunque los primeros resultados obtenidos sugieren que las entidades podran haber sido renuentes al uso de los colchones de capital aun en caso necesario, no es posible determinar cules son las causas de dicha reticencia. En concreto, no est claro si esa falta de disposicin al uso de colchones deriva de una medida de precaucin respecto a posibles prdidas en un momento de incertidumbre, o del deseo de evitar el efecto estigma que podra suponer reducir los niveles de capital. En todo caso, o precisamente por ello, el Comit va a continuar evaluando estos aspectos en los prximos aos, adems de realizar una evaluacin ms amplia sobre el impacto de las reformas iniciales de Basilea III en la ltima dcada. Una tercera conclusin que podemos extraer de las experiencias recientes, y no tan recientes, es que la resiliencia del sistema bancario global no puede darse por sentada. En la medida en que la pandemia contine teniendo efectos y al mismo tiempo se vayan retirando las medidas pblicas de apoyo, podran surgir prdidas adicionales para los bancos. Asimismo, el aumento de los niveles de deuda pblica y empresarial podra incrementar las debilidades estructurales de los balances de las entidades en el largo plazo. Adicionalmente, las recientes vulnerabilidades en la intermediacin no bancaria han puesto de manifiesto su alto nivel de interconexin con los bancos, por lo que no se puede excluir el riesgo de contagio. Permtanme, en esta segunda parte de mi intervencin, trasladarles diversos aspectos de una reflexin realizada a raz de las conclusiones que he mencionado:  En primer lugar, la implementacin de las reformas iniciales de Basilea III ha producido un claro beneficio neto para la economa global y, en general, para la sociedad. Durante la pandemia hemos cosechado estos beneficios colectivamente.
