In this sense, the greatest challenge, from my point of view, arises in how to adequately convey to citizens the complexity of economic problems and their possible solutions, including the limits of knowledge or available information, so that the results of evaluations and analyses are interpreted properly and with due caution. For this, the economic education of information professionals is obviously fundamental. To explain this debate and be able to translate it to citizens in their own language, journalists must first understand the complexities and limitations of economic analysis. I dare say that success in properly translating the results of evaluations d1 including, I repeat, their limitations d1 depends on the fruitful dialogue between ideology and evaluation, to which I referred earlier, so that the former is permeable to it; and, ultimately, to promote the creation of the necessary consensus to implement the appropriate economic reforms. And this challenge is even greater, as pointed out by the former president of the Association of Economic Information Journalists, ea96igo de Barr97n2, in a context in which the polarization and politicization of the media have increased, we are in full battle against disinformation and the influence generated by the competitive pressure exerted on the media by the networks leads in many cases, wrongly, to the use of clickbait as a mechanism to attract readers. 2 I96igo de Barr97n (2019), speech delivered on November 25 during the delivery of the Tintero y Secante Awards 2019 by the Association of Economic Information Journalists. On the contrary, properly feeding the debate among citizens and, ultimately, political decision requires objective information; In particular, on the complexity and on the different trade-offs that any economic policy decision normally generates, both among individuals or population groups and in terms of its temporal impact, among others. In other words, I believe that it is no exaggeration to say that our success as a society in creating a genuine culture of economic policy evaluation, which allows long-term effects on decision-making to be taken into account, depends crucially on the media being able to properly transfer the results of these evaluations to the citizens. Beyond, of course, the role that the institutions have in achieving that objective. Of course, at Banco de Espa96a we believe that, from rigour and independence, we can contribute decisively to it by adopting a culture of permanent evaluation of the actions derived from our responsibilities; providing other economic policymakers with the best analysis and proposals to increase economic growth and citizens' well-being; facilitating and collaborating with the research community in the use of the information we have to contribute to a greater extent to that objective; promoting d0 also in collaboration with the public and private sectors d0 the economic and financial education of citizens, which allows them to understand and properly value public policies and make the best financial decisions that affect them, and collaborating with the media to facilitate the transmission of all this information and analysis to citizens. Thanks a lot.
text_original: 11.11.2021 El papel de los medios de comunicacin en el fomento de polticas basadas en evidencias Entrega de los Premios Lderes/La Informacin Pablo Hernndez de Cos Gobernador Buenas tardes. Permtanme que inicie mi intervencin agradeciendo a La Informacin su amable invitacin a participar en este acto de entrega de la cuarta edicin de los Premios Lderes. Esta invitacin me permite unirme al reconocimiento a los premiados: en este caso, Jose Ignacio Goirigolzarri, presidente de CaixaBank; Joel Balagu, fundador y CEO de Volava, y Luca Comenge, presidenta del grupo PRIM. Enhorabuena a los tres por su trayectoria, que se ve justamente reconocida por este premio. En un acto similar hace unas semanas, en el que el reconocimiento se otorgaba al Banco de Espaa, con la concesin por el Consejo General de Economistas de la Gran Cruz al Mrito en el Servicio de la Economa, habl de la importancia de incorporar las consideraciones de largo plazo en la toma de decisiones de la poltica pblica. Permtanme que retome brevemente algunas de las ideas all expuestas, pero enfatizando ahora el papel que pueden y deben ejercer los medios de comunicacin en la persecucin de ese objetivo. Un acto como este, en el que un medio de comunicacin nos convoca a unirnos al reconocimiento de determinadas personalidades que, con su esfuerzo diario y actuando desde la tica, la sostenibilidad y la contribucin a la sociedad, se han convertido en un modelo a seguir, creo que es una ocasin oportuna para invocar ese papel. En aquel discurso, justifiqu la necesidad de incorporar las consideraciones de largo plazo en la toma de decisiones como algo consustancial a la idea de progreso que deben perseguir los poderes pblicos. En materia de poltica econmica, esto se debe articular a travs de la definicin y la ejecucin de polticas que promuevan la prosperidad y las oportunidades para todos los ciudadanos, no solo actuales, sino tambin futuros. La calidad de las instituciones es un factor que puede contribuir claramente a este objetivo. Este es, de hecho, el argumento que justifica la independencia de los bancos centrales. Pero, ms all de la calidad de las instituciones, para lograr el objetivo de incorporar las consideraciones de largo plazo al proceso decisorio pblico, existen tres aspectos complementarios que, en mi opinin, resultan esenciales, y a los que los medios de comunicacin pueden contribuir decisivamente. El primero de ellos se deriva de la incorporacin de una cultura de evaluacin continua y rigurosa de las polticas pblicas, en el entendimiento de que, en una sociedad democrtica, la evaluacin del diseo y de los efectos de las polticas pblicas cumple una funcin poltica, al promover la transparencia sobre las actuaciones de los responsables polticos y sobre sus resultados, lo que facilita la rendicin de cuentas y el control democrtico por parte del Parlamento y de los ciudadanos. Pero tambin cumple una funcin tcnica, al permitir alimentar el proceso de toma de decisiones con informacin valiosa para mejorar su eficacia y su eficiencia. Por eso, cuando se promueven polticas basadas en evidencias, se trata tanto de un alegato tcnico a favor de la eficacia como de una afirmacin poltica a favor del control democrtico del poder por los ciudadanos y sus representantes. El segundo elemento se refiere a la necesidad de disponer de datos que informen el proceso de toma de decisiones. Los datos son la materia prima que nutre el proceso de evaluacin. Sin datos adecuados, de calidad, disponibles oportunamente y con la suficiente granularidad, una buena evaluacin no es posible. Si en el sector privado se habla de la economa del dato, de manera que las dinmicas competitivas de las empresas se han visto afectadas crucialmente por el uso de los datos o por la tecnologa, el sector pblico no puede quedarse atrs en el tratamiento de los datos. El uso de los datos de los que disponen las distintas administraciones ampla de manera acelerada las capacidades de diagnstico y de evaluacin. Y aade tambin un mecanismo adicional de control de las autoridades, que refuerza la calidad del debate pblico y de la democracia, en particular cuando esta informacin se pone a disposicin de la comunidad investigadora para que pueda ser utilizada con fines cientficos de inters pblico. As pues, datos de calidad, capacidad tcnica, rigor e independencia en el anlisis pareceran los ingredientes necesarios para constituir una cultura de la evaluacin que llevase a la formulacin de polticas pblicas sobre la base de evidencias. El tercer aspecto necesario es lograr una adecuada educacin econmico-financiera de la poblacin en general. Con una ciudadana capacitada para interiorizar crticamente en sus decisiones individuales tanto los resultados fundamentales de las evaluaciones independientes como los distintos beneficios y costes asociados a diferentes cursos de accin, sera ms fcil asentar una cultura de la evaluacin. Como he subrayado en distintas ocasiones, para la consecucin de este objetivo, creo que es fundamental profundizar en la incorporacin de los conocimientos econmicos y financieros en el curriculum escolar, como recomiendan las instituciones internacionales. Este alegato a favor de unas polticas pblicas basadas en evidencias como elemento importante para el progreso y la libertad en las sociedades democrticas no debe entenderse, por contraposicin, como opuesto al sano debate ideolgico propio de las sociedades libres y plurales. Al contrario, creo que ambos elementos han de complementarse. La ideologa tiene, al menos, un doble papel en el proceso decisorio de las polticas pblicas. El primero est relacionado con los fines. Aporta una nocin tica sobre lo que es bueno o malo para la sociedad. Y esto no puede ni debe estar sometido a evaluacin, pues es una cuestin de preferencias personales que, en caso de legtima discrepancia, ha de dirimirse en el mbito poltico a travs del proceso democrtico, en el marco constitucional de cada nacin. El segundo papel de la ideologa es aportar puntos de partida iniciales sobre cmo cabra, a priori, abordar estos fines cuando no contamos con una slida evidencia sobre el mejor curso de accin para su consecucin. En cierto sentido, la ideologa viene a cubrir, en ocasiones, las lagunas de la evaluacin rigurosa basada en datos fiables. En este segundo mbito, existe un amplio campo para el dilogo fructfero entre ideologa y evaluacin, y para ello solo es necesario un prerrequisito: que, por muy firmes que sean los postulados ideolgicos sobre los medios que se deben emplear, los decisores de poltica econmica estn abiertos a dejarse interpelar por los resultados de evaluaciones rigurosas e independientes. De hecho, el fruto de este dilogo puede ser muy enriquecedor para la sociedad: la emergencia de unos consensos mnimos sobre la forma de abordar, mediante las polticas pblicas, determinados retos que sean identificados como tales por un espectro poltico muy amplio. Como ya he comentado en distintas ocasiones, desde que nuestra sociedad y nuestra economa fueron impactadas por la pandemia, estos consensos sociales y polticos bsicos son particularmente necesarios para afrontar situaciones de enorme incertidumbre como la actual, en la que se precisan reformas de calado para mejorar el bienestar de los ciudadanos. Un consenso sobre qu reformas realizar y con qu contenido, apoyadas en los resultados de evaluaciones econmicas slidas, proporcionara a la poltica econmica estabilidad ms all del ciclo electoral y, por tanto, credibilidad frente a los ciudadanos y a los inversores, multiplicando as su impacto positivo. Pues bien, en todo este proceso, creo que los medios de comunicacin pueden y deben desempear un papel fundamental. Desde luego, los medios de comunicacin son cruciales en la identificacin de los problemas a los que se enfrenta la sociedad, que, en ltimo trmino, pueden requerir una accin de poltica econmica para su resolucin. Deca Elas Canetti que el verdadero escritor es el sabueso de su tiempo1, que ha de meter su hocico en todas partes sin que se le escape nada, buscando la verdad. Creo que esta actitud es tambin deseable en los periodistas. 1 E. Canetti (1936), Hermann Broch, discurso pronunciado en su quincuagsimo aniversario (Viena, noviembre), en La conciencia de las palabras, Fondo de Cultura de Mxico, 1981. Los medios tambin desempean un papel fundamental en el proceso de transparencia y de rendicin de cuentas de los poderes pblicos, ms all de la funcin institucional que en esa dimensin ejercen los parlamentos. Y no solo desde la perspectiva de la oferta las autoridades nos servimos habitualmente de los medios de comunicacin para lanzar los mensajes relativos a nuestras actuaciones, sino tambin desde la demanda de los propios medios, exigiendo esa informacin y las explicaciones (evaluaciones) oportunas a las autoridades. Pero me gustara subrayar el papel nico que los medios de comunicacin ejercen trasladando esa informacin, explicaciones o evaluaciones a los ciudadanos. Solo en casos muy limitados, los informes, artculos, evaluaciones o discursos que elabora el Banco de Espaa, por ejemplo, son ledos ntegramente por los ciudadanos. Tenemos que admitir que estos llegan a su conocimiento, casi exclusivamente, a travs de los medios de comunicacin. De ah la importancia que desde el Banco de Espaa hemos concedido a establecer una relacin fluida y estrecha con los medios, reforzando los canales que nos permiten explicar adecuadamente nuestros trabajos, a travs de briefings, entrevistas o la participacin en actos como este. Esa motivacin es la que nos ha llevado a incluir resmenes y extractos que sintetizan nuestros informes, para que los informadores puedan comprenderlos mejor. Intentamos tambin aunque sea difcil en ocasiones esforzarnos en utilizar un lenguaje y unas formas accesibles para todos. Desde esa perspectiva, el papel de los medios de comunicacin contribuyendo a fomentar esa cultura de polticas econmicas basadas en evidencias e, indirectamente, la educacin econmico-financiera de los ciudadanos es fundamental. En este sentido, el mayor reto, desde mi punto de vista, surge en cmo trasladar adecuadamente a los ciudadanos la complejidad de los problemas econmicos y sus posibles soluciones, incluyendo los lmites del conocimiento o de la informacin disponible, de manera que se interpreten adecuadamente y con las debidas cautelas los resultados de las evaluaciones y de los anlisis. Para ello, la educacin econmica de los profesionales de la informacin es obviamente fundamental. Para explicar ese debate y poder trasladarlo a la ciudadana en su propio lenguaje, los periodistas deben, primero, comprender las complejidades y limitaciones del anlisis econmico. Me atrevo a decir que del xito en trasladar adecuadamente los resultados de las evaluaciones incluidas, insisto, sus limitaciones depende que se produzca ese dilogo fructfero entre ideologa y evaluacin, al que me refera con anterioridad, de manera que aquella sea permeable a esta; y, en ltimo trmino, que se favorezca la creacin de los consensos necesarios para aplicar las reformas econmicas adecuadas. Y este reto es an mayor, como sealaba el anterior presidente de la Asociacin de Periodistas de Informacin Econmica, igo de Barrn2, en un contexto en el que se han incrementado la polarizacin y la politizacin de los medios, nos encontramos en plena batalla contra la desinformacin y la influencia que genera la presin competitiva ejercida sobre los medios de comunicacin por las redes lleva en muchos casos, equivocadamente, al uso del clickbait como mecanismo de atraccin de lectores. 2 Iigo de Barrn (2019), discurso pronunciado el 25 de noviembre durante la entrega de los Premios Tintero y Secante 2019 por la Asociacin de Periodistas de Informacin Econmica. Por el contrario, alimentar adecuadamente el debate entre los ciudadanos y, en ltimo trmino, la decisin poltica exige informar objetivamente; en particular, sobre la complejidad y sobre los distintos trade-off que normalmente cualquier decisin de poltica econmica genera, tanto entre individuos o grupos poblacionales como en lo que respecta a su impacto temporal, entre otros. En otras palabras, creo que no es exagerado afirmar que nuestro xito como sociedad en la creacin de una verdadera cultura de la evaluacin de las polticas econmicas, que permita tener en consideracin los efectos de largo plazo en la toma de decisiones, depende crucialmente de que los medios de comunicacin sean capaces de trasladar adecuadamente los resultados de estas evaluaciones a los ciudadanos, ms all, por supuesto, del papel que a las instituciones nos corresponde en la consecucin de ese objetivo. Desde luego, en el Banco de Espaa creemos que, desde el rigor y la independencia, podemos contribuir decisivamente a l adoptando una cultura de evaluacin permanente de las actuaciones derivadas de nuestras responsabilidades; proporcionando a otros decisores de poltica econmica los mejores anlisis y propuestas para aumentar el crecimiento econmico y el bienestar de los ciudadanos; facilitando y colaborando con la comunidad investigadora en el uso de la informacin de la que disponemos para contribuir en mayor medida a ese objetivo; promocionando tambin en colaboracin con los sectores pblico y privado la educacin econmica y financiera de los ciudadanos, que les permita comprender y valorar adecuadamente las polticas pblicas y tomar las mejores decisiones financieras que les afectan, y colaborando con los medios de comunicacin en facilitar la transmisin de toda esa informacin y anlisis a los ciudadanos. Muchas gracias.

Title: Rey Juan Carlos University. "Development and regulation of sustainable finance at the national and international levels"
text: 17.11.2021 Developments and regulation of sustainable finance at the national and international levels Seminar "Economic policy and sustainable finance: a new approach" Rey Juan Carlos University. Margarita Delgado Subgobernadora Good morning, everyone. First of all, I would like to thank the educational community, in this case the Rey Juan Carlos University and, in particular, the Faculty of Legal and Social Sciences for the opportunity to participate in this international seminar on finance and sustainability. This is undoubtedly an issue of unquestionable topicality. I am convinced that it will mark the evolution and transformation of the financial sector in the coming years. To the extent that the economy is reoriented towards a more sustainable model, and by this I mean not only the environmental aspect but also the social aspect, we will also see how the financial sector will adapt. We cannot forget the close interconnections between the real economy and the financial sector as the latter acts as a channelling and distributor of funds. The regulatory agenda for sustainable finance has reached a high degree of ambition in recent times. Today I will take advantage of this forum to review the main regulatory or other developments that have occurred and, above all, those that are in the process of gestation. I will focus on those that particularly affect the activity of the Bank of Spain as a prudential supervisor and as a central bank. Climate risks are relevant for the Bank of Spain because of their potential implications on financial stability due to their impact on inflation, the potential growth of the economy and the transmission of monetary policy. Prudential regulation is one of the tools we have to try to mitigate these risks and facilitate the transition of the economy towards a more sustainable model. To complete this transition, it is not only necessary to adapt the regulation, but also to provide it with economic resources. Although there are various estimates, I will refer to calculations made by the European Commission itself1: One trillion euros of public and private funds need to be mobilised over the next decade. To put this figure in context, I want to recall that Spanish GDP was 1.1 trillion euros in 2020. Additionally, to achieve carbon neutrality in 2050, an additional 260,000 million euros of annual investment would be needed. 1 I will structure my speech by distinguishing the different levels at which regulatory issues are addressed: national, European and international, with which I will begin now. International regulation One of the most active forums in this international arena is the NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System), where 100 members are represented, mainly Central Banks and supervisors, as well as 16 observers such as the Financial Stability Board (FSB) or the Basel Supervisory Committee (BCBS). In this forum, whose task is to promote the role of the financial system in the transition to a more sustainable economy and mobilize capital towards "green" projects, work is being done on several lines: (a) The first assesses the degree of progress made by supervisors in integrating climate and environmental risks into their supervisory frameworks and Activities. It also advances in the study of the risk differential between green assets and other assets. This last point is key to confirm d0 or not d0 whether investment in more sustainable assets inherently entails lower risk and thus assign prudential measures according to that risk. b) A second line of work focuses on the development and updating of climate scenarios, both transition and physical risk, that can be used by both supervisors and central banks and by institutions in the stress exercises of these risks. c) The third line of work deals with green finance, studying the incorporation of sustainable and responsible investment (SRI) criteria in the portfolios of central banks, and in the management of monetary policy. I shall refer to this later. (d) The fourth and final line of work has the essential task of identifying missing data - and necessary - to improve the assessment of risks associated with climate change in the financial system. As I have pointed out on multiple occasions, the absence of data with a sufficient degree of detail and historical depth is one of the main obstacles that both companies and supervisors encounter when measuring and managing climate risk. Another key international body in the field of banking regulation and prudential supervision is the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. This global committee is responsible for issuing international standards of prudential regulation in the banking field. At the same time, it promotes cooperation on supervisory matters to strengthen bank regulation, supervision and practices to strengthen financial stability. Well, this Committee, which has set up a specific task force on climate risk, has published two reports that I would like to highlight. The first refers to climate-related risk factors and their transmission channels. The paper explores how these risk factors affect the banking system through micro and macroeconomic impacts. The second report concerns methodologies for measuring climate-related financial risks. It also affects the need for more data to be able to address the management of these risks. The most relevant conclusion of these two reports is that traditional risk categories (credit, market, liquidity and operational) can serve to capture climate risk, but it is still necessary to find out how they impact these risks through a greater quantity and quality of data. Finally, I would like to mention that the Basel Committee continues to analyse to what extent climate risks can be addressed by the banking prudential framework from regulation, supervision and information to the market. Recently, the Committee has recognized the importance of establishing global standards that improve the consistency, comparability and reliability of information related to the sustainability. For this reason, it has recognized the initiative of the IFRS Foundation (International Financial Reporting Standards) created by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) for this purpose. In addition, the Basel Committee emphasizes that supervisors need to ensure that both the financial system as a whole and individual banks are prepared to identify, measure and mitigate climate risks.2 2 3 If you like, I now turn to regulatory initiatives at European level. European Union Regulation The European Union, for its part, is implementing a European framework for sustainable finance whose main objective is to facilitate the channelling of public and mainly private capital towards sustainable investments. There are two key pieces of this European framework. On the one hand, the sustainable finance action plan that the European Commission published in March 2018 and which has formed the basis of a significant number of legislative and non-legislative initiatives in this area. On the other hand, the renewed strategy3 on sustainable finance that the Commission published in June 2021 as a complement to the 2018 action plan and as a logical consequence of the developments in sustainability since its publication. Among all the initiatives that are based on the two previous documents, action plan and renewed strategy, I will make a reference to those especially relevant for the financial sector and for the Bank of Spain: the Taxonomy Regulation, the Proposal for a Directive on corporate sustainability reporting (CSRD) and the Green Bonds Regulation. I will conclude this part of my speech by dealing in more detail with the changes in the banking prudential framework. I will start, because of its importance, with the Regulation on the establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable investments or Taxonomy Regulation (Regulation EU 2020/852). It is essential to establish, not only at European level, but at global level, a set of common definitions for all actors in the economy, be they banks or companies, given that this is a global problem that cannot be tackled from a local perspective. This Regulation sets out six environmental objectives: (i) climate change mitigation, (ii) adaptation to climate change, (iii) sustainable use of water and marine resources, (iv) transition to a circular economy; (v) pollution prevention and control, and (vi) and biodiversity protection. To consider that an economic activity is aligned with the taxonomy, in addition to contributing to one of the above objectives, it must not cause any significant damage to the rest, and must be carried out in compliance with minimum social guarantees. This regulation is fundamental. It forms the basis of all sustainability regulations. As I have said, the European Commission continues to work on the development of this taxonomy, which includes covering d0 for the objectives (i) and (ii) of climate change d0 those economic activities on those that have not yet been pronounced, such as agriculture, and some more controversial energy sectors, such as nuclear energy or natural gas. In addition, it has yet to develop the technical criteria to classify economic activities as sustainable, in accordance with the rest of the objectives. Additionally, work is being done on the extension of this environmental taxonomy to the so-called "brown" and "neutral" activities, but these works are still in a very incipient phase. Secondly, I would like to mention the Proposal for a Directive on Corporate Sustainability Reporting (CSRD), which amends the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD). It will introduce substantial and necessary improvements to sustainability reporting obligations, which should contribute to a better allocation of financing via an adjustment in asset prices. A clear example of this is the extension of the scope of the NFRD, which will also extend to large companies, whether listed or not, and to all listed companies, including SMEs (with the exception of listed micro-enterprises). Thirdly, I must also highlight the proposal for a regulation on a green bond standard, issued in July this year. This proposal will create a high-quality voluntary standard for all issuers (private and sovereign) to contribute to the financing of sustainable investments. The existence of a European green bond standard will incentivise the creation of a common framework consistent with the Union's objectives related to climate change mitigation and adaptation. Both are two of the environmental objectives set out in the European Taxonomy Regulation that I have already mentioned. The interconnection of these standards with the Taxonomy Regulation is critical to ensure that sustainable economic activities are adequately financed through the issuance of debt instruments. Here I also want to mention the importance of these standards to avoid what we call "greenwashing", which is the process of classifying certain activities as environmentally sustainable when in fact they are not. It is well known that the issuance of ESG securities is becoming increasingly important. A few weeks ago we knew the fact that 14.4% of the assets of Spanish funds are deposited in ESG funds or that the sustainable debt placed until June exceeded all that issued in 2020, or that 40% of Spanish investors consider that ESG criteria are "key" in their investment approach, a percentage higher than the global average. These facts highlight the importance of having a clear definition of what a green bond is. European standards are key to this. Let me make a small parenthesis at this point relating to green emissions. I recall here that the European Central Bank presented in July 2021 its strategy to mainstream climate considerations into its monetary policy framework and, in particular, in the areas of disclosure, risk assessment, collateral arrangements and corporate asset purchases. For its part, the Bank of Spain adhered in February 2021 to the agreement adopted by the Eurosystem for the establishment of a common position on sustainable investments related to climate change in those portfolios denominated in euros not related to monetary policy. Earlier, in 2019, the Bank of Spain had decided to add sustainability and responsibility criteria to the investment policy of its own portfolios. Continuing with the review of European regulation from the prudential field, I must highlight the initiatives taken by the European Banking Authority (EBA) and by the European Commission. 1) First, the European Banking Authority was mandated to analyse how to incorporate ESG risks into the three pillars of Basel banking regulation. Pillar 1 refers to capital requirements, and includes and conforms what is the solvency ratio. The EBA is determining whether specific prudential treatment of exposures related to assets or activities linked to environmental or social objectives would be warranted. This work is still in its infancy. In addition, the analysis that is being done does not focus only on the solvency ratio, but includes other measures in the area of pillar 1, such as the framework of large exposures, leverage ratio, liquidity etc. With regard to Pillar 2, the EBA is assessing the possible inclusion of environmental, social and governance risks in the supervisory review and assessment process. This process, called SREP in common terminology, shows where each entity stands with capital requirements and how it addresses its risks. The SREP concludes with a decision setting out the main objectives to address the weaknesses identified. In June 2021, the EBA published a report4 making a series of recommendations to institutions and supervisors related to the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks into business, governance and risk management strategies. The most relevant aspect of the report is that it establishes common definitions of ESG risks and their transmission channels and identifies appropriate methodologies for their measurement. It outlines how banks should manage ESG risks. It also recommends integrating them into their business strategies, internal governance structures and risk management systems. It also sets out how these risks should be monitored under a principle of proportionality and assessing the long-term resilience of the institutions' strategy. 4 5 Pillar 3 deals with the information to be published by institutions and relates to market discipline. At this point, the EBA published in March 2021 for consultation a draft technical implementation standard5 (ITS) on the information to be disclosed related to ESG risks, both quantitatively and qualitatively. The purpose of this ITS is to provide the market with comparable and quantitative information on the physical and transition risks to which credit institutions are exposed. They will also have to provide the market with information on their green investments through the so-called GAR (Green Asset ratio), which reports on how much of the exposures of financial institutions contribute to the achievement of climate change mitigation and adaptation objectives as defined in the Taxonomy Regulation. In a first phase, only significant credit institutions that have issued listed securities would be subject to this disclosure requirement. But, as I have pointed out, the rule is still in the consultation phase. 2) As regards the Commission's initiatives in the prudential area, I must highlight the banking package published at the end of October. This package goes a step further by explicitly incorporating sustainability into banking prudential regulations (basically in the prudential requirements regulation and directive), in order to ensure better ESG risk management by banks. In addition, and taking into account the principle of proportionality, it has extended to all credit institutions the ESG risk disclosure requirements to which I referred earlier. Finally, I would like to mention that, in its proposal, the Commission has not addressed one of the most controversial issues: the possibility of introducing an adjustment to the Pillar 1 capital requirements associated with green/brown assets. This is an idea that the Commission is still exploring, but on which it does not wish to pronounce until it has the analysis and results of the work being carried out in this area by both the EBA and the BCBS. Allow me again to make another parenthesis in this review of the sustainability regulations to make a small reflection. Until now, I have referred almost exclusively to environmental aspects, but there is no sustainable economy that is not also sustainable from a social point of view. All organizations, companies, public institutions have an impact on society wherever they are based. This social aspect must also be defined and regulated, as we are doing in the environmental field. Unfortunately I cannot give many details because this regulatory development is still at a very early stage. We still have the establishment of a social taxonomy similar to the one that already exists for the environment. It would be desirable for the Commission to be able to make a legislative proposal along these lines over the next year, but it is still too early to venture out. At the moment I can only confirm that work is being done to define what is meant by a "social investment" and what the social objectives are. Perhaps in a few years we will have a clearer framework of social sustainability. We now leave behind the work of European regulators to briefly mention the actions taken at the European Central Bank. This body published, in November last year, the guide on climate-related and environmental risks. It reviews how supervisors believe banks should manage these risks prudently and the mechanisms for communicating them transparently. These guides are aimed at significant institutions whose supervision falls on the European Central Bank, but similarly, the Bank of Spain published in October 2020 expectations in the same sense addressed to less significant institutions, as ultimately responsible for their supervision. The compliance and degree of adherence to them will be subject to review over the next year, although we have already analyzed the self-assessment exercise that the entities have carried out in relation to compliance with these Expectations. No bank is yet in line with these guidelines in full, but we have observed best practices in all geographies and types of entities, so it sheds some optimism about compliance with them in the future. In addition, as I noted earlier, the European Central Bank presented in July this year its plan to include climate change considerations in its monetary policy strategy. This new strategy includes climate issues in four areas: disclosure, risk assessment, collateral system and corporate asset purchases. In particular, the ECB will introduce disclosure requirements on private sector assets as a new eligibility criterion for the purposes of collateral presentation and asset purchases. It will also take into account relevant climate risks when reviewing the risk assessment and control frameworks for collateral provided by counterparties in Eurosystem credit operations. I cannot fail to mention the two stress test exercises between the actions of the European Central Bank. The first, top-down approach, whose results have been recently published. The second, the bottom-up exercise that will be carried out next year to the entities under its supervision. The one already carried out verified the impact of climate change on more than four million companies worldwide and 1,600 banks in the euro area in 3 different climate scenarios6. He concluded that there are clear benefits to acting early on climate change. 6 In conclusion, I would like to review legislative initiatives at national level. Spain I have to mention Law 7/2021 on climate change and ecological transition. The articles of this standard establish that credit institutions must prepare, within the framework of the prudential relevance report, an annual report. In it, an evaluation of the financial impact on society of the risks associated with climate change generated by exposure to it of its activity must be carried out. The risks of the transition to a sustainable economy and the measures taken to address those risks should therefore be included. Specific decarbonisation targets for its loan and investment portfolio aligned with the Paris Agreement will also have to be published from 2023. The content of this report will be determined by normative development within two years of the approval of the law, but in any case it will include the following aspects: (a) The governance of the entity related to the identification, assessment and management of climate risks; (b) The approved strategy to adapt to and mitigate the risks associated with climate change. c) The impacts that the risks and opportunities associated with climate change may have on the organization's activities and strategy, as well as on its financial planning. d) The processes for identifying, assessing, monitoring and managing climate-related risks and how these are integrated into their overall business risk analysis and their integration into overall risk management by institutions. (e) Finally, the metrics, scenarios and targets used to assess and manage relevant risks and opportunities related to climate change. As you can see, the objectives that this point aims to cover are very ambitious and we will have to wait for them to be more detailed in the subsequent legislative development, on which work is already being done7. 7 The Treasury has just launched a consultation to specify the content of this legislative act On the other hand, this law also establishes requirements for the authorities since it indicates that the Bank of Spain, the National Securities Market Commission and the General Directorate of Insurance and Pension Funds, within the scope of their respective competences, will jointly prepare, every two years, a report on the degree of alignment with the climate goals of the Paris Agreement and European Union regulations. This report will be based on future scenarios and will assess the risk that climate change may pose to the Spanish financial system. It will also detail the policies to combat it and will be coordinated within the scope of the Macroprudential Authority Financial Stability Board (AMCESFI). Conclusion As you have heard, legislation around the concept of sustainability is experiencing a regulatory maelstrom across the board. All actors, international, European and, of course, national, are immersed in a process of normative definition in order to build an economic future d1and therefore, financiald1, sustainable in every way to face the enormous challenge of adapting to the new climate environment. I would like to highlight the leading role that the EU has taken in terms of sustainability, but mentioning the importance of coordination at global level, because climate change is a global problem and the lack of coordination could lead to a fragmentation of regulatory frameworks and to problems of level playing field. On the other hand, from the point of view of prudential supervision, I would like to point out d0 by way of summarizing what has been said d0 that, initially, efforts have been made to improve the management of these risks by institutions (pillar 2) as well as their disclosure to third parties (pillar 3). The need to adjust Pillar 1 to reflect these new risks is still under discussion. However, all measures already taken should result in a better allocation of bank financing to more sustainable projects, thus contributing to climate change mitigation. I hope that this intervention has demonstrated the existing commitment on the part of all regulators to work on the creation of a regulatory framework that supports that sustainable economy to which I have referred. However, I would like to stress that the transformation towards this sustainable economy is, without a doubt, the primary responsibility of governments, which with their policies and decisions must guide the change of economic model. It is true that financial institutions play a leading role as elements channeling resources between economic actors, but they are still some more participants, along with the rest of society. The responsibility of entities is to identify, measure and incorporate climate risk into their usual risk management, but the real protagonists of change will be governments with their policies and of course, citizens with their actions. Thanks a lot.

En ella se repasa la manera en que los supervisores consideramos que las entidades de crdito deben gestionar estos riesgos de manera prudente y los mecanismos para comunicarlos con transparencia. Estas guas estn dirigidas a las entidades significativas cuya supervisin recae en el Banco Central Europeo, pero de manera anloga, el Banco de Espaa public en octubre de 2020 unas expectativas en el mismo sentido dirigidas a las entidades menos significativas, como responsable ltimo de su supervisin. El cumplimiento y grado de adherencia a las mismas ser objeto de revisin a lo largo del ao que viene, aunque ya hemos analizado el ejercicio de autoevaluacin que han realizado las entidades en relacin con el cumplimiento de dichas expectativas. Todava ningn banco est en lnea con estas guas al completo, pero hemos observado mejores prcticas en todas las geografas y tipologa de entidades, por lo que arroja cierto optimismo sobre el cumplimiento de las mismas en el futuro. Adicionalmente, como he sealado antes, el Banco Central Europeo present en julio de este ao su plan para incluir consideraciones del cambio climtico en su estrategia de poltica monetaria. En esta nueva estrategia se incluyen los aspectos climticos en cuatro reas: divulgacin de informacin, evaluacin de riesgos, sistema de activos de garanta y compras de activos del sector empresarial. En concreto, el BCE introducir requisitos de divulgacin de informacin sobre los activos del sector privado como nuevo criterio de admisin a efectos de su presentacin como activos de garanta y de las compras de activos. Tambin tendr en cuenta los riesgos climticos relevantes cuando revise los marcos de valoracin y control de riesgos de los activos de garanta aportados por las entidades de contrapartida en las operaciones de crdito del Eurosistema. No puedo dejar de mencionar los dos ejercicios de stress test entre las acciones del Banco Central Europeo. El primero, de enfoque top-down, cuyos resultados han sido publicados recientemente. El segundo, el ejercicio bottom-up que se realizar el ao que viene a las entidades bajo su supervisin. El ya realizado comprob el impacto del cambio climtico en ms de cuatro millones de empresas en todo el mundo y a 1.600 bancos del rea euro en 3 diferentes escenarios climticos6. Lleg a la conclusin de que hay claros beneficios en actuar tempranamente contra el cambio climtico. 6 https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/scpops/ecb.op281~05a7735b1c.en.pdf Para terminar, quisiera hacer un repaso de las iniciativas legislativas de mbito nacional Espaa Tengo que mencionar la Ley 7/2021 de cambio climtico y transicin ecolgica. En el articulado de esta norma se establece que las entidades de crdito debern elaborar, en el marco del informe de relevancia prudencial, un informe de carcter anual. En el mismo ha de realizarse una evaluacin del impacto financiero sobre la sociedad de los riesgos asociados al cambio climtico generados por la exposicin a este de su actividad. Deben por tanto incluirse los riesgos de la transicin hacia una economa sostenible y las medidas que se adopten para hacer frente a dichos riesgos. Asimismo, habrn de publicarse objetivos especficos de descarbonizacin de su cartera de prstamo e inversin alineados con el Acuerdo de Pars a partir de 2023. El contenido de dicho informe se determinar por desarrollo normativo en el plazo de dos aos desde la aprobacin de la ley, pero en cualquier caso incluir los siguientes aspectos: a) La gobernanza de la entidad relacionada con la identificacin, evaluacin y gestin de los riesgos climticos. b) La estrategia aprobada para adaptarse al cambio climtico y mitigar los riesgos asociados al mismo. c) Los impactos que los riesgos y oportunidades asociados al cambio climtico pudieran tener en las actividades de la organizacin y su estrategia, as como en su planificacin financiera. d) Los procesos de identificacin, evaluacin, control y gestin de los riesgos relacionados con el clima y cmo estos se integran en su anlisis de riesgo de negocio global y su integracin en la gestin global del riesgo por parte de las entidades. e) Por ltimo, las mtricas, escenarios y los objetivos utilizados para evaluar y gestionar los riesgos y oportunidades relevantes relacionados con el cambio climtico. Como ven, los objetivos que pretende cubrir este punto son muy ambiciosos y tendremos que esperar a que sean ms detallados en el desarrollo legislativo posterior, en el que ya se trabaja7. 7 El Tesoro acaba de lanzar una consulta para concretar el contenido de este acto legislativo Por otra parte, esta ley tambin establece requerimientos para las autoridades dado que seala que el Banco de Espaa, la Comisin Nacional del Mercado de Valores y la Direccin General de Seguros y Fondos de Pensiones, en el mbito de sus respectivas competencias, elaborarn conjuntamente, cada dos aos, un informe sobre el grado de alineamiento con las metas climticas del Acuerdo de Pars y de la normativa de la Unin Europea. Este informe estar basado en escenarios futuros y evaluar el riesgo que el cambio climtico pueda suponer para el sistema financiero espaol. Tambin detallar las polticas para combatirlo y se coordinar en el mbito de la Autoridad Macroprudencial Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera (AMCESFI). Conclusin Como han podido escuchar, la legislacin en torno al concepto de sostenibilidad est experimentando una vorgine regulatoria en todos los mbitos. Todos los actores, internacionales, europeos y, por supuesto, nacionales estamos inmersos en un proceso de definicin normativa con el fin de construir un futuro econmico y por ello, financiero, sostenible en todos los sentidos para hacer frente al enorme reto de adaptarnos al nuevo entorno climtico. Quiero destacar el papel de liderazgo que ha asumido la UE en materia de sostenibilidad, pero mencionando la importancia de que haya coordinacin a nivel global, pues el cambio climtico es un problema global y la falta de coordinacin podra llevar a una fragmentacin de los marcos regulatorios y a problemas de level playing field. Por otra parte, desde la ptica de la supervisin prudencial me gustara indicar  a modo de resumen de lo dicho  que, inicialmente, los esfuerzos se han puesto en mejorar la gestin de estos riesgos por parte de las entidades (pilar 2) as como su divulgacin a terceros (pilar 3). Est todava en discusin la necesidad de ajustar el pilar 1 para reflejar estos nuevos riesgos. No obstante, todas las medidas ya adoptadas deberan redundar en una mejor asignacin de la financiacin bancaria a proyectos ms sostenibles, contribuyendo de esta manera a la mitigacin del cambio climtico. Espero que esta intervencin haya dejado evidenciado el compromiso existente por parte de todos los reguladores para trabajar en la creacin de un marco normativo que sustente esa economa sostenible a la que he hecho referencia. No obstante, quiero resaltar que la transformacin hacia esa economa sostenible es, sin duda, responsabilidad primera de los gobiernos, que con sus polticas y decisiones deben orientar el cambio de modelo econmico. Cierto es que las entidades financieras juegan un papel protagonista como elementos canalizadores de recursos entre los actores econmicos, pero no dejan de ser unos intervinientes ms, junto con el resto de la sociedad. La responsabilidad de las entidades consiste en identificar, medir e incorporar el riesgo climtico dentro de su gestin habitual de los riesgos, pero los verdaderos protagonistas del cambio sern los gobiernos con sus polticas y por supuesto, los ciudadanos con su actuacin. Muchas gracias.

Title: Future of the banking sector after new regulations, the financial crisis and the pandemic
text: 24.11.2021 Future of the banking sector after new regulations, the financial crisis and the pandemic Conference "New competition, new business and technology in the banking sector"/FUNCAS Margarita Delgado Subgobernadora Good morning to all those attending this conference organized by Funcas in which a current issue will be put on the table and that I think is frankly relevant: the future of the banking sector. Why do I think this is a topical issue? The changing environment in which we live makes us rethink day in and day out, what the future of one sector or another will be. It is true that the world has always been in continuous evolution. But you will agree with me that the pace of social and technological changes and transformations has accelerated, I would almost say exponentially, in recent times. That is, in my opinion, the reason why we are all continuously immersed in a process of rethinking strategies and processes in order to adapt to the new realities in which we live. The banking sector is no stranger to this phenomenon and, if I may, I consider it to be one of the most affected by this transformation process. This is due to the extraordinary development of technology and its direct application to the financial sector. I firmly believe that this trend will not stop in the coming years, quite the opposite. The use of technology will take hold and increase, causing the need to adapt business processes and strategies to the new environment. This undoubtedly constitutes a huge challenge for the entire sector, including supervisors, given that we have to be able to monitor the use of new technologies and incorporate into our processes the use of innovative solutions in such a way that the stability of the financial system is not compromised. As has been pointed out on numerous occasions, the pandemic has only accelerated this digitalization process. Banks had to quickly adapt their processes to continue providing financial services to their customers remotely while incorporating teleworking massively. In these months, consumers have also changed their consumption habits. We now use more frequently digital means of payment instead of cash and we make greater use of online platforms to interact with entities. In this sense, we have also been observing the new phenomenon of the commercialization of financial products or services or others through third-party platforms. Artificial intelligence, big data, cloud services, distributed ledger technologies or decentralized finance are, among many others, relatively new concepts that will play a key role in the near future of finance. Knowing how to fit these new pieces into the puzzle of existing financial markets will be essential to ensure an efficient, solid financial sector adapted to the new reality. Entities will have to continue making an effort to adapt to the new environment in which they operate and will operate in the future. This environment will be very different from the one we know today, not only because of the new way of relating to customers, but also because of the emergence of new actors, new processes or new ways of understanding the financial business. In order to position themselves properly in this new map, they will have to carry out a detailed analysis of the strategy to follow, taking into account the benefits provided by technology, but also undertaking a detailed study of the risks and threats that digitalization entails. To all this, we must add the uncertainties that every transformation entails. In this speech I will make an analysis of the main benefits, risks and challenges that, from my point of view, digitalization brings to the future of the banking sector, as well as a small review of how European regulation is facing this phenomenon. I would like to start with some of the potential benefits that the use of technology can bring to the banking sector. In the first place, digitalization generates cost reductions in the medium term, despite the not inconsiderable amounts of investment it requires. The spectrum of customers that can be reached thanks to the use of digital technology increases considerably since it is not necessary to have a wide network of branches in a territory to access potential customers. This is essential to reduce operating costs in an environment where financial sector returns are low. It is true that, as I have pointed out, digital transformation requires large investments and it is in this environment of narrow margins where entities will have to do an analysis work on the digitalization strategy they want to follow. They must prioritize some processes over others wherever they consider that digitalization provides more added value according to the strategy they have designed. It's not about investing for investing's sake. As in almost all decisions, it will be necessary to analyze where you want to be in the medium term and see how you can achieve that goal with an efficient use of available resources. On this path, many momentous decisions will also have to be taken. For example, see if the development of the projects is done internally or relies on third-party solutions. Another point that must be taken into account is that the investment must contemplate the cultural change in organizations and include staff training, so that the skills of bank employees also adapt to the new environment. As mentioned in the report presented today, some forecasts predict that between 15% and 20% of the new jobs created in this sector will have to do with digitalization. Secondly, we must not only think of digitalization as a mere mechanism to reduce costs, but also to generate higher revenues. On the one hand, by expanding the customer base and, on the other, by creating new business opportunities, for example, by offering their digital platforms in which third parties market their products, or by providing new products that are better adapted to the needs of each client. Customer satisfaction will be an increasingly relevant point given that the degree of fidelity of the same will be lower, being easier to change entity in a digital environment. To take advantage of these opportunities, it is essential to leverage good data management. Data is already the most profitable raw material that exists. The correct use, processing and storage of the same will result in information that serves to create products that generate more value. On the one hand, for the client, from the point of view of satisfying their needs. On the other hand, for entities, which will have a deeper knowledge of the behavior of their customers and therefore will be able to offer products better adapted to their risk profile. In this data processing, the use of artificial intelligence will be an element to take into account. However, at this point I cannot fail to mention the regulations on the protection of personal data, which we must bear in mind at all times, and the future European Regulation on Artificial Intelligence. Thirdly, digitalisation also opens up a world of opportunities in that it can change the business model, making it more global. It is important that entities have a good data governance framework, through which it is possible to obtain quality data from reliable sources. In a second step, for example, the use of a compatible IT platform within the same banking group would facilitate data processing and value obtaining by improving risk management globally. In addition, although there are still certain cross-border barriers in the European environment, such as different financial cultures or traditions, or even the absence of complete harmonisation of regulations, digitalisation favours a change in the way of consuming and can contribute to the creation of a more homogeneous financial system. Therefore, digitalization is highly beneficial in that it allows services to be delivered in a more efficient way, at a lower cost, better adapted to the needs of consumers and potentially expanding the customer base. However, the other side of this coin is the risks and challenges that this digitalization process entails and that must not be forgotten in the analysis. The main direct risk we all face in this environment is cyber risk. The increase in interconnections, both with third parties and with customers, increases the exposure surface and therefore the probability of attacks, which have grown exponentially during the pandemic. It's not just about establishing barriers that protect entities' digital systems and processes so they can operate in a secure environment. Additionally, resilience plans will have to be designed, determining which activities are critical and thus ensuring that entities are able to operate in exceptional circumstances. Zero risk does not exist and the digital world is no exception. Unfortunately, entities are not the only target of network criminals. Banking customers are also suffering numerous and increasingly sophisticated attacks. Is Education and awareness of the dangers of these new digital processes are necessary to create an environment of trust. The last risk I want to refer to today is that of dependence on third parties. There is a consolidated trend in recent years to outsource certain activities, pursuing objectives of cost reduction, increased flexibility and efficiency improvements. Outsourcing to third parties of specific services that provide little value allows entities to focus on more relevant activities. An example we all have in mind is outsourcing to cloud service providers. It is necessary to remember that institutions must carry out an in-depth analysis of the risks that may arise from depending on third parties when providing certain services. In any case, entities may not delegate the responsibility they have when exercising an activity, regardless of whether it is outsourced or not. As for the challenges, there are many that affect the banking sector and to which they will undoubtedly have to adapt, to continue operating in an efficient and profitable manner. From my point of view, the main challenge is to establish a digital strategy that is adequate and that serves to integrate correctly into the new banking ecosystem. It is about seeking a balanced and orderly transformation, which neither leads banks to make too risky decisions pushed by the market nor, on the contrary, leaves them behind in the transformation process. We are looking at new ways to deliver services. The traditional vertically integrated model, offering all kinds of financial products with greater or lesser use of technology, is beginning to coexist with other non-linear models. These non-linear models have burst onto the market in a new way, either by offering specific products through non-proprietary channels or by providing digital platforms1 to offer a range of third-party specialist products. 1 Banks will have to consider various options in the face of this new phenomenon and there may not be a single correct answer. One possibility is to continue with the same vertical model, but progressively incorporating digital elements into products and processes. Another is to follow the most successful trends in finance by responding quickly to innovations. The last one is to be totally innovative and lead these trends and changes in the financial market. On these business strategies and adaptation to digitalization there are no guidelines that are valid for everyone or that guarantee success in this process. Each entity must adapt the design of its strategy to its own objectives, resources and environment. Another relevant challenge is the growing competition in the sector, not only among traditional participants but also due to the emergence of new players. I cannot make an intervention on the future of banking without referring to fintech. I believe that it has been a wise move on the part of the banking sector to see these new players not as a threat or disruptive element in the status quo of finance, but as an opportunity to take advantage of everything they can offer and thus improve their competitive position. There are many examples of collaboration between traditional financial institutions and fintech that have culminated in successful processes. In this analysis of the future of the financial sector I cannot fail to mention another of the new actors on the scene, the large technology companies (bigtech). Today, and at least in the European environment, the irruption of these companies is still not relevant compared to other geographies, mainly China, but we can not ignore this phenomenon. The great advantage that these large technology providers have is the huge amount of data they manage and their ability to process them. This stems not only from the large customer base they have, but from the significant frequency of interactions with them. Other advantages are preferential access to finance and having a good reputation and confidence among consumers. Properly handled and processed data can become a powerful tool for the provision of financial services. For example, these companies could determine the risk profile of borrowers without the need for a credit history. In this way, the big technology companies could promote the financial inclusion of a sector of the population that is currently outside the sphere of influence of traditional banking. This scenario, although in principle would be more plausible in other geographies other than Europe, must also be taken into account when drawing the new financial map of the future. It is important to note that, today, both fintech and bigtech do not normally provide financial services globally. At the moment, they focus on those specific market niches where they generate more added value, such as payment systems and, to a lesser extent, asset management. Also in insurance and loans in less banked countries. There is currently a debate about the emergence of these large companies and how their activity, and the risks they entail, impact the financial sector and the economy. At the level of the European Central Bank, the principle of "same activity, same risk, same regulation and same supervision" has been established2. An example is the rules for the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, which are common to all regardless of the category of the company carrying out an activity. On the other 2 On the other hand, there are also currents that consider that the regulations should be more based on the type of entity and the risks they entail, rather than on the specific activity they exercise3. 3 4 5 This was stated in the strategic guidelines for the period 2019/2024. 6 FinTech Action Plan We must not forget that the banking sector is subject to exhaustive and increasing regulation and supervision due to the implication and impact it has on financial stability. The preservation of it, as well as market integrity, consumer protection and competition, are the objectives pursued by regulators and supervisors. To the extent that these new actors engage in activities that may have a significant impact on financial stability, they should be subject to regulation based on the risks they generate. Today, the financial services provided by bigtechs are not very significant in our environment (cloud services, payments...) and as such, are subject to the regulatory framework established for these specific activities. However, we will have to be attentive to market developments to avoid materialising the risks that these large technology service providers can potentially generate, as well as the systemic risk derived from market concentration and its possible impact on economic and financial stability. I would also like to highlight another additional challenge, in this case related to supervisors. It is essential that we maintain close contacts with the industry to be aware of the state of technology and technological risk in the sector. The dialogue with the different actors is essential to clarify regulatory issues and supervisory expectations. These supervisory dialogues, together with the regulatory sandbox, are some of the ways to achieve this goal. Aware of the rapid digital transformation we are experiencing, the risks that this may entail and the need to adapt regulations to this new environment, I would now like to make a brief review of the European Commission's strategy for digital finance4. Supporting the digital transition in the EU is a key priority for the European Commission5. This strategy builds on the FinTech Action Plan that was developed in 20186. EU actions to promote the digital transformation of financial services run until 2024 and are guided by four priorities: 1) Eliminating fragmentation the Digital Single Market; 2) Adapt the EU regulatory framework to facilitate digital innovation; 3) Create a European financial data space to capitalize on the value of information as a foundation for innovation and 4) Address the challenges and risks associated with digital transformation. In relation to the first priority, the elimination of fragmentation of the Digital Single Market, a series of concrete actions are contemplated such as the new Digital Identification Regulation (e-IDAS), on which there is already a draft. Progress will also be made in harmonizing the regulations on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing (AML/CTF). In addition, it will make it easier for digital financial services to gain scale in the Single Market. To this end, the principle of passport and one-stop shop for authorisation will apply as early as 2024 to all those areas that show high potential for the development of digital finance7. 7 For example, the EU framework for crowdfunding agreed in Dec-19 will introduce a common regime and passport for various types of crowdfunding, and the crypto-asset regulation will introduce a common regime and passport for issuers and crypto-asset service providers. The Commission will also consider the relevance of the passport in other areas, such as prudential regulation in non-bank financing or the certification of RegTech solutions companies and the adoption of common approaches in that field, including interoperability. 8 There is already a proposed pilot scheme: 9 10 Also relevant BIS advisory document: 11 With regard to the second priority, focused on adapting regulation to facilitate digital innovation, the EU will establish a comprehensive framework addressing issues as diverse as the adoption of distributed ledger technology (DLT)8, a proposal for a regulation for crypto-assets (MICA)910 that includes asset-referenced tokens (also known as stablecoins) and utility tokens or the Artificial Intelligence Regulation, for which there is also a draft proposal11. The third priority, data-related, aims to facilitate real-time digital access to all regulated financial information. The aim is to ensure that all public is available in standardized, machine-readable formats, and to promote information technology tools to facilitate reporting and monitoring. Similarly, companies will be encouraged to share data inside and outside the European financial sector (open finance). Finally, regarding the fourth priority, addressing the challenges and risks associated with digital transformation, should be done by safeguarding financial stability, protecting consumers and investors and based on the aforementioned principle of "same activity, same risk, same rules". In summary, the Commission is working hard to ensure that by 2024 EU prudential and conduct regulation and supervision are adapted to digital developments, including in its object traditional financial institutions and technology providers that provide services to the financial sector. This regulation includes a wide range of reforms and new legislation that I have already mentioned, such as the e-IDAS Regulation (electronic identification), MICA (crypto-asset markets), DORA (Digital Operational Resilience), Digital Service Act, Data Act or the Artificial Intelligence Regulation. The aim of the ongoing legislative amendments is to protect end-users of digital finance, safeguard financial stability, protect the integrity of the EU financial sector and ensure a level playing field for all. In this review of the future of the banking sector, I cannot fail to mention another element to take into account: the digital euro. Although we are still in a research phase, in which basic elements of its design are being outlined and defined, it seems clear that, in case its issuance is finally decided, financial institutions will play an important role in its implementation. Finally, I would like to refer briefly to the process of adapting to this digital environment that we supervisors are carrying out. For example, we are advancing projects to automate supervisory processes and take advantage of advanced information analysis. But we are not only working on the development of these tools, but we are also fostering a digital culture in the organization, promoting skills that facilitate and commit to digitalization. As I have pointed out, digitalisation also brings challenges and risks for supervisors. Risks and challenges that we must know and manage, such as the use of external providers in the public cloud, data quality or the lack of specialized profiles, among others. In conclusion, the future of the banking sector is shaping up differently from the one we live in today. New actors, different ways of relating to customers, new ways of carrying out processes and new risks, are the essential elements that will shape the future banking scenario. Now is the time to make transcendental strategic decisions that serve to position yourself adequately in this new banking ecosystem. Regulators, supervisors and banks must be prepared to face these new challenges and those that lie ahead in order to preserve the necessary financial stability that guarantees solid economic growth. Thanks a lot.

En este sentido, venimos observando tambin el nuevo fenmeno de la comercializacin de productos o servicios financieros u otros a travs de plataformas de terceros. Saber encajar estas nuevas piezas en el puzle de los mercados financieros existentes ser esencial para asegurar un sector financiero eficiente, slido y adaptado a la nueva realidad. Este entorno ser bien distinto al que conocemos actualmente, no solo por la nueva forma de relacionarse con los clientes, sino tambin por la irrupcin de nuevos actores, nuevos procesos o nuevas formas de entender el negocio financiero.
