Cierto es que, como he sealado, la transformacin digital requiere grandes inversiones y es en este entorno de estrechos mrgenes donde las entidades tendrn que hacer una labor de anlisis sobre la estrategia de digitalizacin que quieren seguir. Debern priorizar unos procesos sobre otros all donde consideren que la digitalizacin aporta ms valor aadido segn la estrategia que hayan diseado. No se trata de invertir por invertir. Como en casi todas las decisiones, habr que analizar dnde se quiere estar en el medio plazo y ver cmo se puede alcanzar ese objetivo con un uso eficiente de los recursos disponibles. En este camino habr que tomar, adems, muchas decisiones trascendentales. Por ejemplo, ver si el desarrollo de los proyectos se realiza internamente o se apoya en soluciones de terceros. Otro punto que hay que tener en cuenta es que la inversin deber contemplar el cambio cultural en las organizaciones e incluir la formacin del personal, para que las capacidades de los empleados bancarios se adapten tambin al nuevo entorno. Segn se menciona en el informe que hoy se presenta, algunas previsiones vaticinan que entre un 15% y un 20% de los nuevos puestos que se creen en este sector tendrn que ver con la digitalizacin. En segundo lugar, no solo hay que pensar en la digitalizacin como un mero mecanismo para reducir costes, sino tambin para generar mayores ingresos. Por un lado, mediante la ampliacin de la base de clientes y, por otro, creando nuevas oportunidades de negocio, por ejemplo, ofreciendo sus plataformas digitales en las que terceros comercialicen sus productos, o facilitando nuevos productos que se adapten mejor a las necesidades de cada cliente. La satisfaccin del cliente ser un punto cada vez ms relevante dado que el grado de fidelidad de los mismos ser menor, al ser ms fcil cambiar de entidad en un entorno digital. Para aprovechar estas oportunidades es fundamental apalancarse en una buena gestin de los datos. El dato es ya la materia prima ms rentable que existe. La correcta utilizacin, procesamiento y almacenamiento de los mismos dar como resultado informacin que sirva para crear productos que generen ms valor. Por un lado, para el cliente, desde el punto de vista de satisfaccin de sus necesidades. Por otro lado, para las entidades, que tendrn un conocimiento ms profundo del comportamiento de sus clientes y por lo tanto podrn ofrecer productos mejor adaptados a su perfil de riesgo. En este tratamiento de datos, el uso de inteligencia artificial ser un elemento a tener muy en cuenta. No obstante, en este punto no puedo dejar de mencionar la normativa de proteccin de datos personales, que en todo momento tenemos que tener presente, y el futuro Reglamento Europeo sobre Inteligencia Artificial. En tercer lugar, la digitalizacin tambin abre un mundo de oportunidades en cuanto que puede hacer cambiar el modelo de negocio, hacindolo ms global. Es relevante que las entidades tengan un buen marco de gobierno del dato, a travs del cual sea posible obtener datos de calidad provenientes de fuentes confiables. En un segundo paso, por ejemplo, el uso de una plataforma informtica compatible dentro un mismo grupo bancario, facilitara el procesamiento de datos y la obtencin de valor mejorando la gestin de riesgos de manera global. Adems, aunque existen todava ciertas barreras transfronterizas en el entorno europeo, como por ejemplo distintas culturas o tradiciones financieras, o incluso la ausencia de una armonizacin completa de la normativa, la digitalizacin favorece el cambio en la forma de consumir y puede contribuir a la creacin de un sistema financiero ms homogneo. Por lo tanto, la digitalizacin es altamente beneficiosa en cuanto que permite prestar servicios de una manera ms eficiente, a menor coste, adaptndose mejor a las necesidades de los consumidores y ampliando potencialmente la base de clientes. No obstante, la otra cara de esta moneda son los riesgos y retos que este proceso de digitalizacin lleva implcitos y que no hay que olvidar en el anlisis. El principal riesgo directo al que todos nos enfrentamos en este entorno es el ciberriesgo. El aumento de interconexiones, tanto con terceros como con clientes, incrementa la superficie de exposicin y por tanto la probabilidad de ataques, que han crecido de forma exponencial durante la pandemia. No se trata solo de establecer barreras que protejan los sistemas y procesos digitales de las entidades para que puedan operar en un entorno seguro. Adicionalmente se tendrn que disear planes de resiliencia, determinando qu actividades son crticas y as garantizar que las entidades sean capaces de operar en circunstancias excepcionales. El riesgo cero no existe y el mundo digital no es una excepcin. Desgraciadamente, las entidades no son el nico objetivo de los delincuentes de las redes. Los clientes bancarios tambin sufren numerosos y cada vez ms sofisticados ataques. Es necesaria una labor de educacin y concienciacin de los peligros que conllevan estos nuevos procesos digitales para crear un entorno de confianza. El ltimo riesgo al que quiero hacer hoy referencia es el de dependencia de terceros. Existe una tendencia consolidada en los ltimos aos a externalizar ciertas actividades, persiguiendo objetivos de reduccin de costes, aumento de la flexibilidad y mejoras de la eficiencia. La subcontratacin con terceros de servicios concretos que aportan poco valor permite a las entidades centrarse en actividades ms relevantes. Un ejemplo que todos tenemos en mente es la externalizacin en proveedores de servicios en la nube. Es necesario recordar que las entidades deben realizar un anlisis en profundidad de los riesgos que puede suponer depender de terceras partes a la hora de prestar ciertos servicios. En cualquier caso, las entidades no podrn delegar la responsabilidad que tienen al ejercer una actividad, con independencia de que est externalizada o no. En cuanto a los retos, son muchos los que afectan al sector bancario y a los que sin duda se tendrn que adaptar, para seguir operando de una manera eficiente y rentable. Desde mi punto de vista, el principal reto es el establecer una estrategia digital que sea adecuada y que sirva para integrarse correctamente en el nuevo ecosistema bancario. Se trata de buscar una transformacin equilibrada y ordenada, que ni lleve a los bancos a tomar decisiones demasiado arriesgadas empujados por el mercado ni, por el contrario, los deje atrs en el proceso de transformacin. Estamos observando nuevas formas de proveer servicios. El modelo tradicional integrado verticalmente, ofreciendo todo tipo de productos financieros con mayor o menor uso de tecnologa, est empezando a convivir con otros modelos no lineales. Estos modelos no lineales han irrumpido en el mercado de manera novedosa, ya sea ofertando productos especficos a travs de canales no propios o bien facilitando plataformas digitales1 para ofrecer un abanico de productos de terceros especialistas. 1https://www.eba.europa.eu/sites/default/documents/files/document_library/Publications/Reports/2021/1019865/EBA%20Digital%20platforms%20report%20-%20210921.pdf La banca deber considerar diversas opciones ante este nuevo fenmeno y posiblemente no haya una nica respuesta correcta. Una posibilidad es continuar con el mismo modelo vertical, pero incorporando progresivamente elementos digitales en productos y procesos. Otra es seguir las tendencias ms exitosas que se den en el mbito de las finanzas respondiendo rpidamente a las innovaciones que se produzcan. La ltima es ser totalmente innovador y liderar estas tendencias y cambios en el mercado financiero. Sobre estas estrategias de negocio y adaptacin a la digitalizacin no existen unas directrices que sean vlidas para todos ni que garanticen el xito en este proceso. Cada entidad deber amoldar el diseo de su estrategia a sus propios objetivos, recursos y entorno. Otro reto relevante es la creciente competencia en el sector, no solo entre los intervinientes tradicionales sino, tambin, por la aparicin de nuevos actores. No puedo hacer una intervencin sobre el futuro de la banca sin hacer referencia a las fintech. Considero que ha sido un acierto por parte del sector bancario el ver a estos nuevos jugadores no como una amenaza o elemento disruptivo en el statu quo de las finanzas, sino como una oportunidad para sacar provecho de todo lo que pueden ofrecer y as mejorar su posicin competitiva. Son muchos los ejemplos de colaboracin entre entidades financieras tradicionales y fintech que han culminado en procesos exitosos. En este anlisis del futuro del sector financiero no puedo tampoco dejar de mencionar otro de los nuevos actores en escena, las grandes empresas tecnolgicas (bigtech). A da de hoy, y al menos en el entorno europeo, la irrupcin de estas empresas todava no es relevante en comparacin con otras geografas, principalmente China, pero no por ello podemos obviar este fenmeno. La gran ventaja que tienen estos grandes proveedores tecnolgicos es la cantidad ingente de datos que gestionan y su capacidad de procesarlos. Esto se deriva no solo de la amplia base de clientes con que cuentan, sino de la significativa frecuencia de interacciones con ellos. Otras ventajas son el acceso preferente a financiacin y contar con una buena reputacin y confianza entre los consumidores. Unos datos debidamente manejados y procesados pueden convertirse en una poderosa herramienta para la prestacin de servicios financieros. Por ejemplo, estas empresas podran determinar el perfil de riesgo de los acreditados sin la necesidad de disponer de un historial crediticio. De este modo, las grandes tecnolgicas podran promover la inclusin financiera de un sector de la poblacin que actualmente se encontrara fuera del mbito de influencia de la banca tradicional. Este escenario, aunque en principio sera ms plausible en otras geografas distintas a la europea, hay que tenerlo en cuenta tambin a la hora de dibujar el nuevo mapa financiero del futuro. Es importante sealar que, a da de hoy, tanto las fintech como las bigtech normalmente no prestan servicios financieros de manera global. Por el momento, se centran en aquellos nichos de mercado especficos donde generan ms valor aadido, como sistemas de pago y, en menor medida, gestin de activos. Tambin en seguros y prstamos en pases menos bancarizados. Existe en la actualidad un debate en torno a la irrupcin de estas grandes empresas y cmo su actividad, y los riesgos que llevan implcitos, impactan en el sector financiero y en la economa. En el mbito del Banco Central Europeo se ha establecido el principio de misma actividad, mismo riesgo, misma regulacin y misma supervisin2. Un ejemplo son las normas de prevencin del blanqueo de capitales y financiacin del terrorismo, que son comunes a todos sin importar la categora de la empresa que ejerce una actividad. Por otro 2https://www.bankingsupervision.europa.eu/ecb/pub/pdf/ssm.esbceuropeanbankingsupervisionresponsetoeuropeancommissionpublicconsultationdigitalfinancestrategyeuropefintechactionplan2020~b2e6cd0dc4.en.pdf lado, tambin existen corrientes que consideran que la normativa debera estar ms fundamentada en la tipologa de entidad y riesgos que conllevan, ms que en la actividad concreta que ejercen3. 3 https://www.bis.org/fsi/fsipapers17.htm 4 https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en 5 As se hizo constar en las orientaciones estratgicas para el perodo 2019/2024. https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024_es 6 FinTech Action Plan No debemos olvidar que el sector bancario est sometido a una exhaustiva y creciente regulacin y supervisin por la implicacin e impacto que tiene en la estabilidad financiera. La preservacin de la misma, as como de la integridad de mercado, la proteccin del consumidor y la competencia, son los objetivos que perseguimos los reguladores y supervisores. En la medida en que estos nuevos actores ejerzan actividades que puedan incidir significativamente en la estabilidad financiera, deberan someterse a una regulacin fundamentada en los riesgos que generan. Hoy en da, los servicios financieros que prestan las bigtechs son poco significativos en nuestro entorno (servicios de la nube, pagos) y como tal, estn sujetos al marco regulatorio establecido para estas actividades concretas. No obstante, tendremos que estar atentos a la evolucin del mercado para evitar la materializacin de los riesgos que potencialmente pueden generar estos grandes proveedores de servicios tecnolgicos, as como el riesgo sistmico derivado de la concentracin de mercado y su posible impacto en la estabilidad econmica y financiera. Quiero destacar tambin otro reto adicional, en este caso relacionado con los supervisores. Es primordial que mantengamos contactos estrechos con la industria para estar al corriente del estado de la tecnologa y del riesgo tecnolgico en el sector. La interlocucin con los diferentes actores es imprescindible para poder aclarar cuestiones regulatorias y expectativas supervisoras. Estos dilogos supervisores, junto con los espacios controlados de pruebas (regulatory sandbox, en ingls) son algunas de las vas para alcanzar este objetivo. Consciente de la rpida transformacin digital que estamos experimentando, de los riesgos que ello puede conllevar y de la necesidad de adaptar la normativa a este nuevo entorno, quiero hacer ahora un pequeo repaso a la estrategia de la Comisin Europea para las finanzas digitales4. El apoyo a la transicin digital en la UE es una prioridad clave para la Comisin Europea5. Esta estrategia se construye sobre el Plan de Accin de FinTech que se elabor en 20186. Las acciones de la UE para promover la transformacin digital de los servicios financieros se extienden hasta 2024 y estn guiadas por cuatro prioridades: 1) Eliminar la fragmentacin del mercado nico digital; 2) Adaptar el marco regulatorio de la UE para facilitar la innovacin digital; 3) Crear un espacio europeo de datos financieros que permita capitalizar el valor de la informacin como fundamento de la innovacin y 4) Abordar los desafos y riesgos asociados a la transformacin digital. En relacin con la primera prioridad, la eliminacin de la fragmentacin del mercado nico digital, se contemplan una serie de actuaciones concretas como el nuevo Reglamento de identificacin digital (e-IDAS), sobre el que ya hay un borrador. Tambin se avanzar en armonizar la normativa de prevencin de lavado de dinero y financiacin del terrorismo (AML/CTF). Adems, se facilitar que los servicios financieros digitales ganen escala en el mercado nico. Para ello, el principio de pasaporte y ventanilla nica de autorizacin se aplicar ya en 2024 a todas aquellas reas que muestren alto potencial para el desarrollo de las finanzas digitales7. 7 Por ejemplo, el marco UE para crowdfunding acordado en dic-19, introducir un rgimen comn y pasaporte para varios tipos de crowdfunding, y el reglamento de criptoactivos lo har para los emisores y proveedores de servicios de criptoactivos. La Comisin tambin considerar la relevancia del pasaporte en otras reas, como la regulacin prudencial en la financiacin no bancaria o la certificacin de empresas de soluciones RegTech y la adopcin de enfoques comunes en ese campo, incluyendo la interoperabilidad. 8 Existe ya un rgimen piloto propuesto: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52020PC0594 9 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/ES/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52020PC0593 10 Relevante tambin documento consultivo de BIS: https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d519.pdf 11 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021PC0206 Con respecto a la segunda prioridad, centrada en la adaptacin de la regulacin para facilitar la innovacin digital, la UE establecer un marco integral que aborde asuntos tan diversos como la adopcin de la tecnologa de registros distribuidos (DLT)8, una propuesta de reglamento para los criptoactivos (MICA)910 que incluye los tokens referenciados a activos (tambin conocidos como stablecoins) y los utility tokens o el Reglamento de Inteligencia Artificial, sobre el que tambin existe una propuesta de borrador11. Para la tercera prioridad, relacionada con los datos, se pretende facilitar el acceso digital en tiempo real a toda la informacin financiera regulada. Se quiere as asegurar que toda la que sea pblica est disponible en formatos estandarizados y legibles por mquinas, as como promover herramientas de tecnologa de la informacin para facilitar el reporte y la supervisin. Del mismo modo, se fomentar que las empresas compartan datos dentro y fuera del sector financiero europeo (open finance). Por ltimo, en cuanto a la cuarta prioridad, abordar los desafos y riesgos asociados a la transformacin digital, se deber realizar salvaguardando la estabilidad financiera, protegiendo a los consumidores e inversores y basndose en el principio antes mencionado de misma actividad, mismo riesgo, mismas reglas. En resumen, la Comisin est trabajando intensamente para que en 2024 la regulacin prudencial y de conducta de la UE y la supervisin estn adaptadas a la evolucin digital, incluyendo en su objeto las entidades financieras tradicionales y los proveedores tecnolgicos que presten servicios al sector financiero. Esta regulacin comprende una amplia batera de reformas y nueva legislacin que ya he mencionado, como el Reglamento e-IDAS (de identificacin electrnica), MICA (mercados de criptoactivos), DORA (resiliencia Operativa digital), Digital Service Act, Data Act o el Reglamento de Inteligencia Artificial. El objetivo de las modificaciones legislativas en marcha es proteger a los usuarios finales de finanzas digitales, salvaguardar la estabilidad financiera, proteger la integridad del sector financiero de la UE y asegurar la igualdad de reglas para todos (level playing field) En este repaso al futuro del sector bancario no puedo dejar de mencionar otro elemento a tener en cuenta: el euro digital. Aunque todava estamos en una fase de investigacin, en la que se estn perfilando y definiendo elementos bsicos de su diseo, parece claro que, en caso de que finalmente se decida su emisin, las entidades financieras jugarn un papel relevante en su implantacin. Ya por ltimo, quisiera hacer referencia brevemente al proceso de adaptacin a este entorno digital que los supervisores estamos realizando. Por ejemplo, estamos avanzando en proyectos de automatizacin de los procesos supervisores y en el aprovechamiento del anlisis avanzado de la informacin. Pero no slo estamos trabajando en el desarrollo de estas herramientas, sino que tambin estamos fomentando una cultura digital en la organizacin, promoviendo habilidades que faciliten y se comprometan con la digitalizacin. Como he sealado, la digitalizacin tambin conlleva retos y riesgos para los supervisores. Riesgos y retos que debemos conocer y gestionar, como son la utilizacin de proveedores externos en la nube pblica, la calidad de los datos o la falta de perfiles especializados, entre otros. En conclusin, el futuro del sector bancario se perfila diferente al que vivimos en la actualidad. Nuevos actores, distintas formas de relacionarse con los clientes, nuevas maneras de realizar los procesos y nuevos riesgos, son los elementos esenciales que conformarn el escenario futuro bancario. Ahora es el momento de tomar decisiones estratgicas trascendentales que sirvan para posicionarse adecuadamente en este nuevo ecosistema bancario. Los reguladores, los supervisores y las entidades debemos estar preparados para afrontar estos nuevos retos y los que queden por llegar con el fin de preservar la necesaria estabilidad financiera que garantice un crecimiento econmico slido. Muchas gracias.

Title: Appearance before the Senate Budget Committee in relation to the draft General State Budget for 2022
text: 30.11.2021 Appearance before the Senate Budget Committee in relation to the draft General State Budget for 2022 Pablo Hernandez de Cos Governor Ladies and gentlemen, I appear once again in this House on the occasion of the process of discussion of the General State Budget and Social Security (hereinafter, PGE) for the year 2022. On this occasion, my appearance takes place in more favourable circumstances than those we experienced in my previous intervention before this Commission, in December 2020. The epidemiological situation has changed substantially, thanks to the extension of the vaccination process, although, as we see in some countries around us and with the appearance of new variants of the virus, normality is far from full and uncertainty remains high. As usual, I will begin with a description of the evolution and prospects of the Spanish economy. Secondly, I will analyze the main features of the PGE Project. Finally, I will address the medium-term challenges of fiscal policy in our country. 1 Recent developments and prospects for the Spanish economy 1.1 The global context Left graph: GDP growth forecasts. Right graph: Vaccinated population with full schedule (11/28/2021). Economic activity continues to recover worldwide, thanks to the advance of vaccination and the extraordinary support of economic policies. According to the latest forecasts of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), global GDP growth will be 5.9% in 2021 and 4.9% in 2022, after falling by 3.1% in 2020. In 2023 that growth would moderate to 3.6%. However, the pace of recovery is uneven, since, according to these same forecasts, advanced economies would recover pre-pandemic GDP levels next year, while the recovery in emerging economies is weaker, which is largely the result of a slower vaccination process. In the euro area, GDP growth would be 5% in 2021, reaching the pre-pandemic level in the last quarter of the year, and 4.3% in 2022, according to these same forecasts1. Among the main economies in the area, significant GDP gains are expected in France and Italy d0 6.3% and 5.8% in 2021 and 3.9% and 4.2% in 2022. These countries experienced, like Spain, more intense contractions during 2020. In Germany, on the other hand, growth will be lower in 2021, at 3.1%, having been revised downwards due to the comparatively greater impact that global supply shortages are having on some industrial branches. 1 The ECB's September forecast for growth of 5% in 2021, 4.6% in 2022 and 2.1% in 2023. In any case, this global economic scenario is subject to high uncertainty, due to a combination of factors. On the one hand, the pandemic remains a global threat and epidemiological developments will continue to condition economic activity, especially in those regions with a lower percentage of immunized population. On the other hand, the strong recovery in demand following the cessation of the main containment measures has led to widespread disruptions in supply chains. This has been joined by a sharp rise in commodity prices, which is generating significant spikes in inflation rates in the main countries. I will address all these aspects when reviewing the evolution of the Spanish economy. 1.2 Recent developments in the Spanish economy Chart: Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth (%). The initial economic impact of the health crisis on the Spanish economy was one of the most intense among the surrounding countries. The progressive recovery has been marked by the successive subsequent waves of the pandemic and by the maintenance of various measures to limit mobility. After the end of the second State of Alarm in May of this year, in parallel to the progress of the vaccination process, there was a return to the path of growth. GDP grew by 1.1% and 2% quarter-on-quarter in the second and third quarters, respectively, supported by the strength of private consumption. In particular, there was an uptick in spending on services involving a greater degree of social contact. Figure: Real GDP (Dec-19-Sep-21). In any case, the recovery in activity is still clearly incomplete, since the level of GDP in the third quarter still presented a gap of 6.6 pps compared to that observed at the end of 2019. In addition, the pace of recovery is also slower than in other neighbouring countries, as this gap was only 0.5 pps in the euro area or 1.4 pps, for example, in Italy. This delay in the path of recovery is due, to a large extent, to Spain's greater dependence on its tourism sector, whose activity has been hampered by restrictions on international mobility. The fall in foreign tourist arrivals caused a collapse in services exports, which in the third quarter of this year were still 29% below pre-pandemic levels, which contrasts with the behavior of exports of goods, which are already 1% above that level. But it also reflects the weaker weakness of some components of domestic demand, such as household consumption. Left graph: Variation of total affiliation, ERTE and effective affiliation compared to February 2020 (seasonally adjusted series of total affiliation). The labour market suffered a very severe impact in the initial stage of the pandemic. In April 2020, almost one in four people who were affiliated to Social Security before the outbreak of COVID-19 had either lost their job or were in a situation of ERTE. The recovery in employment is, however, more dynamic than that of GDP, which seems to reflect the impact of a set of factors of a very diverse nature, which would include the high weight in the composition of the recovery in activity of the rebound in the branches of services with high social interaction (whose level of productivity is comparatively lower than in other sectors) and the effect of some preventive measures against to the pandemic (which has led to an increase in employment needs for each unit of product). In addition, the strong dynamism of public employment in response to the needs of the pandemic and, perhaps, an early reincorporation of workers affected by ERTEs, favoured by expectations of recovery of activity that, in some cases, would not have been fully materialized, could also have played a certain role. In October of this year, the number of effective Social Security affiliates, a variable that is constructed by subtracting from the number of people affiliated to workers in ERTE, was already practically at the same level as in February 2020 (-0.1% in terms of the seasonally adjusted series). The information referring to the first half of November points to a continuation of this positive trend. The unemployment rate, meanwhile, stood at 14.6% in the third quarter of this year, 1.7 pp below its level last year, but still 0.8 pp above the pre-crisis value. Left graph: Income and expenses of the Public Administrations. Accumulated of 12 months. Right graph: Deficit Public accounts also suffered a very significant deterioration as a result of the pandemic. In particular, the deficit of the Public Administrations rose in 2020 to 11% of GDP, 8.1 pps more than in 2019, mainly due to the increase in expenditure. Approximately two thirds of the increase of almost 63 billion euros in public spending in 2020 (about 3.7pp of GDP) corresponded to the highest disbursements for social benefits to workers and the self-employed, subsidies of social contributions to companies and social and health expenses by the Public Administrations. On the other hand, the fall in revenues was mainly due to indirect taxes, whose collection contracted by 11.8%, in line with the behavior of its tax bases. On the other hand, he highlighted the resistance shown by collection through direct taxes, which was only reduced by 3%, and social contributions, which even increased by 0.8%, thanks to the positive effect of some of the measures deployed by the Government to deal with the pandemic on the bases that determine these revenues. Overall, the weight of government revenue in GDP rose last year. In 2021, a certain correction in the public deficit is being observed, due both to the temporary nature of some of the discretionary measures adopted to deal with the consequences of the pandemic and to the cyclical improvement. However, in September of this year, the deficit still stood at 8.2% of GDP in cumulative twelve-month terms. This evolution was the result of the notable recovery experienced by public revenues and a moderate reduction in expenditures, which still remain well above their levels prior to the outbreak of the pandemic. Left graph: Effective affiliation by branches. Variation between Oct-21 and Feb-20. Center graph: Effective occupancy rate by Autonomous Community. Variation between 3Q21 and 3Q19. Right graph: Effective occupancy rate by age. Variation between 3Q21 and 3Q19. A very remarkable feature of this crisis is the asymmetric nature of its impact by sector, region and population group. Although the relaxation of the measures to contain the pandemic has allowed a gradual reactivation of the most affected sectors, the impact of the health crisis remains very uneven among them. As noted, effective affiliation in the economy as a whole was only 0.1% below the pre-crisis level in October. However, this gap was 12.9% and 10.1% in the hotel and leisure branches, respectively, while in information and communication services and health effective affiliation was well above the pre-crisis level (7.6% and 6.8%). The different sectoral specialization has also been reflected in the economic impact of the pandemic at the regional level. The employment rate in effective terms for Spain as a whole was, in the third quarter of this year, 0.5 pp lower than in the third quarter of 2019, but in the Canary and Balearic Islands, it was 3.6 and 3.7 pps below, respectively. On the contrary, in Murcia and Castilla-La Mancha there were increases, which were 2.3 and 2.2 pp, respectively. By population group, the crisis still disproportionately affects certain groups of workers, particularly the youngest, with temporary contracts and low incomes, given their high weight in the sectors most affected by the pandemic. Moreover, these effects have only been corrected to a limited extent after the start of recovery. Specifically, the employment rate in effective terms for people aged between 16 and 29 was, in the third quarter, 1.2 pp lower than at the beginning of the crisis. This figure stands at -0.9 pp in the age group between 30 and 44 years, and now presents a positive sign in older individuals (0.6). The greater impact on workers with a higher degree of vulnerability and who have more limited resources to sustain their spending could therefore have led to an increase in inequality. 1.3 The macroeconomic outlook Graph: Revisions of the Quarterly National Accounts data. GDP and private consumption. 1. The revision of the INE's QNA assumes a lower level of GDP in the second quarter of 2021. And growth in the third quarter (2%) was lower than expected by the Bank of Spain in September (2.5%) 2. Recent deterioration of some aspects of the external environment: "bottlenecks" and increases in raw materials, energy and other intermediate goods. 3. However, the latest information on economic developments in the fourth quarter has remained relatively favourable. The Bank of Spain published its latest macroeconomic projections last September. They anticipated a maintenance of the recovery, under the assumption of the continuation of the process of improvement of the epidemiological situation both in Spain and in the rest of the world, the prolongation of the expansionary tone of demand policies, both monetary and fiscal, and an intensive use of funds from the Next Generation EU (NGEU) program. However, since the preparation of these projections, there have been some relevant developments. First, the GDP growth figure for the second quarter of this year has been revised sharply downwards, from an initial 2.8% to 1.1% (together with minor revisions in the previous quarters). This entails, mechanically (i.e. if the projected growth rates for the following quarters remain unchanged), a substantial reduction in the average GDP growth rate for 2021 and, to a lesser extent, also in 2022. Additionally, the increase in the economy's output in the third quarter would have been 2%, according to the preliminary estimate, instead of the 2.5% that the Bank of Spain expected in September. Secondly, there has been increasing evidence, at a global level, of alterations in global production chains associated with the reopening of economies after the most acute phase of the pandemic. Thus, in the Spanish case, preliminary data from the Bank of Spain's Survey on Business Activity (EBAE) in November show an increase in the proportion of companies that declare that their production capacity is being limited by the lack of material and/or equipment, as a result of bottlenecks in global supply chains. To this is added the increase in energy costs and other raw materials and intermediate goods. Overall, these developments tend to point to a worsening of the global economic context. Behind these disruptions are different, sometimes interrelated, factors. Among them, it should be noted, first of all, that, as a result of the pandemic, the demand for durable consumer goods has increased in place of spending on restricted services and also as a reflection of the acceleration of the digitalization process. The supply of this type of durable goods is relatively inelastic in the short term, since the expansion of its productive capacity requires some time. Shortages of supplies, such as microchips, have resulted in bottlenecks in the industry that have hit advanced economies hardest. Against this background, it is instructive that the euro area composite output PMI has been declining since spring (despite the upswing in preliminary data in November). The biggest decline has been concentrated in manufacturing (although the services sector has also lost dynamism). A sector especially affected by these disruptions is the automotive industry, since it works with low levels of inventories (just-in-time model) and during the hardest months of the pandemic suffered a sharp drop in demand. Over the past few months, some vehicle manufacturers have been forced to halt production processes, stockpile unfinished vehicles and cut their production forecasts for 2021 and 2022. In addition, the mismatches between supply and demand have led to an increase in prices, particularly pronounced in the case of various industrial and transport metals, and in the case of energy sources, be they primary, such as oil, gas or coal, or secondary, such as electricity, produced in part through some of the primary sources mentioned. But the magnitude of the revision of employment was, in quarter-on-quarter terms, much lower than that of GDP, of 4 decimal points, to 4%. This illustrates the difficulties, in the current recovery phase, in properly assessing the relationship between activity and employment. In any case, the developments I have described allow us to anticipate a significant downward revision of the growth of the current year in Spain. According to these forecasts, pre-pandemic levels of economic activity would not be reached until around the beginning of 2023. 1.4 The main sources of uncertainty Diagram with a list of factors: epidemiological, related to the behavior of the agents, the aftermath of the crisis and the evolution of some recent uncertainties originating in the external context. The expectation of recovery is real, but its speed and depth are subject to a high degree of uncertainty. In the case of the Spanish economy, the outlook in the coming months depends, above all, on several sources of uncertainty related to the evolution of the pandemic, the strength of household consumption, the recovery of tourism, the deployment of European funds, the scars of the crisis on the business fabric, as well as the persistence of bottlenecks and the current episode of inflation. Let me briefly review these sources of risk. First, our projections assume that the process of immunization of the population will allow the impact of the pandemic on economic activity to continue to reduce in the coming months. However, as the most recent evolution of the disease in some countries of Central and Eastern Europe is showing, a more unfavourable epidemiological evolution cannot be excluded, with spikes in infections. In addition, although their probability is, in principle, very low, scenarios with episodes of more serious contagion, linked to an eventual spread of more infectious and, in the worst case, resistant varieties of the virus that require the reintroduction of containment measures, cannot be ruled out. In any case, it should be stressed that the degree of adaptation of economies to the successive waves of the pandemic has increased significantly. Secondly, the economic evolution of the coming quarters will be influenced by the pace of recovery in private consumption, which will be conditioned by the decisions of households to release the accumulated savings stock in 2020, which exceeds 6% of GDP. In principle, there are several reasons that lead to the assumption that households will make partial use of this saving in the medium term. On the one hand, the households that have increased their savings the most compared to the pre-pandemic period have been those with the highest incomes, whose propensity to consume is usually lower. On the other hand, an important part of the expenditure that has not been able to materialize since the beginning of the pandemic due to the restrictions is not easily postponed, since it was concentrated in services such as catering or leisure. Our projections incorporate the assumption that households will only partially draw on this accumulated savings, but admit a high level of uncertainty around this assumption. Third, the other component of demand for which there continues to be a high degree of uncertainty is tourism exports. The September projections assumed that the recovery in the volume of non-resident tourism prior to the pandemic would not be fully completed until 2023. Specifically, with regard to the third quarter of each year, which corresponds to the high season, it was then assumed that the level of tourism exports in 2021 and 2022 would be approximately 45% and 90%, respectively, of the level observed in 2019, the last year before the pandemic, and that we would have to wait until the summer of 2023 to have an almost full recovery. However, it is not easy to anticipate the patterns of behavior of international tourism after the pandemic. Fourthly, the implementation of projects associated with the Next Generation EU (NGEU) programme should boost activity in the coming years. In particular, it should result in high growth rates of public and business investment. The Bank of Spain explicitly incorporated the impact of the NGEU into its projections for the first time in December 2020, once the 2021 PGE Project had provided the first details about the volume of funds allocated for this year. Already then we pointed out that there was a high degree of uncertainty surrounding the timetable for execution. In practice, the rate of use has been lower than that incorporated in the different projection exercises carried out since then, which in the September projections led to a transfer of part of the investment flow associated with European resources from 2021 to 2022 and 2023. Specifically, these projections contemplated the realization of projects for an amount of more than 40 billion euros between 2021 and 2022, with a notable impact on the GDP growth rate of those two years (0.6 and 1.8 pps, respectively). In any case, uncertainty remains very high both in relation to the timing of project implementation and with regard to their multiplier effect on activity and employment, which will decisively condition economic developments in the coming years. Fifth, the magnitude of the persistent damage that the pandemic may have caused to employment and the productive fabric (in terms of destruction of companies and increase in structural unemployment) is also unknown. Our September projections were prepared on the assumption that the policies deployed since the beginning of the crisis will allow, on an aggregate scale, the damage caused by the crisis to the productive and labour fabric in terms of the destruction of companies and increase in long-term unemployment to have a relatively limited effect on the economy. However, some signs of deterioration in the solvency of companies have been detected, mainly concentrated in the sectors most affected by the pandemic. Thus, for example, there has been a certain deterioration in the credit quality of some loan portfolios of banks, an increase in the dissolutions of commercial companies and a rebound in the number of companies that are in bankruptcy, despite the moratorium on these procedures that will be in force until mid-2022. In any case, the most recent data show a certain moderation in these trends. Thus, for example, the number of dissolutions of commercial companies, which stood in May, in seasonally adjusted terms, around 12% above the average levels of 2019, has been gradually reduced since then, although in September it still exceeded by 5% the values registered before the pandemic. Sixth, bottlenecks in the supply of certain intermediate energy and non-energy goods could persist or be amplified, putting at risk the intensity of the recovery, particularly affecting industrial branches. Hern87ndez de Cos (2021), Inflation: recent developments, prospects and monetary policy implications Indeed, from February, one year after the last month before the start of the pandemic, until November, inflation has picked up from -0.1% to 5.6% in Spain. If the evolution between February and October (the last month for which disaggregated data are available) is analyzed, the increase is explained, above all, by the contribution of energy prices, which contributed 3.7 pp at the rate of 5.4% observed in October. This contribution of energy prices has been greater than in the euro area countries, as these goods have a greater weight in our consumption basket and as retail electricity prices react to wholesale price changes to a greater extent than in the euro area average. Overall, the contribution of the electricity price increase was about half of the component's increase. But there has also been an acceleration in core inflation, from 0% to 1.4%, mainly due to the services component, which has gone from -0.1% to 1.6%, while that of non-energy industrial goods has increased from 0.3% to 0.9%. The phenomena underlying the upswing in inflation have a transitory essence and an origin external to the Spanish economy. It is true, however, that the phenomenon is showing greater persistence than a few months ago and that, for the foreseeable future, we will continue to observe relatively high rates of inflation. At the same time, the degree of persistence of current increases in consumer prices depends on how much external shocks and also the reaction of national actors are prolonged. This assumption of transience is based on various arguments. The first of these has to do with the base effects derived from the decline in 2020 in the prices of some services whose consumption had been particularly damaged by the pandemic, such as those related to tourism and leisure. These positive base effects have been particularly pronounced in the case of non-electricity energy goods, a component that had registered a sharp decline in 2020 due to the fall in oil prices. Thus, the base effect in this component would have contributed between February and October 2021, in cumulative terms, a total of 1.3 pp of the acceleration observed in general inflation. In the case of services, the base effects did not begin to manifest themselves until the summer of 2021, but, in any case, they have had an upward impact of 0.6 pp. Overall, therefore, around 30% of the acceleration observed in the aggregate inflation would have been due to the base effects described. By its very nature, this effect should, in principle, be purely transitory. Secondly, energy prices, especially gas, have experienced very significant increases. Indeed, if we take, for example, the evolution in the wholesale electricity market in Spain, prices have multiplied by a factor of 4.4 from the end of last year until mid-November. Almost 80% of this increase is explained by the increase in the price of gas, while that of emission rights contributed almost 10% more. However, in principle, this increase is expected to be transitory in nature, as anticipated by the prices quoted in the futures markets of these commodities, which point to a reduction throughout 2022. But it cannot be excluded that the increase in prices will persist in the coming months, given the increase in energy consumption during the winter, in a context in which the volume of oil and gas stocks is relatively small. A third reason for this upswing in inflation is the proliferation of bottlenecks that obstruct or impede the functioning of value chains and the increase in the price of maritime transport, which have resulted in a sharp acceleration in industrial production prices, in particular in the prices of manufacturing intermediate goods. This is despite the fact that, for the moment, companies would be only partially transferring to the sale prices of their products the increase in the prices of their inputs. That is, there would be a decrease in margins. In any case, this phenomenon should be equally transitory, as long as supply is able to adapt to the rebound in demand after the reopening of the economy. There are, however, some uncertainties about this price scenario. The first arises from a possible filtering of increases in the costs of energy and non-energy intermediates to consumer prices. For the time being, as I pointed out, this increase has extended to a limited extent. However, a prolongation of higher costs, for example by delaying the resolution of bottlenecks or lengthening difficulties in normal gas supply in Europe, would reduce the chances that corporate margins can continue to absorb cost increases. Moreover, the evidence indicates that the transmission of the prices of intermediate goods occurs with a certain lag, so past increases could contribute to increased inflationary pressures on final goods in the coming months. A second source of uncertainty arises from wage trends and, therefore, from the possible appearance of what are known as "second-round effects". At the moment, these effects are contained, with a wage increase until October of 1.6%, two tenths less than in 2020. However, in the newly signed agreements, the increases agreed for 2021 have gone from 1.1% in January to 1.7% in cumulative terms until October. One factor that would support expectations that the magnitude of runoff effects will be modest is the low prevalence of safeguard clauses in collective agreements, which has, in fact, fallen sharply in recent years, from around 70% before the onset of the global financial crisis to 17% today. On the other hand, it is observed that wage increases are being higher in those sectors in which employment is showing a more favorable evolution and, therefore, there is less slack. In other words, wage increases in certain sectors reflect, for the time being, factors consistent with a more favourable cyclical position in some sectors, and not with generalised and indiscriminate increases in wages. In addition, although estimating the degree of slack in the economy is particularly difficult to carry out in the context of the pandemic, it must be borne in mind that, in Spain, the level of real GDP is still far from its pre-pandemic level and even more from the trend that preceded the crisis. In any case, in relation to the two previous factors, it is obvious, the longer that duration, the greater the probability that the increase in inflation will gain persistence, both because cost increases filter more intensely to final prices and because the rise in these gives rise to higher wage demands. On the other hand, it must be borne in mind that the Spanish economy is very dependent on external energy, so the current disturbance implies a deterioration of the real terms of trade and, therefore, a real loss of income for families and companies, with potential negative effects on consumption and investment. In fact, real wages are falling and corporate margins are shrinking. And it is true that the high savings accumulated by families during the crisis should make it possible to mitigate these negative effects, but we also know that a very significant part of the accumulated savings has been concentrated in high-income families that normally have a relatively low propensity to consume. It follows from this argument that the current inflationary episode introduces an element of additional risk to activity. With regard to the specific episode of the rise in the price of electricity, the internal estimates obtained in the Bank of Spain through different methodologies can serve as a guide, which would point to an impact of between 2 and 3 tenths of GDP after three years for a permanent increase of 10% in the price of electricity paid by consumers. 1.5 The role of economic policies in the current situation 1. In the current and projected context, monetary and fiscal policies should avoid a premature withdrawal of stimulus. 1.1 Recent developments in inflation remain consistent with a return to moderate inflationary pressures over the medium term. Hence the desirability of monetary policy maintaining a patient approach when assessing a possible revision of its current accommodative tone. 1.2 Fiscal policy support will be necessary in 2022, but in a more selective way, focused on companies and population groups still affected by the crisis, and limited in time, so as not to widen the structural deficit. 2. In parallel, the design of a consolidation programme should be initiated to gradually reduce the high levels of public deficit and debt, with a view to its implementation once the recovery is solid. 3. Economic policy should also facilitate the adaptation of companies and workers to the new realities that have emerged after the pandemic. To this end, the use of the adjustment mechanisms provided by legislation should be allowed to adapt the specific situation of companies, improve debt restructuring procedures, and strengthen training policies and job search aids for workers. 4. Medium-term challenges must also be addressed with a determined agenda of structural reforms, also supported by the use of European funds. The speed and forcefulness of the economic policy response to the pandemic has been crucial to limit its effects. The unprecedented scale of the shock also had an unprecedented policy response, which has alleviated short-term costs, avoided even more extreme negative scenarios and is likely to reduce the medium- and long-term damage of the crisis. The reaction of the European Central Bank (ECB) d0 with its pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP) d0 and the increase in the euro area's public deficit of more than 6.5 points of GDP in 2020 illustrate this forcefulness. The recovery remains subject to many uncertainties and also depends on the course of economic policies. Premature withdrawal of the supporting measures of the agents concerned would entail damage that exceeds the possible costs of maintaining them until recovery shows sufficient robustness. In the case of monetary policy, when analysing the implications of the current situation, it is appropriate to start from the ECB's new strategic framework, which sets a symmetric 2% target over the medium term5. Well, as I have pointed out, recent developments in inflation remain consistent with a return to moderate inflationary pressures over the medium term. Hence the desirability of monetary policy maintaining a patient approach when assessing a possible revision of its current accommodative tone, in order to stabilise the medium-term inflation rate at around 2%6. However, we must pay attention to the possibility of the appearance of 5 See P. Hern87ndez de Cos (2021), The European Central Bank's New Monetary Policy Strategy. 6 See P. Hern87ndez de Cos (2021), Inflation: recent developments, perspectives and monetary policy implications. Signs of unanchoring expectations, since this would be the main factor that would confer persistence to this episode of high inflation. In the case of fiscal policy, it is necessary to maintain an expansionary tone, but with an increasingly focused character, especially in the sectors and agents most affected and with a growing weight of growth considerations in the medium and long term. Thus, the identification of possible structural changes and damages is crucial. Economic policy should not sustain indefinitely activities that could structurally reduce their weight in the economy in the future, but facilitate their adaptation to the new reality and the efficient reallocation of resources. In addition, it is important that the measures are temporary so as not to increase the structural deficit further. And once the pandemic is over, it will be necessary to rebuild fiscal margins and reduce public debt, through a gradual multiannual strategy. The design of this plan must be anticipated, with a view to its implementation once the recovery is solid. I will dwell on this later. In the case of the business sector, for example, it is still important to focus aid on reversing the deterioration of the solvency situation generated by the crisis in companies that are considered viable. The extension of the term of some of the measures to support the business sector until mid-2022, approved by the Council of Ministers on November 23, could contribute to this end by allowing viable companies that have been most negatively affected by the crisis and whose activity is recovering at a comparatively slower pace to benefit for longer from this support. In addition, economic policy should facilitate the adaptation of companies to the new situation arising from the health crisis, which would require, on the one hand, allowing the use of the adjustment mechanisms provided by legislation, in particular labor legislation, and that these be adapted to the specific conditions of companies. On the other hand, it should also be complemented by a more streamlined functioning of judicial and out-of-court insolvency procedures that allow a greater number of viable companies to continue their activity and facilitate the exit of those that are not7. These include, in addition to the inadequate functioning of our labour market, low productivity, the fight against climate change, population ageing or high inequality. Finally, allow me to mention, as the main novelty compared to previous hearings, the challenge of also properly managing economic policy in the context of the inflationary upswing we are experiencing. Recent developments create a complex environment for the course of economic policies. On the one hand, the ECB would have been experiencing, prior to the pandemic, difficulties in reaching its inflation target for a very long period of time. Against this background, the Governing Council of the ECB is determined, as I indicated above, to continue to provide the monetary stimulus necessary to ensure that, over the medium term, inflation will reach the 2% target on a lasting basis, without reacting prematurely to temporary shocks. On the other hand, fiscal policy needs to adopt a medium-term perspective in which budgetary consolidation, once the recovery is established, moves to a priority level. This does not mean that it should stop paying attention, as I have just emphasized, to supporting the layers of society that are being most affected by the consequences of the pandemic as well as by the current inflationary upturn. But it is an additional argument to justify that support should be selective and that a generalized fiscal impulse should be avoided, which, if it occurs, could translate into an increase in the bottlenecks already existing in the most stressed sectors, which would end up filtering into additional inflationary pressures. Finally, companies and workers must internalize the fundamentally transitory nature of some of the main factors behind the current rise in prices and seek an equitable distribution of the decline in income of the national economy compared to the rest of the world implied by recent cost increases, in many cases concentrated in goods and services that our economy does not produce. But it needs, either as intermediate goods of the productive process or as final goods for consumption or investment. In this respect, two risks should be highlighted that would affect, in opposite directions, the fulfilment of this objective. In the first place, and as I mentioned earlier, the macroeconomic picture presented in the PGE project is subject to downside risks. If they materialize, such risks would result in a higher public deficit. On the other hand, and in the opposite direction, historical evidence indicates that the execution of expenditure related to public investment, one of the items that increases the most in the PGE Project, tends to be significantly below the initially budgeted expenditure. This observation would mean that the forecast of public expenditure for all the Public Administrations would be subject to downside risks, which could offset the risks to the public deficit derived from the potential lower economic growth. In the same sense, it should be borne in mind that the budget execution data for 2021 show a greater dynamism of tax collection than anticipated, which could lead to a lower than expected closure of the public deficit in 2021. As for the stance of fiscal policy, which is a measure of the economic stimulus provided by the Public Administrations, this is a difficult concept to quantify, given the complications arising from correctly identifying where we are in the economic cycle, especially in a context such as the current one, with an asymmetric recovery as a shock of a high magnitude. Beyond these difficulties, when considering the orientation of fiscal policy approximated by the change in the structural government balance, the effect of European funds channelled through the RRF should also be included. These funds do not affect the level of deficit in accounting terms, but they do affect the tone of fiscal policy, since they imply a significant increase in spending, but, given their financing scheme, they are not the result of direct collection on resident agents. In this way, the tone of fiscal policy, measured by the variation in the structural balance contained in the Budget Plan, would go from being expansionary in 2021 (-0.9 pp.) to being practically neutral in 2022, once the impact of European funds is included. However, if we consider the temporary profile of execution of the expenditure of European funds contemplated in the forecasts of the Bank of Spain, the tone of fiscal policy would be significantly expansionary in 2022. In the same vein, in a recent report, the European Fiscal Board advocates setting the tone for fiscal policy using the level of the primary structural balance. Thus, this institution recommends referring to the change in the structural balance as "fiscal impulse" and the level as "fiscal position" or "budgetary stance". The fiscal policy response, needed to combat the economic effects of the pandemic, has increased this deterioration. This phenomenon has materialized in some standard metrics of the health of public finances. Thus, according to the estimates of the structural balance prepared by the European Commission, this would have gone from 3.7% of GDP in 2019 .2.5 pp above that observed in the average of EMU economies., to 4.9% in 2021. This trend is also reflected in the public debt-to-GDP ratio, which has increased by more than 26 pps between the end of 2019 and the third quarter of 2021, when it stood at 122.1% of GDP. The value reached in the second quarter, at 123% of GDP, was substantially higher than the euro area average (98.3%). Graph: EVOLUTION OF PUBLIC DEBT UNDER DIFFERENT ASSUMPTIONS (2016-2036). In addition, the simulation exercises carried out by the Bank of Spain suggest that, under plausible assumptions about the future evolution of economic growth and interest rates, in the absence of policies to correct the current budgetary imbalances, the public debt ratio would remain at very high values over the next 15 years. In this regard, it should be noted that the evidence available suggests that maintaining a level of public debt over an extended period of time could entail at least two sources of vulnerability. In the first place, it cannot be ruled out that the financial markets register greater volatility and there will be an increase in the rate of return demanded by investors for the purchase of public debt. In this sense, and thanks to the extraordinary measures implemented by the ECB, the financing costs of the Spanish Treasury have remained at historically very low levels, the new macroeconomic context, propitiated by a gradual recovery in activity and prices, has already begun to affect the yield required of sovereign bonds in the long term in the countries of our environment. An example is the case of Spain, where the rate of 10-year public debt is currently around 0.4% compared to 0% at the beginning of the year. The lengthening observed in recent years of the average maturity of Spanish public debt would, however, soften the transfer of these increases to the interest burden. Secondly, high public indebtedness leads to an absorption of resources for its financing, either in the form of higher taxes or reduction of potentially productive spending, which could be used for alternative uses. In addition, it may adversely affect the financing conditions of private actors. Based on these arguments, and as I have already stressed on several occasions, the deterioration of public finances is a challenge that requires a response in the form of a fiscal consolidation plan that allows fiscal authorities to provide room for manoeuvre to act in the face of possible negative economic shocks in the future. This plan should be designed rigorously and promptly, for gradual implementation once the recovery is solid. The plan should specify the budgetary targets, the details of the composition of the adjustment that will enable those objectives to be achieved and the time frames within which it will be developed. These characteristics would help to give the process credibility. In this sense, the preparation of the Update of the Stability Programme of Spain that must be presented next spring may be a good time to lay the foundations of this plan. 3.2 Improving the quality of public accounts In addition to ensuring the sustainability of public finances, Spain faces another major challenge in fiscal matters: improving the quality of public accounts. These two major challenges should not be seen in isolation: a recomposition of public finances that contributes to the structural transformation that the Spanish economy has to address in the coming years will result in greater potential growth, and, therefore, in an improvement in the sustainability of public accounts. To address the analysis of this second great challenge, I will articulate my comments around two dimensions: the composition and efficiency of public expenditures and revenues in our country and the role that the NGEU program can play. 3.2.1 The composition and efficiency of public expenditure and revenue The relative importance that each chapter of expenditure or income represents on public accounts should be due to the preferences that society shows for the policies that these headings represent.
