However, it is not only necessary to know the changes that are taking place in the market, but also to be a participant in them. Initiatives such as the digital euro project or the regulatory sandbox are good examples. As you may know, the Eurosystem decided last year to launch a research project for the possible issuance of a digital euro. It is a complex issue with a multitude of implications and aspects to be analyzed. The aim is to be prepared to be able to react in an agile manner if, for example, the role of central bank money as an anchor of the monetary system is weakened by the evolution of the payments ecosystem. We are currently in a phase where we are analysing the changes that are taking place and exploring the possibilities offered by technology to determine how best to avoid unwanted distortions in the stability of the financial system. This will form the basis for designing a solution that is safe, efficient and adapted to the preferences and needs of all parties involved. To this end, communication with the different market agents is essential. In this regard, I would like to highlight the recent publication of a report that includes the conclusions of the first exercise of interaction with users. As for the sandbox, as you well know, it is a tool that financial authorities have to improve their knowledge of new technologies and to help agents to better understand supervisory and regulatory expectations. The Spanish sandbox began operating at the beginning of 2021 and we are currently immersed in the reception of applications for the third cohort, while preparing the exit of the projects presented in the first wave. In the first 2 calls, we have received a total of 49 projects from the Bank of Spain, of which 36 have been formally evaluated and 11 have had a prior favorable evaluation. It is a dynamic tool that is very enriching for both financial authorities and developers. In the field of payments, innovative projects have been presented that can represent important advances. For example, some of these projects use distributed ledgers and artificial intelligence to reduce the need for liquidity of companies when settling their debts or to promote the real-time reconciliation of positions at an international level of the same business group. The test environment is a unique opportunity for the authorities to learn about the opportunities posed by the application of these new technologies in the field of payments, but also their potential risks, through specific projects. Another essential element that I would like to emphasise in my speech is the need for international coordination and cooperation, both at European and global level, to improve payment services. Payments have changed a lot in recent years, and generally for the better. But there are clear asymmetries depending on the geographical area we consider. At the strictly national level, the improvements in infrastructure, services and means of payment have been truly remarkable and allow us to carry out transactions quickly, securely and at modest costs for users. Making a person-to-person payment immediately using our mobile phone and without having to remember account numbers or other cumbersome details is not a chimera, but a reality in our country for some time now. It is an achievement that is also due to a collective effort of which I believe we can legitimately be proud and which shows that Spain is a leader in this field. However, it is clear that limiting ourselves to the national level is not enough. One of the most visible effects of digitalisation is probably the blurring of borders. We have become accustomed, and even more so after the pandemic, to buying and accessing online content regardless of where the provider is. This requires harmonised, efficient and secure payment services across national borders. In the Eurozone, the fact of sharing currency has made evident, for years, the need to harmonize and improve the functioning of the payment market. Looking back at the time that has elapsed since its creation, we can say that the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) has been a resounding success. Transfers and debits throughout the area are exchanged in homogeneous formats, under the same conditions and at the same prices as domestic payments. Highlighting the success of SEPA does not mean, far from it, that we can be complacent. The environment is tremendously dynamic and it is no secret that we are facing new challenges, many of which have been mentioned in the round tables: the implementation of PSD2 and, in particular, the opening of account information has generated problems and frictions, for example; The emergence of unregulated con assets poses challenges in multiple areas; the payment experience at the point of sale is not yet homogeneous in Europe; the scope of immediate payments does not cover the whole of SEPA either... The list is long. At the Bank of Spain, as a member of the Eurosystem, and in the sector in general, I believe that we are aware of these challenges and of the need to continue evolving payment services in Europe to respond to the challenges posed by new technologies and new developments. To give an example, the response to the challenge posed by cryptoassets is being articulated through the MiCA regulation, given that in some cases these assets could serve as a means of payment. But I would like to go beyond the European environment and consider the global situation. It is clear that cross-border payment services, beyond the SEPA area, have also improved in recent years. In some cases, for some specific providers or specific brokers, payments are fast and efficient. But it is also clear that, in general, international payment services are more expensive, slower, less accessible and transparent than domestic payments (or those made in the eurozone, in our case). The efficiency gap may have even widened, as progress at the global level has been much slower. Digitalisation and globalisation only highlight these shortcomings much more clearly. In this context, it is increasingly necessary to promote and coordinate change on a much larger scale than the European scale in order to achieve something equivalent to a "global SEPA". Public authorities are no strangers to this challenge and in early 2020 the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors approved the launch of an ambitious programme to improve cross-border payments. It is a collective initiative involving various global committees and authorities (the BIS Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, IOSCO, etc.) and is coordinated by the Financial Stability Board. (FSB). Since 2021, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the other committees involved have begun the implementation of a roadmap, which will include descriptive work, but also the establishment of quantitative targets to assess improvements in the cost, speed, accessibility and transparency of international payments. The regular publication of these indicators will certainly help to maintain momentum and track progress in an effort that will take several years to complete. Despite its clear ambition, the international coordination effort does not end with this programme. Given the growing importance of crypto-assets, and in particular stablecoins, and their potential use for payment transactions, I would also like to cite the work of the CPMI and IOSCO to apply to this crypto-asset class the standards and principles that already apply to systemically important infrastructure. The so-called stablecoins are those cryptoassets that try to control their volatility using backing assets, whether currencies or other goods, as collateral. In this regard, the FSB has published a report assessing the regulatory, supervisory, and oversight challenges associated with global stablecoins, identifying a set of high-level recommendations to mitigate potential risks to financial stability. I remind you that stablecoins, especially global stablecoins, are the most worrying because excessive panic about them could stress money markets and, therefore, infect the entities that act as custodians of the hedging assets. The Basel Committee and the FSB are also assessing the macro- and microprudential implications of the development of these crypto-assets, exercises that also serve as a basis for the design of possible actions in this regard. The Basel Committee is also discussing the characteristics of the regime that will define the prudential treatment applicable to the exposures of credit institutions. All these elements are part of a debate that is still open, which is expected to materialize in concrete actions in the short and medium term. In short, the challenge posed by improving payment services is not just a national or European effort, but a global one. Central banks around the world are committed to this initiative for the ultimate benefit of the society we serve, but the success of this effort depends crucially on the active participation of industry and dialogue with all stakeholders. A complex path on which we will undoubtedly encounter difficulties. Russia's recent invasion of Ukraine, for example, in addition to the terrible human drama it entails, is also a threat to various areas of the financial sector, including payment services, which are at clear risk of fragmentation. I would like to conclude by highlighting the three main messages that I have pointed out throughout my speech. Firstly, the need for coordination to solve the challenges posed by the improvement of payment services. These services form a dense network of interconnections of various entities and infrastructures, so that the improvement of the network can only be achieved through collaboration between the various actors. In this regard, central banks will continue to act as catalysts for change. Second, optimism. It is true that we will encounter difficulties and even momentary setbacks - I mentioned the case of Ukraine - but in the long term the trend is positive. If we look back and look at the current situation in perspective, we can see great progress. Digitalisation can help us achieve additional efficiency gains. Finally, an invitation to ambition, to think big. Payment services have room for improvement in our immediate area, but above all it is on a global scale where there is a gap to overcome. Regulatory and supervisory authorities need to continue working to analyse international standards and guidelines and determine whether the principles applicable to entities or infrastructures require a more uniform implementation or have differences that need to be addressed. I encourage you to actively follow the progress and to participate in this collective effort, which is undoubtedly complex, but also exciting. Thanks a lot.
text_original: BANCO DE ESPAA Eurosistema 06.04.2022 IV Foro Fintech & Open Banking del diario Expansin Clausura de honor Margarita Delgado Subgobernadora Agradezco al diario Expansin la invitacin para cerrar este IV Foro Fintech & Open Banking. Es un placer para m participar en este evento, centrado en los recientes avances en los medios de pago, y me gustara compartir con ustedes algunas reflexiones sobre la innovacin en este mbito, as como sobre el papel de los bancos centrales y otras autoridades, no solo en el contexto nacional, sino tambin europeo e incluso global. La digitalizacin de los servicios de pago tiene numerosos beneficios para la sociedad: incrementos de eficiencia, reduccin de costes, mayor acceso a los servicios financieros, seguridad reforzada... la lista es larga. La puesta en marcha de las transferencias inmediatas o la posibilidad de pagar con el mvil son solo dos ejemplos que lustran a la perfeccin las ventajas que estos avances representan para los ciudadanos. Sin embargo, las nuevas tecnologas, agentes y productos que estn emergiendo conllevan tambin riesgos. En algunos casos, son similares a los que plantean los pagos tradicionales y que ya estamos habituados a gestionar. En otras ocasiones, por el contrario, se plantean nuevos riesgos que es necesario identificar y evaluar a fin de determinar el mejor modo de abordarlos. Las autoridades financieras debemos ser conscientes de esta combinacin de riesgos y oportunidades y para ello es necesario tener un conocimiento de los nuevos desarrollos en el sector, algo que cada vez resulta ms complicado, dada la velocidad a la que suceden las innovaciones, su heterogeneidad y su carcter global. Sin embargo, no solo es preciso conocer los cambios que se estn produciendo en el mercado, sino tambin ser partcipe de los mismos. Iniciativas como el proyecto del euro digital o el sandbox regulatorio son buenos ejemplos. Como sabrn, el Eurosistema decidi el ao pasado iniciar un proyecto de investigacin para la posible emisin de un euro digital. Se trata de una cuestin compleja con multitud de implicaciones y aspectos a analizar. El objetivo es estar preparados para poder reaccionar de manera gil si, por ejemplo, el rol del dinero de banco central como anclaje del sistema monetario se viera debilitado por la evolucin del ecosistema de pagos. Actualmente nos encontramos en una fase de en la estamos analizando los cambios que se estn produciendo y explorando las posibilidades que ofrece la tecnologa para determinar la mejor manera de evitar distorsiones no deseadas en la estabilidad del sistema financiero. Esto constituir la base para disear una solucin segura, eficiente y adaptada a las preferencias y necesidades de todas las partes implicadas. Para ello, la comunicacin con los distintos agentes del mercado resulta fundamental. En este sentido, me gustara destacar la reciente publicacin de un informe que recoge las conclusiones del primer ejercicio de interaccin con los usuarios1. En cuanto al sandbox, como bien saben se trata de una herramienta con la que cuentan las autoridades financieras para mejorar su conocimiento sobre las nuevas tecnologas y para ayudar a los agentes a conocer mejor las expectativas supervisores y regulatoas. El sandbox espaol comenz a operar a principios de 2021 y en estos momentos estamos inmersos en la recepcin de solicitudes para la tercera cohorte, al tiempo que se prepara la 1 https://www.ecb.europa.eu/paym/digital euro/investigation/profuse/shared/fles/dedocs/ecb.dedocs220330 reporte 1 salida de los proyectos presentados en la primera oleada. En las 2 primeras convocatorias hemos recibido en el Banco de Espaa un total de 49 proyectos de los que se han evaluado formalmente 36 y 11 han tenido una evaluacin previa favorable. Se trata de una herramienta dinmica muy enriquecedora tanto para las autoridades financieras como para los promotores. En el mbito de los pagos, se han presentado proyectos innovadores que pueden suponer importantes avances. Por ejemplo, algunos de estos proyectos utilizan los registros distribuidos y la inteligencia artificial para reducir la necesidad de liquidez de las empresas a la hora de saldar sus deudas o para favorecer la reconciliacin en tiempo real de posiciones a nivel internacional de un mismo grupo empresarial. El entorno de pruebas supone una oportunidad nica para que, a travs de proyectos concretos, las autoridades podamos conocer de cerca las oportunidades que supone la aplicacin de estas nuevas tecnologas en el mbito de los pagos, pero tambin sus potenciales riesgos. Otro elemento esencial que quiero destacar en mi intervencin es la necesaria coordinacin y cooperacin internacional, tanto a escala europea como global, para mejorar los servicios de pago. Los pagos han cambiado mucho en los ltimos aos, y en trminos generales a mejor. Pero existen claras asimetras dependiendo del mbito geogrfico que consideremos. En la esfera estrictamente nacional, las mejoras en infraestructuras, servicios y medios de pago han sido realmente notables y nos permiten realizar transacciones de forma rpida, segura y a unos costes modestos para los usuarios. Hacer un pago persona a persona de forma inmediata utilizando nuestro mvil y sin tener que recordar nmeros de cuenta u otros detalles engorrosos no es una quimera, sino una realidad en nuestro pas desde hace ya un tiempo. Es un logro que adems se debe a un esfuerzo colectivo del que creo que podemos enorgullecemos legtimamente y que evidencia que Espaa es lder en este campo. Sin embargo, es evidente que limitarnos al mbito nacional no es suficiente. Uno de los efectos ms visibles de la digitalizacin es, probablemente, la difuminacin de las fronteras. Nos hemos acostumbrado, y an ms tras la pandemia, a comprar y acceder a contenidos online sin importarnos donde est el proveedor. Esto requiere unos servicios de pago armonizados, eficientes y seguros ms all de las fronteras nacionales. En la Eurozona, el hecho de compartir moneda hizo evidente, desde hace aos, la necesidad de armonizar y mejorar el funcionamiento del mercado de pagos. Con la perspectiva del tiempo transcurrido desde su creacin, podemos afirmar que la Zona nica de Pagos en Euros (SEPA por sus siglas en ingls) ha sido un rotundo xito. Las transferencias y adeudos en toda el rea se intercambian con formatos homogneos, en las mismas condiciones y a los mismos precios que los pagos nacionales. Resaltar el xito de la SEPA no quiere decir, ni mucho menos, que podamos ser complacientes. El entorno es tremendamente dinmico y a nadie se le oculta que nos enfrentamos a nuevos retos, muchos de los cuales se han mencionado en las mesas redondas: la aplicacin de la PSD2 y, en particular, de la apertura de la informacin sobre cuentas ha generado problemas y fricciones, por ejemplo; la aparicin de cptoactivos no 2 regulados plantea retos en mltiples reas; la experiencia de pago en el punto de venta todava no es homognea en Europa; el alcance de los pagos inmediatos tampoco abarca a toda la SEPA... la lista es larga. Desde el Banco de Espaa, como miembro del Eurosistema, y desde el sector en general, creo que somos conscientes de esos desafos y de la necesidad de seguir evolucionando los servicios de pago en Europa para responder a los retos que plantean las nuevas tecnologas y los nuevos desarrollos. Por poner un ejemplo, la respuesta al desafo que plantean los criptoactivos se est articulando a travs del reglamento MiCA dado que en algunos casos estos activos podran servir como medio de pago. Pero me gustara ir ms all del entorno europeo y considerar la situacin global. Es evidente que los servicios de pago transfronterizo, ms all del rea SEPA, tambin han mejorado en los ltimos aos. En algunos casos, para algunos proveedores concretos o corredores especficos, los pagos son rpidos y eficientes. Pero tambin es evidente que, en general, los servicios de pago internacionales son ms caros, lentos, menos accesibles y transparentes que los pagos nacionales (o que los realizados en la eurozona, en nuestro caso). La brecha de eficiencia puede que incluso se haya agrandado, ya que el progreso experimentado en el mbito global ha sido mucho ms lento. La digitalizacin y globalizacin no hacen sino poner de relieve estas deficiencias de forma mucho ms clara. En este contexto se hace cada vez ms necesario impulsar y coordinar el cambio a una escala mucho mayor que la europea para poder conseguir algo equivalente a una SEPA de mbito global. Las autoridades pblicas no son ajenas a este reto y a principios de 2020 los ministros de economa y gobernadores de bancos centrales del G20 aprobaron el lanzamiento de un ambicioso programa de mejora de los pagos transfronterizos. Se trata de una iniciativa colectiva en la que participan diversos comits y autoridades globales (el Comit de Pagos e Infraestructuras de Mercado del BIS -CPMI-, el Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea -BCBS-, el Banco Mundial, el Fondo Monetario Internacional, IOSCO2...) y que se desarrolla bajo la coordinacin del Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera. (FSB). Desde 2021, el Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera (FSB) y el resto de Comits implicados han comenzado la implementacin de una hoja de ruta, que incluir trabajos descriptivos, pero tambin el establecimiento de unos objetivos cuantitativos para evaluar las mejoras en el coste, la rapidez, la accesibilidad y la transparencia de los pagos internacionales. La publicacin peridica de estos indicadores ayudar sin duda a mantener el impulso y hacer un seguimiento de los progresos en un esfuerzo que requerir varios aos para completarse. Pese a su clara ambicin, el esfuerzo de coordinacin internacional no acaba con este programa. Dada la creciente importancia de los criptoactivos y en especial de las stablecoins, y su posible uso para las operaciones de pago, me gustara citar tambin los trabajos del CPMI y de IOSCO para aplicar a esta clase de criptoactivos los estndares y principios que ya se aplican a las infraestructuras de importancia sistmica. 2 International Organization of Securities Commissions 3 Los denominados stablecoins son aquellos criptoactivos que tratan de controlar su volatilidad usando activos de respaldo, sean monedas u otro bien, a modo de colateral. En este sentido, el FSB ha publicado un informe evaluando los retos reglatenos, supervisores y de vigilancia asociados a las stablecoins globales, identificando un conjunto de recomendaciones de alto nivel para mitigar los posibles riesgos para la estabilidad financiera. Les recuerdo que las stablecoins, en especial las global stablecoins, son las que ms preocupacin generan porque un pnico excesivo sobre las mismas podra tensionar los mercados monetarios y, por lo tanto, contagiar a las entidades que acten como custodios de los activos de cobertura. El Comit de Basilea y el FSB estn asimismo evaluando las implicaciones macro y microprudenciales del desarrollo de estos criptoactivos, ejercicios que sirven tambin de base para el diseo de posibles actuaciones al respecto. Tambin en el Comit de Basilea se estn debatiendo las caractersticas del rgimen que definir el tratamiento prudencial aplicable a las exposiciones de las entidades de crdito. Todos estos elementos son parte de un debate an abierto, que se espera que se materialice en acciones concretas en el corto y medio plazo. En resumen, el reto que plantea la mejora de los servicios de pago no es solo un esfuerzo nacional o europeo, sino global. Los bancos centrales de todo el mundo estamos comprometidos con esta iniciativa en beneficio ltimo de la sociedad a la que servimos, pero el xito de este esfuerzo depende crucialmente de la participacin activa de la industria y del dilogo con todas las partes interesadas. Un camino complejo en el que sin duda nos encontraremos con dificultades. La reciente invasin rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, adems del terrible drama humano que supone, es tambin una amenaza para diversas reas del sector financiero, incluyendo los servicios de pago, que corren un claro riesgo de fragmentacin. Me gustara terminar destacando los tres mensajes principales que he do apuntando a lo largo de mi intervencin. En primer lugar, la necesidad de coordinacin para resolver los desafos que plantea la mejora de los servicios de pago. Estos servicios forman una red tupida de interconexiones de diversas entidades e infraestructuras, por lo que la mejora de la red solo puede lograrse mediante la colaboracin entre los diversos actores. En este sentido, los bancos centrales seguiremos actuando como catalizadores para el cambio. En segundo lugar, optimismo. Es cierto que nos encontraremos con dificultades e incluso retrocesos momentneos -he mencionado el caso de Ucrania- pero a largo plazo la tendencia es positiva. Si echamos la vista atrs y contemplamos la situacin actual con perspectiva, se aprecian grandes avances. La digitalizacin nos puede ayudar a conseguir incrementos de eficiencia adicionales. Finalmente, una invitacin a la ambicin, a pensar a lo grande. Los servicios de pago tienen margen de mejora en nuestro mbito ms cercano, pero sobre todo es a escala global donde hay una brecha que superar. Las autoridades regulatorias y supervisores tenemos que seguir trabajando para analizar estndares y guas internacionales y determinar si los principios aplicables a entidades o infraestructuras requieren una implementacin ms uniforme o presentan diferencias que es necesario abordar. 4 Les animo a seguir activamente los progresos y a participar en este esfuerzo colectivo, sin duda complejo, pero tambin ilusionante. Muchas gracias. 5

Title: Conference "Disclosure of Climate Alignment and Net Zero Commitments of the Financial Sector"
text: 28.04.2022 Reporting the financial sectors climate alignment and net zero commitments* Seminar organised by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and the Banco de Espana Margarita Delgado Deputy Governor * English translation from the original in Spanish. Good morning everyone. I would like to begin by thanking the organisers of this event, both the WWF and the Banco de Espanas Regulation Department, and, needless to say, the participants, including regulators, such as the European Commission and the Spanish National Securities Market Commission (CNMV), and industry representatives. I would also like to take a moment to welcome the audience, and to celebrate the enormous interest this event has attracted. Tasked with channelling resources, the financial sector has a key role to play in the process of transitioning the economy towards more sustainable models. The role of the financial supervisors and regulators involves ensuring that banks identify, manage and report on the risks posed by climate change. The incorporation of these risks into their management decisions will help to change the relative prices of financial instruments in favour of those that fund more sustainable activities. Regulators, supervisors and banks have all encountered significant challenges throughout this process of adaptation to comply with the 2015 Paris Agreement. Key among these is the one addressed in todays seminar: the need for granular data to draw on. Data with sufficient quality and historical depth, constructed on the basis of robust, internationally agreed standard definitions. Aware of the challenge posed by this new risk, I would like to highlight the creation of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), of which the Banco de Espana forms part, with a view to furthering the development of suitable climate and environmental risk management. This group analyses an array of sustainability- related aspects and their potential impact on financial stability. One of the NGFS most recent pieces of research, published in March, concerns the loss of biodiversity and the economic and financial repercussions this may have. Meanwhile, this Tuesday saw the publication of another report on how to improve transparency in the financing of the green transition. Todays first session will look at some of the most important current reporting initiatives at European level. The session will address, for example, the proposal for a corporate sustainability reporting directive (CSRD), currently at the final stage of negotiation, as well as the European Banking Authoritys Implementing Technical Standards on disclosure by banks of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks, published at the start of this year. These regulations represent a very significant step towards improving the information available to market participants and supervisors, though they will admittedly call for a considerable effort on the part of the institutions affected. But the lack of data is a global issue and, as such, is also being addressed at an international level. The creation of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) in November 2021, under the auspices of the IFRS Foundation, was a key milestone in this regard. It is crucial to ensure that the European standards are compatible with the work being performed by the ISSB at a global level. Todays final two sessions concern the so-called climate alignment and net-zero target setting metrics. Initiatives such as the report published by the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) in October 2021 or the creation of the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) bear witness to the momentum behind and growing importance of these metrics for businesses in general and the financial sector in particular. 1 The panel discussion in the second session and the round table planned for the third will offer a chance to reflect on these issues. While the financial sector is clearly a key player when it comes to financing this transition, the process cannot be efficiently managed without sufficient information from businesses and households. Lastly, as supervisors, we also face the challenge of ensuring that our processes account for this new risk. To this end, we have already set in place a range of initiatives, from the issue of specific supervisory expectations to the conduct of stress test exercises from various perspectives. The one currently underway will prove crucial for learning about and understanding climate risk and will help identify best practices as the basis for establishing criteria to manage such risk. I encourage you to pay close attention to todays round tables, at which all of these issues will be debated from the standpoint of the industry, the regulators and the organisations involved in this area. Thank you. 2

Title: Conference "The technological revolution in banking: Engine of growth for Spanish SMEs"
text: 06.05.2022 The technological revolution in banking: a driver of growth for Spanish SMEs* elEconomista business conference Margarita Delgado Deputy Governor * English translation from the original in Spanish I would like to thank the newspaper El Economista for inviting me to close this conference on the technological revolution in banking. It is a pleasure for me to participate in an event that has sought to discuss the challenges that need to be addressed by the banking sector to boost the competitiveness of the Spanish economy and promote the growth of Spanish firms. This conference has identified many challenges posed by the digitalisation of banking services, along with its numerous benefits for the economy in terms of greater efficiency, cost cutting and ease of access to financial services, among others. However, as the scope of financial services offered by the banking sector is very broad, today I am going to focus on payment services. These are key to the functioning of the economy in general and of firms in particular, as well as being a benchmark in the application of financial innovation. Specifically, I would like to share some thoughts on innovation and digitalisation in this area, focusing in particular on the concept of open banking. Payment services have changed much in recent years. Technological developments have enabled new services to be offered and paved the way for greater competition in the sector. They have also allowed the entry of specialist providers, many of which have established collaborations or acted in step with the banking sector, the traditional provider of such services. Nevertheless, technological developments and the entry of new players have been a wake-up call for the banking sector to accelerate changes in this area. In this modern digital environment, both the general public and firms have seen banking services adapt to their new needs and payment habits. Among the growing demands from users are immediacy and online access to services. The expansion of instant transfers and the ability to make and receive mobile payments are two examples of how the banking sector is responding to these demands, a response that is being spearheaded by Spanish banks. The sector has often collaborated to tackle these enormous challenges, with one clear success story being Bizum, an instant payment solution in Spain with close to 20 million users. Since its launch, a billion instant transfers have been made through Bizum, chiefly between individuals. This platform has also supported payments for online purchases since 2019. Thanks to Bizums exponential growth over the last two years, 43% of transfers processed in Spain are now instant, putting Spain at the forefront of instant payments in Europe. The Spanish financial sector is also working on a collaborative solution in the so-called Request-To-Pay arena, which enables payees to issue a request for payment through instant payment mechanisms. This will, for example, allow the instant payment of electronic invoices and taxes, enabling firms to optimise their cash management, pay invoices 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and make immediate refunds to customers, among other advantages. All this progress has naturally been accompanied by legislative developments, such as the Revised Payment Service Directive, known as PSD2. The main objectives of this legislation were none other than introducing greater competition in the payment services market, 1 facilitating online payments and providing greater security to users, with the ultimate aim of creating a fully integrated, efficient and secure European payments market. PSD2 has obliged banks to make major changes to comply with the strong customer authentication requirements. Implementing these requirements without undermining the user experience presents a major challenge which is driving, and in turn benefiting from, the development of new technologies, such as biometrics. The legislation also requires banks to open up their systems to payment initiation and account information service providers. As account servicing payment providers (ASPSPs), banks have had to establish secure communications with these payment service providers, either through a specific technological interface (known as Application Programming Interfaces, or APIs) or through the same channel they use to communicate with their customers. These changes are prompting banks to invest in technological infrastructures to support a higher volume of requests, owing to their storage or hardware needs. Sometimes this involves outsourcing to cloud service providers. All this progress is driving open banking in the payments area, enabling any customer, be they an individual or a firm, with online access to their payment account to use a different entity to either initiate payments or access account information. Banks and FinTech firms are thus responding to customer demands for swift and secure transactions, along with easy access to, and information on, all their accounts, regardless of which banks they are with. In my opinion, open banking offers customers more freedom to choose their financial provider(s) and enables them to take out different products with different providers, according to their interests. Secure third-party access fosters the development of new business models that cover customers specific needs in a digital environment. Some examples can be found in businesses geared towards cash management at firms. Here, by combining account information and payment initiation services, comprehensive information on a firms payment accounts can be viewed online and in real time, and personalised reports can be obtained (income and expense forecasts, reconciliations, etc.). It is also possible to react immediately to that information, ordering payment transactions from the same interface. Another example is firms offering accounting management services, which, following customer authorisation, can now have instant access to all the aggregated information on a customers payment accounts through a single account information service provider. Such access has also benefited traditional businesses. A case in point are merchants that use customers payment account information, again with their prior consent, to feed credit scoring tools, enabling them to decide almost immediately on whether to finance customers purchases and on the conditions of such financing. 2 In short, together with PSD2, open banking has opened up a range of opportunities for the financial sector. In view of this experience, the European Commission is working to establish a broader framework for open finance, defined in the Digital Finance Strategy as announced a few weeks ago. I have so far endeavoured to list examples showcasing the potential advantages of open banking. However, in order to progress towards broader open banking, it seems appropriate to consider the lessons learned so far. In particular, we need to consider the challenges and risks it poses. The main challenge posed by open banking is customers' reticence to share their data. According to a survey conducted in the United Kingdom, 74% of customers would not consider sharing their data to check if they could afford a mortgage, loan or credit card. Nor would 65% share their data to check if they could get a better deal for their insurance. Further, 69% of UK adults said they are not comfortable sharing personal data with banks or big tech companies to access financial services. These findings seem to indicate how important privacy is for the general public. As regards the risks posed for traditional banks by opening banking, we could first of all mention competition. By sharing information with other parties, they are opening up access to their most valuable commodity, namely data, to other players that may be better placed to compete. Although the spirit of open banking is none other than increasing competition and, therefore, improving the products and services offered to customers, it is without doubt something that traditional financial institutions will have to bear in mind. This brings me on to the risk of disintermediation, as open banking allows third parties to offer products and services that have traditionally been provided by such financial institutions. Banks will have to adapt to the new market conditions if they want to avoid losing part of the services they currently provide and missing out on any more innovative services developed in the future. Another clear risk posed by open banking is the increase in cyber risk: the higher number of connections and actors involved means greater exposure to attack, potentially compromising firms and individuals financial data. Fraudulent use of the technology may have a direct cost for the general public and firms that are users of financial and payment services. It could also come with a high reputational cost for the financial system as a whole that could erode its functioning. As you are aware, the Ministry for the Economy, along with the National Securities Market Commission (CNMV), the Banco de Espana and a host of other institutions and authorities, has recently signed the Action Plan against Financial Fraud (PAFF, by the Spanish acronym) to combat potentially fraudulent financial products and services. Through such initiatives we are demonstrating our commitment to combating fraud. n-finance- frameworkb. l . 3 An additional risk to be considered when discussing digitalisation in general is the risk of exclusion. Customers with lower digital skills, such as some of the older generation, may miss out on certain financial services if they are not provided through traditional channels. Again, from the customers perspective, there is a risk of losing control over their own data. Although the European Commission has indicated that the development of open banking will be linked to users having control over their own data, it is also true that they may inadvertently share their data with a third party that is not registered or authorised by the competent authority. In conclusion, digitalisation in the financial sector is a reality from which there is no going back. Today I have wanted to focus on how it is applied to payment systems and open banking, but it also has a clear impact on other areas and is evolving at an unprecedented speed. From the standpoint of financial stability, digitalisation has important benefits. First, it leads to efficiency gains that help reinforce the soundness and resilience of the banking sector and, second, it opens up new business opportunities and increases competition. Although it has transitory costs and affects the general public in different ways, the balance is positive, and players will need to address the transition costs that doubtless exist. Both from the standpoint of financial system players (banks and new entrants) and of customers, digitalisation calls for an overhaul of various business models and a rigorous analysis of the associated risks. On this note of caution, which no speech by the supervisor can overlook, I would encourage you to continue driving digitalisation and providing increasingly efficient and secure services to customers, to the benefit of all. Thank you. 4

Title: Institutional inauguration of ING's corporate headquarters in Madrid
text: BANK OF SPAIN Eurosystem 17.05.2022 Keynote Address Institutional inauguration of ING's corporate headquarters in Madrid Margarita Delgado Deputy Governor Good morning everyone. First of all, I would like to express my gratitude to ING for the invitation to participate in the inauguration of this new headquarters, which confirms the firm commitment of this entity to its business in Spain. Almost three years ago I participated in the twentieth anniversary and on that occasion I already highlighted the agility that characterizes ING to adapt to new environments. This new corporate headquarters is another example of this since, as we can see, it is fully aligned with the new times, new ways of working and, in addition, following the best building standards in relation to sustainability and energy consumption. Russia's invasion of Ukraine is a new disruption that adds uncertainty to the recovery, with foreseeable consequences for economic activity and also puts additional pressure on inflation. Although the financial exposures of Spanish banks to these two countries are minimal and the commercial channel of the Spanish economy is not relevant, the indirect effects can be significant, especially through the channel of confidence and uncertainty with impacts on the economy. The European banking sector in general and the Spanish banking sector in particular are facing this new disruption from a situation of recovery and resilience, having recovered pre-pandemic levels of profitability and with stable solvency levels. However, in Spain there are still sectors that have not fully returned to their level of activity after the health crisis or are being more affected by energy and raw material shocks. That is why I take this opportunity to once again send the message that, in the face of the foreseeable tightening of financing conditions with a greater impact on more indebted companies and vulnerable families, financial institutions must continue to monitor their credit quality and take measures that allow them to properly manage their credit risk. In this context, allow me to refer to the two structural challenges that banks face and that they already presented before the pandemic. Specifically, firstly, the concepts of profitability/efficiency, digitalisation and competition from new players and secondly, the challenges of transforming the economic model towards a more sustainable one. As we will surely witness in the dialogues that will take place afterwards, adapting to new ways of doing business, as well as sustainability are two of the challenges, perhaps the main ones, that financial institutions face in these times. I am going to make a small reference to both, starting with the challenge of digitalization. ING is well aware of this, given that since its implementation for individuals in Spain in 1999 it has been characterised by the marketing of its products, including the popular orange account, through alternative channels, initially by telephone and later by Internet. The pandemic has accelerated the digitalisation process of Spanish banks. According to Eurostat data from 2021, 65% of Spaniards would have used banking on Une in the 3 months prior to the survey, above the 60% average for the Eurozone. This is significant considering that 5 years earlier, in 2016, this figure was 43%, lower than the Eurozone average (49%). This means that the growth of digitalisation, especially in Spain, is very significant. Likewise, it is not only the new ways of interacting with customers that must be taken into account, but also the emergence of new players, new contact channels and new ways of providing services. As for the new players, we have to refer to FinTechs, which are those companies with a high technological component, which provide flexibility since they do not carry the drawbacks of old operating systems and therefore can adapt to changes more quickly and which, in addition, tend to be focused on those segments of the value chain with the highest return. Currently, this sector tends to operate more in payments, loans on Une, wealth management or exchange of assets. On the other hand, the incorporation of BigTechs into the financial sector could be much more disruptive given the amount of information they treasure and the economies of scale they already have. To all this, other technological elements are added such as cloud computing infrastructures, artificial intelligence, artificial learning (machine learning), as well as other phenomena such as the distribution of financial services through non-financial channels (Banking as a Service) or the use of banking platforms to offer financial and non-financial services. own or third parties. Of course, it is also necessary to think that the profile of jobs in the sector will have to adapt to this new digital ecosystem and the risk culture of the entities will also have to take this fact into account. The operational risk associated with digitalization is becoming increasingly relevant. In conclusion, the degree to which the banking business is evolving is so accelerated that it is currently considered one of the greatest challenges facing the sector. To be properly positioned, it is necessary that the heads of the entities are fully aware of this fact and are knowledgeable about the matter to avoid the fear of the unknown, which would lead to avoiding innovations and leave the entities in a vulnerable situation to the rest of the sector. The second challenge referred to today and which is also very present on the supervisory agenda is that of sustainability. The political commitment reached at the Paris Summit in 2015 to the fight against climate change is firm and has triggered a whole wave of very important regulatory changes to adapt the economy to the new sustainability requirements. The financial sector, as a channel of resources, is key in this process of adaptation of the economy towards more sustainable models. Undoubtedly, this fact is already leading to a transformation in risk management, in which sustainability factors are already an element to be taken into account. A proper analysis of how physical and transition risks influence the risk profile of institutions is essential for proper climate risk management. To this end, obtaining quality data, with sufficient historical depth and based on clear and homogeneous definitions at the international level, is key. This is a global risk that must be addressed in a coordinated manner at the international level. Institutions will have to make a great effort to collect, analyse and report data, following the instructions that the European Banking Authority has recently published. Institutions will have to collect and process information from their borrowers, whether companies and households, and it will require a great deal of effort. We are therefore immersed in a process of adaptation to new environments that require a phase of learning and adjustment. On the part of the supervisors, we have issued guides on supervisory expectations in this area, carrying out specific analyses on the degree of adaptation of the entities to them. We have also enhanced stress tests with different scopes to see the degree of resistance of entities to the challenges posed by climate change. We are currently in the execution phase of the last of them. The establishment of homogeneous taxonomies, clear and comparable definitions, data collection and analysis, are the elements that make up the new climate risk management framework on which there is still a long way to go. The ultimate goal is for the financial sector to be able to channel the necessary resources to transform the economy towards more sustainable models. This transformation must be orderly, making it easier for the most polluting sectors to also receive the necessary resources for their conversion to the green and sustainable economy. ING, as a Dutch entity, is fully aware of this challenge given that the Netherlands was a pioneer in putting climate risk on the international agenda. To conclude, I would like to congratulate ING on the new corporate headquarters, which is an example of the bank's commitment to modernity and sustainability. Two essential elements for success today.

Para ello, la obtencin de datos de calidad, con la suficiente profundidad histrica y basados en definiciones claras y homogneas a nivel internacional es clave. Las entidades tendrn que hacer un gran esfuerzo de recopilacin, anlisis y reporte de datos, siguiendo las instrucciones que la Autoridad Bancaria Europea ha publicado recientemente. Tambin hemos realzado pruebas de estrs con distinto alcance para ver el grado de resistencia de las entidades a los retos que supone el cambio climtico. En la actualidad estamos en la fase de ejecucin del ltimo de ellos. El establecimiento de taxonomas homogneas, definiciones claras y comparables, recopilacin y anlisis de datos, son los elementos que configuran el nuevo marco de gestin del riesgo climtico sobre los que todava queda un camino por recorrer. Dicha transformacin deber ser ordenada, facilitando que aquellos sectores ms contaminantes tambin reciban los recursos necesarios para su conversin hacia la economa verde y sostenible. ING, como entidad holandesa es plenamente consciente de este reto dado que los Pases Bajos fueron pioneros a la hora de poner el riesgo climtico en la agenda internacional. Title: Annual Meeting of Self-Control
text: BANK OF SPAIN Eurosystem 26.05.2022 Opening Speech General Assembly of Autocontrol Margarita Delgado Deputy Governor I would like to thank Autocontrol for its invitation to open this General Assembly. It is a pleasure for me to be able to participate in this event. This is not the first time that the Bank of Spain has inaugurated a general assembly of Autocontrol. In 2017, the Director of the Department of Conduct of Entities participated in an event like today's. It is precisely this Department of the Bank of Spain, within the new Directorate General for Financial Conduct and Banknotes, that maintains a regular collaboration with Autocontrol, always with the aim of ensuring that the advertising of bank products and services is clear, balanced, objective and sufficient. These objectives and principles are common to advertising in all sectors of the economy, not just the financial sector, and are covered by Autocontrol's activity. Advertising is the first point of contact between a company and a potential customer, so the messages and information that are transmitted in it usually have a great impact on the generation of expectations about the product, and on the consequent decision-making process. It is necessary that potential customers have the confidence to move in a sphere of sufficient protection that also contributes to less conflictive relationships after the purchase or contract. In the field of banking products and services, if we take into account that the economic commitments acquired by the bank customer are in many cases long-term, this entity-customer relationship is especially relevant. For this reason, the supervision of the advertising activity of financial institutions is an essential element of the conduct framework, to ensure that the relationship between institutions and their customers is properly initiated and developed. In recent years, it has become clear that institutions behave appropriately with their customers and improve the level of financial education of the general public for financial stability, the reputation of the sector and for confidence in the system itself. The important role played by financial institutions in channelling funds to the real economy justifies the financial sector being a regulated sector . In addition, the sector is subject to exhaustive supervision. This supervision seeks, on the one hand, to guarantee the solvency of financial institutions and, on the other hand, to preserve the proper conduct of the institutions, thereby trying to ensure proper protection of the banking customer. The proper functioning of the financial services market requires, without a doubt, the trust of citizens. In recent years, we have witnessed an increase in conflicts between banks and their customers, which has also received great media attention and has affected this necessary principle of trust. Monitoring the conduct of institutions is now a key element in restoring that trust. Let me mention that, at the end of April 2022, the Governing Council of the Bank of Spain approved the creation of the new Directorate General for Financial Conduct and Banknotes, with the aim of highlighting the importance of the conduct of institutions and better exploiting the synergies that can occur within the Bank of Spain to promote financial education. Therefore, conduct monitoring is key and must be carried out at all stages of the bank's relationship with its customer. Advertising activity is, as I mentioned before, the first meeting point in this relationship and requires a specific regulation to which I am now going to refer. The regulations on transparency and protection of banking customers have evolved over time and, with them, the specific regulations that regulate the advertising activity of banking products and services. It should not be forgotten that until 2010 in Spain there was a regime of prior administrative authorisation for the advertising of credit institutions. The entry into force of Order EHA/1718/2010 put an end to this unique prior authorisation regime and replaced it with an advertising control system based on a two-pronged approach: a preventive one, consisting of the preparation by the Bank of Spain of criteria for the clarity, sufficiency and objectivity of advertising messages, and in the establishment by the entities of internal procedures and controls that guarantee their compliance. The second approach is corrective, allowing the cessation or rectification of advertising that does not comply with the regulations, as well as the eventual sanction of inappropriate conduct. The general criteria and principles to which advertising must conform, and the general criteria on the minimum content and format of the advertising message were determined in Circular 6/2010. I would like to highlight that one of the great novelties introduced by this regulation was to encourage the adhesion of entities to advertising self-regulatory bodies, systems that enjoy undoubted recognition by the European authorities. Subsequently, through Circular 4/2020, the regulations adapted the scope of application of the advertising rules to new subjects such as real estate lenders and credit intermediaries, among other aspects. For example, the latter circular has sought to adapt the principles and criteria to adjust advertising to developments in the advertising sector and, in particular, to the impact of digital technology, while ensuring more effective monitoring. The progress of digitalisation is evident in all areas and in this one in particular it allows us to take advantage of the advantages it offers for the dissemination of advertising messages. In 2021, digital media occupied the first place in advertising investment volume for the third consecutive year, with more than 45% of the total investment of this investment. The financial sector is second in the ranking of investment in advertising, only surpassed by the distribution and restaurant sector. Following the European model, the current advertising regulations try to guarantee good management of advertising activity through two elements. Firstly, the aim is to design advertising that rests on the responsibility of the entities themselves through the development of commercial communication policies and appropriate internal procedures. The idea is to strengthen discipline in the marketing of banking products and services through the involvement of the governing bodies of the institutions, and especially their internal control functions. Also, through the voluntary adhesion by the entities to advertising self-regulation bodies. The aim is to promote clarity and honesty in its advertising activity and, with this, protect the interests of customers, while minimising the specific legal and reputational risks of financial institutions. Secondly, it is a matter of guaranteeing the correction of possible inappropriate conduct through the ex-post control of advertising activity by the Bank of Spain, and the possibility for the supervisor to issue requests for the cessation or rectification of campaigns and advertising pieces. Since the implementation of the current ex-post control system for advertising, the Bank of Spain has been making requests for the cessation or rectification of campaigns and advertising pieces and supervisory actions aimed at verifying compliance with advertising regulations. It has also developed an important regulatory and interpretative activity in this field. In 2021, the Bank of Spain's Conduct of Institutions Department, in its work of supervising advertising activity, has paid special attention to the way in which institutions have adapted to Bank of Spain Circular 4/2020, as well as to other aspects of particular interest, such as the marketing of revolving cards and car financing. In addition, the commercial communication policies of the new entities that started advertising activity were analyzed. A total of 146 requests for cessation or rectification of advertising were submitted, of which 57 (39%) culminated in cessation and 77 in rectification of the advertising piece (53%). Having said that, I would like to highlight the positive assessment that this supervisor has of self-regulation in various areas of conduct, and in particular in advertising activity. The actions of the entities must not be limited to mere compliance with the regulation. They must go further by implementing a culture of good practices in their organizations and always acting honestly, professionally, taking into account the rights and interests of customers. Autocontrol is, to date, the only advertising self-regulatory body in Spain, with a history of more than two decades, and to which around 120 entities in the banking sector are currently adhered. At the European level, self-regulation mechanisms are considered useful and effective instruments to ensure the adequacy of the commercial relations and practices of the different economic agents and work is being done to define their space and promote their role, especially from the European Economic and Social Committee. Permissive to conclude. Advertising introduces us to product knowledge, helping the customer to choose the one that best suits their needs. With an ever-increasing offer of products and services marketed in more innovative channels, the importance of the clarity and veracity of the advertising message becomes more relevant. It is also an essential factor in the game of competition between institutions, which I have already highlighted as fundamental to preserve the best interest of customers in their financial choices. It is the responsibility of all of us  entities, advertisers, self-regulatory systems and supervisors  to convey to citizens an advertising message that is clear, objective, and that generates reasonable expectations in accordance with the real characteristics of the product. On the part of the Bank of Spain, we are committed to this work, both through the supervision of conduct and through our participation in the agreements and measures that are designed to promote financial education. In addition, in response to this changing environment, the new internal organisation will allow us to take better advantage of the synergies and proximity to the public offered by the branch network. This network will give increasing support to our actions in the areas of behavioural supervision and financial education, to which they will give greater capillarity. And I have no doubt that advertisers, supervised entities, and Autocontrol itself will also maintain, and reinforce, their commitment in this area, for which they will always count on our collaboration. Thanks a lot.
